# Introduction

The *Varahi Samhita* <note>also known as the Brihat Samhita</note> is a primary text of astrology and astronomy. Its creator, the teacher Varahamihira, was the son of Aditya-dasa and a resident of Avanti <note>modern-day Ujjain</note>. After studying all the sciences from his father, Varahamihira went to the city of Kapittha, where he performed penance to the Sun God and received a boon. Whatever the case may be, in the introduction to this book, we must determine the time period of Varahamihira and the creators of the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The Sun Canon, a foundational Sanskrit astronomical text</note>. By establishing their era, the timing of many other astronomers can also be determined. Varahamihira wrote in his book titled *Pancha-Siddhantika* <note>The Five Treatises</note>:

-> "The southward journey of the Sun once began from the midpoint of the constellation Ashlesha, and the northward journey from the beginning of Dhanishtha." <-
-> "This was certainly true at some time, as stated in the ancient scriptures." ||1|| <-
-> "Currently, the Sun’s southward journey begins from the start of Cancer, and the other (northward) from the start of Capricorn." <-
-> "The deviation from the ancient records is evident through direct observation." ||2|| <-
-> "One should recognize this through distant markers at the rising or setting of the Sun," <-
-> "or by the marks of the entry and exit of the shadow on a large circle <term>Gnomon: a vertical pillar used to measure the sun's shadow</term>." ||3|| <-
-> "If the Sun turns back without reaching Capricorn, it destroys the South and West; if it turns back without reaching Cancer, it destroys the North and East." ||4|| <-
-> "Returning after completing the northward journey brings an increase in well-being." <-
-> "When the Sun follows its natural course, it is auspicious; a distorted movement brings fear." ||5|| <-

In ancient times, the <term>Dakshinayana</term> <note>the Sun's six-month southward journey/Winter Solstice</note> began in the middle of the Ashlesha constellation and the <term>Uttarayana</term> <note>the Sun's six-month northward journey/Summer Solstice</note> began at the start of Dhanishtha, because such accounts exist in the ancient scriptures ||1||. Currently, the Sun's southward journey begins at the start of Cancer and the northward journey at the start of Capricorn; therefore, in the absence of the ancient <term>Ayana</term> <note>solstice point/precession</note>, its change is clearly perceived ||2||. (Method for knowing the change of the solstice): One should know this through distant markers <term>such as constellations</term> at the time of the Sun's rise and set, or by observing the entry and exit of the shadow from fixed marks on a large circle <note>referring to a sundial or astronomical circle</note> ||3||. If the Sun turns back in its northward journey without reaching Capricorn, the South-West direction is harmed; if it turns back in its southward journey without reaching Cancer, the North-East direction is destroyed ||4||. By returning after reaching the start of Capricorn, the Sun is a bringer of auspiciousness, and this is its natural motion; if the motion is distorted from this, the Sun becomes a bringer of inauspiciousness ||5||.

From these first two verses of the teacher Varahamihira, we receive help in identifying the eras of two astronomers: first, the author of the ancient scriptures, and second, Varahamihira himself. Bhattotpala, the commentator on Varahamihira's work, has identified the "ancient scripture" as the *Parashari Samhita*. He has also quoted statements regarding the state of the seasons from that scripture in his commentary.

## Introduction

> For example,—“From the beginning of Dhanishta to the middle of Paushna <note>original: "Paushna" refers to the nakshatra Revati</note> is the cool season (Shishir). From the middle of Paushna to the end of Rohini is spring (Vasanta). From the beginning of Saumya <note>original: "Saumya" refers to Mrigashira</note> to the middle of Ashlesha is summer (Grishma). From the middle of Ashlesha to the end of Hasta is the rainy season (Pravrit/Varsha). From the beginning of Chitra to the middle of Jyeshtha is autumn (Sharad). From the middle of Jyeshtha to the end of Shravana is the winter season (Hemanta).”

From the beginning of Dhanishta to the first half of Revati is the cool season. From the remaining half of Revati to the end of Rohini is the springtime. From the beginning of Mrigashira to the first half of Ashlesha is the summer season. From the remaining half of Ashlesha to the end of Hasta is the rainy season. From the beginning of Chitra to the first half of Jyeshtha is the autumn season. From the remaining half of Jyeshtha to the end of Shravana is the winter season.

The zodiac <note>Rashichakra</note> is divided into twenty-seven parts. In each part resides one <term>Constellation</term> (Nakshtra); therefore, the span of each constellation occupies 13 degrees and 20 minutes of the zodiac. In the spring season, the point in the zodiac where the Sun is positioned when day and night are equal <note>the vernal equinox</note> is considered the beginning of the sign of Aries (Mesha). At that location resides the junction star <note>Yogatara</note> Revati of our Indian astronomy and <term>Piscium</term> <note>original: "Piscum"; likely Zeta Piscium</note> of Western astronomy. According to the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit text on astronomy</note>, the junction star Revati is located at 359 degrees and 50 minutes of the zodiac. However, according to the view of Brahmagupta and others, Revati resides at 360 degrees—that is, at the very beginning of the zodiac. The coordinates (polar longitudes and latitudes) of the constellations as determined by astronomers will be published in their proper places.

By looking at the list written below, it will become clear which positions of the zodiac were occupied by all the seasons as determined by Parashara:

| Beginning | End | Season |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| From 283° 20' | to 353° 20' | Cool (Shishir) <gloss>}</gloss> |
| 353° 20' | to 53° 20' | Spring (Vasanta) <gloss>}</gloss> **Northern Solstice** |
| 53° 20' | to 113° 20' | Summer (Grishma) <gloss>}</gloss> |
| 113° 20' | to 173° 20' | Rainy (Varsha) <gloss>}</gloss> |
| 173° 20' | to 233° 20' | Autumn (Sharad) <gloss>}</gloss> **Southern Solstice** |
| 233° 20' | to 293° 20' | Winter (Hemanta) <gloss>}</gloss> |

In the time of Varahamihira <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer</note>, all seasons began at the start of the zodiac signs; therefore, in his time, the cool season began when the zodiac reached 270 degrees. This means that from the time of the author of the *Parashara Samhita* to the time of Varaha, the solstice <note>Ayana</note> had advanced by (293° 20' - 270°) = 23 degrees and 20 minutes. This implies that the seasonal changes occurring in the era of the *Samhita* author were shifting 23° 20' earlier by Varaha's time. In English, this motion is called the Precession of the Equinoxes <note>original: "advance of the equinoctial point or ecliptic intersection to the east"</note>. According to Western mathematical theory, the annual rate of the precession is 50.1 seconds; therefore, it takes 1676 years for a shift of 23° 20'. For this reason, according to Western mathematics, a difference of this many years is seen between the two astronomers. Once the era of Varahamihiracharya is firmly established, the time in which Parashara lived can be known.

Now it must be observed how many degrees the solstice has advanced eastward from the time of Varahamihiracharya to the present day. From examining the almanacs <note>Panjikas</note> of Bengal, it is known that in the Shaka era—

# Introduction

At the beginning of the year 1815, the precession <note>original: "ayana"</note> had advanced 20 degrees, 54 minutes, and 36 seconds <term>Vikala: a unit of angular measurement equivalent to a second of arc</term> toward the east. This means that in the present time, all seasons begin earlier by that specific amount compared to the time of Varaha <note>Varahamihira, a 6th-century Indian astronomer</note>. Since the current zodiac signs have been determined, a relationship has been established between the signs and the months. Therefore, by adding the degrees of precession <term>Ayanamsha: the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term> to the zodiac signs, the true position of the sun for the present time is clearly proven.

The seasons as calculated in the almanacs <note>Panchang</note> of the Bengal region can be presented in this manner:

| Approx. Date | Start | Season | Remarks |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10 Pausha | Capricorn | } | |
| | | } Shishir (Dewy) | Winter Solstice. |
| 10 Magha | Aquarius | } | |
| 10 Phalguna | Pisces | } | Northern Transit <note>Uttarayana</note>. |
| 10 Chaitra | Aries | } Vasanta (Spring) | Vernal Equinox <note>original: "Krantipata"</note>. |
| 10 Vaishakha | Taurus | } | |
| 10 Jyeshtha | Gemini | } Grishma (Summer) | Summer Solstice. |
| 10 Ashadha | Cancer | } | |
| 10 Shravana | Leo | } Varsha (Monsoon) | Southern Transit <note>Dakshinayana</note>, |
| 10 Bhadrapada | Virgo | } | Autumnal |
| 10 Ashvina | Libra | } Sharad (Autumn) | |
| 10 Kartika | Scorpio | } | Equinox, |
| 10 Margashirsha | Sagittarius | } Hemanta (Winter) | |

Therefore, by maintaining an annual motion of 54 seconds, 1394 years of precession have passed since the degrees recorded in the Bengali papers. Thus, according to the opinion of the aforementioned papers, the time of Varaha and the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy</note> is known to be the year 421 of the Shaka era <note>approx. 499 CE</note>. Different degrees of precession are given in the almanacs of our country. According to some, the precession for the current year is 22-53. According to others, it is 22-39. Some opinions match the Bengali papers. Bapudeva Shastri's almanac is purer <note>more accurate</note> than all other papers. By examining it, it is known that in the current year, the precession is moving at 22 degrees, 9 minutes, and 24 seconds. Now, by fixing the annual motion of the equinox <note>Krantipata</note> at 50.1 seconds and performing the calculation, it is known that Varahamihiracharya lived approximately 1592 years before the present time. To support this conclusion, I publish the celestial observation results of the famous astronomers Hipparchus of Egypt <note>Hipparchus was Greek, though associated with Alexandrian/Egyptian observations</note> and Europe.

Hipparchus wrote that in his time, the star Chitra <note>Spica</note> was 6 degrees west of the equinoctial point, and Mr. Herschel <note>William Herschel, the British astronomer</note> wrote that at the beginning of 1750 CE, the said star was at the equinox...

# Introduction

<page-num>6</page-num>

It has advanced 26 degrees and 24 minutes to the east. Therefore, from the time of Hipparchus to the time of Herschel <note>William Herschel, the 18th-century British astronomer</note>, the equinoctial point <term>Kranti-pata-bindu: the point where the celestial equator intersects the ecliptic</term> has moved 26 degrees and 24 minutes eastward. Thus, through precise mathematical calculation, it is known that Hipparchus observed the heavens 1897 years before Herschel, or before 147 BCE. In the time of Hipparchus, the star Chitra <note>Spica</note> was located at 174 degrees of the zodiac. However, in the time of the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* and Varaha <note>Varahamihira</note>, it had advanced 6 degrees eastward; that is, the equinox and the star Chitra were at the same position in the zodiac, or at 180 degrees. Therefore, by fixing the annual precession of the equinox <term>Ayana: the movement of the equinoxes</term> at 50.1 seconds and calculating, it is known that the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* and Varaha lived 431 years after Hipparchus, or in the year 284 CE. It has already been stated that the author of the *Parashari* published the positions of the seasons 1676 years before Varaha; therefore, he existed 1392 years before the Christian Era.

Now it is revealed that Adityadasa did not personally write the *Surya Siddhanta*. Varahamihiracharya has written his father's name as Adityadasa in the *Varahi Samhita* and the *Brihat Jataka*. At the end of the *Brihat Jataka*, there is this verse:

> ->The son of Adityadasa, having obtained knowledge from him,<-
> ->In the town of Kapittha, having received the grace of the Sun God,<-
> ->Varahamihira of Avanti, having thoroughly studied the views of the sages,<-
> ->Composed this beautiful work on Horoscopy. (9)<-
> ->This intellect, graced by bowing at the feet of the Sun, the Sages, and the Teacher,<-
> ->Has compiled this scripture; salutations to the ancient creators.<-
<note>Original Sanskrit: "Adityadasatanayastadavaptabodhah..." translated here into English.</note>

Varahamihira, a resident of Avanti and son of Adityadasa (who was learned in the Vedas), having obtained the grace of the Sun God in the city of Kapittha and having well-considered the opinions of the wise, composed this sweet *Hora-shastra* <term>Horoscopy/Astrology</term>. The grace produced by bowing to the Sun, the Sages, and the feet of the Guru is the primary cause for the collection of this scripture; therefore, he bows to them repeatedly.

From observing the positions of the lunar mansions <term>Nakshatras</term> given in the *Surya Siddhanta* for that period, it is known that it was composed during the time of Varaha. Now we arrive at these conclusions: 1. Perhaps Varaha himself composed the *Siddhanta* and named it after his father or the Sun, or 2. His father himself composed it and named it the *Surya Siddhanta*. In his book *Pancha-siddhantika*, Varaha has listed the *Saura-siddhanta* among the five systems; for this reason, it is clearly revealed that the *Surya Siddhanta* was not composed by him. Therefore, it appears that the said book was written by his father Aditya—

<header>Introduction</header>

# Introduction

During the time of Brahmagupta, the star Chitra <note>Spica</note> was situated at 183 degrees; that is, from the time of the author of the *Surya Siddhanta* and Varaha, the star Chitra advanced three degrees eastward. Therefore, Brahmagupta was born 215 years after Varahamihiracharya, specifically in the Shaka year 421 <note>approx. 499 CE</note>.

It is said that at the court of the Persian Shah Naushikhan <note>Khosrow I</note>, there was a minister named "Buzurjmeher." This Shah reigned from 534 CE to 590 CE. Because there is some slight similarity between this name and the name Varahamihira, some might speculate that he was a member of Shah Naushikhan's court. If such people were to learn the facts, their misconception would be removed, as it is believed that the *Panchatantra* of Vishnusharma was translated into the Persian language by the order of this very minister. Furthermore, another reason is that Vishnusharma has written the name of Varahamihiracharya within the *Panchatantra*; how then could Varahamihiracharya have belonged to the time of Naushikhan?

Varahamihiracharya, in his work *Brihat Jataka*, has listed the names of many astronomers who preceded him. For example: Maya, Yavana, Manittha, Shakti, Satya, Bali, Vishnugupta, Devaswami, Siddhasena, Jivasharma, Prithuyasha, and so on. Varaha also acknowledged that the <term>Ionians</term> <note>original: "Yavanas"</note> and <term>Greeks</term> possessed special expertise in astronomy. He says:

> "The Yavanas are indeed foreigners <note>original: "Mlechha"</note>, yet this science is well-established among them. Therefore, even they are honored like sages; how much more so then a Brahmin who is a knower of the divine science?"

Among the "Mlechha" (those of foreign conduct) Yavanas, there is a specialized study of this science (predictive astrology). For this reason, they are worthy of worship like sages; if the knower of the scripture is a Brahmin, then what more need be said? Seeing this statement, it is estimated that Varaha also had contact with Egyptian astronomers.

Before determining the time of Aryabhata, it is necessary to write something regarding the Precession of the Equinoxes <note>original: "Ayanamsha"</note>. Just as our astronomers do not agree on the measurement of the year, their views on the Precession are not uniform. Even the primary ancient astronomers, such as the author of the *Parashari*, considered the state of the Precession to be fluctuating. However, Vishnuchandra, the author of the *Vashistha Siddhanta*, was the first to reveal the revolution of the celestial node <note>the point where the ecliptic and equator intersect</note> like a circumference.

According to the view of Aryabhata, in one *Kalpa* <note>an eon of 4,320,000,000 years</note>, there are 1,582,237,500,000 sidereal risings; therefore, in these many years, there are 157,791,750,000 days. Many astronomers who came later have used the measurements of the year determined by the Aryabhatas in their own books. The author of the *Brahma Siddhanta* has written that in one *Kalpa*, there are "fifteen trillion, eight hundred twenty-two billion, three hundred sixty-four million, five hundred thousand" <note>original Sanskrit numeral: "privatavichutustayasharabdhirasagunayamadvivasutithayah"</note> sidereal risings. Brahmagupta, the author of the *Brahma Sphuta Siddhanta*, has also written this. As follows:

> "The planetary mathematics spoken by Brahma, which had become decayed over a long period of time, is now being stated clearly by Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu. I shall explain the defects, such as the differences in the start of the Yugas, of those whose vision is blocked by the veil of ignorance and who speak differently from the Brahma Siddhanta."

It also introduces the mathematical constants used by Aryabhata and Brahmagupta to calculate celestial cycles.</summary>

<header>Introduction</header>

Four zeros, five, the Vedas <note>original: "Veda" representing the number 4</note>, the flavors <note>original: "Rasa" representing 6</note>, fire <note>original: "Agni" representing 3</note>, the twins <note>original: "Yama" representing 2</note>, the fortnights <note>original: "Paksha" representing 2</note>, eight, the arrows <note>original: "Shara" representing 5</note>, and the moon <note>original: "Indu" representing 1</note>—these are the revolutions of the stars in a Kalpa <term>Kalpa: An aeon in Hindu cosmology, equal to 4.32 billion years</term>.
<note>The Sanskrit verse uses word-numerals to express the number 1,582,236,450,000.</note>

The planetary calculations established by Brahma have become obsolete due to their antiquity; for this reason, Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu, writes a clear correction <note>original: "sphuta"</note> of them. He describes the flaws in the Epoch-divisions <note>original: "Yugadi-bheda"</note> cited by those ignorant people who speak in contradiction to the *Brahma-Siddhanta*. In one Kalpa, there are 1,582,236,450,000 sidereal risings.

Bhaskaracharya, who held Brahmagupta in the highest regard, also illuminated the year-measurements and stellar positions determined by Brahmagupta in his own work, the *Shiromani*.

The author of the *Surya Siddhanta* and other prominent astronomers have proposed the theory of the oscillating motion of the equinoxes <term>Ayana: The precession of the equinoxes</term>. However, to refute this view, Bhaskara wrote in his *Vasana-Bhashya* commentary: "If this was not observed, why was it stated by the authors of the *Surya Siddhanta* as authoritative tradition, like the circumference of the planetary orbits?" That is to say, if the era of the *Surya Siddhanta* and others was entirely within the precessional shift, why did they not reveal the theory of the stellar circle's revolution according to the views of Nara (the *Vasistha Siddhanta*)? However, Bhaskaracharya expressed this view without truly knowing the reason, which shall be written later. It is stated in the *Surya Siddhanta*:

->The circle of stars librates eastward thirty times in a Great Age.<-
->From that multiplier, divided by the terrestrial days of the age, the result is obtained from the total days.<-
->That sine multiplied by three and divided by ten gives the degrees known as the Precession <note>original: "Ayanansha"</note>.<-

In one Great Age <note>original: "Mahayuga"</note>, the stellar circle advances eastward 600 (30 $\times$ 20) times. By multiplying the desired days <note>original: "Ahargana"</note> or years by 600 and dividing by the terrestrial days or years of the Age, one takes the result's arc <note>original: "Bhuja"</note>, multiplies it by three, and divides by ten to obtain the Precessional Degrees <note>original: "Ayanansha"</note>. Both the writing and the meaning of this verse are extremely complex. The core issue is: why put so much effort into explaining something that should be simple? This method is not desirable in mathematics. The alternative meaning understood by Bhaskaracharya will be written later.

The final quarter of another primary verse defining the precession has also become complex in meaning. For example:

->In an Age, the stellar circle indeed librates eastward six hundred times.<-
->That multiplier, divided by the terrestrial days, the total days become the precessional traveler.<-

Here, if the word "Dyuguna" is not interpreted as the "Total Days" <note>original: "Ahargana"</note>, it cannot be reconciled with the previous verse in any way. Mr. Davis <note>original: "डेंमिस" (likely a misspelling of Samuel Davis)</note> also did not interpret this verse correctly. He wrote: "Multiply Ahargan (Number of mean solar days for which calculation is made) by 600 and divide the product by solar days in a yug, of quotient take sine and multiply 3 and divide by 10 to get ayanansha." <note>The original text contains several printer's errors in the English quote, such as "qays" for "days" and "prodnct" for "product".</note>

Whatever the case may be, it is understood from the first verse that according to the *Surya Siddhanta*, the annual motion of the precession is 54 seconds <note>original: "Vikala"</note>.

Parashara’s view is that in one Kalpa, the stellar circle moves 581,709 times...

# Introduction
<page-num>(11)</page-num>

According to the view of Aryabhata, it moves 578,159 times; therefore, according to both these views respectively, the precession <note>Ayana: the shifting of the equinoxes</note> advances eastward by 52.3 and 52.1 seconds <term>Vikala: a second of arc in ancient Indian astronomy</term> every year. The *Parashari Samhita* is the very foundation of Aryabhata’s system; this is inferred from the excerpts quoted in his book. The author of the *Parashari* was the first to propose the shifting state of the equinoxes. According to his view, the equinoctial cycle oscillates between two points, 27 degrees east and west of the sign of Aries. Aryabhata compared his own celestial observations with those recorded in the *Parashari* and applied his intellect to other matters as well. In the text *Aryashtashatika*, he recorded a different opinion regarding the precession—according to him, "The cycle should move 24 degrees in both directions" <note>original: "चतुर्विंशत्यंशचक्रमुभयतो गच्छेत्"</note>. In his later work, the *Dashagitika*, he set aside that opinion and upheld the ancient view. From these two published opinions, it is inferred that by writing 24 degrees, he was indicating the limit of the precession based on an estimate of his own time. Therefore, it is known that he was born when the equinoctial cycle had advanced 24 degrees from the western point. At the time of Varahamihira and the author of the *Surya Siddhanta*, the cycle had advanced 27 degrees; thus, in Aryabhata’s time, the cycle was 3 degrees west of Aries. For this reason, he was born 215 years before Varahamihira, or 9 years before the Shaka era <note>The Shaka era began in 78 CE; this places Aryabhata around 69 CE by this specific calculation</note>. Mr. Apurva Chandra says that Aryabhata lived 16 centuries after Yudhishthira. Mr. Colebrooke is of the opinion that Aryabhata was a contemporary of Diophantus, the inventor of Greek algebra. Diophantus was born sometime around 319 CE. The honorable Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a resident of Pune, published a book titled *Orion* <note>referring to the constellations Mrigashira and Ardra</note> and, using Vedic evidence, showed that the shifting state of the equinoxes is mathematically incorrect.

The *Garga Samhita* is also an ancient text of astrology. Varahamihira has repeatedly mentioned the name of this text in the *Brihat Samhita*. Professor Kern, the English translator of the *Brihat Samhita*, quoted passages from the *Garga Samhita* and wrote that it was composed 44 years before the Christian era. That passage is as follows:

> Then, having attacked Saketa, the Panchalas, and Mathura,
> the Greeks <note>Yavanas: historically referring to Indo-Greeks</note>, possessing wicked prowess, will reach the City of the Flower-Standard <note>Kusumadhvaja: another name for Pataliputra/Patna</note>.
> Once they reach the famous and prosperous City of Flowers <note>Pushpapura</note>,
> all the provinces will undoubtedly fall into chaos.

The wicked Greeks will attack Saketa, Panchala, and Mathura and proceed to Pataliputra (Patna). Reaching Kusumapura, they will loot it and cause utter destruction. Professor Kern says that during the time of the Bactrian King Menander, 144 years before the Christian era, an invasion of Saketa took place. Therefore, the author of the *Garga Samhita* lived after this invasion. Whatever Garga has written regarding the precession, it is known that he took this subject from the *Parashari*, because both expressed the same opinion when describing the auspicious and inauspicious effects of the precession!

As stated by Parashara:

> When [the sun] reaches the end of the constellation Shravana <note>original: Vaishnavanta</note> and enters the northern path,
> or when it enters the southern path in Ashlesha, it leads to great fear.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the history of Indian astronomy, specifically focusing on the calculation of the equinoxes and the movement of the solstices.</meta>

# Introduction

Garga writes—
> When the Sun reaches the end of the constellation Shravishtha <note>original: "Shravishtha," another name for Dhanishtha</note> during its northern course, and begins its southern course upon reaching Ashlesha, one should know that a time of great fear is at hand.

Both verses carry the same meaning: the <term>Uttarayana</term> <note>The northern progress of the sun after the winter solstice</note> occurs as the Sun travels through the end of Dhanishtha, and one should suspect great danger when the <term>Dakshinayana</term> <note>The southern progress of the sun after the summer solstice</note> begins after it travels to Ashlesha. The antiquity of Parashara’s writings is evident from the very meter of his verses.

The cyclical rotation of the <term>Krantipata</term> <note>The precession of the equinoxes; the point where the celestial equator and ecliptic intersect</note> was first revealed among Hindu astronomers by **Vishnuchandra**, the author of the <term>Vasishtha Siddhanta</term> <note>An ancient Indian astronomical treatise</note>. His view is that the precession completes 189,411 revolutions in one Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic cycle of time</note>; therefore, it is understood that according to his view, the solstice moves forward in the east by 60.06 seconds of arc <note>original: "vikala"</note> every year. Whether this view was taken from the books of the Greek astronomers **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**, or was discovered by the **Aryan astronomers** <note>referring to ancient Indian scholars</note> themselves, we cannot fully determine. However, looking at the annual motion of the solstice determined by both groups of astronomers, it appears that Vishnuchandra expressed this independently. According to Hipparchus, the equinox moves forward by one degree in approximately 85 years, and according to Ptolemy, one degree in 100 years.

Bhaskara has written—Chapter 6 of the <term>Shiromani</term> <note>referring to the Siddhanta Shiromani, a major work by Bhaskaracharya</note>:
> The intersection of the equator and the ecliptic is called the Krantipata (equinox).
> Its revolutions, as stated in the Surya Siddhanta, are thirty thousand in a Kalpa, moving in a reverse direction. ||17||
> The movement of the solstice (Ayana-chalana) was described by Munjala and others; it is the same thing.
> In their school, the revolutions in a Kalpa are 199,669. ||18||

The meeting point of the equator and the ecliptic is called the <term>Krantipata</term>. According to the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, its revolutions in one Kalpa are thirty thousand. <term>Ayana-chalana</term> <note>The shifting of the solstices/precession</note> and Krantipata are the same thing. According to **Munjala** and others, there are 199,669 revolutions of the solstice in one Kalpa. **Munishvara**, the commentator on the *Shiromani*, in order to reconcile this with the *Surya Siddhanta*, interpreted the word "Vyasta" (reverse) as—Vi = twenty <insert>multiplied by thirty thousand, making 600,000 (six hundred thousand),</insert> but according to Munjala and others, the annual motion of the solstice is 59.09 seconds of arc.

According to some astronomers, the <term>Ayanamsha</term> <note>The angular distance between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</note> began in the Shaka year 444. These astronomers believe that the solstice moves forward by one degree every 60 years. Their formula is as follows:—
> Subtract 444 from the Shaka year and divide by 60; the result is the Ayanamsha.
> This should be added to the clear Sun (Nirayana) to obtain the Sayan Sun for the purpose of calculating the ascendant and other factors.

Subtract 444 from the Shaka year and divide by 60 to obtain the Ayanamsha; by adding that to the <term>Nirayana Ravi</term> <note>The sidereal Sun</note>, the ascendant and the "ascensional difference" (Chara) of the <term>Sayana Ravi</term> <note>The tropical Sun</note> will also be found. It is estimated that later astronomers derived the above erroneous view from **Bhaskaracharya’s** <term>Karanakutuhala</term> <note>An astronomical handbook written in 1183 CE</note>. The *Karanakutuhala* was written in 1105 Shaka, and in it, eleven (11) degrees of Ayanamsha are recorded. Therefore, at the rate of one degree every 60 years, 11 degrees equal 660 years. Later astronomers subtracted 660 from 1105 Shaka to find the beginning of the precession. However, we do not consider Bhaskaracharya’s view to be correct. Bhaskara has written:—

> Brahmagupta and others did not calculate the <term>True Latitude</term><note>original: "sphuta-shara"</note> because the difference was very slight. Because the stars are fixed (they do not move), only the true latitudes of the stars are recorded; similarly, the true <term>Polar Longitudes</term><note>original: "dhruvaka"</note> of the stars, corrected by <term>Visibility Correction</term><note>original: "drik-karma"</note> and precession, are also recorded. In an inscription of Bhojaraja, the years 919 Samvat and 784 Shaka are written. From this, it is known that there have been several individuals named Bhojaraja in India. For this reason, one must perform every task with a steady and discerning eye.

Shatananda composed the book named <term>Bhasvati</term> in the Shaka year 1021. This is a small <term>Karana text</term><note>A concise astronomical manual used for practical calculations</note>; in this, the mathematics determined by the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> and Varahamihira are written in a summarized form.

> "Having bowed to the lotus feet of Murari (Vishnu), the illustrious one known as Shatananda speaks this *Bhasvati* for the benefit of his disciples, in the Shaka year measured by the Moon (1), the wings (2), the void (0), and the One (1) [Shaka 1021]. When subtracted by the arrows (5), the sacrificial fire (3), and the moon (1) [135], it becomes the Shaka year in this world."

Seeing the phrase "following the teachings of Mihira" written by Shatananda, Mr. Bentley concluded that Varahamihira was Shatananda's teacher and therefore he lived in 1060 AD. But, dear readers! You should well remember that Bentley did not understand the meaning of this.

Ganesha Daivajna, the son of Keshav Samvatsar, composed the *Grahalaghava* or *Siddhanta-Rahasya* in the Shaka year 1442 <note>approx. 1520 AD</note>. The writing of this gentleman is extremely complex.

Up to this point, the chronology of the astrologers has been determined. Although we only intended to determine the time of Varahamihiracharya, several matters were critiqued as the context arose. The book named *Brihat Samhita* is such that by reading it, a person becomes skilled in all tasks. It was a matter of wonder that such an excellent book did not have a Hindi commentary and was not printed in Bombay. <meta>This page marks the beginning of the Varahi Samhita (Bṛhat Saṃhitā). It establishes the cosmological and methodological framework for the work, transitioning from ancient sage-authored texts to a more concise, accessible format.</meta>

# Here Begins the Work Composed by the Best of Scholars, the Teacher Varahamihira
## The Varahi Samhita
### With Hindi Commentary

->Chapter One<-

Victorious is the Sun, the source of the entire universe, the soul of the world, the natural ornament of the sky. He is adorned with a garland of a thousand rays that resemble molten gold. <note>Verse 1: An invocation to Surya, the Sun God, common in Sanskrit scientific texts.</note> ||1||

Having observed the truth-filled scriptures spoken by the first sages <note>original: "muni"</note>, and considering the vastness of those works, I am now prepared to speak clearly, using a composition that is neither too brief nor too expansive. ||2||

If it is argued that only that which is ancient and composed by sages is good, and not that which is composed by men—I ask: when the meaning is the same, what is the difference in the specific statement, provided it is not a sacred mantra, simply because the syllables differ? ||3||

If the Creator <note>original: "Pitamaha" (Brahma)</note> says, "The day of the Son of Earth <note>Mars</note> is not auspicious," or if a man says, "Tuesday is unfavorable," what is the difference between the human and the divine word? ||4||

Having looked at the vast extent of the scriptures that have emerged in succession starting from Brahma, I am encouraged to produce this work as a concise summary. ||5||

Indeed, this universe was once darkness. Within that, in the waters, a golden egg of light was formed. In that egg, the Self-Born Brahma, the creator of the universe, manifested with the Sun and Moon as his eyes. ||6||

Kapila <note>founder of the Samkhya school</note> says Primordial Matter <note>Prakriti</note> is the cause; Kanada <note>founder of the Vaisheshika school</note> says it is atoms; some say Time is the cause, others say Nature, and others say Action <note>Karma</note>. ||7||

But enough of these extensive debates on various theories. Here, I must state the definitive conclusions regarding the branches of the science of Jyotish <note>term: Jyotish (astronomy and astrology)</note>. ||8||

The science of Jyotish deals with many subjects and stands upon three pillars <note>original: "skandhas"</note>. The sages call the complete collection of these the "Samhita." In this system, the movement of the planets determined by calculation is called "Tantra" <note>mathematical astronomy</note>; the second is "Hora" <note>horoscopy/natal astrology</note>; and the third is the determination of the various limbs or branches. ||9||

I have already described the retrograde and re-retrograde motions, the settings and risings of the star-planets in my work on astronomical calculation <note>referring to the Pancha-siddhantika</note>. I have also previously described birth charts in detail, along with journeys and marriages <note>referring to the Brihat Jataka and Vivaha Patalam</note>. ||10||

Leaving aside the minor details of questions and answers and the origins of planets which are of little use, I shall now speak of the essential truths, full of substance and meaning for all. ||11||

->Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira.<-

**Hindi Commentary Translation:**
May the Sun God be supremely victorious—He who is the place of origin for the entire world, who is the soul of the entire world, who is the natural ornament of the sky, and who is beautiful with a garland of rays like molten gold. ||1||

Having observed the truthful scriptures described in detail by the first sage (Brahma), I, the teacher Varahamihira, am prepared to describe that same knowledge in a clear manner through a composition that is neither too short nor too long. ||2||

If you say that only those scriptures composed by sages (Brahma and others) and which are ancient are excellent, and that a scripture composed by a human cannot be excellent—to that, it is said: other than sacred mantras, if the meaning is the same, what is the difference between the words of a sage and a human...

<summary>This page serves as the formal opening of Varahamihira's Bṛhat Saṃhitā, offering a prayer to the Sun and justifying the creation of a new, concise scientific text that summarizes ancient wisdom. It defines the three branches of Jyotish: Tantra (mathematics), Hora (horoscopy), and Samhita (general astrology/omens).</summary>
<keywords>Varahamihira, Bṛhat Saṃhitā, Jyotish, Astronomy, Astrology, Brahma, Sun God, Tantra, Hora, Samhita</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory framing of the Varahi Samhita (Brihat Samhita), where the author justifies the need for a new, concise compendium of astrological knowledge.</meta>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>The Varahi Samhita</header>

If the meaning is identical and only the syllables differ, what special merit does a sentence written by an ancient sage <note>such as Brahma, the creator</note> hold over a sentence written by a common man? For instance, in a text composed by Brahma it is written: "The day of the Son of the Earth is not auspicious" <note>original Sanskrit: *Kshititanayavasaro na shubhakrit*</note>, while in a human-authored text it is written: "The day of Mars is unfavorable" <note>original Sanskrit: *Kujadinamanishtam*</note>. Aside from the variation in wording, what excellence does the sage’s version have over the man’s? That is to say, none. Seeing the excessive length of all the scriptures composed by Brahma and others, I am inspired to illuminate this science in a systematic and concise form. ||3||4||5||

At the time when there was no creation, this entire universe was filled with darkness. Within that very darkness, a radiant golden egg was produced in the waters. It split into two pieces, forming Heaven and Earth. From those pieces, Brahma was born, whose eyes are the Sun and the Moon. ||6||

Regarding the origin of the universe, many different opinions are observed among the sages. Kapila says that *Pradhana* <note>the root-nature or primordial matter</note> is the cause of the universe. The sage Kanada says that substances and other material categories are the cause of the world's origin. Some say Time is the cause, others say Nature <note>inherent character</note> is the cause, and the followers of Mimamsa say that Action <note>Karma</note> is the cause of the world. ||7||

There is no need for further elaboration on the description of the world's origin. To settle this topic, many subjects would have to be described, and the matter is not small. Therefore, leaving aside this contemplation, we must here only determine the branches of the science of Jyotish <note>astrology and astronomy</note>. ||8||

The science of Jyotish, which has many divisions, is divided into three parts: *Samhita*, *Tantra*, and *Hora*. That which describes all the subjects of Jyotish is called the *Samhita* branch. That in which the movement of the planets is described through mathematics is called the *Tantra* branch. And that in which the determination of limbs <note>individual destiny</note>, such as journeys and marriages, is described is called the *Hora* branch. ||9||

In my own composition, the astronomical treatise named *Pancha-Siddhantika*, I have described the retrograde motions, direct paths, settings, and risings of the five star-planets <note>Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>. And in works such as the *Brihat Jataka* and *Brihat Vivaha-patala*, I have already described births, journeys, and marriages in great detail. ||10||

Now, at the beginning of the various treatises composed by sages like Garga, there are questions asked by disciples and answers given by the sages, along with various types of stories and useless accounts of the origin of the Sun and other planets. Furthermore, there are ancient accounts in the old *Samhita* texts that contradict the reality of the celestial sphere and are of very little practical use. Therefore, discarding all those hollow accounts, I describe in this book the essential and factual matters. ||11||

->Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Introduction to the Science," in the Hindi commentary<-
->written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province,<-
->on the Brihat Samhita composed by the illustrious teacher Varahamihira. ||1||<-

<summary>Varahamihira explains his rationale for writing the Brihat Samhita, emphasizing conciseness over ancient verbosity and defining the three branches of Jyotish: Samhita, Tantra, and Hora. He dismisses mythological filler in favor of essential astronomical and astrological facts.</summary>
<keywords>Varahamihira, Brihat Samhita, Jyotish, Samhita, Tantra, Hora, cosmology, Pancha-Siddhantika, Baldev Prasad Mishra, astrology branches</keywords>

# Chapter Two

### Now, therefore, we shall explain the "Sutras for the Astrologer."

The <term>Samvatsara</term><note>A Royal Astrologer or Master of the Year</note> should be of noble birth, pleasant to look upon, modest in dress, truthful, free from envy, and impartial. He should have well-knit and well-proportioned limbs, with no physical defects, and possess beautiful hands, feet, nails, eyes, chin, teeth, ears, forehead, eyebrows, and head. He should be of noble physique and have a deep, majestic voice. For generally, internal virtues and defects follow the physical form of the body. ||1||

Regarding his virtues: he must be pure, dexterous, bold, eloquent, possessed of ready wit, a knower of place and time, and endowed with <term>Sattva</term><note>The quality of goodness, clarity, and harmony</note>. He should not be intimidated by assemblies and should be superior to his fellow students. He must be skillful, free from vices, and well-versed in the arts of pacification, nourishment, magic, and ritual bathing. He should be devoted to the worship of the gods, observances, and fasting. His scientific power should be demonstrated by the wonders of his independent knowledge. He should be able to answer questions correctly, except when faced with the inscrutable will of destiny. He must be a master of the three branches of the science: <term>Grahaganita</term><note>Mathematical Astronomy</note>, <term>Samhita</term><note>Natural Astrology/Omens</note>, and <term>Hora</term><note>Horoscopy/Predictive Astrology</note>. ||2||

In the branch of Mathematical Astronomy, he must be a knower of time and space as described in the five <term>Siddhantas</term><note>Scientific treatises or systems</note>—namely the <term>Paulisha</term>, <term>Romaka</term>, <term>Vasishtha</term>, <term>Saura</term>, and <term>Paitamaha</term>. He must understand the divisions of time from the Great Age (<term>Yuga</term>), year, solstice, season, month, and fortnight, down to the day, night, hour (<term>Muhurta</term>), minute, second, and the smallest fractions of a breath. ||3||

He must understand the causes of the four types of months—Solar, Civil, Sidereal, and Lunar—as well as the occurrence of intercalary months (<term>Adhimasa</term>) and omitted days (<term>Avama</term>). ||4||

He must know the lords of the sixty-year cycle, the years, months, days, and hours, and their beginnings and endings. He must be expert in demonstrating the similarities and differences between the various measurements of time, such as the Solar system. Even when there are differences in the treatises, he must be skillful in demonstrating the truth through observation, using the shadow, water-clocks, and the alignment of the meridian, ensuring that calculation matches observation. He must understand the causes of the fast, slow, northern, southern, low, and high motions of the Sun and other planets. He must be a predictor of the eclipses of the Sun and Moon: their beginning, end, direction, magnitude, duration, intensity, and color. He must also predict the conjunctions and planetary wars of the planets yet to come. He must be skilled in determining the distance of each planet's orbit in <term>Yojanas</term><note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> and the rotation of the Earth. He must be an expert in the geometry of time, including the celestial sphere, the latitude, the equinoctial shadow, and the rising of the zodiac signs. His speech should be refined by the study of various objections and questions, like gold purified by the touchstone and fire. He is a true Master of the System. As it has been said:

> How can one be known as a knower of the scriptures who does not lead to a clear conclusion, who cannot answer a single question when asked, and who does not teach his disciples? * A man who interprets the text one way and the meaning another, or who performs calculations incorrectly, is like a vulgar man who, approaching a grandfather, praises an unworthy stranger. * When the system is well understood, the ascendant determined by the shadow and water-clock, and the meaning of the horoscopy well-established, the words of the predictor never go in vain. * And as was said by the noble <term>Vishnugupta</term><note>Also known as Chanakya or Kautilya</note>: A man crossing the ocean might perhaps reach the other side by the force of the wind, but no one who is not a Seer (<term>Rishi</term>) can ever, even in thought, reach the far shore of the great ocean known as the "Person of Time" (<term>Kalapurusha</term>).

In the branch of Horoscopy (<term>Hora</term>), he must understand the strengths and weaknesses of the signs, hours, decans, ninth-parts, twelfth-parts, and thirtieth-parts. He must determine the various strengths of planets through their direction, place, time, and movement. He must understand the temperaments, elements, substances, castes, and activities associated with them. He must be expert in the moments of conception and birth, the calculation of longevity, periods (<term>Dashas</term>) and sub-periods, the eight-fold divisions (<term>Ashtakavarga</term>), and the various yogas (planetary combinations) such as Raja-yoga, Chandra-yoga, and Nabhasa-yoga. He must judge the results of these based on the planetary aspects and positions, and provide omens for the present moment, marriages, and other ceremonies...

<summary>This page defines the rigorous physical, moral, and intellectual requirements for a Royal Astrologer, emphasizing mastery over the five astronomical systems and the mathematical calculation of time.</summary>
<keywords>Samvatsara, Siddhanta, Astronomy, Horoscopy, Varahamihira, Vishnugupta, Five Siddhantas, Kalapurusha</keywords>

# The Varahi Samhita

(20)

...and the performance of rituals for those in distress. Regarding expeditions: the lunar day, the weekday, the <term>Karana</term><note>A Karana is half of a lunar day or Tithi</note>, the lunar mansion (<term>Nakshatra</term>), the auspicious moment (<term>Muhurta</tt>), the rising sign (<term>Lagna</term>), the <term>Yoga</term>, the twitching of limbs, dreams, the ceremonial bath of victory, sacrifices to the planets, communal sacrifices, the sacred fire, the characteristics of idols, the movements of elephants and horses, the rumors within the army, the gestures of the soldiers, the six-fold diplomatic policy, the means of overcoming calamities, auspicious and inauspicious omens, the encampment of the army, the color of the fire, and the timely employment of ministers, spies, messengers, and forest-dwellers, as well as the methods for capturing an enemy's fortress—all these have been explained by the ancient teachers. 

The science is spread across the world, as if painted on the mind or poured into the heart. The life of one who does not know the movements of the heavenly bodies is fruitless. ||5|| 

One who has mastered the entire <term>Samhita</term><note>The branch of astrology dealing with collective omens and natural phenomena</note> becomes a true diviner of fate. In this work, the following subjects are contained: the movements of the Sun and other planets; their natural states, transformations, size, color, rays, brilliance, shapes, settings, risings, paths, transitions from one path to another, retrograde and re-retrograde motions, and their conjunctions. The results of these are judged according to the division of countries based on the "Star-Tortoise" (<term>Nakshatra-Kurma</term>) arrangement. 

It also covers the movements of the star Canopus (<term>Agastya</term>) and the Seven Sages (<term>Saptarishi</term>/Great Bear); the distribution of countries among the planets; the arrangement of the lunar mansions; the "triangle" and "conjunction" configurations of planets; planetary wars; the yearly results of planetary positions; the signs of pregnancy in the clouds; the conjunctions of the Moon with the stars Rohini, Svati, and Ashadha; immediate rainfall; the flowering of plants and creepers; halos and circles around the sun and moon; mock suns; winds; meteors; the glowing of the quarters; earthquakes; the colors of twilight; "cities of the Gandharvas" <note>mirages in the sky</note>; dust storms; the fluctuation of prices; the birth of crops; the festival of Indra’s banner; Indra’s bow (the rainbow); the science of architecture (<term>Vastu-vidya</term>); the science of bodily marks; the science of crows; the circle of internal omens; the circles of deer, horses, and winds; the characteristics of palaces and temples; the characteristics of idols and their installation; the "Ayurveda" of trees (botany); the finding of underground water; the lustration of horses and elephants; the movements of the wagtail; the pacification of portents; the variegated spots of the peacock; the "Ghee-blanket" ceremony; the characteristics of swords, silk cloths, roosters, tortoises, cows, goats, horses, elephants, men, and women; the concerns of the inner harem; the characteristics of umbrellas, shoes, torn clothes, fly-whisks, staffs, beds, and seats; the examination of gems; the characteristics of lamps; and the good or bad omens associated with tooth-sticks. 

These general omens affecting the world, as well as those affecting individual men and kings, must be contemplated every moment by an astrologer who is devoted to no other task. It is not possible for a single person to observe all omens day and night. Therefore, a well-paid astrologer should employ four other experts. One should watch the East and South-East; another the South and South-West; another the West and North-West; and another the North and North-East. This is because omens like falling meteors occur suddenly. Their results depend on their shape, color, glossiness, size, and the planets or stars they strike. ||6||

As the Great Sage Garga has said: 
"The King who does not honor the astrologer who is skilled in all branches and sub-branches of the science, and who is a master of horoscopy and mathematical astronomy, meets with destruction." ||7||

"Even those who dwell in the forest, who are free from 'mine-ness' and possess nothing, even they inquire of the astrologer who is an expert in the movements of the stars." ||8||

"As the night is without a lamp, and as the sky is without the sun, so does a King without an astrologer wander like a blind man on a path." ||9||

"The auspicious moments, the lunar days, the stars, the seasons, and the solstices—all would become confused if there were no royal astrologer." ||10||

"Therefore, a King who desires victory, fame, wealth, enjoyment, and spiritual merit should approach a learned and leading astrologer." ||11||

"One who desires prosperity should not live in a land where there is no astrologer; for where he resides as the 'eye' of the land, no sin exists." ||12||

"One who studies the science of the stars does not fall into hell; the diviner of fate attains a place in the world of Brahma." ||13||

"The twice-born man who knows this entire science in both text and meaning deserves to be the first to eat at a funeral feast (<term>Shraddha</term>); he is honored and purifies the company." ||14||

"The Greeks (<term>Yavanas</term>) are indeed foreigners, but this science is well-established among them..." <note>original: "mlecchā hi yavanāsteṣu samyak śāstramidaṃ"</note>

# Chapter 2: With Hindi Commentary

...established. Even those who live like sages are worshipped; how much more so a Brahmin who knows the divine science? || 15 ||
One who gives predictions based on hidden tricks, sorcery, or by overhearing whispers <note>original: "karnopashruti" - a divination technique involving listening to chance words</note> should not be consulted; he is not a true knower of the divine. || 16 ||
He who claims to be an astrologer without knowing the scriptures is a sinner who defiles the assembly; he should be known as a "Star-Gazer" <note>A derogatory term for a pretender who only looks at stars without scientific knowledge</note>. || 17 ||
He who observes a fast suggested by such a "Star-Gazer" goes to the hell of "Blinding Darkness" <note>Andhatamisra</note> along with that pretender. || 18 ||
The predictions of the ignorant are like the accidental fulfillment of a vow made to a lump of clay at the city gate; if they come true, it is merely by chance. || 19 ||
One who makes predictions by mere luck, who is fond of interrupted or inconsistent talk, and is intoxicated by knowing only a fraction of the scripture, should be abandoned by the King. || 20 ||
But he who thoroughly understands the three branches—**Horoscopy** <term>Hora: natal astrology</term>, **Mathematics** <term>Ganita: astronomy and calculations</term>, and **Natural Astrology** <term>Samhita: omens and mundane astrology</term>—should be honored and accepted by a King desiring victory. || 21 ||
A single astrologer who knows the right time and place can achieve what a thousand elephants or four thousand horses cannot. || 22 ||
Bad dreams, evil thoughts, ill omens, and sinful deeds quickly perish upon hearing the moon's alignment with the stars from an astrologer. || 23 ||
Neither the King's father, mother, relatives, nor friends desire his fame and growth as much as a well-wishing, competent astrologer does for the King and his army. || 24 ||

->Thus ends the Second Chapter, titled "The Rules for the Astrologer," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 2 ||<-

Here, the definition of the first **Samvatsara** <term>Royal Astrologer</term>, that is, the Astrologer, is stated:
He should be born of a noble family, be pleasant to look at, modest in dress, truthful, not a fault-finder of others' virtues, and possess a body perfect in all limbs. He should not be physically disabled, and his hands, feet, nails, eyes, chin, teeth, ears, forehead, and head—all these parts—should be marked with excellent signs. His body should be robust and handsome, and he should have a deep, resonant voice. Such a person is fully entitled to the name "Astrologer," because generally, virtues and flaws follow the form and shape of the body. || 1 ||

He must be pure, clever, bold (meaning one who speaks well in assemblies), skilled in conversation, quick-witted, a knower of time and place, free from deceit in his heart, fearless in gatherings, and not subject to humiliation by his peers. He should be skillful and free from all types of addictions. He must be knowledgeable in the sciences of **Pacification** <term>Shantik: rituals to calm evil omens</term>, **Prosperity** <term>Paushtik: rituals for growth</term>, **Exorcism** <term>Abhichara</term>, and ritual bathing. He should be devoted to worshipping the gods, vows, and fasting. He should spread his glory by creating wonder through his astronomical calculations. He should be able to answer questions about the future and, even without being asked, should advise on pacification rituals to ward off the divine calamities arising from various portents. He must be an astrologer who knows the full meaning of all the texts including **Calculations**, **Compendiums**, and **Horoscopy**. || 2 ||

He must be an astrologer who knows **Calculations** <note>Ganita</note>, specifically the five systems of astronomy: **Paulisha, Romaka, Vashishtha, Surya, and Paitamaha**. Within these five Siddhantas <term>scientific treatises</term>, he must understand the divisions of time such as the Aeon <term>Yuga</term>, Year, Solstice, Season, Month, Fortnight, Day-and-Night, three-hour periods, Muhurta, Ghatika, Pala, breath-length <term>Prana</term>, Truti, and the further subdivisions of a Truti. Furthermore, he must know the divisions of space: minutes, seconds, degrees, and zodiac signs. || 3 ||

He must be an astrologer who understands the causes of the four types of months—**Solar, Civil, Sidereal, and Lunar**—as well as intercalary months <term>Adhimasa</term> and lost months <term>Kshayamasa</term>. || 4 ||

He must know the sixty years of the cycle beginning with **Prabhava** and **Vibhava**, and within them, the twelve-year cycles <note>Yuga</note>...

# Varahi Samhita

<page-num>22</page-num>
<header>Varahi Samhita</header>

He should be one who understands the uninterrupted knowledge of the lords of the years (in cycles of five years), months, days, and <term>Hora</term><note>An hour or a specific astrological division of time</note>. He must be expert in discerning which of the various measurements—Solar, Lunar, and others—prescribed in the scriptures are correct or incorrect. If differences appear in the Solar measurements within the Siddhanta texts, he should be skilled in performing <term>Drig-ganita</term><note>Calculations verified by direct observation</note> using shadows and water-clocks, based on the visible celestial equator at the time of the solstices <note>original: "Ayana"</note>. Furthermore, he must understand the causes of the fast, slow, southern, northern, low, and high motions of the Sun and other planets. 

In the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, he should be able to predict the time of contact, the time of release, the directions of contact and release, the duration of the eclipse, the <term>Vimarda</term><note>Total darkness or maximum obscuration</note>, the color, the location, and future planetary conjunctions or planetary wars. He must understand the space, time, and cause regarding the schemes of planetary revolutions, latitudes, co-latitudes, the radius of the diurnal circle, the ascensional difference, the rising periods of the zodiac signs, shadows, the <term>Nadi</term><note>A unit of time, 24 minutes</note>, and the <term>Karana</term><note>Half of a lunar day</note>. 

He must be truthful in answering various types of questions. Only one who speaks the scripture as clearly as gold that has been rubbed on a touchstone, heated in fire, and purified by a grindstone can be called a <term>Tantrajna</term><note>A master of the technical/mathematical systems of astronomy</note>. It is said: how can one be considered a knower of scripture if he cannot state a definite meaning, cannot answer when questioned, and cannot teach a student? An ignorant man who interprets a text one way while the meaning is another, and who confuses the calculation manuals, is like a debauched man who praises a prostitute in the presence of Lord Brahma. The words of a man who knows the technical system, who can determine the ascendant <note>Lagna</note> through shadows, water-clocks, and instruments, and who is an expert in <term>Horashastra</term><note>Predictive astrology</note>, can never be false. 

<note>Arya Vishnugupta likely refers to Chanakya/Kautilya</note> Arya Vishnugupta has also said that if a man wishes to cross the ocean, he might do so by the force of the wind, but this ocean of the Science of Time <note>Jyotish Shastra</note>, which is the very form of the Time-Purusha, cannot be crossed even in the mind by anyone other than a Sage. 

In <term>Horashastra</term>, there is the determination of planetary strength through various means: signs, hours, decans <note>Drekkana</note>, ninth-parts <note>Navamsha</note>, twelfth-parts, thirtieth-parts, strengths and weaknesses, places of reception, time, and motivation. It covers the reception of nature, elements, substances, castes, and actions; conception, the time of birth, wonders, faith, commands, early death, longevity, major and minor planetary periods, the eight-fold divisions <note>Ashtakavarga</note>, royal yogas, lunar yogas, two-planet yogas, and the results of all yogas like the Nabhasa yogas. It includes the results of houses, aspects, departures, motions, and the auspicious or inauspicious causes of all questions of that time. It describes the reasons for all marriage rituals, journeys, lunar dates, days, half-lunar days, constellations, auspicious moments, the ascendant, and unions. It covers the twitching of body parts, dreams, victory, ritual baths, planetary sacrifices, group travels, the signs of fire, signals of elephants and horses, the movements of army rumors, the six-fold diplomatic measures, omens of good and bad fortune, the grounds for army encampments, the color of fires, and the timely employment of ministers, spies, messengers, and forest-dwellers. The methods for capturing an enemy's fort and the nature of all journeys—all these matters are spoken of in the <term>Horashastras</term>. 

The teachers have said: the commands of one who knows this scripture—including the revolutions of the stars—as if it were popularized in the world, written in his intellect, and cast into his heart, never go in vain. Only those expert in the Samhitas of Astrology can be <term>Daivajnas</term><note>Diviners or knowers of fate</note>. Because in the Samhitas, all these matters are described, such as: the movement of the Sun and other planets, and therein the nature and transformations of all the planets...

<summary>This page outlines the rigorous technical and ethical requirements for an astrologer, emphasizing the need for observational accuracy and mastery over both mathematical astronomy (Tantra) and predictive astrology (Hora).</summary>

# Chapter 2: The Samhita (Continued)

The determination of time is made through the measurement, color, rays, light, shape, rising, setting, and paths—including distinct, retrograde, and post-retrograde paths—of the **Nakshatras** <note>Lunar mansions or star clusters</note> and **Grahas** <note>Planets, including the Sun and Moon</note>, as well as their conjunctions. This science reveals the effects on all countries through the divisions of the stars and the *Kurma-vibhaga* <note>original: "कूर्मविभाग"; a traditional geographical division of India shaped like a tortoise</note>. 

It further encompasses:
*   The movement of Agastya <note>The star Canopus</note> and the Seven Sages <note>The Big Dipper/Ursa Major</note>.
*   *Graha-bhakti* <note>Planetary influences over specific regions or materials</note> and the arrangement of the stars.
*   Planetary triangles, planetary wars, and conjunctions.
*   Eclipses and the prediction of rainfall.
*   The signs of pregnancy in clouds <note>Garbha-lakshana: an ancient method of predicting rain months in advance</note>.
*   The yogas <note>conjunctions</note> of Rohini, Swati, and Ashadha.
*   Immediate rainfall, the blooming of flowers and vines.
*   Atmospheric phenomena: halos (*paridhi* and *parivesha*), mock suns (*parigha*), winds, meteors (*ulka*), and the "burning of the quarters" <note>an ominous red glow on the horizon</note>.
*   Earthquakes, the glowing of the twilight, "cities of the Gandharvas" <note>mirages in the sky</note>, dust storms, and thunderclaps.
*   Economic fluctuations: the rise in prices of goods and the production of grain.
*   The festival of Indra’s Banner and the appearance of rainbows.
*   **Vastu Vidya** <note>The science of architecture and sacred geometry</note>, the science of bodily limbs (*Anga-vidya*), and the science of crows (*Vayasa-vidya*).
*   The cycles of animals: deer, horses, and the cycle of winds.
*   The characteristics of palaces, idols, and the consecration of idols.
*   **Vrikshayurveda** <note>The science of plant life and health</note> and the treatment of trees.
*   *Udargala* <note>The art of finding underground water</note>.
*   The lustration of arms (*Niranjana*), the appearance of wagtails, and the pacification of portents.
*   The variegated patterns of peacock feathers.
*   The examination of qualities in ghee, blankets, swords, and royal sashes.
*   The characteristics of roosters, tortoises, goats, dogs, horses, and elephants.
*   The physiognomy of men and women, and concerns regarding the inner apartments <note>the harem or private royal quarters</note>.
*   The signs of caskets, pearls, tears in garments, chowries <note>fly-whisks</note>, staffs, beds, and seats.
*   The examination of gems, the signs of lamps, and the use of tooth-sticks.

All these auspicious and inauspicious omens are revealed through this **Samhita**. It is proper for the **Daivajnya** <note>The "knower of fate"—an astrologer-astronomer</note> to disregard other tasks and constantly contemplate all ordinary and extraordinary signs, both auspicious and inauspicious, for the world and for every individual. 

However, determining the good or evil of these matters day and night is not a task for a single man. Therefore, a king should appoint four other men who are well-versed in these scriptures to assist a well-supported **Daivajnya**. 
*   One man should observe the East and the Southeast (*Agni* corner).
*   The second should observe the South and the Southwest (*Nairrita*).
*   The third should observe the West and the Northwest (*Vayu* corner).
*   The fourth should observe the North and the Northeast (*Ishana* corner).

This ensures that omens like falling meteors are noticed immediately, for the effects of such meteors depend on their shape, color, glossiness, size, and their relation to the planets and stars at the time of impact. 

The sage **Garga** has said: "A king who does not honor a **Daivajnya** who is skilled in all branches of the science, proficient in *Hora* <note>predictive astrology</note> and mathematics, will soon meet his destruction." **|| 6-7 ||**

Even forest-dwellers, those free from worldly attachments, and those who accept nothing, still inquire about all matters from the scholars who know the movements of the planets and stars. **|| 8 ||**

Just as a night without a lamp and a sky without the sun, a king without a **Daivajnya** does not shine; rather, he wanders like a blind man on a treacherous path. **|| 9 ||**

Without a **Daivajnya**, the auspicious moments (*Muhurta*), lunar dates (*Tithi*), stars, seasons, and the sun's solstices (*Ayana*) would all become confused and overturned. **|| 10 ||**

For this reason, a king who desires victory, fame, fortune, enjoyment, and auspiciousness should approach a learned and leading **Daivajnya** to know all things. **|| 11 ||**

It is not proper to reside in a country where no **Daivajnya** lives; for where the **Daivajnya**, who acts as the eye for all matters, resides, no sin remains. **|| 12 ||**

By studying under a **Daivajnya** or by teaching a **Daivajnya**, one does not go to hell; rather, by being a contemplator of fate, one gains honor in the world of Brahma. **|| 13 ||**

Those **Brahmans** who know this subject thoroughly, according to the text and its meaning, are the first to be fed at funeral feasts (*Shraddha*) and, being purifiers of the assembly, are honored everywhere. **|| 14 ||**

Even if this science resides with a *Mlechchha* <note>a foreigner or non-Aryan</note> or a *Yavana* <note>originally meaning Greek, later any foreigner</note>, they should be worshipped like sages; how much more then for a **Brahman** who contemplates the divine...

<summary>This page lists the extensive subjects covered by the Samhita, ranging from meteorology to physiognomy, and emphasizes the political and spiritual necessity of the astrologer (Daivajnya) to the state.</summary>

<header>The Varahi Samhita (The Compendium of Varahamihira)</header>

What more need be said? ॥15॥ One should not ask anything of an astrologer who is shrouded in deceit <note>original: *kuhaka* - referring to fraud or juggling</note>, pride, or who is worthy of censure for what is heard by the ears; nor should such an astrologer speak. ॥16॥ That man who becomes an astrologer without knowing the Shastras <note>sacred scientific treatises</note> is a defiler of the assembly and a sinful soul; he should be known as a "Star-Gazer" <note>original: *Nakshatra-suchaka*, a derogatory term for a pretender</note>. ॥17॥ A person who observes fasts and rituals prescribed by such a "Star-Gazer" falls, along with that pretender, into the hell known as *Andhatamisra* <note>The "Blinding Darkness" hell</note>. ॥18॥ Just as a prayer offered to a mere lump of clay at a city gate might by chance be answered <note>referring to accidental success</note>, the predictions of an ignorant man may occasionally come true by sheer coincidence. ॥19॥ A king should abandon an astrologer who is fond of "wealthy" talk (boasting of many meanings) or "wealth-less" talk (nonsense), and who becomes intoxicated with pride despite possessing only a small amount of knowledge. ॥20॥ Kings desiring victory should worship and accept an astrologer who possesses excellent knowledge in *Hora* <note>predictive/natal astrology</note>, *Ganita* <note>mathematics/astronomy</note>, and *Samhita* <note>omens and mundane astrology</note>. ॥21॥ What a single astrologer <note>original: *Daivachintaka* - one who contemplates the divine/fate</note> who knows the specifics of place and time is capable of achieving, a thousand elephants or four thousand horses cannot accomplish. ॥22॥ By hearing the dialogue regarding the Moon’s constellations from the mouth of a true astrologer, bad dreams, ill omens, and the effects of evil deeds are quickly destroyed. ॥23॥ To increase their own fame, astrologers act in the interest of a powerful king in a way that even the king's father, mother, kinsmen, or brothers cannot. ॥24॥

->Thus ends the second chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the Great Teacher Varahamihira.<-

### Chapter Three

The southward journey of the sun <note>the summer solstice</note> once began from the middle of the constellation *Ashlesha*, and the northward journey <note>the winter solstice</note> from the beginning of *Dhanishtha*. This was certainly the case at one time, as stated in the ancient Shastras. ॥1॥ Currently, the sun's solstice begins from the start of Cancer <note>Karkataka</note> and the other from the start of Capricorn <note>Mriga/Makara</note>. The absence of what was previously stated is a deviation; this is clearly visible through direct observation. ॥2॥ This can be verified by observing the sun at sunrise or sunset against distant markers, or by the marks of the entry and exit of shadows on a large graduated circle. ॥3॥ If the sun turns back without reaching Capricorn, it destroys the South and the West. If it turns back without reaching Cancer, it destroys the North and the East. ॥4॥ Having passed the northern solstice, if the sun turns back, it brings welfare and the growth of grain. Even when following its natural course, it does so; however, a distorted movement of the sun <note>original: *Ushnanshu* - the hot-rayed one</note> creates fear. ॥5॥ Even without an eclipse, a dark spot called *Twashtar* sometimes appears on the solar disc. This destroys seven kings and the people through weapons, fire, and famine. ॥6॥ There are thirty-three "sons of Rahu" known as *Tamasakila* <note>Dark Spikes/Sunspots</note> or *Ketus*. One should predict results after observing their color, position, and shape on the sun. ॥7॥ When these appear on the solar disc, they yield evil results; on the lunar disc, they are generally auspicious. However, if they take the shape of a banner, a headless trunk, or a weapon, they are evil even on the Moon. ॥8॥ At their appearance, the waters become turbid, the sky is filled with dust, and a fierce wind carrying grit strikes the peaks of mountains and trees. ॥9॥ Trees bloom out of season, animals and birds appear distressed, the quarters of the sky seem to burn, and portents such as meteors and earthquakes occur. ॥10॥ If these sunspots are seen simultaneously with comets <note>Shikhi</note>, *Kilas*, or Rahu <note>eclipses</note>, their individual effects are not judged separately; one should declare the results based on the primary cause of their appearance. ॥11॥ In whichever land these spots on the solar disc are visible...

# Chapter 3: The Solar Course (Continued)

In each of these instances, the misfortunes of kings must be understood. <note>Verse 12</note> Even sages, their bodies withered by hunger, abandon their righteous conduct; and people, their children's arms devoid of flesh, migrate to foreign lands with great difficulty. <note>Verse 13</note>

The virtuous, their wealth plundered by thieves, sigh deeply with eyelids closed; their bodies tremble, and their vision is choked by tears born of sorrow. <note>Verse 14</note> Wasted and filled with self-loathing, men are oppressed by their own kings and by foreign invasions; some speak ill of their own king’s conduct and past deeds. <note>Verse 15</note>

Even when clouds are formed, they do not release abundant water; rivers dwindle to a trickle, and crops grow only in scattered places. <note>Verse 16</note>

If a <term>Kabandha</term><note>A headless trunk or spectral form appearing in the sky</note> appears in the solar disc, it signifies the death of the king by execution or fear of disease. If a crow-like shape appears, there is fear of thieves; if a <term>Kilaka</term><note>A wedge-shaped spot or "pin" on the sun</note> is present, it portends famine. <note>Verse 17</note>

If the Sun is pierced by shapes resembling royal insignia—such as the parasol, banner, or fly-whisk—it brings about a change in the monarchy. If it appears with sparks or smoke, it destroys the people. <note>Verse 18</note> A single spot causes famine; two or more lead to the destruction of the king. If the Sun is pierced by spots of white, red, yellow, or black, it destroys the corresponding <term>Varna</term><note>The four social classes: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra</note>. <note>Verse 19</note>

From whichever direction these great portents arise on the solar disc, fear will come to the people from that very direction. <note>Verse 20</note>

A Sun with upward-pointing rays destroys the commander-in-chief. A yellow Sun kills the king's son, while a white Sun kills the royal priest. <note>Verse 21</note> A variegated or smoke-colored Sun throws the earth into confusion; if it does not quickly bring rain, it brings death by thieves and weapons. <note>Verse 22</note>

The Sun is auspicious if it is:
*   Copper-colored or tawny in the <term>Shishira</term><note>Late Winter</note> season.
*   The color of a lion or saffron in <term>Madhu</term><note>Spring/Chaitra</note>.
*   Pale gold in Summer.
*   White in the Rainy season. <note>Verse 23</note>
*   Like the interior of a lotus in Autumn.
*   Like blood in <term>Hemanta</term><note>Early Winter</note>.
*   Glossy during the Monsoon.
A Sun that reflects the natural colors of all seasons is also a giver of blessings. <note>Verse 24</note>

A rough, white Sun destroys the Brahmins; a reddish one destroys the Kshatriyas. A yellow Sun destroys the Vaishyas, and a black one destroys the others. A glossy Sun is beneficial. <note>Verse 25</note> In Summer, a red Sun causes both good and bad; in the Rainy season, a black Sun causes drought. In Early Winter, a yellow Sun soon brings fear of disease. <note>Verse 26</note>

The Sun, if its body is split by a rainbow, causes conflict among kings. In the Monsoon, if it shines with clear brilliance, it brings immediate rain. <note>Verse 27</note> During the Rainy season, a Sun resembling the <term>Shirisha</term> flower <note>Albizia lebbeck, a pale greenish-yellow flower</note> brings immediate rain. If it resembles a peacock's feather, there will be no rain for twelve years. <note>Verse 28</note>

If the Sun is dark, there is fear of insects; if it looks like ash, there is fear of foreign armies. If it appears with a hole in the constellation of the king, that ruler faces destruction. <note>Verse 29</note> When the Sun in the sky looks like rabbit's blood, battles occur. If it looks like the Moon, the king is killed and another king quickly takes his place. <note>Verse 30</note>

A Sun shaped like a pot causes hunger and death; a fragmented Sun kills the king; one without rays causes fear. A Sun shaped like an archway destroys the city; one like a parasol leads to the destruction of the country. <note>Verse 31</note> If the Sun looks like a banner or a bow, or if it is trembling and rough, wars break out. If a black line appears on the Sun, it kills the king, and then his minister. <note>Verse 32</note>

When meteors, thunderbolts, or lightning strike the rising Sun, one should know it signifies the death of the king and the installation of another ruler. <note>Verse 33</note> If the Sun is surrounded by a halo every day at both twilights, or if it rises and sets blood-red, it brings another king to power. <note>Verse 34</note>

If the Sun is hidden at both twilights by clouds shaped like weapons, it causes war. If the clouds resemble deer, buffalo, birds, donkeys, or young camels, it brings fear. <note>Verse 35</note> From the intense heat of the Sun's rays, the earth suffers great pain.

It provides a seasonal guide for "natural" versus "portentous" solar colors and describes how specific shapes in the solar disc affect different social classes.</summary>
