### Chapter Twelve

### The Course of Agastya <note>The star Canopus</note>

> The Vindhya mountain range, whose peaks grew high enough to obstruct the path of the Sun, was brought to a standstill by him; the demon Vatapi, the enemy of the gods, was digested after entering his belly; the ocean was drunk up by him, who is an ocean of penance; and the southern direction is adorned by him—I now approach the description of the course of that Sage Agastya, who possesses the brilliance of milk. || 1 || The ocean, whose peaks were once uprooted by the claws of crocodiles and which contained hidden mountains, was instantly made beautiful by him through the removal of its water; it appeared as if to mock the gods with its piles of excellent jewels and gems mixed with falling pearls, like ancient white jeweled crowns. || 2 || Even when its water was removed, the ocean shone even more brilliantly, adorned by coral-bearing mountains and by the serpents emerging from them. || 3 || Though the great ocean, where whales once frolicked and which scattered heaps of jewels, fell into a state of distress <note>being dried up</note>, it was restored to celestial glory by him who drank its waters. || 4 || Even with its water gone, the Lord of Rivers <note>the Ocean</note>, filled with scattered shells and where whales once moved, bears the beauty of a lake in autumn, adorned with waves, white lotuses, and swans. || 5 || With whales acting as dark clouds, jewels as stars, crystals as the moon, and the rays atop the hoods of serpents as the fire-colored planets, the ocean resembled the winding sky... <note>The text cuts off mid-description of the dried ocean bed</note>

# Chapter 12: The Course of Agastya

...who performed [this deed]. || 6 || Hear now of the rising of that Sage <note>Agastya, identified with the star Canopus</note> who restrained the Vindhya mountains. Those mountains had risen up to block the path of the sun's chariot; their moving peaks were beautiful with fluttering banners, held aloft in the sky as they provided support for the bodies of the Vidyadharas <note>Celestial beings</note> who were busy embracing their beloveds clinging to their shoulders. The mountain's inner caves and waterfalls were frequented by lions who wore, as if they were ear-ornaments, swarms of bees following the scent of the ichor <note>rutting fluid</note> mixed with blood licked from the temples of elephants. Its peaks, inhabited by hyenas, bears, tigers, and monkeys, seemed to touch the sky; they echoed with the deep humming of intoxicated bees wandering in fear as trees were uprooted by elephants. The mountain appeared as if embraced by the sky for the sake of a lover in a secret tryst; it was filled with gardens inhabited by gods and populated by Brahmins who lived on water, moss, or air. || 7 ||

Upon the rising of the Sage named Agastya, the waters—which had been defiled by the mud of the flowering season—become pure again by their own nature, just like the hearts of virtuous men [after a period of turmoil]. || 8 ||

The river, with Ruddy Sheldrakes <term>Chakravaka: birds symbolic of fidelity</term> stationed on both banks and nourishing a row of crying swans, shines like a woman with a laughing face, her teeth stained red by chewing betel nut. || 9 ||

The river, filled with blue and white lotuses and adorned with rows of wandering bees, shines like a clever woman casting side-long glances with the movement of her arched eyebrows. || 10 ||

At night, the white water-lily opens its petals—in which bees are nestled—like a beautiful eye with dark pupils and lovely lashes, in order to behold the moon’s splendor which has been restored by the departure of the clouds. || 11 ||

The Earth, with her "hands" in the form of lakes filled with various colorful lotuses, swans, ruddy geese, and ducks, offers a respectful libation <term>Arghya: a ritual offering to a guest</term> to the one named Agastya, consisting of abundant gems, flowers, and fruits. || 12 ||

The water that was abandoned by the gods and poisoned by the fire-like venom of serpents whose bodies were hidden in the clouds, becomes auspicious and pure again upon the sight of Agastya. || 13 ||

The son of Varuna <note>Agastya</note> removes sins even by mere remembrance, let alone by hymns of praise. I shall describe the ritual of the libation for him as declared by the Sages, for the benefit of the King. || 14 ||

The learned man should announce the visibility of the star in every country by calculating its position. In Ujjain <note>A major center of Indian astronomy</note>, this occurs when the Sun has reached the sign of Virgo and is at seven degrees. || 15 ||

When the darkness of night is slightly broken by the rays of the dawn in the southern direction, the King—having been informed of the direction by the astronomer—should devoutly offer the libation upon the ground. || 16 ||

With fragrant seasonal flowers, fruits, gems from the ocean, gold, garments, a cow, a bull, and excellent cooked rice mixed with other foods, along with unhusked rice, fragrant incense, and ointments. || 17 ||

The King who offers this libation with faith becomes free from disease and conquers his enemies. If he performs this properly for seven years, he becomes the lord of the entire Earth, which is girdled by the oceans. || 18 ||

The Brahmin [who performs this] attains the Vedas; the Kshatriya wins victory; the Vaishya gains cattle and great wealth; and the Shudra attains the fruit of dharma. All gain freedom from disease. || 19 ||

If Agastya appears harsh and copper-colored, he causes disease; if smoke-colored, he causes drought; if flickering, he brings fear; if the color of madder <note>a reddish dye</note>, he brings hunger and war; and if he appears very small, he causes the siege of cities. || 20 ||

If he appears like gold or clear like crystal, bathing the earth with his rays, then the land becomes rich in food, free from fear, and populated by healthy people. || 21 ||

If he is struck by a meteor or a comet, he brings hunger and pestilence. He is said to become visible when the Sun enters the constellation Hasta, and he sets when the Sun enters Rohini. || 22 ||

->Thus ends the twelfth chapter, "The Course of Agastya," in the Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira.<-

<header>Varāhī Saṃhitā</header>

A brief account is given here of that Agastya, the purifier of the waters: who halted the Vindhya mountains when they grew tall to block the path of the Sun God; who digested the demon named Vatapi, a foe of the gods and a piercer of the bellies of sages; who drank the entire ocean; who adorned the southern direction through the ocean of his penance; and by whom, in ancient times, the sudden destruction of the water-mass seemed to offer a slight to the crown-wearing and jewel-bearing gods. When the waters vanished, the ocean bed became more beautiful than the full sea, revealing peaks uprooted by the claws of sea monsters, underwater mountains, and falling pearls mixed with heaps of excellent gems. The Lord of Rivers (the Ocean), though devoid of water, shone intensely, adorned by treeless mountains, gems, jewels, coral, and the serpents emerging from within. He drank the waters of the great ocean, which moved turbulently with leaping crocodiles and water-elephants; thus the ocean, though a seat of calamity <note>referring to its drying up</note>, attained a heavenly splendor. At that time, though its water was stolen, the Lord of Rivers was filled with floating crocodiles, oyster shells, and conchs, bearing the beauty of a lotus-pond in autumn—wavy, white-hued, and graced by lotuses and swans. He created a waterless, autumn-like "ocean-sky" where the white clouds were the darkness, the gems were the stars, the crystals were the moon, and the jewels on the hoods of serpents shone like radiant comets. **1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6**

The Vindhya mountain was growing continuously to block the path of the Sun's chariot. At that time, the <term>Vidyadharas</term> <note>celestial musicians/beings</note> living on its peaks were startled and nearly falling due to the mountain's upward quivering; because of this, the beautiful women resting on their shoulders anxiously stretched their bodies into the lap of the sky. At that moment, the garments on their laps and bodies began to shine like fluttering banners; thus, those elevated, flag-like Vidyadharas were beautifying the Vindhya mountain. Lions dwelt in the caves and waterfalls of the Vindhya; on the heads of these lions, rows of bees shone like garlands of <term>Bana</term> flowers, drawn by the sweet scent of blood from the temples of elephants. By the pulling of blossoming trees by massive elephants, the intoxicated rows of bees, terrified and agitated, created a deep musical sound. With its peaks echoing the cries of hyenas, bears, tigers, and <term>Shakhamrigas</term> <note>monkeys; literally "branch-deer"</note>, the Vindhya mountain seemed to be writing something upon the sky. The forests of Vindhya are inhabited by the gods. Listen now to a description of the rising of that Sage, who halted the Vindhya mountain—which is filled with many Brahmins who live only on water, or fast from grain, or eat only roots, or live on air—and which is embraced in its waterless regions by the River <term>Reva</term> <note>the Narmada River</note> like a woman intoxicated with passion. **7**

Just as the heart of a good man, defiled by the filth of association with evil people, becomes naturally pure the moment he sees a saint, so too the water mixed with mud due to the monsoon rains becomes naturally pure as soon as the Sage Agastya rises. **8**

Just as a white row of teeth shines in the middle of the red lips stained by betel-juice when a beautiful woman laughs, so too Agastya—

# Chapter 12: With Hindi Commentary
### Page 71

With the rising of the star Agastya, the rivers shine with rows of sounding Hamsa birds <note>Indian geese or swans</note> seated between two red-colored Chakravaka birds <note>Ruddy shelducks</note> stationed on both banks. ||9||

Upon the rising of the Sage Agastya, the rivers—filled with white lotuses situated near blue lotuses, over which rows of bees hover—appear like a clever woman overcome by love, casting side-long glances full of emotion. ||10||

The long ponds, appearing as amorous women wearing bracelets in the form of rippling waves, seem to open their excellent-lidded eyes—whose dark pupils are water-lilies surrounded by bees—specifically to behold the majesty of the moon, which has increased now that the clouds of the rainy season have departed at night. ||11||

The Earth, possessing hands in the form of lakes filled with various beautiful lotuses, swans, ruddy shelducks, and ducks, offers an *Arghya* <note>a respectful libation or offering</note> to the Sage Agastya with many jewels, flowers, and fruits. ||12||

The water poured down by the command of Indra, even if it was nourished by the poisonous fire emitted from the hoods of serpents while enveloped in the clouds, becomes auspicious and purifying upon the sight of the Sage Agastya. ||13||

To what extent can we describe the fruit of praising Agastya, the son of Varuna, by whose mere remembrance a multitude of sins are washed away? The procedure for the *Arghya* offering to Agastya, as prescribed by the sages for the benefit of kings, is now stated. ||14||

Learned scholars, having calculated the rising of Agastya according to the rules of mathematics, shall issue decrees in all lands. When the true longitude of the Sun is seven degrees less than the sign of Virgo (i.e., 4 signs and 23 degrees; this usually occurs around the 22nd, 23rd, or 24th day of the month of **Bhadrapada**), then the rising of the Sage Agastya occurs in the city of Ujjayini. ||15||

When the darkness of night is somewhat destroyed by the rays of the Sun (at the hour of dawn), and the quarters of the sky are pointed out by the astrologer <term>Daivajna: one who knows the divine/fate</term> (having received the command: "This is the South; offer the *Arghya* to Lord Agastya in this direction"), it is proper for the King to offer an *Arghya* upon the earth toward the South. This offering should be composed of seasonal autumn flowers, fruits, gems from the sea, gold, garments, cows, bulls, sweet rice, edible delicacies, curd, unbroken grains, fragrant incense, and sandalwood. ||16-17||

If a King performs this offering with faith, he shall be free from disease and conquer all his enemies. If he continues to give this offering for seven years, he shall become the lord of the earth girt by the oceans—a *Chakravartin* <note>a universal sovereign</note>. ||18||

If **Brahmins** offer *Arghya* to Agastya with whatever items they can obtain, they shall become masters of the four Vedas and gain beautiful wives and sons. If merchants <note>Vaishyas</note> likewise offer *Arghya* with whatever they have acquired, they obtain cattle and great wealth. ||19||

If the star Agastya appears "harsh" (rough or dry), it portends disease; if it is tawny in color, it signifies drought; if it is smoke-colored, it is inauspicious for cattle; if it is throbbing or trembling, it portends fear; and if its color is like madder-red, it signifies hunger, war, and...

<margin>* "The word *shatakumbha* can refer to both gold and silver; however, here it refers to silver." Thus says Mahotpala <note>Bhattotpala, the famous 10th-century commentator on Varahamihira</note>.</margin>
If the star is minute, it causes the siege of cities. ||20|| If the star Agastya <note>Canopus</note> appears as bright as *shatakumbha* (silver) or crystal, and satiates the earth with its rays, then the earth becomes abundant with grain and filled with people free from fear and disease. ||21|| If Agastya is struck by meteors or comets, then hunger, fear, and plague occur. When the Sun enters the constellation of Hasta, Agastya becomes visible in all regions; when the Sun enters Rohini, it sets (disappears) in all lands. ||22||

->Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Hindi commentary of the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Shri Varahamihiracharya, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. ||12||<-

### Now Begins the Thirteenth Chapter
#### The Course of the Seven Sages (Saptarshi)

**The northern direction appears like a woman wearing a single-string pearl necklace, adorned with a garland of white lotuses, smiling and protected by her lord, because of the Seven Sages (the Big Dipper). ||1|| Following the instruction of the Pole Star (Dhruva), their leader, the northern direction seems to dance repeatedly with the wandering Sages. I shall describe their course according to the opinion of the Elder Garga. ||2|| The Sages were in the Magha constellation when King Yudhishthira was ruling the earth; the era of that king is 2526 years before the Shaka era. ||3|| They remain in each constellation for a hundred years. They always rise in the North-East along with Arundhati. ||4|| In the eastern part stands the Lord Marichi; to the west of him is Vashistha; then Angiras, then Atri, and near him is Pulastya. ||5|| Then Pulaha and Kratu—thus the Lords are situated in order from the east. There, the virtuous Arundhati remains closely attached to the great sage Vashistha. ||6|| If they are struck by meteors, lightning, or smoke, or if they are discolored, rayless, or small, they destroy their respective classes of people. If they are large and bright, they bring prosperity to them. ||7|| Marichi is known to preside over the Gandharvas, gods, demons, charms, medicines, Siddhas, Yakshas, and Nagas. ||8|| Vashistha, if struck, destroys the Shakas, Yavanas <note>Greeks/Ionians</note>, Daradas, Paratas, and Kambojas, as well as hermits living in forests; if full of rays, he grants them prosperity. ||9|| Angiras is said to rule over those endowed with knowledge, the wise, and Brahmins. Atri rules over those born in forests, water-products, the ocean, and rivers. ||10|| Pulastya is remembered as the lord of Rakshasas, Pisachas, Danavas, Daityas, and serpents. Pulaha rules over roots and fruits, and Kratu over sacrifices and those who perform them. ||11||**

->**Thus ends the thirteenth chapter on the Course of the Seven Sages in the *Brihat Samhita* of Shri Varahamihira. ||13||**<-

#### Hindi Commentary Chapter 14

The <term>Saptarshi</term><note>The Seven Sages, identified with the stars of the Big Dipper</note> were present; by adding 2526 to the Shaka era year, the time of Yudhishthira is known. ||3|| They wander through each <term>Nakshatra</term><note>Lunar mansion or star cluster</note> for a hundred years. They always rise in the north-east direction accompanied by the chaste Arundhati. ||4|| In the eastern part resides Lord Marichi; to the west of Marichi is Vashistha; behind him is Angira; then Atri; near him are Pulastya, Pulaha, and Lord Kratu, seated in order toward the east. Among them, the chaste Arundhati has taken refuge with the great sage Vashistha. ||5||6|| If these stars are struck by meteors, thunderbolts, or smoke, or if they become discolored, lusterless, or small, they destroy their respective classes of people. If they are large or bright, they cause their respective classes to prosper. ||7|| If Marichi is afflicted in any way, it causes pain to the Gandharvas, gods, demons, medicinal charms, Siddhas, Yakshas, Nagas, and Vidyadharas. ||8|| If Vashistha is afflicted, he destroys the Shakas, Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners</note>, Daradas, Paratas, Kambojas, and forest-dwelling ascetics, but if he is radiant, he brings prosperity. ||9|| If Angira is struck, he destroys wise men, intellectuals, and Brahmins. If Atri is obstructed, those born in forests, aquatic products, the ocean, and rivers are destroyed. ||10|| From an obstacle to Pulastya, the Rakshasas, Pisachas, Danavas, Daityas, and serpents suffer; from a breach in Pulaha, roots and fruits suffer; and from an obstacle to the sage Kratu, those who perform sacrifices face difficulties. ||11||

# Now Begins the Fourteenth Chapter
## The Division of the Tortoise

The countries of <term>Bharatavarsha</term><note>Ancient India</note> are divided into nine parts starting from the center and moving toward the East and other directions, based on groups of three constellations arranged from the south-east onwards. ||1|| The central region includes Bhadra, Arimeda, Mandavya, Salva, Nipa, Ujjihana; also Maru, Vatsa, Ghosha, the Yamuna and Saraswati regions, Matsya, and Madhyamika. ||2|| Mathura, Upajyotisha, Dharmaranya, Anishurasena, Gauragriva, Uddehika, Gudashvattha, and the Panchalas. ||3|| Saketa, Kanka, Kuru, Kalakoti, Kukura, the Pariyatra mountains, Audumbara, Kapishthala, and Gajahvaya—these constitute the Middle Country. ||4|| Now in the East: the Anjana, Vrishabhadhvaja, Padma, and Malyavat mountains; the Vyaghramukha (tiger-faced), Sukshma, Karbata, Chandrapura, and Shurpakarna (sieve-eared). ||5|| The Khasas, Magadha, Shibira mountain, Mithila, Samatata, Odra, Ashvavadana (horse-faced), and Danturaka; Pragjyotisha, the Lauhitya river, the Milky Ocean, and the Purushada (cannibals). ||6|| The Udayagiri (Sunrise Mountain), Bhadra, Gauda, Paundra, Utkala, Kashi, Mekala, Ambastha, Ekapada (one-footed), Tamaliptaka, Koshala, and Vardhamana. ||7|| In the South-East direction: Koshala, Kalinga, Vanga, Upavanga, Jathara, Anga, Shaulika, Vidarbha, Vatsa, Andhra, Chedi, and the Urdhvakanthas (high-necked). ||8|| Vrishanalikera, Charmadvipa, the inhabitants of the Vindhyas, Tripura, the Smashrudhara (bearded ones), Hemakuta, Vyalagriva (serpent-necked), and Mahagriva (long-necked). ||9|| Kishkindha, Kanakasthala, the Nishada nations, Purika, Dasharna, along with the Nagnaparnas and Shabaras; these countries are associated with the triad of stars beginning with Ashlesha. ||10|| Now in the South: Lanka, Kalajina, Saurikirna, Talikata, Girinagara, Malaya, Dardura, Mahendra, and Malini mountains, and the Marukacchas. ||11|| Kankata, Tankana, the inhabitants of Vanavasi, Shibika, Phanika—

### Chapter Fifteen

->The Array of the Constellations<-
<note>Sanskrit: Nakshatra-Vyuha. This chapter details which professions, items, and people are governed by each lunar mansion.</note>

Under **Krittika** <note>The Fire-god's star</note> are those who deal in white flowers, those who maintain the sacred fires, experts in mantras, and those skilled in the commentaries on the ritual sutras. Also included are miners, barbers, Brahmins, potters, priests, and astronomers. || 1 ||

Under **Rohini** are those of noble vows, merchants, kings, the wealthy, and those who drive carts. It also governs cattle, bulls, aquatic animals, farmers, and those possessing the majesty of great mountains. || 2 ||

Under **Mrigashira** are fragrant things, garlands, lotuses, flowers, fruits, gems, forest-dwellers, and birds. Also included are deer, the Moon-god's followers, those who travel by foot, musicians, lovers, and letter-carriers. || 3 ||

Under **Ardra** <note>The Fierce star</note> are those fond of killing, binding, lying, adultery, theft, deceit, and creating discord. It also governs husked grains, sharp weapons, mantras, sorcery, and those skilled in the rituals of spirits. || 4 ||

Under **Punarvasu** <note>The star of the Adityas</note> are those endowed with truth, generosity, purity, noble lineage, beauty, intellect, fame, and wealth. It governs superior grains, merchants, those devoted to service, and artisans. || 5 ||

Under **Pushya** are barley, wheat, rice, sugarcane, forests, ministers, kings, those who live by water, holy men, and those devoted to performing sacrifices. || 6 ||

Under **Ashlesha** <note>The Serpent star</note> are artificial things, bulbs, roots, fruits, insects, snakes, and poisons. It also governs those fond of stealing others' wealth, husked grains, and all types of physicians. || 7 ||

Under **Magha** <note>The Ancestor star</note> are those rich in wealth and grain, granaries, those who take refuge in the East, devotees of the ancestors, merchants, heroes, meat-eaters, and those who dislike women. || 8 ||

Under **Purva-Phalguni** are actors, young women, the amiable, musicians, artisans, and commodities. It also governs cotton, salt, honey, oil, and young boys. || 9 ||

Under **Uttara-Phalguni** <note>The star of Aryaman</note> are those devoted to mildness, purity, humility, asceticism, charity, and the scriptures. It governs fine grains, great wealth, those devoted to righteousness, and kings. || 10 ||

Under **Hasta** are thieves, elephants, chariot-drivers, mahouts, artisans, and commodities. It also governs husked grains, those afflicted by hunger, merchants, and the elements of light and wind. || 11 ||

Under **Chitra** <note>The star of Tvashtar</note> are those skilled in ornaments, gems, dyes, painting, music, and perfumery. It also governs clever mathematicians, weavers, ophthalmic surgeons, and royal grains. || 12 ||

Under **Svati** are birds, wild animals, horses, merchants, and grains that are wind-heavy <note>likely meaning light or airy grains</note>. It also governs those with unstable friendships, the weak-willed, ascetics, and those skilled in trade. || 13 ||

Under **Vishakha** <note>The star of Indra and Agni</note> are trees with red flowers and fruits, sesame, and green gram. It also governs cotton, black gram, chickpeas, and devotees of Indra and the Fire-god. || 14 ||

Under **Anuradha** <note>The star of Mitra</note> are those endowed with bravery, leaders of groups, those fond of the company of holy men, and all virtuous people in the world, as well as everything produced in the autumn. || 15 ||

Under **Jyeshtha** <note>The star of Indra</note> are the very brave, those endowed with lineage, wealth, and fame, and those who seize others' property. It governs kings desiring victory and the leaders of armies. || 16 ||

Under **Mula** are medicines, physicians, heads of guilds, and those who deal in flowers, roots, and fruits. Seeds...

## Chapter 15: Accompanied by Hindi Commentary

...endowed with wealth. Those who live on fruits and roots. **(17)** Under **Shatabhisha** <note>original: "Aapye" referring to the water deity Varuna</note> are the gentle, those who travel by water-ways, those endowed with truth, purity, and wealth; bridge-builders, those who live by water, fruits, flowers, and aquatic products. **(18)** Under **Purva Bhadrapada** <note>original: "Vishveshvare"</note> are high officials, wrestlers, those who cross waters, horses, devotees of the gods, stationary warriors, those possessing great enjoyment, and those endowed with vigor. **(19)** Under **Uttara Bhadrapada** <note>original: "Shravane" here refers to the deity Ahirbudhnya</note> are those clever in illusion, always active, capable in their duties, enthusiastic, righteous, devotees of the Lord, and speakers of truth. **(20)** Under **Revati** <note>original: "Vasubhe"</note> are men free from pride, the impotent, those with fickle friendships, those disliked by women, those fond of giving gifts, the very wealthy, and those devoted to tranquility. **(21)** Under **Varuna** <note>Shatabhisha</note> are those who use nets, fishermen, aquatic creatures, and water-dwelling beings; also swineherds, washermen, distillers, and bird-catchers belong to this group. **(22)** Under **Purva Ashadha** <note>original: "Aaje"</note> are thieves, animal herders, the violent, those with low or deceitful conduct, those devoid of religious vows, and men skilled in combat. **(23)** Under **Uttara Ashadha** <note>original: "Ahirbudhnye"</note> are Brahmins, those endowed with sacrifice, charity, and penance, those of great wealth, forest hermits, heretics, kings, and excellent grains. **(24)** Under **Revati** <note>original: "Paushne"</note> are aquatic products, fruits, flowers, salt, gems, conch-shells, pearls, lotuses, fragrant flowers, perfumes, merchants, and ship-pilots. **(25)** Under the **Ashvins** <note>Ashwini</note> are horse-stealers, army commanders, physicians, servants, horses, horse-riders, handsome merchants, and horse-keepers. **(26)** Under **Yama** <note>Bharani</note> are those who consume blood and flesh, the cruel, those addicted to killing, binding, and beating, husked grains, those born of low families, and those devoid of courage. **(27)**

The three **Purvas** <note>Purva Phalguni, Purva Ashadha, Purva Bhadrapada</note> along with **Krittika** belong to the Brahmins; the **Uttaras** <note>Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, Uttara Bhadrapada</note> along with **Pushya** belong to the Kshatriyas (kings). **Revati**, **Anuradha**, **Magha**, and **Rohini** belong to the farmers. **(28)** **Punarvasu**, **Hasta**, **Abhijit**, and **Ashwini** are said to be the stars of the merchant class. **Mula**, **Ardra**, **Swati**, and **Shatabhisha** belong to the fierce classes and those of great power. **(29)** **Mrigashira**, **Jyeshtha**, **Chitra**, and **Dhanishta** are assigned to the servant class and masters. **Ashlesha**, **Vishakha**, **Shravana**, and **Bharani** are designated for the outcaste classes. **(30)**

When a star is occupied by the Sun or Saturn, or is damaged by the retrograde motion or piercing of Mars, or is hit by an eclipse or a meteor, or is definitely afflicted by the Moon— **(31)** it is called "stricken." Also, if it undergoes a natural reversal. The destruction of the mentioned groups occurs then; conversely, if the star is healthy, it leads to prosperity. **(31-32)**

### Thus ends the Fifteenth Chapter, "The Array of Nakshatras," in the Brihat Samhita of Shri Varahamihira.

### Now begins the Sixteenth Chapter:

The Sun <note>original: *Bhaskara*</note> is the lord of the eastern half of the Narmada river, the source of the Shone river, the regions of Anga, Suhma, Kalinga, and Balkh; the Shakas, Yavanas <note>Greeks or foreigners from the West</note>, Magadha, Shabara, Pragjyotisha <note>ancient Assam</note>, China, and Kamboja; || 1 || the Mekala, Kirata, and Vitaka tribes, those born in the inner and outer mountains, and the Pulindas; the eastern half of the Dravida country and the southern bank of the Yamuna; || 2 || Champa, Udumbara, Kaushambi, Chedi, the Vindhya forests, and Kalinga; the Pundra, Golangula, Shriparvata, and Vardhamana regions; || 3 || the Ikshumati river, and then thieves, the Parata people, forest-dwellers, and those who live by cattle-breeding; husk-grains, pungent substances, gold, fire, poison, and brave men; || 4 || medicines, physicians, four-legged animals, farmers, kings, violent men, travelers, and thieves; and those who are sharp, famous, and associated with snakes. || 5 ||

The Son of Earth <note>original: *Vasudhasuta*, referring to Mars</note> is the lord of those residing in the western half of the Shone, Narmada, and Bhimaratha rivers; the Nirvindhya, Vetravati, Shipra, Godavari, and Vena rivers; || 9 || the Mandakini, Payoshni, Mahanadi, Sindhu, Malati, and Para rivers; the northern Pandyas, Mount Mahendra, the Vindhyas, the Malaya mountains, and the Cholas; || 10 || the Dravidas, Videhas, Andhras, Ashmakas, Bhasapuras, Konkanas, Mantrishikas, Kuntalas, Keralas, Dandakas, Kantipura, and those of mixed Mleccha <note>foreign or non-Vedic</note> origin; || 11 || Nasik, Bhogavardhana, Virata, and the countries bordering the Vindhya mountains; those who drink the good waters of the Tapi and the Gomati; || 12 || city-dwellers, farmers, the Parata people, fire-worshippers, and those who live by their wits or weapons; forest-dwellers, fort-keepers, those in marketplaces, killers, the cruel, and the arrogant; || 13 || princes, elephants, the deceitful, children, those who strike, and cattle-herders; red fruits and flowers, coral, commanders, jaggery, wine, and sharp things; || 14 || those born in treasuries, performers of fire-sacrifices, mineral mines, Buddhist monks <note>original: *Shakya-bhikshu*</note>, and thieves; and those with long-standing enmities and great appetites. || 15 ||

# The Varahi Samhita

### The Domain of Mercury (The Son of the Moon)
Those who dwell by waterways, traders, those living in holes <note>likely referring to cave-dwellers or miners</note>, and mountain residents. **(17)** Experts in water-engines <note>mechanical pumps or irrigation systems</note>, musicians, painters, and those skilled in the preparation of gems, dyes, and perfumes. Those who excel in drawing, grammar, mathematics, grooming, and the science of longevity <note>Ayurveda</note> or crafts. **(18)** Spies, jugglers, infants, poets, the deceitful, informers, and those devoted to sorcery. Messengers, eunuchs, wits, and those knowledgeable in demonology and illusionism <note>magic</note>. **(19)** Guards, actors, dancers, and those dealing in ghee, oil, fats, seeds, and bitter things. Ascetics, those skilled in alchemy, and mules belong to the **Son of the Moon** <note>Mercury</note>. **(20)**

### The Domain of Jupiter (The Preceptor)
The eastern part of the Indus river, Mathura, the western half of Bharata, the Sauviras, Srughna, the northern regions, the Vipasha and Shatadru rivers, Maru, and the Salvas. **(21)** The Traigartas, Pauravas, Ambasthas, Paratas, Vatadhanas, Yaudheyas, the Saraswatas, Arjunayanas, and the Matsyas—their villages and nations. **(22)** Those devoted to elephants, horses, royal priests, kings, ministers, and rites for prosperity and nourishment. Those endowed with craftsmanship, truth, purity, religious vows, learning, charity, and virtue. **(23)** Citizens, the wealthy, those learned in linguistics and the Vedas, and those skilled in sorcery and politics. The regalia of kings, such as umbrellas, banners, and fly-whisks. **(24)** Bitumen, spikenard, valerian, costus, resins, rock salt, creepers, sweet juices, beeswax, and the herb *choraka* belong to **Jupiter**. **(25)**

### The Domain of Venus (The Son of Bhrigu)
Taxila, Martikavata, the Bahugiri mountains, Gandhara, Pushkalavataka, Prasthala, Malava, Kaikaya, Dasharna, Ushinara, and the Shibis. **(26)** Those who drink from the Vitasta, Iravati, and Chandrabhaga rivers. Those possessed of chariots, silver mines, elephants, horses, high officials, and wealth. **(27)** Fragrant flowers, ointments, gems, diamonds, ornaments, lotus-beds, beautiful young men and women, poetic equipment, and those who eat delicious and sweet food. **(28)** Those endowed with gardens, water, desire, fame, happiness, generosity, and beauty. Scholars, ministers, merchants, potters, those born from eggs <note>birds</note>, and the *triphala* fruits. **(29)** Silk, fine cloth, blankets, wool, *lodhra* bark, cinnamon, nutmeg, aloe-wood, sweet flag, long pepper, and sandalwood belong to **Venus**. **(30)**

### The Domain of Saturn (The Son of the Sun)
Anarta, Arbuda, Pushkara, Saurashtra, the Abhiras, Shudras, and Raivatakas. The region where the river Saraswati disappeared, and the western country. **(31)** The people of Kurukshetra, Prabhasa, Vidisha, the Vedasmriti river, and those born on the banks of the Mahi. The wicked, the soiled, the lowly, those without oil, and those whose virility is impaired. **(32)** Prisoners, bird-catchers, the impure, fishermen, the deformed, the elderly, and vintners. Leaders of guilds, those who have fallen from their vows, and the impoverished Pulindas. **(33)** Pungent and bitter substances, alchemical elixirs, widows, serpents, thieves, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, chickpeas, and those afflicted by wind-disorders or pulses belong to the **Son of the Sun** <note>Saturn</note>. **(34)**

### The Domain of Rahu (The Enemy of the Sun and Moon)
Those settled on mountain peaks, in glens, and caves; the Mleccha <note>foreign/non-Vedic</note> tribes and Shudras. Jackal-eaters, the Shulikas, Bokkanas, horse-faced people, and the deformed. **(35)** Family-destroyers, the violent, the ungrateful, thieves, and those devoid of truth, purity, and charity. Donkey-riders, wrestlers, the intensely angry, and the lowly. **(36)** The afflicted, the hypocritical, demons, those who sleep excessively, and all creatures abandoned by virtue. Black gram and sesame belong to the **Enemy of the Sun and Moon** <note>Rahu</note>. **(37)**

### The Domain of Ketu (The Comet/Tail)
Mountain fortresses, the Pallavas, White Huns, Cholas, Afghans, Maru, and China. Those living on the frontiers, the wealthy, the noble, and those endowed with industry and valor. **(38)** Those fond of others' wives, the hot-tempered, those interested in others' affairs, the intoxicated, fools, and those ambitious for religious victory are declared to belong to **Ketu**. **(39)**

### Conclusion on Planetary Strength
If a planet is glossy-beamed, large, and in its natural state at the time of its rising—provided it is not struck by portents, meteors, dust, or planetary conflict—and if it is in its own house or exaltation and aspected by a benefic planet, it brings prosperity to those over whom it is said to rule. **(40)** If the characteristics are the opposite of those mentioned, the people and things under its domain suffer decline.

# Chapter 16: On the Jurisdictions of the Planets

> People and kings alike become distressed, afflicted by the fear of riots and disease. || 41 || If the fear for kings is not caused by enemies, then it arises by necessity from their own past deeds or from their ministers. For the common folk, distress arises from drought and the forced migration from ancient cities to mountains and river valleys. || 42 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Jurisdictions of the Planets," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the illustrious Varāhamihira. || 16 ||

The Sun is the lord of the eastern half of the Narmada river, the Shon, Odra, Vanga <note>modern Bengal</note>, Suhma, Bahlika, Shaka, Yavana <note>Greeks or foreigners from the West</note>, Magadha, Shabara, Pragjyotisha <note>Assam</note>, China, Kamboja, Mekala, Kirata, Vitaka, the Vichala mountains, the outer Pulindas, the eastern half of Dravida, the right bank of the Yamuna, Champa, Udumbara, Kaushambi, Chedi, the Vindhya forests, Kalinga, Pundra, Golangula, Shriparvata, Vardhamana, and the Ikshumati river. He also rules over thieves, the Parata people, wildernesses, cowherds, grains that ripen in the forest, bitter trees, gold, fire, poison, heroes of war, medicines, physicians, four-legged animals, farmers, kings, violent infantry, robbers, deadly serpents, and the sharp-toothed creatures of the forest. || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 || 5 ||

The Moon is the lord of mountains, water, fortresses, Kosala, Maruchha, the ocean, the Romakas <note>Romans or Westerners</note>, the Tushara forest-dwellers, Tangana, Hala, the Kingdom of Women, the islands of the Great Ocean, sweet juices, flowers, fruits, water, salt, conch shells, pearls, lotuses, Shali rice, barley, pulses, wheat, those who drink Soma at sacrifices, Brahmins born of royal lineages, beautiful white horses, clever young women, army commanders, food, clothing, horned animals, night-roaming creatures, farmers, and those knowledgeable in sacrifices. || 6 || 7 || 8 ||

Mars is the lord of the Shon and Narmada rivers, all kings of the western half of the Bhimaratha, the Nirvindhya, Vetravati, Godavari, Shipra, Vena, Mandakini, Payoshni, Mahanadi, Sindhu, Malati, and Paradi rivers, the northern forests, Mount Mahendra, the Vindhyas, the regions near Malaya, Chola, Dravida, Videha, Andhra, Ashmaka, Bhasapura, Konkan, Samantrishika, Kuntala, Kerala, Dandaka, Kantipur, the Mlechhas <note>foreigners/non-Aryans</note>, those of mixed caste, the people of Nasik, Bhogavardhana, and Virankarat. He rules those who live near the Vindhyas and drink the sweet waters of the Tapti and Gomti rivers, city-dwellers, farmers, those who earn a living through fire or weapons, forest-dwellers, fortresses, small towns, executioners, the proud, monarchs, princes, elephants, the deceitful, children, those who strike others, herders, jeweled fruits and flowers, coral, generals, virtues, intoxication, sharp treasuries, mansions, those who maintain sacred fires, mines of metals, monks, thieves, rogues, those who hold long grudges, and those who eat excessively. || 9 || 10 || 11 || 12 || 13 || 14 || 15 ||

Mercury is the lord of the Lauhitya and Indus rivers, the Sarayu, Gambhirika, Rathalha, Ganges, and Koshiki rivers, Kamboja, Vaideha, the eastern half of Mathura, the Himalayas, the kingdoms of Gomanta and Chitrakoot, bridges, waterways, commodities found in holes and mountains, wells, scholars, painting, those who know grammar and mathematics, spies, sorcerers, children, poets, rogues, heralds, those engaged in black magic, messengers, eunuchs, jesters, those knowledgeable in demonology and illusionism, guards, actors and dancers, ghee, oil, fats, seeds, bitter things, those observing vows, alchemy, skilled men, and mixed-grain dishes. || 16 || 17 || 18 || 19 || 20 ||

Jupiter is the lord of the eastern part of the Indus river, the western half of Mathura, Bharata, Sauvira, the northern direction of Sudhna, the Vipasha and Shatadru rivers, Ramatha, Shalva, Traigarta, Paukha, Ambashtha, Parata, Vatadhana, Yaudheya, Saraswata, Arjunayana, and the villages and kingdoms of the middle region. He also rules over elephants, horses, priests, kings, ministers, those engaged in auspicious and nourishing rites, and great wealth...

Those who know the meaning of words <note>philologists or grammarians</note>, those who know the Vedas, students of magic <term>Abhichara: incantations or rituals for malevolent purposes</term> and politics, flags, fly-whisks and other honors of kings, bitumen <note>original: "shailaj"</note>, spikenard, tagara, koot, mercury, rock salt, substances produced from creepers, sweet juices, wax, and the plant *choraka*—all these are ruled by Jupiter. ||21||22||23||24||25||

The people of Taxila, Martikavat, Bahugiri, Gandhara, Pushkalavat, Prasthala, Malwa, Kaikala, Dasharna, Ushinara, and the Shibi country; those who drink the waters of the Vitasta <note>Jhelum</note>, Iravati <note>Ravi</note>, and Chandrabhaga <note>Chenab</note> rivers; chariots, silver, mines, elephants, horses, mahouts, wealthy people, fragrant flowers, ointments, gems and diamonds, ornaments, lotus beds, excellent young women, those resembling the god of love, purified grains, men who eat sweet substances, gardens, water, passionate people, fame, happiness, generosity, and handsome scholars, ministers, merchants, potters, variegated birds, the three fruits <term>Triphala: Haritaki, Bibhitaki, and Amalaki</term>, silk clothes, blankets, hemp, leaves, wool, Lodhra leaves, cinnamon, nutmeg, agarwood, calamus, and sandalwood—all these are under the influence of Venus. ||26||27||28||29||30||

Anarta, Arbuda, Pushkara, Saurashtra, the Abhira and Shudra tribes, Raivataka, the region where the Saraswati river disappears, the western lands, Kurukshetra, Prabhasa, Vidisha, the Vedasmriti river, those living on the banks of the Mahi; all crude substances, the wicked, the filthy, the lowly, oil-pressers, those lacking vitality, eunuchs, prisoners, hunters, the impure, fishermen, the ugly, the elderly, pig-breeders, leaders of guilds, those who have abandoned their vows, the Shavara and Pulinda tribes, the poor, bitter and pungent things, alchemy, widows, snakes, thieves, buffaloes, donkeys, young camels, chickpeas, peas, and chaff—all these things are under the control of Saturn. ||31||32||33||34||

Mountain peaks, Mlechha <note>foreign or non-Vedic</note> tribes living in caves and valleys, Shudras, jackal-eaters, those who execute by impalement, the Vokkana, the horse-faced <note>possibly a reference to a specific tribe or a physical deformity</note>, the disabled, those who disgrace their families, the violent, the ungrateful, thieves, those devoid of truth, purity, and charity, mules, wrestlers, those with severe faults, the lowly, the afflicted, hypocrites, demons, those who sleep excessively, the godless, creatures, black gram, and sesame—these are under the power of Rahu. ||35||36||37||

Mountain fortresses, the White Huns, Cholas, Afghans, the Maru desert, China, frontier lands, the wealthy, those who trade with great effort, the courageous, those devoted to others' wives, the quarrelsome, the Parandakas, the curious, the arrogant, the foolish, and the religious who desire victory—these are under the influence of Ketu. ||38||39||

When planets are naturally great, bright-rayed, and not struck by portents, meteors, dust storms, or planetary conflict; when they are situated in their own houses, in their exaltation, and are seen by benefic planets as they rise—they bring prosperity to those things and people they rule. ||40|| If the opposite characteristics occur, all substances governed by those planets suffer destruction; at such times, kings and people who are cowardly or afflicted by disease suffer greatly. ||41|| If kings do not have security from their enemies, sons, or ministers, or if there is a drought in the land, it is proper to move to new cities, mountains, or rivers according to the prescribed rules. ||42||

->Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western Province, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the venerable Acharya Varahamihira. ||16||<-

## Chapter Seventeen

### Planetary War

The time and manner in which a "war" between planets is predicted by those who know the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note> was established by me in my astronomical treatise based on the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Canon," a foundational Sanskrit text on astronomy</note>. || 1 ||

To the eye, the planets moving in the sky appear to meet as equals, though they actually stay in their own distinct paths, one above the other, at vast distances. || 2 ||

The sages, such as Parashara and others, have stated that there are four types of planetary war caused by their close approach: *Bheda* (occultation), *Ullekha* (grazing), *Anshumardana* (clashing of rays), and *Apasavya* (passing from the south). || 3 ||

In a *Bheda* <note>literally "piercing" or occultation</note> encounter, there is a failure of rain and the breaking of friendships between great families. In an *Ullekha* <note>grazing</note> encounter, there is fear of weapons, conflict among ministers, and a scarcity of favorite foods. || 4 ||

In an *Anshumardana* <note>clashing of rays</note> encounter, there are wars between kings, injuries from weapons, and suffering from hunger. In an *Apasavya* <note>passing to the south</note> encounter, wars likewise break out among rulers. || 5 ||

The Sun is the "Crier" (*Akranda*). A planet in the middle is "Urban" (*Paura*); one in the east is "Urban," and one in the west is "Marching" (*Yayi*). Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are always "Urban" planets; the Moon is always a "Crier." || 6 ||

Ketu <note>the descending lunar node</note>, Mars, Rahu <note>the ascending lunar node</note>, and Venus are "Marching" planets. If these are defeated, they destroy the Criers, Marchers, and Urban classes respectively; if victorious, they grant victory to their own class. || 7 ||

When an Urban planet is defeated by another Urban planet, the city-dwelling kings are destroyed. The same logic applies to the Marching and Crying planets. || 8 ||

A planet is considered "defeated" if it is situated to the south, looks harsh, is trembling, retreats without reaching its goal, is small, is mounted upon, looks unnatural, is lusterless, or is discolored. || 9 ||

A planet possessing the opposite characteristics is declared "victorious": if it is large, glossy, bright, and even if situated to the south, it is considered a winner if it is exceptionally brilliant. || 10 ||

If both planets are large, glossy, and full of rays during their meeting, there is mutual affection between them <note>a peaceful conjunction</note>. If they are the opposite, they destroy their own parties. || 11 ||

Whatever effects are indicated by the characteristics of the planets in war or conjunction, the same results should be predicted without hesitation for the kings on Earth. || 12 ||

When Mars is defeated by Jupiter, the people of Bahlika <note>Bactria</note>, the Marching types, and those who maintain the sacred fires suffer. When Mercury is defeated, the Shurasenas, Kalingas, and Salwas are oppressed. || 13 ||

When Mars is defeated by Saturn, the Urban citizens are victorious but the common subjects suffer. When Venus is defeated, there is distress for granaries, foreigners, and the warrior class. || 14 ||

When Mercury is defeated by Mars, trees, rivers, ascetics, the Ashmaka people, and kings suffer. Those in the north and those initiated for sacrifices also face distress. || 15 ||

When Mercury is defeated by Jupiter, foreigners, the lower classes, thieves, wealthy citizens, and the people of Trigarta and the mountains suffer; the Earth also trembles. || 16 ||

When Mercury is destroyed by Saturn, sailors, warriors, aquatic products, the wealthy, and pregnant women suffer. When Venus is defeated by Saturn, there is anger from fire and destruction of crops and clouds. || 17 ||

When Venus is struck by Jupiter, the people of Kuluta, Gandhara, Kaikaya, Madra, Salwa, Vatsa, and Vanga suffer; cattle and crops are destroyed. || 18 ||

When Jupiter is defeated by Mars, the Middle Country and its rulers suffer. When defeated by Saturn, the Arjunayanas, Vasatis, Yaudheyas, Shibis, and Brahmins suffer. || 19 ||

When Jupiter is defeated by Mercury, foreigners, the truthful, and those bearing arms perish; the Middle Country and the fruits of devotion are also destroyed. || 20 ||

When Jupiter is defeated by Venus, the "Marching" leaders meet their end. There is conflict between priests and warriors, and Indra <note>the rain god</note> does not release water. || 21 ||

The people of Koshala, Kalinga, Vanga, Vatsa, Matsya, and the Middle Country suffer greatly, as do eunuchs and the Shurasenas. || 22 ||

When Venus is defeated by Mars, there is the death of army chiefs and battles between kings. When defeated by Mercury, the mountain dwellers... || 23 ||

# Varahi Samhita (Brihat Samhita)

The destruction of milk and meager rainfall. || 23 || When Venus is defeated by Saturn, the leaders of guilds, those who live by weapons <note>soldiers or mercenaries</note>, and the warrior class suffer. Aquatic creatures are also afflicted; other effects follow the general planetary assignments. || 24 || When Saturn is defeated by Venus, there is a half-increase in prosperity, but pain for those who deal with snakes, birds, and those who are prideful. When defeated by Mars, the regions of Tankan, Andhra, Kashi, and Bahlika suffer. || 25 || When Saturn is defeated by Mercury, the people of Anga, merchants, birds, cattle, and elephants are distressed. When defeated by Jupiter, women, buffaloes, and the Khasas suffer. || 26 || These specific results are declared for the defeat of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. One should state the results based on the planetary assignments; otherwise, the defeated planets destroy their own assigned subjects. || 27 ||

->Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Planetary Conflict," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 17 ||<-

Regarding the time of upcoming planetary conflicts as decreed by the pundits who know the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note>: I have already spoken of this in the *Karana* text <note>original: "Panchasiddhantika"</note> according to the views of the *Surya Siddhanta*. || 1 || That which appears to be an encounter of planets—situated far apart in their own distinct paths—due to their alignment in the line of sight from a great distance, is called "Planetary Conflict" <term>Graha Yuddha: an astronomical conjunction where planets appear to clash</term> by the learned. || 2 || Sages such as Parashara have described four types of planetary conflict based on their proximity: *Bheda* (Cleaving), *Ullekha* (Grazing), *Anshumardana* (Clashing of rays), and *Apasavya* (Passing to the south). || 3 || In a *Bheda* conflict, there is a failure of rains and discord between friends and noble families. In an *Ullekha* conflict, there is fear of weapons, opposition among ministers, and famine. || 4 || In an *Anshumardana* conflict, there is war among kings, distress from weapons, disease, and hunger. In an *Apasavya* conflict, the kings engage in battle. || 5 || The Sun is designated as the "Crier" <note>Akrand</note> at noon; in the forenoon, the "City" planets <note>Paur</note> are active, and in the afternoon, the "Malefic" planets are designated as Criers. Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are always "City" planets. The Moon is eternally a "Crier." || 6 || Ketu, Mars, Rahu, and Venus are "Marchers" <note>Yaayi: planets representing mobile forces or invaders</note>. When these planets are defeated, the Criers, Marchers, and City-dwellers are destroyed accordingly; when victorious, they grant victory to their own classes. || 7 || When a City planet clashes with another City planet, the citizens and the city kings are destroyed. Similarly, when Marcher and Crier planets, or City and Marcher planets, defeat one another, they destroy their respective subjects. || 8 || A planet should be known as defeated if it appears in the southern direction, looks rough, trembling, fails to reach its position, is retreating (retrograde), small, obscured by another planet, fierce, lusterless, or discolored. The planet with the opposite characteristics is called the victor. However, even if in the south, if a planet has a large orb, is glossy, and radiant, it is declared the winner. || 9 || 10 || During a planetary conflict, if two planets both possess rays, large orbs, and are glossy, this is called "Mutual Affection." In such a case, there will be equality between kings on Earth even during wartime. If the opposite occurs, one's own side will be destroyed. || 11 || Whatever results are observed through the signs of conflict or conjunction, the same results will be experienced by the kings on Earth. || 12 || If Jupiter defeats Mars, then the people of Bahlika, the Marchers, and those who live by fire <note>blacksmiths, cooks, etc.</note> suffer. If Mercury defeats Mars, the regions of Shurasena, Kalinga, and Shalva suffer. || 13 || If Mars is defeated by Saturn, the city-dwellers are victorious, but the subjects become agitated and are destroyed...

If Venus defeats Mars, then storehouses <note>original: *kostha gara*</note>, barbarians <note>original: *mleccha* - often referring to non-Vedic or foreign tribes</note>, and the warrior class <note>Kshatriyas</note> suffer distress. ||14|| If Mercury is struck by Mars, then trees, rivers, ascetics, the Ashmaka people, kings, and those initiated into sacrifices in the northern direction suffer. ||15|| If Mercury is conquered by Jupiter, then barbarians, the laboring class <note>Shudras</note>, thieves, wealthy citizens, the Trigarta people, and mountain dwellers suffer pain, and the earth trembles. ||16|| If Mercury is destroyed by Saturn, then boatmen, warriors, aquatic products, the wealthy, and pregnant women suffer; and if Mercury is defeated by Venus, there is an outbreak of fire, and grain, clouds, and travelers are destroyed. ||17|| If Jupiter is struck by Venus, then the people of Kuluta, Gandhara, Kaikaya, Madra, Shalva, Vatsa, Vanga, as well as cattle herds and grain, face destruction. ||18|| If Jupiter is struck by Mars, then the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha</note>, kings, and cows suffer; if struck by Saturn, the Arjunayana, Vasati, Yaudheya, and Shibi tribes, along with the priestly class <note>Brahmins</note>, suffer; and if Jupiter is conquered by Mercury, then barbarians, truth-tellers, those who live by the sword, and the Middle Country all face depletion. However, the results should be determined according to the principles of planetary associations <note>original: *grahabhakta*</note>. ||19||20|| If Venus is struck by Jupiter, then great travelers are destroyed, there is conflict between priests and ministers, and Indra <note>the god of rain</note> does not send rain. ||21|| The inhabitants of Kosala, Kalinga, Vanga, Vatsa, Matsya, and the Middle Country, along with the Shurasena people and eunuchs, suffer great pain. ||22|| If Venus is conquered by Mars, there is the killing of army commanders and war between kings. If Venus is conquered by Mercury, there is distress in all mountainous regions, loss of milk, and meager rainfall. ||23|| If Venus is defeated by Saturn, then leaders of guilds, those living by the sword, the warrior class, and aquatic creatures are afflicted, and grain becomes ordinary; this is the result of planetary association. ||24|| If Saturn is struck by Venus, then high prices, snakes, birds, and proud people suffer. If Saturn is struck by Mars, then the people of Tangana, Andhra, Odra, Kashi, and Bahlika suffer. ||25|| If Saturn is defeated by Mercury, then the Anga region, merchants, birds, animals, and snakes are distressed; and if struck by Jupiter, then women, buffaloes, and men of the Shaka <note>Scythian</note> race are distressed. ||26|| This specific result of the mutual striking of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn has been stated. In other instances—namely, the "war" of planets with ordinary stars—the results should be stated according to what was described in the previous chapter titled "Associations" <note>Bhakti</note>. However, when planets are struck in various positions, they destroy the specific objects assigned to them. ||27||

<margin>1. This characteristic applies only to Venus, because it is written in the section on warfare that no planet except Venus, upon being victorious, moves to the southern direction. It should be known that whether Venus is in the north or the south, it is usually the victor in war: **"Whether situated in the north or the south, the son of Bhrigu <note>Venus</note> is generally the victor."** ||2|| The meeting of planets is called "War" <note>Yuddha</note>, "Association" <note>Samagama</note>, and "Setting" <note>Astamana</note>. According to the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>an ancient astronomical treatise</note>, the meeting of the five planets (Mars, etc.) with one another is called "War"; their meeting with the Moon is called "Association"; and their meeting with the Sun is called "Setting" <note>Combustion</note>.</margin>

## Chapter Eighteen

### The Conjunction of the Moon with Planets and Stars

If the Moon passes to the north of the asterisms <note>original: "bhānāṃ" - the 27 lunar mansions or Nakshatras</note> or the planets, it is called "Pradakshina" <note>meaning "clockwise" or "circumambulatory," a sign of respect and auspiciousness</note>. This brings prosperity to mankind. However, if the Moon passes to the south, it is not auspicious for people. || 1 ||

When the Moon passes to the north of Mars <note>original: "maṇḍala" / "vakra" implied; the Hindi commentary clarifies this refers to the red planet</note>, there is victory for the powerful mountain-dwelling tribes; the warrior class <note>Kshatriyas</note> rejoices along with the travelers, and the Earth becomes delighted, being filled with abundant grain. || 2 ||

If the Moon passes to the north of Mercury <note>original: "svasutasya" - literally "his own son," as Mercury is mythologically the son of the Moon</note>, it brings victory to city-dwellers, creates abundance, increases the harvest, brings joy to the people, and fills the treasuries of kings. || 3 ||

When the Moon passes to the north of Jupiter, there is an increase in the righteousness <note>Dharma</note> of city-dwellers, warriors, Brahmins, scholars, and the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha, the central heartland of ancient India</note>; there is plenty of food, and the subjects are satisfied. || 4 ||

If the Moon passes to the north of Venus, there is an increase in wealth, elephants, and horses; victory comes to travelers and archers, and the grain harvest is of the highest quality. || 5 ||

If the Moon should pass to the south <note>The Sanskrit text says "pradakshina" (right/north) while the Hindi commentary interprets the Saturn movement specifically</note> of Saturn, there is victory for the city kings, and the Shakas, Bahlikas, Sindhus, Pahlavas, and Yavanas <note>These refer to various Indo-Scythian, Bactrian, and Greek-descended groups in the northwest of ancient India</note> live in prosperity. || 6 ||

When the cool-rayed Moon passes to the north of the asterisms without any affliction, it nourishes the resources, the citizens, and the devoted regions; but by passing to the south, it destroys them. The fruits of the Moon being situated to the north of a planet have been described; if it is to the south, the results are entirely opposite. Thus the conjunctions of the Moon with the stars and planets are declared; however, a "planetary war" <note>term: Graha-yuddha; a specific astronomical calculation where planets compete for brilliance</note> never actually occurs between the Moon and the stars. || 7–8 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Conjunction of the Moon with Planets," in the *Bṛhat Saṃhitā* composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 18 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Hindi commentary on the *Bṛhat Saṃhitā* of Sri Varahamihira, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western provinces. || 18 ||

It concludes by clarifying that the Moon does not engage in "planetary combat" like other planets do.</summary>

# Chapter Nineteen
## The Results of the Planetary Years

The earth everywhere is covered with sparse crops; the forests are consumed by the fires of the gods <note>original: "devāgni," likely referring to forest fires caused by lightning</note> and filled with poisonous rains. The rivers do not flow with much water, and medicinal herbs are not possessed of great strength or potency. ॥ 1 ॥

The son of Aditi <note>The Sun</note> burns fiercely even during the winter season; the clouds, though appearing heavy, do not release much water. The moon loses its brilliance, the sky is distressed, and the communities of ascetics suffer along with the herds of cows. ॥ 2 ॥

Kings, accompanied by elephants, horses, and infantry endowed with unbearable strength and intoxication, roam about with bows, swords, and clubs in excess. They destroy countries in battle along with their followers during the year, month, or day of the Sun. ॥ 3 ॥

The sky is pervaded by clouds resembling moving mountains, possessing the luster of snakes, collyrium, bees, or buffalo horns. They fill the entire earth with pure waters and the quarters of the sky with deep, thrilling thunder. ॥ 4 ॥

The waters are filled with lotuses, lilies, and blue water-lilies; the orchards have trees in full bloom echoed by the humming of bees. The cows yield abundant milk and are pleasing to the eye; women, through their charms, constantly delight their lovers. ॥ 5 ॥

The earth is rich in fields of wheat, rice, barley, and excellent sugarcane; it is protected by kings and abounds in cities and mines. Marked by various wonders and echoing with the sounds of seasonal sacrifices, the earth shines when the year of the Cold-Rayed One <note>The Moon</note> has commenced. ॥ 6 ॥

The fire, driven by the wind, wanders extremely fiercely, desiring to burn villages, forests, and cities. The multitudes of men on earth cry out "Alas! Alas!", struck down by bands of robbers, deprived of their wealth and cattle. ॥ 7 ॥

Even when clouds rise high in the sky with gathered forms, they do not release much water anywhere. The crops on the borders of the land wither away, and even those that reach maturity are carried off by others due to lawlessness. ॥ 8 ॥

Kings do not have their minds capable of proper protection; there is an abundance of diseases arising from bile <note>term: Pitta - one of the three humors in Ayurvedic medicine</note> and provocation of serpents. This progeny is thus afflicted and the crops fail in the year of the Son of the Earth <note>Mars</note>. ॥ 9 ॥

There is an increase in magicians, illusionists, deceivers, and city-dwellers; also of those skilled in music, painting, mathematics, and weapons. Kings, desiring victory, wish to give gifts to one another that produce satisfaction upon seeing them. ॥ 10 ॥

The news in the world is true; the Three Vedas <note>term: Trayi - the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas</note> are practiced without deficiency, and the science of government <note>term: Dandaniti</note> functions properly as in the time of Manu. Some have their minds deeply intent on the Supreme Syllable <note>The sacred syllable Om</note> and seek the highest state through the science of logic <note>term: Anvikshiki</note>. ॥ 11 ॥

The Son of the Moon <note>Mercury</note> creates affection for jesters, envoys, poets, children, and eunuchs; for those skilled in logic, and those living near bridges, water, or mountains, in his own year or month; he also brings an abundance of medicinal herbs to the earth. ॥ 12 ॥

The sound of chanting uttered at sacrifices goes to the heavens, breaking the hearts of those who would steal the sacrifice. It wanders constantly, bringing joy to the hearts of the best of the twice-born <note>term: Dvija - the upper castes, specifically Brahmins here</note> and the gods who partake in the sacrificial offerings. ॥ 13 ॥

The earth possesses excellent crops and is rich in many elephants, horses, wealth, and great herds of cows. Prospering under the protection of kings, the people then appear as if they are rivals to the inhabitants of heaven. ॥ 14 ॥

The earth is covered by various clouds, towering with lightning, satisfying the ground with water. In this auspicious year of the Teacher of the King of Gods <note>Jupiter</note>, the earth has many crops and is endowed with the best prosperity. ॥ 15 ॥

The earth, possessing rice and sugarcane, has its embankments filled with water released by the clouds that rest on the mountain peaks. Scattered with beautiful lotuses and filled with water-tanks, she shines like a young woman with her body radiant with new ornaments. ॥ 16 ॥ The warrior class on earth...

<summary>This page describes the astrological effects of the years ruled by the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, and Jupiter. It details the environmental, social, and political consequences, ranging from famine and war under Mars to prosperity and religious devotion under Jupiter.</summary>

->**The Varahi Samhita**<-

...[The king] protects the earth, which is rich in cities and mines, having destroyed the forces of his many powerful enemies, and having filled the quarters of the world with the repeated sounds of various shouts of victory. The groups of the wicked are destroyed, while the righteous are filled with joy. **(17)** In the year of Venus <note>Sanskrit: *Sita*, referring to the planet Venus</note>, wine is drunk constantly in the spring with beloved women; songs that captivate the ear are sung to the accompaniment of flutes and lutes. Guests, friends, and kinsmen feast together, and there is a loud proclamation of the victory of Love <note>Sanskrit: *Madana*, the god of desire</note>. **(18)**

In the year of Saturn <note>Sanskrit: *Sani* or *Divakarasuta*, the son of the Sun</note>, nations are troubled by many battles with bands of bold bandits, and are deprived of many cattle and much wealth. People wail for their slain kinsmen, and families are afflicted by the best of diseases <note>ironic usage for severe plagues</note> and by hunger. **(19)** The atmosphere is devoid of clouds, which are driven away by the wind; the surface of the earth has its trees scorched; the sky is covered with dust, its sun and moonbeams lost; and even the rivers, in their hope for water, are waterless and thin. **(20)** In some places, the crops perish due to lack of water; in others, they thrive when sprinkled with water. When the enemy of Vritra <note>Indra, the god of rain</note> rains but slowly, such is the constant trend in the year of the Son of the Sun. **(21)**

A planet that is small, with dull rays, or occupying a low position <note>astrological debilitation</note>, or defeated by others, does not give its full fruit. The opposite is true for a planet that is otherwise. Whatever inauspiciousness occurs in an inauspicious year due to the month, that increases; and the same applies to auspicious results. In a mixture of conditions, the results are mediocre. **(22)**

### Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Results of the Planets as Lords of the Year," in the Brihat Samhita composed by the illustrious Varahamihira.

If the **Sun** is the Lord of the Year, the Lord of the Month, or the Lord of the Day, then everywhere on earth grain will be scarce. In the forests, trees will be infested with insects in various places. The rivers will not have much water. Due to suffering, medicinal herbs will lose their potency. Even in the winter season, the sun will cast fierce heat. Clouds as large as mountains will not rain much water. The luster of the moon and stars in the sky will vanish. The families of cows and ascetics will experience grief. Kings, possessed of endurable strength in the form of elephants, horses, and infantry, will wander about destroying all countries, carrying many arrows, bows, swords, and clubs, accompanied by their followers. **(1–3)**

If the **Moon** is the master of the year, then clouds—black like moving mountains, or like collyrium <note>eye-black</note>, bees, and buffaloes—pervade the sky. Filling all directions with deep, longing sounds, they saturate the earth with pure water. In the lakes, the white, red, and blue lotuses bloom. The gardens are filled with blossoming trees and the sound of bees. Cows give plenty of milk. Women, who bring joy to the eyes, cause men to sport without ceasing due to their attachment. Sugarcane, rice, barley, and excellent grains grow in abundance. The earth is protected by kings, marked by small temples <term>Chaitya: small shrines or sacred monuments</term>, and echoing with the holy sounds of sacrifices and fire-offerings. **(4–6)**

If **Mars** is the master of the year, then a very fierce fire, raised by the wind, seeks to burn villages, forests, and cities. The people of the earth, struck down by thieves, wander about crying out in distress, helpless and deprived of cattle. The clouds in the void are low and compact in form, yet they do not rain much water anywhere. The ripened grain almost withers away, and even if it survives somehow, other men seize it due to lawlessness. In the year of Mars, kings do not protect their subjects well. There is an excess of diseases arising from bile <note>Pitta</note>. There is the wrath of serpents. In this way, the people of the subjects become poor, wretched, and like the dead, without grain. **(7–9)**

If **Mercury** is the master of the year, then men who practice illusion, sorcery, and magic, as well as celestial musicians...

### Chapter 19 with Hindi Commentary

Those who possess knowledge of writing, mathematics, and weaponry increase in number. Kings, desiring mutual affection, wish to gift one another wonderful sights and pleasing objects. In the world, commerce and the <term>Triple Veda</term><note>original: "Trayi Shastra"; refers to the three foundational Vedas: Rig, Yajur, and Sama</note> remain intact and truthful. <term>Dandniti</term><note>The science of government and the administration of justice/punishment</note> flourishes as it did in the time of Manu. Some apply their intellect to the knowledge of the scriptures, while others strive to attain the supreme state through <term>Anvikshiki</term><note>The science of logic and metaphysics</note>. In his year or month, the planet Mercury thus satisfies messengers skilled in humor, poets, children, eunuchs, those knowledgeable in strategy, and those living near bridges, water, and mountains; and medicinal herbs grow in abundance on the earth. ||10||11||12||

If Jupiter is the lord of the year, the vast sound of the Vedas uttered in sacrifices travels through the sky, piercing the hearts of those who would destroy the sacrifice, while bringing joy to the hearts of the noble Brahmins and the deities who receive their sacrificial portions. The earth—truthful, excellent, and filled with many elephants, horses, <term>four-fold armies</term><note>chaturanga: infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants</note>, great wealth, herds of cows, and riches—is protected and nourished by kings, appearing as if competing in splendor with the inhabitants of heaven. Clouds of various colors cover the earth with satisfying rain. In the auspicious year of Jupiter, the preceptor of the gods, the earth becomes rich and filled with much grain. ||13||14||15||

If Venus is the lord of the year, the earth—filled with water released by mountain-like clouds and crowded with ponds whose waters are hidden by beautiful lotuses—shines like a woman with bright limbs adorned with new jewelry. It produces <term>shasthi</term><note>a variety of rice that ripens in sixty days</note> and sugarcane. Kings, destroying their enemies and nourishing their subjects, make the directions resound with cries of victory; they protect the prosperous earth, including its cities and mines, by satisfying the disciplined and destroying the wicked. In the spring season, men repeatedly drink wine with their beloveds, singing songs that please the ear accompanied by the flute and lute, and eating food with guests, friends, and kinsmen. In the year of Venus, the god of love <insert>Kamadeva</insert> is thus victorious. ||16||17||18||

When Saturn is the lord of the year, all kingdoms become distressed due to thieves with evil vows and the occurrence of many battles. Many lose their livestock and wealth. Men weep greatly due to separation from their kinsmen; they are highly agitated by hunger and disease. As soon as clouds appear in the sky, the wind blows them away. Not a single leaf on earth remains healthy. In the sky, the rays of the sun and moon are obscured by dust. Reservoirs become waterless and rivers become thin. In some places, crops are destroyed for lack of water; in others, they flourish in water-logged land. In this way, in the year when Saturn is the lord, Indra <note>the god of rain</note> grants rain that yields grain only very slowly. ||19||20||21||

A planet that is small, has weak rays, is moving toward its sign of debilitation, or is defeated by another planet cannot grant full or nourishing results. If an inauspicious planet is the lord of the year or the lord of the month, the results produced by its influence are obtained; otherwise, auspicious results are also attained. ||22||

### Chapter Twenty

### The Conjunction of Planets in Geometric Figures
<note>Sanskrit: Grahashringataka. This refers to specific triangular or "singhara-nut" shaped alignments of planets.</note>

In whichever direction the star-planets <note>The five visible planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are seen entering the Sun, the inhabitants of that direction will suffer fear from weapons, hunger, and intense anxiety. || 1 ||

When the planetary configurations appear in the shapes of a **discus**, a **bow**, a **shringataka** <note>a triangle or crossroad shape</note>, a **staff**, a **city**, a **morsel**, or a **thunderbolt**, there will be hunger and drought in the world, and kings will engage in war. || 2 ||

At the end of the day, when the Sun has set, if a "garland of planets" <note>a line of multiple planets</note> is visible in a particular portion of the sky, that region will fall under the rule of a foreign king and suffer great distress from enemy invasions. || 3 ||

The planets destroy the people associated with the specific lunar mansion <note>Nakshatra</note> in which they meet. However, if they do not clash with one another and their rays remain bright and clear, it brings auspiciousness to those people. || 4 ||

The planetary conditions are named **Samvarta** (The Whirl), **Samagama** (Meeting), **Sammoha** (Delusion), **Samaja** (Assembly), **Sannipata** (Collision), and **Kosha** (Treasury). I shall now describe their specific characteristics and effects. || 5 ||

When four or five "traveling" planets <note>Yayins</note> meet with "city" planets <note>Pauras - planets stationary in specific signs</note> in a single lunar mansion, it is called **Samvarta**. If Rahu or Ketu <note>The lunar nodes/eclipsing shadows</note> join them, it is called **Sammoha**. || 6 ||

A meeting of "city" planets with other "city" planets, or "travelers" with "travelers," is called **Samaja**. If another planet enters the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, it is known as **Kosha**. || 7 ||

If one planet rises in the West and another in the East simultaneously, it is called **Sannipata**. In a **Samagama** (specifically a meeting with the Moon), if the planets are undistorted, glossy, and large, they are considered blessed and bring prosperity. || 8 ||

The results of **Samvarta** and **Samagama** are neutral; **Sammoha** and **Kosha** bring fear to the subjects; **Samaja** is declared to bring excellent balance; and **Sannipata** surely brings enmity and anger. || 9 ||

->Thus ends the twentieth chapter, named "The Conjunction of Planets in Geometric Figures," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira.<-

# Chapter 21
## **Signs of the Rain-Embryo**

Food is the life-breath of the world, and food is dependent on the rainy season. Therefore, the rainy season must be examined with great effort. <note>The text emphasizes that predicting rain is essential for survival in an agrarian society.</note> || 1 ||

Having seen the signs recorded by the ancient sages, I now compose this work based on the teachings of Garga, Parashara, Kashyapa, Vatsya, and others. || 2 ||

Indeed, the astrologer who remains focused day and night on the signs of the rain-embryo will find that his words, like those of a sage, never prove false regarding the prediction of water. || 3 ||

What science is greater than this? By knowing it, one becomes a seer of the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note> even in this destructive age of Kali. || 4 ||

Some say the days of embryo formation begin after the end of the bright half of the month of Karttika <note>October-November</note>. However, that is not the opinion of the majority; I shall state the view of Garga and others. || 5 ||

The signs of the embryos should be known starting from the first day of the bright half of the month of Margashirsha <note>November-December</note>, when the Moon reaches the lunar mansion of Purvashadha. || 6 ||

An embryo formed when the Moon is in a particular lunar mansion will come to birth <note>fall as rain</note> 195 days later, according to the Moon's transit through that same mansion. || 7 ||

Embryos formed in the bright fortnight are born in the dark fortnight; those formed in the dark are born in the bright. Those formed at night are born by day; those formed by day are born at night. Those formed at dawn are born at dusk, and vice versa. || 8 ||

Embryos formed from the mansion of Mrigashirsha onwards yield little fruit in the bright half of Pausha. The dark half of Pausha indicates the rainfall for the bright half of Shravana <note>July-August</note>. || 9 ||

Embryos arising in the bright half of Magha come to birth in the dark half of Shravana. Those from the dark half of Magha indicate the rainfall for the bright half of Bhadrapada <note>August-September</note>. || 10 ||

Those arising in the bright half of Phalguna are to be assigned to the dark half of Bhadrapada. Those born in the dark half of Phalguna result in rain during the bright half of Ashwayuja <note>September-October</note>. || 11 ||

Rain-clouds formed in the bright half of Chaitra give water in the dark half of Ashwayuja. Those formed in the dark half of Chaitra rain in the bright half of Karttika. || 12 ||

Clouds formed in the east later rain in the west; those formed in the west rain in the east. The same reversal applies to the other directions and the wind. || 13 ||

A pleasant, soft, northerly wind; a clear sky; the Sun and Moon surrounded by glossy, thick, white halos—these are good signs. || 14 ||

A sky filled with large, thick, glossy clouds shaped like needles, or razors, or colored red; or clouds dark like a crow's egg, while the Moon and stars remain clear. || 15 ||

A rainbow, deep rumbling thunder, lightning, and a "mock sun" <note>parhelion</note> at a pleasant twilight; birds and deer crying peacefully in the north, northeast, or east. || 16 ||

Planets that are large, moving clockwise, with glossy rays and free from afflictions; trees with healthy sprouts; and humans and four-legged animals being joyful. || 17 ||

All these are nourishers of the embryos. I shall now describe the specific characteristics of the growth of the embryos according to the nature of each season. || 18 ||

In the month of Margashirsha and Pausha: twilight colors, clouds with halos, and not too much cold in Mrigashirsha, but heavy frost in Pausha. || 19 ||

In Magha: strong winds, the Sun and Moon dimmed by frost, extreme cold, and the Sun rising or setting behind clouds are auspicious. || 20 ||

In the month of Phalguna: rough, violent winds; glossy drifting clouds; incomplete halos; and a Sun that is tawny or copper-colored is beneficial. || 21 ||

In Chaitra: embryos accompanied by wind, clouds, rain, and halos are auspicious; clouds, wind, water, lightning, and thunder are for the good of the people. <note>The text breaks here mid-verse.</note>
