# Page 92
## Varahi Samhita

In the month of Vaishakha <note>April-May</note> || 22 || Clouds that shine like pearls or silver, or possess the dark hue of the Tamala tree, blue lotus, or collyrium <note>eye-salve</note>, and are shaped like aquatic animals, are pregnant with abundant water. || 23 || Clouds that have been heated by the intense rays of the sun and are accompanied by a gentle breeze will release water in torrents like an angry outburst at the time of delivery <note>the time of rainfall</note>. || 24 ||

The signs of a "miscarriage" <note>failure of rain</note> of the clouds include: meteors, thunderbolts, dust storms, and a "burning" of the horizon. Also, earthquakes, the appearance of "city-like" formations in the sky <note>Fata Morgana</note>, spikes in the sky, comets, and planetary wars. || 25 || The appearance of blood-like rain, unnatural phenomena, atmospheric halos, rainbows, and eclipses of the sun or moon—by these three types of portents and others, the "pregnancy" of the cloud is destroyed. || 26 ||

Growth of the pregnancy occurs through natural characteristics suited to the season; the opposite occurs if those characteristics are reversed. || 27 || If the pregnancy develops during the constellations of Bhadrapada, Ashvini, Rohini, or Itijya <note>Pushya</note>, it will result in a great deal of rain in all seasons. || 28 || A pregnancy associated with Shatabhishak, Ashlesha, Ardra, Swati, or Magha is auspicious; it nourishes the clouds for many days, unless destroyed by the three types of portents. || 29 ||

Starting from the month of Margashirsha, the delivery occurs after 195 days <note>calculated by the moon's transit through the asterisms</note>. || 30 || If the clouds are associated with cruel planets, they produce rain accompanied by hail, thunderbolts, and even "fish-rain" <note>unusual atmospheric deposits</note>. If the Moon or Sun is joined or aspected by benefic planets, they bring abundant rain. || 31 ||

Excessive rain during the time of "pregnancy" leads to the loss of that pregnancy. If the rainfall exceeds one-eighth of a *Drona* <note>a traditional unit of volume</note>, the pregnancy is considered "leaked" or aborted. || 32 || If a healthy pregnancy does not rain at the time of delivery due to planetary afflictions, it will later release that water mixed with hail. || 33 || Just as milk held too long in the udder of a cow becomes thick and hard, so does the water of a cloud turn into hail when its time has passed. || 34 ||

Through five specific causes, rain falls over an area of a hundred *Yojanas* <note>ancient measure of distance</note>, or half that, or half again. || 35 || In a pregnancy formed by five causes, a *Drona* of rain is produced: three *Adhakas* <note>sub-unit of Drona</note> due to wind, six due to lightning, nine due to clouds, and twelve due to thunder at the time of delivery. || 36 || A cloud accompanied by wind, water, lightning, thunder, and specific cloud-forms is full of water. If it releases too much water during the pregnancy period, it will only produce a fine mist at the time of delivery. || 37 ||

-> Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Signs of Cloud Pregnancy," in the Brhat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. <-

Food is the very life of the world, and food is dependent on the rainy season; for this reason, one should examine the rainy season with great effort. || 1 || I have composed these "Signs of Pregnancy" after observing all the signs of rain recorded by sages such as Garga, Parashara, Kashyapa, and Vatsya. || 2 || Those men who know the divine and keep their minds focused and alert on the signs of cloud pregnancy day and night—their words regarding the calculation of clouds, like those of the sages, never prove false. || 3 || What science is greater than this, knowing which people can become seers of the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note> even in this destructive Age of Kali? || 4 || Some say that the days of pregnancy begin after the bright fortnight of the month of Kartika; however, this is not universally accepted. Therefore, I am expressing the opinion of many sages like Garga. || 5 || From the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Agrahayana <note>Margashirsha</note>, when the Moon is in the constellation of Purvashadha, the signs of all pregnancies should be known. || 6 || From the moment the Moon reaches the constellation where the cloud becomes "pregnant," by the power of the Moon, 195...

# Chapter 21: With Hindi Commentary

During the day, that pregnancy will reach its time of delivery <note>original: "prasava," referring to the falling of rain</note>. ||7|| A pregnancy conceived during the bright fortnight <note>Shukla Paksha, the waxing moon</note> will be delivered in the dark fortnight <note>Krishna Paksha, the waning moon</note>, and a pregnancy of the dark fortnight will be delivered in the bright fortnight. A pregnancy of the day is delivered at night, a pregnancy of the night is delivered during some part of the day, and a pregnancy of the twilight is delivered in the opposite twilight. ||8||

Pregnancies conceived during the constellation of Mrigashira and those conceived in the bright fortnight of the month of Pausha <note>December-January</note> yield weak results. Through the dark fortnight of Pausha, the bright fortnight of Shravana <note>July-August</note> should be predicted. ||9|| A pregnancy from the bright fortnight of the month of Magha <note>January-February</note> reaches its delivery time in the dark fortnight of Shravana. Through the dark fortnight of Magha, the bright fortnight of the month of Bhadrapada <note>August-September</note> is determined. ||10||

Pregnancies born in the bright fortnight of Phalguna <note>February-March</note> should be delivered in the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada. Those pregnancies born in the dark fortnight of Phalguna are delivered in the bright fortnight of the month of Ashvina <note>September-October</note>. ||11|| Pregnancies born in the white <note>bright</note> fortnight of Chaitra <note>March-April</note> give water in the dark fortnight of Ashvina; and pregnancies produced in the bright fortnight of Chaitra shower water in the bright fortnight of Kartika <note>October-November</note>. ||12||

Clouds of the eastern direction fly to the west, and clouds of the west rise in the eastern direction; similarly, in the remaining directions, there is an exchange of clouds and wind. ||13|| In the North, North-East, and East, when the wind blows, the sky is clear, joyful, and soft. The Moon and Sun are oily <note>glossy/lustrous</note>, white, and mostly surrounded by halos. ||14|| When the sky is filled with thick, very glossy clouds, or clouds resembling a crow's egg or a peacock's feather, the stars and the moon possess a pure radiance. ||15||

When there are rainbows and deep thundering, clouds facing the sun and flashing lightning are situated in the North, North-East, and East, and when birds and deer make peaceful sounds, the evening time is truly delightful. ||16|| When many planets moving in a clockwise direction are free from disturbances and have glossy rays, when trees are free from the sprouts of disease, and humans and four-legged animals appear with joyful eyes, then there is nourishment of the pregnancies. However, this is said regarding their own season and natural pregnancy. ||17||18||

In the months of Agrahayana <note>November-December</note> and Pausha, if the clouds are colored with evening twilight and are circular, and if there is extreme cold in Agrahayana and heavy snowfall in Pausha, the pregnancy does not become nourished. ||19|| In Magha, if the wind is strong, and the rays of the Moon and Sun are as tattered and cold as frost, then the setting and rising of the sun behind clouds is desirable. ||20|| If in the month of Phalguna the wind blows dry and fierce, and glossy clouds gather—if they are complete and the sun is reddish-brown and copper-colored like fire—it is auspicious. ||21||

If in Chaitra all pregnancies are accompanied by wind, clouds, rain, and halos, it is auspicious. If in Vaishakha <note>April-May</note> there are clouds, wind, water, and thundering lightning, it serves the benefit of the pregnancy. ||22|| Clouds shaped like pearls or silver, or with the luster of Tamala <note>dark bark</note>, blue lotus, or collyrium, or shaped like aquatic creatures, will rain much water. When the pregnancy is heated by the rays of the sun and the wind blows gently, the clouds, as if enraged at the time of delivery, shower streams of water. ||23||24||

Meteors, thunderbolts, falling dust, fires in the directions, earthquakes, "cities of Gandharvas" <note>mirages</note>, spikes <note>atmospheric phenomena</note>, comets, planetary wars, thunderclaps, or the raining of blood and such—through all these portents or even three such portents, the destruction of the pregnancy occurs. ||25|| Pregnancies that grow by the ordinary characteristics of the season's nature are changed by contrary characteristics. ||26|| In all seasons, pregnancies grown in the constellations of Purva-Bhadrapada, Uttara-Bhadrapada, Purva-Ashadha, Uttara-Ashadha, and Rohini give much water. ||27|| Pregnancies joined with Shatabhisha, Ashlesha, Ardra, Svati, and Magha are auspicious and provide nourishment for many days.

...they cause destruction; if struck by the three types of portents <note>terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial</note>, they cause ruin. ||28|| When the Moon resides in any one of these five constellations <note>Nakshatras</note>, then in the six months from Agrahayana to Vaishakha <note>roughly November to May</note>, rain occurs sequentially for 8, 6, 16, 20, 24, and 3 days respectively. ||29|| If joined by cruel planets <note>malefics like Mars or Saturn</note>, the "cloud-embryos" rain down hail, thunderbolts, and even fish; but if the Moon or Sun are joined by or aspected by auspicious planets <note>benefics like Jupiter or Venus</note>, they produce abundant rain. ||30|| If excessive rain occurs without cause during the gestation period, the embryo is lost; if it rains more than one-eighth of a *Drona* <term>Drona: a traditional unit of rainfall measurement</term>, the embryo is destroyed. ||31|| If a fully developed embryo does not rain due to planetary affliction, then at the time of delivery, it rains water mixed with hail during its own gestation period. ||32|| Just as milk kept for a long time in a cow becomes hard, so too the cloud-embryo becomes hardened after many days have passed. ||33|| An embryo nourished by five types of causes spreads and rains up to a hundred *Yojanas* <term>Yojana: a distance of about 8-9 miles</term>; in the absence of each single cause, the rainfall area is reduced by half. ||34|| That is, a four-cause embryo rains for 50 Yojanas (200 *Kosh*), a three-cause for 25 Yojanas (100 *Kosh*), a two-cause for 12.5 Yojanas (50 *Kosh*), and a single-cause embryo rains up to 5 Yojanas (20 *Kosh*). An embryo with five causes rains one *Drona* of water; one caused by wind rains three *Adhakas*, and one caused by lightning rains 6 *Adhakas*. ||35|| An embryo possessing the five causes—wind, water, lightning, thunder, and clouds—gives much water. If it rains heavily during the gestation period, then at the time of delivery, only droplets will fall. ||36||

### Now begins the Twenty-Second Chapter
#### On the Retention of Cloud-Embryos

The four days starting from the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeshtha <note>May-June</note> are the days for observing wind retention. Gentle and auspicious winds are praised, as is a sky covered with glossy, thick clouds. ||1|| If it rains in the four constellations starting with Swati in that same period, then the four months starting with Shravana <note>July-August</note> will have rainfall; these are known as the "retentions." ||2|| If these signs are uniform, they are auspicious; if interrupted, they do not bring well-being and are said to bring fear of thieves. Here are also the verses of Vasistha <note>referring to the ancient sage Vasistha</note>: ||3|| Retentions accompanied by lightning, droplets, dust-storms, and the Sun and Moon being covered are auspicious retentions. ||4|| When the lightning is excellent and appears in the North-East, the wise man should predict the growth of all crops. ||5|| Rain with dust, and even the auspicious play of children and the sweet sounds of birds, or their playing in dust and water, are good signs. ||6|| Halos around the Sun and Moon that are glossy and not excessively distorted indicate rain for the prosperity of all crops. ||7|| Clouds that are glossy, compact, and move in a clockwise direction <note>Pradakshina</note> will bring great rain that fulfills the purpose of all crops. ||8||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, named "The Retention of Cloud-Embryos," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. ||22||

# Chapter 23: On Rainfall
## With Hindi Commentary

The four days starting from the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeshtha <note>May–June</note> are the days for observing the <term>conception of clouds</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Garbhadharana*; the period when the atmosphere "conceives" the rain that will fall months later</note> via the wind. If there is a gentle, auspicious wind or if the sky is covered with smooth, glossy clouds, it is considered excellent. ||1|| If it rains during these four days under the four <term>lunar mansions</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Nakshatras*</note> starting with Swati, then the "conception" is considered dissolved in the months starting from Shravana <note>July–August</note>; that is, there will be no rain. ||2|| If the weather remains consistent across these four days, it is auspicious; if contrary, it is not beneficial and instead brings fear of thieves. The verses spoken by the sage Vashistha on this subject are as follows: ||3|| If there is lightning, water droplets, and wind mixed with dust, and if the Moon or Sun are veiled by clouds, such a "conception" is superior. ||4|| When excellent lightning flashes in auspicious directions, the wise man should declare that there will be an increase in grain. ||5|| If children at play scatter water or dust, or if birds make sweet sounds and frolic in the dust or water, it is auspicious. ||6|| If the circles <note>halos</note> around the Sun and Moon are glossy and not excessively distorted, the rain of this period will increase all types of grain. ||7|| If the clouds are smooth, dense, and move in a clockwise direction, there will be heavy rain that achieves the success of all crops and wealth. ||8||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the illustrious teacher Varahamihira. ||22||

---

->**Now begins the Twenty-Third Chapter:**<-
->**On Rainfall**<-

> After the full moon of Jyeshtha has passed, the wise, who understand these matters, should predict the good or bad results and the quantity of water based on the rainfall occurring under Purva-Ashadha and other lunar mansions. ||1||
> The measurement of water is determined using a bowl one cubit <note>approx. 18 inches</note> wide. An *Adhaka* <note>a unit of volume</note> is defined as fifty *Palas*; one should measure the fallen water by this standard. ||2||
> The first measurement of water is told by that rain which leaves a mark on the earth or creates droplets on the tips of grass. ||3||
> Some say the rainfall covers a radius of ten *Yojanas* <note>approx. 80-90 miles</note>; however, the opinion of Garga, Vashistha, and Parashara is that it extends no further than twelve *Yojanas*. ||4||
> It usually rains again under the same lunar mansions in which it rained previously. If it does not rain under any of the mansions starting with Purva-Ashadha, then a drought occurs. ||5||
> Under Hasta, Purva-Ashadha, Mrigashira, Chitra, Revati, and Dhanishtha, the measure is sixteen *Dronas*. Under Shatabhisha, Jyeshtha, and Swati, it is four. Under Krittika, it is ten. ||6||
> Under Shravana, Magha, Anuradha, Bharani, and Mula, it is fourteen. Under Phalguni, it is twenty-five. Under Punarvasu, it is twenty *Dronas*. ||7||
> Under Vishakha and Uttarashadha, it is twenty. Under Ashlesha, it is thirteen. Under Uttarabhadrapada, Uttaraphalguni, and Rohini, it is twenty-five. ||8||
> Under Purvabhadrapada and Pushya, it is fifteen. Under Ashwini, it is twelve. Under Ardra, it is eighteen *Dronas*—provided these mansions are not afflicted by portents. ||9||
> If a lunar mansion is afflicted by the Sun, Saturn, or comets, or hit by three types of portents from Mars, there is no welfare nor rain. If associated with auspicious planets and free of portents, there is welfare. ||10||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "On Rainfall," in the Brihat Samhita composed by the illustrious Varahamihira. ||23||

One should determine the measurement of water by using a vessel one cubit wide. If this fills up, one should weigh the fallen water to declare the year's rainfall results. The weight of said vessel is fifty <term>Palas</term><note>A traditional unit of weight, approximately 48 grams</note>. When this is filled with water, the result of the rainfall is one <term>Adhaka</term><note>A unit of volume used for measuring rainfall in ancient India</note>. ||2|| The first measurement of rainfall for the year should be calculated from that rain which leaves a mark upon the earth or stays as droplets on the tips of blades of grass. ||3|| Some say that rain occurs only as far as the eye can see; others say, based on the aforementioned signs, that rain occurs within a circle of ten <term>Yojanas</term><note>A Yojana is roughly 8 to 9 miles</note>. However, according to the opinions of the sages Garga, Vasistha, and Parashara, rain does not extend beyond twelve Yojanas (that is, 48 <term>Koshas</term>). ||4|| Rain usually occurs during the "delivery period" <note>original: "Prasava-kala," referring to the time when the clouds "give birth" to rain</note> under the same lunar mansions <note>original: "Nakshatras"</note> in which the initial rainfall was observed. However, if it does not rain in any mansion from Purvashadha to Mula, then there will be a drought <note>original: "Anavrishti"</note> across all mansions. ||5||

If the Moon is undisturbed and positioned in Hasta, Purvashadha, Mrigashira, Chitra, Revati, or Dhanishtha, it rains sixteen <term>Dronas</term><note>A Drona is a large unit of liquid measure, equal to 4 Adhakas</note>; in Shatabhisha, Jyeshtha, and Swati, 4 Dronas; in Krittika, 10 Dronas; in Shravana, Magha, Anuradha, Bharani, and Mula, fourteen; in Phalguni, twenty-five; in Punarvasu, 20; in Vishakha and Uttarashadha, twenty; in Ashlesha, thirteen; in Uttarabhadrapada, Uttaraphalguni, and Rohini, twenty-five; in Purvabhadrapada, Pushya, and Ashvini, twelve; and in Ardra, eighteen Dronas of water are rained. ||6||7||8||9|| If all the lunar mansions are afflicted by the Sun, Saturn, or Ketu, and are struck by the three types of portents caused by Mars, there will be no rain; however, if they are peaceful and undisturbed, it is auspicious. ||10||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the venerable teacher Varahamihira. ||23||

### Chapter Twenty-Four
### The Conjunction of Rohini

In the gardens filled with the humming of bees clinging to the flowers of trees born in the crevices of golden mountain peaks, echoing with the quarrels of many birds and the deep sounds of the songs of celestial maidens— ||1|| On the summit of the mountain that is the abode of the gods, Jupiter <note>Lord Brihaspati</note> spoke these truths to Narada; and Garga, Parashara, Kashyapa, and Maya spoke them to their circles of disciples. ||2|| Having observed those teachings regarding the conjunction of the Moon with the star Rohini <note>original: "Prajapatya," a name for Rohini</note>, I am now prepared to speak them myself in a concise volume. ||3|| An astrologer, having observed the Moon approaching the star Rohini in the dark fortnight of the month of Ashadha, should predict the good or evil fortune of the world according to the scriptural teachings. ||4|| The prediction of the conjunction should be made before it occurs; I have already described the conjunction of the lunar mansions in the section on "Karana." The results should be declared based on the size, brilliance, color, and path of the Moon, as well as any sudden portents. ||5|| A Brahmin, having fasted for three days, should stay at a spot north or east of the city and remain devoted to the sacred fire. # Chapter 24: The Signs of Rain and Wind

One should perform a fire sacrifice using water and Darba grass <note>sacred *Desmostachya bipinnata* grass used in Vedic rituals</note> while reciting hymns dedicated to the Wind-god and the Moon.

### The Banner Test for Wind
One should prepare a smooth, black banner, equal in length to its staff and three times as high. After first determining the cardinal directions, the wind should be observed by means of this banner when the Moon is in conjunction with the star Rohini.

In this observation, the watches of the day <note>a *prahara* is a 3-hour period</note> represent the fortnights of the rainy season, and smaller divisions of time represent the days. A wind blowing from the left <note>clockwise/auspicious direction</note> is always a bringer of good fortune. The direction in which the wind remains steady and strong is the dominant wind for that period.

### The Seed Germination Test
During this conjunction, various seeds are placed in a water-pot. Those seeds which sprout during the ritual will thrive and see an increase in their yield during the coming year; those that do not sprout will not prosper.

### Observations of the Sky and Clouds
When the Moon is joined with Rohini, if the directions are peaceful and the cries of birds and animals are calm, the sky is clear, and the wind is blameless, it is highly praised. Now, the results of the clouds and winds will be told:

*   **Cloud Formations:**
    *   Clouds may appear black and white, or entirely white, or entirely black like serpents.
    *   Some appear with only their bellies and backs visible, flickering with tongues of lightning.
    *   Others are as white as the interior of a blooming lotus, with edges tinted by the glow of the dawn sun.
    *   The sky may be variegated with clouds the color of bees <note>black</note>, saffron <note>orange-yellow</note>, or the Kimshuka flower <note>bright red</note>.
    *   The sky might be blocked by dark clouds, decorated by flickering lightning and Indra’s Bow <note>a rainbow</note>, resembling a forest filled with elephants and buffaloes being overtaken by a forest fire.
    *   Or the sky may be covered by clouds resembling heaps of black antimony stone, or clouds as beautiful as snow, pearls, conch shells, or moonbeams.

### The Elephant-Clouds
Clouds may resemble "Cloud-Elephants" (*Abdanaga*), with lightning as their golden girths, cranes as their white teeth <note>tusks</note>, and falling rain as their ichor <note>the fluid secreted by elephants in rut</note>. With their moving edges acting as trunks and decorated with the banners of rainbows, they cover the sky.

### Auspicious Signs for Plenty
If the sky is blocked for three days, two days, or even one day by clouds of the described forms, there will be a "Good Alms" <term>Subhiksha: a time of plenty and easy living</term>, the people will be joyful, and the earth will be abundant with water.

### Inauspicious Signs
Clouds that are rough, small, scattered by the wind, and shaped like camels, crows, ghosts, or monkeys—or other condemned forms—and which remain silent <note>without thunder</note>, do not bring welfare or rain.

If the sun shines with soft rays in a cloudless sky, it brings rain. Similarly, if the night sky is as clear as a lake full of blooming lilies and the stars are bright, it bodes well for a good harvest.

### Predictions by Direction
*   **East:** Clouds rising here bring successful crops.
*   **South-East:** Fire hazards.
*   **South:** Crops will perish.
*   **South-West:** Half the crops will be lost.
*   **West:** Excellent rain.
*   **North-West:** Wind and rain.
*   **North:** Strong, nourishing rain.
*   **North-East:** The best crops.

The wind carries these same fruits according to the direction from which it blows. Meteors, falling stars, lightning, thunderbolts, "glow of the directions" <note>auroras or atmospheric glows</note>, earthquakes, and the cries of animals and birds should all be observed just like the clouds.

### The Water-Pot (Kumbha) Oracles
One should place pots named after the months, starting with Shravana <note>July-August</note>, in a clockwise circle.
*   If a pot remains full, that month will provide plenty of water.
*   If it leaks or is empty, the rain will be deficient.
Other pots may be marked with the names of kings or specific regions. Their breaking, leaking, or fullness predicts the fortune or misfortune of those individuals or lands accordingly.

In the delightful gardens situated on the peak of **Mount Sumeru**, filled with the humming of bees attracted to the flowers of the trees growing there, the chirping of various birds, and the soft, deep songs of the celestial maidens—there, **Brihaspati** <note>The preceptor of the Gods</note> spoke to **Narada** regarding the **Rohini** conjunction. Having decided on the first day, he should know from that flag for how many moments and in which direction the wind blows. || 9 || For one watch of the day <note>approx. 3 hours</note> in one direction...

If the wind blows, there will be rain for 15 days; one should then determine the portion of the day based on the duration of the wind's flow. (From the months of Shravan to Kartik <note>July to November</note>, each of the eight fortnights should be indicated by one specific portion). If the wind moves toward the left direction, it is immediately auspicious; if it moves toward a fixed target—that is, in a single direction—that wind is considered established and powerful. ||10|| After this planetary union <note>the conjunction of the Moon and the Rohini star</note> has passed, among the seeds kept in a jar, whichever ones sprout will see growth in their respective shares, and others will not. ||11|| If all directions become calm during the Moon's union with Rohini, and birds or deer make pleasant sounds, the sky is clear, and the wind is pleasing, then there is great success for the land. Following this, the results of the clouds and winds are described in order. ||12||

If the sky is surrounded by massive, serpent-shaped clouds—some white mixed with black, some pure white, some black, some with twisted bellies and visible backs (appearing like a coiled snake whose back and belly are seen as it strikes), with tongues like flashing lightning and making great noise; or if the sky is beautified as if painted by variegated clouds that are clear and reddish like a blooming lotus at the edges, or like honeybees, saffron, or the Flame-of-the-Forest flower; or if the sky is covered with black clouds or decorated with flashing lightning and rainbows, appearing like a forest on fire crowded with elephants and buffaloes; or if the sky is covered with clouds like the black stones of a mountain of antimony <term>Anjan; a dark mineral used for eye-paint</term>; or if the sky is covered by clouds that steal the luster of snow, pearls, conch shells, and moonbeams; or if the entire sky is covered by elephant-shaped clouds that are dark blue like the Tamala tree or a bumblebee, possessing golden belts of lightning, tusks of wind, and dripping water like rut <note>the fluid secreted by elephants in heat</note>, appearing like the great form of Indra adorned with high banners; or if blue lotus-like clouds situated in the twilight-colored sky steal the splendor of Lord Hari <note>Vishnu</note> wearing yellow garments—if the deep thunder of such clouds joins the cries of peacocks, Cuckoo-fishes <note>Chataka birds</note>, and frogs, then these sky-spanning clouds spread in all directions will pour much water upon the earth. ||13||14||15||16||17||18||19|| If the sky remains covered by such clouds for two or three days, there will be abundance <term>Subhiksha; a time of plenty and easy access to food</term>, people will be happy, and much rain will fall on the earth. ||20||

Clouds that are dry, expanded by slight winds, and shaped like camels, crows, ghosts, or monkeys, or other condemned forms, and are silent when they rise, are not auspicious and do not bring rain. ||21|| Alternatively, if the sky is cloudless but the sun's rays are intense, it will rain; and if at night the sky is clear with stars, blooming like a pond of lilies, the rainfall will be good. ||22||

From clouds arising in the East, the grain ripens well; from clouds rising in the Southeast <note>Agneya</note>, there is the wrath of fire; from clouds arising in the South, there is a loss of grain; from clouds rising in the Southwest <note>Nairrita</note>, there is dearness <note>inflation/scarcity</note>; and from clouds rising in the West, there is beautiful rain. ||23|| From clouds rising in the Northwest, there is wind and rain only in some places; from clouds arising in the North, there is nourishing rain; and from clouds rising in the Northeast <note>Ishan</note>, there is excellent grain. The same results apply to the winds blowing from these four directions.

If a white animal leads, there will be moderate rain. If a multi-colored animal is in front, even rain-bearing clouds will not pour water. || 35 || If the Moon, joined with Rohini, cannot be seen in a sky covered by clouds, there is a great fear of disease, yet there will be much water and grain upon the earth. || 36 ||

## Now begins the Twenty-Fifth Chapter
### The Conjunction of Swati

**The results of the Moon's conjunction with Rohini <note>Aldebaran</note> are the same as those for its conjunction with Swati and Ashadha. Having considered all these during the bright fortnight of the month of Ashadha <note>June-July</note>, I shall now explain the specific distinctions found herein. || 1 || If it rains during the first part of the night while the Moon is in Swati, all crops will flourish. In the second part, sesame, green gram, and black gram will grow; in the third part, summer crops will thrive, but autumn crops will not. || 2 || If it rains in the first part of the day, there will be good rainfall throughout the season; in the second part, it brings pests and snakes. Rain in the middle or latter part of the day indicates moderate rain, while rain throughout the day and night signifies a year of excessive rainfall. || 3 || The star to the north of Chitra <note>Spica</note> is called Apamvatsa <note>The Child of the Waters</note>. When the Moon is near that star during the Swati conjunction, it is considered auspicious. || 4 || If, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Magha <note>January-February</note>, during the Swati conjunction, there is frost, or a fierce wind blows, or water-laden clouds thunder incessantly, or the sky is filled with streaks of lightning and the sun, moon, and stars are obscured—then the rainy season will bring joy to the countryside and be filled with all types of grain. || 5 || Similarly, one should observe the Swati conjunction in the dark fortnights of Phalguna, Chaitra, or Vaishakha, but it should be known especially in the month of Ashadha. || 6 ||**

**Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Conjunction of Swati," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 25 ||**

Just as the results are determined by the Moon's conjunction with Rohini, so too are the results for the Moon's conjunction with the constellations Swati and Ashadha. After carefully considering this in the bright half of the month of Ashadha, the specific details are stated: || 1 || If rain falls in the first part of the night during the Swati constellation, all types of grain increase. In the second part, sesame, mung beans, and urad dal grow; in the third part, summer grains are produced, but the autumn harvest does not occur. || 2 || Rain in the first part of the day leads to a good rainy season; in the second part, it produces snakes and insects. If it rains in the middle or later part of the day, there is good rain, and if it rains day and night, there will be a great deal of rain that year. || 3 || The star to the north of Chitra is called *Apamvatsa* <note>1</note>. When the Swati conjunction occurs with the Moon near that star, it results in welfare. || 4 || If frost falls during the Swati conjunction on the seventh tithi <note>lunar day</note> of the dark fortnight of the month of Magha, or if a gale-force wind blows, water-bearing clouds thunder, and the sky is filled with lines of lightning while the light of the moon, sun, and stars is hidden, then in the rainy season the districts will be happy and endowed with all grains. || 5 || Such a Swati conjunction also occurs in the dark fortnights of Phalguna, Chaitra, or Vaishakha, but the Swati conjunction in the month of Ashadha should be understood as particularly significant. || 6 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Hindi commentary on the Brihat Samhita, composed by Sri Varahamihira Acharya and written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the northwestern region. || 25 ||

(From the chapter on the Conjunction of Stars and Planets in the Surya Siddhanta).</note>

# (102)
# The Vārāhī Compilation (Vārāhīsaṃhitā)

### Chapter Twenty-Six
### The Conjunction of the Month of Ashadha (Ashadhoyoga)

On the full moon day of the month of Ashadha <note>June/July</note>, one should weigh equal amounts of various seeds and leave them overnight. On the following day, whichever seed increases in weight will flourish in growth; that which decreases will not thrive. The following incantation should be recited for the consecration of the scales: || 1 ||

"O Goddess Saraswati, the embodiment of Truth, you should be praised with this mantra. You are devoted to the vow of truth; therefore, reveal that which is true. || 2 || By that Truth through which the Sun, Moon, planets, and the host of stars rise in the East and set in the West; || 3 || that Truth which resides in all the Vedas, that Truth found among the knowers of the Supreme Spirit (Brahmavadis), and that Truth which exists in the three worlds—let that Truth be manifested here. || 4 || You are the daughter of Brahma, celebrated as Aditya, belonging to the lineage (gotra) of Kashyapa, and known by the name 'Tula' (The Scales)." || 5 ||

The scales should be made with a beam of six finger-widths (angulas), suspended by four silken threads. The length of the strings should be ten finger-widths, and the distance between the two pans should be six finger-widths. || 6 || Place gold in the southern pan and the other substances or water in the northern pan. If the water used is from a well, a spring, or a lake, it indicates poor, medium, or excellent rainfall respectively. || 7 ||

Elephants are represented by ivory, cattle and horses by their hair, kings by gold, and Brahmins by beeswax. The various regions, years, months, and directions are represented by the nature of the remaining substances. || 8 || A scale made of gold is best, silver is middling, and if these are unavailable, it should be made of Khadira wood <term>Khadira: Acacia catechu, a very hard wood used in rituals</term>. Alternatively, it may be made from the wood of a tree hit by an arrow, and its length should be one span (vasti). || 9 ||

A decrease in weight signifies destruction; an increase signifies growth; and if the weight remains the same, the result will be stable. This secret of the "Scale-Treasury" has been told; a man should perform this even during the conjunction of Prajapati (Rohini). || 10 || Malefic planets are not auspicious when positioned in the constellations of Swati, Ashadha, or Rohini. If there is a leap month (intercalary month), the observation should be performed twice. || 11 || When all three conjunctions yield similar results, the prediction is certain. If they differ, the results observed during the Rohini conjunction are considered superior. || 12 ||

The winds from the East and other directions indicate respectively: successful harvest, danger from fire, scanty rain, medium rain, excellent rain, excessive rain with wind, and a healthy, prosperous season. || 13 || On the fourth day of the dark fortnight following the Ashadha full moon, if it rains under the constellation of Ajaikapada (Purva Bhadrapada), the rainy season will be excellent; if not, it will not be so. || 14 || If a North-Easterly wind blows on the full moon of Ashadha as the sun sets, the harvest of crops will be magnificent. || 15 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Conjunction of Ashadha," in the Brihat Samhita of Shri Varahamihira. || 26 ||

You are the keeper of the vow of truth regarding all things true; therefore, please reveal the truth to me." || 2 || By the power of that Truth by which the Moon... <note>The Hindi translation follows the Sanskrit verses provided above.</note>

# Chapter 26: The Hindi Commentary

The Sun, the planets, and the <term>Jyotirgana</term><note>The collective host of stars and celestial bodies</note> rise in the east and set in the west. Whatever is true in all the Vedas, whatever is true among the seekers of Brahman, and whatever is true in the three worlds—may you manifest that truth here. For you are renowned as the daughter of Brahma, named Aditya; you belong to the lineage of Kashyapa and are known by the name <term>Tula</term><note>The Balance or Scales</note>. ||3-4||

The scale is made of hemp, consisting of four strings and a beam six fingers wide. The measurement of each of the four strings should be ten fingers long. In this manner, a <term>kaksha</term><note>The central handle or pivot point held to lift the scales</note> of six fingers' measure should be placed between the two pans. ||5||

In the right-hand pan, gold should be placed; in the other pan, the remaining substances and water should be placed. By performing this ritual with water from a well, a pond, or a river, one predicts low, medium, or excellent rainfall respectively. That is to say: if the well water becomes slightly heavier on the second day compared to the first, there will be no rain. If the rainwater becomes heavier, there will be medium rain. If the river or pond water becomes heavier, there will be appropriate rainfall. If all water samples increase in weight, there is excessive rain (<term>ativrishti</term>), and if all decrease, there is drought (<term>anavrishti</term>). ||7||

The growth or decline of various groups is known through specific items: ivory for the <term>Nagas</term><note>Serpent deities or perhaps a specific tribe</note>, greed for cattle, horses, and livestock, and "heaven" for kings. Through a <term>siktha</term><note>A lump of wax the size of a single mouthful</note>, the prosperity or decline of the twice-born <note>The Brahmin, Kshatriya, and Vaishya castes</note> is known. Similarly, for the central region, the year, the month, the quarters of the sky, and other commodities (like grain), one should weigh the actual object whose increase or decrease one wishes to know and then pronounce the result. A balance-beam made of gold is best, silver is medium; if these are unavailable, the beam should be made of Khair wood. Alternatively, it should be shaped like the arrow that pierces a man and be one <term>vitasti</term><note>A span; the distance between the tip of the thumb and the little finger</note> in length. ||8-9||

In weighing with the scales, that which is lighter rises and that which is heavier sinks; this is the secret of the "Balance-Casket" (<term>Tula-kosha</term>). Men also observe this during the <term>Rohini-yoga</term><note>The conjunction of the Moon with the star Rohini</note>. ||10||

The conjunction of malefic planets in the constellations of Swati, Rohini, and Ashadha is not auspicious. However, in a year where there is an <term>Adhimasa</term><margin>An intercalary or "extra" month added to the lunar calendar to align it with the solar year.</margin> (specifically an extra Ashadha month), both previously mentioned conjunctions shall be considered. ||11||

If the results of all three omens (Rohini, Swati, and Ashadhi) are identical, then one should declare the auspicious or inauspicious result without any doubt. If the results differ, the result derived from Rohini is considered the most significant. ||12||

If an easterly wind blows, the grain will be successfully harvested. If the wind blows from the southeast (the direction of Agni), there will be the wrath of fire. Similarly, following the clockwise direction from the south, the winds indicate light rain, medium rain, excellent rain, stormy rain, nourishing rain, and auspicious rain. ||13||

If it rains during the <term>Krishna Chaturthi</term><note>The fourth day of the dark lunar fortnight</note> following the Ashadhi full moon, and while the moon is in the Purva-Ashadha constellation, the rainfall for the season will be good; otherwise, it will not. ||14||

At the time of sunset on the Ashadhi full moon, if the wind blows from the northeast, then the grain on earth will be of excellent quality. ||15||

->Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter of the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the great teacher Varahamihira.<-

<note>1. A lunar month in which no solar transition (Sankranti) occurs is called an Adhimasa or Malamasa (impure month). "That month without a transition is clearly an Adhimasa." (Siddhanta Shiromani)</note>

Varāhī Saṃhitā

# Now begins the Twenty-Seventh Chapter¹
## The Wind Circle

When the East wind blows from the sky at the time of the Āṣāḍhī conjunction <note>A specific lunar alignment in the month of June-July</note>, churning the crests of the eastern ocean waves and struck by the matted hair-like rays of the sun and moon, one should know that the earth will be covered by clusters of dark clouds, enriched by the autumn harvest, and adorned with the lush crops of spring. ॥ 1 ॥

When the South-east wind, skillful in striking the peaks of the Malaya mountains, blows as the divine Sun sets, then the earth—constantly burning and embraced by flickering flames—vomits a heap of ashes through the hot sighs of its own body <note>This indicates severe drought or fire</note>. ॥ 2 ॥

When the noble South wind blows during this conjunction, making the monkeys dance among the canopies of palm trees and creepers, and rising with full effort like an elephant, then the clouds—struck by the wind as if by elephant-goads—release slow drops of water like weary farmers. ॥ 3 ॥

When the South-west wind blows continuously at sunset, tossing heaps of fine cardamom, lavalī, and cloves in the ocean, the earth appears like a drunken female ghost—fierce and trembling, covered by a spread of human bone fragments and plagued by hunger and thirst. ॥ 4 ॥

When the West wind blows at the time of sunset, flickering with the pride of its great mane of dust, then the earth—though possessed of crops—will see wars started by great kings, and in various places, it will be soaked with constant fat, flesh, and blood. ॥ 5 ॥

If at the time of the Āṣāḍhī festival, as the Lord of Rays (the Sun) sets, the North-west wind blows with increased speed—the enemy of clouds yet mimicking the movement of a snake—one should know the earth will be delighted by streams of water, echoing with the croaking of frogs, marked by the brilliance of crops, and filled with happiness like an army of good fortune. ॥ 6 ॥

When the North wind, fragrant with the scent of Kadamba flowers, blows at the end of summer as the Sun’s rays are swallowed by Mount Meru, then the clouds—intoxicated by the play of lightning—fill the earth with water like madmen, reflecting the rays of the moon. ॥ 7 ॥

If the North-east wind should blow—cool, served by the hosts of gods, fragrant with Punnāga, Aguru, and Pārijāta <note>Heavenly and aromatic trees</note>, and making a fierce sound—then the earth will be filled with the youth of abundant water and lush crops; righteous kings, having bowed their enemies, will then protect the social orders. ॥ 8 ॥

**Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, named "The Wind Circle," in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā composed by Sri Varāhamihira. ॥ 27 ॥**

If the wind blows <note>referring to the North-West wind mentioned previously</note>, the earth remains constantly inflamed; embraced by the crests of light at its base, it seems to vomit ashes through breaths born from the heat of its own body. ||2||

When, in this alignment, the harsh Southern wind continues to howl, making the groups of Palmyra trees and creepers dance along with the monkeys, then despite all efforts, the clouds—resembling tall elephants or elephants struck by a goad <term>ankusha: a hooked tool used by mahouts to guide elephants</term>—yield only meager rain, like a miserly man giving charity. ||3||

At the time of sunset, when the South-Western wind swirls the small cardamom and clove trees along the seashore, it makes the earth appear fierce and restless, like the bride of a mad ghost, covered under the weight of straw bundles and the bone fragments of those who died of hunger and thirst. ||4||

At twilight, when the wind blows in the West, restless due to the scattering of saffron dust and prideful in its movement, then the earth becomes a battlefield for great kings, filled with grain yet equally covered in places by fat, flesh, and blood. ||5||

On the full moon of the month of Ashadha <note>June-July</note>, if at the time of sunset the "enemy of the clouds"—the North-Western wind—moves with the speed of Garuda <note>the divine eagle-king</note>, then the earth, blooming with streams of water and echoing with the croaking of frogs, appears like a fortunate army, possessing the beauty of grain and attaining great happiness. ||6||

At the end of summer, when the sun's rays reach the base of Mount Meru and the fragrant Northern wind blows, scented with the aroma of Kadamba flowers, then lightning swirls within the clouds. Those clouds, intoxicated by their own brilliance, fill the earth—which is otherwise bereft of the moon's rays—with water like a madman. ||7||

If the fierce-sounding North-Eastern wind, fragrant with Punnaga, Aguru <term>agarwood</term>, and Parijata flowers, is cool and worthy of the gods, then the earth becomes full of youthful vigor and ripe crops, and righteous kings, subduers of their enemies, protect the Dharma <note>the moral and cosmic order</note>. ||8||

## Now begins the Twenty-Eighth Chapter
### Signs of Immediate Rain

In a query regarding rain, if the Moon occupies a water-sign <note>Cancer, Scorpio, or Pisces</note> and is situated in the Ascendant, or if it is in a Quadrant <term>Kendra: the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses</term> during the bright fortnight, it brings abundant water. If aspected by benefics, there is much rain; if by malefic planets, there is little. During the monsoon season, Venus acts just like the Moon in this regard. ||1||

If the person asking the question <insert>the querent</insert> touches a wet object, or something named after water, or stands near water, or is about to perform an action related to water, it should be said: "There is no doubt, water will come soon." The same applies if the word "water" is heard at the time of the inquiry. ||2||

If the Sun, situated on the eastern mountain <note>at sunrise</note>, is difficult to look at due to extreme brilliance, resembling molten gold or the luster of a polished beryl stone, it brings rain that very day. The same occurs if the Sun, having reached the middle of the sky, shines with intense, scorching heat. ||3||

Tasteless water, water resembling the eyes of a cow <note>original: "gonetrābhaṃ"; likely referring to a specific clarity or brownish-blue tint</note>, a clear sky, and a change in the taste of salt; when the sky takes on the color of a crow's egg, when the wind dies down, and when fish leap frequently or frogs croak repeatedly while moving on land—these are causes for the arrival of water. || 4 ||

Cats scratching the ground intensely with their claws, an accumulation of rust on metals with a raw, fleshy smell <note>original: "visragandhaḥ"</note>, and children building bridges out of dust in the streets—these announce that water will arrive shortly. || 5 ||

If the mountains resemble heaps of collyrium <note>a black eye-salve</note> or if their caves are blocked by vapor; and if the halos around the moon resemble the eyes of a partridge <note>original: "kṛkavāku"; can also mean a rooster</note>, they are givers of rain. || 6 ||

The migration of ants with their eggs without any external disturbance, the mating of snakes, the climbing of trees by serpents, and the leaping of cows are signs of rain. || 7 ||

Chameleons perched on the tips of trees with their gaze fixed on the sky, and if the upward gaze of cows falls toward the sky, then water will fall before long. || 8 ||

If domestic animals do not wish to leave the house, shake their ears and hooves, and if dogs behave in the same manner as these animals, one should indicate that water is about to fall. || 9 ||

When dogs stay on the roofs of houses or bark with their faces turned upward toward the sky; and if lightning appears during the day in the direction of the Northeast <note>original: "pinākidigbhava"; the direction of Shiva/Pinaki</note>, then the earth becomes satisfied with excessive water. || 10 ||

When the moon resembles the eyes of a parrot or a pigeon, or is the color of honey, and when a "mock moon" <note>original: "pratiśaśī"; a paraselene or lunar parhelion</note> shines in the sky, then water falls from the heaven without delay. || 11 ||

If there is thunder at night and lightning during the day, appearing red like blood and standing straight like a rod; and if the wind is cool and comes from the front, then the arrival of water will occur. || 12 ||

If the sprouts of creepers point upward toward the sky, if birds bathe in moving dust, and if reptiles sit on the tips of grass, then the fall of water is imminent. || 13 ||

When the twilight clouds have colors like peacocks, parrots, blue jays, or ruddy geese, or steal the luster of the Hibiscus flower and the lotus; and if they resemble crocodiles, turtles, boars, or fish emerging from water, and are piled in many layers, they give water shortly. || 14 ||

Clouds that are white as lime or the moon at their edges, but have the luster of collyrium or bees in their center, which are glossy, multi-layered, dripping with water drops, and shaped like broken flights of stairs—if such clouds arise in the East and move West, or arise in the West and move East, they release abundant water on the earth before long. || 15 ||

If rainbows, "halos of the sun" <note>original: "parigha"</note>, mock suns, or lightning halos appear at the time of the sun's rising or setting, one should predict abundant water immediately. || 16 ||

If the sky resembles the feathers of a partridge <note>original: "tittiri-patra"; likely referring to cirrocumulus "mackerel" clouds</note> and flocks of birds chirp joyfully at the rising or setting of the sun, the clouds release water day and night without delay. || 17 ||

If the rays of the sun are "unfailing" <note>original: "amogha"; clear and piercing</note> and rise up like the peaks of the sunset mountain, and if the clouds thunder with a sound that seems to touch the earth, that is a great sign of rain. || 18 ||

During the rainy season, if the Moon is in the seventh house from Venus and is aspected by a benefic planet, or is in the ninth, fifth, or seventh house from Saturn, it leads to the arrival of water. || 19 ||

Generally, at the time of the rising or setting of planets, at their conjunctions, at their entry into a new planetary circle, at the end of a fortnight, at the end of the sun's northern or southern course, and when the sun enters the lunar mansion of Ārdrā, rain occurs by rule. || 20 ||

Water falls during the conjunction of Mercury and Venus, Mercury and Jupiter, or Jupiter and Venus.

### **Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Signs of Immediate Rain," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 28 ||**

If a question regarding rain is asked and at that time the Moon occupies a <term>watery sign</term><note>Cancer, Aquarius, Pisces, Virgo, or the latter half of Capricorn</note> and is situated in the <term>Ascendant</term><note>Lagna, the rising sign</note> or a <term>quadrant</term><note>Kendra, the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses</note> and is aspected by a benefic planet, then much water will fall. If it is aspected by a <term>malefic planet</term><note>planets like Mars or Saturn that bring harsh influence</note>, little water falls and rain does not occur for a long time. Venus gives results similar to the Moon. || 1 || If at the time of inquiry, the questioner touches a wet object, water, or an object named after water, or is engaged in work near water or related to water, or if a word signifying water is heard, it can be said without doubt that rain will come very soon. || 2 || During the rainy season, on the day when the Sun, positioned on the eastern mountain, has a luster that pains the eyes or has a smooth brilliance like molten gold or <term>beryl</term><note>original: "Vaidurya-mani", a cat's eye or greenish gem</note>, it will rain on that day; and if the Sun reaches high in the sky and burns with sharp rays, it will rain at that time. || 3 || 

The spoiling of the taste of water, the sky becoming the color of a cow's eye, the directions becoming clear, the sweating of salt, the rising of clouds colored like a crow's egg, the sudden stopping of the wind, fish repeatedly leaping out of the water, and frogs croaking again and again—these are signs of the <insert>arrival</insert> of water. || 4 || Cats scratching the earth with their claws, a smell like raw meat coming from iron due to the accumulation of rust, and children building bridges of sand in the path—these reveal the signs of immediate rain. || 5 || If all the mountains become the color of a heap of <term>collyrium</term><note>black eye-salve</note>, their caves fill with vapor, and the halo around the Moon becomes the color of a rooster's eye, there will be rain. || 6 || 

The movement of ants carrying their eggs from one place to another without any disturbance, snakes mating or climbing trees, and cows leaping and skipping—these bring rain. || 7 || If a chameleon climbs a tree and looks toward the sky, or if cows lift their gaze upward to look at the Sun, water will fall soon. || 8 || If domestic animals do not wish to go out of the house and keep shaking their ears and hooves, and if dogs behave in the same manner as these animals, it should be stated that it will rain. || 9 || When dogs sit on the roofs of houses or look upward continuously, and when lightning flashes in the <term>Northeast</term><note>original: "Ishan-kon"</note> during the day, the earth will be flooded by excessive rain. || 10 || When the Moon is red like the eye of a parrot or pigeon, or the color of honey, and when a second Moon <note>a parhelion or "mock moon" phenomenon</note> is seen in the sky, water will soon fall from the heavens. || 11 || If there is the sound of thunder at night, or if streaks of lightning resembling blood or a staff are seen during the day, and if the wind is cool from the front, then the arrival of water occurs.

...12. If the new leaves of creepers point upward toward the sky, if birds bathe in water or dust, and if snakes or insects sit atop the tips of grass, there will be immediate rain. 13. When the clouds in the evening sky take on the colors of a peacock, parrot, Indian roller, or cuckoo, or mimic the luster of the hibiscus <note>original: *japakusuma*</note> or lotus, and if the water ripples take the shapes of mountains, crocodiles, tortoises, boars, or fish, it will soon rain. 14. Clouds that are straight at the four edges, white like the moon, yet dark as collyrium <note>eye salve</note> or bees in the center, dripping with glistening droplets, piled one atop another like stairs, and moving from the east toward the west—these clouds will soon pour much water upon the earth. 15. If at sunrise or sunset a rainbow, a *parigha* <note>a line of clouds crossing the sun</note>, a mock sun, a rod-like cloud formation, or a halo like lightning appears, it rains heavily very soon. 16. If at sunrise or sunset the sky becomes the color of a partridge's wing and birds chirp joyfully, the clouds will soon release much water. 17. If at the setting of the thousand-rayed sun, rays as high as the sunset mountains and "unfailing" <note>original: *amogha*</note> rays are visible, and if clouds thunder close to the earth, these are considered great signs of approaching rain. 18. If during the rainy season the Moon is aspected by auspicious planets, or is in the seventh house from Venus, or the ninth, fifth, or seventh from Saturn, this causes the arrival of water. 19. Rain usually occurs according to rule during the rising or setting of planets, during their transition through circles <note>mandala</note>, at their conjunctions, at the end of a fortnight, at the end of a solstice <note>ayana</note>, and when the Sun enters the lunar mansion of Ardra. 20. The conjunction of Mercury and Venus, Mercury and Jupiter, or Jupiter and Venus causes rain. However, if Saturn and Mars join without being aspected by or joined with a benefic planet, there is a fear of fire. 21. When planets following the Sun remain to the west or even to the east of the Sun, they turn the earth into a sea <note>indicating extreme flooding</note>. 22.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Hindi commentary of the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Acharya Varahamihira, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region.

By observing the abundance of fruits and flowers on vegetation, the ease of obtaining goods and the success of agriculture can be known. || 1 || From an abundance of *Shal* flowers and fruits, white *Shashti* rice grows; from *Dudhi*, *Panduka* grain; from blue *Ashoka*, the growth of hogs. ## Chapter 30
### Signs of Twilight
<note>Sanskrit: Sandhyā-lakṣaṇam. This refers to the transitional periods of dawn and dusk.</note>

The period of twilight lasts from the time the sun is half-set (or half-risen) until the stars become indistinct in the sky. During this time, the following signs indicate specific results: 1

Observations should be made of wild animals, birds, the wind, halos <note>pariveṣa</note>, mock suns <note>paridhi</note>, atmospheric bars <note>parigha</note>, clouds, "cloud-trees," and rainbows; as well as the "city of the Gandharvas" <note>fata morgana or mirage</note>, sunbeams <note>danda</note>, dust, glossiness, and colors. 2

If a wild animal cries out loudly and fiercely, it foretells the destruction of a village. If such a sound comes from the south, facing the sun, it indicates the destruction of an army. 3

If animals move to the left, it signifies war; if to the right, it signifies the meeting of armies. If the wind is calm, or if the "circle of animals" <term>mṛga-cakra: a specific grouping of animals used in divination</term> or the wind moves in a mixed fashion during twilight, rain will follow. 4

The cries of animals and birds facing the sun at morning twilight foretell the ruin of the country. If they cry from the south with their mouths facing the sun, it indicates the capture of a city. 5

A twilight is inauspicious if the wind is strong enough to damage houses and gateways, or if it raises dust and clods of earth, or if it is accompanied by harsh, terrifying noises and falling birds. 6

A twilight is considered blessed if the wind is gentle, barely moving the leaves of the trees, or if there is no wind at all, and if the cries of birds and animals are sweet and peaceful. 7

During the twilight hour, if the sunbeams, lightning, "cloud-fish," halos, and mock suns are glossy, and if rainbows and "Indra's cables" <note>irāvata: a type of atmospheric phenomenon</note> appear, they bring immediate rain. 8

Sunbeams that are broken, uneven, scattered, distorted, crooked, or turning to the left—as well as those that are thin, short, faint, or dusty—bring war and a lack of rain. 9

Sunbeams that are radiant, clear, straight, long, and turning to the right bring prosperity to the world when the sun shines in a cloudless sky. 10

The white rays of the sun that reach the zenith during the day, which are glossy, continuous, and straight, are called "Infallible" <note>amogha</note> and are bringers of rain. 11

Rays that are variegated, tawny, reddish-brown, or colored like madder, green, or spotted, and which stretch toward the heavens, bring rain within seven days but also cause slight fear. 12

Copper-colored rays foretell the death of a commander-in-chief; yellow-red rays indicate his calamity. Green rays signify the destruction of cattle and crops, while smoke-colored rays portend the loss of cows. 13

Madder-colored rays bring fear of weapons and fire; tawny rays bring wind and rain. Rays the color of ash indicate a lack of rain, and thin, spotted, or variegated rays indicate general weakness. 14

When dust the color of the Bandhuka flower or powdered collyrium <note>black eye-salve</note> approaches the sun, the people will be afflicted by hundreds of diseases. White dust, however, brings peace and prosperity to the world. 15

A "Staff" <note>daṇḍa</note> is a phenomenon formed by the union of sunbeams, clouds, and wind. If it appears in the intermediate directions, it is inauspicious for people; if in the cardinal directions, it is inauspicious for the twice-born <note>the priestly and noble classes</note>. 16

If seen at dawn, midday, or dusk, it brings fear of weapons and disease. A white "Staff" affects the Brahmins, and it destroys whichever direction it faces. 17

A "Cloud-Tree" <note>abhra-vṛkṣa: a vertical cloud formation</note> that is blue with a curd-like top, covering the sun and reaching the mid-sky, or clouds streaked with yellow and thick at the base, bring abundant rain. 18

If a "Cloud-Tree" rises in the direction of a marching king's travel, it foretells his death. If it resembles a sapling, it signifies the death of the crown prince or a minister. 19

Twilight that is colored like a blue lily, lapis lazuli, or the filaments of a lotus, and is free from wind but illuminated by sunbeams, brings immediate rain. 20

Twilight accompanied by ill-shaped clouds, mirages, mist, dust, or smoke causes drought during the rainy season and war at other times. 21

In the seasons beginning with Winter, the natural colors of twilight are crimson, yellow, white, variegated, lotus-like, and blood-red respectively. These are auspicious in their own seasons; any other color is a portent of change.

# Chapter 30: On the Signs of Twilight

|| 22 || A cloud shaped like a king bearing weapons, if it appears broken and moves toward the Sun, indicates danger from an enemy. If a white cloud shaped like a city is overtaken by the Sun, it signifies the capture of a city; if it is pierced through, it signifies destruction. || 23 || A very thick white covering of clouds to the left of the Sun brings rain. If the Sun is surrounded by clouds resembling the *Veerana* <note>original: "वीरण" - a type of fragrant grass (Vetiver)</note> bush appearing in a non-blazing direction, it is auspicious. || 24 || A white *Parigha* <note>term: Parigha - a horizontal cloud formation resembling a cross-bar or bolt</note> brings calamity to the king. One colored like blood causes the fury of the army. One with the color of gold, appearing at sunrise, increases the strength of the army. || 25 || Two *Paridhis* <note>term: Paridhi - a halo or solar arc</note> on both sides of the Sun bring abundant water. However, if these halos surround all quarters, not even a drop of rain will fall. || 26 || Clouds shaped like banners, umbrellas, mountains, elephants, or horses at the two twilights lead to victory. Those resembling blood lead to battle. || 27 || Clouds resembling heaps of straw smoke increase the strength of the king's enemies. || 28 || Hanging clouds shaped like trees, shining with a harsh red light, are auspicious at twilight. Those shaped like cities are also beneficial. || 29 || The cries of birds, jackals, or deer in a "blazing" <note>The "blazing" direction refers to the quarter where the sun is currently positioned or its opposite, considered astrologically intense.</note> direction, or the presence of "rods" of light, dust, or *Parighas*, or daily abnormalities of the Sun, lead to the destruction of the country's ruler and the famine of the people. || 30 || Omens in the East bear fruit immediately; those in the West at night or within three days. Halos, dust, and *Parighas* show results within seven days if not immediate. Similarly, solar centers, rainbows, lightning, mock suns, clouds, and winds show results that same day or on the eighth; birds within seven days, and deer immediately. || 31 || The glow of twilight illuminates one *yojana* <note>term: Yojana - a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>; lightning illuminates six. The sound of thunder travels five *yojanas*. There is no sound when a meteor falls. || 32 || A mock sun is three *yojanas* in extent; a *Parigha* is five. The circle of a halo is visible for five or six *yojanas*, while the bow of Indra <note>note: "Indra's Bow" is the traditional Sanskrit term for a rainbow.</note> shines for ten. || 33 ||

->Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "Signs of Twilight," in the *Brihat Samhita* of Sri Varahamihira. || 30 ||<-

The period from the setting of the Sun until the stars are clearly visible in the sky is known as the evening twilight (*Sandhya*). Similarly, the period from the appearance of stars until the Sun is half-risen is the morning twilight. || 1 || The effects of twilight are told through these signs: deer, birds, wind, halos (*Parivesha*), solar arcs (*Paridhi*), cross-bar clouds (*Parigha*), clouds, trees, rainbows, solar rays, "rods" of light (*Danda*), dust, glossiness, and color. || 2 || A deer making a loud, terrifying sound repeatedly indicates the destruction of the village. If a deer on the right side of the army faces the Sun and cries loudly, the army will be destroyed. || 3 || If the deer is in the South and is quiet, it signifies battle; if on the left, it signifies the meeting of armies. If at twilight the deer, the *Chakravaka* bird, and the wind move in mixed directions, there will be rain. || 4 || In the morning twilight, the sound of deer and birds facing the Sun in the East announces the destruction of the country. If deer and birds cry facing the Sun in the South, the city will be captured by enemies. || 5 || A wind that blows down houses, trees, and gateways, or lifts clods of earth with dust, or makes birds fall with its fierce speed and harsh sound, makes for an inauspicious twilight. || 6 || If at twilight a gentle breeze blows, or it is windless, and birds and deer cry sweetly in a "quiet" direction, that twilight is worshipped as auspicious. || 7 || At twilight, if the "rods" of light, lightning, "fish" clouds, circles, halos, rainbows, the *Airavata* <note>note: Airavata is the celestial elephant of Indra, here referring to a specific rainbow or cloud formation.</note>, and the Sun's rays are all glossy, it brings immediate rain. || 8 || Clouds that are broken, crooked, destroyed, terrifying, distorted, or leaning to the left... <note>The text ends mid-sentence, continuing the description of inauspicious cloud shapes.</note>

If the sun’s rays at twilight are broken, small, weak, and dim, there will be war and no rain. || 9 ||
In a cloudless sky, if the sun’s rays are clear, pleasant, straight, long, and rotate in a clockwise direction <note>original: "pradakshina"</note>, it brings auspiciousness to the world. || 10 || If the sun’s rays appear at the beginning, middle, and end of the day and are glossy, unbroken, straight, and white, they bring rain; these rays are named *Amogha* <term>Amogha: literally "unfailing" or "productive"</term>. || 11 || If those same rays become black, yellow, tawny, red, or green—appearing in many forms across the sky—they are causes for rain, but for one week they may indicate some danger. || 12 ||

If they are copper-colored, the commander-in-chief dies; if they are yellow and red, the commander-in-chief suffers distress; if they are green, cattle and grain are destroyed; if smoke-colored, cattle perish; if they have the luster of madder <note>a reddish-purple dye</note>, there is fear of weapons and fire. If they appear behind <insert>the sun</insert>, rain comes with wind; if they are ash-colored, there is drought; and if they are strong and variegated in color, the rainfall becomes scanty. || 13 || 14 ||

When the dust of twilight becomes as black as a midday flower or collyrium powder <note>eye makeup soot</note> and moves toward the sun, men suffer from hundreds of diseases. If this dust is white, it causes the growth and peace of mankind. || 15 || If the sun’s rays combine with water and wind to take the shape of a staff <note>a vertical pillar of light</note>, this is called a *Danda*. If it stands in the intermediate directions, it is inauspicious for kings; if it stands in the cardinal directions, it is inauspicious for the twice-born classes <note>the upper castes: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas</note>. || 16 ||

If a *Danda* is seen before sunrise or during the midday transition, it causes fear of weapons and disease. If it is white, it harms the Brahmins and the directions in which it stands. || 17 || A blue cloud in the sky with edges like curd that covers the sun is called an *Abhrataru* <term>Abhrataru: literally "cloud-tree"</term>. This, or a yellow cloud that is "thick-rooted" (having a mouth-like opening at the bottom), pours down much water. || 18 || If an *Abhrataru* follows a king marching against an enemy and suddenly vanishes, the crown prince and the minister will perish. || 19 ||

A windless twilight, possessing the luster of a blue lotus, lapis lazuli, or the filaments of a lotus, brings rain if illuminated by the sun's rays. || 20 || A twilight filled with ill-shaped clouds, "cities of Gandharvas" <term>Gandharva-nagara: a complex mirage or Fata Morgana appearing like a celestial city</term>, frost, dust, or smoke (fog) reduces rain during the monsoon; in other seasons, it provokes the fury of weapons. || 21 ||

In the seasons starting with *Shishira* <note>the cool season</note>, the natural colors of twilight—red, yellow, white, variegated, or like a lotus or blood—are auspicious if they match the season. Any other color indicates a disturbance. || 22 || If clouds shaped like men bearing weapons appear before the sun and are broken, there is fear of the enemy. If a "city of Gandharvas" in a white sky covers the sun, an attacking king will capture a besieged city. If the sun-city pierces the Gandharva-city, the city is destroyed by the enemy. || 23 ||

White clouds with white edges that cover the sun from the left, or clouds arising from a dull direction resembling a thicket of *Ushira* <note>Vetiver grass</note> that cover the sun, will bring rain. || 24 || If a white halo <note>original: "paridhi"</note> is seen at sunrise, the king faces calamity; a red one causes the army’s anger; one with the appearance of gold increases strength. || 25 || If the halo on both sides of the sun takes on a "body" (becomes thick), it rains heavily. If the entire halo surrounds the directions, not a single drop of water falls. || 26 ||

If twilight clouds take the form of a flag, umbrella, mountain, elephant, or horse, it leads to victory. If they are as red as blood, they lead to battle. || 27 || Clouds with a glossy form like the smoke of straw increase the power of kings. || 28 || Clouds at twilight [facing] the sharp sun...

If the light-givers <note>referring to the sun or moon</note> appear in the shape of a tree or seem to bow down, it is auspicious. ### Now Begins the Thirty-First Chapter
#### Signs of the Burning of the Quarters

A yellow glow in the sky <note>Digdaha: literally "burning of the directions," referring to abnormal atmospheric glows or wildfires on the horizon</note> causes fear for the king; a fire-colored glow causes the destruction of the country. If it is blood-red and accompanied by a wind from the south-west, it destroys the crops. || 1 || That glow which is intensely bright and casts shadows like the sun, and which resembles the color of blood, brings great fear to the king and provokes the fury of weapons <note>war</note>. || 2 || If the glow appears in the East, it causes suffering to kings and the warrior class <term>Kshatriyas</term>. In the South-East, it troubles artisans and youths. In the South, it brings suffering to fierce men, the merchant class <term>Vaishyas</term>, messengers, and remarried women. || 3 || In the West, it affects the laboring class <term>Shudras</term> and farmers. In the North-West, it affects thieves along with horses. In the North, it brings suffering to the priestly class <term>Brahmins</term>, and in the North-East, it affects heretics and traders. || 4 || If the sky is clear, the stars are bright, the wind blows clockwise <note>Pradakshina</note>, and the glow of the quarters is as pure as gold, it is for the benefit of the world and its rulers. || 5 ||

->Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, named "Signs of the Burning of the Quarters," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 31 ||<-

A yellow-colored glow in the sky is a cause for fear of the king; a fire-colored glow is a cause for the destruction of the country; and a red-colored glow with a southern wind destroys the grain. || 1 || A glow that is extremely bright and reveals shadows (inner light) like the sun, and is red like blood, gives great fear to the king and manifests the fury of weapons. || 2 || If the glow is in the East, kings and warriors are troubled; in the South-East, it troubles groups of youths and artisans; in the South, it is painful for fierce men, merchants, messengers, and women married a second time. || 3 || In the West, laborers and farmers; in the North-West, thieves along with horses; in the North, Brahmins; and in the North-East, heretics and merchants are troubled. || 4 || When the sky...

### Now begins the Thirty-Second Chapter
## Signs of Earthquakes
<term>Bhukampa-lakshanam: The diagnostic signs and characteristics of earthquakes.</term>

Some say an earthquake is caused by massive creatures living deep within the waters of the underworld. Others say it arises from the resting breath of the "Elephants of the Quarters" <note>Diggajas: Mythical elephants who support the earth at the cardinal points</note> when they grow weary of the earth's weight. || 1 ||

Some teachers say that air, when struck by other winds, falls to the earth with a great roar; others claim it is caused by an unseen, supernatural force. || 2 ||

In ancient times, the Earth was shaken by mountains that possessed wings, as they constantly flew up and crashed down. Trembling, the Earth approached the Grandfather <note>Pitamaha: A title for Brahma, the Creator</note> in the assembly of the gods, filled with shame. || 3 ||

"O Lord! The name 'Achala' <note>Achala: Literally "The Immovable One," a common Sanskrit name for the Earth</note> you gave me is no longer true. With these moving mountains, I am unable to endure this distress." || 4 ||

Seeing her face—her voice choking with emotion, her lips slightly trembling, her head bowed, and her eyes filled with tears—the Grandfather spoke: || 5 ||

"O Indra! Remove the sorrow of the Earth Mother. Cast your thunderbolt to shatter the wings of the mountains." Indra replied, "It shall be done," and told the Earth, "Do not fear." || 6 ||

"However, the Wind, Fire, Indra, and Varuna <note>The gods of Air, Fire, Sky/Rain, and Water</note> shall shake the earth in the first, second, third, and fourth parts of the day and night respectively, to signal the arrival of good or evil results." || 7 ||

### The Vayavya (Wind) Circle
The four stars beginning with Aryaman <note>Uttara Phalguni</note>, along with Hasta, Chitra, Svati, Mrigashira, and Ashwini, constitute the Wind Circle. Its signs appear seven days prior: || 8 ||

The sky is filled with smoke, and the wind blows violently, scattering dust from the ground and breaking trees. The sun appears with weak, dull rays. || 9 ||

When an earthquake occurs in the Wind Circle, it is said to cause the destruction of crops, water, forests, and medicinal herbs. It brings about swelling, breathing difficulties, insanity, fevers, and coughs, and causes distress to merchants. || 10 ||

Those who are handsome, soldiers, physicians, women, poets, musicians, traders, and artisans suffer; as do the regions of Saurashtra, Kuru, Magadha, Dasharna, and Matsya. || 11 ||

### The Agneya (Fire) Circle
Pushya, Krittika, Vishakha, Bharani, Magha, and Purva Phalguni—this group is known as the Fiery Circle. It produces the following signs: || 12 ||

Falling stars and meteors appear, and the sky seems to be on fire, accompanied by glows in the quarters. For seven days, the wind blows accompanied by fire. || 13 ||

In a Fiery earthquake, there is the destruction of clouds, the drying up of water reservoirs, and enmity between kings. It brings skin diseases like herpes and scabies, as well as fevers, erysipelas, and jaundice. || 14 ||

Men of great luster and fierce temperament suffer, as do the people of Ashmaka, Anga, Bahlika, Tangana, Kalinga, Vanga, Dravida, and various tribes of Shabaras. || 15 ||

### The Aindra (Indra/Sky) Circle
Abhijit, Shravana, Dhanishtha, Rohini, Jyeshtha, Uttarashada, and Anuradha constitute the Circle of Indra. Its signs are as follows: || 16 ||

Clouds, as massive as moving mountains and roaring deeply, accompanied by lightning and resembling the color of buffalo horns, bees, or snakes, pour down water. || 17 ||

An earthquake in Indra's circle destroys famous kings and leaders of prominent families and castes. It leads to outbreaks of diarrhea, throat constriction, mouth diseases, and severe vomiting. || 18 ||

It causes distress to the regions of Kashi, Yugandhara, Paurava, Kirata, Kira, Abhisara, Hala, Madra, Arbuda, Suvastu, and Malwa, yet it brings beneficial rain. || 19 ||

It details the environmental omens and the specific social and regional impacts of earthquakes occurring under the Wind, Fire, and Indra circles.</summary>
