# Chapter 32: Signs of Earthquakes

The constellations of Revati, Ardra, Ashlesha, Mula, Shatabhisha, and Varuna <note>original: "Varuna-devani," referring to the deity of the waters</note> belong to the **Varuna Circle**. These are its signs: || 20 ||

Clouds appear with the luster of blue lotuses, bees, or collyrium <note>black eye pigment</note>, making sweet sounds and being very dense. Their bodies are illuminated by lightning, and they pour down streams of water like goads. || 21 ||

The Varuna earthquake brings dense clouds to oceans and rivers, yet it may result in a lack of rain <note>or "unseasonable rain"</note> and the cessation of hostilities. It strikes the people of Gonarda, Chedi, Kukura, Kirata, and Videha. || 22 ||

An earthquake yields its results within six months, while a "nirghata" <note>a thunder-like sound from the sky without clouds</note> ripens its effects in two. Other sages have described further calamities associated with these circles: || 23 ||

Meteors, the appearance of "Harishchandra-puram" <note>a fata morgana or illusory city in the sky</note>, dust storms, thunderous sounds, earthquakes, and the burning of the horizons; fierce winds, eclipses of the sun and moon, and unnatural movements of the constellations and stars; || 24 ||

Rain from a cloudless sky, or unnatural rain and wind; smoke and sparks or flames from the fire; wild animals entering the middle of the village; or the appearance of a rainbow <note>original: "Indra's bow"</note> at night; || 25 ||

Abnormalities in the twilight, fragments of halos around the sun or moon, rivers flowing backward, and the sound of trumpets in the sky. Any other natural phenomenon that is contrary to its usual nature should be judged according to these circles. || 26 ||

The Indra circle destroys the effects of the Vayu circle, and Vayu destroys Indra's; likewise, the Varuna and Agni circles counteract each other. Earthquakes born from the constellations of their respective periods are also affected. || 27 ||

The two circles of Vayu <note>Wind</note> and Agni <note>Fire</note> lead to the death of famous kings or great calamities. People are also tormented by hunger, fear, plague, and drought. || 28 ||

The circles of Varuna and Indra lead to abundance, welfare, rain, and joy in the world. Cows give a great abundance of milk, and kings cease their hostilities. || 29 ||

The Wind circle bears fruit in four fortnights, the Fire circle in three, the Indra circle in seven days, and the Varuna circle yields results immediately, provided no other time has been specified for these wonders. || 30 ||

The Wind shakes the earth for two hundred leagues <note>original: "yojanas"</note>, Fire for one hundred and ten, Varuna for eighty, and Indra for sixty. || 31 ||

If another earthquake occurs on the third, fourth, or seventh day, or after a month, a fortnight, or three fortnights, it portends the destruction of the principal king. || 32 ||

->**Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Signs of Earthquakes," in the Brihat Samhita of Shri Varahamihira.**<-

***

One school of thought says that earthquakes are caused by large creatures living in the water; others say they are caused by the resting of the <term>Diggajas</term> <note>the eight "Direction Elephants" who support the world</note> who have grown tired of carrying the weight of the earth. || 1 || Others say that when wind strikes wind and falls, it creates an earthquake accompanied by sound; and some say it is a cause of auspicious or inauspicious actions. Some teachers hold this view: In ancient times, the mountains used to fall from the sky to the earth and fly from the earth into the sky. Because of this falling and flying, the earth was shaken and, feeling ashamed before the gods, she spoke to Lord Brahma: "O Lord! You gave me the name <term>Achala</term> <note>The Immovable One</note>, but because of these moving mountains, I have become 'Sachala' (the moving one). Therefore, I cannot bear this suffering." || 2 || 3 || 4 || Hearing these choked words of the Earth, and seeing her face with trembling lips, slightly bowed, and eyes filled with tears, Brahma said: "O Indra! Remove the grief of the Earth. Bring your thunderbolt to clip the wings of the mountains." Indra said, "So be it," and told the Earth: "Have no fear. However, Vayu, Agni, Indra, and Varuna will shake you during the first, second, third, and fourth parts of the day and night to indicate good and bad fruits." || 5 || 6 || 7 || First, the constellations Uttara Phalguni, Hasta, Chitra, Swati, Revati, Mrigashira, and Ashwini constitute the **Vayu Circle**; its results manifest within one week. || 8 || In this circle, in a sky covered with smoke, the dust of the earth is blown about...

From an earthquake in the **Vayavya** <note>North-western or Airy circle</note> division, there is a depletion of grain, water, and forest herbs. Merchants suffer from swelling, asthma, insanity, fever, and coughs. || 10 || Handsome men, weapon-bearers, physicians, women, poets, singers, traders, and craftsmen are afflicted, as are the regions of Saurashtra, Kuru, Magadha, Dasharna, and Matsya. || 11 ||

The stars named Pushya, Agneya <note>Kruttika</note>, Vishakha, Bharani, Pitrya <note>Magha</note>, Aja <note>Purva Bhadrapada</note>, and Bhagya <note>Purva Phalguni</note> belong to the **Hutabhuj** <note>Fire/Agni</note> group. When an earthquake occurs in this **Agneya** <note>Fiery</note> group, there is destruction of clouds, drying up of reservoirs, hatred toward kings, and outbreaks of ringworm, scabies, fever, erysipelas, and jaundice. Abhijit, Shravana, Dhanishtha, Rohini, Jyeshtha, Uttarashadha, and Anuradha—these seven stars belong to the **Indra** <note>Lord of Heavens</note> circle. Their nature is such: clouds shaped like moving mountains, making deep sounds, accompanied by lightning, and as black as forests, buffaloes, bees, or snakes, pour down water. When an earthquake occurs in the Indra group, kings and leaders living near oceans and rivers are destroyed, and there is an outbreak of diarrhea, throat infections, mouth diseases, and vomiting. || 16 || 17 || 18 || The regions of Kashi, Yugandhara, Paurava, Kirata, Kira, Abhisara, Hala, Madra, Arbuda, Suvastu, and Malava suffer, though rain falls according to desire. || 19 ||

Revati, Purvashadha, Ardra, Ashlesha, Mula, Uttarabhadrapada, and Shatabhisha—these seven stars belong to the **Varuna** <note>Water deity</note> circle. Their appearance is like the blue lotus, bees, or collyrium, reflecting a brilliant luster. With bodies illuminated by lightning, many clouds making sweet sounds rain down in sprouts of water. || 20 || 21 ||

If an earthquake occurs in this Varuna circle, those seeking refuge in the sea and rivers are destroyed. It brings rain, is free from malice, but destroys the inhabitants of Gonarda, Chedi, Kukura, Kirata, and Videha. || 22 ||

The fruit of an earthquake ripens in six months; the fruit of a **nirghata** <note>a sudden thunderous sound in a clear sky</note> occurs in two months. Any other portents occurring in these circles will also yield their results within these two months. || 23 || Meteors, "cities of Gandharvas" <note>mirages</note>, dust storms, calamities, earthquakes, the burning of the quarters, fierce winds, and eclipses of the sun and moon are described as disturbances of the stars and planets. || 24 ||

Rain falling without clouds, unnatural changes, sparks of fire in flames, rain accompanied by wind, heat, wild animals entering villages, rainbows appearing at night, disturbances at twilight, halos, the reversal of river currents, and the sounding of trumpets in the sky—whatever other abnormalities occur in the world, their results are explained through these groups. || 25 || 26 ||

When the Indra circle strikes the Vayavya circle, or the Vayavya circle destroys the Indra group—similarly, if the Varuna and Agneya circles strike each other—it is called a **Vela-nakshatra-jata** <note>time-star-born</note> quake. || 27 || From the collision of the Agneya and Vayavya circles, a famous king dies or falls into calamity, and men suffer from hunger, plague, and lack of rain. From the collision of the Varuna and **Paurandara** <note>Indra</note> circles, there is abundance, auspicious rain, and affection; cows give much milk, and kings abandon their mutual animosity. || 28 || 29 ||

For disturbances like the twitching of limbs where the timing of the result is not stated: if they occur in the Vayavya circle, the result happens within two months; in the Agni group, within three fortnights; in the Indra group, after a week; and the Varuna group yields results quickly. || 30 || The wind group [affects] two hundred leagues...

### Now Begins the Thirty-Third Chapter

#### Characteristics of Meteors <note>original: *Ulka-lakshanam*</note>

Meteors are the forms of those who, having exhausted the fruits of their merit in heaven, are now falling. They are divided into five types: *Dhishnya* (fireballs), *Ulka* (meteors), *Ashani* (thunderbolts), *Vidyut* (lightning), and *Tara* (falling stars). || 1 || A meteor yields its fruit <note>the predicted event</note> within a fortnight; similarly, a fireball and a thunderbolt yield results within three fortnights. Lightning gives results in six days, and a falling star does the same. || 2 || A falling star is said to give one-quarter of the predicted result, and a fireball gives half. The other three—lightning, meteors, and thunderbolts—give the full result. || 3 ||

A thunderbolt <note>original: *Ashani*</note> falls with a great roar upon men, elephants, horses, wild animals, stones, houses, trees, and cattle; it is circular in shape and tears open the surface of the earth. || 4 || Lightning <note>original: *Vidyut*</note> causes terror to living beings, making a crackling sound; it is crooked, wide, and falls suddenly, ignited upon piles of fuel or living creatures. || 5 || A fireball <note>original: *Dhishnya*</note> has a thin tail and is seen for a distance of ten cubits <note>original: *dhanushi*</note> or more; it resembles a glowing coal and is two cubits in size. || 6 ||

A falling star <note>original: *Tara*</note> is one cubit long, white or copper-colored like a lotus fiber; it moves horizontally, downwards, or upwards in the sky as if being carried by the wind. || 7 || A meteor <note>original: *Ulka*</note> is wide at the head and grows as it falls, with a very thin tail; it is as long as a man, and many varieties of it exist. || 8 || Those shaped like ghosts, weapons, donkeys, young camels, crocodiles, monkeys, tusks, tails, or deer are inauspicious, as are those resembling iguanas, smoke, or those with two heads. || 9 ||

Those resembling a banner, fish, elephant, mountain, lotus, moon, horse, molten silver, or a swan—or shaped like the *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious mark</note>, a thunderbolt, a conch, or a swastika—bring peace and plenty. || 10 || Many meteors falling from the middle of the sky portend the destruction of the king and the nation. If they wander aimlessly above the sky, they indicate public confusion. || 11 || If they touch the Sun or Moon, or emerge from them, or are accompanied by clouds and tremors, they cause fear of foreign invasion, the death of a king, famine, and lack of rain. || 12 ||

A meteor passing to the left of the Sun or Moon destroys those outside the city; one passing to the right is auspicious for a traveler if it emerges from the front of the Sun. || 13 || White, red, yellow, and black meteors destroy the four castes <note>Brahmins, etc.</note> respectively, depending on whether the color is at the head, sides, or tail. || 14 || A rough meteor falling from the North or other cardinal directions is harmful to the respective castes; however, if it is straight, glossy, unbroken, and falls low, it brings prosperity to them. || 15 ||

Meteors that are dark, blue, blood-red, or the color of black ash, rough, appearing at twilight, or crooked and broken, indicate fear of an enemy invasion. || 16 || If they strike a lunar mansion <note>original: *Nakshatra*</note> or a planet, they indicate the destruction of the people associated with them. If they strike the Sun or Moon at sunrise or sunset, they portend the death of the king or his subjects. || 17 || If the mansions of *Purva Phalguni*, *Rohini*, *Dhanishtha*, or *Mula* are struck by a meteor, it harms young women. If *Pushya*, *Sravana*, or *Swati* are struck, it harms Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and traders. || 18 || If the "fixed" or "gentle" mansions are struck, it harms kings; if the "fierce" or "sharp" mansions are struck, it harms thieves.

# The Varahi Samhita

When [meteors] strike the <term>Kshipra</term> <note>refers to a specific group of lunar mansions or "Nakshatras" characterized as "swift"</note> and those skilled in the arts, it causes distress; the same occurs when they strike the <term>Sadharana</term> <note>the "ordinary" or "mixed" lunar mansions</note> stars. || 19 || If these fall upon the idols of deities, they bring fear to the King and the nation. If they fall upon the <term>Indradhvaja</term> <note>the ceremonial banner of Indra</note>, they cause suffering to kings; if upon houses, to their masters. || 20 || If a meteor strikes a particular direction, it harms the countries in that quarter and those engaged in agriculture on the threshing floors. Falling upon a <term>Chaitya</term> tree <note>a sacred fig or a tree serving as a local shrine</note>, it causes distress to those who are honored or virtuous. || 21 || If it falls at the city gate, the city faces destruction; if upon the <term>Indrakila</term> <note>the main pillar or threshold of a city gate</note>, it is said to cause the death of the people. Falling upon a temple of Brahma, it destroys the Brahmins; in a cow-pen, it destroys the cattle-owners. || 22 || When sounds of hissing, clapping, musical instruments, singing, or loud shouting are heard at the time of a meteor's fall, it portends fear for the nation and its King. || 23 || A meteor that remains visible in the sky for a long time in the shape of a staff brings fear to the King. So too does one that appears suspended in the sky as if held by a thread, or one that resembles the Great Banner of Indra. || 24 || One that moves backward harms the merchant class; one that moves horizontally harms the wives of kings. One that falls vertically downward destroys kings, while one that moves upward destroys the Brahmins. || 25 || One shaped like a peacock's tail brings about the destruction of the people. One that glides like a serpent brings misfortune to women. || 26 || A circular meteor destroys the city; one shaped like a parasol destroys the royal priest. One that appears like a thicket of bamboo causes defects and harm to the nation. || 27 || One resembling a wild beast or a boar, or one adorned with a garland of sparks, or one that breaks into pieces or falls with a great noise, brings sin and calamity. || 28 || One resembling the bow of Indra <note>a rainbow</note> that dissolves in the sky destroys the clouds. One that moves against the wind, or travels a crooked path, or turns back, is not considered auspicious. || 29 || From whichever direction a meteor overcomes a city or an army, fear will come to the King from that very direction. However, if a King marches toward the direction where a meteor falls with a bright glow, he will soon conquer his enemies. || 30 ||

### Thus ends the Thirty-Third Chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Meteors," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 33 ||

Meteors are the forms of those who, having enjoyed the fruits of their merits in heaven, are now falling [to be reborn]. There are five types of meteors: <term>Dhishnya</term>, <term>Ulka</term> (Meteor), <term>Ashani</term> (Thunderbolt), <term>Vidyut</term> (Lightning), and <term>Tara</term> (Star). || 1 || The effects of an *Ulka* manifest in 15 days; similarly, the *Dhishnya* and *Ashani* manifest in three fortnights (45 days); and the effects of a *Tara* or *Vidyut* occur within six days. || 2 || A *Tara* gives one-quarter of the predicted result, a *Dhishnya* gives half, while *Vidyut*, *Ulka*, and *Vajra* (Thunderbolt) give the full result. || 3 || The *Ashani* is shaped like a wheel; with a great sound, it tears the earth and falls upon men, elephants, horses, deer, stones, houses, trees, and cattle. || 4 || Making a *tad-tad* sound, the *Vidyut* (lightning) suddenly causes terror to living beings; it is crooked, vast, and burning as it falls upon creatures and heaps of fuel. || 5 || The *Dhishnya* has a thin, small tail, resembles a glowing ember, and is seen for a distance of a little more than ten bows <note>approx. 60 feet</note>; its size is two cubits. || 6 || A *Tara* (falling star) is copper-colored, lotus-colored, wire-like, or white; its width is one cubit. It moves horizontally or slightly upward in the sky as if being pulled. || 7 || The *Ulka* has a very thin tail but a large body; it grows as it falls, but its tail becomes smaller. Its length is equal to that of a man, and it has many varieties. || 8 || Sometimes it takes the shape of a corpse, a weapon, an ass, a camel, a crocodile, a monkey, a tusked animal, or a deer. Sometimes it appears as a monitor lizard, a snake, or smoke, or with two heads. These forms are sinful/inuspicious. || 9 || Sometimes it appears like a banner, a fish, an elephant, a mountain, a lotus, the moon, a horse, glowing dust, or a swan; or it shines in the form of a <term>Shrivatsa</term> <note>an auspicious mark</note>, a thunderbolt, a conch, or a swastika. All these are heralds of welfare and abundance. || 10 || However, meteors of many forms, wandering constantly in the sky, fall from the heavens...

# Chapter 33: With Hindi Commentary
### Page 119

If a meteor touches the Moon or the Sun and falls from them, or if the earth trembles at that moment, then the city will fall under the control of a foreign king; it signifies the death of a monarch, famine, drought, and terrifying times. || 12 || If a meteor falls to the right of the Sun or the Moon, it destroys those who dwell in the forests. If a meteor emerging from the Sun <note>original: "divakara," a name for the Sun</note> comes directly toward a traveler, it is auspicious for their journey. || 13 ||

Meteors of white, red, yellow, and black colors destroy the four classes of society <note>the varna system</note> respectively. Even if these colors are situated in the head, chest, sides, or tail of the meteor, they still destroy the four classes—starting with Brahmins—in that same order. || 14 || If a meteor falls harshly in the directions starting from the North in a clockwise manner, it destroys the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively. However, if the meteor is straight, smooth, unbroken, and moves through the lower part of the sky, it brings prosperity to the aforementioned classes. || 15 ||

The falling of a meteor that is dark, reddish-brown, blue, blood-red, fiery, black, or dry like ash—whether it appears during the twilight or during the day, or if it is crooked or fragmented—is a cause for fear of the enemy. || 16 || If a meteor causes a "star-strike" <term>Nakshatraghata: the striking or occultation of a lunar mansion by a meteor</term> or a "planet-strike" <term>Grahaghata: the striking of a planet</term>, then the devotion or prosperity previously mentioned is destroyed, and the specific objects associated with those stars perish. If a meteor strikes the Sun or Moon at the time of rising or setting, forest-dwellers are killed. || 17 ||

If a meteor strikes the junction-stars of the lunar mansions <note>Nakshatras</note> of Purva Phalguni, Punarvasu, Dhanishta, or Mula, young women will suffer. If it strikes Pushya, Swati, or Shravana, Brahmins and Kshatriyas will suffer. || 18 || If a meteor afflicts Rohini, the three Uttaras <note>Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, Uttara Bhadrapada</note>, Mrigashira, Chitra, Anuradha, or Revati <note>referred to here as 'kheti' or agriculture-related</note>, then kings will suffer. If a meteor strikes the three Purvas <note>Purva Phalguni, Purva Ashadha, Purva Bhadrapada</note>, Bharani, Magha, Ardra, Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, or Mula, then thieves will suffer. If Ashwini, Pushya, Abhijit, Krittika, or Vishakha are pierced by a meteor, then those who know the arts, such as singing and dancing, will suffer. || 19 ||

If a meteor falls upon the idol of a deity, it portends danger to the King and the Kingdom. If it falls on the Banner of Indra <note>Indradhwaja: a ceremonial festival pole</term>, it brings pain to kings; if it falls inside a house, it brings suffering to the masters of the house. || 20 || If a meteor falls upon a house belonging to the guardian of a specific direction, it affects the residents of that direction. If it falls in a threshing floor, it harms farmers. If a meteor falls on a tree planted near a small temple, it brings suffering to holy men <note>Sadhus</note>. || 21 ||

If a meteor falls on the city gate, the city will decline. If it falls upon the "Indra-bolt" <term>Indrakila: the main pillar or bolt of a city gate</term>, it is said to cause the destruction of men. If it falls on a temple of Brahma, it kills Brahmins, and if it falls in a cowshed, it kills many wealthy cattle-owners. || 22 || If at the time of a meteor's fall there is the sound of a "Shveda" <note>the lion-like roar of a warrior during battle</note>, or loud sounds of clapping, instrumental music, singing, or wailing, then there is fear for the kingdom and its ruler. || 23 ||

A meteor that takes the shape of a staff and remains in the sky for a long time is a cause of fear for kings. One that stays in the sky as if suspended by a string, or appears like the Banner of Indra, is also dangerous to the King. || 24 || A meteor that moves in reverse—that is, returns to the place from which it emerged—causes fear to merchants <note>Sheths</note>. A crooked-moving meteor destroys queens; one with its "face" pointing downward destroys kings; and one moving upward destroys Brahmins. || 25 || A meteor shaped like a peacock's tail causes the destruction of people, and one that moves like a snake brings misfortune to women. || 26 ||

A meteor in the shape of a circle destroys the city; one shaped like an umbrella destroys the priest; and one shaped like a bamboo bundle creates defects in the country. || 27 || If a meteor appears shaped like a serpent, a boar, or is accompanied by sparks, or is lump-shaped, or moves with a loud noise, it is a bringer of sin and misfortune. || 28 || If it resembles a rainbow, it destroys the kingdom; if it vanishes into the sky, it destroys the clouds; and if it moves crookedly against the direction of the wind...

# The Varahi Samhita

If a meteor travels toward a certain direction and then returns, it is not an auspicious sign. <note>verse 29</note> From whichever direction a meteor falls upon a city or an army, the King will face danger from that specific direction. However, if a meteor falls while illuminating a certain direction and the King marches toward that direction, he will soon be capable of conquering his enemies. <note>verse 30</note>

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baladevprasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the great teacher Sri Varahamihira.

### Now Begins the Thirty-Fourth Chapter
->Characteristics of Halos<-

The rays of the Sun and Moon, when displaced by the wind and formed into a circular shape, appearing in various colors and forms in a sky filled with thin clouds, are called <term>Parivesha</term> <note>halos or atmospheric circles around celestial bodies</note>. <note>verse 1</note> These halos may be red, blue, pale, pigeon-colored, cloud-like, variegated, green, or white. They are created respectively by Indra, Yama, Varuna, Nirriti, Vayu, Brahma, and Agni. <note>verse 2; these are the directional deities</note>

Kubera <note>the god of wealth</note> creates a blackish halo. Others are formed by the combination of these qualities. A halo created by the wind vanishes frequently and yields little result. <note>verse 3</note> A halo that resembles the color of a blue jay, a peacock’s neck, silver, oil, milk, or water, appearing in its proper season, perfectly circular and glossy, brings peace and abundance of food. <note>verse 4</note>

A halo that spans the entire sky, has multiple colors, resembles blood, or appears rough and dry is inauspicious. Similarly, one shaped like an incomplete cart, a bow, or a <term>shringataka</term> <note>a triangular nut or a crossroad shape</note> is considered evil. <note>verse 5</note> A halo colored like a peacock's throat brings excessive rain; one with many colors indicates the death of a king; a smoky one brings fear; one resembling a rainbow indicates war, as does one with the color of Ashoka flowers. <note>verse 6</note>

When a halo is of a single color, thick, glossy, and surrounded by clouds shaped like razors, it brings immediate rain. A yellow halo with a blazing sun does the same. <note>verse 7</note> If birds and wild animals cry out toward a blazing sun, and a very large, murky halo rises during the three periods of twilight, it brings fear. If struck by lightning or meteors, it indicates the king will be killed by a weapon. <note>verse 8</note>

If the Sun and Moon appear red day and night for a long time while surrounded by halos, or if they are frequently encircled while rising, setting, or in the mid-sky, it foretells the death of the sovereign. <note>verse 9</note> A double halo brings fear to the commander-in-chief but does not cause much conflict with weapons. A triple halo or more indicates war, danger to the crown prince, or the siege of a city. <note>verse 10</note>

If a planet, the Moon, or a constellation is obstructed within the halo, there will be rain within three days or a month, or else a conflict. A halo appearing in the <term>Hora</term> <note>astrological hour</note>, the ascendant of birth, or the birth star is inauspicious for the King. <note>verse 11</note> Saturn situated within the halo destroys small grains, causes wind and rain, and kills those who depend on the earth and agriculture. <note>verse 12</note>

When Mars enters the halo, there is a retreat of the prince’s and commander’s armies, and fear of fire and weapons. When Jupiter is in the halo, the royal priest, ministers, and the King suffer. <note>verse 13</note> Mercury in the halo brings prosperity to ministers, landowners, and scribes, along with good rain. Venus in the halo brings suffering to traveling warriors and kings, but food remains dear. <note>verse 14</note>

Fear arises from hunger, fire, death, and the King's weapons when Ketu is in the halo. Rahu in the halo indicates danger to pregnancies, disease, and fear of the King. <note>verse 15</note> Know that wars occur when two planets are within the halo. If three are present—including the Sun or Moon—fear of famine and rain is foretold. <note>verse 16</note>

If four planets are present, the King, along with his ministers and priest, falls into the clutches of death. If five or more planets are within the circle, know it to be like the destruction of the world. <note>verse 17</note> A halo rising separately around a star-planet <note>non-luminary planets like Mars or Venus</note> or a constellation causes the death of the King, provided Ketu is not visible. <note>verse 18</note>

From the first day of the lunar fortnight onwards, the halo affects Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively. From the fifth day onwards, it is inauspicious for guilds, cities, and treasuries. <note>verse 19</note> On the eighth day, it affects the crown prince, and for the three days following that, it affects the King...

# Chapter 34: Characteristics of Halos

...is harmful. A halo on the twelfth day of the lunar month causes a siege of the city; on the thirteenth day, it causes turmoil in the army. ||20||
A halo appearing on the fourteenth day causes suffering to the King's wife. If it appears on the fifteenth day <note>the full moon or new moon</note>, it causes suffering to the Sovereign himself. ||21||
The inner line of the halo's circle should be understood to affect the city-dwellers, while the outer line affects those who are traveling or outside. The middle line affects the "crying" <note>those seeking protection or the common folk</note>. ||22||
Those whose portion of the halo is red, dark, or rough will face defeat. Those whose portion is glossy, white, and radiant will achieve victory. ||23||

->Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, named "Characteristics of Halos," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the illustrious Varahamihira. <-

When the rays of the sun or moon are reflected upon the vapors and, driven by the wind into a circular shape, appear in various colors and forms in a sky with few clouds, they are called a <term>Parivesha</term> <note>a halo or atmospheric corona</note>. ||1||
Halos that are red, blue, slightly white, pigeon-colored, cloud-colored, variegated (multi-colored), green, and bright white are produced respectively by the deities Indra, Yama, Varuna, Nirriti, Vayu, Mahadeva, Brahma, and Agni. ||2||
Kubera, the giver of wealth, produces a black-colored halo. A halo that repeatedly dissolves due to the interaction of the elements is caused by Vayu (the wind god) and yields little result. ||3||
A halo that has the luster of a peacock's neck, silver, oil, milk, or water, appears in its proper season, is an unbroken circle, and is glossy, brings about abundance and auspiciousness. ||4||
A halo that moves across the entire sky, has many lusters, looks like blood, is rough, or shaped like a broken cart, a bow, or a triangle, is considered sinful and ominous. ||5||
If the halo is like a peacock's neck, there will be excessive rain. If it is multi-colored, the King will be killed. A smoke-colored halo brings fear. If it is radiant like a rainbow or an Ashoka flower, war will occur. ||6||
In whatever season a halo is very glossy with a single color, surrounded by small clouds shaped like razors, or if the sun's rays appear yellow, rain will come quickly. ||7||
A very large halo appearing during the three periods of twilight <note>dawn, noon, and dusk</note>, accompanied by the cries of birds and beasts facing the sun, is terrifying. However, if this halo is pierced by a meteor or lightning, the King will die by a weapon. ||8||
If a halo appears around the sun or moon every day and night, the King is killed. Even if multiple halos appear in a single day—at sunrise, sunset, or midday—the result is the same: the death of the King. ||9||
A halo with two concentric circles is frightening for the commander-in-chief but does not cause extreme violence by weapons. A halo with three or more circles causes weapon-strife, danger to the Crown Prince, and the siege of the city. ||10||
If any planet like Mars, the Moon, or a constellation is within a halo, rain occurs in three days or war within a month. If the halo occurs during the King's birth constellation or the ruling sign of his horoscope, it is inauspicious for him. ||11||
If Saturn is within the halo's circle, it destroys small grains and, by killing farmers and stationary beings, produces rain accompanied by wind. ||12||
If <insert>Mars</insert> is in the halo, there will be distress for the prince, the commander, and the army, and fear of fire and weapons. If Jupiter is in the halo, the priests, ministers, and kings suffer. ||13||
If Mercury is in the halo, there is prosperity for ministers, permanent residents, and scribes, and good rain occurs. If Venus is in the halo, kings who are on the march and the warrior class (Kshatriyas) suffer, and famine occurs. ||14||
If Ketu is in the halo, fear arises from hunger, fire, death, the king, and weapons. If Rahu is in the halo, there is danger to pregnancies, disease, and fear of the king. ||15||
The halos of the Sun and Moon...

If two planets are within the halo, a war occurs; if three planets are in the halo, there is fear of famine and a lack of rain. || 16 || If there are four planets in the halo, the King may die along with his minister and priest; if five or more planets are in the circle, it is as if the world faces dissolution <note>Pralaya: the cosmic destruction at the end of an eon</note>. || 17 || If the star-planets—namely Mars and the others—or groups of lunar mansions <note>Nakshatras</note> appear in separate halos, the King is usually assassinated. However, if a comet <note>Ketu</note> has not risen, and then a comet does rise, its specific fruit takes precedence over the effects of the star-planets. || 18 || If a halo appears on the dates from the first to the fourth of the lunar fortnight, then in that order, the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras <note>The four traditional social classes</note> are destroyed. From the fifth to the seventh date, it is inauspicious for guilds, cities, and the royal treasury. || 19 || If a halo occurs on the eighth date, there is trouble from all sides; if it occurs in the three dates following that, the King is at fault. A halo on the twelfth date leads to the siege of the city, and on the thirteenth, it causes agitation from weapons <note>warfare</note>. || 20 || A halo on the fourteenth date causes suffering to the Queen; on the fifteenth <note>Full or New Moon</note>, it causes suffering to the King. || 21 || If a line is seen inside the halo, the city dwellers suffer; if the line is outside the halo, the attacking kings suffer; if it is in the middle, one should judge the good or bad fortune of the "cry of help" <note>Akrandasara: likely referring to the strength of allies or those coming to the rescue</note>. || 22 || By dividing the country according to planetary devotion or the "Tortoise Division" <note>Kurma-vibhaga: an ancient method of mapping the geography of India onto the body of a cosmic tortoise</note>, the region where the halo appears red, dark, or rough will face defeat. Those regions where the halo is glossy, white, or brilliant will be victorious. || 23 ||

# Chapter Thirty-Five

## Characteristics of Indra’s Weapon (The Rainbow)

The multi-colored rays of the sun, when struck by the wind in a cloudy sky, appear in the form of a bow; that is the Rainbow <note>Indradhanush: literally "Indra's Bow"</note>. || 1 || Some teachers say it is produced by the breath of the infinite lineage of serpents <note>Ananta-kula-uraga: mythical snakes associated with the underworld and atmosphere</note>. For those setting out on a journey, seeing it directly in front of them brings defeat. || 2 || A rainbow that is unbroken, touching the earth, bright, glossy, thick, multi-colored, and appearing as a double reflection in the same direction is considered excellent and bestows rain. || 3 || If it appears in the intermediate directions, it destroys the lords of those directions; if it appears in a cloudless sky, it causes plague. Reddish-pink, yellow, and blue colors bring faults caused by weapons, fire, and hunger respectively. || 4 || If seen in the middle of water, it means a lack of rain; on the ground, the destruction of crops; if situated on a tree, disease. On an anthill, it brings fear of weapons; at night, the rainbow of Indra signifies the killing of a minister. || 5 || During a drought, the rainbow brings rain; during a rainy period, it stops the rain. After the rain, the bow of the thunderbolt-bearer <note>Indra</note> always indicates more rain. || 6 || A rainbow at night in the East causes suffering to the King. If it arises in the South, West, or North, it kills the General, the Leader, and the Minister respectively. || 7 || A white-colored rainbow at night causes suffering to the Brahmins and others. In whichever direction it is visible, it shall soon destroy the chief of kings in that region. || 8 ||

->Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, named "Characteristics of Indra’s Weapon," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 35 ||<-

The multi-colored rays of the sun, obstructed by the wind, appear in the shape of a bow in the cloudy sky—this is the rainbow. || 1 || Some teachers say that it is born from the breath of the great serpents named Ananta...

It is produced from the breath <note>original: "श्वास" (shvasa); referring to the breath of the sun or atmospheric vapors</note>. If a rainbow appears in a cloudless sky, a plague or epidemic follows. If it is the color of a trumpet-flower <note>pale red/pink</note>, yellow, or blue, then calamities involving weapons, fire, and famine arise. ||4|| A rainbow appearing in water indicates a drought; on the earth, it means loss of grain; on a tree, it signifies disease; on an anthill <note>original: "वल्मीक" (valmika)</note>, it brings fear of weapons; and at night, it causes the death of a minister. ||5|| If a rainbow appears in the East during a drought, it brings rain; if it appears in the East during the rainy season, it stops the rain. If a rainbow appears in the West, it always brings rain. ||6|| A rainbow in the East at night causes suffering for kings. A rainbow rising from the South, West, or North destroys the commander-in-chief, the leader, and the minister. ||7|| If a rainbow at night is white, red, yellow, or black, it destroys the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras <note>The four traditional social classes of ancient India</note> respectively. However, the kings of whichever direction the rainbow appears in will soon face destruction. ||8||

# Now Begins the Thirty-Sixth Chapter

## Celestial Cities <note>original: "गंधर्वनगरम्" (Gandharva-nagaram); literally 'City of the Gandharvas,' referring to complex mirages or Fata Morgana in the sky</note>

> **If a celestial city appears in the North and other directions, it brings misfortune to the priest, the king, the army commander, and the crown prince respectively. If it is white, red, yellow, or black, it leads to the destruction of the Brahmins and the other classes. ||1|| If located in the North, it brings victory to the city and the king. If located in the intermediate directions <note>Northeast, Southeast, etc.</note>, it causes the destruction of the low-born. If seen in a peaceful direction with ornamental arches <note>taranas</note>, it signifies victory for the king. ||2|| If it rises in all directions or remains constantly visible, it brings fear to kings and their nations. If it resembles smoke, fire, or a rainbow, it kills thieves and forest-dwellers. ||3|| A pale white celestial city brings lightning strikes and wind. If it is glowing, the king dies; if on the left, there is fear of enemies; if on the right, there is victory. ||4|| When a city appears in the sky with many colors and shapes, adorned with banners, flags, and arches, then the earth drinks the blood of many elephants, men, and horses in battle. ||5||**

**Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Celestial Cities," in the Brihat Samhita by Sri Varahamihira. ||36||**

If a celestial city appears in the North, East, South, or West, it brings obstacles to the priest, king, commander, and crown prince respectively. If it is white, red, yellow, or black, it causes the destruction of the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras. ||1|| In the North, it grants victory to cities and kings. If situated in the Northeast, Southeast, or Northwest corners, the lower classes are destroyed. If a celestial city with arches is seen in a peaceful direction, the king will be victorious. ||2|| A celestial city that appears constantly in all directions is terrifying for both the king and the kingdom; if it looks like smoke, fire, or a rainbow, it strikes down thieves and forest-dwellers...

# Chapter 37
->Characteristics of the Mock Sun<-

> **A mock sun <term>Pratisurya: a parhelion or "mock sun" caused by ice crystals in the atmosphere</term> is auspicious if it possesses the color and brilliance of the sun of that season, is glossy, clear like a beryl stone, and white; such brings well-being and abundance. || 1 || If yellow, it produces disease; if it bears the color of an Ashoka flower <note>bright red</note>, it leads to the fury of weapons (war). A "garland" of mock suns—that is, the rising of many mock suns—destroys through fear of thieves, terror, and the death of the king. || 2 || A mock sun situated to the north of the sun brings rain; to the south, it brings wind. If situated on both sides, there is danger from floods. If situated above the sun, it destroys the king; if below, it destroys the people. || 3 ||**

**Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, named the Circle of Mock Suns, in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 37 ||**

If the mock sun is the same color as the sun in its respective season, and is similarly glossy, clear as a beryl gem, and white-red in hue, it brings peace and a good harvest. || 1 || If it is yellow, it creates illness; if it takes the color of an Ashoka flower, it causes the "fury of weapons" (conflict). If a "garland" of mock suns appears—meaning many mock suns rise at once—it results in fear of bandits, panic, and the ruin of the king. || 2 || If the mock sun is in the north, it rains water; if in the south, it moves the winds; if in both directions, there is fear of water (floods). If positioned above, it destroys the king, and if below, it destroys the common people. || 3 ||

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter <note>Original text says "सप्तविंशो" (27th) but context and numerals confirm 37th.</note> in the Hindi commentary of the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra of Moradabad. || 37 ||

# Chapter 38
->Characteristics of Dust<-

> **They say the destruction of the ruler is foretold by dust that resembles a mass of thick darkness, by which mountains, cities, and trees become invisible and all directions are covered. || 1 || In whichever direction the mass of dust first arises or in whichever direction it perishes, fear will certainly arrive in that very place within seven days; of this there is no doubt. || 2 || When a thick cloud of dust is white, there will be suffering for the ministers and the populace. Before long, weapons will be provoked (war), but success will be achieved through great difficulty. || 3 || If at sunrise the dust expands for one or even two days, as if veiling the surface of the sky, it announces a most terrible fear. || 4 || If it carries a continuous accumulation for one full night, it kills the principal king; for the remaining wise men, it brings peace...**

...of kings. ||5|| In whichever kingdom a thick cloud of dust spreads for two consecutive nights, the arrival of an enemy army <note>original: "parachakrasya-gamanam"</note> should be understood as imminent. ||6|| If the dust falls for three or four nights, it leads to the destruction of blindness <note>likely referring to a loss of vision or metaphorical darkness/ignorance</note>. If the dust persists for five nights, there will be turmoil in the kings' armies. ||7|| When dust is released from the rising of comets <note>term: Ketu (comets or meteors)</note> and similar phenomena, it brings intense fear. The Teachers <note>referring to ancient sages/authorities</note> say this result is fully realized in seasons other than the cool season <note>term: Shishira (late winter/cool season)</note>. ||8||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Dust," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. ||38||

When a mass of dust, like a thick group of darkness, covers all directions such that mountains, cities, or trees are not visible, then know for certain that the King will be destroyed. ||1|| In whichever direction the mass of dust is first seen, or in whichever direction that dust first subsides, fear will undoubtedly arrive there within seven days. ||2|| If the cloud-like mass of dust is white in color, it causes distress to ministers and the rural districts <note>term: Janapada (inhabited territories or administrative districts)</note>. Conflict with weapons arrives quickly, and tasks are accomplished only with great difficulty. ||3|| If, at the time of sunrise, dust covers and illuminates the sky for one or two days, it is said to be a matter of grave fear. ||4|| If dust continues to accumulate for one full night, the primary King dies, though it brings auspicious results for the remaining wise kings. ||5|| In a country where thick dust spreads for two consecutive nights, it should be well understood that another king will rule that land. ||6|| If dust continues to fall for three or four nights, grain and juices <note>referring to essential fluids or sap/essences</note> are destroyed; if it falls for five nights, there is chaos in the kings' armies. ||7|| If dust falls after the rising of comets (Ketu) etc., there is intense fear. The Teachers say that this has a greater effect in seasons other than the cool season. ||8||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the Hindi commentary on the Brihat Samhita, composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. ||38||

# Chapter Thirty-Nine
## Characteristics of Atmospheric Concussions <note>term: Nirghata (a sudden noise in the sky, often interpreted as a thunder-clap or atmospheric explosion without clouds)</note>

When wind, struck by wind, falls from the sky to the earth, it is then called a "Nirghata." It is sinful/ominous if accompanied by the cries of birds facing the sun. ||1|| If it occurs at sunrise, it destroys judges <note>term: Adhikaranika (officials or magistrates)</note>, kings, the wealthy, warriors, women, merchants, and courtesans. If it occurs during the first part of the day <note>term: Praharansha (a division of time, roughly 3 hours)</note>, it strikes goat-herders, the laboring class <note>term: Shudra</note>, and city-dwellers. ||2|| Until midday, it troubles those who serve the king and the priestly class <note>term: Brahmins</note>. In the third part of the day, it affects the merchant class <note>term: Vaishyas</note> and clouds; in the fourth part, it affects thieves. ||3|| After sunset, in the first watch of the night, it destroys the lowly and the crops. In the second watch of the night, it oppresses those who resemble ghosts <note>term: Pishacha (spirits or demons)</note>. ||4|| In the third watch, it destroys horses and elephants, and in the fourth, those who are traveling. From whichever direction the terrifying, cracking sound comes, it destroys that direction. ||5||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Atmospheric Concussions," in the Brihat Samhita by Sri Varahamihira. ||39||

When wind collides with wind and falls to the earth, it is called a Nirghata. If birds cry out while facing the sun during that concussion, it is an omen of sin. ||1|| If a Nirghata occurs at sunrise, then judges, kings, the wealthy, warriors, women, merchants, and courtesans are destroyed. If it lasts until the first watch, then goat-herders, the laboring class, and...

### Now begins the Fortieth Chapter
### The Birth of Crops <note>Sasya-jataka: The astrological study of crop yields and agricultural success</note>

These are the auspicious and inauspicious combinations for the summer and autumn crops, as stated by the sage Badarayana <note>An ancient authority often cited by Varahamihira</note>, based on the entry of the Sun into the signs of Scorpio and Taurus. || 1 || When the Sun enters Scorpio, if the angles <note><term>Kendras</term>: The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses in a horoscope, considered the pillars of a chart</note> are occupied by or aspected by powerful benefic planets, there is an increase in the summer crops. || 2 || When the Sun is in the eighth sign, and Jupiter and the Moon are in Aquarius and Leo, or both are in Leo and Aquarius, the summer crop reaches completion. || 3 ||

If Venus or Mercury (or both together) are in the second house from the Sun, or even in the twelfth house, the crop reaches completion, especially if aspected by Jupiter. || 4 || If the Sun in Scorpio is placed between benefics, and Jupiter and the Moon are in the seventh house, there is supreme prosperity. If the Sun is in the first house and Jupiter is in the second, there is half-completion of the crop. || 5 || If Venus, the Moon, and Mercury are in the eleventh, fourth, or second houses from the Sun in Scorpio, there is supreme prosperity of the crop; if Jupiter is in the tenth house, there is prosperity for the cattle. || 6 ||

If Jupiter is in Aquarius, the Moon in Taurus, the Sun at the beginning of Scorpio, and Mars and Saturn are in Capricorn, there is a great harvest, but later there is fear of foreign armies and disease. || 7 || If the Sun in Scorpio is between two malefic planets, it destroys the crop. A malefic in the seventh house destroys the crop as soon as it is born. || 8 || A cruel planet <note>malefic</note> in the second house, not aspected by benefics, destroys the first-born crop; however, the crop sown later will clearly reach completion. || 9 ||

If two malefic planets are in the seventh house or the angles from the Sun in Scorpio, they cause the ruin of the crop, unless they are aspected by benefics. || 10 || When two malefic planets are in the seventh and sixth houses from the Sun in Scorpio, there is a loss of half the crop yield. || 11 || By this same method, the destruction or welfare of the autumn crops should be known by experts when the Sun enters Taurus. || 12 ||

When the Sun moves through the three signs starting with Aries, joined or aspected by benefics, it makes the summer grain abundant and fit for use. || 13 || Similarly, when the Sun is in Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, it affects the autumn crop; however, at the time of harvest, the opposite should be understood if there are malefic aspects or conjunctions. || 14 ||

->Thus ends the fortieth chapter, named "The Birth of Crops," in the Brihat Samhita by Sri Varahamihira. || 40 ||<-

At the time of the Sun's entry into the sign <note>Scorpio is implied by context</note>, if all its cardinal houses—namely Scorpio, Aquarius, Taurus, and Leo—are occupied by auspicious planets or aspected by powerful auspicious planets, then the summer grain crops will flourish. || 2 || When the Sun enters the eighth sign (Scorpio), if at that time Jupiter is in Aquarius and the Moon is in Leo, or if Jupiter is in Leo and the Moon is in Aquarius, the grain produced in summer increases. || 3 || If Venus or Mercury moves into the second sign from the Sun, or if they both enter the twelfth sign from the Sun simultaneously, the grain will be similarly abundant; and if there is an aspect from Jupiter upon them, that grain will be of excellent quality. || 4 || If there are two auspicious planets on either side of the Sun while it is in Scorpio, and the Moon and Jupiter are in the seventh house from it, there will be a very excellent harvest. and if Jupiter is in the tenth house <term>Karma</term><note>The 10th house in astrology, relating to action and results</note>, great prosperity is obtained for the cattle. || 6 || At the time the Sun enters Scorpio, if Jupiter is in Aquarius, the Moon in Taurus, and Mars and Saturn are in Capricorn, the grain grows well, but later there is a fear of foreign invasions <term>Parachakra</term> and disease. || 7 || If the Sun in Scorpio is situated between two malefic planets, it destroys the grain; if at this time it <note>the malefic influence</note> is situated in Taurus, it destroys the grain as soon as it is produced. || 8 || If a cruel <note>malefic</note> planet situated in the house of wealth <note>2nd house</note> is not aspected by an auspicious planet, it destroys the early-sown crops, but the late-sown crops will yield well. || 9 || Cruel planets situated in the seventh house or in the cardinal houses from the Sun in Scorpio destroy the crops, but if an auspicious planet aspects them, they cannot destroy the grain everywhere. || 10 || When two cruel planets are in the seventh and sixth houses from the Sun in Scorpio, the crops grow, but the prices remain expensive. || 11 || Upon the Sun's entry into Taurus, the learned should predict either the destruction of the produced grain or the cause of auspiciousness <term>Mangala</term>. || 12 || If the Sun, situated in the three signs starting with Aries, is joined with or aspected by an auspicious planet, the summer harvest will be strong and the grain will be so cheap that people can secure both this world and the next <note>meaning they have enough surplus to perform acts of charity/Alms-giving</note>. || 13 || The Sun situated in Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius affects the autumn-produced crops in the same way; however, during the time of grain collection, if there is an aspect or conjunction of a cruel planet, one should know the result will be the opposite. || 14 ||

## Chapter Forty-Two
### On Commodity Prices and Trading (*Arghakanda*)

> If one observes heavy rain, meteors, halos around the sun or moon, eclipses, or dust storms on the New Moon or Full Moon days, ||1|| one should predict the specific fluctuations in prices for each month as the Sun progresses through the zodiac signs. Portents occurring on other lunar days signify wars and danger for kings. ||2|| When the Sun enters Aries <note>Aries: Mesha</note>, one should collect summer grains. When in Taurus <note>Taurus: Vrisha</note>, collect forest roots and fruits; profit from these will be realized in the fourth month. ||3|| When the Sun is in Gemini <note>Gemini: Mithuna</note>, gather all types of juices, liquids, and grains; by selling them in the sixth month, one obtains a vast profit. ||4|| When the Sun is in Cancer <note>Cancer: Karka</note>, store honey, perfumes, oils, ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, and molasses. In the second month, the profit is doubled, though it may vary slightly. ||5|| In Leo <note>Leo: Simha</note>, store gold, gems, leather, weapons, pearls, and silver. In the fifth month, the seller gains profit; otherwise, there is a loss. ||6|| When the Sun enters Virgo <note>Virgo: Kanya</note>, the buyer of fly-whisks, donkeys, camels, and horses will obtain double profit by selling them in the sixth month. ||7|| In Libra <note>Libra: Tula</note>, one should acquire woven cloth, vessels, gems, blankets, glass, and yellow flowers, as well as grains; after six months, the investment is doubled. ||8|| When the Sun resides in Scorpio <note>Scorpio: Vrishchika</note>, fruits, bulbs, roots, and various gems stored for two years yield double profit. ||9|| When in Sagittarius <note>Sagittarius: Dhanu</note>, one should purchase saffron, conch shells, coral, glass, and pearls; after one year, they increase to double their value. ||10|| When the Sun is in Capricorn or Aquarius <note>Makara or Kumbha</note>, one should acquire iron vessels and grains; by waiting one month before selling, the seeker of profit gains double. ||11|| When the Sun reaches Pisces <note>Pisces: Meena</note>, by storing roots, fruits, bulbs, vessels, and gems for half a year, one attains the desired profit. ||12|| In whichever sign the Moon <note>original: "शिशिरमयूख" - the cool-rayed one</note> or the Sun <note>original: "सहस्रकिरण" - the thousand-rayed one</note> is joined or aspected by a "great friend" <note>a specific astrological relationship</note>, the aforementioned profit is indicated. ||13|| The Moon, when full or joined with the Sun, and joined or aspected by benefics, is said to cause an immediate rise in prices. If joined or aspected by malefics, it destroys prices. Likewise, one should predict good or bad results by understanding the nature of the Sun's transit through the signs. ||14||
> Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "On Commodity Prices," in the *Brihat Samhita* of Varahamihira. ||42||

Every month, when all the zodiac signs transition through the Sun, one should observe disturbances such as halos <note>perivesha</note>, eclipses, circles of light, torrential rain, meteors, and staff-like formations <note>danda-rupa utpata</note> during the New Moon or Full Moon. Based on these, predictions for all subjects should be made in sequence. The disturbances occurring on specific lunar days <note>tithis</note> manifest a fear of turmoil for kings. ||1-2||

When the Sun enters **Aries**, it is proper to collect grains produced in the summer. When in **Taurus**, one should collect wild fruits and roots; profit is gained from these in the fourth month. ||3|| When the Sun reaches **Gemini**, one should collect all types of liquids <note>rasas, such as oils or juices</note> and all types of grains; selling them in the sixth month yields great profit. ||4|| When the Sun is situated in **Cancer**, by protecting—that is, storing—honey, perfumes, oil, ghee, and sugar, one gains double profit in the second month. However, if the timing is slightly off, there may be less profit or even loss. ||5|| When the Sun is in **Leo**, one should collect gold, gems, hides, armor, weapons, pearls, and silver; selling them in the fifth month brings profit to the seller, while doing otherwise results in loss. ||6|| When the Sun is in **Virgo**, if one purchases fly-whisks <note>chamar</note>, donkeys, elephant calves, and horses and sells them in the sixth month, the profit is doubled. ||7|| When the Sun is in **Libra**, by collecting cotton thread and clothes made from it, vessels, gems, blankets, glass, yellow flowers, and all types of grains, their price later increases twofold. ||8|| When the Sun is in **Scorpio**, if one gathers tubers, roots, fruits, and various kinds of gems and keeps them for two years, the profit is doubled. ||9|| When the Sun is in **Sagittarius**, one should collect saffron, conch shells, coral, pearls, and fruits; after six months of purchase, their price becomes double. ||10|| When the Sun is in **Capricorn** and **Aquarius**, one should acquire iron, vessels, and grains. One seeking profit should keep these items for one month before selling to gain double. ||11|| When the Sun reaches **Pisces**, if one acquires roots, fruits, tubers, vessels, and gems and sells them after six months, the profit is as desired. ||12||

Whichever sign the Sun or Moon occupies, if they are aspected by "great friend" <note>adhimitra</note> planets, they bring profit to the items associated with that sign. If on a New Moon or Full Moon, the Moon is joined with or aspected by a benefic planet, it is said to cause a rapid increase in prices <note>arghavriddhi</note>. If the Sun is aspected by or joined with a malefic planet, obstacles occur. In this manner, one should announce good and bad results by knowing the state of each planet. ||13-14||

# Chapter 43
## The Glory of Indra’s Banner

> The immortals said to Brahma: "O Blessed One, we are unable to withstand the demons <note>Asuras</note> in battle. Therefore, we have come to you, the refuge of those seeking shelter." ||1|| The Blessed One said to the gods: "In the Ocean of Milk, Keshav <note>Vishnu</note> will give you a banner <note>ketu</note>. Upon seeing it, the demons will not be able to stand against you in war." ||2|| Having received this boon, the gods, led by Indra, went to the Ocean of Milk and offered praises to the one marked with the Shrivatsa, whose chest was illuminated by the rays of the Kaustubha gem. ||3||

# Chapter 43: The Festival of the Indra-Banner
### With Hindi Commentary

->To the Lord of Fortune <note>Sripati</note>, the unthinkable, the incomparable, who dwells within all embodied beings, the subtle, the Supreme Soul, the beginningless, the All-Pervading One <note>Vishnu</note> whose limits are unknown.<- ||4||

Praised by the gods, the Lord Narayana was pleased and granted them a Banner—a sun to the frost-like lotus-faces of the wives of the demons <note>meaning it destroys the joy of the enemies of the gods</note>. ||5|| Indra rejoiced upon receiving that banner, which was born from the splendor of Vishnu, possessed eight wheels, and stood upon a brilliant chariot adorned with gems, shining like the sun in autumn. ||6|| With that raised banner of the King of Immortals, decorated with networks of small bells and equipped with umbrellas, bells, and baskets, he brought destruction to the enemy armies in battle. ||7||

The Lord of Immortals then gave a bamboo staff to Vasu, the King of Chedi. That lord of men worshipped it according to the sacred rites. ||8|| Pleased by the sacrifice <note>the Maha festival</note>, Indra said: "Those kings who act like Vasu shall be highly honored; their commands shall be fulfilled on earth. ||9|| Their subjects shall be joyful, free from fear and disease, and possessed of abundant food. The Banner itself, through omens, shall declare the good or evil fate of the world." ||10||

I shall now describe, according to tradition, the worship of that banner as performed by kings of old who desired an increase in strength and victory, by the command of Indra. ||11|| At an auspicious time, on a favorable day and lunar mansion <note>Nakshatra</note>, and at a lucky moment, the astrologer <term>Daivajna: a specialist in celestial omens</term> and the master carpenter <term>Sutradhara: the 'holder of the string' or chief architect</term> should set out for the forest. ||12||

Trees growing in gardens, temples, cemeteries, anthills, on roads, or near funeral pyres are to be avoided. Also unsuitable are trees that are stunted, withered at the top, thorny, or covered in creepers and parasites. ||13|| Trees that house many birds, have hollows, or have been damaged by wind or fire, as well as those with feminine names, are not auspicious for Indra’s Banner. ||14||

The best trees are the Arjuna, Ashvakarna, Priyaka, Dhava, and Udumbara—these five. One should choose one of these or another commendable tree. ||15|| After first worshipping the tree growing in pale or dark soil according to the rites, the priest should approach it alone at night, touch it, and recite this prayer: ||16||

"To whatever spirits dwell here, greetings and salutations to you! Having accepted this offering, please change your residence. ||17|| The King chooses you; may it be well with you, O best of trees! Accept this worship for the sake of the Banner of the King of the Gods." ||18||

At dawn, he should cut the tree while facing North or East. The sound of the axe being cracked or harsh is not desired; a smooth, deep sound is beneficial. ||19|| A fall toward the East or North that is unimpeded and straight brings victory to the king; if it falls in any other way or gets caught, it should be abandoned. ||20|| Having cut four inches from the top and eight from the base, one should place the staff in water. After taking it out, it should be brought to the city gate by cart or by men. ||21||

If a spoke breaks, it signifies a split in the army; if the rim breaks, the army's destruction. If the axle breaks, wealth is lost; if the linchpin breaks, the carpenter suffers. ||22|| On the eighth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada <note>August-September</note>, the King, surrounded by citizens, the astrologer, ministers, chamberlains, and priests, all well-dressed, ||23|| should lead the staff of Indra into the city. It should be wrapped in new cloth, adorned with garlands, perfumes, and incense, accompanied by the sound of conchs and trumpets. ||24||

The city should be decorated with blood-red banners, arches, and forest garlands; the people should be joyful, the streets swept and sprinkled, and crowded with well-dressed courtesans. ||25|| The shops and houses should be honored, the sound of Vedic chants for a holy day should be loud, and the crossroads filled with actors, dancers, and singers. ||26||

There, white banners bring victory; yellow ones bring disease. Variegated banners bring triumph, while red ones lead to the fury of weapons. ||27|| If elephants or other animals knock the staff down while it is entering, it signifies fear. If children clap their hands or there is fighting among animals, it foretells war. ||28|| After the carpenter has fashioned it again, he should raise the staff with a machine according to the rites. A vigil is kept on the eleventh day...

# The Varahi Samhita

The King shall cause this to be performed. ## 29 ## Wearing white garments and a white turban, the Royal Priest <note>Purohita</note> shall offer oblations into the fire using hymns <note>mantras</note> sacred to Indra and Vishnu, while the Astrologer <note>Samvatsara</note> observes the omens. ## 30 ##

If the fire takes the shape of auspicious objects, is fragrant, glossy, thick, and possesses bright flames, it brings good fortune. Anything other than this is considered undesirable; this has been explained at length in the section on "Marches" <note>Yatra: a chapter regarding military expeditions</note>. ## 31 ##

If, at the conclusion of the "Svaha" <note>the ritual exclamation when offering into fire</note>, the fire-god <note>Hutabhuj</note> spontaneously bursts into bright, glossy flames circling to the right, he brings under the King's control the Earth, which wears the waters of the Ganges and the Yamuna <note>literally: daughter of the Sun</note> as a beautiful necklace and the ocean as a girdle. ## 32 ##

When the fire resembles the color of gold, the Ashoka flower, the Kurantaka, the lotus, beryl, or the blue water-lily, darkness finds no place in the palace, and the King's enemies—who would steal his gems—are defeated. ## 33 ##

Those whose sacrificial fire roars like a multitude of chariots, the ocean, a thundercloud, an elephant, or a drum, will find the directions darkened by the dust raised by their soldiers, blinded with battle-fury, as they march to victory. ## 34 ##

The Earth—with the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains as her breasts—comes under the sway of those kings whose fire takes the shape of a banner, a water-pot, a horse, an elephant, or a mountain. ## 35 ##

When the fire is perfumed with the scent of elephant-ichor <note>Mada: a fragrant secretion from elephants in rut</note>, damp earth, lotuses, and fried grain, the Earth appears as if strewn with the luster of the crest-jewels of prostrate rival kings. ## 36 ##

Whatever good or evil omens have been described regarding the Seven Seers <note>the Big Dipper constellation</note> when Indra’s Banner is raised, those should also be considered during birth-sacrifices, planetary pacification rituals, marches, and marriages. ## 37 ##

Having honored the Brahmins with sweets, cakes, milk-rice, and monetary gifts, the banner should be raised on the twelfth lunar day under the Shravana asterism, or at another time if Shravana is not available. ## 38 ##

The expert should create the "Daughters of Indra" <note>Shakra-kumari: smaller poles or decorative side-posts</note>; Manu says there should be seven or five. Two, named Nanda and Upananda, should be three-quarters and one-half the height of the main pole respectively. ## 39 ##

Two others, Jaya and Vijaya, are one-sixteenth taller than those, and two more are called Vasundhara. In the middle of these stands the "Mother of Indra," which is one-eighth taller than the others. ## 40 ##

One should then attach the various ornaments <note>Pitakas: basket-like decorative boxes or frames</note> in order, which were fashioned in ancient times by the delighted gods for the Banner of the King of Heaven. ## 41 ##

The first, square and resembling the red Ashoka flower, was given by Vishvakarma <note>the divine architect</note>. The second, a girdle of many colors, was given by Savitri <note>the Creator</note> and Shiva. ## 42 ##

The third ornament, eight-sided and colored blue and red, was given by Indra. The fourth, a radiant "lentil-shaped" ornament <note>Masuraka</note>, was given by dark Yama <note>God of Death</note>. ## 43 ##

The fifth, given by Varuna <note>God of the Waters</note>, is six-sided, colored like madder, and resembles the waves of the sea. The sixth, a peacock-blue armlet <note>Keyura</note>, was given by Vayu <note>God of the Wind</note>. ## 44 ##

Skanda <note>God of War</note> gave his own armlet as the seventh, which is highly multicolored. The eighth, resembling the flames of fire, was given by Agni <note>the Fire-god</note>. ## 45 ##

The Moon gave the ninth, a necklace <note>Graiveyaka</note> resembling beryl. The tenth, radiant and shaped like a chariot wheel, was given by the Sun and Tvashtar. ## 46 ##

The eleventh, a lotus-like ornament without a central pole, was given by the Vishvedevas. The twelfth, also without a pole and resembling a blue water-lily, was given by the Sages. ## 47 ##

The thirteenth ornament, slightly protruding at the top and bottom but wide in the middle, was given by Brihaspati and Shukra <note>the preceptors of the gods and demons</note>; it is the color of liquid lac. ## 48 ##

Whatever ornament was fashioned by whichever deity for the sake of the banner, the wise should understand that ornament to be presided over by that specific deity. ## 49 ##

The circumference of the first ornament <note>Pitaka</note> is one-third the height of the banner. Each subsequent ornament is one-eighth smaller than the one preceding it. ## 50 ##

On the fourth day, the expert in the scriptures should complete the Indra-dhvaja ritual. Being self-controlled, he should recite these mantras sung in the tradition of Manu: ## 51 ##

"By Shiva, the Sun, Yama, Indra, and the Moon; by the Lord of Wealth <note>Kubera</note>, Fire, and the Noose-bearer <note>Varuna</note>; by the hosts of Great Sages, the directions, and the celestial nymphs; by Shukra, Angiras, Skanda, and the Maruts— ## 52 ##

Just as you were honored by these with many strength-giving forms and noble ornaments, so too here..."

# Chapter 43: The Glory of Indra's Banner

"O God, accept these auspicious ornaments with a pleased mind." [53] You are the unborn, the imperishable, the eternal, the one-formed Vishnu, the Boar <note>The Varaha avatar</note>, the ancient Primeval Person. You are the Ender <note>Yama/Death</note>, the All-Destroyer, the Fire, the Thousand-Headed, and the Praiseworthy One of a hundred sacrifices. [54] I invoke the wise, seven-tongued <note>referring to Agni/Fire</note> protector, Indra the guardian, the Lord of the Gods, the powerful one, the slayer of Vritra, who possesses a fine army; may our heroes be victorious. [55]

During the filling, the raising, the entry, the bathing, the arranging of garlands, and the dismissal, the King—having fasted—should recite these auspicious mantras of the many-invoked Banner. [56]

The Banner should be decorated in all directions with umbrellas, flags, mirrors, fruits, half-moons, variegated garlands, plantain stalks, and sugarcane stalks; with carvings of serpents and lions, with baskets and lattice-windows, and with the Guardians of the Quarters. [57] With unbroken ropes, firm wooden cross-bars <note>term: Matrika, the supporting wooden frame</note>, well-fitted mechanical bolts, and a decorated base-arch, one should raise the symbol of the Thousand-Eyed One <note>Indra</note>, accompanied by the "Maidens" <note>term: Kumarika, smaller side-poles</note> made of heartwood that are not broken. [58]

Amidst the continuous roar of the people, with auspicious blessings and prostrations, with the sound of sharp drums, clay drums, conchs, and kettledrums, and with Brahmins repeatedly chanting words ordained by the Vedas, one should raise the Banner, which is white and brings welfare. [59] With citizens holding fruits, curds, ghee, parched grain, honey, and flowers in their hands, bowing their heads and feeling satisfied, the Lord of the people <note>the King</note> should have the Banner of the Lord of the Immortals <note>Indra</note> raised. It should not lean toward the enemy's city, as that would lead to the destruction of the learned. [60]

A raising that is neither too fast nor too slow, without trembling, and where the decorations like garlands and baskets do not fall, is considered desirable; anything otherwise is inauspicious. The priest should pacify such ill-omens with restorative rites for the King. [61]

If carnivorous birds, owls, pigeons, crows, or vultures perch on the Banner, they signify great fear for the King. A blue jay indicates danger to the Crown Prince, and a hawk falling upon it causes eye disease. [62] If the umbrella breaks or falls, the King dies; if bees settle on it, it brings danger from thieves. A meteor hitting it kills the priest, and a lightning strike kills the King's consort. [63]

A fallen flag causes the King's destruction; the falling of a basket causes a lack of rain. If the Banner breaks at the middle, the tip, or the base, it kills the ministers, the King, or the citizens respectively. [64] If shrouded in smoke, there is fear of fire; if by darkness, there is mental delusion. If broken or fallen due to serpents <note>or perhaps carvings of them</note>, the ministers will perish. If the color fades starting from the water-pot decoration, the Brahmins and other castes suffer in order. If the "Maiden" pole breaks, the death of a harlot is foretold. [65]

If the rope snaps, it brings suffering to children; if the cross-bar <note>Matrika</note> breaks, it brings suffering to the King's mother. Whatever children or wandering performers do <note>mimicking the ceremony</note>, that same result—whether good or evil—will come to pass. [66]

After the Banner has been raised and worshipped for four days, the King, on the fifth day, should dismiss the symbol of the Destroyer of Strength <note>Indra</note> along with his subjects, for the increase of his own power. [67] This ritual was first started by King Uparichara Vasu and has been continuously performed by kings since. By following this procedure, a ruler shall face no fear from his enemies. [68]

->Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Achievement of Indra's Banner," in the Brihat Samhita of Sri Varahamihira.<-

Seeing that Banner, the demons will no longer be able to stand before you in battle." [2] Thus, having received the boon, all the gods with Indra went to the Ocean of Milk...</margin>

# Varahi Samhita
<page-num>134</page-num>
->Varahi Samhita<-

They began to praise Lord Vishnu, the husband of Lakshmi, the Supreme Soul, who is without beginning, whose chest is illuminated by the rays of the Kaustubha gem <note>A celebrated jewel obtained during the churning of the ocean, worn by Vishnu</note>, who is inconceivable (beyond the reach of thought), who views all equally, who dwells within the hearts of all beings, who is subtle, and whose limits are immeasurable. ||3|| When the gods praised Narayana in this manner, He satisfied them by giving them a banner. This banner acted like the sun to the lotus-forest of the faces of the gods and their wives <note>making them bloom with joy</note>, and like the moon to the lotus-forest of the faces of the wives of the demons <note>causing them to wither or close in sorrow</note>. ||5|| King Indra was delighted to receive that banner, which was born from the splendor of Vishnu, possessed eight wheels, was radiant, and was placed in a chariot decorated with jewels, shining like the autumnal sun. ||6|| Adorned with clusters of small bells, garlands, umbrellas, bells, and *pitakas* <term>pitaka: a specific type of ornament or basket-like structure attached to the banner</term>, King Indra destroyed the enemy armies in battle with that extremely high banner. ||7||

Indra, the king of the gods, gave this staff made of bamboo to Uparichara Vasu, the King of Chedi; the King worshipped that staff thoroughly. ||8|| Pleased by this festival, Indra declared that those kings who perform this festival like Uparichara Vasu will become wealthy like Vasu and will be known as masters of success on earth. All their subjects will be satisfied, free from fear and disease, and possessed of much grain—meaning their houses will be filled with much corn. This banner itself, acting as an omen in the world, will reveal the good and bad fruits (results) for the world. ||9||10||

I shall now describe here, according to the scriptures, how the Indra-dhvaja <note>Indra's Banner</note> was previously worshipped by kings desiring victory and the growth of their armies by the command of Indra. ||11|| The method of that worship is that when there is an auspicious *karana* <note>an astrological division of a day</note>, day, lunar mansion (*nakshatra*), and a favorable moment (*muhurta*) suitable for travel, the astrologer (*daivajña*) and the carpenter (*sūtradhāra*) should go into the forest. ||12||

Trees that are in flower gardens, temples, cemeteries, on anthills, on roads, or near funeral pyres are not auspicious for the Indra-ketu <note>another name for Indra's banner</note>. Likewise, trees that are stunted, dried up while standing, thorny, covered in creepers, or those with parasites (*banda*), those with many bird nests, or those afflicted by wind and fire, or trees with feminine names (such as the Khirni tree) are not auspicious. ||13||14||

The five trees—Arjuna, Ashvakarna, Priyaka, Dhava, and Udumbara (Wild Fig)—are the best. If none of these trees are available, any other tree may be taken, and that too is fine. ||15|| After first worshipping a tree grown on white or black soil according to the rites, a Brahmin should go into the uninhabited forest at night, and touching such a tree, should recite this mantra:

> "May it be well with the beings who reside on this tree; I bow to them. Accepting this offering, may those beings dwell elsewhere. O best of trees! For the sake of the King of Gods' banner, the King desires to obtain you. May you be blessed; please accept this worship."

||16|| ||17||18||

Following this, at dawn, one should cut the tree while facing North or East. At that time, if a cracking or harsh sound comes from cutting the tree, it is inauspicious; the emergence of a pleasant and deep sound is auspicious. ||19|| The tree should fall without breaking, it should not be crooked, and it should not fall while leaning against another tree. If it falls toward the East or North, it brings victory to kings. A tree falling in any other way gives the opposite result. ||20|| After cutting four finger-widths from the top and eight finger-widths from the root, the wood should be placed in water. Then, after taking the tree out of the water, it should be brought to the city gate by means of a cart or carried by men. ||21|| If the spoke of the cart breaks while bringing it, then the army...

The breaking of the <term>aksha<note>The axle of the wheel.</note></term> leads to the loss of wealth, and the breaking of the <term>ani<note>The linchpin or the bolt at the end of the axle.</note></term> results in the death of the carpenter. ||22||

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhadrapada <note>August-September</note>, the King, accompanied by citizens in fine attire, the <term>daivajña<note>The royal astrologer or seer.</note></term>, ministers, the <term>kañcukī<note>The chamberlain or overseer of the harem.</note></term>, and Brahmins, should have the citizens raise the Indra-banner. It should be covered with unblemished cloths, adorned with garlands, scents, and incense, and brought into the city to the sound of conches and trumpets. ||23|| ||24||

At that time, the city should be decorated with charming banners, triumphal arches, and forest garlands.
