The city squares should be filled with actors, dancers, and those knowledgeable in music. ||26||

At such a time, the hoisting of a white banner is a cause for victory; a yellow banner brings disease; a multi-colored banner grants triumph; and a red banner indicates the provocation of the enemy's weapons. ||27|| If, while the pole is being brought into the city, any animal such as an elephant knocks it down, it is a cause for fear. If groups of children clap their hands at that time, or if any creatures fight, it indicates that a battle will occur. ||28||

Then the carpenter should properly shave the pole and place it on the lathe; it is proper for the King to keep a vigil on the eleventh day <note>Ekadashi</note>. ||29|| The King’s priest, wearing white clothes and a turban, should perform a burnt offering in the fire using <term>Aindra<note>Mantras dedicated to Indra.</note></term> and <term>Vaishnava<note>Mantras dedicated to Vishnu.</note></term> mantras. A fire that takes a shape resembling desired wealth, is fragrant, smooth, dense, and has flickering flames is auspicious; any fire other than this does not grant the desired fruit. This has been described in detail in the *Yogayatra* <note>A work by Varahamihira regarding the travels and expeditions of kings.</note>. ||31|| If, while offering <term>ghṛta<note>Clarified butter (ghee).</note></term> into the fire for the deity, the sacrificial fire at the end of the mantra recitation spontaneously develops a bright white flame, is oily, and circles toward the right, then the Earth—which wears the beautiful necklace of the waters of the Ganges and Yamuna and the waistband of the oceans—will come under the King's control. ||32||

If the fire is the color of gold, Ashoka flowers, Kurantaka, lotus, lapis lazuli, or a blue lotus, then darkness, afflicted by the light of jewels, finds no place in the King’s palace—that is, darkness does not remain. ||33|| If the fire makes a sound like the ocean, a cloud, an elephant, or a kettle-drum, then at the time the King sets out for war, all directions will appear as black as darkness, filled with herds of intoxicated elephants. ||34||

If the fire resembles a banner, a pot, a horse, or an elephant, then the Earth—which supports the mountains of sunrise and sunset and possesses the Himalaya and Vindhya mountains as its breasts—will come under the King's control. ||35|| If the fire has a fragrance like elephant musk, the earth, a lotus, rice-pudding, ghee, or honey, then the royal assembly will be permeated by the luster of the jewels set in the crowns of kings who are bowing down in salutation. ||36||

The auspicious and inauspicious signs described through the nature of the fire at the time of raising the Indra-banner should also be considered at the time of birth, sacrifices, planetary pacification rituals, journeys, and marriages. ||37|| After worshipping the Brahmins with jaggery, flour-cakes, rice-pudding, and donations, one should raise the banner on the twelfth day <note>Dwadashi</note> during the Shravana Nakshatra <note>A specific lunar mansion/constellation</note>. On top of the banner, one should place five or seven <term>shatrukumārī<note>Literally "enemy-maidens"; these are smaller decorative poles or cross-bars attached to the main banner.</note></term>, as Lord Manu has said. # The Varahi Samhita
<page-num>136</page-num>

One should create the "Shakra-kumari" <note>Indra's daughters; smaller auxiliary poles</note> named *Nanda*, equal to one-fourth of the main banner's size, and *Upananda*, equal to half its size. Two *Vasundharas* named *Jaya* and *Vijaya* should be made slightly larger than a sixteenth part, and in the middle, the "Mother of Indra" should be made larger than eight parts. In ancient times, the gods joyfully gave ornaments to Indra’s banner; one should offer all those ornaments and *pitakas* <note>term: pitaka; decorative baskets or boxes attached to the pole</note> in their proper sequence. ||38-41||

First, Vishvakarma <note>the divine architect</note> gave a square ornament as red as a red Ashoka flower. Second, Brahma and Shiva gave a multi-colored girdle. Indra gave the third ornament to the banner: an eight-sided piece of blue and red color. ||42-43||

Following this, Varuna <note>god of the waters</note> gave the fifth ornament, shining like madder-dye and shaped like water ripples with six corners. The Wind God (Pavan) gave the sixth ornament called a *Keyura* <note>term: Keyura; traditionally an armlet, here a pole decoration</note>, which was the color of a peacock and blue like a rain cloud. ||44||

Lord Kartikeya gave the seventh ornament, his own *Keyura* decorated with many pictures. Agni, the god of the sacrificial fire, gave the eighth ornament, bright like a flame. ||45||

The Moon gave the ninth ornament, a neck-piece resembling a cat's-eye gem (*Vaidurya*). Tvashta (the Sun/Divine Smith) gave the tenth ornament, radiant like the wheel of a chariot. ||46||

The Vishvedevas <note>the "All-Gods" group</note> gave the eleventh ornament, shaped like a lotus. The Sages gave the twelfth ornament called *Nivansha*, resembling a blue lotus. Brihaspati and Shukra <note>the preceptors of the gods and demons</note> placed the thirteenth ornament upon the head of the banner; it was large, the color of red lac, and curved from the bottom upwards. ||47-48||

The wise should know that whichever deity fashioned an ornament for the banner remains the presiding master of that specific ornament. ||49||

The circumference of the first *pitaka* is one-third the measure of the banner itself. Thereafter, each subsequent circumference is one-eighth smaller than the one preceding it. ||50||

On the fourth day, a man learned in the scriptures should complete the Indra-banner with sacred chants (*mantras*) and recite these verses spoken by Manu from the ancient traditions: ||51||

-> "O Lord! Just as you were honored by Mahadeva, Surya, Yama, Indra, Chandra, Kubera, Agni, Varuna, the Great Sages, all the Directions, the Apsaras, Shukra, Angira, Kartikeya, Vayu, and the Gana-deities with these radiant, multi-formed, and noble ornaments—so now, being pleased, accept all these jewels. O Lord! You are unborn, changeless, eternal, and of a single essence. You are the Primordial Being and the celestial bodies. You are Yama, the Destroyer, and the Fire. You are the thousand-headed one, the worshipful one. I invoke you—the Poet, the Seven-Tongued, the Protector, Lord of the Gods, the Savior, the Slayer of Vritra, known as Shakra and Sushena. May all our warriors be victorious in the North!" <- ||52-55||

The King, having fasted, should recite these auspicious mantras during the completion, the raising, the entry, the bathing, the garlanding, and the immersion of the Indra-banner. ||56||

One should decorate this banner on all sides with umbrellas, flags, mirrors, half-moons, wondrous garlands, plantain trees, sugarcane, black snakes, lions, *pitakas*, latticed windows, and the Guardians of the Directions. ||57||

The King should raise the banner—the symbol of the thousand-eyed Indra—made of an unbroken tree, bound with unbroken ropes, adorned with the figures of maidens, and equipped with mechanical devices, bolts, pedestals, and ceremonial arches. ||58||

Amidst auspicious blessings, prostrations, and the sweet sounds of drums, *mridangas*, conchs, and trumpets, and the repeated Vedic recitations of the Brahmins, the King should raise the banner, accompanied by the cheers of the people. ||59||

<header>With Hindi Commentary Chapter 44</header>

Holding ghee, parched grain, honey, and flowers in their hands, the citizens shall offer praises while bowing their heads. Once the Indra-banner is raised, the King <note>original: "Prajapati"</note> should cause the tip of that banner to lean toward the city of his enemies to ensure their destruction. ||60|| If the banner rises very quickly without trembling, and its garlands, baskets <note>ornamental baskets or 'pitakas'</note>, and other ornaments do not fall, it is beneficial for him. Any other manner of raising it is inauspicious. The King’s priest <note>term: Purohit (royal chaplain)</note> should perform a peace-ritual <note>Shanti</note> to remove all obstacles. ||61|| If meat-eating birds, owls, pigeons, crows, or vultures sit upon the Indra-banner, it brings great unrest to the King. If a blue jay <note>Neelkanth</note> sits upon it, fear is predicted for the Crown Prince. A hawk falling upon the banner creates a danger to the eyes. ||62|| The breaking of the ceremonial umbrella or the falling of the banner reveals the impending death of kings. If bees build a honeycomb on the banner, it signifies the death of thieves. If a meteor strikes the banner, the priest dies; if a lightning bolt strikes, the King’s Queen dies. ||63|| The falling of the flag signifies the destruction of the Queen, and the falling of the ornamental basket brings drought. If the middle, top, or base of the Indra-banner breaks, it destroys the ministers, the King, and the citizens respectively. ||64|| If smoke surrounds it, there will be delusion; if it breaks in the middle and falls, there will be a lack of ministers. If it breaks and falls toward the North or other four directions, it creates distress for the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras <note>the four social classes</note> in order. If the smaller 'daughter' poles are torn or broken, then unchaste women shall perish. ||65|| If the banner gets stuck on its path while being raised, it causes suffering to children. The breaking of the wood placed beside the gateway causes suffering to the Queen Mother. Whatever actions children or messengers perform near the banner, the results will be sinful (if the actions are bad) or auspicious (if the actions are good). ||66|| After the raised and worshipped banner has been honored for four days, the King should dismantle it on the fifth day along with his subjects; this increases the strength of the King’s army. ||67|| This ritual was started by King Uparichara Vasu and has been performed by kings ever since. Those kings who worship the Indra-banner in this manner shall never suffer fear from their enemies. ||68||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter of the Hindi commentary on the Brihat Samhita composed by Acharya Varahamihira, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region.

### Now Begins the Forty-Fourth Chapter
### The Neerajan Ritual <note>A purification ritual involving lamps and water for the army and horses</note>

> When the Goddess of Fortune <note>Lakshmi</note> awakens the lotus-navelled Lord <note>Vishnu</note> during the season of clouds <note>monsoon</note> when the moon and sun are the eyes, one should perform the Neerajan ritual for horses, elephants, and men. ||1|| This peace-ritual named Neerajan should be performed on the twelfth, eighth, or fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kartik, or during the month of Ashvin. ||2|| In the North-East direction of the city, on auspicious ground, a gateway <note>Torana</note> should be constructed of auspicious wood, sixteen cubits high and ten cubits wide. ||3|| The gateway should be made of branches from the Sarja, Udumbara, or Kakubha trees, adorned with peace-garlands and plenty of Kusha grass, and decorated with fish-banners and wheels made of bamboo. ||4|| One should tie amulets <note>Pratisara</note> around the necks of the horses containing marking-nut, rice, costus, and white mustard.

<summary>This page details the omens associated with the Indra-banner festival and concludes Chapter 43, before introducing the Neerajan ritual for purifying the military in Chapter 44.</summary>

# For Prosperity and the Propitiation of the Royal Quarters

### Verse 5–7
For seven days, one should perform propitiatory rites <term>Shanti: rituals to avert evil or bring peace</term> for the horses in the sanctuary using mantras dedicated to the Sun, Varuna, the Vishvedevas, Prajapati, Indra, and Vishnu. The horses should be honored and never addressed with harsh words, nor should they be struck. They should be kept free from fear by the sounds of holy chants, conch shells, and musical instruments.

### Verse 8–11
On the eighth day, an ashram-like enclosure covered with Kusha grass and bark should be constructed to the south of the ceremonial arch <term>Torana: a ritual gateway</term>, facing north. An altar and a ritual fire should be prepared in front of it. The following substances should be placed in water jars:
Sandalwood, Kustha, Samanga, Orpiment, Realgar, Priyangu, Vacha, Danti, Amrita, Anjana, Rajani, Suvarnapushpa, and Agnimantha; also white flowers, Saparnakosha, Katambhara, Trayamana, Sahadevi, Nagakusuma, Svagupta, Shatavari, and Somaraji.
After placing these in the jars, one should properly offer sacrifices consisting of various types of food, especially honey, milk-rice, and barley-gruel.

### Verse 12–14
The sacrificial fuel <term>Samidh: sticks used for the sacred fire</term> should be made from Khadira, Palasha, Udumbara, Kashmarya, or Ashvattha wood. A person desiring prosperity should use a sacrificial ladle <term>Sruk</term> made of gold or silver. The King, looking magnificent and facing east, should sit on a tiger skin near the fire, accompanied by the horse-physician and the astrologer. The characteristics of the altar, the priest, and the fire should be observed as prescribed in the chapters on the "Expedition," the "Sacrifice to the Planets," and the "Banner of Indra."

### Verse 15–16
A horse and a noble elephant possessing auspicious marks should be consecrated and bathed. They should be honored with fresh white garments, perfumes, garlands, and incense. They should then be led to the base of the ceremonial arch while being soothed with gentle words, as the sounds of musical instruments, conch shells, and holy blessings fill the quarters.

### Verse 17–19
If the horse, when brought forward, stands lifting its right foot, the King will soon conquer his enemies without effort. If it is terrified, it is not auspicious for the King. Other behaviors of elephants and horses should be interpreted as explained in the chapter on "Expeditions." The priest should consecrate a ball of food with mantras and offer it to the horse; if the horse smells it or eats it, it brings victory. If it acts otherwise, the result is said to be the opposite.

### Verse 20–22
The priest should dip a branch of the Udumbara tree into the water from the jars and sprinkle the horses, as well as the army including the King and the elephants, while reciting propitiatory and restorative mantras. After performing the rites for the prosperity of the nation, the priest should pierce a clay image of the enemy in the chest with a spear using <term>Abhichara: malevolent magic/exorcism</term> mantras. Then the priest should give the bit to the horse after consecrating it; the King should then mount and, having been purified by the lustration rite, set out with his army toward the north-east.

### Verse 23–25
With elephants delighted by the sound of drums and conch shells, the air fragrant with the scent of their flowing ichor <term>Mada: a secretion from rutting elephants</term>, the King shines like the sun at the end of the rainy season, glowing with the mass of light reflecting from the crest-jewels of his vassals. Surrounded by white fly-whisks <term>Chauris</term> fluttering like rows of swans, his beautiful garlands and garments are stirred by the scented breeze. Adorned with crowns, earrings, and armlets set with various colored gems and diamonds, he reflects the splendor of a rainbow through the rays of his many jewels.

### Verse 26–28
Surrounded by horses that seem to leap into the sky and elephants that seem to tear the earth, the King should march like Indra surrounded by the gods who have conquered their foes. Or, adorned with pearls and diamonds, wearing white garlands, a turban, and white ointments, he may ride an elephant under a raised umbrella, looking like the son of Bhrigu <note>The planet Venus</note> atop a dark cloud. A King whose army is joyful—men, horses, and elephants alike—whose weapons shine brightly, and who remains calm while terrifying the enemy, will soon conquer the entire earth.

# Chapter 44: With Hindi Commentary
<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>With Hindi Commentary Chapter 44</header>

The clouds are His eyelids, and the Moon and Sun are His two eyes; when that Lord Padmanabha <note>The "Lotus-Navelled" Vishnu</note> opens His eyes—that is, when He awakens—then one should perform the *Neerajan* <note>A ritual involving the waving of lights or purification of weapons and animals</note> for horses, elephants, and men. ||1|| One should perform the propitiation known as *Neerajan* on the full moon, the twelfth day, or the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kartik, or during the month of Ashvin. ||2|| In the north-eastern direction of the city, upon excellent ground, one should construct a *Toran* <note>A ceremonial archway</note> made of fine wood, sixteen cubits high and ten cubits wide. ||3|| Build a "House of Propitiation" using the wood of the *Vijaysar*, *Gular* <note>Cluster fig</note>, and *Arjun* trees, and place plenty of *Kush* grass within it. In its doorway, place fish, banners, and wheels made of bamboo. ||4|| For the sake of the propitiation house and the nourishment of all, it is proper to bind marking-nut, *Shathi* grain, *Kuth* <note>Costus</note>, and mustard seeds around the necks of the horses using the <term>Pratisara Mantra</term> <note>A protective incantation used while tying a ritual thread or amulet</note>. ||5|| For one week, perform the propitiation of the horses in the "House of Propitiation" using the mantras of the Sun, Varuna, the Vishvedevas, Prajapati, Indra, and Vishnu. ||6|| Those horses should be rendered fearless and honored with auspicious recitations, the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, and songs; they must not be frightened or threatened with harsh words or any other means. ||7|| When the eighth day arrives, establish the sacrificial fire—covered with *Kush* grass and bark—upon the altar, moving it from the south side of the archway toward the north. ||8|| Sandalwood, *Kuth*, madder, yellow orpiment, realgar, foxtail millet, sweet flag, *Amrit*, collyrium, turmeric, gold, flowers, and *Ganiyari*... ||9|| ...white alum, *Purnakosha*, *Kutki*, *Trayaman*, the *Sahadevi* herb, white *Purnakosh*, *Nagkeshar*, *Konch*, *Shatavari*, and *Somvalli*. ||10|| Taking all these items in equal measure, place them into water-pots and offer a <term>Bali</term> <note>A ritual offering or sacrifice</note> properly along with plenty of honey, rice-pudding, barley-gruel, and various other substances. ||11|| Make the <term>Samidha</term> <note>Sacrificial fuel/kindling</note> from the wood of *Khair*, *Dhak*, *Gular*, *Gambhari*, and *Peepal* trees; one who desires prosperity should have a <term>Sruva</term> <note>A small wooden sacrificial ladle</note> made of gold or silver. ||12|| Seated upon a tiger skin and facing the east, the illustrious King should sit near the fire along with the horses, physicians, and astrologers. ||13|| The characteristics of the altar, the priest, and the fire that have been described in the rules for planetary sacrifices, for journeys, and regarding the banner of Indra should all be understood to apply to this ritual as well. ||14|| After giving <term>Diksha</term> <note>Ritual initiation or preparation</note> to the elephants and horses of excellent qualities, bathe them, dress them in new garments, and worship them with garlands of flowers, perfumes, and incense. ||15|| Speaking sweet words to soothe and encourage them, bring them slowly near the base of the ritual archway, accompanied by various musical instruments, conchs, and auspicious sounds that fill the directions with their resonance. ||16|| If the horse, when brought forward, stands with its right hoof raised first, the King will conquer his enemies quickly and without effort; however, if the horse is terrified, it portends fear for the King. The results of other movements of elephants and horses, as described in the <term>Yatradhyaya</term> <note>The chapter concerning journeys and military expeditions</note>, should be considered here with proper reasoning. ||17||18|| The priest, reciting mantras, should offer a ball of food for the horse to eat; if the horse smells it or eats it, it is a sign of victory. The opposite is said to be inauspicious. ||19|| The priest or a Brahmin should touch the King, the army (including elephants), and the horses with a branch of the *Gular* tree soaked in water from the ritual pot while reciting nourishing mantras for their peace; for the increase of the kingdom, he should repeatedly perform propitiation while reciting *Abhichara* <note>Incantations for overcoming enemies</note> mantras. It is proper for the priest to make an image of the enemy out of clay and pierce its chest with a spear. ||20||21|| The priest, reciting mantras, should place the reins in the horse's mouth; then the King, having been purified by the *Neerajan* ceremony, should mount that horse and proceed toward the north with his army. ||22|| He, fragrant with the scent of the ichor of joyful elephants whose temples are dripping with fluid, amidst the sound of drums and conchs—

The king, refreshed by the breeze and delighted, wears a crown set with jewels whose flickering radiance makes him appear like the sun emerging from behind clouds. # Chapter 45
## The Sight of the Wagtail
<note>The Wagtail (Khanjana) is considered a highly significant bird in Indian augury, particularly when first sighted after the rainy season.</note>

I shall now proclaim the fruits (results) described by the sages regarding the first sighting of the bird known as the Wagtail. ||1|| The variety called *Bhadra* (the Auspicious) is large, with an uplifted neck and a black throat; it brings prosperity. The variety called *Sampurna* (the Full), which is black from the throat to the face, fulfills all desires. ||2|| The one called *Rikta* (the Empty) has a black spot on its throat and white cheeks; it brings loss. The yellow variety, known as *Gopita*, is seen as a bringer of distress. ||3|| Now, the Wagtail brings fortune if seen upon trees bearing sweet and fragrant fruits or flowers, near sacred bodies of water, or upon the heads of elephants, horses, or snakes, or on palaces, gardens, and mansions. ||4|| It also brings prosperity if seen near cow-pens, gatherings of good people, sacrificial festivals, kings, or Brahmins; or upon elephant and horse stables, umbrellas, banners, and yak-tail whisks. ||5|| Furthermore, it brings wealth if seen on gold, clean white garments, lotuses, water-lilies, worshipped objects, freshly plastered floors, vessels of curd, or heaps of grain. ||6||

If seen in mud, it signifies the attainment of sweet food; on cow dung, it signifies wealth in cows; on green grass, the acquisition of clothes; but if seen on a cart, it signifies the ruin of the country. ||7|| On the roof of a house, it means loss of wealth; on a leather strap, it means imprisonment; and on an impure place, it signifies disease. If seen on the backs of goats or sheep, it quickly brings a meeting with a beloved person. ||8|| If situated on a buffalo, camel, donkey, bone, cremation ground, the corner of a house, gravel, or a mountain, or on a rampart, ashes, or hair, it is inauspicious and brings death, disease, or fear. ||9|| It is inauspicious if it is shaking its wings, but auspicious if it is drinking water or standing by a river. A Wagtail seen at sunrise is praised, but it does not yield desirable results at sunset. ||10|| After the lustration ceremony <note>The *Nirajana* ritual mentioned in the previous chapter.</note> is completed, the king should observe the direction in which the Wagtail flies; the enemy in that direction will quickly come under his control. ||11|| Wherever it performs a mating act, there is a hidden treasure; wherever it vomits, there is glass <note>or crystal</note> beneath the ground. They also say that charcoal is found where... <insert>it drops its excrement</insert>

If the bird is seen on excrement, one should dig the earth to remove the curiosity <note>original: "kautuka"; referring to the hidden objects mentioned in the previous verse</note> of what lies beneath. || 12 || A bird that is dead, mutilated, deformed, or diseased yields results equal to its own physical state <note>i.e., bad luck or illness</note>. A bird that is seen hiding or settling down brings wealth, and one seen in the sky brings a meeting with kinsmen. || 13 || Even a King, after seeing a wagtail in an auspicious place in the sky, should perform auspicious rites on the earth. By offering an *Arghya* <note>a respectful offering of water, flowers, etc.</note> consisting of fragrant flowers and incense, he attains prosperity and is congratulated. || 14 || Even if a King sees an inauspicious wagtail, he will not suffer ill effects if he remains devoted to the worship of Brahmins, gurus, saints, and gods, and if he abstains from eating meat for seven days. || 15 || The results of the first sighting last for a year; however, for daily sightings, the result lasts for the remainder of the day. One should deduce the effects based on the direction, location, form, the rising sign (Lagna), the asterism (Nakshatra), and whether the bird is in a "peaceful" or "blazing" state. || 16 ||

### Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter titled "The Sight of the Wagtail" in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. || 45 ||

All the fruits/results that the sages have declared regarding the first sighting of the bird named <term>Khanjana</term> <note>The Wagtail bird, considered a significant omen-bearer in Indian augury</note> are now described. || 1 || A wagtail with a thick neck, high posture, and a black throat is called <term>Bhadra</term> <note>meaning "auspicious" or "blessed"</note>; this wagtail is a bringer of good fortune. If it is black from the mouth to the throat, its name is <term>Sampurna</term> <note>meaning "complete" or "full"</note>. This wagtail fulfills all hopes. || 2 || One that has whiteness and a safflower-red color at the end of a black spot on its throat is called <term>Rikta</term> <note>meaning "empty" or "void"</note>; its result is fruitless. A yellow-colored wagtail is named <term>Gopita</term>; its sight brings distress. || 3 ||

If the wagtail is seen near trees laden with sweet fragrant fruits and flowers, pure water bodies, the heads of elephants, horses, or snakes, palaces, flower gardens, balconies, cow-sheds, gatherings of noble people, sacrifices, festive houses, or near kings and Brahmins; or on elephant stables, horse stables, umbrellas, banners, and fly-whisks, gold, white clothes, lotuses, lilies, places that are worshipped or smeared with cow dung, vessels of curd, or heaps of grain—then one attains Lakshmi <note>Goddess of wealth; implies the acquisition of riches</note>. || 4, 5, 6 ||

If the wagtail is sitting in mud, one receives delicious food; if sitting on cow dung, wealth in the form of cattle/milk; if sitting on green grass, one obtains clothes; and if situated on a cart, it signifies the destruction of the country. || 7 || When the wagtail sits on the roof of a house, there is a loss of wealth; if it sits on a hole/crack, it signifies imprisonment; and if seen in an impure place, disease occurs. If it sits in a place where goats and sheep are kept, there will be a swift meeting with a beloved person. || 8 || If it is situated on a buffalo, camel, donkey, bone, cremation ground, corner of a house, gravel, mountain, rampart, ashes, or hair, it is inauspicious and brings the fear of death. || 9 || A wagtail flapping both its wings is inauspicious; if it is drinking water in a river, it is auspicious. Seeing the wagtail at the time of sunrise is excellent, but at the time of sunset, the desired fruit is not obtained. || 10 || After the <term>Nirajana</term> <note>a military lustration ceremony involving the waving of lights</note> ritual, if a wagtail is seen moving in the direction the King is facing, and the King travels in that direction, his enemies will soon come under his control. || 11 || In the place where the wagtail mates, a hidden treasure is found; where the wagtail vomits, glass/crystal lies beneath that earth; where it leaves its droppings, coal lies beneath. To test this wonder, one should dig the earth. || 12 || A dead, mutilated, or diseased wagtail bird [gives results according to] its body...

If seen flying in the sky, it brings wealth and a reunion with brothers and kinsmen. ||13|| If a King, upon seeing a suspicious wagtail in a favorable place, offers an auspicious *arghya* <note>a respectful offering of water, flowers, and grains</note> consisting of fragrant flowers and incense upon the earth, then all blessings will increase. ||14|| Those Kings who are devoted to the worship of the twice-born <note>Brahmins</note>, gurus, saints, and deities, and who abstain from eating meat for one week after seeing an inauspicious wagtail, will not suffer the evil effects. ||15|| The result of the first sighting of a wagtail lasts for one year; however, if another wagtail is seen within that period, the result of that sighting lasts only until sunset of that same day. ## Now begins the Forty-Sixth Chapter
### Signs of Portents

I shall now describe the portents <term>Utpata: unnatural disturbances or omens</term> as told by the sage Garga. In brief, a portent is any deviation from the natural state of things. ||1|| Due to the misconduct of men and the accumulation of sins, calamities occur. These portents are of three types: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial. ||2|| Because of the misdeeds of humans, the deities—being displeased—create these signs. To counter them, the King should perform *Shanti* <note>propitiatory rites or peace-making rituals</note> in the kingdom. ||3|| Celestial portents involve unnatural changes in planets and stars, meteors, thunderbolts, high winds, and halos. Atmospheric portents include things like "cities of the Gandharvas" <note>mirages in the sky</note> and Indra’s bows <note>rainbows appearing at unusual times</note>. ||4|| Terrestrial portents are those occurring in moving or stationary objects; these are pacified by specific rituals. Some say atmospheric portents can be softened, but celestial ones cannot be averted. ||5|| However, even celestial portents are pacified by generous gifts of gold, cows, and land, and by the *Koti-homa* <note>a ritual involving ten million offerings</note> and milking cows on the grounds of a temple of Rudra <note>Shiva</note>. ||6|| The divine ripening of these portents affects the King in eight ways: through himself, his son, his treasury, his vehicles, his priest, and his subjects. ||7|| The spontaneous breaking, moving, sweating, weeping, or speaking of idols in temples indicates the destruction of the King and the country. ||8|| The breaking or falling of divine processions, carriages, axles, wheels, yokes, or banners, as well as their inversion or sinking, is not auspicious for the country or the King. ||9|| Disturbances related to the images of Sages, the God of Dharma, the Ancestors, or Brahma bring evil to the twice-born classes. Those arising from Rudra or the World-Protectors are harmful to cattle. ||10|| Disturbances in the images of Jupiter, Venus, or Saturn affect the royal priests; those of Vishnu affect the general population; those of Skanda or Vishakha affect provincial rulers and Kings. ||11|| Portents involving Vedavyasa affect the ministers; Vinayaka <note>Ganesha</note> affects the army commanders; and disturbances in the images of the Creator <note>Brahma</note> or Vishwakarma are said to bring ruin to the entire world. ||12|| If disturbances occur in the images of young gods, goddesses, or female attendants, it affects the King’s sons, daughters, wives, and servants respectively. ||13|| The same should be predicted for portents involving Rakshasas, Pisachas, Guhyakas, or Nagas <note>various classes of spirits and serpent deities</note>. The results of all these manifest within eight months. ||14|| Having observed a divine abnormality, the royal priest, being pure, having fasted for three days and bathed, should worship the idol with baths, flowers, ointments, and garments...

### Chapter 46: With Hindi Commentary

15. The priest should worship the deity with *Madhuparka* <note>a traditional offering of honey, curd, and ghee</note>, various foods, and offerings according to the prescribed rites. He should perform a burnt offering (*homa*) of *Sthālīpāka* <note>cooked rice or grains</note> using the appropriate mantras associated with that specific deity.

16. Thus, when there are abnormalities in divine images, a seven-night peace ceremony (*śānti*) should be performed, involving the worship of Brahmins and the host of gods, accompanied by songs, dance, and festivals.

17. Kings who perform these rites according to the rules do not suffer the ripening of sins, as the evil is obstructed by the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
**Thus ends the section on Portents of Divine Images.**

18. In a kingdom where fire breaks out without a source, or where a fire does not burn even when supplied with fuel, it should be known as a sign of distress for the king and his nation.

19. If fire burns wet meat or water, it signifies the death of the king. If it breaks out in weapons, a fierce battle is coming. Fire in the army, village, or city causes destruction and creates a fear of fire.

20. If palaces, houses, gateways, or banners are burnt by fire or struck by lightning, the arrival of an enemy army is certain within six months.

21. Smoke rising where there is no fire, or dust and darkness appearing during the day, brings great fear. The disappearance of stars in a clear night sky, or their appearance during the day, is also harmful.

22. Fire appearing on city squares, four-legged animals, birds, or humans is said to be terrifying. Death is indicated if smoke, fire, or sparks appear on beds, clothes, or hair.

23. If weapons appear to burn, crawl, or make sounds, or if they spontaneously leave their sheaths or tremble, it is a portent; otherwise, one should predict a fierce and chaotic battle.

24. To remedy portents of fire, one should offer oblations into the fire using mantras, fuel from milk-yielding trees <note>such as Banyan or Peepal</note>, mustard seeds, and clarified butter (*ghee*). In this ceremony, gold must be given to the Brahmins.
**Thus ends the section on Portents of Fire.**

25. If the branches of trees break suddenly, it indicates preparations for war. If trees appear to laugh, it means the ruin of the country; if they weep, it means an abundance of disease.

26. If a young tree flowers out of season, it signifies the death of children; if it happens in a mature tree, it means the division of the kingdom. If sap/milk flows from a tree, it leads to the destruction of all goods.

27. If wine flows, it means the loss of vehicles; if blood, war; if honey, disease. If oil flows, there is fear of famine; if water flows, there is great fear.

28. If dry trees sprout, the strength and food supply will perish; if healthy trees wither, it is the same. If fallen trees rise on their own, it signifies fear caused by the gods.

29. If a worshipped tree produces flowers or fruit out of season, it is designated as a sign for the king's death. Smoke or flames appearing on such a tree also lead to the king's death.

30. If trees appear to move or speak, the destruction of the people is foretold. The results of tree portents ripen within ten months.

31. One should worship the tree with garlands, scents, incense, and cloth, and place an umbrella over it. Then, a prayer to Shiva (*Rudra-japa*) and a six-part oblation (*ṣaḍaṅga-homa*) to the Rudras should be performed.

32. The king should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and ghee. The great sages have declared that in the case of tree portents, the earth (land) should be given as the sacrificial fee.
**Thus ends the section on Portents of Trees.**

33. If two or three stalks emerge from a single lotus or similar plant, it signifies death. If flowers and fruits grow in pairs (joined), it tells of the death of the owner.

34. If there is an excessive growth of crops, or if various types of fruits and flowers appear on a single tree, the arrival of an enemy army is certain.

35. When sesame seeds yield only half the usual oil, or no oil at all, or if food loses its natural taste, one should know that a very great fear is approaching.

36. Any deformed flower or fruit should be taken outside the village or city. A mild *caru* <note>sacrificial porridge</note> should be prepared, or an animal should be sacrificed for the sake of peace (*śānti*).

37. Upon seeing a deformity in the crops, that field should first be given to the Brahmins. By performing a *caru* offering to Mars (*Bhauma*) in the middle of that field, one does not encounter the predicted evils.

Famine occurs when there is rain out of season; fear of hunger and invasion by enemy armies occurs during excessive rain. Disease follows when rain falls in the wrong season, and the death of a king is foretold when rain falls from a cloudless sky. || 38 ||

When cold and heat are reversed, or when the seasons do not manifest correctly, there will be danger to the kingdom, fear of disease, and divine calamities within six months. || 39 ||

Continuous rain for seven days at an unusual time indicates the death of a prominent king. If the rain is red <note>likely referring to dust storms or atmospheric phenomena</note>, there will be preparations for war; if it rains flesh, bones, or fat, a plague will follow. || 40 ||

One should recognize danger when it rains grain, gold, bark, fruits, or flowers. If it rains charcoal or dust, that city will face destruction. || 41 ||

When hailstones fall without clouds, or when strange creatures fall as rain, or if there is a gap <note>unusual cessation</note> during heavy rain, it causes the "iti" <term>iti: the six traditional calamities of agriculture: drought, floods, locusts, rats, birds, and foreign invasion</term> to afflict the crops. || 42 ||

If it rains milk, clarified butter, honey, curds, blood, or hot water, the destruction of the country is known; a rain of bones indicates a war between kings. || 43 ||

If the shadow of the sun is not seen in a clear sky, or if it appears reversed, one should point out that a very great danger has arrived for the country. || 44 ||

When a rainbow is seen in a cloudless sky during the day or at night, in the east or the west, there will be a great fear of hunger. || 45 ||

The conjunction of the Sun, Moon, Rain-god, and Wind-god is remembered during the time of unnatural rain. To pacify the evil, one should give gifts of grain, food, cows, and gold; then the sin attains peace. || 46 || **Thus ends the section on unnatural phenomena in rain.** <note>original: "vrishti-vaikritam"</note>

The receding of rivers from a city soon causes it to become empty. The drying up of lakes and other bodies of water that are usually perennial is also an omen. || 47 ||

Rivers carrying oil, blood, or flesh, or those that are turbulent, turbid, or flowing backward, announce the arrival of an enemy army within six months. || 48 ||

When wells produce flames, smoke, or boiling water, or if sounds of weeping, shouting, singing, or chattering come from them, it is predicted to lead to a plague among the people. || 49 ||

The appearance of water where no hole was dug, or a change in the smell and taste of water, or any unnatural state of a reservoir, indicates great danger. Here is the pacification for that: || 50 ||

In the event of a water disturbance, one should perform a worship of Varuna <note>the Vedic deity of the waters</note> using the Varuna-mantras. Through the chanting and fire-offerings of those same verses, the evil attains peace. || 51 || **Thus ends the section on unnatural phenomena in water.** <note>original: "jala-vaikritam"</note>

Regarding unnatural births: if women give birth to two, three, four, or more children at once, or if the birth is too early or too late, it leads to the destruction of the country and the family. || 52 ||

If twin births occur among mares, camels, buffaloes, cows, or she-elephants, it indicates their death. The result of such a birth manifests in six months. Regarding the pacification, there are two verses spoken by Garga: || 53 ||

<margin>Garga was an ancient sage and astronomer often cited by Varahamihira.</margin>

"Such women should be abandoned to another territory by one who desires welfare. One should gratify the twice-born <note>Brahmins</note> with their desires and have the pacification ritual performed here." || 54 ||

"Four-legged animals [who give birth unnaturally] should be removed from their herds to foreign lands. Otherwise, they will destroy the city, the master, and the herd." || 55 || **Thus ends the section on unnatural phenomena in births.** <note>original: "prasava-vaikritam"</note>

It is inauspicious when animals approach those of a different species, or when cows are approached by others. Or if two bulls drink from each other, or if a dog drinks from a cow. || 56 ||

Within three months, one should know that an enemy invasion will certainly occur. To counter that, these two verses were specified by Garga: || 57 ||

"Abandonment, exile, or donation [of the animal] will quickly bring good. One should gratify the Brahmins here and have chanting and fire-offerings performed." || 58 ||

"The priest should sacrifice to the Creator with a cooked offering and an animal, using the Prajapatya mantra, and give a large fee for the ritual." || 59 || **Thus ends the section on unnatural phenomena in four-legged animals.** <note>original: "catushpada-vaikritam"</note>

If a vehicle moves without being yoked to draft animals, or if it fails to move when yoked, there will be danger to the kingdom and the breaking or sinking of wheels. || 60 || If the sound of a trumpet occurs without being struck...

When forest birds or wild animals enter the city without fear, or when diurnal creatures roam at night and nocturnal ones roam by day; || 66 || or if deer and birds form circles at both twilights, or huddle together crying out toward a "blazing" <note>the direction of the sun</note> quarter, it brings great fear. || 67 || If dogs stay at the door wailing like humans, or if jackals howl at the sun, or if a pigeon or an owl enters the King's palace; || 68 || or if a rooster crows at dusk, or a cuckoo sings in the winter; or if hawks and other birds of prey fly in circles against the sun in the sky—these are all fearful signs. || 69 ||

If the banner of Indra, the sacrificial pillar, the main pillars, or the gates break; or if the doors, arches, and flags are destroyed, it signifies the death of the King. || 74 || If both twilights appear unnaturally bright, or if smoke rises in the forest without a fire, or if the earth cracks without a hole or trembles, it brings fear. || 75 ||

To counteract these, the Sage Garga has prescribed this rite of pacification <term>Śānti: a ritual to calm malevolent forces</term>. || 80 || Great pacification rites, offerings, and grand feasts should be organized. One should worship the Great Indra with hymns dedicated to him. || 81 || **Thus ends the portents of Indra's banner and pillars.**

# The Varahi Samhita

...joyful minds. || 84 || When trees produce an abundance of sap, resin, flowers, and fruit; when there is an increase in the prosperity of cattle and birds—these are signs of auspiciousness in the months of Madhu and Madhava <note>The spring months of Chaitra and Vaishakha</note>. || 85 ||

A sky clouded by the fall of stars and meteors; the solar and lunar discs appearing tawny like copper; the air struck by smoke, dust, and wind without the presence of actual fire or combustion; || 86 || the twilight sky glowing red like a crimson lotus or resembling a turbulent ocean; and the drying up of river waters—if these are seen in the Summer, one should declare them as auspicious <note>original: "shubham"; these events are normal for the heat of summer and thus not omens of evil</note>. || 87 ||

The appearance of Indra’s bow <note>a rainbow</note>, halos, lightning, and the sprouting of dry vegetation; earthquakes, tremors, and unnatural movements of the earth; the roaring or cracking of the ground; || 88 || the rising of lakes, rivers, and wells, or the floating and swimming of things that usually sink; the shifting of mountains and houses—none of these bring fear if they occur during the Rainy Season. || 89 ||

The miraculous sight of celestial women, spirits, Gandharvas <note>celestial musicians</note>, and divine chariots; the visibility of planets, constellations, and stars in the sky during the daytime; || 90 || the sound of singing and musical instruments echoing from forests and mountain peaks; the flourishing of crops and the receding of waters—these are considered sinless <note>harmless</note> in the Autumn. || 91 ||

Cold winds and heavy frost; the roaring of wild beasts and birds; the appearance of Rakshasas, Yakshas <note>nature spirits</note>, and other beings; hearing unearthly voices; || 92 || the directions being shrouded in smoke and darkness; the sky, forests, and mountains appearing obscured; and the sun rising or setting with great intensity—these are considered auspicious in the Pre-Winter season. || 93 ||

Snowfall and atmospheric disturbances; the sight of deformed or miraculous beings; the sky appearing dark like black eye-salve or variegated by the fall of stars and meteors; || 94 || diverse or unusual pregnancies among women, cows, goats, horses, wild animals, and birds; and abnormalities in leaves, sprouts, and creepers—these are auspicious in the Late Winter season. || 95 ||

Indeed, these phenomena are auspicious when seen in their proper season, as they belong to the nature of that season. However, if these same portents are seen outside of their proper season, they are considered extremely terrible. || 96 ||

The songs and verses of the intoxicated, the spontaneous talk of children, and the casual words of women—these do not fail to come true <note>they are considered prophetic</note>. || 97 || The divine will first moves among the gods and then reaches humanity; speech does not manifest without a cause, for it is the goddess Saraswati <note>the goddess of wisdom and speech</note> herself who speaks the truth through them. || 98 ||

Even one who is not an expert in mathematics <note>astronomy</note>, by understanding these portents, becomes famous and a favorite of kings. This secret teaching of the sages has been told; by knowing it, a man becomes a seer of the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note>. || 99 ||

->Thus ends the Forty-Sixth Chapter, named "The Characteristics of Portents,"<-
->in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira.<-

The portents that the great sage Garga described to Atri are now being described here. To be contrary to nature is the definition of a "portent" <term>Utpata: a calamity or supernatural omen</term>. This is its brief meaning. || 1 || Due to the accumulation of sins from the wrongful conduct of men, calamities arise. Divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents provide ample warning of these. || 2 || When men behave improperly, the gods become displeased and create these portents. To ward off these calamities, it is proper for a King to perform ceremonies of peace <note>Shanti rites</note> in his kingdom. || 3 ||

Here, abnormalities of the stars, meteors, thunderbolts, winds, and solar halos are "Divine" portents. Fata Morgana <note>original: "Gandharva-pur," cities in the clouds</note>, rainbows, and similar sights are called "Atmospheric" portents. || 4 || Portents arising from animate (moving) and inanimate (fixed) objects are known as "Terrestrial" portents. These portents are neutralized by peace-making rituals. Some say that atmospheric portents are lessened by such rituals, but divine portents can never be fully averted. || 5 || However, in a temple of Shiva...

Such is the procedure described by the Great Sages. ||32||

->**Thus ends the section on Abnormalities of Trees.**<-

If two or three stalks emerge from a single stem of a lotus or barley, or if two flowers or two fruits grow where there should be one, it portends the death of their owner. ||33|| If there is an excessive growth of grain or if many types of fruits and flowers appear on a single tree, then by the laws of fate, an enemy army will surely enter that country. ||34|| When only half of a sesame seed contains oil, or if no oil comes out of the sesame, a very great fear arises due to the tastelessness <note>loss of essence</note> of the grain. ||35|| It is proper to discard abnormal flowers or fruits outside the village or town. To pacify this, one should perform a <term>Charu</term> <note>an oblation of boiled rice</note> named *Saumya* and also offer an animal—specifically a goat—for peace. ||36|| If an abnormality is seen in the field, one should first donate that field to Brahmins; then, by performing a <term>Charu</term> for the Earth-deity, the defects arising from it can no longer persist. ||37||

->**Thus ends the section on Abnormalities of Crops.**<-

Famine results from drought, the arrival of a foreign army and fear of hunger result from excessive rain, disease results from rain occurring out of season, and the king is killed if it rains from a cloudless sky. ||38|| If winter and summer exchange places, or if all seasons do not behave properly, there will be fear of divine wrath, fear for the kingdom, and fear of disease for six months. ||39|| If it rains continuously for a week out of season, the primary king dies; if it rains blood, there is preparation for weapons <note>war</note>; and if it rains meat, bones, or fat, a plague occurs. ||40|| Fear arises from the raining of grain, gold, bark, fruit, and flowers. The city where charcoal and dust rain down is destroyed. ||41|| The falling of hail without clouds, the abnormal appearance of creatures like donkeys, camels, cats, and jackals, or if rain falls in patches <note>raining in some spots but not others</note> during heavy rains, then fears such as locusts arise for the crops. ||42|| The country is destroyed by the raining of milk, ghee, honey, or hot water, and war occurs among kings if it rains blood. ||43|| If no shadow is seen in the clear sun, or if a reversed shadow is seen, it should be said that there will be great terror in the country. ||44|| When a rainbow appears in the east or west in a cloudless sky during the day or night...

If such signs are seen, a severe famine <term>durbhiksha; a period of extreme food scarcity</term> occurs. ||45|| During the time of unnatural rain, one should perform a sacrifice to the Sun, Moon, and Wind. At that time, giving donations of grain, food, cows, and gold will pacify the sin. ||46|| **Thus ends the section on Unnatural Rain.**

If rivers that flow below a city shift away from those cities, or if the city's perennial reservoirs, ponds, etc., dry up, then the city soon becomes deserted. ||47|| If oil, blood, or flesh flows in the rivers, if the water becomes foul, or if it begins to flow backward, then within six months, an enemy army will attack the city. ||48|| If flames or a glare are seen in a well, if the water begins to boil, or if sounds of weeping, singing, or nonsensical chatter are heard, these occurrences are causes of plague <term>mari; an epidemic or mass death</term>. ||49|| The emergence of water without digging, a change in the smell and taste of water, or the corruption of a reservoir is a cause of great fear. Its pacification should be done in this manner: in the event of water corruption, one should worship Varuna <note>The Vedic deity of water</note> with the Varuna-mantra and perform chanting and fire-sacrifices with this same mantra; in this way, this sin will be pacified. ||50|| 51|| **Thus ends the section on Unnatural Water.**

If there is a disorder in childbirth among women, such as giving birth to two, three, or four children at once, or if birth occurs significantly after or before the expected time, then the country and the lineage are thoroughly destroyed. ||52|| If a mare, a female camel, a buffalo, a cow, or a female elephant gives birth to two offspring at once, it results in their own death. The fruit of unnatural birth manifests after six months. For its pacification, Sage Garga has spoken two verses: a man seeking welfare should leave these women <note>referring to the animals or the afflicted</note> in a distant land. He should satisfy the Brahmins according to their wishes and perform pacification in this manner: move the four-legged animals away from their usual place and leave them in another's land; otherwise, the lord of the city and one's own herd will be destroyed. ||53|| 54|| 55|| **Thus ends the section on Unnatural Birth.**

If an animal of one species mates with an animal of another species, it is inauspicious. Or if two bulls suckle each other's udders, or if a dog suckles a cow's calf, it is inauspicious. ||56|| If this happens, an enemy army undoubtedly arrives within three months. To prevent this, Sage Garga has spoken these two peace-giving verses:

> "By abandoning them, removing them, or donating them, auspiciousness soon follows. For this reason, one should satisfy the Brahmins and have chanting and fire-sacrifices performed. It is proper for the priest to perform the <term>sthalipaka; a ritual offering of cooked rice</term> with the Prajapatya-mantra and worship the Creator (Dhata) with the animals, giving a large amount of grain as a donation."

||57|| 58|| 59|| **Thus ends the section on Unnatural Quadrupeds.**

If chariots, carriages, or other vehicles begin to move without being yoked to horses or oxen, or if a vehicle yoked to oxen does not move and the wheel sinks into the earth, there is a threat to the kingdom. ||60|| If the sound of a trumpet occurs without being blown, or if a trumpet does not sound when blown, or if it produces "derivation" <note>original: vyutpatti</note>—meaning various strange sounds—then the arrival of an enemy army or the death of the king occurs. ||61|| When there is an echo in the sky, or the trumpet sounds, or there is an inverted alignment of the zodiac signs like Cancer, then disease or death occurs. If the sound of the trumpet is toneless, it signifies the defeat of the enemy. ||62|| The sudden yoking of an ox and a plow, the appearance of some corruption in household items like a ladle (spoon), or the howling of a jackal are causes for fear of weapons. The Sage has described its pacification in this way:

> "In this atmospheric disorder <term>vayavya vikara; disturbances related to the wind or air</term>, the king should worship the Wind with barley-meal and have the Brahmins chant the five Rigvedic verses beginning with 'A Vayo'. By giving sweet rice-porridge and donations to the Brahmins..."

# Varahi Samhita

“...satisfy them, diligently give plenty of food as a ritual gift <term>Dakshina: a sacrificial fee or gift given to priests</term>, and perform the fire sacrifice.” ||63||64||65||

Thus ends the **Portents of the Wind**. If domesticated birds of the house become wild, or if wild forest birds enter the city without fear; if those that roam by day wander at night, or those of the night wander by day; if deer and birds sit in circles during the two twilights <note>dawn and dusk</note>, or if they gather and shriek facing the sun, it brings fear. ||66||67|| If dogs remain stuck at the door wailing, or if jackals howl facing the sun; if pigeons or owls enter the royal palace, or if a rooster crows at dusk; if the cuckoo sings out of season during the winter months, or if hawks and other birds fly in reverse circles in the sky, it is a sign of danger. ||68||69|| If a flock of birds descends upon a house, a sacred tree <term>Chaitya: a shrine or holy tree</term>, a gateway, or a door; or if honeycombs, termite mounds, or lotus-like growths appear in these places, it signifies the destruction of said locations. ||70|| If dogs bring bones or parts of a corpse into the house, it causes a plague. If animals or weapons speak like humans, the King will die. To pacify these omens, the Sage <note>likely referring to Garga</note> has spoken these words:

> “In the event of abnormalities among deer and birds, one should perform a fire sacrifice along with ritual gifts. Five Brahmins should be made to chant the mantra ‘Devah Kapota’ <note>original: ‘देवाः कपोत’ - a Vedic hymn used to ward off the ill effects of a dove entering a house</note>, and after giving gifts with the ‘Sudevah’ mantra, it is proper to chant the Shakuna-Sukta <note>hymns related to omens</note> or the ‘Manovedashiramsi’ mantra.” ||71||72||73||

Thus ends the **Abnormalities of Deer and Birds**. If the banner of Indra <term>Indradhwaja: a ceremonial pole raised during festivals</term>, the Indra-bolt, pillars, doors, gates, or flags break or fall, the King dies. ||74|| The appearance of unnatural light during the two twilights, the rising of smoke in a forest where there is no fire, and the cracking or trembling of the earth without a visible hole are all terrifying signs. ||75|| The country whose King is a hypocrite, a devotee of atheists, does not behave like the virtuous, is of a wrathful nature, envious, and sets his mind on cruel conflicts—that country shall be destroyed. ||76|| When children take up weapons, wood, or stones and strike one another while shouting “Kill, seize, cut, break,” then fear shall soon follow. ||77|| If images of the dead are drawn on the walls of a house with charcoal or red chalk, or if a portrait of the master is made at the time of destruction, fear arrives quickly there. ||78|| In a house where spiderwebs are thick, where no worship is performed at twilight, where there is constant strife, and where women remain habitually impure, fear also resides. ||79|| The appearance of demons <term>Rakshasas</term> is a sign of an impending plague from all sides. To prevent this, Garga has prescribed this pacification:

> “Great peace is achieved by offering delicious edible items and sacrifices <term>Bali: ritual offerings</term>, and one should worship Mahendra <note>the Great Indra</note> thoroughly with all the mantras dedicated to him.” ||80||81||

Thus ends the **Portents of Indra’s Banner and Pillars**. In the destruction of a King or country, during the rising of a comet <term>Ketu</term>, or during eclipses of the Moon and Sun, the occurrence of portents out of their proper season is not considered a fault <note>meaning they are expected during such major events</note>. ||82|| Regarding portents that do not produce ill effects, the son of the Sage <note>Rishiputra</note> has described them in these two verses as being natural to the seasons: “Thunderbolts, lightning, the shaking of the earth, twilight glows, clashing sounds, halos, dust storms, smoke, and the sun appearing red at rising or setting; the appearance of grain, sap, oil, and many flowers in trees, and the increase of vigor in cows and birds—these are signs of auspiciousness during the months of Chaitra and Vaishakha <note>March–May</note>.” ||83||84||85|| Stars and meteors—

The appearance of a reddish-brown circle around the Moon and Sun caused by a fall <note>likely referring to atmospheric phenomena like halos</note>, making a sound like a flame without fire; smoke, dust stirred by the wind, and a twilight glow colored like a red lotus; the sky appearing like a surging ocean, and the drying up of river waters—all these produce auspicious results if they are seen during the summer season. || 86 || 87 ||

The appearance of rainbows, halos, lightning, the sprouting of buds on withered trees, the shaking of the earth, its overturning, changes in its form, the earth making sounds or cracking open; the rising of lakes, rivers, and wells or their overflowing their banks, the flooding of water, and the shaking of mountains and houses—these are not fearful <note>i.e., they are considered natural/harmless</note> during the rainy season. || 88 || 89 ||

The sight of celestial women, spirits, celestial musicians <term>Gandharvas</term>, flying chariots <term>Vimanas</term>, and other wonderful visions; the appearance of planets, constellations, and stars in the sky during the day; the sound of songs and musical instruments heard from the peaks of mountains and forests; an increase in grain and a decrease in water—these are said to be auspicious in the autumn season. || 90 || 91 ||

Coldness in the wind and frost, the calling of deer and birds, the sight of beings such as demons <term>Rakshasas</term> and nature spirits <term>Yakshas</term>, divine voices, a smoky or dark sky, the covering of forests, mountains, and directions, and the rising and setting of the sun in high altitudes—these are said to be auspicious in the <term>Hemanta</term> <note>early winter</note> season. || 92 || 93 ||

The falling of snow, disturbances of the wind, deformed and wonderful sights, a sky like black ointment, the sky appearing variegated due to falling stars or meteors; the birth of strange offspring among cows, goats, horses, deer, birds, and women; and abnormalities in leaves, creepers, and sprouts—these are auspicious in the <term>Shishira</term> <note>late winter</note> season. || 94 || 95 ||

If these abnormalities, which arise from nature, are seen in their respective seasons, they are auspicious; if these abnormalities are seen in other seasons, they are extremely terrible. || 96 || The songs and stories of the mad, the words of children, and whatever a woman says—these are not to be disregarded <note>they are seen as prophetic</note>. || 97 || This Goddess of Speech <term>Saraswati</term>, who is the form of truth and unprompted, first circulated among all the gods and then reached mankind. || 98 || Even an astrologer who does not know the science of mathematics, if he understands the knowledge of portents <term>Utpatas</term> well, he too becomes famous and beloved by the king. This is the secret of the sage's words, by knowing which a man can become a seer of the three periods of time <note>past, present, and future</note>. || 99 ||

### Now Begins the Forty-Seventh Chapter

#### The Variegated Beauty of the Peacock <note>original: "Mayurachitrakam"</note>

> I have previously described in detail the auspicious and inauspicious results depending on the heavens and the atmosphere, mostly regarding the movements, conjunctions, and conflicts of the planets and their paths. || 1 ||
> It is not proper for Varahamihira to do this again, as he is a maker of summaries; that would be his fault. However, those who know the science should not say this, for I am repeating the results already mentioned in what is famously known as the "Peacock's Variegation" <note>original: "Mayurachitrakam"</note>, which is a beautiful limb of this science. || 2 ||
> This is merely a description of its own nature. Even if I do not say this, I would still be subject to criticism here. || 3 ||
> All those planets situated in the Northern path <note>original: "Uttaravithi"</note> that are bright bring safety, abundance of food, and welfare. Those that have gone to the Southern path and are devoid of luster bring hunger, fear, and thieves—

# The Varahi Compendium
<note>original: वाराहीसंहिता (Varahi Samhita), a 6th-century encyclopedic work by Varahamihira covering astrology, planetary movements, and omens.</note>

(152)

...they are the ones who cause death. || 4 ||
When Venus <note>original: भृगुपुत्र (Bhrigu-putra), son of Bhrigu</note> enters the royal treasury <note>a specific astrological house</note> and Jupiter <note>original: गिरां प्रभु (Giram-prabhu), the Lord of Speech</note> is situated in the constellation of Pushya, kings become free from enmity and enjoy happiness, and the people are delighted and free from disease. || 5 ||

If the planets, excluding the Sun, afflict the constellations of Krittika, Magha, Rohini, Shravana, or Jyeshtha <note>original: ऐन्द्र (Aindra), belonging to Indra</note>, then the western direction is afflicted by lawlessness. || 6 ||

If at the end of the day these planets stand in the east like a banner, there will be conflict among the kings of the eastern regions. If they are in the middle, there is distress in the Middle Country <note>Central India</note>; this occurs when they are harsh, but not when they possess beautiful rays. || 7 ||

If they occupy the southern quarter, there is a loss of clouds <note>drought</note> in the Deccan <note>Southern India</note>. If they are diminished and harsh in appearance, there is war; if they are endowed with thick bodies and bright rays, it is auspicious. || 8 ||

In the northern path, if their rays are clear, they bring peace to those kings. If they have short bodies and the color of ash, they bring trouble to the kings of those countries. || 9 ||

If the stars of the constellations and the planets are accompanied by smoke, flames, and sparks, or if they lose their visibility, the entire world along with its kings faces destruction. || 10 ||

When two moons appear to shine in the sky, there is a great and immediate increase in the prosperity of the priestly class. If two suns appear, there is a war between the castes, and if three or four appear, it signifies the dissolution of the world. || 11 ||

If a comet <note>original: शिखी (Shikhi), the crested one</note> touches the Seven Sages <note>the Big Dipper</note>, Abhijit, the Pole Star <note>Dhruva</note>, or the constellation of Magha, it causes the destruction of clouds, ruins good deeds, and brings sorrow. If it touches them with a serpentine coil, there is a certain failure of rain, and the countryside, filled with distressed children, quickly goes to ruin. || 12 ||

When Saturn <note>original: रविपुत्र (Raviputra), son of the Sun</note> moves through the eastern gates of the constellations and undergoes retrograde motion, he causes famine, terrible fear, enmity among friends, and a lack of rain. || 13 ||

If Saturn, Mars <note>original: रुधिर (Rudhira), the blood-red one</note>, or a comet pierces the "Cart of Rohini" <note>a specific V-shaped star configuration in Taurus</note>, what can I say? The entire world falls into an ocean of misfortune and meets its end. || 14 ||

Whenever a comet rises continuously or traverses the entire circle of constellations, the world, including all moving and unmoving beings, experiences the evil fruits of its past deeds. || 15 ||

The Moon, when situated in the shape of a bow, looking harsh and red like blood, foretells hunger and fear, but also the mobilization of armies and victory for the side it faces. If its "horns" point downward, it kills cattle and destroys crops; if it appears to be burning or smoking, it signifies the death of a king. || 16 ||

When the Moon is glossy, thick, has even "horns," is wide and high, and moves in the northern path through the "Path of the Air," and is seen with benefic planets and separated from malefic ones, it brings great joy to the people. || 17 ||

When the Moon passes through the constellations of Magha, Anuradha, Jyeshtha, Vishakha, and Chitra, and moves to the south of them, it is not auspicious; it is beneficial only if it moves to the north or through the middle. || 18 ||

The *Parigha* is a line of clouds that appears horizontally at sunrise or sunset. The *Pratisurya* is a mock sun <note>parhelion</note>, and the *Danda* is a straight phenomenon resembling a rainbow. || 19 ||

The long rays of the Sun at sunrise or sunset are called *Amogha*. A straight fragment of a rainbow is called *Rohita*, and a long one is called *Airavata*. || 20 ||

The period from when the sun is half-set until the stars become visible is called the evening twilight (*Sandhya*). Similarly, it lasts from the time the Sun's light begins to fade until it rises. || 21 ||

During this twilight time, good or bad fortune should be predicted by these signs. If all these signs are glossy, there is immediate rain; if they are harsh, there is fear. || 22 ||

When the *Parigha* line is unbroken, the sky is clear, the Sun's rays are dark-hued but glossy, the rainbow is white, and lightning appears in the northeast; or when a "cloud-tree" is glossy and embraced by the Sun's rays, there will be rain. Rain also occurs if a great cloud covers the Sun at the time of its setting. || 23 ||

If it is broken, crooked, black, short, or pierced by signs like crows... [text continues]

### Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, named Mayurachitrakam, in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. || 47 ||

---

We have described all the auspicious and inauspicious fruits regarding the movement of planets, their conjunctions, planetary wars, and their paths <term>Vithi</term><note>specific longitudinal belts in the sky</note>, mostly concerning divine and atmospheric phenomena. ||1|| It is not proper for Varahamihira to repeat these things frequently, for his only fault is that he is a condenser <note>one who summarizes</note>; however, by creating this excellent section called *Mayurachitrakam* <note>The Variegated Peacock</note>, which yields results, the pundits who know this work will not find any fault in him. ||2|| (Regarding the clouds mentioned previously) that is the very nature of the *Mayurachitrakam*, therefore they should not be described again; yet, even if not described, criticism may not be avoided. ||3|| If the planets move in the Northern Path and are bright, there is well-being, abundance of food, and prosperity; if they go to the Southern Path and are lusterless, they cause famine, fear of thieves, and death. ||4|| If the planet Venus is in the "Storehouse" <note>the Magha constellation</note> and Jupiter is seated in the Pushya constellation, then kings remain without enemies, and the subjects remain happy, joyful, and free from disease. ||5|| If planets other than the Sun afflict the constellations of Krittika, Magha, Rohini, Shravana, and Jyeshtha, then the Western region suffers due to injustice. ||6|| If at the time of twilight the planets appear in the East like banners, there will be war among the kings of the East; if this happens in the middle of the sky, the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha</note> suffers; however, if these are dry yet beautiful or possess rays, the Middle Country is not pained. ||7|| If the planets are in the South, there is a depletion of the Southern Path and the clouds; if at this time the planets have diminished bodies and harsh appearances, there is conflict; but if they have large bodies and are radiant, it is auspicious. ||8|| If they shine with clear rays in the Northern Path, they bring peace to the kings there; if they have small bodies and are the color of ash, they bring faults to the country and the kings. ||9|| If the stars of the planets and constellations are joined with laps of smoke and sparks, or if they lose their light without cause, then the entire world is destroyed along with the king. ||10|| When two moons appear radiant in the sky, it is extremely auspicious for the Brahmins; the appearance of two suns indicates war for the Kshatriyas and others; and the rising of three, four, or many such suns and moons indicates the dissolution of the world. ||11|| If the "crested one" <note>the comet Ketu</note> touches the Great Bear <term>Saptarishi-mandala</term>, Abhijit, the Pole Star <term>Dhruva</term>, or the constellation Jyeshtha, it causes the destruction of clouds, loss in good deeds, and sorrow. If it touches the Ashlesha constellation...

If [Saturn] touches [the constellation], it surely destroys the rains, and in the districts characterized by sandy soil, disturbances arise and they are quickly brought to ruin. ||12|| If Saturn wanders through the "Eastern Gate," namely the seven constellations beginning with <term>Kruttika</term> <note>The Pleiades</note>, and becomes retrograde, it causes famine, fear, and enmity among friends, and it does not bring rain. ||13|| If Saturn, Mars, or Ketu <note>The South Node of the Moon, often appearing as a comet</note> should pierce the <term>Rohini Shakata</term> <note>The "Cart of Rohini," a specific V-shaped configuration in Taurus</note>, then such unspeakable misfortune befalls the entire world that it cannot be described. ||14|| When Ketu is constantly rising or wanders through many circles of constellations, the world continuously experiences the fruits of all the evil deeds it has committed. ||15||

If the Moon is shaped like a bow, appears rough, and has the color of blood, it produces hunger and fear; whichever direction the "bowstring" of this Moon faces indicates the mobilization and victory of an army. If the horn of the Moon points downward, there is a destruction of grain and cattle, and if it emits flames and smoke, it causes the death of kings. ||16|| A Moon that is glossy, thick, with equal horns, vast and high, wandering in the northern direction in the <term>Nagavithi</term> <note>The "Serpent's Path," a specific celestial latitude</note>, and is separated from malefic planets while being viewed by benefic planets, gives great joy to mankind. ||17|| If the Moon reaches the constellations of Magha, Anuradha, Jyeshtha, Vishakha, and Chitra and moves to the south, the result is not auspicious; if it stays in the north or the center, it is beneficial. ||18||

The line of clouds seen at the time of sunrise or sunset is named <term>Parigha</term> <note>An atmospheric bar or "bolt"</note>. If it is slanted, it is called <term>Parigha</term>; if it is an object resembling the sun, it is called <term>Pratisurya</term> <note>A mock sun or parhelion</note>; and a straight cloud resembling Indra’s bow <note>a rainbow</note> is called <term>Danda</term> <note>The Staff</note>. A long ray of the sun is called <term>Amogha</term> <note>The Unfailing</note>, and a long, straight rainbow is called <term>Airavata</term> <note>Named after the celestial elephant</note>. ||19||20||

The period from when the sun is half-hidden and the stars have not yet appeared, starting from the loss of brilliance until half the sun has risen, is called <term>Sandhya</term> <note>Twilight/Juncture</note>. ||21|| At that time of twilight, one should predict auspicious or inauspicious results by observing these signs; if all these signs are glossy, there will be immediate rain, and if they are rough, there will be fear. ||22|| An unbroken <term>Parigha</term>, a clear sky, dark rays of the sun, a glistening luster, a white-colored bow of the gods <note>a white rainbow</note>, lightning appearing in the northeast, or when the Badar tree becomes glossy from the falling rays of the sun, or when a great cloud covers the sun at the time of its setting—then rain occurs. ||23|| In a country where the sun appears fragmented, crooked, black, small, pierced by signs like a crow's foot, and rough, there is often an absence of a king. ||24||

Those kings desiring war whose armies are joined from behind by meat-eating birds face a great fear for their forces; however, if the birds fly ahead of them, victory is achieved. ||25|| At the time of sunrise or sunset, if an image of <term>Gandharvapur</term> <note>A "City of Celestial Musicians," referring to a complex mirage or Fata Morgana</note> equipped with banners blocks the sun, it reveals that the king will encounter a fearful battle. ||26|| A twilight with glossy and sweet winds, where the sounds of birds and deer are heard in the eastern direction, is good; but if the twilight is destroyed by dust or is as rough as blood, the district shall be destroyed. ||27||

That which the Sages have described in great detail, I have stated in this treatise while omitting all those repetitions. Upon hearing the song of the cuckoo, it is the nature of the crow to caw; in truth, the crow's cawing is not intended to defeat the cuckoo. ||28||

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the Northwest region, on the <term>Brihat Samhita</term> composed by the venerable Acharya Varahamihira. ||47||
