# Now begins the Forty-Eighth Chapter
## The Royal Ablution (Pushya Snana)

The King is the very root of the tree of his subjects; it is from the protection or injury of that root that evil or good arises in the world. Therefore, the welfare of the King is the primary concern. **(1)** <note>This verse establishes the "Organic Theory" of the state, where the monarch's spiritual health dictates the nation's fate.</note>

The ritual of pacification <term>Shanti: a rite to avert evil</term> which was originally explained by the Self-Born <note>Brahma</note> to the Teacher of the Gods <note>Brihaspati</note> for the sake of Great Indra, was received by the Elder Garga; listen now as he relates it to Bhaguri. **(2)**

The Royal Ablution <term>Pushya Snana: a ritual bath performed when the moon is in the asterism of Pushya</term> must be performed for the King by the Astrologer and the Royal Priest. There is no greater purifier than this, nor anything more effective at ending all portents of evil. **(3)**

The site should be free from trees like the *Shleshmantaka* <note>Cordia myxa</note>, the *Aksha* <note>Terminalia bellirica</note>, or those that are thorny, pungent, bitter, or foul-smelling. It should be avoided by birds of ill omen such as owls and vultures. **(4)**

It should be a forest region covered with young trees, shrubs, and spreading creepers, filled with pleasant, sweet-smelling trees with undamaged leaves and sprouts. **(5)**

The area should be made beautiful by the presence of wild cocks, Greek partridges, parrots, peacocks, woodpeckers, blue jays, and green pigeons; by the *krakara* partridges, the moon-birds, the *kapinjala*, the *vanjula*, and the lovely pigeons. **(6)**

The outskirts of the forest, a field, or a clean house should resound with the humming of bees drunk on floral nectar and the songs of the male cuckoo and other birds. **(7)**

Or the rite may be performed on the charming sandy banks—the "hips" of the river-nymphs—which are marked by the "nail-scratches" of the claws of water-birds. One should do this with a joyful heart among pleasant people. **(8)**

Or by a lake that bears the beauty of the Thousand-Eyed One <note>Indra</note>, where the umbrellas are leaping swans, the music is the song of the cranes and herons, and the eyes are the blossoming blue lotuses. **(9)**

Where the lotus-plant "ladies" have faces of full-blown lotuses, speak in the melodious tones of the swans, and possess high breasts in the form of budding flowers. **(10)**

Or it may be performed in a cow-pen that is not white-washed <note>original: "agauram"</note>, not fierce, free from the foam of other animals, and marked by the hoof-prints of dogs; a place celebrated for the lowing of recently delivered cows and the play of calves. **(11)**

Or perhaps on the seashore, crowded with jewel-laden ships that have safely arrived, its borders dappled by white birds and aquatic creatures resting in the thickets of *nichula* trees. **(12)**

Or in those hermitages where the lion is conquered by patience as if by anger, and is surpassed by the deer; where safety is granted to the young of birds and fawns. **(13)**

Or in a place where the steps of deer-eyed women are hindered by the jingling of their waist-bands and anklets, and which resounds with their sweet voices like the warbling of the cuckoo. **(14)**

The rite should be done during the *Pushya* lunar mansion, in temples, at holy watering places <term>Tirthas</term>, in gardens, or beautiful regions; on ground that slopes to the East or North, where water flows in a clockwise direction. **(15)**

The ground must be free from ashes, charcoal, bones, barren soil, husks, hair, whiskers, and the dwellings of crabs, porcupines, or mice, and free from anthills. **(16)**

The earth that is firm, fragrant, glossy, sweet, and level leads to victory. Such a site should also be selected for a military camp as appropriate. **(17)**

Having left the city, the Astrologer, the Minister, and the Sacrificers should offer a sacrifice <term>Bali</term> in the East, the North, or the North-East. **(18)**

The Royal Priest, being restrained and bowed in devotion, should perform the Invocation with parched grain, unbroken rice, curd, and flowers. The following mantra was ordained by the Sages for this purpose: **(19)**

"May all the Gods come who desire worship here; the Directions, the Serpent-gods, the Twice-born <note>Brahmins</note>, and whoever else is entitled to a share." **(20)**

Having thus invoked them all, the Priest should say: "After receiving worship tomorrow, they shall depart, having granted peace to the King." **(21)**

After the invocation and worship, they should stay there for the night. The rules for interpreting dreams—whether good or bad—have already been stated in the section on 'Marching.' **(22)**

On the following morning, he should gather the materials of the specified quality and go to the designated spot of earth. Here are the verses sung by the Sages: **(23)**

Drawing a mystical circle <term>Mandala</term> there, he should fashion a representation of the Earth, containing various mines of jewels and diverse places. **(24)**

The Priest... <meta>catchword: The Priest (purohito)</meta>

One should place the Serpents <note>Nagas</note>, the Nature Spirits <note>Yakshas</note>, the Gods, and the Ancestors <note>Pitris</note> in their respective positions. Likewise, place the Celestial Musicians <note>Gandharvas</note>, the Heavenly Nymphs <note>Apsaras</note>, the Sages, and the Perfected Beings <note>Siddhas</note>. || 25 ||

The Planets should be placed along with the Constellations <note>Nakshatras</note>, and the Roaring Ones <note>Rudras</note> along with the Divine Mothers. Also place Skanda <note>the god of war</note>, Vishnu, Vishakha, the Guardians of the Quarters <note>Lokapalas</note>, and the Goddesses. || 26 ||

Having fashioned these figures with various colors that are pleasing and endowed with fragrant qualities, the wise practitioner should worship them according to their nature with perfumes, garlands, and ointments. || 27 ||

They should be offered various types of foods, fruits, roots, and meat, as well as various delightful drinks such as wine, milk, and fermented liquors. || 28 ||

Hereafter, I shall describe the specific worship for those depicted here. For the Planets, the procedure prescribed in the *Sacrifice to the Planets* <term>Grahayajna: a specific Vedic ritual to appease planetary deities</term> should be performed. || 29 ||

The Spirits <note>Pishachas</note>, the Sons of Diti <note>Asuras</note>, and the Demons <note>Danavas</note> are to be worshipped with meat-rice and wine. The Ancestors are worshipped with oil-massages, collyrium <note>eye-salve</note>, sesame seeds, and also meat-rice. || 30 ||

The Sages are worshipped with the melodies of the Sama Veda, the sacrificial formulas of the Yajur Veda, and the hymns of the Rig Veda, along with perfumes, incense, and garlands. The Serpents <note>Nagas</note> should be worshipped with non-clashing colors <note>original: "ashleshaka-varna"</note> and the "Three Sweets" <note>honey, clarified butter, and sugar</note>. || 31 ||

The Gods <note>Vibudhas</note> are worshipped with incense, offerings of clarified butter, garlands, gems, hymns of praise, and prostrations. The Celestial Musicians and Nymphs are worshipped with perfumes and highly fragrant garlands. || 32 ||

For the remaining deities, one should place offerings of all colors. For all of them, one should provide protective wrist-bands <note>pratisara</note>, garments, banners, ornaments, and sacred threads. || 33 ||

Having prepared the sacrificial fire in the western or southern part of the circle <term>Mandala: a sacred consecrated space</term> on the altar, the priest should gather the requirements, including a bull and long Vedic texts. || 34 ||

Parched grain, clarified butter, unbroken rice, curd, honey, white mustard, perfumes, flowers, and incense; yellow orpiment <note>gorochana</note>, eye-salve, sesame seeds, and sweet fruits of the current season. || 35 ||

There should be bowls of milk-porridge with clarified butter and those aforementioned materials. The worship should be performed on the western altar; that is the altar for the ritual bath. || 36 ||

At its corners, one should place firm water-pots <term>Kalashas: ceremonial jars representing abundance</term> with their necks wrapped in white thread, covered with the sprouts of milk-exuding trees <note>such as the Banyan or Peepal</note> and fruits. || 37 ||

Filled with water mixed for the *Pushya-bath* <note>a ritual bath performed when the moon is in the asterism of Pushya</note> and containing gems, one should add the groups of herbs prescribed for the Pushya-bath. || 38 ||

<margin>List of medicinal and auspicious herbs</margin>
Jyotishmati, Trayamana, Abhaya, Aparajita, Jiva, Vishveshvari, Patha, Samanga, and Vijaya; || 39 ||

Saha, Sahadevi, Purnakosha, Shatavari, Arishtika, Shiva, and Bhadra—these should be placed into those jars. || 40 ||

Brahmi, Kshema, Aja, all types of seeds, gold, auspicious items as available, all-healing herbs, and essences; || 41 ||

Gems, all types of perfumes, Bilva and Vikankata wood, herbs with praiseworthy names, gold, and auspicious objects. || 42 ||

First, one should spread the skin of a bull that has died of old age <note>indicating a natural, non-violent death</note>, which possessed excellent marks, with its neck facing east. || 43 ||

Over that, the red, unblemished skin of a fighting bull; third, the skin of a lion; and after that, the skin of a tiger. || 44 ||

These four skins should be spread upon that altar. When the auspicious moment <term>Muhurta: a unit of time approx. 48 minutes</term> arrives, joined with the Moon in the Pushya constellation; || 45 ||

A "Throne of Fortune" <note>Bhadrasana</note> made of either gold, silver, or copper, or fashioned from a milk-exuding tree, should be placed upon the skins. || 46 ||

Its height may vary: one cubit, a cubit and a quarter, or a cubit and a half. Such a throne, placed within the mandala, brings good fortune to all kings. || 47 ||

Having placed a piece of gold beneath him, the King should sit there with a composed mind, surrounded by his ministers, trusted friends, the royal priest, the astrologer, and virtuous citizens. || 48 ||

With the sounds of "Auspicious Day!" proclaimed by bards, citizens, and Brahmins, and with the sounds of prosperity from conch shells and musical instruments, all ill-fortune is destroyed. || 49 ||

The royal priest, wearing unwashed <note>new</note> silk garments, should cover the King with a woolen blanket and, having performed the offerings and worship, should sprinkle him using the jars filled with clarified butter.

50. The quantity of water jars should be eight, twenty-eight, or one hundred and eight. As the number increases, the merit increases proportionally. This <term>mantra</term><note>A sacred chant or formula</note> sung by the sages is used here:

51. "Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme destroyer of sins. Clarified butter is the food of the gods; upon clarified butter all the worlds are established."

52. "Whatever misfortune has come to you from the earth, the atmosphere, or the heavens—may all of that perish through the touch of this clarified butter."

53. Then, having removed the woolen blanket, the priest should sprinkle the lord of men with the waters of the <term>Pushyasnana</term><note>A ritual bath performed when the moon is in the asterism of Pushya</note>, which contain fruits and flowers, while reciting this prayer:

54. "May the gods consecrate you, as well as the ancient perfected beings: Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, the <term>Sadhyas</term><note>A class of minor celestial deities</note>, and the hosts of Maruts."

55. "The <term>Adityas</term><note>Solar deities</note>, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Ashvins—the best of physicians; Aditi, the mother of the gods, Svaha, Siddhi, and Sarasvati."

56. "Kirti, Lakshmi, Dhriti, Shri, Sinivali, and Kuhu; Danu, Surasa, Vinata, and Kadru."

57. "The wives of the gods who have not been named, and the mothers of the gods; may all of them and the celestial hosts of <term>Apsaras</term><note>Heavenly nymphs</note> consecrate you."

58. "The lunar mansions, the auspicious hours, the fortnights, the days and nights, the twilights, the years, the lords of the days, the divisions of time—the <term>Kalas</term>, <term>Kasthas</term>, <term>Kshanas</term>, and <term>Lavas</term>."

59. "May all the auspicious limbs of Time consecrate you. The gods who travel in celestial chariots, the <term>Manus</term><note>Progenitors of humanity</note>, along with the oceans."

60. "The Seven Sages with their wives, and those who dwell in the station of the North Star: Marichi, Atri, Pulastya, Kratu, and Angiras."

61. "Bhrigu, Sanatkumara, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatana, Daksha, Jaigishavya, and Bhagandara."

62. "Ekata, Dvita, Trita, Jabali, and Kashyapa; Durvasa, Durvinita, Kanva, and Katyayana."

63. "Markandeya, Dirghatapas, Shunahshepha, Viduratha, Urva, Samvartaka, Chyavana, Atri, and Parashara."

64. "Dvaipayana, Yav akrita, the King of the Gods <note>Indra</note> with his younger brother; these and other sages devoted to the vows of the Vedas."

65. "May they, rich in penance, consecrate you along with their disciples and wives. The mountains, trees, vines, and holy sanctuaries."

66. "The highly fortunate rivers, the <term>Nagas</term><note>Serpent deities</note>, and the <term>Kimpurushas</term><note>Celestial beings</note>; the noble <term>Vaikhanasa</term> ascetics and the twice-born who dwell in the sky."

67. "Prajapati, Diti, and the cows who are the mothers of the universe; the divine vehicles and all worlds, moving and unmoving."

68. "The fires, the ancestors, the stars, the clouds, the sky, the directions, and the water. These and many others of holy renown and auspicious nature—"

69. "May they consecrate you with waters that destroy all calamities. May they bring about your welfare, long life, and health."

70. With these and other prayers prescribed in the <term>Atharvakalpa</term><note>Ritual texts associated with the Atharva Veda</note>, along with the Rudra-hymns, and those seen by Kushmanda, Maharohina, and Kubera, and with prosperity—

71. Having whispered the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are the source of happiness" <note>original: "Apo hi stha..."</note> and the four verses beginning with "The golden-colored..." <note>original: "Hiranyavarna..."</note>, the king, having bathed, should put on a pair of cotton garments.

72. To the sound of the auspicious <term>Shankha</term><note>Conch shell</note>, having sipped water for purification and honored the gods, gurus, and priests, he should then perform the worship of his umbrella, banner, and weapons.

73. He should put on new, victorious ornaments that have been consecrated with the hymns for "Long Life," "Vigor," and "Increase of Wealth."

74. Going to the second altar, the king should sit upon animal skins. These skins should be placed one on top of the other in this order:

75. The skin of a bull, a cat, a <term>Ruru</term> deer, and a spotted deer. Upon those, the skin of a lion, and finally, the skin of a tiger.

76. In the principal place, the priest should offer oblations into the fire with fuel sticks—

One should worship the Three-eyed One <note>Shiva</note>, Indra, Brihaspati, Narayana <note>Vishnu</note>, the Wind-god, and the Fire-god. || 77 || The astrologer should announce the omens of the fire as specified for the Banner of Indra. Even without the Pushya star, this "Ablution of the Month of Pausha" was declared of old to be fruitful. || 82 || In times of national calamity, epidemics, the appearance of Rahu or Ketu <note>eclipses or comets</note>, and the affliction of planets, one should perform the Pushya-snana. || 83 || There is no calamity in the world that is not pacified by this; there is no other auspicious rite that surpasses this. || 84 || For a King desiring supreme sovereignty or the birth of a son, this procedure is highly recommended before his consecration. || 85 || The great-famed Brihaspati spoke this for the sake of Mahendra <note>Indra</note>. This bath is the ultimate means of securing long life, the growth of progeny, and good fortune. || 86 || He who bathes elephants and horses according to this same procedure will attain supreme success, freed from all fear. || 87 ||

## Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Pushya Ablution," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. || 48 ||

The King is like the root for the tree that is the citizenry; the subjects experience the good and bad fruits of the King's transformative rituals. Therefore, one should always be concerned with the welfare of the King. || 1 || Listen to that pacification ritual which Brahma himself told to Brihaspati for Indra, and which the elder Garga, having obtained it, told to Bhaguri. || 2 || It is proper for the King to perform the Pushya-snana through astrologers and priests. Besides this, there is no other rite so pure and capable of destroying all types of calamities. || 3 || The Pushya-snana should be performed in a forest filled with many sweet trees, charming with intact leaves and sprouts, and free from trees like the *Shleshmataka* <note>Cordia myxa</note>, *Aksha* <note>Beleric myrobalan</note>, thorny trees like *Khair* <note>Acacia catechu</note>, or those that are pungent, bitter, or scentless. It should be away from trees frequented by ominous birds like owls. The site should be resonant with the delightful sounds of the *Kukvaku* <note>chameleon/wild cock</note>, *Jivaka* <note>partridge</note>, parrots, peacocks, woodpeckers, blue jays, pigeons, and bees intoxicated by drinking the nectar of flowers. This pacification should be done in a sacred temple-garden near such a forest. || 4 || 5 || 6 || 7 || Or, this pacification should be performed on the beautiful, thigh-like sandbanks of a river—a lady-like river whose waters are marked by the scratches of water-birds, pleasing to the eyes and mind. || 8 || Or it should be performed on the banks of a sacred lake that bears the form of the thousand-eyed Indra, where lotus-like faces bloom, where the speech is the melodious warbling of swans, and where the high breasts are the lotus buds. There, the flying swans serve as the royal umbrella, and the sounds of the *Karandava* <note>coot</note>, *Kurara* <note>osprey</note>, and cranes provide the music. || 9 || 10 || Or in a place where foam has fallen from the rumination of cows, and where the earth is struck by their hooves...

# Chapter 48: With Hindi Commentary
<page-num>159</page-num>

The ritual of the **Pushya Bath** <note>A royal consecration or purification bath performed when the moon is in the lunar mansion of Pushya</note> should be performed in a cow-pen, where cow dung is scattered all around and where the lowing and frolicking of newborn calves creates a festive atmosphere. || 11 ||

Or, it should be performed on the seashore, where ships have arrived safely, where there are heaps of gems, dense *Nichula* (water-cane) trees, and where the shoreline has become multicolored due to the presence of aquatic creatures and white birds. || 12 ||

Just as anger is conquered by forgiveness, the ritual should be performed in a hermitage where lions are humbled by the presence of deer, and where birds and fawns roam without fear. Alternatively, it may be performed in a magnificent house filled with lotus-eyed women who speak as sweetly as the cuckoo and move gracefully—their pace slowed by the weight of their heavy hips and the jingling of their waist-bells and anklets. || 13 || || 14 ||

Or, the **Pushya Bath** should be performed in a sacred temple, at a holy pilgrimage site, in a beautiful garden, or on a piece of land that slopes toward the East or North, where water flows according to the prescribed circumambulation <note>Pradakshina</note> route. || 15 ||

The ground that is dense, fragrant, smooth, sweet, and level—free from ashes, charcoal, bones, barren soil, husks, hair, pits, or the presence of crabs, predatory animals, and mice—and where there are no termite mounds, is the cause of victory. This should also be planned accordingly within a military camp. || 16 || 17 ||

The **Astrologer** <term>Daivajña: one who knows the movements of the stars</term>, the Minister, and the **Priest** <term>Purohita: the royal chaplain</term> should leave the city and go to these locations in the East, North, or Northeast direction. Thereafter, the Priest, having offered salutations, should perform a sacrifice with parched grain, unbroken rice, curd, and flowers. The Sages have provided this **Invocation Mantra** <note>original: "Avahana Mantra"</note> for this purpose:

-> "May all the deities who desire worship here, the Guardians of the Directions, the Serpent-gods, the Brahmins, and whoever else is entitled to a share, please come." || 18 || 19 || 20 || <-

After this, the Priest should call upon everyone and say:

-> "May you all receive the auspicious worship tomorrow, grant peace to the King, and then depart." || 21 || <-

After worshipping the invited deities, everyone should spend the night there. The good or bad fruits of the dreams seen during that night should be interpreted as described in the *Chapter on Journeys*. || 22 ||

The next morning, having brought the prescribed materials, one should go to that ground. Regarding what must be done there, these are the verses sung by the Sage:

-> "The learned Priest should draw a mandala <note>sacred circle</note> there, representing the Earth as a mine of various gems, and designate various positions. He should place the **Nagas** (Serpents), **Yakshas** (Nature Spirits), **Pitris** (Ancestors), **Gandharvas** (Celestial Musicians), **Apsaras** (Celestial Nymphs), Sages, and **Siddhas** (Perfected Beings) in their respective places. He should arrange the Planets of the Constellations, **Rudra** (Shiva), **Skanda** (Kartikeya), **Vishnu**, **Vishakha**, and the **Lokapalas** (World Protectors) along with the **Matrikas** (Mother Goddesses) and the wives of the gods in their proper stations. Then, having colored them with various hues, he should worship them according to tradition with fragrant and beautiful garlands, sandalwood paste, various edible offerings including meat, and various delightful liquids such as wine, milk, and decoctions." || 23 || 24 || 25 || 26 || 27 || 28 || <-

I shall now describe how the desired deities should be worshipped; the same procedure prescribed for the worship of planets in the *Graha-Yajna* <note>Sacrifice to the Planets</note> should be followed here. || 29 || In that ritual, the **Pishachas** (Spirits), **Daityas** (Titans), and **Danavas** (Demons) should be worshipped with meat, cooked grain, and fish. The Ancestors should be worshipped with ointments, collyrium, sesame, meat, and cooked food. || 30 || The Sages should be worshipped with the chanting of the Sama, Yajur, and Rig Vedas, along with fragrant incense and garlands. The Nagas should be worshipped with various colors and the *Trimadhu* <note>A mixture of honey, ghee, and sugar</note>. || 31 || The Gods should be worshipped with incense, offerings of ghee, garlands, gems, hymns of praise, and prostrations. The Gandharvas and Apsaras should be worshipped with the finest fragrant substances and garlands. || 32 || All others should be worshipped with a universal multi-colored offering...

### Page 160

One should offer garments, banners, ornaments, and the sacred thread to all [the deities]. || 33 || Having established the fire upon the altar in the western or southern part of the ritual enclosure, one should donate kusha grass and all necessary materials. Offer parched grains, ghee, rice, curd, honey, white mustard, flower garlands, incense, *gorochana* <note>a bright yellow pigment found in the gallbladders of cattle, used for tilaks</note>, collyrium, sesame seeds, sweet seasonal fruits, and shallow earthen bowls filled with ghee and rice pudding along with all these materials. The altar situated to the west of the principal altar should be worshipped; that very altar is the bathing-altar (*snana-vedi*). || 34 ||

|| 35 || 36 || Tie threads around the necks of all the sturdy water-pots (*kalashas*), cover them with the leaves and fruits of milky trees <note>trees that exude a milky sap, such as Banyan or Peepal, considered auspicious</note>, and place them systematically at the four corners of the altar. Fill all the pots with water mixed with the substances prescribed for the <term>Pushyasnana</term> <note>a ritual bath performed when the moon is in the Pushya asterism to ensure a king's victory and prosperity</note> and place all types of gems within them. The materials for the <term>Pushyasnana</term> as stated by the <term>Sage Garga</term> <note>an ancient Vedic seer and astronomer</note> are as follows:

> "Foxtail millet, *trayamana*, *abhaya* (myrobalan), *aparajita* (clitoria), *jiva* (sweet flag), *vishweshwari* (dry ginger), *patha*, *samanga*, *bhanga*, *saha* (field pumpkin), *sahadevi*, *purnakosha* (nutgrass), *shatavari*, *arishtika* (soapnut), *shiva*, *bhadra*, *aja* (a specific medicinal herb), *kshema* (a fragrant resin), *brahmi*, all types of seeds, gold, auspicious substances, all kinds of medicinal herbs, juices, gems, all varieties of perfumes, a bull, *vikankata* (flacourtia), the herb named *prashasta*, gold, and whatever other auspicious materials can be found—all these should be placed into these water-pots. || 37 || 38 || 39 || 40 || 41 || 42 ||"

First, spread the hide of a bull that possessed excellent marks and died of old age, with its neck facing the east. || 43 || Then, spread the red, intact hide of a warrior bull. Over that, spread a lion's skin, and over that, a tiger's skin. When the Pushya constellation and an auspicious moment arrive, these four types of skins should be spread upon the altar. || 44 || 45 || Place a beautiful seat made of gold, silver, or copper, or a beautiful seat made from the wood of a milky tree, upon these skins. The height of this seat is of three types: one cubit, one and a quarter cubits, or one and a half cubits. If all seats are of the prescribed height and laid out thus, they bring victory and auspiciousness to all kings desiring a kingdom, making them <term>Mandali-kantara-jit</term> <note>one who conquers the territories of neighboring rulers</note>. || 46 || 47 || The noble-minded King, covered in gold, should sit upon that throne surrounded by his ministers, trusted confidants, priests, astrologers, citizens, and those named 'Kalyana' (Auspicious). || 48 || The celebratory sounds of bards and townspeople, the sacred chants uttered by Brahmins, and the auspicious sounds of drums, conch shells, and trumpets destroy the King's misfortunes. || 49 || Then, the priest should thoroughly cover the King—who is wearing intact silk garments and has performed sacrifices and worship—with a blanket, and perform the <term>Abhisheka</term> <note>ritual anointing or sprinkling</note> over the King using a pot filled with ghee. || 50 || There may be eight, twenty-eight, or one hundred and eight pots; the more pots there are, the more the merit increases. Regarding this, the mantra spoken by the Sage is:

> "Ghee (*ajya*) is the supreme radiance; ghee is the best and the destroyer of sins. Ghee is the food of the gods, and all the worlds are established in ghee. O King! Whatever sins—terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial—reside upon you, they are all destroyed upon contact with the ghee." || 51 || 52 || 53 ||

Then, the priest should remove the blanket from the King's body and perform the King's consecration with the Pushyasnana water, which is filled with fruits and flowers. The mantra for that is:

> "May Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, the Maruts, the Sadhyas, and the deities who are perfected and ancient, consecrate you. May the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Ashvins (the best of physicians), Aditi (the mother of the gods), Svaha, Siddhi, Saraswati, Kirti, Lakshmi, Dhriti, Shri, Sinivali, Kuhu, Danu, Surasa, Vinata, Kadru, the mothers of the gods, and the celestial nymphs—may all these [consecrate] you..."

May they perform your <term>Abhisheka</term><note>Ritual bathing or consecration</note>; may the auspicious parts of time—the lunar mansions, the elective moments, the fortnights, day, night, twilight, the year, the most excellent days, and the divisions of time such as the *Kala*, *Kastha*, *Kshana*, and *Lava*—consecrate you. May the gods residing in celestial chariots, the oceans, Manu, the seven Sages with their wives, the entire celestial pole, Marichi, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Angira, Bhrigu, Sanatkumara, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatana, Daksha, Jaigishavya, Bhagandara, Ekata, Dvita, Trita, Jabali, Kashyapa, Durvinita, Durvasa, Kanva, Katyayana, Dirghatapa, Markandeya, Shunahshepha, Viduratha, Urdhva, Samvartaka, Chyavana, Atri, Parasara, Dvaipayana, Yavkrita, the King of Gods <note>Indra</note> with his younger brother, the ascetic sages who study the Vedas along with their disciples and wives, all the mountains and trees, the vines, and the holy temples consecrate you. May the most fortunate rivers, the Nagas, the Kimpurushas, those following the forest-dweller's path, the highly blessed twice-born ones who dwell in the sky, Prajapati, Diti—the mother of the Daityas—all the cows, all divine vehicles, all the moving and unmoving worlds, the fires, the ancestors, the stars, all the clouds, the sky, all the directions, the waters, and the waters that remove all types of calamities, which are auspicious and celebrated for great merit, consecrate you and grant you welfare, long life, and health." || 54-70 ||

The <term>Kushmanda</term> and <term>Maharauhina</term> mantras associated with the Rudras, the mantras of Kubera and others, and the beautiful mantras mentioned in the <term>Atharvakalpa</term> <note>Ritual texts associated with the Atharvaveda</note> should be used for the consecration for all types of prosperity. One should chant the three verses beginning with "Apohishtha" <note>Latin/Sanskrit: *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* - "O Waters, you are indeed..."</note> and the four verses beginning with "Hiranyavarna" <note>Latin/Sanskrit: *Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* - "Golden-colored..."</note>. Then the King, having bathed, should wear two cotton garments. || 71-72 ||

Thereafter, the King, having performed the <term>Achamana</term> <note>Ritual sipping of water</note> amidst the sounds of conch shells and the recitation of auspicious prayers, should worship the Gods, the Guru, and the Brahmins, and then include the royal umbrella, the flag, and all weapons in his worship. || 73 ||

By chanting the verses "For long life, for luster, for the increase of wealth" over the ornaments, the King should put on new ornaments for victory. || 74 || Then the King should go to another altar and sit upon all the skins mentioned previously. The skins mentioned hereafter should be placed one on top of the other. || 75 || He should place the skins of a bull, a cat, a *Ruru* deer, a spotted deer, a lion, and a tiger one over the other in this manner. || 76 || The <term>Purohita</term> <note>Royal priest</note> should offer oblations of sacrificial wood, sesame seeds, and clarified butter into the fire in the center of the altar, using the verses dedicated to Shambhu, Indra, Brihaspati, Narayana, and Vayu. || 77 || The <term>Daivajña</term> <note>Astrologer/Diviner</note> should explain all the omens of the fire as described in the chapter on Indra's Flag, and having completed everything, the priest should say with folded hands:

> "O Gods! May all of you deities, having received worship from the King and granting him great success, depart to return again."

|| 78-79 || Then the King should worship the astrologer and the priest by giving them much wealth, and he should honor those worthy of sacrificial fees and the Vedic scholars according to their merit. || 80 || He should grant safety to his subjects, release animals that have been taken to the slaughterhouse, and release all prisoners except those who have committed internal <note>treasonous</note> crimes. || 81 || This <term>Shanti</term> <note>Peace-making/Propitiatory rite</note> which increases happiness, fame, and wealth should be performed in every *Pushya* constellation. If the *Pushya* constellation does not fall on the full moon of the month of Pausha, it gives only half the fruit. The rites to be performed therein have been described previously. || 82 || When there are calamities in the kingdom or other types of disturbances, or upon the appearance of Rahu and Ketu <note>Eclipses/Comets</note>, or when the planets are harrassing, one should perform the *Pushya* bath. || 83 || There is no calamity on this earth that cannot be removed by this rite, and there is no inauspiciousness capable of overcoming this peace-rite. || 84 || For this reason, for a King desiring to sit upon the throne or desiring the birth of a son, this method of consecration is the most excellent and primary. || 85 || The highly renowned Brihaspati spoke this for Indra. This excellent method of the *Pushya* bath [grants] long life—

### Chapter 49
### Characteristics of the Royal Tiara <note>Sanskrit: *Patta-lakshanam*. A 'Patta' is a decorative gold band or tiara worn on the forehead as a mark of rank.</note>

The characteristics of tiaras which have been described in great detail by the ancient teachers are here summarized by me, encompassing all the essential meanings. || 1 || A tiara that is eight fingers <note>The *angula* or 'finger-breadth' was a standard unit of measurement in ancient India.</note> wide in the center brings good fortune to Kings. One of seven fingers is prescribed for the Queen-consort, and one of six fingers for the Crown Prince. || 2 || A tiara of four fingers' width in the center is for the Commander-in-Chief, and one of two fingers is called the 'Tiara of Favor' <note>A *Prasada-patta* was a simplified band gifted by the King as a mark of honor.</note>. These five types of tiaras are celebrated. || 3 || All of them should be twice as long as they are wide, and their width at the sides should be half of their width in the center. All should be crafted from pure gold to increase prosperity. || 4 || The King’s tiara has five crests <note>Sanskrit: *shikha*, referring to the pointed or ornamental peaks of the crown.</note>; those of the Crown Prince and the Queen-consort have three crests; the Commander-in-Chief’s has one crest; and the Tiara of Favor is without any crest. || 5 || If, while being fashioned, the gold leaf of the tiara expands easily, it signifies the growth and victory of the King, as well as the happiness and wealth of the subjects. || 6 || A blemish appearing in the center causes the destruction of life and the kingdom. If it is cracked in the middle, it must be discarded; if cracked at the sides, it causes obstacles. || 7 || Upon the appearance of such inauspicious omens, the scholar of the scriptures should prescribe a rite of pacification <note>Sanskrit: *shanti*, a ritual intended to avert evil or bad luck.</note> for the King. A tiara with auspicious signs leads to the expansion of the King’s nation. || 8 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Royal Tiara," in the *Brihat Samhita* by the venerable Varahamihira. || 49 ||

The characteristics of the tiara which the teachers have spoken of in detail are here stated in brief, containing all the relevant meanings. || 1 || A crown with a width of eight fingers in the middle is auspicious for Kings; if it is seven fingers wide, it is auspicious for the Queen, and if it is six fingers wide, it is auspicious for the Crown Prince. || 2 || A crown with a width of four fingers in the middle is auspicious for the Commander-in-Chief; a band of two fingers' width is called the 'Tiara of Favor.' These five types of crowns have been described. || 3 || All crowns should be twice as long as their width, and their side-width should be half [of the center]; if all are made of pure gold, they increase auspiciousness. || 4 || A crown with five crests is auspicious for the King, a crown with three crests for the Crown Prince and the Queen, and a crown with one crest for the Commander-in-Chief; the Tiara of Favor without a crest is also auspicious. || 5 || If the leaves crafted for the crown spread out with ease, then the King attains growth and victory, and the subjects attain happiness and wealth. || 6 || If there are stains on the leaf, it destroys life and the kingdom; if it is broken in the middle, it is proper to discard it; if its two sides are torn, it causes obstacles. || 7 || In this way, upon the occurrence of inauspicious omens, those who know the scriptures should order a rite of pacification; by wearing a crown that has no inauspicious marks, the King's empire grows. || 8 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the venerable teacher Varahamihira, with the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province. || 49 ||

# Now begins the Fiftieth Chapter
## The Characteristics of Swords

A sword of fifty <term>Angulas</term> <note>An 'Angula' is a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's breadth, approx. 0.75 inches</note> is considered excellent; one of twenty-five is the minimum. One should judge the <term>Vrana</term> <note>Literally 'wound,' but here referring to spots, marks, or indentations on the blade</note> based on these measurements; marks situated on odd-numbered units are inauspicious. ||1||

Marks resembling the <term>Shrivatsa</term> <note>An auspicious symbol associated with Vishnu</note>, the <term>Vardhamana</term> <note>A stepped-pyramid symbol</note>, a leaf, a Shiva-linga, an earring, or a lotus are praised; so too are those resembling a banner, a weapon, or a swastika. ||2||

Marks shaped like a lizard, a crow, a heron, a headless trunk, or a scorpion are not givers of good fortune, nor are those that follow the grain of the metal or are too numerous. ||3||

A sword that is cracked, short, blunt, broken at the spine, or unpleasing to the eye is not conducive to growth. One that makes no sound when struck is considered undesirable; the opposite of these traits yields desired results. ||4||

A <term>clanging sound</term> <note>original: "svanitam"</note> is said to portend death; a sword slipping from its scabbard predicts defeat. If it unsheathes itself, war is imminent; if the sword appears to blaze with light, victory follows. ||5||

A king should not unsheathe his sword without cause, nor should he rattle it, look at his reflection in it, mention its price, or name its place of origin. He must treat the blade with reverence and never touch it while in an impure state. ||6||

Blades shaped like a cow’s tongue, a blue lotus, or a bamboo leaf are auspicious, as are those resembling a oleander leaf, a spear-point, or a rounded tip. ||7||

Once finished, a sword should not be shortened; it should be made to the correct proportions using a whetstone. If the base is cut, the master dies; if the tip is cut, his mother dies. ||8||

Just as a mark on a woman’s body—such as a mole on the face or the private parts—reveals her character, so too do the marks on a sword reveal its nature. ||9||

Alternatively, by observing which part of his own body a petitioner touches while holding a sword, a wise man can predict the location of a mark on the blade while it is still in its scabbard, by knowing this science. ||10||

If the head is touched, the mark is at the first finger-breadth; the forehead, the second; between the brows, the third; and the eyes, the fourth. ||11||

The nose, lips, cheeks, jaw, ears, neck, and shoulders correspond to the fifth through eleventh units. At the twelfth is the chest, and at the thirteenth, the armpits. ||12||

The breasts, heart, stomach, belly, and navel correspond to the fourteenth through eighteenth. From the nineteenth, the marks are at the base of the navel, the waist, and the private parts. ||13||

At the twenty-second are the thighs; at the twenty-third, between the thighs; at the twenty-fourth, the knees; and at the twenty-fifth, the shanks. ||14||

The middle of the shanks, the ankles, the heels, the feet, and the toes correspond to the twenty-sixth through the thirtieth units, according to the opinion of <term>Garga</term> <note>An ancient sage and authority on astrology and omens</note>. ||15||

Death of a son, gain of wealth, loss of wealth, prosperity, and imprisonment: one should predict these results respectively for marks located at each finger-breadth starting from the first. ||16||

Gain of a son, quarrel, acquisition of elephants, death of a son, and gain of wealth; then destruction, obtaining a woman, and mental grief follow from the sixth unit onwards. ||17||

Gain, loss, obtaining a woman, slaughter, growth, death, and contentment are known from the fourteenth; loss of wealth occurs at the twenty-first. ||18||

Acquisition of riches, liberation, arrival of money, death, prosperity, and poverty; then power, death, and kingship follow in order up to the thirtieth unit. ||19||

Beyond this, there are no specific results, though marks on odd units generally give evil or good results. Some say marks beyond thirty units up to the tip are without effect. ||20||

A sword smelling of oleander, lotus, elephant-must, ghee, saffron, jasmine, or champaka brings good fortune. One smelling of cow urine, mud, or fat is undesirable. ||21||

A scent resembling tortoise fat or wood-ash brings fear and sorrow. A blade with the luster of <term>beryl</term> <note>original: "vaidurya"</note>, gold, or lightning brings victory, health, and growth. ||22||

This is the <term>tempering of weapons</term> <note>original: "shastrapana"</note> according to Ushanas: for one desiring radiant fortune, temper with blood; for one desiring virtuous sons, with clarified butter; for one desiring inexhaustible wealth, with water. ||23||

<note>The following verses are in Sanskrit, providing alchemical recipes for hardening steel.</note>

If one desires success in wealth through a sinful <note>original: "papena"</note> act, one should drink goat's milk. If a sword is smeared with the bile of a fish, a deer, a horse, or a goat, mixed with the milky sap of the *Calotropis* plant and the seeds of the palmyra palm, it becomes incredibly strong. || 24 ||

A paste made of *Calotropis* milk, the soot from a burnt ram's horn, and the excrement of pigeons and mice should be applied to the blade. After being tempered in oil and then sharpened, the sword will not break even when struck against stones. || 25 ||

An iron weapon that is soaked for a day in a solution of wood-ash from a banana tree mixed with buttermilk, and then properly sharpened, will not break against stone, nor will its edge be blunted by other metals. || 26 ||

---

A sword measuring fifty fingers <term>Angula: a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger</term> is excellent, while a sword of twenty-five fingers is of the lowest quality. One should identify flaws <term>Vrana: literally 'wounds' or 'scars,' referring here to structural defects or spots in the metal</term> based on these finger-measurements; if a flaw appears at an odd-numbered measurement, such as 3, 5, 7, or 9, it is inauspicious. || 1 ||

Marks resembling the Shrivatsa <note>a sacred curl of hair</note>, a Vardhamana <note>a ritual vessel</note>, an umbrella, a Shiva-linga, an earring, a lotus, a banner, a weapon, or a swastika are auspicious. || 2 ||

A sword with marks shaped like a lizard, a crow, a vulture, a beast of prey, a headless torso, or a scorpion, or one with many marks like a bamboo stalk, is not auspicious. || 3 ||

A sword that is cracked, too small, blunt, notched, unpleasing to the eye and mind, or one that makes no sound when struck is harmful; the opposite qualities bring desired results. || 4 ||

If a sword suddenly makes a sound on its own, it portends death. If it rattles in its scabbard, it indicates defeat. If it unsheathes itself, it signifies war, and if it glows brightly, it signifies victory. || 5 ||

A King should not draw his sword from its scabbard without cause, nor should he shake it. He should not look at his reflection in it, mention its price, or name its place of origin. Furthermore, he must not touch it while in an impure state. || 6 ||

Swords shaped like a cow's tongue, a blue lotus, a bamboo leaf, or an oleander leaf, as well as those with pointed or rounded tips, are all considered good. || 7 ||

It is not proper to test or cut the aforementioned high-quality swords against a whetstone. If the tip of the sword breaks, the owner of the sword will die; if the hilt breaks, the owner's mother will die. || 8 ||

Just as one can predict the presence of moles on a woman's hidden parts by seeing moles on her face, one can predict the flaws <gloss>Vrana</gloss> within a sword by observing the marks on its hilt. || 9 ||

When a sword-bearer asks a question (such as "Tell me where the flaws are in this sword"), the astrologer <term>Daivajña: a knower of fate or an astrologer</term> should observe which part of the body the questioner touches. According to the science of weapons, he can then determine exactly where the flaws are located on the sword. || 10 ||

If the questioner touches their head at the time of the inquiry, it should be said that the flaw is in the first finger-length of the sword. If they touch the forehead, the flaw is in the second finger-length; if between the eyebrows, the third; if the eyes, the fourth. || 11 ||

If the questioner touches the nose, lips, cheeks, chin, ears, neck, or shoulders, the flaw is located at the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh finger-lengths respectively. Touching the [chest] indicates the twelfth, and touching both armpits indicates the thirteenth finger-length. || 12 ||

By touching the breasts, heart, stomach, flanks, or navel, one should indicate flaws from the fourteenth to the eighteenth finger-lengths in order. Touching the base of the navel, the waist, or the private parts indicates flaws at the nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first finger-lengths. || 13 ||

Touching both thighs indicates the 22nd finger-length; touching the space between the thighs indicates the 23rd. Touching the knees indicates the 24th, and touching the shanks indicates the 25th finger-length. || 14 ||

At that time, if the questioner touches the space between the shanks, the ankles, the heels, the feet, or the toes, then in that order—

<header>Chapter 50 with Hindi Commentary</header>

The presence of a flaw <term>vrana<gloss>a spot, scar, or blemish on the metal</gloss></term> in the area from twenty-six to thirty <term>anguls<gloss>a traditional unit of measurement, roughly a finger's width</gloss></term> should be examined; this is the opinion of the sage Gargacharya. || 15 || If a flaw on the sword is located between one and five anguls from the hilt, the results are as follows in order: death of a son, gain of wealth, loss of wealth, prosperity, and imprisonment. || 16 ||

The results for flaws located from the sixth angul onwards are, in order: gain of a son, distress, acquisition of an elephant, death of a son, gain of wealth, destruction, obtaining a wife, and mental sorrow. || 17 || From the fourteenth to the twentieth angul, the results are: gain, loss, obtaining a wife, slaughter, growth, death, and satisfaction. A flaw at the twenty-first angul results in the loss of wealth. || 18 || From the twenty-second to the thirtieth angul, the results for these nine positions are: acquisition of wealth, lack of salvation <note>original: "anirvan"</note>, arrival of money, death, prosperity, poverty, glory, death, and kingship. || 19 || No specific results are mentioned beyond this; however, some say that a flaw at an odd-numbered angul is inauspicious, while an even-numbered one is auspicious. Others claim that beyond thirty anguls, a flaw anywhere else on the blade carries no specific significance. || 20 ||

A sword that smells like oleander, water-lily, elephant ichor <term>mada<gloss>the scent of an elephant in rut</gloss></term>, ghee, saffron, jasmine, or champaka is a bringer of good fortune. However, if it smells like cow urine, mud, or fat, it is harmful. || 21 || If it smells like a tortoise, marrow, blood, or potash, it brings fear and sorrow. A sword that shines like lapis lazuli, gold, or lightning increases victory and health. || 22 || Those who desire to attain Lakshmi <note>The Goddess of Wealth and Fortune</note> should "quench" <note>original: "paan dena" - the process of tempering or ritual feeding of the blade</note> their weapons with blood. One desiring a virtuous son should quench the weapon with ghee, and one desiring eternal wealth should quench the sword with water; such is the opinion of the scripture composed by Shukracharya. || 23 ||

If the blade is quenched with the milk of a mare, a female camel, or a female elephant, one's goals are successfully achieved even through sinful deeds. If quenched in a mixture of fish gall, deer, horse, and goat milk combined with the juice of <term>talmethi<gloss>a medicinal plant</gloss></term>, the sword becomes so sharp it can sever an elephant's trunk. || 24 || First, rub the weapon with oil, then apply a paste made of the resin of the <term>Aak<gloss>Calotropis procera, the giant milkweed</gloss></term> tree, ashes of a ram's horn, and the droppings of pigeons and mice. After sharpening it, even if struck against stone, the edge will not break. || 25 || If one mixes the potash of a banana tree root with buttermilk and lets it sit for a day, and then the iron sword "drinks" this mixture, the blade will not break even when struck against stone, nor will it become blunt <note>original: "khutla"</note> when striking other iron. || 26 ||

# The Varāhī Saṃhitā (The Compendium of Varāhamihira)

### Chapter 51
### The Science of Bodily Gestures <gloss>1</gloss>

The astrologer <note>original: "daivajña" - one who knows the divine will through stars and omens</note> should predict good or bad fortune by observing the direction, the spoken word, the location, and any sounds or impacts. He must also mentally analyze the time and the specific movements of the limbs of the questioner, whether they belong to the questioner himself or another. For the All-Knowing Lord, being the soul of all moving and unmoving things, is all-seeing; He reveals the fruits of good and bad fortune to seekers through gestures and speech. ||1||

A favorable location is one that is level, shaded by trees with auspicious names, covered in glossy leaves, and bearing beautiful flowers and abundant fruit. It should be a place where pleasant birds gather, a residence of gods, sages, twice-born <note>priestly or scholarly classes</note>, holy men, or perfected beings <note>Siddhas</note>. It should be sprinkled with fine flowers and grain, providing joy through the purity of sweet water and lush green grass. ||2||

Locations are not auspicious if the trees are cut, broken, infested with worms, thorny, scorched, rough, or crooked. Nor is it good if the trees are inhabited by cruel birds, have contemptible names, or are covered in dry, withered, and rustling leaves. ||3||

A cemetery, a deserted house, a crossroads, or a place that is unpleasant, uneven, or salty/barren is not good. Similarly, a place covered in rubbish, charcoal, skulls, ashes, chaff, or dry grass is unfavorable. ||4||

It is not auspicious if the place is occupied by ascetics, naked mendicants, barbers, enemies, prisoners, butchers, or those of the lowest castes <note>original: "svapaca" - literally 'dog-cookers'</note>. Nor is it good if it is filled with gamblers or those oppressed by suffering, or where weapons and liquor are sold. ||5||

The East, North, and Northeast directions are praised for the questioner; the directions of the Wind (NW), Water (W), Death (S), Fire (SE), and Demons (SW) are not. Success comes in the forenoon, not at night, nor during the two twilights, nor in the afternoon for the one asking the question. ||6||

Whatever good or bad omens were described for the undertaking of a journey should also be applied here. One should observe what is in front, what is brought by the people, or what is held in the questioner's palm or clothing. ||7||

The masculine limbs include the upper chest, testicles, feet, teeth, arms, hands, cheeks, hair, throat, nails, and thumb; also the temples, armpits, shoulders, ears, anus, and joints. In a woman, the eyebrows, nose, buttocks, skin-folds <note>on the abdomen</note>, waist, fine lines, and the collection of fingers are considered. ||8||

The tongue, neck, calves, the pair of heels, shanks, navel, earlobes, the nape of the neck, the face, back, collarbone, knees, bones, sides, heart, palate, eyes, penis, chest, and the sacrum... ||9||

...as well as the head and forehead, are termed "neuter." Success may occasionally come through these neuter parts, but never through those that are rough, wounded, broken, or emaciated. ||10||

If the big toe is clearly seen or moved, a desire for sugarcane arises. If a finger is moved, it indicates grief regarding a daughter. If the head is struck, there is fear of the king. ||11||

A movement of the chest indicates separation from one's own body/kin. Touching a rag or torn cloth brings misfortune. If one grasps a cloth by its edge or tail and applies it to the feet, it signifies pervasive influence or gain. ||12||

If the questioner scratches the ground with the big toe, he is thinking of matters related to land. If he scratches his feet with his hand, he is thinking of a female slave. ||13||

Seeing a palm leaf, birch bark, or a cloth suggests thoughts of clothing. Seeing hair, chaff, bone, or ash suggests thoughts of wild animals. Seeing a rope, a net, or tree bark suggests that disease or imprisonment is approaching. ||14||

Through the mention of long pepper, black pepper, dry ginger, or nutgrass; or through lodh-tree bark, costus, clothing, lotus, or valerian; or through fragrant spikenard, dill, or tagara-powder, one should declare the thoughts of the questioner. ||15||

One should predict the destruction of women, men, those afflicted by faults, travelers, sons, wealth, grain, children, or two-legged and four-legged creatures and birds, based on the specific omens seen or mentioned. ||16||

Seeing the dung of elephants, cows, or dogs indicates the destruction of wealth, women, or friends. ||18|| By seeing cattle, elephants, buffaloes, lotuses, silver, or tigers, one obtains wealth in the form of sheep, clothing, sandalwood, silk, and a collection of ornaments. ||19||

When a query is made by men upon seeing an elderly Buddhist monk <note>Shravaka</note> or a wandering ascetic <note>Parivrajaka</note>, the matter concerns friends, gambling, or wealth; or it relates to a courtesan, a king, or a desire for offspring. ||20|| Through Buddhist monks, teachers, Jain monks <note>Arhat/Nirgrantha</note>, omen-readers, merchants, or fishermen; or through thieves, army commanders, traders, female slaves, warriors, shopkeepers, or those condemned to death. ||21|| If an ascetic or a vintner <note>liquor-seller</note> is seen, the traveler's query concerns the tending of cattle. If the querent is anxious, it indicates failure in their livelihood. ||22||

If the querent says, "I wish to ask," "Speak," "Look, Noble One," or "Command me," the concern arises from family connections or relates to gains and power. ||23|| If they say "Point it out," "Speak," "Victory to the traveler," or "Look and tell me what I am thinking," or "Let it be seen quickly by everyone," the matter concerns relatives or thieves. ||24||

If the querent touches an internal limb, it refers to a kinsman; if an external limb, a stranger. By the movement of the big toe or other toes, it refers to male or female slaves. Touching the shanks refers to a servant; the navel to a sister; the heart to one's wife; and touching the heels or the toes indicates a son or daughter. ||25|| Touching the belly refers to the mother; the head to a teacher <note>Guru</note>; the right and left arms to a brother and his wife—thus should one point out the person involved in a theft. ||26||

If the querent leaves an internal limb and touches an external one, or if they discharge phlegm, urine, or feces, or drop an object held in their palm. ||27|| Or if they excessively bend their limbs or crack their joints, or if they see someone carrying an empty vessel, or see a thief; or if words like "stolen," "fallen," "wounded," "forgotten," "destroyed," "broken," "gone," "robbed," or "dead" are heard—then the stolen property will not be recovered. ||28||

All these signs, along with husks, bones, or poison, indicate death. For those in pain, they coincide with weeping or sneezing. If the querent touches an internal limb while the wind <note>Vata humor</note> is strong, or speaks while satiated after a heavy meal, the following applies: ||29|| Touching the forehead or seeing a porcupine indicates eating rice; touching the chest indicates sixty-day rice <note>Shashtika</note>; touching the neck indicates barley. ||30|| Touching the side, breast, belly, or knee indicates beans, flour, or sesame gruel. If they smack their lips or lick them, a sweet taste is known. ||31||

If they smack their tongue, it is sour; if they contort their face, it is pungent, bitter, or astringent; if they hiccup or spit, it is salty. ||32|| If they discharge phlegm, it is dry or bitter; if they hear a carnivore or a messenger, it involves meat. Touching the eyebrows, cheeks, or lips is an omen that such food has been eaten. ||33|| Touching the head, throat, hair, jaw, temples, ears, shanks, or bladder indicates the meat of elephants, buffaloes, rams, boars, cows, hares, or deer has been eaten. ||34|| If such omens are seen or heard, one should say fish or lizard meat was eaten. In a query regarding a pregnant woman, one should predict the fall of the fetus <note>miscarriage</note> based on these signs. ||35||

Whether a male, female, or eunuch is seen, inferred, standing in front, or behind—that will be the gender of the birth. Seeing drinks, food, flowers, or fruits is auspicious. ||36|| If the querent touches the eyebrows or the belly with the thumb or a finger, the concern is about pregnancy. This involves honey, ghee, gold, gems, coral, or the mother, nurse, and child. ||37|| If the belly is touched, she is pregnant; but due to bad omens, there may be indifference. If the belly is squeezed or if a seat or the hand is pressed, it indicates labor. ||38|| For the nose...

### Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, named "Anga Vidya" (Science of Limbs), in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. ॥51॥

By observing the direction, the objects brought by the questioner, and the physical movements of the questioner, oneself, or others, an astrologer <term>Jyotishi: a practitioner of Vedic astrology and divination</term> can use their intellect to predict auspicious or inauspicious results. One who possesses thorough knowledge of stationary <gloss>plants/minerals</gloss> and moving <gloss>animals/humans</gloss> entities is considered an all-knowing <term>Daivajña: one who knows the divine will</term>, an all-seer, equal to the Lord Narayana <note>Vishnu</note>. This is because through these gestures and conversations, they reveal the good and bad fortunes of those seeking wealth and success. ॥ 1 ॥

A place that is adorned with the beautiful "smile" of flowers, laden with many fruits, possesses trees with smooth bark, is free from ominous birds, and features trees with noble names; a place that is level and serves as the dwelling of deities, sages, Brahmins, and perfected beings <term>Siddhas: enlightened or semi-divine beings</term>; where noble men and grain abound, and which is green with fresh grass springing from the joy of pure, delicious water—such a place is auspicious for making an inquiry. ॥ 2 ॥

A place where trees are broken, worm-eaten, thorny, burnt, withered, or crooked; a place surrounded by cruel birds, or trees with bad names, or those that are shriveled and consist mostly of leaves—such a place is inauspicious. ॥ 3 ॥

A place that is a crossroads, or resembles a desolate house near a cremation ground, or is unpleasant to the mind, crooked, always elevated, uninhabited, or covered in charcoal, human skulls, and dry straw—this is not conducive to success. ॥ 4 ॥

A place occupied by monks, naked ascetics <gloss>Nagas</gloss>, barbers, enemies, prisoners, butchers, outcasts <gloss>Chandals</gloss>, rogues, hermits, or afflicted people, or a place where weapons and liquor are sold, is not auspicious. ॥ 5 ॥

The East, North, and Northeast <gloss>Ishana</gloss> directions are best for the questioner, but the Northwest <gloss>Vayu</gloss>, West, South, and Southwest <gloss>Nairrita</gloss> directions are not good. It is not auspicious to ask questions at night, during the two twilights <gloss>dawn and dusk</gloss>, or in the late afternoon. ॥ 6 ॥

The auspicious and inauspicious omens mentioned in the rules of travel should be applied here by observing the objects brought before the questioner or the marks on their clothing. ॥ 7 ॥

The thighs, lips, breasts, scrotum, feet, teeth, arms, hands, cheeks, hair, throat, nails, thumb, temples, shoulders, ears, anus, and joints are masculine words <note>referring to the grammatical gender in Sanskrit which influences the divination</note>. The eyebrows, nose, buttocks <gloss>fleshy part of the waist</gloss>, waist, and fingers with beautiful lines are feminine words. The tongue, neck, calves <gloss>Pindika</gloss>, heels, thighs, navel, earlobes, nape of the neck <gloss>Krikati</gloss>, ankles, face, back, collarbone, knees, ribs, heart, palate, eyes, phallus, chest, the three bones at the base of the spine <gloss>Trika</gloss>, head, and forehead—these limbs are neuter words. # Varahi Samhita
### Page 170

If the questioner avoids touching their inner limbs and instead touches their outer limbs, or if they pass phlegm, urine, or feces while dropping an object from their hand, or if they bend their body excessively or stretch out of laziness; if they see a person with an empty vessel, see a thief, or if during the time of the inquiry words like "seized," "fallen," "cut," "forgotten," "destroyed," "broken," "stolen," or "died" are heard, then the stolen object will not be recovered. **(27–28)**

All these aforementioned signs, when accompanied by the sight of chaff, bone, or poison, or the sound of weeping or sneezing, indicate the death of a patient. If the questioner touches a firm inner limb and takes a deep breath, the <term>Daivajña</term><note>An astrologer or diviner; literally "one who knows the divine."</note> should declare that the questioner is satisfied from having eaten a large meal. **(29)**

If the questioner touches their forehead and sees <term>Shuka-dhanya</term><note>Awned grains or bearded cereals like barley.</note>, say that they have eaten Shali rice. By touching the chest, it is Shali rice, and by touching the neck, it is barley. **(30)**

If the questioner touches the flank, breast, stomach, or knee, then respectively declare the consumption of black gram, milk, sesame, or pulses. If they lick both lips, know they have tasted something sweet. **(31)**

If the questioner is <term>Vishtambhi</term><note>Constipated or experiencing abdominal obstruction.</note>, licks the corners of the mouth with the tongue, or puckers the face, they have eaten something sour. Hiccups arise from eating pungent, bitter, astringent, or hot substances. If they spit, they have eaten rock salt. **(32)**

If at the time of inquiry they expel phlegm, or see a dry, sharp object or a carnivorous bird (or hear its name), they have eaten food mixed with meat. By touching the eyebrow, cheek, or lip, say they have eaten the meat of a <term>Shakuna</term> bird. **(33)**

By touching the head, throat, hair, chin, temple, thigh, or pelvis, the questioner has respectively eaten the meat of an elephant, buffalo, ram, boar, cow, rabbit, or deer. **(34)**

Seeing or hearing evil omens indicates the consumption of monitor lizard or fish meat. Through these signs, the miscarriage of a pregnant woman can also be revealed. **(35)**

In questions regarding pregnancy, whether the child is male, female, or a hermaphrodite is determined by the limbs touched or the objects seen. The birth is predicted based on what is touched in front of the diviner. However, seeing betel leaves, food, flowers, or fruit is auspicious. **(36)**

If one asks a question while touching the eyebrow, stomach, or a finger with the thumb, the questioner is worried about a pregnancy. If honey, ghee, gold, jewels, coral, or a mother, nurse, and son are seen standing ahead, these also reveal concerns regarding pregnancy. **(37)**

If the hands are placed on—that is, touching—the stomach, the woman is indeed pregnant. However, if evil <term>Nimitta</term><note>Omens or signs.</note> are seen, the fetus will be destroyed. If the questioner presses and pulls at the stomach or rubs their hands together while asking, the fetus will also be lost. **(38)**

In an inquiry about conception, if the questioner touches the right nostril, conception will occur after one month. If they touch the left nostril or left ear, conception will occur after four months. **(39)**

Touching the root of the topknot indicates three sons and two daughters will be born. Touching the ear indicates five sons, and touching the hand indicates three sons. If the questioner touches the big toe or both heels at the time of inquiry, one daughter is born. Similarly, touching the little finger indicates five daughters, the ring finger four, the middle finger three, and the index finger two daughters. **(40)**

Touching the right breast indicates two daughters, and touching the left thigh indicates two sons. Touching the middle of the forehead indicates four daughters, and touching the edge of the forehead indicates three daughters. **(41)**

# Now begins the Fifty-Second Chapter
## Signs of Pimples

White, red, yellow, and black pimples <note>original: "pitaka"</note> belong to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively. They yield results for the first-born <note>Brahmins</note> and the other classes in that order. || 1 || Those that are very glossy and of clear beauty bring wealth. If they arise on the head, they bring good fortune; if near the eyebrows, misfortune; if arising from the eyebrows themselves, a meeting with beloved persons; and if arising from the middle of the eyebrows, they quickly bring bad character and grief. If located on the eyelids, they indicate a pleasant sight for the eyes; if in the region of the temples, they indicate renunciation <note>becoming a wandering ascetic</note>; and if located in the places where tears fall, they indicate extreme anxiety. || 2 || On the nose and cheeks, they give clothing and sons; on the lips, they bring the gain of food; similarly, those on the chin bring much wealth; and on the forehead, likewise. On the jaws and the throat, they bring ornaments, food, and drink; on the ears, they bring a collection of ornaments and also self-knowledge. || 3 || Located on the crown-joint, the neck, the heart, the breasts, the sides, or the chest, they indicate a blow from an iron weapon, a wound, the gain of sons and wealth, or even grief. On the shoulder, they bring the attainment of the beloved, but also wandering or begging for alms repeatedly. Those arising in the armpits bring the destruction of wealth and much happiness <note>The text suggests a mix of loss and subsequent comfort</note>. || 4 || Those born on the back and the pair of arms bring the destruction of a multitude of sorrows and enemies. Those born on the wrist bring self-restraint, and those arising from the upper arms bring ornaments and the like. || 5 || Those on the fingers and the belly bring the acquisition of wealth, good fortune, and also grief. On the navel, they bring good food and drink; below it, the theft of wealth by thieves. On the bladder, they bring wealth and grain; on the penis, good sons; and those born on the anus or testicles bring wealth or good fortune. || 6 || On the thighs, they bring the gain of vehicles and women; on the knees, injury from enemies. On the shanks, injury by a weapon; and on the ankles, they give the distress of being bound or fettered. || 7 || Those born on the buttocks, heels, and feet bring loss of wealth, forbidden sexual encounters, and travel. On the collection of toes, they bring imprisonment, and on the thumb, honor from one's kinsmen. || 8 || Pimples or boils caused by portents <note>unnatural occurrences</note> are auspicious for men if on the right side, and for women if on the left; those caused by injury are the opposite. || 9 || Thus the division of pimples has been told from the head downwards. The division of scars and moles <note>original: "vrana-tilaka"</note> should be understood in the same way. Similarly, the marks of birthmarks and hair-whorls <note>original: "mashaka-lakshma-avarta"</note> existing on the bodies of living beings produce the results as stated. || 10 ||

If they are smooth and beautiful, they reveal results according to the <gloss>1</gloss> classes <note>original: "varna"; the four social-cosmic orders</note> starting with the Twice-born; otherwise, they are fruitless. That is, white-colored boils are fruitful for Brahmins, and red-colored boils are fruitful for Kshatriyas. || 1 ||

If a boil is on the head, wealth comes; if on the forehead, the attainment of good fortune; if on both eyebrows, misfortune occurs along with the meeting of a beloved person. If it is between the eyebrows or on the eyelid, there is grief. If on both eyes, it indicates a favorable sight <note>or the gaze of a loved one</note>; if on the temple, it makes one an ascetic; if in the place where tears fall, anxiety arises. || 2 ||

If on the nose and cheek, it bestows clothing and a son; if on both lips, gain of food is achieved; if below the chin, food is obtained. If on the skull, there is gain of much wealth; if on both jawbones, there is also gain of much wealth. If on the throat, there is gain of ornaments, food, and drink; if it arises in the ear, one obtains ear-ornaments and knowledge of one's true nature. || 3 ||

If <term>pitaka</term> <note>a small boil, pustule, or carbuncle</note> arise on the joints of the head, the neck, the heart, the breasts, the flanks, or the chest, the results are respectively: injury by a weapon, a blow, the gain of a son, grief, and the attainment of a beloved. If on the shoulder, there is wandering for alms and destruction. If on the side of the abdomen, many pleasures are obtained through wealth. || 4 ||

If they arise on the back or both arms, there is destruction of sorrow and enemies. If on the wrist, there is restraint; if near both arms, the attainment of ornaments and such occurs. || 5 ||

If a <term>phunsi</term> <note>a small pimple or boil</note> is on the hand, the finger, or the stomach, the results are respectively: attainment of wealth, good fortune, and grief. If on the navel, attainment of excellent drink and food occurs; if below it, loss of wealth through thieves. If on the bladder, wealth and grain; if on the penis, a young woman and a beautiful son; and if on the private parts or above the scrotum, it ordains wealth and good fortune. || 6 ||

If on both thighs, one obtains a vehicle and a wife; if on both knees, one suffers loss from enemies. On both shins, a wound from a weapon; and if on the ankle, the distress of travel and bondage. || 7 ||

However, if they are on the buttocks, the heel, or the feet, there is destruction of wealth, consorting with an unworthy woman, and the gain of a journey. If on the cluster of toes, there is bondage; and if on the big toe, one receives honor from kinsmen. || 8 ||

The boil that occurs on the right side of a man is called "**Utpataganda**" <note>a boil signifying a sudden portent or calamity</note>; a boil on the left side is called an "**Abhighata**" <note>a boil signifying a blow or injury</note> boil. Such boils on the right side of a man bring grain; however, for women, the result is the opposite. That is, a boil on the right side of a woman is called "**Abhighata**" and on the left side "**Utpataganda**." These are auspicious for women on the left side; otherwise, they yield inauspicious results. || 9 ||

Starting from the head, the classification and results of boils on all parts of the body have been stated. The results of a wound or a mole (there is a black-colored mole) should be known in the same way. And the two types of marks called <term>mashaka</term> <note>a mole or freckle</note> or <term>avarta</term> <note>a hair-whorl</note>—if these marks are on the bodies of living beings, they also give the same results. || 10 ||

# Now begins the Fifty-Third Chapter
## Architecture (Vastu Vidya)

The knowledge of architecture, which has come down through the lineage of sages from the Lotus-born <note>The god Brahma</note>, is now being composed by me for the pleasure of learned astrologers. ||1||

It is said that once there was some being <note>The Vastu Purusha or "Building Spirit"</note> who obstructed the earth and sky with his body. The host of gods suddenly seized him and cast him face-downwards. ||2||

Whichever limb was held down by a particular deity, that deity remained stationed there. The Creator <note>Brahma</note> then ordained that being, composed of all the gods, to be the "Spirit of the Site" (Vastu-Nara). ||3||

The house of a King should be one hundred and eight cubits <term>Hasta: a unit of measurement roughly 18 inches</term> in width. There are five types of such houses, each decreasing by eight cubits in width, while their lengths are one and a quarter times their widths. ||4||

The houses of Commanders-in-Chief start at sixty-four cubits and decrease by six cubits for each of the five types; their length is their width plus one-sixth part. ||5||

The houses of Ministers are of five types, starting from sixty cubits and decreasing by four; their length is their width plus one-eighth part. The houses of the Queens are half the size of these. ||6||

The houses of the Crown Prince start at eighty cubits and decrease by six; their length is their width plus one-third. The houses of the younger princes are half the size of the Crown Prince's. ||7||

The houses of the great feudal lords and high royal officials are sized between those of the King and the Ministers. The houses of chamberlains, courtesans, and artists are sized between those of the King and the Crown Prince. ||8||

The houses of all superintendents and officers are equal to the treasury and pleasure-houses. The houses of factory overseers and messengers are sized between those of the Crown Prince and the Ministers. ||9||

The houses of the Astrologer, the Royal Priest, and the Physician start at forty cubits and decrease by four for each of the five types; their length is their width plus one-sixth. ||10||

In architecture, the width is the same as the height for auspicious results. In houses with halls (Shalas), the length is twice the width. ||11||

The width for the four castes starts at thirty-two cubits and decreases by four, down to sixteen cubits. For those of very low status, the size is even smaller. ||12||

The length for Brahmins is the width plus one-tenth; for Kshatriyas, width plus one-eighth; for Vaishyas, width plus one-sixth; and for Shudras, width plus one-quarter. ||13||

The treasury and pleasure-houses are sized between the King's and the Commander's houses. The houses of royal officers are sized between the Commander's and the four castes' houses. ||14||

For those of mixed castes (Parasavas, etc.), the house is built according to their own proportions. A house that is smaller or larger than its prescribed measure brings ill fortune to all. ||15||

For hermits, granaries, armories, and fire-houses, there is no fixed limit, but the authorities do not desire a height exceeding one hundred cubits. ||16||

For the houses of Commanders and Kings, when the width is increased by seventy and divided by two, the hall (Shala) is one-fourteenth of that, and the veranda (Alinda) is one-thirty-fifth. ||17||

In houses of thirty-two cubits and so on, the halls are 4, 4, 3, 3, and 3 cubits wide, with additional inches <term>Angula: a finger-breadth</term> of 17, 3, 15, 13, and 4 respectively. ||18||

The decrease in inches for these is 3, 3, 2, 2, and 2. The remaining inches are 19, 8, 20, 18, and 3. ||19||

A gallery (Vithika) equal to one-third of the hall should be made outside the house. If it is in front, the building is called "Soshnisha" (Turbaned). ||20||

If it is at the back, it is "Sayashraya"; if at the sides, "Savastambha"; and if all around, it is "Samsthita." All these are praised by the experts of the Shastras. ||21||

The height of a house should be its width plus one-sixteenth, plus four cubits. For multi-story buildings, the height of each successive floor is reduced by one-twelfth. ||22||

The thickness of the wall for all houses made of burnt bricks is one-sixteenth of the width. For wooden houses, there are different options. ||23||

The width of the King's and Commander's houses is increased by one-eleventh part; the height of the door in inches is equal to...
