# Varāhī Saṃhitā (The Compendium of Varāhamihira)

The width <note>original: *viṣkambha*</note> is half [of the height]. **24** For the four classes starting with the Brahmins <note>original: *vipra*</note>, the width is 50, 48, 46, and 44 digits <note>original: *aṅgula*</note> respectively. The width of a door is half its height plus one-eighth. **25** The thickness of the door frame should be as many digits as the measure of the height in cubits <note>original: *hasta*</note>. This thickness applies to the two side-posts; for the threshold and the lintel, it should be one and a half times that amount. **26**

The width of these posts is one-eightieth of seven times the height. For a pillar <note>original: *stambha*</note>, the width is one-eightieth of nine times the height, and it should diminish by one-tenth at the top. **27**
A square pillar is called *Rucaka*; an octagonal one is *Vajra*; a sixteen-sided one is *Dvivajra*; a thirty-two-sided one is *Pralīnaka*; and a circular one is called *Vṛtta*. **28**

Dividing the pillar into nine parts: the base <note>original: *vahana*</note> is one part; the pot-capital <note>original: *ghaṭa*</note> is another part; the lotus-motif <note>original: *padma*</note> and the upper lip <note>original: *uttaroṣṭha*</note> should each be made with one part. **29** The thickness of the main beams <note>original: *bhāratulā*</note> is equal to the pillar's width; for the secondary beams <note>original: *tulā*</note> and minor beams <note>original: *upatulā*</note> placed above them, the thickness decreases by one-quarter for each level. **30**

A building with an unobstructed veranda <note>original: *alinda*</note> all around is called *Sarvatobhadra* (Good on All Sides). It is suitable for kings and assemblies of scholars and should have four doors. **31** A *Nandyāvarta* house has verandas running clockwise from the hall walls; in this layout, the western door should be omitted, and the rest constructed. **32** If the veranda on the door-side is continuous and the others follow clockwise, it is auspicious; this is the *Vardhamāna* (Increasing) style, but it should not have a southern door. **33**

If the western veranda is continuous, and the eastern ones are also continuous and rising from it, while the others are open to that limit, it is a *Svastika* (Cross) layout; an eastern door here brings misfortune. **34** If the eastern and western verandas are continuous and the remaining two are limited by them, it is a *Rucaka*; a northern door is not auspicious here, but others are praised. **35** The *Nandyāvarta* and *Vardhamāna* are the best of all; the *Svastika* and *Rucaka* are middling, and the rest are auspicious for kings and others. **36**

A three-winged house <note>original: *triśālaka*</note> lacking a northern wing is called *Hiraṇyanābha* (Golden-Navel) and is blessed. One lacking an eastern wing is *Sukṣetra* (Good Field) and brings prosperity. **37** One lacking a southern wing is *Cullī* (Oven) and causes loss of wealth. One lacking a western wing is *Pakṣaghna* (Wing-Destroyer) and causes the death of sons and enmity. **38**

A house with wings only on the west and south is *Siddhārtha*; on the west and north is *Yamasūrya*; on the north and east is *Daṇḍākhya*; on the east and south is *Vātākhya*. **39** Wings on the east and west are *Gṛhacullī*; on the south and north are *Kāca*. Wealth is gained in *Siddhārtha*; death of the master occurs in *Yamasūrya*. **40** Punishment <note>original: *daṇḍa*</note> occurs in *Daṇḍākhya*; constant quarrel and anxiety in *Vātākhya*; loss of wealth in *Cullī*; and conflict with kinsmen is recorded for *Kāca*. **41**

In a grid of eighty-one squares <note>the *Ekāśīti-pada Vāstu Puruṣa Maṇḍala*</note>, there are ten lines running east-to-west and ten north-to-south. Within these, thirteen deities are stationed in the interior and thirty-two in the outer compartments. **42** Starting from the northeast: *Śikhi*, *Parjanya*, *Jayanta*, *Indra*, *Sūrya*, *Satya*, *Bhṛśa*, and *Antarikṣa*. *Anila* (Wind) is in the southeast corner. **43** Then *Pūṣan*, *Vitatha*, *Bṛhatkṣata*, *Yama*, *Gandharva*, *Bhṛṅgarāja*, and *Mṛga*. Then *Pitṛs*, *Dauvārika*, *Sugrīva*, *Puṣpadatta*, *Varuṇa* <note>original: *ambupati*</note>, and *Asura*. **44** Then *Śoṣa*, *Pāpayakṣman*, and *Roga* in the corner; then *Ahi* and *Mukhya*. Then *Bhallāṭa*, *Soma*, *Bhujaga*, *Aditi*, and *Diti* in sequence. **45**

In the center is *Brahmā*, lord of nine squares. To his east stands *Aryaman*. Clockwise from him, separated by one square each, are *Savitṛ* and *Vivasvān*. **46** Then the Lord of Gods (*Indra*), then *Mitra*, then *Rājayakṣman*, then *Pṛthvīdhara* and *Āpavatsa*—these are on the perimeter of Brahmā. **47** *Āpa* is in the northeast corner; *Sāvitra* in the southeast; *Jaya* in the southwest; and *Rudra* in the northwest, in the inner positions. **48** *Āpa*, *Āpavatsa*, *Parjanya*, *Agni*, and *Diti*—this group of five deities occupies one square each in the corners. **49** The remaining twenty outer deities are said to occupy two squares each. # Chapter 53: With Hindi Commentary

### The Disposition of Deities on the Body

The deities Aryaman and others occupy three squares in the cardinal directions. **(50)** The head of this Spirit <note>Vastu Purusha</note> lies toward the North-East; he lies face down. Upon his head sits Agni <note>the Fire-god, here called Shikhi</note>. In the region of the face is Apah <note>Water</note>, and upon the breasts are Aryaman and Apavatsa. **(51)**

The external deities, starting with Parjanya, are located on the eyes, ears, chest, and shoulders. Satya and the four others are on the arm. Savitar and Savitra are on the hand. **(52)** Vitatha and Brihatkshata are on the flank. Vivasvan is situated in the belly. The thighs, knees, shanks, and buttocks are occupied by Yama and the others. **(53)**

These are the positions on the right side; the same applies to those on the left side. In the genitals are Shakra and Jayanta. In the heart resides Brahma, the Grandfather, while his feet extend to the center. **(54)**

### The Grid and the Vital Points

Having divided the area into sixty-four squares <note>the 8x8 grid</note> and drawn the diagonal lines, Brahma occupies the four central squares. The deities at the corners of Brahma's area occupy half a square. **(55)** Eight deities on the outer corners occupy half a square, while those adjacent to them occupy one and a half squares. The remaining twenty deities occupy two squares each. **(56)**

The intersections of the main lines <term>Vanshas | central structural axes</term> and the centers of the squares are known as the <term>Marmas | vital sensitive points</term>. A wise man should not obstruct them. **(57)** If these points are oppressed by impure vessels, nails, pillars, or <term>Shalyas | foreign objects/hidden debris</term>, they cause pain to the master of the house in the corresponding part of his own body. **(58)**

### Omens and Hidden Defects

If the master of the house feels an itch in a limb, or if an omen occurs during a sacrificial pouring, or if the fire shows an abnormality, there is a hidden object <note>Shalya</note> at that spot. **(59)** If wood is buried there, it causes loss of wealth; if bone, it causes pain to cattle and fear of disease. If iron, there is fear of weapons; if skulls or hair, death may occur. **(60)**

Charcoal brings fear of thieves; ashes always indicate fear of fire. A hidden object located on a vital point <note>Marma</note> is extremely inauspicious, unless it is gold or silver. **(61)** Even a heap of chaff, whether on a vital point or not, blocks the arrival of wealth. Even a peg <note>Nagadantaka</note> placed on a vital point becomes a source of defect. **(62)**

<column-break/>

The lines are drawn from the hair to the wind, from the ancestors to the fire, from the thread of decay to Vitatha, from Mukhya to Bhrisha, and from Jayanta to Bhriga, and from Aditi to Sugriva. **(63)** The nine intersections of these lines are designated as "Extreme Vital Points" <note>Ati-marmas</note>. The measure of a vital point is said to be one-eighth of a square. **(64)** The width of a "bone" <note>Vansha/structural line</note> is equal to the number of fingers in a cubit; the width of a "vein" <note>Shira</note> is prescribed as one and a half times that. **(65)**

### The Welfare of the Inhabitants

A householder seeking happiness should carefully protect Brahma, who resides in the center of the house. If Brahma is afflicted by leftovers or impurities, the master of the house suffers. **(66)** If the "Site-Man" <note>Vastu Purusha</note> lacks a right arm, wealth is lost and the women suffer; if the left is missing, wealth and grain are lost. If the head is missing, all virtues are lost. **(67)**

Defects in the limbs lead to troubles for women, death of sons, and servitude. In a house where the Spirit is complete, the inhabitants enjoy honor, wealth, and happiness. **(68)** These deities are established similarly in houses, cities, and villages. The various classes, such as Brahmins, should reside in their appropriate quarters. **(69)**

The residences of Brahmins and others should be known to start from the North. As one enters the respective houses, they should be situated to the right. **(70)** When the site is divided by nine or eight lines <note>creating 81 or 64 squares</note>, the doors placed in the positions of Agni and others yield specific results. **(71)**

### Results of Door Placements

**East side:** Fear of fire, birth of daughters, great wealth, favor of the king, excessive anger, falsehood, cruelty, and theft. **(72)**
**South side:** Few sons, servitude, meanness, increase in food and drink, increase in sons, ferocity, ingratitude, poverty, and destruction of the sons' valor. **(73)**
**West side:** Affliction to sons, increase of enemies, no gain of wealth or sons, attainment of sons, wealth and strength, abundance of wealth, fear of the king, loss of wealth, and disease. **(74)**
**North side:** Slaughter and imprisonment, increase of enemies, gain of wealth and sons, possession of all virtues, attainment of sons and wealth, excellence, and defects caused by sons...

# The Varāhī Compendium
## Chapter on Residential Architecture (Vāstuvidyā)

...causes poverty for the woman of the house. ॥ 75 ॥ A door is considered inauspicious if it is "pierced" <note>obstructed or aligned directly with</note> by a road, a tree, a corner, a well, a pillar, or a water-channel. However, if the distance between the door and the obstruction is twice the height of the house, there is no defect. ॥ 76 ॥ A door pierced by a road leads to ruin; one pierced by a young tree causes harm to the children. A door situated in mud brings sorrow, while one that leaks water causes excessive expenditure. ॥ 77 ॥ A well in front of the door causes epilepsy; a temple or divine image causes destruction. A pillar causes defects related to the wife, and if the door faces a Brahma-temple <note>or perhaps a central courtyard pillar</note>, it leads to the ruin of the entire lineage. ॥ 78 ॥

If a door opens by itself, it causes madness; if it closes by itself, the family is destroyed. If the door is larger than the prescribed measurements, there is fear of the king; if it is too low, there is fear of thieves and general distress. ॥ 79 ॥ A door placed directly above another door is not for welfare, nor is one that is too narrow. A crooked door brings fear of hunger, and a "hunchbacked" <note>warped or sagging</note> door ruins the family. ॥ 80 ॥ A door that is too tightly fitted causes pain; one that leans inward leads to poverty. If it leans outward, it causes constant travel or exile, and if it is misaligned with the cardinal directions, there is trouble from thieves. ॥ 81 ॥ The main entrance should not be overshadowed by other doors; it should be richly decorated. One should adorn it with auspicious symbols such as water-pots, fruits, leaves, and images of forest-spirits <note>original: "pramatha"</note>. ॥ 82 ॥

In the corners starting from the North-East, outside the house, reside these spirits: Carakī, Vidāriṇā, Pūtanā, and Rākṣasī. ॥ 83 ॥ The defects that reside in the corners of cities, houses, and villages are amplified by the presence of outcasts <note>original: "śvapaca", literally "dog-cookers"</note> living in those specific spots. ॥ 84 ॥

Trees with inauspicious fruits should be avoided in the South and other directions in sequence. In the North and other directions, the following are praised: the Plakṣa, the Banyan, the Udumbara, and the Peepal. ॥ 85 ॥ Thorny trees near the house bring fear of enemies; trees with milky sap cause loss of wealth; fruit-bearing trees cause the loss of offspring. Even the timber from these trees should be avoided. ॥ 86 ॥ If one cannot cut down these trees, one should plant auspicious ones between them: the Punnāga, Aśoka, Ariṣṭa, Bakula, Jackfruit, Śamī, and Śāla. ॥ 87 ॥

Land that is rich in medicinal herbs, trees, and vines, and is sweet-smelling, fragrant, glossy, and level, brings prosperity to men. If such land provides relief even to weary travelers, how much more so will it bless a permanent home? ॥ 88 ॥

Loss of wealth occurs if the house is near a minister's residence; death of a son if near a rogue's house. Anxiety arises near a temple, and infamy if built at a crossroads. ॥ 89 ॥ Near a sacred tree <note>original: "caitya"</note>, there is fear from planetary influences; in places full of anthills or pits, there are calamities. A house in a hollow causes constant thirst, and land shaped like a tortoise shell causes loss of wealth. ॥ 90 ॥

A slope toward the North is preferred for Brahmins, and so on in clockwise order for the other castes. A Brahmin may live anywhere, but others should prefer land suited to their own class. ॥ 91 ॥

**The Pit Test for Soil Quality:**
Dig a pit one cubit deep in the center of the site and then refill it with the same earth. If the earth does not fill the hole, it is inauspicious; if it is level, it is mediocre; if there is earth left over, it is excellent. ॥ 92 ॥ Alternatively, fill the pit with water and walk a hundred paces; if the water level has not dropped upon your return, the land is blessed. <note>The text also mentions a weight-based test involving 64 palas of water.</note> ॥ 93 ॥ Or, place a lamp in an unbaked clay pot inside the pit. The direction in which the flame burns brightest indicates which caste the land is best suited for. ॥ 94 ॥ Flowers left in the pit overnight that do not wither indicate the land is auspicious for the corresponding caste. Ultimately, that land is auspicious where one's mind feels at peace. ॥ 95 ॥

White, red, yellow, and black soils are praised for Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively. The smell of the earth should resemble ghee, blood, food, or wine. ॥ 96 ॥ Land covered with Kuśa grass, Śara reeds, Dūrvā grass, or Kāśa grass respectively brings growth to the corresponding castes. The tastes should be sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent. ॥ 97 ॥

After finding land that has been plowed, where seeds have sprouted, where cows have rested, and which has been praised by Brahmins, the architect should begin construction at the time appointed by the astrologer. ॥ 98 ॥ Having performed worship of the deities with various foods, curd, unbroken grain, fragrant flowers, and incense, and having honored the architects and Brahmins... ॥ 99 ॥ The Brahmin should touch his head, the Kshatriya his chest, the Vaishya his thighs, and the Shudra his feet... <note>This refers to a ritual of consecration or measurement based on the body parts associated with the origins of the four castes.</note>

# Chapter 53: On the Characteristics of House Construction
## (Page 177)

At the beginning of a house's construction, the architect should touch the ground and draw a line. **[100]** This line should be drawn with the thumb, the middle finger, or the forefinger. If the ground is touched with gold, gems, silver, pearls, curd, fruits, flowers, or unbroken grains <note>Sanskrit: *akshata*, used in rituals</note>, it is considered auspicious. **[101]**

If the line is drawn with a weapon, there is a risk of death by weapons; if with iron, there is a risk of imprisonment; if with ash, there is a fear of fire. If drawn with grass, there is a fear of thieves, and if scratched with wood, there is a fear of the king <note>likely meaning legal or governmental trouble</note>. **[102]**

A crooked line or one drawn with the foot brings fear of weapons and distress. A line drawn with leather, charcoal, bone, or a tooth brings misfortune to the builder. **[103]** Lines drawn from right to left <note>counter-clockwise</note> indicate enmity, while those drawn from left to right <note>clockwise</note> indicate prosperity. Harsh words, spitting, or sneezing at this time are declared inauspicious. **[104]**

When the architect enters the house—whether it is half-finished or fully built—the homeowner should observe the omens: where the architect stands and which part of his body he touches. **[105]** If a bird facing the sun cries out harshly at that moment, a bone <note>an impurity buried in the ground</note> should be predicted in the part of the site corresponding to the body part touched by the architect. **[106]**

If, at the time of the bird's cry, other animals like elephants, horses, or dogs make a sound, the bone belongs to that specific animal and is located in the corresponding limb. **[107]** If a donkey brays while the measuring line is being stretched, it indicates a "thorn" <note>Sanskrit: *shalyam*, meaning a hidden defect or foreign object</note> of bone. If a dog or jackal jumps over the line, a hidden defect is also indicated. **[108]**

When a bird chirps sweetly from a peaceful direction, it signifies wealth at that spot or in the limb of the owner's body corresponding to that direction. **[109]** If the measuring line breaks, it signifies death; if the foundation peg is driven in upside down, it signifies great disease. If the homeowner or the architect suffers a lapse in memory, death is predicted. **[110]**

If the water-pot slips from the shoulder, it causes headaches; if the pot is broken, it signifies the death of the workers, unless it was free from defects. If it slips from the hand, the death of the homeowner is predicted. **[111]**

After performing worship in the South-East corner, the first stone should be laid. The remaining stones and pillars should be raised in a clockwise direction. **[112]** The pillar should be raised adorned with umbrellas, garlands, and clothes, and treated with incense and ointments. The height of the door should be constructed with similar care. **[113]**

The results of birds perching on the pillars, or the pillars shaking, falling, or being poorly positioned, are similar to the results described for Indra's Banner <note>referring to a specific set of omens regarding ritual poles</note>; these can be auspicious or inauspicious. **[114]**

If the North-East is elevated, there is a loss of wealth and sons; if there is a foul smell, it signifies the death of a son. If the building is crooked, it leads to the destruction of kinsmen; if the directions are confused <note>the house is not aligned with the cardinal points</note>, there will be no pregnancies. **[115]**

If one desires the growth of the house, it should be expanded equally on all sides. Expanding in only one direction is a defect, though it may be done toward the East or the North. **[116]** Expansion to the East causes enmity with friends; to the South, fear of death; to the West, loss of wealth; and to the North, mental anguish. **[117]**

The prayer room <note>Sanskrit: *devagriham*</note> should be in the North-East; the kitchen in the South-East; the storage for household goods in the South-West; and the granary or wealth in the North-West. **[118]**

Water located in the East and other directions causes: loss of sons, fear of fire, fear of enemies, quarrels with women, wickedness in women, poverty, and (finally, in the North) growth of wealth and children. **[119]**

Trees that are homes for birds, broken, dried up, burnt, located in temple grounds or cemeteries, or trees like the Milk-tree, Dhava, Vibhitaka, Neem, and Arani should be avoided for timber. **[120]** A tree should be cut during the day after performing offerings and worship at night and walking around it. It is lucky if it falls toward the North or East; otherwise, it should not be used. **[121]**

If the cut surface is clear, the wood is auspicious for the house. If there is a yellow circle, a lizard is hidden inside; **[122]** if madder-red, a frog; if blue, a snake; if reddish, a chameleon; if bean-colored, a stone; if brownish, a mouse; and if sword-colored, water. **[123]**

One who desires prosperity should not sleep on grain, cows, teachers, fire, or wine; nor under a main beam, nor with the head toward the North or West, nor naked, nor with wet feet. **[124]**

### Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, named "The Science of Architecture," in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā composed by Sri Varāhamihira. ||53

That same Science of Architecture <note>Vāstu-vidyā: the ancient Indian system of architecture and design</note>, which came from Lord Brahmā to the sages, is now being recounted for the pleasure of scholars and astrologers. ||1|| In ancient times, a certain being <note>a spirit or 'bhuta'</note> was born who obstructed the Earth and the Sky with his body. He was struck down by the gods and fell face-down upon the earth. ||2|| Whichever deity took possession of a particular part of his body became the presiding lord of that area. Subsequently, Lord Brahmā ordained that being of divine body to be the "Vāstu Puruṣa" <note>The "Building Personified," a cosmic man whose body forms the grid for architectural planning</note>. ||3|| (In this world, there are five types of residential houses for men.) Among them, the first is the best, the second is inferior to the first, and so on. First, the measurements for a King's house are stated: it is one hundred and eight (108) cubits <gloss>1</gloss> wide and 135 cubits long. Among the five types of royal houses, this is the best. The second and the other four types of houses will decrease by eight cubits in both length and width respectively. For example: the second is 125 cubits long and 100 cubits wide; the third is 115 long and 92 wide; the fourth is 105 long and 84 wide; and the fifth is 95 cubits long and 76 cubits wide. ||4|| The best house for a Commander-in-Chief is 64 cubits wide, and its length is determined by adding a sixth part to that width. For example: the first is 64 cubits wide and 74 cubits and 16 digits <note>angul</note> long; the second is 58 wide and 67 cubits 16 digits long; the third is 52 wide and 60 cubits 16 digits long; the fourth is 46 wide and 53 cubits 16 digits long; and the fifth is 40 cubits wide and 46 cubits 16 digits long. ||5|| The houses of Ministers are also of five types. The primary house among them is 60 cubits wide. Then, four cubits are reduced successively from 60—meaning they are 56, 52, 48, and 44 cubits wide respectively. The length is determined by adding one-eighth of the width to the width itself. The measurements are as follows: the first is 67 cubits 12 digits, the second is 63, the third is 58 cubits 12 digits, the fourth is 54, and the fifth is 49 cubits 12 digits long. The houses for Queens should be half the size of these in length and width. Lengths: first 33:18, second 31:12, third 29:6, fourth 27:0, fifth 24:18. Widths: first 30, second 28, third 26, fourth 24, and fifth 22 cubits. ||6|| The houses of the Crown Prince <note>Yuvarāja</note> are also of five types. The best house among them is 80 cubits wide; the width of the other houses decreases by six cubits successively. Their length is determined by adding one-third of the width. For example: the first is 80 cubits wide and 106 cubits 16 digits long; the second is 74 wide and 98 cubits 16 digits long; the third is 68 wide and 90 cubits 16 digits long; the fourth is 62 wide and 82 cubits 16 digits long; the fifth is 56 wide and 74 cubits 16 digits long. Among these best and other types...

The houses of the younger brothers of the Crown Prince <note>original: *Yuvraj*</note> should be half the size of the royal residences. Their widths are measured at 40, 37, 34, 31, and 28 cubits <note>original: *haath*, a traditional unit of length approximately 18 inches</note>, and their lengths are 53.8, 49.8, 45.8, 41.8, and 37.8 cubits respectively. ||7|| The difference in size between the houses of the King and the Minister is the same as the difference for the houses of the Feudal Lords <note>original: *Samanta*</note> and high-ranking officials. In order of excellence, their widths are 48, 44, 40, 36, and 32 cubits, and their lengths are 67.12, 62.10, 56.12, 51.10, and 45.12 digits <note>original: *angul*, a finger's width</note>. The difference between the houses of the King and the Crown Prince is the same as the difference for the houses of chamberlains, courtesans, and performers. In order of excellence, their lengths are 28.8, 26.8, 24.8, 22.8, and 20.8 digits, and their widths are similarly 28, 26, 24, 22, and 20. ||8|| The dimensions for the houses of all superintendents and officers are equal to the dimensions of the treasury and the pleasure-house. The difference between the houses of the Crown Prince and the Minister is the same as the difference for the houses of the heads of labor and messengers. Their widths are 20, 18, 16, 14, and 12 cubits, and their lengths are 39.4, 35.16, 32.4, 28.16, and 25.4. ||9|| The width of the best house for an astrologer, a priest, or a physician should be 40 cubits. These are also of five types; for this reason, following the sequence, each will decrease by four cubits, and their length will be their width plus one-sixth part of that width. The widths are 40, 36, 32, 28, and 24 cubits. The lengths are 46.16, 42.0, 37.16, 32.16, and 28.0 digits. ||10|| It is auspicious if a house is as high as it is wide. However, for houses consisting of only a single hall <note>original: *shala*</note>, the length should be double the width. ||11||

From this, it is understood that Brahmins are entitled to five types of houses of such breadth and diameter, Vaishyas to three types, Shudras to two types, and those of the lowest caste to one type of house.

The difference found between the houses of the common people and the Commander-in-Chief shall be the measure for the <term>Koshagriha</term> <note>Treasury or storehouse</note> and the <term>Ratigriha</term> <note>Pleasure house or private chamber</note>. ...will be of the measure of eight fingers, two cubits and twenty fingers, two cubits and eighteen fingers, and two cubits and three fingers. ||18||19||

One-third of the previously mentioned hall measurement should be kept as open ground outside the building; the name of this ground is <term>Vithika</term> <note>a gallery or veranda</note>. If this <term>Vithika</term> is located on the eastern side of the building, the structure is named **"Soshnisha"**. If the <term>Vithika</term> is on the western side, it is called a **"Sayashraya"** building. If the <term>Vithika</term> is in the north or south direction, it is called **"Savashtambha"**. If such a <term>Vithika</term> surrounds all four sides of the building, it is called **"Samsthita"**. The authors of the scriptures always worship all these types of buildings; that is, such architecture is extremely auspicious. ||20||21||

Whatever the width of the house may be, adding four cubits to its sixteenth part will give the height of that house. The height of the remaining four types of houses will be progressively less by twelve parts in comparison. ||22||

The measure of the wall is exactly one-sixteenth of the diameter of all houses; this measurement applies to houses made of fired bricks. However, for a house made of wood, the thickness of the wall should be determined according to one's preference. ||23||

Take the diameter of the house of a King or a General, add seventy to it, and divide by 11 (eleven); the resulting figure in cubits will be the width of its main entrance. The height will be as many cubits as there are fingers in the width measurement. Half of the door's width is known as the <term>Vishkambha</term> <note>the width of the door-post or pillar</note>. ||24||

For the houses of other castes such as Brahmins, adding eighteen fingers to one-fiftieth of the house diameter will give the measurement of the door. One-eighth of the door measurement is the <term>Vishkambha</term> of the door, and the height of the door will be higher than the <term>Vishkambha</term>. ||25||

As many cubits as it is in height, it shall be that many fingers in thickness. Both side-frames of the house shall be thus, and the measure of the <term>Udumbara</term> <note>the threshold or door-sill</note> is one and a half times the measure of the side-frames. ||26||

Multiply the height of a house in cubits by 17 (seventeen) and divide by 80 (eighty); the result is the width of its base (foundation). Multiply the height by nine, divide by eighty, and subtract one-tenth of that cubit-measure; the remainder is the measurement of the top part of the column. ||27||

If the middle part of the column is square, it is called **"Ruchaka"**. If it is octagonal, its name is **"Vajra"**. A sixteen-sided column is called **"Dvivajra"**, a thirty-two-sided one is **"Pralinaka"**, and a circular one is called a **"Vritta"** column. These five types of columns are the ones that yield auspicious results. ||28||

When the column measurement is divided by nine, the resulting parts are collectively called the <term>Vahana</term> <note>the supporting members or tiers</note>. Among these, the bottom-most ninth part is named **"Vahana"**; the eighth part is **"Ghatagra"**; the seventh part is **"Padma"** <note>lotus-shaped capital</note>; the sixth is **"Uttaroshta"**; the fifth is **"Bharatula"**; the fourth part is **"Tula"** <note>main beam</note>; the third part is **"Upatula"** <note>minor beam</note>; the second part is **"Apratishiddha"**; and the first part is the **"Alinda"** <note>lattice or balcony</note>. These will be reduced by one-fourth relative to each other in sequence. A building that has such <term>Vahana</term> and doors on all four sides is called a **"Sarvatobhadra"** building. This is auspicious for Kings, those dependent on Kings, and for the Gods. ||29||30||31||

A building in which the <term>Alinda</term> <note>veranda/balcony</note> runs all the way down in a circumambulatory (clockwise) order is called a **"Nandyavarta"** building. This will have no door in the West, while doors will exist in the other directions. ||32||

A building where the <term>Alinda</term> runs down to the lower part of the door in a circumambulatory order is auspicious; the name of this building is **"Vardhamana"**. It has no door in the South...

# Varahi Samhita
## Page 182

One should build a house where there is one hall in the west and two in the east extending to the ends, with the other two sides having raised halls and the remaining boundaries left open; this is called the **"Svastika"** <note>literally "auspicious sign"</note> type of architecture. For this type, an east-facing door is not considered good. ||33||34||

A house where the two halls in the east and west are lowered (or absent) and the remaining two extend to the east and west limits is called **"Ruchaka"**. For this house, a north-facing door is not good, while all other doors bring blessings. ||35||

The **Nandyavarta** and **Vardhamana** types of architecture are auspicious for everyone. **Svastika** and **Ruchaka** give moderate results, while the remaining types of architecture are auspicious only for kings. ||36||

A three-walled house that lacks a hall on the north side is called **"Hiranyanabha"** <note>Golden-naved</note>; one lacking a hall in the east is called **"Dhanya"** <note>Wealthy</note>; and one lacking a hall in the east but otherwise well-proportioned is **"Sukhetra"** <note>Good Field</note>. These are auspicious. ||37||

A house lacking a hall in the south is called **"Chulli-Trishalaka"**; this destroys wealth. A house lacking a western hall is called **"Pakshaghna"** <note>Side-destroyer</note>; this leads to the loss of sons and creates enmity. ||38||

A house with halls only in the west and south is called **"Siddhartha"**. Halls in the west and north are called **"Yamasurya"**. Halls in the north and east are called **"Danda"** <note>The Staff/Punishment</note>, and halls in the east and south are called **"Vata"** <note>Wind</note>. ||39||

A house with halls only in the east and west is called **"Griha-Chulli"**, and one with halls in the south and north is called **"Kacha"**. The Siddhartha layout brings wealth. The Yamasurya layout leads to the death of the master of the house. The Danda layout leads to punishment and execution. The Vata layout leads to constant struggle and distress. The Chulli leads to the destruction of finances, and the Kacha layout leads to conflicts within the family or caste. ||40||41||

<note>Types of Vastu Mandalas and details of the Deities</note>

There are two types of Vastu Mandalas <note>sacred diagrams used in site planning</note>: the 81-square grid (Ekashitipada) and the 64-square grid. For the 81-square grid, one should draw ten lines facing east and ten lines facing north over them to create eighty-one squares. In this 81-square Vastu Mandala, forty-five (45) deities reside. Among them, thirteen reside in the center and thirty-two on the outer perimeter.

They are as follows: Shikhi, Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Surya, Satya, Bhrisha, and Antariksha. All these deities reside in order starting from the Northeast corner (Ishan) toward the lower section. In the Southeast corner (Agni) is Anila; following him in order are Pusha, Vitatha, Brihatkshata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhrigaraja, and Mriga. Starting from the Southwest corner (Nairitya) are Dauvarika (Sugriva), Kusumadatta, Varuna, Asura, Shosha, and Rajayakshma. Starting from the Northwest corner (Vayu) are Tata, Ananta, Vasuki, Mallara, Soma, Bhujaga, Aditi, and Diti. All these deities reside there. ||42||43||44||45||

In the central ninth square, Lord Brahma resides. To the east of Brahma are Aryama, followed by Savita, Vivasvan, Indra, Mitra, Rajayakshma, Shosha, and Apavatsa; these deities reside around Brahma in a clockwise direction, each separated by one square. The deity named Apa resides in the Northeast corner of Brahma. Savitra is in the Southeast, Jaya is in the Southwest, and Rudra is in the Northwest. All these reside in the interior. ||46||47||48||

Apa, Apavatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti are all "class" deities. In these five classes, five deities reside; these are "five-footed" (occupying five units). The remaining outer deities are "two-footed" (occupying two units), and there are twenty of them. The four deities like Aryama who surround Brahma are "three-footed" (occupying three units). ||49||50||

The Vastu-Purusha <note>the personification of the site's energy</note> lies with his face downward and his head in the Northeast corner (Ishan). Shikhi is situated on his head. On his face—

## With Hindi Commentary

->**The Deities of the Vastu Purusha**<-

The deity **Apah** is situated on the breast, and **Aryama** is on the chest, while **Apavatsa** resides upon the chest as well. ||51|| The four external deities—**Parjanya**, **Jayanta**, **Indra**, and **Surya**—are located respectively on the eyes, ears, chest, and shoulders. The five deities starting with **Satya** are located on the arms. **Savita** and **Savitra** are situated on the hands. ||52|| **Vitatha** and **Brihatkshata** are on the flanks, **Vivasvan** is on the stomach, **Yama** is on the thighs, **Gandharva** is on the knees, **Bhrungaraja** is on the shanks, and **Mriga** is above the buttocks. ||53||

These deities are stationed on the right side of the **Vastu Purusha** <note>the personified spirit of the architectural site</note>. Similarly, deities are also situated on the left side: **Prithvi** <note>Earth</note> on the left breast, **Diti** on the lower eye, **Aditi** on the ear, **Bhujanga** <note>the Serpent</note> on the left side of the chest, **Soma** on the shoulder, and the five deities **Bhallata**, **Mukhya**, **Ahiraga**, and **Papayakshma** are on the arm. On the left hand are **Rudra** and **Rajayakshma**; on the flanks are **Shosha** and **Asura**; on the thighs is **Varuna**; on the knees is **Kusumadanta**; on the shanks is **Sugriva**; and on the buttocks is **Dauvarika**. These deities reside in the left portion of the **Vastu Purusha**. **Indra** and **Jayanta** are situated on the phallus, **Brahma** resides at the heart, and **Pita** is at the feet. This describes the division of the **Vastu** into eighty-one <term>Pads</term> <note>square divisions or modules</note> for cities, villages, and houses. Now, the sixty-four pad Vastu is described. ||54||

Alternatively, one may construct a Vastu of sixty-four squares; that is, by drawing nine lines east-to-west and nine lines north-to-south, sixty-four squares are created in the Vastu. Two diagonal lines should be drawn across the four corners. In this layout, **Brahma** is the lord of the four central squares. The eight deities situated near the "ears" of Brahma are **Apavatsa**, **Savita**, **Savitra**, **Indra**, **Jayanta**, **Rajayakshma**, and **Rudra**. ||55||

The eight deities stationed in the outer corners are **Agni**, **Antariksha**, **Vayu**, **Mriga**, **Pita**, **Papa**, **Yakshmaroga**, and **Diti**; all of these are lords of half a square each. Flanking them are **Parjanya**, **Bhrisha**, **Bhrungaraja**, **Dauvarika**, **Sheshanaga**, and **Aditi**, who are lords of one-and-a-half pads each. The remaining twenty deities—**Jayanta**, **Indra**, **Surya**, **Satya**, **Vitatha**, **Brihatkshata**, **Yama**, **Gandharva**, **Sugriva**, **Kusumadanta**, **Varuna**, **Asura**, **Mukhya**, **Bhallata**, **Soma**, **Bhujanga**, **Aryama**, **Vivasvan**, **Mitra**, and **Prithvidhara**—are all lords of two squares each. This is the description of the sixty-four pad Vastu. ||56||

The intersections of the <term>Vamshas</term> <note>directional lines/beams</note> which will be described hereafter, and the exact centers of the pads, are known as the **Marma** <note>vital/sensitive</note> spots of the Vastu. A wise man should never cause "affliction" <note>physical pressure or damage</note> to these spots. ||57|| If the **Marma** spots in a Vastu are afflicted by impurities, vessels, nails, pillars, or <term>Shalya</term> <note>hidden foreign objects/obstacles</note> (which will be discussed later), they cause pain to the owner of the house in the corresponding limb of their own body. ||58||

If the owner of the house scratches a particular limb during a <term>Homa</term> <note>fire ritual</note> or at the time of a query, a **Shalya** <note>hidden defect</note> exists in that corresponding limb of the Vastu. Furthermore, if during an offering to a deity like **Agni**, an ill <term>Shakun</term> <note>omen</note> occurs—such as sneezing or weeping—or if some abnormality appears in the sacrificial fire, one should understand that the limb of the **Vastu Purusha** associated with that deity contains a **Shalya**. ||59||

The presence of a wooden **Shalya** leads to loss of wealth; a **Shalya** of bones causes suffering to livestock and fear of disease; an iron **Shalya** brings fear of weapons; and a **Shalya** of skulls or hair leads to death. ||60|| A **Shalya** of charcoal brings fear of thieves, and a **Shalya** of ash brings a constant fear of fire. Except for gold and silver, any other **Shalya** lodged in the **Marma** of the **Vastu Purusha** is extremely inauspicious. ||61|| If husks of grain or similar items are in the **Marma** spots or elsewhere, they block the arrival of wealth. An elephant's tusk is auspicious, but if it is located in a **Marma** spot, it becomes harmful. ||62||

In the **Vastu Purusha**, one should draw lines from the deity named **Roma** to **Anila**, from **Pita** to **Shikhi**, from **Vitatha** to **Shosha**, from **Mukha** to **Bhrisha**, from **Jayanta** to **Bhrunga**, and from **Aditi** to **Sugriva**. ||63|| Of these lines, nine...

-># Barahi Samhita<-

The intersections of the <term>Vastu Purusha</term> <note>The "Vastu Purusha" is the mystical spirit of a structure, envisioned as a man lying face down within the building's foundation grid</note> are called the "extreme vital points" (*ati-marma*); the measurement of such a vital point is said to be one-eighth of a square (*pada*). ||64||

The "lineage" (*vansha*) of the six previously mentioned lines is now described. The ten horizontal and ten vertical lines drawn for the division of the site are called *shira* (veins). However many cubits the width of one square is in the site, the width of one *vansha* should be that many finger-breadths (*angul*). The width of a *shira* is one and a half times the width of a *vansha*. ||65|| If the master of the house desires happiness, he must carefully protect the area of Brahma located in the center of the site. By throwing leftovers or refuse upon the Brahma-space, the owner of the house suffers distress. ||66|| If the right arm of the <term>Vastu Purusha</term> is deficient, it leads to the destruction of wealth and defects regarding the wife; if the left arm is deficient, there is a loss of money and grain. If the head of the <term>Vastu Purusha</term> is missing, all virtues including wealth and health are destroyed. ||67|| If the <term>Vastu Purusha</term> is without feet, there are troubles for the wife, the death of sons, and a state of servitude. If all the limbs of the <term>Vastu Purusha</term> are complete, those living in that site enjoy honor, wealth, and happiness. ||68|| In houses, cities, and villages, this Vastu deity resides in the same manner. In those cities and villages, one should settle the various classes (*varnas*), such as Brahmins, in their proper order. ||69|| In the four directions—North, East, South, and West—the <term>Chatushala</term> <note>A traditional four-winged house surrounding a central courtyard</note> houses in a village or city should be occupied by Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively. These houses should be built such that when entering the courtyard of one's home, the residential quarters remain on the right side. ||70|| In a site of eighty-one squares divided by nine lines, and a site of sixty-four squares divided by eight lines, there are thirty-two gates starting from Agni. Their results are described in order. ||71||

From Agni to Antariksha, there are eight deities in the Eastern part of the <term>Vastu Purusha</term>. If a door is placed over them, the results in order are: fear of fire, birth of daughters, great wealth, favor of the King, irritability, speaking falsehoods, cruelty, and thievery. ||72|| From Pavana to Mriga, in the squares of the eight deities of the South, the results of a door are: few sons, servitude, meanness, increase in food, drink and sons, ferocity, ingratitude, poverty, and the destruction of sons and strength. ||73|| From Pitra to Papa, the results of placing a door on the eight deities of the West are: suffering of sons, increase in enemies, lack of wealth and sons, attainment of sons, wealth and strength, prosperity, fear of the government, loss of wealth, and disease. ||74|| From Yakshma to Diti, the results of placing a door on the eight deities of the North are: death, imprisonment, increase in enemies, gain of sons and wealth, possession of all virtues, attainment of sons and wealth, enmity with sons, defects in the wife, and poverty. ||75||

A door obstructed by a roadside tree, the corner of another house, a well, a pillar, or a water drainage channel is considered inauspicious. That is, these should not be directly in front of the house door. However, if the obstruction is at a distance of twice the height of the door, there is no defect. ||76|| If the path to the door is obstructed, it leads to the destruction of the house owner; a tree obstruction causes defects in children; a mud obstruction (if mud remains constantly in front of the house) causes grief. A drainage channel obstruction leads to the depletion of wealth. ||77|| A well obstruction causes <term>epilepsy</term> <note>original: "mrigi-roga"</note>, an obstruction by a deity's idol leads to the destruction of the house owner, a pillar obstruction causes defects in the women of the house, and a door directly facing the Brahma-center leads to the destruction of the lineage. ||78|| In a house where the door leaf opens by itself without being touched, the residents suffer from insanity. If the door leaf closes on its own, the lineage is destroyed. If the door is larger than its prescribed proportions...

If [the door] is [too large], there is fear of the king <note>original: "raja-bhaya"; likely referring to legal troubles or government interference</note>, and if it is too small, there is fear of thieves and it causes suffering. ||79||

If the door of the second story is placed directly above the main door, it is not auspicious; similarly, a door that is too low is not good. A door that is excessively wide creates a fear of hunger <note>poverty or lack of resources</note>, and a crooked or hunched door causes the destruction of the family lineage. ||80|| A door that is heavily pressed down by the upper timber <note>the lintel</note> causes pain to the master of the house. If it leans inward, it causes the death of the master. If it leans outward, the master remains in foreign lands, and if it looks toward [an incorrect] direction, he is troubled by thieves. ||81||

The appearance of the main entrance of the house should not be like ordinary doors; that is, the main entrance should be superior in beauty to the other doors. One should decorate the main entrance with auspicious ornaments such as water-pots <term>Kalash</term>, fruits, leaves, and the attendants of Lord Shiva <note>Ganas</note>; these images should be carved upon the door. ||82|| Outside the house, in the four corners starting from the Northeast <term>Ishan</term>, reside four deities in order: Charki, Vidari, Putana, and Rakshasi. ||83|| Those who live in the four corners of a house, village, or city suffer various types of distress; however, if low castes such as the <term>Shvapach</term> <note>traditionally dog-cookers or those outside the varna system</note> live in those corners, they experience growth. ||84||

The Pilkhan, Banyan <term>Vat</term>, Gular <note>Cluster Fig</note>, and Peepal trees are inauspicious if they are located in the South, West, North, and East of the house respectively. However, if these trees grow in the North, East, South, and West in that order, they are auspicious. ||85|| If thorny trees like Khair are near the house, they create fear of enemies. Milky trees like Aak <note>Milkweed/Calotropis</note> cause the destruction of wealth. Fruit-bearing trees like Mango cause the decline of progeny. The wood of these trees should also not be used in the construction of the house. ||86||

If these [inauspicious] trees are near the house and one does not cut them down, then one should plant auspicious trees alongside them. The Nagkeshar, Ashoka, Neem, Maulsari, Jackfruit <term>Kathal</term>, Jant, and Shaal trees are auspicious. ||87||

If travelers walking on a path sit for even a moment to relieve their exhaustion on land that is smooth, level, without holes, sweet-smelling, and endowed with excellent medicinal herbs and vines, that land grants them prosperity <term>Lakshmi</term>. What then to say of the prosperity attained by those whose very houses are built on such land and who always reside there? ||88||

If the house of a king's minister is near one's home, it causes loss of wealth. If the house of a cheat is nearby, it causes the death of a son. If a temple of a deity is close, the mind remains in sorrow. If a crossroads <term>Chatuspath</term> is nearby, it brings infamy. ||89|| If a <term>Chaitya</term> <note>a sacred or prominent tree</note> is near the house, the master fears the influence of the planets. If a snake's burrow or pitted land is near the house, calamity follows. A pit near the house causes diseases of thirst, and land shaped like a tortoise near the house destroys the master's wealth. ||90||

Land that slopes toward the North <term>Udakplav</term> is auspicious for Brahmins. Similarly, land sloping East, South, and West is auspicious for Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras respectively. Brahmins may live on all types of land regardless of the direction of the slope. For other castes, land following their order is auspicious: East, South, and West slopes for Kshatriyas; South and West slopes for Vaishyas; and only West-sloping land for Shudras. ||91||

Dig a pit one cubit <note>the length of a forearm</note> wide and one cubit deep in the house, then fill it back up with the same soil. If the soil is insufficient to fill the pit, the house is inauspicious. If the soil fills the pit exactly, it is neither auspicious nor inauspicious. And if the pit is filled and soil remains left over, then [it is very auspicious]...

That house is auspicious in every way. ||92|| According to the previously mentioned method, one should dig a pit and fill it with water; then walk a hundred steps and return. If, in that time, the water in the pit has not decreased at all, that land is auspicious. Furthermore, if one fills an <term>Adhak</term> with the dust of that place and weighs it, and that dust weighs sixty-four <term>Palas</term>, then that land is also auspicious. <note>An Adhak is a wooden vessel for measuring grain which holds approximately four seers (about 3.7 kg) of grain; forty Mashas make one Pal.</note> ||93|| One should place a lamp with four wicks in an unbaked clay vessel. Assign the four castes, starting with <term>Brahmins</term>, to the wicks in the North and other directions, light them, and place the vessel in the pit. The direction in which the wick burns for the longest time indicates that the land is auspicious for that specific caste. ||94|| Take four flowers of colors corresponding to the castes—namely white, red, yellow, and black—place them in the pit in the evening, and check them the next day. The land is auspicious for the caste whose corresponding flower has not withered. Alternatively, if one's mind feels at peace with the land, that land is auspicious; there is no need for further consideration. ||95|| White, red, yellow, and black soils are auspicious for the four castes—Brahmin and the others—respectively. Land that smells like ghee, blood, grain, or wine is auspicious for the castes in that same order. ||96|| Land where Kusha grass, Shar reed, milk-grass, or Kans grass grows abundantly is auspicious for the four castes respectively. Similarly, land where the soil is sweet, astringent, sour, or bitter is auspicious for the four castes in order. ||97||

If one wishes to build a house on a piece of land, they should first plow it and sow seeds. When those seeds have ripened, cows should rest on that land for one night, and Brahmins should praise the land. A person wishing to begin construction on such land should go at an auspicious <term>Muhurta</term> <note>A calculated astrological moment or time period</note> advised by an astrologer. After offering various types of sweets, fried cakes, and other edibles, along with curd, unbroken rice, fragrant flowers, and incense to the <term>Kshetrapal</term> <note>The guardian deity of the field or territory</note> and other deities, the craftsman should draw the lines for the <term>commencement of the house</term>. ||98||99||

At the time of drawing the lines, a Brahmin should touch his head, a Kshatriya his chest, a Vaishya his thigh, and a Shudra his feet while drawing. ||100|| At the start of the house, if the master of the house draws the line using gold, gems, silver, pearls, curd, fruit, flowers, or unbroken rice with his thumb, middle finger, or index finger, it is auspicious. ||101|| If the line is drawn with a weapon, the master of the house may die by a weapon; if with iron, there is imprisonment; if with ash, fear of fire; if with straw, fear of thieves; and if the line for the <term>commencement of the house</term> is drawn with wood, there is fear of the government. ||102|| A crooked line, one drawn with the foot, or an ugly-looking line brings fear of enemies and distress. Lines drawn with leather, charcoal, bone, or teeth bring misfortune to the master of the house. ||103|| A line drawn from right to left causes enmity; a line drawn from left to right brings wealth. If someone speaks harsh words, spits, or sneezes at the time of starting the house, it is said to be inauspicious. ||104|| Whether the house is partially or fully built, the craftsman entering it should observe auspicious and inauspicious signs, noting which part of the <term>Vastu-Purusha</term> <note>The metaphysical "spirit of the site" or architectural man</note> the owner is leaning on and which part of his own body he is touching. ||105|| At that time, if a bird makes a harsh sound while perched in a direction illuminated by the sun, one should know that a bone is buried beneath the spot where the master of the house is standing. Furthermore, the bone belongs to the same limb that the master of the house is touching at that moment. At the time of sunrise, the sun resides in the eastern direction...

Furthermore, during the eight watches <note>Prahars; a unit of time lasting approximately 3 hours</note> of the day and night, the Sun travels through the eight directions in sequence. The direction the Sun has just left is called **Angarini** (Smoldering); the direction in which it currently resides is **Dipta** (Blazing); and the direction it is about to enter is called **Dhumita** (Smoky). Avoiding these three, the remaining five directions are considered **Shanta** (Peaceful). ||106||

At the time of observing omens <term>Shakuna; the science of interpreting signs or bird calls</term>, if a creature such as an elephant, horse, or dog makes a sound while facing the "Blazing" direction, one should understand that a bone from the same body part of that animal is buried in the ground at the spot where the homeowner is currently standing—specifically corresponding to the body part the homeowner is touching at that moment. ||107||

If a donkey brays while the measuring cord is being laid, a bone is buried beneath where the homeowner is sitting. If a dog or a jackal jumps over the measuring cord, one should also conclude there is an extraction-worthy obstacle <term>Shalya; literally "thorn" or "splinter," referring to impure objects like bones or charcoal buried in the foundation</term> in that spot. ||108||

At that time, if birds make sweet sounds while facing a "Peaceful" direction, then wealth is buried in the earth, either where the bird is perched or beneath the limb of the **Vastu Purusha** <note>The "Building Spirit" or cosmic man mapped onto a floor plan</note> where the master of the house is positioned. ||109||

If the cord breaks while being stretched, the owner of the house will die. If the foundation peg is driven in with its head facing downward, it foretells great disease. If the homeowner and the craftsman lose their memory or become confused at that moment, it signifies their impending death. ||110||

If the water pitcher falls from the shoulder while being carried, the homeowner will suffer from head diseases. If the pitcher falls and turns upside down, calamity will strike the homeowner's lineage. If it breaks, the laborer will die, and if the pitcher simply slips from the hands, the homeowner will die. ||111||

One should perform worship in the South-East corner and install the first stone there; thereafter, other stones should be installed in a clockwise direction. Pillars should also be erected in the same sequence. ||112||

A pillar should be decorated with a ceremonial umbrella, flower garlands, and cloth, and then erected after being worshipped with perfumes and incense. The door frame should also be erected with similar care. ||113||

If a bird perches atop a pillar or door frame, or if they shake, fall, or are not set straight during installation, the result should be understood as similar to the **Indra-dhvaja** <note>The Festival of Indra's Banner; refers to a specific chapter on omens regarding ceremonial poles</note>. That is, the auspicious or inauspicious results mentioned in the chapter on Indra's Banner apply here as well. ||114||

If the site <term>Vastu; the building or plot</term> is higher in the East or North, it leads to the loss of wealth and sons. If the site has a foul odor, it leads to the death of a son. If the site is crooked, it leads to the destruction of kinsmen. If the site is so poorly laid out that the directions cannot be distinguished, the women living there will remain barren. ||115||

If one desires the growth of the household, the site should be expanded equally on all four sides, not unevenly. If there is a flaw on one side of the site—meaning an extension—it should be extended toward the East or the North. ||116||

If the site is extended toward the East, it leads to enmity with friends. If extended toward the South, there is fear of death. If extended toward the West, wealth is destroyed. If extended toward the North, it causes mental agony. The fault of extending toward the East or North is considered minor; for this reason, it was stated in the previous verse that if an extension is necessary, it should be toward the East or North. ||117||

The prayer room should be built in the North-East corner (**Ishana**), the kitchen in the South-East (**Agni**), the storage for general household goods in the South-West (**Nairitya**), and the room for storing wealth and grain in the North-West (**Vayavya**). ||118||

If water is situated in the directions starting from the East, the results are respectively: death of a son, fear of fire, auspiciousness <note>original: "shubh-bhay" likely implies a typo for "shubh" or "fear of the auspicious/excess"</note>, distress among women, immorality in women, poverty, increase in wealth, and increase in sons. ||119||

Trees that have bird nests, or are broken, dried, burnt, located in a temple or a cremation ground, or those that exude milky sap, as well as Vacha, Baheda, Neem, and Aralu—all these should be avoided for the house...

<page-num>188</page-num>
<header>(188) Varahi Samhita</header>

...should be cut for use. ||120|| Having offered worship and sacrifices to the tree at night, one should cut the tree during the day, starting from the northeast direction and proceeding clockwise. If the tree falls toward the North or the East, it is considered auspicious; if it falls in other directions, it should not be accepted. ||121|| If the cut surface of the tree is free from defects at the time of felling, that wood is auspicious for the house. If a yellow-colored circle is seen in the cut of the tree, it should be said that a monitor lizard <note>original: "goh"</note> resides within that tree. ||122|| If a red circle resembling madder <note>a plant-based red dye</note> is seen, there is a frog; if a blue circle, a snake; if a blood-red circle, a chameleon; if a green circle (the color of mung beans), a stone; if a brown circle, a rat; and if a circle the color of a sword <note>metallic/grey</note> is seen in the cut, it indicates the presence of water in the middle of the tree. ||123|| A man desiring prosperity <note>literally: "desiring Lakshmi"</note> should not sleep upon grain, cows, his teacher <term>Guru</term>, fire, or deities; nor should he sleep on a bed placed under bamboo. He should not sleep with his head toward the North or the West, nor sleep naked, nor with wet feet. ||124|| One should enter a house that is adorned by a large gathering of people, equipped with ceremonial archways <term>Torana</term>, beautified with full water-pots, where the deities have been worshipped with incense, fragrance, and offerings, and where Brahmins are chanting the Vedas. ||125||

->Thus ends the fifty-third chapter in the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the Northwest country, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the great teacher Varahamihira. ||53||<-

# Now begins the Fifty-Fourth Chapter
## On the Exploration of Water <note>original: "Udakargalam"</note>

I shall now describe the sacred and glorious science of "Water-Bolts" <note>Udakargala: the science of dowsing or detecting underground water</note> by which water is discovered. Just as there are veins <term>shira</term> in the bodies of men, so too are there veins situated high and low within the earth. ||1|| The water falling from the sky is of one color and one taste, but it acquires various tastes and many colors due to the specific nature of the soil. Therefore, one must examine the water as being equal to the earth it rests in. ||2|| Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Vayu, Soma, and Shiva <note>The deities of the eight directions: East, SE, South, SW, West, NW, North, and NE</note> are to be known respectively as the lords of the directions starting from the East. ||3|| The veins are named after these lords of the directions, and the ninth vein in the center is named "Mahashira" (The Great Vein). From these, hundreds of others have emerged, known by various names. ||4|| The veins that rise upward from the netherworld <term>Patala</term> and those situated in the four cardinal directions are auspicious. Those arising from the corner directions are not auspicious. I shall now describe the omens of these veins. ||5|| If a Cane reed <note>original: "Vetasa"</note> is found in a waterless region, then three cubits <term>hasta</term> to its West, at a depth of one and a half man-lengths <term>purusha</term>, a western vein of water flows. ||6|| The signs there at a depth of one and a half man-lengths are a pale frog and yellow soil. There is a layer of stone there, and water lies beneath it. ||7|| If there is a Rose-apple tree <note>original: "Jambu"</note> facing North, then three cubits to its East, at a depth of two man-lengths, a vein flows. The soil there smells of iron and is pale; at a depth of one man-length, a frog is found. ||8|| If an anthill is situated to the East of a Rose-apple tree, then on its southern side, at a depth of two man-lengths, there is sweet water. ||9|| At a depth of half a man-length, there is a fish and a stone resembling a pigeon. The soil there is blue, and the water is long-lasting and abundant. ||10|| Three cubits to the West of a Cluster Fig tree <note>original: "Udumbara"</note>, at a depth of two and a half man-lengths, there is a white snake and a stone—

...a water vein resembling the color of horse-gram <note>original: *kulatthavarno*</note> or collyrium <note>eye salve</note> exists below, providing excellent water. ||11||

If a termite mound <term>valmika (termite mound)</term> is seen to the north of an Arjuna tree, then at a distance of three cubits <note>approx. 4.5 feet</note> from that tree, water will be found at a depth of three and a half <term>purushas (the height of a man with arms raised, approx. 6-7 feet)</term> to the west. ||12||

**Signs of Excavation:**
At a depth of half a *purusha*, a white lizard <note>original: *godha*</note> will be found; then the soil becomes grey, then black, then yellow, then white with sand, after which an infinite supply of water should be predicted. ||13||

If a Nirgundi tree is covered by a termite mound, then at a distance of three cubits to the south, at a depth of two and a quarter *purushas*, there is sweet water that never dries up. ||14||

A Rohita fish is found at half a *purusha* depth; the soil is brownish-red, then pale white; further down is sand mixed with gravel, and then water appears in due order. ||15||

At half a *purusha*, a green frog appears; the earth is like yellow orpiment; the stone resembles a cloud. The northern vein carries auspicious water. ||30||

Whenever a frog <note>original: *dardura*</note> is seen sitting under any tree, water is one cubit from that spot at a depth of four and a half *purushas*. ||31||

# The Varahi Samhita
## Chapter on Water Divination (Dakargala)

The earth <note>original: "Jma"</note> reveals its secrets. The **Mahendri** vein <note>The "Indra" or Eastern vein</note> carries water that is always frothy. ||36||

If a glossy anthill is found to the south of a **Tilaka** tree and is covered with **Kusha** grass, water will be found at a depth of five *purushas* <note>A 'purusha' is a unit of measurement roughly equal to the height of a man with upstanding arms, approx. 6-7 feet</note> in the western direction; this is the first vein. ||37||

When there is a snake's nest to the west of a **Kadamba** tree, water lies to the south of it. At a distance of three cubits <note>original: "hasta", approx. 18 inches</note> from that spot, at a depth of six *purushas*, lies the fourth vein to the north. ||38||

Here, the **Kauberi** <note>Northern</note> vein flows; the water smells of iron but is inexhaustible. At a depth of one *purusha*, a gold-colored frog will be found, and the soil will be yellow. ||39||

If a **Palmyra** or a **Coconut** tree is surrounded by anthills, water is found six cubits to the west at a depth of four *purushas*; this is the southern vein. ||40||

If a **Kapittha** tree <note>Wood-apple</note> is inhabited by snakes, water should be predicted to its north. Leaving a distance of seven cubits and digging to a depth of five *purushas*, water is found. ||41||

At the depth of one *purusha*, a variegated snake appears; the stone is black and "death-breaking" <note>extremely hard</note>. To the west, the clay is white, and the vein then turns north. ||42||

If to the left of an **Ashmantaka** tree a **Badari** <note>Jujube</note> tree is seen, or a snake's hole, water is found six cubits to the north at a depth of three and a half *purushas*. ||43||

At the first *purusha* of depth, a turtle is found; the stone is grey and the soil is sandy. The first vein is to the south, and the second is to the northeast. ||44||

If an anthill is to the left of a **Haridra** <note>Turmeric</note> tree, water is to the east. At a distance of three cubits, it is found at a depth of five and a third *purushas*. ||45||

At one *purusha*, a blue snake is found; the soil is yellow and the stone resembles an emerald. The earth is first black; the vein is western and southern, none other. ||46||

In a waterless region, if signs of marshy plants are seen—such as **Birana** or soft **Durva** grass—water is found there at a depth of one *purusha*. ||47||

Where **Bharngi**, **Vivrita**, **Danti**, **Shukarapadi**, **Lakshmana**, or **Navamalika** <note>various medicinal and flowering plants</note> are found, water is two cubits to the south at a depth of three *purushas*. ||48||

Trees that are glossy, have long hanging branches, or are stunted but lush indicate water nearby. Conversely, trees with holes, withered leaves, or a parched appearance are devoid of water. ||49||

The **Tilaka, Amrataka, Varunaka, Bhallataka, Bilva, Tinduka, Ankola, Pindara, Shirisha, Anjana, Parushaka, Vanjula,** and **Atibala** trees— ||50||

If these are found very glossy and surrounded by anthills, water is three cubits to the north at a depth of four and a half *purushas*. ||51||

Where a patch of grass exists on grassless ground, or a grassless patch on grassy ground, a vein is indicated; or one may say wealth <note>buried treasure</note> is hidden there. ||52||

Where thorny trees grow among thornless ones, or vice versa, water is three cubits to the west at a depth of three and a third *purushas*; or there may be wealth. ||53||

If the ground sounds deep/hollow when struck by the feet, water is there at a depth of three and a half *purushas*; the vein there is the **Kauberi** (Northern) one. ||54||

If a single branch of a tree is bent down or appears pale, water should be known to exist under that branch at a depth of three *purushas*. ||55||

If a tree shows abnormal fruit or flowers, a vein is three cubits to its east at a depth of four *purushas*; beneath is stone and yellow earth. ||56||

If a **Kantakarika** plant is seen without thorns and with white flowers, water is under it at a depth of three and a half *purushas*. ||57||

Where a **Date Palm** with two heads is found in a waterless region, water should be pointed out to its west at a depth of three *purushas*. ||58||

If there is a **Karnikara** or a **Palasha** tree with white flowers, water is found two cubits to its left at a depth of three *purushas*. ||59||

Where the earth gives off heat or smoke, there is water...

## Page 191

In a depth of two men <note>A "man" (purusha) is a traditional unit of measure, roughly the height of a man with arms upraised, approx. 6-7 feet</note>. A vein of water should be pointed out there with a great flow of water. ||60||

In whatever area of a field the crops produced meet with destruction, or appear glossy and extremely pale, there is a great water-vein at a depth of two men. ||61||

Now I shall further describe how water-veins exist in the **desert region** <note>Marudesha</note>. The veins in the earth run like the necks of camels. ||62||

If there is an ant-hill to the northeast of a **Toothbrush tree** <note>Pilu; Salvadora persica</note>, water is found to the west. The vein should be known to flow toward the north at a depth of five men. ||63||

The first sign is a frog; then the earth is tawny-colored; after that it becomes green; and at the depth of one man there is a stone. Below that, water should be indicated. ||64||

If an ant-hill is to the east of that same **Toothbrush tree**, then below that at five cubits <note>hasta</note> distance in the southern direction, water should be declared at a depth of seven men. ||65||

At the first man's depth, there is a black-and-white snake a cubit long. The vein flows to the south, providing abundant but brackish water. ||66||

If there is a snake-dwelling <note>ant-hill</note> to the south of a **Caper bush** <note>Karira; Capparis decidua</note>, water is to the north. It is to be known at a depth of ten men; here, at one man's depth, there is a yellow frog. ||67||

If there is a snake-dwelling to the west of a **Rohitaka tree** <note>Tecomella undulata</note>, then at three cubits to the south, after digging twelve men deep, there is a brackish vein to the west. ||68||

If an ant-hill is seen to the east of an **Arjuna tree** <note>Indrataru</note>, the vein is one cubit to the west. After digging fourteen men, a tawny-colored lizard is found at the first man's depth. ||69||

Or if there is a snake-dwelling to the left of a **Golden-colored tree** <note>Suvarnanama/Amaltas</note>, then at two cubits to the south, water is found at the end of fifteen men. ||70||

The water here is brackish; a mongoose is found at half a man's depth, along with a copper-like stone. The earth is red, and the vein flows to the south there. ||71||

If a **Jujube tree** <note>Badari</note> and a **Rohitaka tree** are found joined together without an ant-hill, water is found three cubits to the west at a depth of sixteen men. ||72||

The water is sweet; first a vein flows to the south and another to the north. There is a stone like flour <note>powdered/soft stone</note>, white earth, and a scorpion at half a man's depth. ||73||

If a **Jujube tree** is combined with a **Caper bush**, water is three cubits to the west. At eighteen men's depth, there is a vein in the northeast with much water. ||74||

A **Jujube tree** joined with a **Toothbrush tree** at a distance of three cubits in the eastern direction: at twenty men's depth, there is inexhaustible water, though it is brackish. ||75||

Where an **Arjuna tree** <note>Kakubha</note> and a **Caper bush** are joined together, or an **Arjuna** and a **Bael tree** <note>Bilva</note>, water is two cubits to the west at a depth of twenty-five men. ||76||

When pale **Durva** and **Kusha** grasses are on top of an ant-hill, a well should be placed in the middle; water is here at twenty-one men. ||77||

Where **Durva** grass is seen on an ant-hill surrounded by **Kadamba** trees, water is three cubits to the south at twenty-five men. ||78||

When a **Rohitaka tree** is in the middle of three ant-hills, surrounded by various other trees, water should be declared there. ||79||

At four cubits from the center and sixteen inches to the north, water is found. After digging forty men, a vein is found from a stone. ||80||

In a place where a **Shami tree** <note>Prosopis cineraria</note> has many knots and an ant-hill to its north, water is found five cubits to the west at a depth of fifty men. ||81||

When five ant-hills are in one place and the middle one is white, a vein is declared there at a depth of fifty-five men <note>sixty minus five</note>. ||82||

Where a **Shami tree** is joined with a **Palasha tree**, water is in the western part at sixty men. At half a man's depth, there is first a snake, then sandy and yellow earth. ||83||

Where there is a white **Rohitaka tree** surrounded by an ant-hill, at one cubit to the east...

# Varāhī Saṃhitā
## Chapter on Water Divination (Dakārgala)

At a depth of seventy <term>man-lengths</term><note>A "man-length" or "purusha" is a traditional unit of measure, roughly the height of a man with arms upraised, approximately 6-7 feet.</note>, there is water. ||84|| Where there is a white <term>Shami</term><note>Prosopis cineraria</note> tree with many thorns, water is found to the south. With five men added to seventy <note>i.e., 75 man-lengths deep</note>, there is a snake and half a man-length further down, water. ||85|| The signs found in the desert are not the same as those in the forest; water should be indicated accordingly. Where there is a <term>Jambu</term><note>Rose apple</note> or <term>Vetasa</term><note>Reed/Cane</note> tree, the depth in the desert is double that of the forest. ||86||

The following plants: <term>Jambu</term>, <term>Trivrta</term>, <term>Murva</term>, <term>Shishumari</term>, <term>Sariva</term>, <term>Shiva</term>, <term>Shyama</term>, the creepers <term>Varahi</term>, <term>Jyotishmati</term>, and <term>Garudavega</term>, ||87|| <term>Sukari</term>, <term>Mashaparni</term>, and <term>Vyaghrapada</term>—if these are found at the abode of a snake, then three <term>cubits</term><note>Original: "kara" (hand/forearm length)</note> north of the anthill, water is found at a depth of three man-lengths. ||88|| This applies to marshy lands; in jungle lands, it is at five man-lengths; by these same signs in the desert, one should say it is at seven man-lengths. ||89||

Where the earth is of uniform appearance, devoid of grass, trees, anthills, or shrubs, but shows a specific "deformity" <note>an anomaly in the soil texture or color</note>, water is located there. ||90|| Where the ground is moist, low-lying, sandy, or produces an echo, water is found at four-and-a-half or five man-lengths. ||91|| To the south of glossy/oily trees, there is abundant water at four man-lengths. Even in a thicket of trees, if one tree looks "deformed" <note>distinct from the others</note>, one should predict water in the same way. ||92||

Where the earth sinks, water is at one-and-a-half man-lengths in jungle or marshy land. Or where there are many insects without a visible nest, water is also there. ||93|| Where the earth is partly hot and partly cold, water is at three-and-a-half man-lengths. If there is a rainbow-colored patch, a fish-shaped mark, or an anthill, water is within four cubits. ||94|| In a row of anthills, if one is taller than the rest, the water-vein is beneath it. Where crops dry up or fail to grow, there is water below. ||95|| Where the <term>Nyagrodha</term><note>Banyan</note>, <term>Palasha</term>, and <term>Udumbara</term> trees grow together, water is beneath them. The same is said for a combination of <term>Vata</term> and <term>Pippala</term> trees; the vein is to the north. ||96||

If a well is made in the southeast corner of a village or town, it constantly causes fear and usually brings about fires involving humans. ||97|| In the southwest corner, it causes the loss of children; in the northwest, fear from women. Avoiding these two or three directions, wells in the remaining directions bring prosperity. ||98||

Having observed the "Science of Water" <note>Dakārgala</note> composed by the Sage Sarasvata, I have composed this in <term>Arya</term> verses; I shall also speak of it in <term>Manava</term> <note>Anushtubh</note> meter. ||99||

Where trees, shrubs, and creepers are glossy, with leaves free of holes, a water-vein exists. Also where there are Lotuses, Sugarcane, <term>Ushira</term>, <term>Guda</term>, <term>Kasha</term>, <term>Kusha</term>, <term>Nalika</term>, or <term>Nala</term> reeds. ||100|| Or where there are Date palms, <term>Jambu</term>, <term>Arjuna</term>, <term>Vetasa</term>, or trees, shrubs, and creepers exuding milky sap. Also <term>Chhatra</term>, <term>Ibhanaga</term>, <term>Shatapatra</term>, <term>Nipa</term>, <term>Naktamala</term>, and <term>Sindhuvara</term>. ||101|| Where <term>Vibhitaka</term> or <term>Madayantika</term> <note>Henna</note> exists, water is at three man-lengths. If there is a mountain upon another mountain, water is at the base at three man-lengths. ||102||

Where the soil is blue, mixed with gravel, and contains <term>Maunja</term>, <term>Kasha</term>, or <term>Kusha</term> grasses, the water is abundant and tasty. The same applies to black or red soil. ||103|| Gravelly, copper-colored earth makes water astringent; alkaline earth <note>Kapila/tawny</note> makes it salty. In pale white earth, the water is said to be salty; in blue earth, it is sweet. ||104|| <term>Shaka</term>, <term>Ashvakarna</term>, <term>Arjuna</term>, <term>Bilva</term>, <term>Sarja</term>, <term>Shriparni</term>, <term>Arishta</term>, <term>Adhava</term>, and <term>Shimshapa</term> trees—if their leaves have holes and the trees/shrubs appear parched—indicate that water is far away. ||105|| Earth colored like the sun, fire, ashes, camels, or donkeys is declared waterless. If there are red sprouts, milky sap, <term>Karira</term> plants, and the earth is red, water is beneath the stone. ||106|| A rock that looks like lapis lazuli, a kidney bean, a cloud, or a ripe <term>Udumbara</term> fruit, or like a bee or collyrium, or is tawny—know that rock to have much water nearby.
