# Chapter 54: On the Exploration of Water Springs (Continued)

(193)
-> Hindi Commentary Included <-

**107-108.** A rock that resembles a pigeon, honey, or clarified butter <note>Ghee</note>, or one that has the color of linen cloth, or is similar in appearance to the Moon-plant <note>Soma-valli</note>, provides an inexhaustible supply of water.

**109.** A rock that is speckled with copper-colored spots, or resembles the pale grey of ashes, camels, or donkeys, is waterless. Similarly, a rock colored like the *Bhringopagangusthapushpika* flower <note>likely a species of Clerodendrum or a similar small wildflower</note>, or one having the color of the sun or fire, contains no water.

**110.** Rocks that have the appearance of the Moon, the Sun, crystal, pearls, or gold; those that shine like sapphire, cinnabar, or collyrium; and those with the tint of the rising sun or yellow orpiment—these are considered auspicious. This is the opinion of the sages, expressed here in verse.

**111.** These rocks are pure and celestial, constantly frequented by the *Yakshas* <note>nature spirits</note> and *Nagas* <note>serpent deities</note>. In the kingdoms of kings where such rocks exist, there will never be a famine caused by lack of rain.

**112.** When a rock is too hard to be broken, one should cover it with wood from the *Palasha* <note>Flame of the Forest</note> and *Tinduka* <note>Persimmon</note> trees and set them ablaze. When the rock becomes red-hot like fire and is then sprinkled with lime-water <note>water mixed with calcium</note>, it will crack open.

**113.** Or, one may prepare a solution of the ashes of the *Mokshaka* tree <note>Schrebera swietenioides</note> mixed with the stalks of *Shara* grass <note>Saccharum munja</note>. If this is poured seven times over a rock heated by fire, it will cause it to burst.

**114.** A mixture of sour gruel <note>kanjika</note>, fermented liquor, horse-gram, and jujube fruits, kept for seven nights and then poured over a heated rock, will surely cause it to split.

**115.** Take the leaves and bark of the Neem tree, sesame stalks, *Apamarga* <note>Prickly Chaff-flower</note>, *Tinduka*, and *Guduchi* <note>Heart-leaved moonseed</note>. A decoction made from the ashes of these, mixed with cow urine and poured six times over a heated stone, will break it.

**116.** A paste made of the milky sap of the *Arka* plant <note>Calotropis</note>, the powder of a ram's horn, pigeon droppings, and rat droppings, mixed with oil and rice-water, should be applied to the edge of a tool. Once sharpened, such a tool will not be blunted even by the hardest stones.

**117.** An iron tool tempered in a solution of plantain <note>banana</note> ashes mixed with buttermilk and kept for a day, will not break when striking stone, nor will it be blunted by other metals.

**118.** A large oblong pond <note>Vapi</note> extending from East to West retains water for a long time, whereas one extending North to South does not, as it is often breached by waves driven by the wind. If one wishes to prevent this, the banks should be reinforced with strong timber or paved with stones and packed earth on both sides.

**119.** The banks should be shaded by trees such as *Kakubha*, Banyan, Mango, *Plaksha*, *Kadamba*, *Nichula*, Jamun, Cane, *Neepa*, *Kurabaka*, Palm, Ashoka, *Madhuka*, and *Bakula*.

**120.** The outlet for the water should not be placed in the Southwest corner. The sluice-gate should be made of solid wood, without any gaps, and then reinforced with earth.

**121.** A mixture of *Anjana* <note>collyrium</note>, *Musta* <note>nut-grass</note>, *Ushira* <note>vetiver</note>, *Rajakoshataki*, and *Amalaka* <note>Indian gooseberry</note> powder, combined with the fruit of the *Kataka* <note>Clearing Nut tree, Strychnos potatorum</note>, should be put into a well.

**122.** If the water is turbid, bitter, salty, or foul-tasting, this mixture will make it clear, tasty, fragrant, and endowed with other excellent qualities.

**123.** The constellations *Hasta*, *Magha*, *Anuradha*, *Pushya*, *Dhanishtha*, the three *Uttaras*, *Rohini*, and *Shatabhishaj* are recommended for commencing the construction of wells.

**124.** Having offered a sacrifice to Varuna <note>the god of waters</note>, one should first drive a stake of Banyan or Cane into the spot identified as the spring, after worshipping it with flowers, perfumes, and incense.

<header>Varaha Samhita</header>

> Having surpassed the views of Jyeshtha and having observed the opinions of Baladeva and others, this second method of water divining <term>Dakargala: The science of locating subterranean water</term> is correctly stated by Varahamihira through the grace of the Sages.<gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "muniprasādāt"</note> || 125 ||

### Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, named Dakargala, in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. || 54 ||

Now the "Water-Bolt" <note>Udakargala, another term for water divining</note> which bestows righteousness and fame is described, through the knowledge of which the water situated within the earth is known. Just as veins are situated in the bodies of men, in the same way, there are many high and low veins <term>shira: literally 'veins' or 'channels', referring here to underground water currents</term> within the earth. || 1 ||

When rain falls from the sky, all water falls with the same single taste; however, due to the specific characteristics of the soil, it acquires various colors and tastes. Its examination should be done according to the soil—meaning, the water will be of the same nature as the land. || 2 ||

Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Vayu, Soma, and Ishana—these eight deities are the lords of the eight directions starting from the East, respectively. || 3 ||

Eight water-veins are famous by the names of the lords of these eight directions, such as Aindri (Eastern), Agneyi (South-eastern), Yamya (Southern), etc. In the center, one large vein is famous by the name "Mahashira" (Great Vein). From these, hundreds of other veins have emerged, which are famous by their own respective names. || 4 ||

The vein that rises straight up from the netherworld <note>Patala</note> and those veins located in the four cardinal directions (East, etc.) are auspicious. Those veins located in the four corners (South-east, etc.) are not auspicious. Now, the signs for identifying these veins are stated. || 5 ||

In a waterless region, if there is a Vetasa tree <note>Indian Willow</note>, then three cubits <note>approx. 4.5 feet</note> to the west of that tree, at a depth of one and a half "man-lengths," there is water, and there the western vein flows. A "man-length" <term>purusha: a unit of measurement</term> is defined as the height of a man with his arms raised; it consists of one hundred and twenty fingers <note>angul</note>. || 6 ||

The sign there is that upon digging half a man-length, a somewhat white-colored frog is found. Then yellow-colored earth appears, followed by layered stone, beneath which lies the water. || 7 ||

In a waterless region, if there is a Jamun tree <note>Black Plum</note>, then three cubits to its north, at a depth of two man-lengths, there is an eastern vein. Upon digging there, earth smelling like iron is found, followed by pale-white earth, and a frog is found at a depth of one man-length. || 8 ||

If an anthill is found near a Jamun tree in the eastern direction, then three cubits south of that tree, at a depth of two man-lengths, there is sweet water. || 9 ||

Upon digging half a man-length, a fish is found, then pigeon-colored stone, and blue earth is found here. The water is abundant and extremely dark. Where the Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> has not specified the measurement of cubits, the previously mentioned measurement should be understood; since the measurement was not stated here, one should assume the aforementioned three cubits. || 10 ||

In a waterless region, if a Gular tree <note>Cluster Fig</note> is seen, then three cubits to its west, at a depth of two and a half man-lengths, there is a vein. At a depth of one man-length, a white snake is found, then stone as black as eye-liner <note>Anjana</note> appears, beneath which is a vein of beautiful water. || 11 ||

If an anthill is seen three cubits north of an Arjuna tree, then three cubits west of that Arjuna tree, at a depth of three and a half man-lengths, there is water. || 12 ||

Upon digging half a man-length, a white-colored monitor lizard is found. At a depth of one man-length, grey-colored earth appears, then black, yellow, and white earth mixed with sand is found...

---

<note>1. This verse is considered an interpolation (later addition) as it is not mentioned in the commentary.</note>

...there is much water to be found beneath it. ||13|| If there is a Nirgundi tree (also known as the Sindhuvara tree) associated with an anthill, then three cubits to the south of it, at a depth of two and a quarter <term>Purusha</term> <note>A 'Purusha' is a traditional unit of measurement based on the height of a man with his arms raised, roughly 6 to 7 feet.</note>, there is sweet water that never dries up. ||14|| Upon digging half a Purusha, a Rohu fish is found. Then, in sequence, tawny-colored soil, pale-white soil, and sand mixed with fine stone particles appear; beneath that is the water. ||15|| If there is an <term>anthill</term> <note>original: "Valmika"</note> to the east of a Ber (Jujube) tree, then water should be declared three cubits west of that tree at a depth of three Purushas. At a depth of half a Purusha, a white-colored lizard appears. ||16||

In a waterless region, if a Ber tree is found joined with a Dhak (Palash) tree, then three cubits to the west, at a depth of three and a quarter Purushas, there is water. The sign there is that after digging one Purusha, a type of non-venomous snake appears. ||17|| Where a Bel tree and a Gular (Cluster Fig) tree grow together, water is found three Purushas deep, three cubits to the south of them. Digging half a Purusha reveals a black-colored frog. ||18|| If an anthill is very close to an Ak-Gular tree, then by digging three and a quarter Purushas directly beneath that anthill, a <term>vein</term> <note>original: "Shira" - referring to an underground water channel</note> flowing to the west is found. ||19|| Pale and yellow soil appears. A stone as white as cow's milk-whey is found, and at half a Purusha deep, a white mouse resembling a white lily flower is seen. ||20||

If a Kapila tree is seen in a waterless region, then three cubits to the east of that tree, at a depth of three and a quarter Purushas, a southern vein flows. ||21|| First, soil the color of a blue lotus appears, then soil the color of a pigeon is seen. One cubit deeper, a fish is found which smells like a Chakora bird; there, a small amount of salty water is found. ||22|| If a <term>Shyonaka tree</term> <note>Oroxylum indicum, or the Indian Trumpet Flower tree</note> is seen in a waterless region, then by going two cubits in the northwest direction and digging, a vein is found at three Purushas. ||23|| If an <term>anthill</term> <note>original: "Vamai"</note> is near a Baheda tree, the vein is one and a half Purushas deep, two cubits east of that tree. ||24|| If the anthill is to the west of the Baheda tree, the vein is four and a half Purushas deep, one cubit north of the tree. ||25|| First, after digging one Purusha, a white-colored Vishambharaka (a type of small creature/insect) is seen. Then a saffron-colored stone appears. Beneath that, a vein flowing westward is found; however, after three years, that vein is destroyed—meaning the water dries up. ||26||

If there is a white-colored soil anthill covered with Kusha grass in the northeast of a <term>Kovidara tree</term> <note>Bauhinia variegata, or Orchid tree; also identified here as Saptaparna</note>, then between the Kovidara tree and the anthill, there is much water at five and a half Purushas deep. ||27|| In the first Purusha of depth, a snake colored like the center of a lotus flower appears, then red earth, then a stone called Kuruvinda; these signs should be noted. ||28|| In a waterless region, if there is a Saptaparna tree with an anthill, water should be declared five Purushas deep, one cubit to the north. ||29|| Here too there are signs: digging half a Purusha reveals a green frog, followed by yellow earth like orpiment, then a black stone like a rain cloud. Beneath all these is a northern vein with sweet water. ||30|| Beneath whatever tree a sitting frog is seen, water exists four and a half Purushas deep, one cubit to the north of that tree. ||31|| One Purusha down, a mongoose appears, then sequentially blue, yellow, and white soil appears, followed by a stone the color of a frog. ||32||

If an anthill <note>original: "valmika"</note> is seen to the south of a **Karanja** tree <note>Indian Beech</note>, then a water vein <note>original: "shira"</note> exists two cubits south of that tree at a depth of three and a half **men** <term>purusha: a unit of depth equivalent to the height of a man with his arms raised, roughly 12 feet</term>. ||33|| Half a **man** deep, a tortoise is found, and then water flows from a primary eastern vein; a second northern vein flows with sweet water. First, a green-colored stone appears, and the water lies beneath it. ||34|| If there is an anthill to the north of a **Mahua** tree, then five cubits west of that tree, at a depth of eight and a half **men**, there is water. ||35|| Upon digging one **man** deep, a large snake is seen. Then smoke-colored earth and a stone the color of horse-gram <note>reddish-brown</note> appear, followed by an eastern vein which always flows with frothy water. ||36|| If there is a glossy anthill accompanied by **Kusha** and **Durva** grass to the south of a **Tilaka** tree, then five cubits west of that tree, at a depth of five **men**, there is water and an eastern vein flows there. ||37|| If there is an anthill to the west of a **Kadamba** tree, then three cubits south of that tree, at a depth of five and three-quarters **men**, there is water. ||38|| A northern vein emerges there; the water is abundant but smells of iron. Digging one **man** deep reveals a gold-colored frog, followed by yellow soil. ||39|| If a **Palm** tree or a **Coconut** tree is surrounded by an anthill, then six cubits to the west of that tree, at a depth of four **men**, there is a southern vein. ||40|| If there is an anthill to the south of a **Kaitha** <note>Wood Apple</note> tree, then digging seven cubits north of that tree reveals water at a depth of five **men**. ||41|| One **man** deep, a variegated snake, black soil, and layered stone appear, followed by white clay; then the northern vein is found. ||42|| If there is a **Ber** <note>Jujube</note> tree or an anthill to the left of an **Ashmantaka** tree, then six cubits north of that Ashmantaka tree, at a depth of three and a half **men**, there is water. ||43|| Digging the first **man** reveals a tortoise, then grey-colored stone and soil mixed with sand; first the southern vein emerges, followed by the vein of the **northeast** <note>original: "ishankon"</note> direction. ||44|| If there is an anthill to the left of a **Haridra** <note>Haldina</note> tree, then three cubits east of that tree, at a depth of five and one-third **men**, there is water. ||45|| One **man** deep, a blue snake appears, then yellow soil, green-colored stone, and black earth; first a western vein emerges, followed by a southern vein. ||46|| In an arid region, if signs of a water-rich land are seen, and where **Veeran** <note>Khas grass</note> and **Durva** grass are extremely soft, water is found at a depth of one **man**. ||47|| Where the medicinal herbs **Bharangi**, **Nisot**, **Danti**, **Sukarpadi**, **Lakshmana**, or **Malati** are found, water exists two cubits south of them at a depth of three **men**. ||48|| Where trees are small and spreading but possess glossy, long branches, water is near; where trees have holes, withered leaves, and appear dry, there is no water. ||49|| Where **Tilaka**, **Amra** <note>Hog Plum</note>, **Varun**, **Bhilawa**, **Bel**, **Tendu**, **Ankol**, **Pindar**, **Siris**, **Anjan**, **Phalsa**, **Ashoka**, and **Atibala**... ||50|| ...these trees are found surrounded by extremely glossy anthills, water exists three cubits north of these trees at a depth of four and a half **men**. ||51|| In a land where no grass grows but one spot is seen with grass, or if the entire land is covered in grass but one spot is bare, then at that spot, at a depth of four and a half **men**, there is either a water vein or buried treasure. ||52|| Where among thorny trees there is one tree without thorns, or among thornless trees there is one tree with thorns, then three cubits west of that tree, digging three and one-third **men** deep reveals water or...

...wealth is found. ||53|| Where the ground produces a deep, resonant sound when struck by the feet, water exists at a depth of three and a half <term>purushas</term> <note>A 'purusha' is a unit of measurement based on the height of a man with upraised arms, roughly 6 feet.</note>, and a northern vein of water emerges. ||54|| If a single branch of a tree is bending toward the ground or has turned yellow, water is found by digging three <term>purushas</term> deep beneath that branch. ||55|| If the fruits and flowers of a tree appear deformed or abnormal, a water vein exists three cubits east of that tree at a depth of four <term>purushas</term>; stones will be found below, and the soil will be yellow. ||56|| Where a <term>Kateri</term> tree <note>Yellow-berried nightshade</note> is found without thorns and bearing white flowers, water is found by digging three and a half <term>purushas</term> beneath it. ||57|| In a waterless region, if a Date Palm tree has two heads <note>a bifurcated trunk</note>, one should say water exists two cubits west of that palm at a depth of three <term>purushas</term>. ||58|| If there is a <term>Karnikara</term> tree <note>Indian Bay Cedar</note> with white flowers or a <term>Dhaka</term> tree <note>Flame of the Forest</note>, water is found two cubits south of that tree at a depth of three <term>purushas</term>. ||59|| In land where steam or smoke is seen rising, one should declare a vein of abundant flowing water at a depth of two <term>purushas</term>. ||60|| In a field where crops grow and then perish, or where the crops are exceptionally lush, or where they turn yellow after sprouting, there is a great deal of water at a depth of two <term>purushas</term>. ||61|| Regarding the nature of water veins in the Marwar <note>desert</note> region: the veins run deep and shallow in the earth, undulating like the neck of a camel. ||62|| If there is a termite mound in the northeast of a <term>Pilu</term> tree <note>Salvadora persica or Toothbrush tree</note>, a northward-flowing vein exists four and a half cubits west of that mound at a depth of five <term>purushas</term>. ||63|| Upon digging there, a frog is found in the first <term>purusha</term>, followed by tawny and green-colored soil and stones; water lies beneath all these signs. ||64|| If the termite mound is to the east of the <term>Pilu</term> tree, water should be declared seven <term>purushas</term> deep and four and a half cubits south of that tree. ||65|| In the first <term>purusha</term> of digging, a black-and-white snake one cubit long appears, followed by a southward vein of very salty water. ||66|| If there is a termite mound to the north of a <term>Karira</term> tree <note>Capparis decidua</note>, sweet water should be known to exist ten <term>purushas</term> deep and four and a half cubits south of that tree. Digging one <term>purusha</term> here reveals a yellow frog. ||67|| If a termite mound is to the west of a <term>Rohitaka</term> tree <note>Desert Teak</note>, a westward vein of salty water is found by digging twelve <term>purushas</term> deep, three cubits south of the tree. ||68|| If a termite mound is seen to the east of an <term>Arjuna</term> tree, a vein is found by digging fourteen <term>purushas</term> deep, one cubit west of the tree. Here, a tawny-colored monitor lizard is seen in the first <term>purusha</term>. ||69|| If a termite mound is on the left side of a <term>Dhatura</term> tree, water is found fifteen <term>purushas</term> deep and two cubits south of that tree. ||70|| That water is very salty; half a <term>purusha</term> down, a mongoose, copper-colored stones, and red earth are found, followed by a southward-flowing vein. ||71|| If a Jujube tree and a <term>Rohitaka</term> tree are seen growing together even without a termite mound, water exists sixteen <term>purushas</term> deep and three cubits west of those trees. ||72|| Here the water is extremely sweet. First a southern vein and then a northern vein flows. Stones white as flour, white earth, and a scorpion at half a <term>purusha</term> are seen. ||73|| If a Jujube tree is found with a <term>Karira</term> tree, water is found by digging eighteen <term>purushas</term> deep and three cubits west; there lies a northeast-flowing vein with abundant water. ||74|| If a Jujube tree is found with a <term>Pilu</term> tree, salty water that never dries up is found twenty <term>purushas</term> deep and three cubits to the east. ||75||

Where the **Arjuna tree** <note>Terminalia arjuna</note> and the **Karira tree** <note>Capparis decidua</note> grow together, or where the **Arjuna tree** and the **Bael tree** <note>Aegle marmelos</note> grow together, there is water twenty-five *purushas* <note>A 'purusha' is a unit of depth roughly equal to a man's height with upraised arms, approx. 6-7 feet</note> deep, two cubits to the west of them. ||76|| If **Durva grass** and white **Kusha grass** are found atop an anthill <note>original: 'valmika', often referring to termite mounds used as hydro-geological indicators</note>, then by digging a well beneath that anthill, water emerges at a depth of twenty-one *purushas*. ||77|| Where **Kadamba trees** are planted in the ground and **Durva grass** is seen atop an anthill, there is water twenty-five *purushas* deep, two cubits south of that Kadamba tree. ||78|| If a **Rohitaka tree** <note>original: 'ruhida', Tecomella undulata</note> is found between three anthills and is accompanied by three different types of trees, water should be predicted there. ||79|| At a distance of four cubits and sixteen fingers north of the centrally located Rohitaka tree, stone is found after digging forty *purushas*. Below that lies the water-vein <note>term: 'shira' - an underground stream or aquifer</note>. ||80|| Where there is a **Shami tree** <note>Prosopis cineraria</note> with many knots and an anthill to its north, there is water fifty *purushas* deep, five cubits west of the Shami tree. ||81|| If there are five anthills in one place, the central one being a white anthill, the water-vein emerges after digging fifty-five *purushas*. ||82|| Where there is a Shami tree joined with a **Palash tree** <note>Butea monosperma</note>, there is water sixty *purushas* deep, five cubits west of those trees. Upon digging the first half-*purusha*, a snake is found, followed by yellow soil mixed with sand. ||83|| Where a white Rohitaka tree is surrounded by anthills, there is water seventy *purushas* deep, one cubit east of that tree. ||84|| Where there is a white Shami tree with many thorns, there is water seventy-five *purushas* deep, one cubit south of that tree; a snake is found after digging half a *purusha*. ||85||

These signs of water-knowledge <note>term: 'jal-gyan' - the science of dowsing</note> mentioned for the **Maru region** <note>Arid/Desert region</note> should not be applied to the **Jangala region** <note>Semi-arid/Bushland</note>; that is, water cannot be identified by these specific signs in the Jangala region. The signs previously mentioned for water-knowledge involving trees like the **Jaman** <note>Java Plum</note> and **Bed-majanu** <note>Willow-like tree</note>—if those signs are seen in the Maru region, the depth of the water should be considered double the *purushas* previously stated. A region with abundant water is called **Anupa**. A region lacking water is called **Marusthal** (Desert). A region distinct from these two, where water is neither too much nor too little, is the **Jangala** region. In this manner, there are three types of regions. ||86|| If the following medicinal herbs are found atop an anthill: **Jaman**, **Nisot**, **Murva**, **Shishumar**, **Sharivan**, **Shiva**, **Shyama**, **Varahi-Kangani**, **Garudavega**, ||87|| **Sukarika**, **Mashavan**, and **Vyaghrapada** (Tiger-claw), then there is water three *purushas* deep, three cubits north of that anthill. ||88|| This depth of three *purushas* should be predicted for the **Anupa** region. If these signs are seen in the **Jangala** region, predict water at five *purushas* instead of three. If these same signs are seen in the **Marusthal**, predict water at seven *purushas*. ||89||

In a land of uniform color where there is no grass, trees, anthills, or shrubs <note>term: 'gulma' - a cluster of many branches arising from a single root</note>, if the ground appears "altered" or different in some way, there is water five *purushas* deep. ||90|| Where the ground is moist, low-lying, and sandy, or where a sound is produced when stepping on it, there is water at four-and-a-half or five *purushas*. ||91|| Where there are many lush trees, one should predict abundant water four *purushas* deep to the south of those trees. If among many trees one tree is "deformed"—meaning its fruits and flowers are of a different type—then there is water four *purushas* deep to the south of that tree. ||92|| In whichever Jangala or Anupa region the ground sinks when stepped upon, there [is water] at one-and-a-half...

...one <term>Purusha</term> <note>A unit of measurement based on a man's height with arms raised, roughly 120 digits or 6-7 feet</note> deep. Where many insects are seen but there is no visible anthill for them to live in, water is found one and a half *Purushas* deep. ||93|| Where the entire ground is warm but one spot is cold, or where the entire ground is cool but one spot is warm, water resides at a depth of three and a half *Purushas*. Where a rainbow, a fish-shaped mark, or an anthill is seen in a desert or marshy region, water is four cubits deep. ||94|| Where there is a row of many anthills in a desert or marshy land and one anthill is taller than the rest, a <term>Shira</term> <note>Literally "vein"; refers to an underground water stream</note> emerges by digging four cubits beneath that tall anthill. Where crops wither after growing or do not grow at all, water is also four cubits deep. ||95|| Where the Banyan, Peepal, and Cluster Fig trees are found together, water emerges by digging three cubits beneath them. Where the Banyan and Peepal are found together, water also emerges three cubits below them; in both these locations, the water vein flows toward the North. ||96|| If a well is situated in the <term>Agni-kon</term> <note>The South-East direction, associated with the Fire element</note> of a village or city, it causes constant fear and often leads to fires in the settlement where even humans may perish. ||97|| If a well is in the <term>Nairitya-kon</term> <note>The South-West direction</note>, it leads to the loss of children; if in the <term>Vayavya-kon</term> <note>The North-West direction</note>, it brings fear to women. Excluding these three directions, wells in the remaining five directions are auspicious. ||98|| Having observed the <term>Udakargala</term> <note>The science of groundwater detection</note> as described by the <term>Saraswat-muni</term> <note>The Sage Saraswat</note>, I have also described this *Udakargala* through the <term>Arya Chhanda</term> <note>A specific Sanskrit metrical meter</note>. Now, I shall describe the *Udakargala* as told by Manu in various verses. ||99|| In land where trees, shrubs, and creepers are glossy and have leaves without holes, a water vein exists three *Purushas* deep. Or where there are grasses such as the Land-Lotus, Tribulus, Khus, Kul, slow-growing <gloss>Reed</gloss>, Kans grass, Kusha, Nalika, or Nal. ||100|| And where there are Date palms, Jamun, Arjun, or Cane trees, or where trees, shrubs, and creepers yield milky sap, or trees like the Chhatri, Hastikarni, Nagkesar, Lotus, Kadamba, Naktamala, or Sindhuvara. ||101|| Where Baheda and Madayantika are found, water is three *Purushas* deep. Where one mountain sits atop another, water is also found three *Purushas* deep at the base of the upper mountain. ||102|| Land filled with Munj, Kans, and Kusha grass, where there is blue soil mixed with stone particles, contains abundant and sweet water. Where there is black or red soil, the water is also plentiful and sweet. ||103|| If the land is <term>Sharkara</term> <gloss>copper-colored and mixed with stone fragments</gloss>, the water extracted will have an astringent taste. In tawny-colored soil, the water is brackish; in pale-colored soil, the water tastes of salt; and in blue-colored soil, the water is sweet. ||104|| Where trees like Shala, Ashwakarna, Arjun, Bael, Sarja, Shriparni, Arishta, and Sheesham have leaves full of holes, and where shrubs and vines also have perforated leaves and appear dry, water is very deep. ||105|| Land that is the color of the sun, fire, ash, camels, or donkeys is waterless. In red soil where red-sprouted Karir trees grow and yield milky sap, water is found beneath the stones. ||106|| Stones that are dark like Lapis Lazuli, <gloss>Moong</gloss> beans, or clouds, or colored like a ripe Cluster Fig—or stones that, when broken, appear pitch black like kohl or are tawny—indicate that much water is very near that stone. ||107|| Stones that are the color of a <gloss>pigeon</gloss>, honey, ghee, linen cloth, or the Soma plant used in sacrifices...

# Varahi Samhita

If the stone is the color of a wood-apple, it also quickly produces inexhaustible water. ||108|| A stone that has copper-colored spots or variegated spots, or is pale white, or is blue and red like the flowers of the *Angushthika* tree, or is the color of the sun or fire, should be known as waterless. ||109|| A stone that is the color of moonlight, crystal, pearl, gold, or sapphire; or very red like cinnabar; or very black like eye-salve; or very red and shining like the rays of the rising sun; or yellow like orpiment—such a stone is auspicious. The verses following in this section are the words of the Sages, meaning they are authoritative. ||110|| All the stones mentioned previously are auspicious; therefore, these stones should not be broken. These stones are always served by *Yakshas* <note>Nature spirits or guardians of treasures</note> and *Nagas* <note>Serpent deities associated with water</note>. In the kingdoms of kings where such stones exist, there is never a drought. ||111||

If a stone appears while digging a well and it cannot be broken, one should burn the wood of the Flame-of-the-Forest (*Palash*) and the Leopard-tree (*Bakul*) over it to make the stone red-hot. Then, if water mixed with lime is sprinkled over it, the stone breaks. ||112|| If one boils water mixed with the ashes of the *Maruva* tree, adds the salt of *Shar* reed, and sprinkles that water seven times over a stone heated by fire, the stone breaks. ||113|| If buttermilk, fermented gruel, liquor, horse-gram, and jujube fruits are kept together in a vessel for seven nights, and then sprinkled repeatedly over a stone heated by the previously mentioned method, the stone breaks. ||114|| If the ashes of lemon leaves, lemon bark, sesame stalks, *Apamarga* (prickly chaff-flower), leopard-tree fruit, and *Giloy* are strained with cow urine, and then sprinkled six times over a heated stone, that stone breaks. ||115||

If one burns the horn of a ram and grinds the soot with the droppings of pigeons and mice, mixes them into the milk of the *Aak* (calotropis) plant to make a paste, and applies it to a weapon, and then tempers the <term>Tanka</term> (<term>Stone-breaking tool</term>) by dipping it in oil, the edge of this weapon will not break even when struck against stone. ||116|| If buttermilk is mixed with the salt of a plantain tree and left for a day, and then used to temper iron, that iron becomes so sharp that it does not break even when struck against stone, nor does it become notched when hitting other iron. ||117||

Water remains for a long time in a <term>Vapi</term> <note>A rectangular step-well</note> that is long from East to West, but it does not stay in one that is long from South to North because it is broken by large waves raised by the wind. If one wishes to make a <term>Pushkarini</term> <note>A lotus pond or reservoir</note> long from South to North, then to protect against the impact of the water, its banks should be bound with strong wood or lined with stone, brick, etc. During construction, each layer of soil should be trampled by horses, elephants, etc., so that the soil is compressed and does not break from the pressure of the water. ||118|| Trees such as Arjuna, Banyan, Mango, White Fig, Kadamba, Nichula, Jamun, Vetasa, Neem (a variety of Kadamba), Kurabaka, Palmyra, Ashoka, Mahua, and Moulshree should be planted on the banks of that <term>Vapi</term>. ||119|| For the exit of water, a path should be made on one side, which should be reinforced with stones. That path should be covered with a gapless wooden plank and pressed down with soil from above. ||120|| One should grind *Anjana* (antimony), *Motha* (nut grass), *Khas* (vetiver), *Rajkoshataki* (large luffa), *Amala* (gooseberry), and *Kataka* (clearing nut) into a powder and put it into the well. ||121|| Water that is muddy, bitter, salty, tasteless, or...

If the water is foul-smelling, by adding this powder it becomes clear, sweet, fragrant, and endowed with many other excellent qualities. ||122|| It is best to begin the construction of a well during the <term>Nakshatras</term><note>Lunar mansions or star clusters used in Vedic astrology</note> of Hasta, Magha, Anuradha, Pushya, Dhanishtha, the three Uttaras (Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, Uttara Bhadrapada), Rohini, and Shatabhisha. ||123|| After offering a sacrifice to Varuna <note>The deity of water</note>, one should worship a stake made of Banyan or Vetasa wood with perfumes, flowers, and incense; then, first drive that stake into the ground at the location of the water vein. ||124|| The knowledge of water during the rainy season after the Jyeshtha full moon is the "Cloud-related Water-finding" (<term>Dakargala</term>), which I have already stated after observing the opinions of sages like Baladeva and others. # Now begins the Fifty-Fifth Chapter
## The Science of Plant Health (Vrikshayurveda)

Water reservoirs are not pleasing if they are devoid of shade on their banks; therefore, one should plant gardens and orchards along the edges of the water. ||1|| Soft soil is beneficial for all types of trees; one should first sow sesame seeds in it. When the sesame plants bloom, they should be tilled back into the earth; this is the first step in preparing the ground. ||2|| Soapnut, Ashoka, Punnaga, Sirisha, and Priyangu trees are auspicious; they should be planted first in a garden or near houses. ||3|| Jackfruit, Ashoka, Banana, Rose-apple, Lakucha, Pomegranate, Grape, Pali-vata, Citron, and Atimuktaka: ||4|| these trees should be planted as cuttings after being smeared with cow dung. They should be planted with care, either by cutting the root or the trunk. ||5|| Plant those without branches in the winter, those with branches in the early spring, and those with well-developed trunks at the onset of the rainy season, ensuring they face the same direction as they did before. ||6|| For the successful transplanting and growth of trees, they should be smeared from root to trunk with a mixture of ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, Usheera <note>vetiver</note>, sesame, honey, Vidanga <note>false black pepper</note>, milk, and cow dung. ||7|| After becoming pure and performing the worship of the tree with baths and ointments, one should plant it; once planted, it will thrive with its own leaves. ||8|| Planted trees should be watered every evening and morning at the end of summer; every other day in winter; and during the rainy season, only when the earth appears dry. ||9|| Rose-apple, Vetasa, Vaneera, Kadamba, Udumbara, Arjuna, Citron, Grape, Lakucha, Pomegranate, ||10|| Vanjula, Nakhtamala, Tilaka, Jackfruit, Timira, and Amrataka—these sixteen are known as water-loving species. ||11|| An interval of twenty cubits <note>approx. 30 feet</note> between trees is best, sixteen cubits is medium, and twelve cubits is the minimum distance to be maintained. ||12|| Trees planted too close together, touching one another, with their roots entangled, do not yield fruit properly as they are "oppressed" <note>competing for nutrients</note>. ||13|| Due to cold, wind, or heat, diseases arise causing yellowing of leaves, lack of growth in shoots, drying of branches, and oozing of sap. ||14|| To treat these, first clean the affected areas with a blade, then apply a paste of Vidanga, ghee, and silt...

...one should sprinkle with milk and water. || 15 || If the fruit is destroyed, a decoction of horse-gram, black-gram, mung beans, sesame, and barley, cooled after boiling, should be sprinkled to increase flowers and fruit. || 16 || Take two <term>Adhakas</term><note>A traditional unit of volume, roughly 3 kilograms</note> of powdered sheep and goat dung, one <term>Adhaka</term> of sesame, one <term>Prastha</term><note>Approx. 750 grams</note> of barley meal, one <term>Drona</term><note>Approx. 12 liters</note> of water, and one <term>Tula</term><note>Approx. 4 kilograms</note> of beef. || 17 || These should be kept for seven nights; this mixture should then be used to sprinkle on trees, shrubs, and creepers to ensure they always bear fruit and flowers. || 18 || For ten days, seeds should be soaked in milk, then handled with hands smeared with ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, rubbed repeatedly with cow dung, and fumigated with the flesh of a boar. || 19 || When planted in prepared soil and mixed with the fat of fish and pigs, then sprinkled with water mixed with milk, the plant will bloom with flowers instantly. || 20 || Even a tamarind seed produces a creeper if treated with the powder of rice, black-gram, and sesame, sprinkled with fermented flesh, and constantly fumigated with turmeric. || 21 || To turn a Wood-Apple <note>Kapittha</note> into a creeper, take the roots of <term>Asphota</term>, <term>Dhatri</term>, <term>Dhava</term>, and <term>Vasika</term>, along with <term>Palashani</term>, <term>Vetasa</term>, <term>Suryavalli</term>, <term>Shyama</term>, and <term>Atimukta</term>—these eight roots. || 22 || Boil these in milk and let it cool; soak Wood-Apple seeds in this for a hundred pulses. Once dry, burn the pit and coat it with a paste of honey, ghee, and ash. || 24 || Fill it with soil mixed with powdered black-gram, sesame, and barley. Add water mixed with fish flesh and beat the soil until it reaches a thick consistency. || 25 || Plant the seed four fingers deep and sprinkle with fish-water and meat-water. A creeper with beautiful sprouts will quickly grow and cover the pavilion, causing wonder. || 26 || If a seed is treated with the pulp of the <term>Ankolla</term> fruit a hundred times, or with its oil, or with the fruit of the <term>Shleshmataka</term> <note>Cordia myxa</note> tree, || 27 || and then planted in soil mixed with hail-water, it germinates instantly. Is it any wonder then that the branches will be weighed down with fruit? || 28 || A wise man should take <term>Shleshmataka</term> seeds, remove the husks, and soak them seven times in the sticky juice of <term>Ankolla</term> in the shade. || 29 || Rub them with buffalo dung, store them in dry cow dung, and when planted in a mix of soil and hail-water, they bear fruit in a single day. || 30 || The constellations <term>Rohini</term>, <term>Mrigashira</term>, <term>Mula</term>, <term>Vishakha</term>, <term>Anuradha</term>, <term>Uttarashada</term>, <term>Uttarabhadrapada</term>, <term>Uttaraphalguni</term>, <term>Shravana</term>, <term>Ashwini</term>, and <term>Hasta</term> are declared by the divine-sighted seers to be auspicious for the planting of trees. || 31 ||

# Chapter 55 with Hindi Commentary

Trees that have not yet produced <insert>fruit or flowers</insert> should be uprooted from one location and transplanted to another in their proper direction during the *Shishira* season <note>Late Winter, typically Jan-Feb</note>. Those that have developed branches should be moved in the *Hemanta* season <note>Early Winter, Nov-Dec</note>, and trees with well-developed, large branches should be transplanted during the rainy season. ||6||

One should grind together ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, *Khas* <note>vetiver</note>, sesame, honey, *Vidanga* <note>False Black Pepper, used as an antimicrobial</note>, milk, and cow dung. Apply this paste to the trees from the roots up to the branches, then uproot them from one place and plant them in another. ||7||

Being purified, having bathed and applied fragrant unguents, one should worship the tree. If the tree is then moved to another location, it will take root with its original leaves intact—that is, it will not wither. ||8||

Transplanted trees should be watered both morning and evening during the summer; in the winter, they should be watered every other day; and in the rainy season, they should be watered only when the ground becomes dry. ||9||

Rose-apple, cane, *Vanira* <note>a variety of cane</note>, *Kadamba*, cluster fig, *Arjuna*, citron, grape, *Badahar* <note>Monkey Fruit</note>, and pomegranate. ||10||

*Banjula*, *Naktamala* <note>Indian Beech</note>, *Tilaka*, jackfruit, *Timira*, and *Ambada* <note>Hog Plum</note>—these sixteen trees are *Anupaja* <term>Anupaja: plants that thrive in marshy or water-rich regions</term>. ||11||

It is best if a distance of twenty cubits <note>approx. 30 feet</note> is kept between one tree and the next; sixteen cubits is middling, and a distance of twelve cubits is considered poor. ||12||

Trees that grow too close together, touch one another, or whose roots become entangled, suffer "distress" and for this reason, they do not bear fruit properly. ||13||

Trees fall ill due to excessive cold, strong winds, or intense sun; then their leaves turn yellow, new shoots do not grow, branches wither, and sap begins to leak out. ||14||

One should treat a sick tree in this manner: first, any part seen to be rotting or dried up should be cut away with a blade. Then, apply a paste of *Vidanga*, ghee, and silt to the tree, and afterwards water it with a mixture of milk and water. ||15||

If a tree does not bear fruit, one should boil horse-gram, black gram, mung beans, sesame, and barley in milk. Once cooled, water the tree with this milk to encourage the growth of fruits and flowers. ||16||

Take two *Adhaka* <note>ancient unit of volume, approx. 3kg</note> of powdered sheep and goat dung, one *Adhaka* of sesame, one *Prastha* <note>approx. 750g</note> of barley meal, one *Drona* <note>approx. 12kg</note> of water, and one *Tula* <note>approx. 5kg</note> of beef. Place all these in a single vessel. ||17||

Keep this for seven nights. Afterwards, water the trees, shrubs, and creepers with this liquid to produce fruits and flowers. ||18||

Take the seed of any tree and coat it with hands greased with ghee, then drop it into milk. Repeat this daily for ten days, coating it with greasy hands and placing it in milk. Then, rub it many times with cow dung to dry it. Fumigate that seed with the smoke of pork and venison. ||19||

Then, sow that seed—along with the fat of fish and pigs—into soil that has been purified by previously sowing sesame. Water it with milk and water. The tree that grows from that seed will emerge already laden with flowers. ||20||

Even the tamarind seed, which is extremely hard, if treated with a powder of grain, black gram, and sesame, along with barley meal and decomposed meat, and then fumigated with turmeric, will produce new sprouts. If even such a seed sprouts, what doubt can there be of others? ||21||

If one wishes to grow a vine from a Wood Apple (*Kapittha*) seed, one should take the roots of these eight: *Vishnukranta*, Amla, *Dhav*, *Basa* <note>Malabar Nut</note> with its leaves, *Vetas* <note>Cane</note>, Sunflower, *Nisot*, and *Atimuktaka* <note>Mountain Jasmine</note>. ||22||

Take the leaves of the cane as well and boil them all in milk. After cooling the milk, place the Wood Apple seed in it for as long as it takes to clap one's hands a hundred times. Then remove it and dry it in the sun. Repeat this process daily for one month before sowing the seed. ||23||

Dig a pit one cubit long, one cubit wide, and two cubits deep...

Once the water has dried, burn the hole with fire and smear it with a mixture of honey, ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, and ashes. ||24|| Fill the hole with a powder made of black gram, sesame, and barley. Water it with fish-water and meat-water. Soon, a creeper with excellent leaves will emerge and cover the pavilion, causing wonder to all who see it. ||26|| Take any seed and give it a hundred "infusions" <term>Bhavana: a process of soaking and drying to impregnate a substance with the properties of a liquid</term> with the pulp or oil of the Ankola fruit, or with the pulp or oil of the Shleshmantaka <note>Lasoora or Glueberry</note> fruit. ||27|| If one then sows this seed in soil moistened by hail-water, it sprouts that very instant and becomes a creeper bent under the weight of its flowers. There is no doubt in this; it truly happens. ||28|| A wise man should take Shleshmantaka seeds, remove their husks, and infuse them seven times in the shade with the "lightning" <note>original: *bijali*, referring to the viscous, translucent fluid</note> of the Ankola fruit, drying them in the shade each time. ||29|| Then, rub those seeds with buffalo dung and store them in a heap of dry buffalo dung. When the earth is later moistened by falling hail, sow those seeds in that hail-soaked soil; they will become a tree and bear fruit in a single day. ||30|| The three Uttaras <note>Uttara Phalguni, Uttara Ashadha, Uttara Bhadrapada</note>, Rohini, Mrigashira, Revati, Chitra, Anuradha, Mula, Vishakha, Pushya, Shravana, Ashwini, and Hasta—these lunar mansions <term>Nakshatras</term> have been declared the best for planting trees by the divine-sighted Lords of Sages. ||31||

# Chapter Fifty-Six
## On the Characteristics of Temples

Having ensured an abundance of water and having laid out gardens, one should build a temple to increase one's fame and religious merit. ||1|| For one who desires to attain those worlds reached through the performance of *Ishta* <note>sacrificial rites</note> and *Purta* <note>charitable works like building wells or gardens</note>, a house for the gods should be built; both merits are seen to be achieved here. ||2|| The gods always draw near to those places which possess woods and water, whether they be natural or man-made. ||3|| Near lakes where the sun's rays are repelled by the umbrellas of lotus leaves, and where the waters are made pure by the ripples stirred by swans tossing white water-lilies. ||4|| Where the sounds of swans, ducks, cranes, and ruddy geese are heard, and where water-creatures rest in the shade of the *Nichula* trees on the banks. ||5|| Where rivers have cranes for their tinkling waist-bells, the song of swans for their voice, the water for their silken garment, and glistening fish for their jewelry. ||6|| Where the flowering trees on the banks are their head-ornaments, the confluences are their broad hips, the sandbanks are their high breasts, and the laughter of swans is their smile. ||7|| The gods always take delight in the regions near forests, rivers, mountains, and springs, and in cities possessing beautiful gardens. ||8|| The types of soil prescribed for Brahmins and the other castes in the context of residential architecture are also recommended for their respective temples. ||9|| A temple should always be designed on a sixty-four-square grid. The door should be placed in the middle, aligned with the cardinal directions...

# Chapter 56: Characteristics of Temples

...is praised. || 10 || Whatever the width of a temple may be, its height should be double that measure. The "waist" <note>the middle section or terrace of the structure</note> is known to be equal to one-third of that height. || 11 || The inner sanctum <note>original: "garbha"</note> should be half of the total width, with the remaining half forming the walls all around. The door should be as wide as one-quarter of the sanctum's width, and its height should be twice its width. || 12 || The doorpost <note>original: "shakha"</note> and the threshold <note>original: "udumbara"</note> should each be one-quarter of the door's height in width. The thickness of the doorposts is traditionally one-quarter of their own width. || 13 || It is recommended that the doorposts be divided into three, five, seven, or nine vertical sections. At the bottom fourth of the doorpost, the two door-keepers <note>statues of guardians</note> should be placed. || 14 || The remaining space should be decorated with auspicious birds, the Tree of Prosperity <note>Shrivriksha</note>, the swastika, holy water-pots <note>ghatas</note>, amorous couples <note>mithunas</note>, creeping vines, and playful spirits <note>pramathas</note>. || 15 || The idol, including its pedestal, should be one-eighth less than the measurement of the doorway. Of that total, the idol itself should take up two parts, and the pedestal <note>pindika</note> one-third. || 16 ||

### The Twenty Types of Temples
The names of the temples are:
1. Meru
2. Mandara
3. Kailasa
4. Vimana-chhanda
5. Nandana
6. Samudra
7. Padma
8. Garuda
9. Nandivardhana
10. Kunjara
11. Guharaja
12. Vrisha
13. Hansa
14. Sarvatobhadra
15. Ghata
16. Simha
17. Vritta (Round)
18. Chatuskona (Square)
19. Shodashashri (Sixteen-sided)
20. Ashtashri (Eight-sided)

These twenty temples have been declared by me by name. I shall now describe their characteristics in the order they were mentioned. || 17–19 ||

Among them, the **Meru** is hexagonal, has twelve stories, varied dark cavities <note>galleries or niches</note>, four doors, and is thirty cubits wide. || 20 || The **Mandara** is thirty cubits wide, has ten stories and a spire. The **Kailasa** also has a spire and is twenty-eight cubits wide with eight stories. || 21 || The **Vimana** is twenty-one cubits wide and features latticed windows. The **Nandana** has six stories, is thirty-two cubits wide, and is adorned with sixteen small domes <note>andas</note>. || 22 || The **Samudra** is circular. The **Padma** is shaped like a lotus, has eight stories, a single spire, and only one main floor level. || 23 || The **Garuda** is shaped like the mythical bird. The **Nandi** is twenty-four cubits wide, has seven stories, and is decorated with twenty small domes. || 24 || The **Kunjara** is shaped like an elephant's back and is sixteen cubits wide at the base. The **Guharaja** is sixteen cubits wide with three roof-windows <note>chandrashalas</note> and a barrel-vaulted roof <note>valabhi</note>. || 25 || The **Vrisha** has one story, one spire, is twelve cubits wide, and is circular all around. The **Hansa** is shaped like a swan, and the **Ghata** is eight cubits wide, shaped like a water-pot. || 26 || The **Sarvatobhadra** has four doors, many spires, many beautiful roof-windows, is twenty-six cubits wide, and has five stories. || 27 || The **Simha** is covered with lion figures, has twelve corners, and is eight cubits wide. The four types—dark-colored, square, and five-domed—are also described. || 28 ||

According to the architect Maya, the height of a story is 108 finger-widths. However, Vishwakarma <note>the divine architect</note> says it is three and a half cubits. || 29 || Learned architects say that when the cornice <note>kapotapali</note> is added, these two different measurements actually become equal. || 30 ||

These characteristics of temples have been described by me in brief. Everything composed by the sage Garga is included here. I have also consulted the extensive works written by Manu and others to create this authoritative summary. || 31 ||

**Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Temples," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira.**

...if they remain undisturbed, then the gods reside in those places. ||3|| The gods always sport in such lakes where the sun's rays are warded off by the umbrellas of lotus leaves, and where white lotuses are moved by the shoulders of swans as they make their way through the clear waters that fill these reservoirs. ||4|| Where the sounds of swans, ducks, cranes, and ruddy geese resound, and where aquatic creatures rest in the shade of the *Nichula* trees <note>The Indian Willow or Barringtonia acutangula</note> along the banks. ||5|| The gods dwell in places near rivers that flow downward—rivers whose waist-belts are the cranes, whose sweet speech is the sound of swans, whose garment is the water, whose girdle is the fish, whose ear-ornaments are the blossoming trees on the banks, whose broad hips are the confluence of land and water, and whose high breasts are the sandbanks and the swans themselves. ||6||7||

The gods constantly take pleasure in the lands near forests, rivers, mountains, and springs, and they also sport in cities filled with gardens. ||8|| The same types of land previously described for building houses for the four castes—starting with the Brahmins—are also considered excellent for constructing temples for those respective castes. ||9||

In a temple, one should always employ the previously mentioned <term>Vastu of sixty-four squares</term> <note>A sacred architectural grid or mandala used in Hindu temple design</note>. In that temple, it is best if the main door is situated exactly in the middle of a cardinal direction. ||10|| The height of the temple should be double its width. The <term>Kati</term> <note>literally "waist"; the basement or plinth of the temple</note> of the temple is equal to one-third of the height; the point where the temple structure begins above the stairs is called the *Kati*. ||11||

The <term>Garbha</term> <note>literally "womb"; the inner sanctum or cella</note> is half of the total width. The remaining half of the width is used for the walls on all sides. The width of the door is equal to one-fourth of the *Garbha's* width, and the height of the door is twice its width. ||12|| The width of the <term>Shakha</term> <note>the vertical doorposts or side-frames</note> and the <term>Udumbara</term> <note>the threshold or lintel</note> is equal to one-fourth of the door's height. The thickness of the *Shakha* is equal to one-fourth of its own width. ||13||

A door is considered excellent if it has three, five, seven, or nine *Shakhas* (vertical moldings) within the stated width. In the lower fourth part of the two doorposts, the figures of two divine doorkeepers should be carved. ||14|| The remaining three-fourths of the doorposts should be decorated with auspicious birds like swans, creepers, *Svastikas*, lucky signs, pitchers, <term>Mithuna</term> <note>amorous couples or pairs of men and women</note>, leaves, and various vines. ||15||

Subtracting one-eighth from the height of the door gives the measurement for the divine idol including its <term>Pindika</term> <note>the pedestal or base upon which the deity is installed</note>. Dividing the total height of the idol and pedestal into three parts: two parts should be the height of the idol and one part should be the height of the *Pindika*. This proportion is prescribed for all <term>Prasadas</term> <note>palatial temples or mansions of the gods</note>. ||16||

The twenty types of temples are: <term>Meru</term>, <term>Mandara</term>, <term>Kailasa</term>, <term>Vimanachhanda</term>, <term>Nandana</term>, <term>Samudra</term>, <term>Padma</term>, <term>Garuda</term>, <term>Nandivardhana</term>, <term>Kunjara</term>, ||17|| <term>Guharaja</term>, <term>Vrisha</term>, <term>Hansa</term>, <term>Sarvatobhadra</term>, <term>Ghata</term>, <term>Simha</term>, <term>Vritta</term>, <term>Chatushkona</term> (Square), <term>Shodashashri</term> (Sixteen-sided), and <term>Ashtashri</term> (Eight-sided). ||18|| We have named these twenty types of temples; now we shall describe their characteristics in the order of their names. ||19||

The temple named *Meru* is hexagonal; it has twelve stories and is equipped with various types of internal windows. It has four doors in the four cardinal directions. Its width is thirty-two cubits and its height is sixty-four cubits. ||20|| The *Mandara* temple is thirty cubits wide, has ten stories, and is adorned with spires. The *Kailasa* temple also has spires, is twenty-eight cubits wide, has eight stories, and is hexagonal. ||21|| The temple with latticed windows and a width of twenty-one cubits...

## Chapter 57 with Hindi Commentary

The **Vimanachhanda** temple is characterized by having eight stories and a hexagonal shape. The **Nandana** temple is also hexagonal but has six stories; it is thirty-two cubits <note>A "hand" or cubit is roughly 18 inches</note> wide and is adorned with sixteen "eggs" <gloss>1</gloss>. The temple named **Samudra** is circular. Both of these temples are eight cubits wide, possess a single spire (shringa), and consist of only one story. ||22-23||

The **Garuda** temple is shaped like the mythical bird Garuda, though it lacks wings and a tail. Both of these <note>referring to Garuda and likely a variant mentioned in related texts</note> should be twenty-four cubits wide, seven stories high, and decorated with twenty-four "eggs." ||24||

The **Kunjara** temple is shaped like the back of an elephant and measures sixteen cubits wide at its base. The **Guharaja** temple is built in the form of Guha <note>The deity Kartikeya</note> and is also sixteen cubits wide. The sloping roofs (valabhi) of both these temples are equipped with three "moon-chambers" <note>Chandrashala: arched dormer windows or decorative niches</note> each. ||25||

The temple named **Vrisha** (Bull) has one story and one spire. It is twelve cubits wide and is circular on all sides. The **Hansa** (Swan) temple is shaped like a swan, complete with a beak, wings, and a tail; it is also twelve cubits wide with one story and one spire. The temple named **Ghata** (Pot) is shaped like a water-pot and is eight cubits wide, also featuring one story and one spire. ||26||

The **Sarvatobhadra** temple is equipped with four doors facing the four cardinal directions. It is beautified by many spires and numerous lovely "moon-chambers." It is twenty-six cubits wide, square in shape, and has five stories. ||27||

The **Simha** (Lion) temple is decorated with the image of a lion, has twelve corners, and is eight cubits wide. The remaining four temples—**Vriksha** (Tree), **Chatushkona** (Square), **Shodashasra** (Sixteen-sided), and **Ashtasra** (Eight-sided)—have shapes corresponding to their names. These four are "dark-formed" (Anjanarupa), meaning their interiors remain dark as outside light does not reach them. ||28||

According to the school of **Maya** <note>The divine architect of the Asuras</note>, the measurement of one story is one hundred and eight digits (anguls). However, **Vishwakarma** <note>The divine architect of the Devas</note> has stated the measurement of a single story to be three and a half cubits. ||29||

Wise craftsmen say the opinions of Maya and Vishwakarma are actually the same. Their reasoning is that when Vishwakarma cited three and a half cubits (which is eighty-four digits), he was excluding the "pigeon-rail" <note>Kapotapalika: a decorative cornice or molding</note>. If the measurement of the pigeon-rail is added to it, it becomes equal to the measurement given by Maya. ||30||

These characteristics of temples have been described by us in brief. However, all the characteristics composed by the sage **Garga** are included herein. We have established this authority here to preserve the memory of the great treatises on temple architecture written by masters such as **Manu, Vashistha, Maya, and Nagnajit**. ||31||

*Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the Hindi commentary of the Brihat Samhita composed by Acharya Varahamihira, as translated by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region.*

# The Varahi Samhita

Once the decoction has been taken off the fire, it should be mixed with the following substances to form a paste: **||2||** Resin of the *Pinus longifolia* <note>original: "Shrivasaka"</note>, Myrrh <note>original: "Rasa"</note>, Guggulu <note>a fragrant resin used in incense and medicine</note>, Bhallataka <note>marking nut</note>, Kunduru <note>frankincense</note>, Sarjarasa <note>resin of the Sal tree</note>, Linseed, and Bilva fruit. This paste is known as **Vajralepa** <note>literally "Diamond Plaster" or "Adamantine Glue"</note>. **||3||** When heated and applied to temples, mansions, balconies, Shiva-lingas, idols, walls, and wells, it lasts for ten thousand years. **||4||**

Lac, Kunduru, Guggulu, soot from the house <note>original: "Grihadhumaka"</note>, the pulp of Kapittha and Bilva fruits, the fruits of Nagabala, Tinduka, Madana, Madhuka <note>honey tree</note>, and Manjistha <note>Indian madder</note>, **||5||** Sarjarasa, and Amla fruits—this constitutes the second variety of paste. This too is called **Vajra** and possesses the same qualities as the first, intended for the same purposes. **||6||**

Another paste, named **Vajratara** <note>meaning "More Adamantine"</note>, is made from the horns of cows, buffaloes, and goats; the hair of donkeys; and the hides of buffaloes and cows, combined with the juices of Neem and Kapittha. **||7||** Eight parts of lead, two parts of bell-metal <note>original: "Kansya"</note>, and one part of brass <note>original: "Reetika"</note>—this alloy, as described by Maya <note>the legendary architect of the Asuras</note>, is known as **Vajrasanghata** <note>Adamantine Union/Alloy</note>. **||8||**

->Thus ends the Fifty-Seventh Chapter, named Vajralepa,<-
->in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira.<-

Unripe fruits of Tinduka, unripe fruits of Kapittha, flowers of the Silk-cotton tree, seeds of the Sallaki tree, bark of the Bandhana tree, and Vacha <note>sweet flag</note>. **||1||** Boil all these in one *Drona* <note>a traditional unit of volume, approx. 8 liters</note> of water until only an eighth part remains, then remove it from the heat. **||2||** Afterward, grind and add the resin of the Sarala tree, Myrrh, Guggulu, Bhilawa, Kunduru <note>resin of the Deodar tree</note>, Ral <note>Sal resin</note>, Linseed, and the pulp of Bilva fruit. This is the preparation called **Vajralepa**. **||3||** This Vajralepa should be heated and applied to divine temples, mansions, balconies, Shiva-lingas, idols of deities, walls, and wells; this coating lasts for a thousand years. **||4||**

Lac, Kunduru, Guggulu, cobwebs/soot from the house, Kapittha fruit, Bilva pulp, fruits of Nagabala <note>Gangeran</note>, fruits of Mahua, and Manjistha. **||5||** By mixing the paste of all these substances into a *Drona* of water prepared as before, the second Vajralepa is perfected. It has the same qualities as the first and is used for temples and other structures in the same manner. **||6||** From the horns of the cow, buffalo, and goat; the hides of the donkey, buffalo, and cow; and the fruits of Neem, Kapittha, and Indigo, the third paste is perfected as before. Its name is **Vajratara**. It possesses the aforementioned qualities and is used for the same tasks. **||7||** Melt together eight parts lead, two parts bell-metal, and one part brass. This is the formula spoken by Maya, and its name is **Vajrasanghata**. **||8||**

Thus ends the Fifty-Seventh Chapter in the Hindi commentary of the Brihat Samhita, composed by Shri Varahamihira Acharya and annotated by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province.

# Chapter Fifty-Eight
## The Characteristics of Images
<note>Sanskrit: Pratimalakṣaṇam. This chapter outlines the system of iconometry—the mathematical proportions used by ancient Indian sculptors to ensure a deity's form was auspicious and aesthetically perfect.</note>

When the sun passes through a lattice window, the smallest particle of dust that is visible is known as a **Particle** <note>original: *paramāṇu*</note>; this is the first unit of measurement. |1|

Eight **Particles** make one **Speck of Dust** <note>original: *rajas*</note>; eight of those make a **Hair’s Tip** <note>original: *bālāgra*</note>; eight of those make a **Nit** <note>original: *likṣā*</note>; eight of those make a **Louse** <note>original: *yūkā*</note>; eight of those make a **Barley-corn** <note>original: *yava*</note>; and eight barley-corns make one **Digit** <note>original: *angula*, roughly 3/4 of an inch</note>. This is the progression of numbers. |2|

Take the height of the temple door and reduce it by one-eighth; one-third of that remaining height is the measurement for the **Pedestal** <note>original: *piṇḍikā*</note>. The **Image** <note>original: *pratimā*</note> itself should be twice the size of the pedestal. |3|

The face should be twelve **Digits** in both width and length, according to the artist's own digit-measure. However, **Nagnajit** <note>An ancient authority on art and architecture</note> states that in the **Dravidian** <note>Southern Indian</note> style, the face is said to be fourteen digits in length. |4|

The nose, forehead, chin, and neck are each four digits long, as are the ears. The jaws are two digits; the chin is two digits wide. |5|

The forehead is eight digits wide. Beyond that, the temples are two digits each. The temples themselves are four digits long, and the ears are two digits in thickness. |6|

The outer edge of the ear should be made at a level of four and a half digits along a level line. The ear-hole and the delicate part of the ear <note>the tragus</note> should be level with the corner of the eye. |7|

**Vasistha** <note>A legendary sage and authority</note> says that the distance between the corner of the eye and the ear is four digits. The lower lip is one digit in thickness, and the upper lip is half of that. |8|

The **philtrum** <note>original: *gocchā*, the groove above the upper lip</note> is half a digit. The mouth should be made four digits long. When closed, it is one and a half digits wide; when open, it is three digits. |9|

The two nostrils are each two digits wide. From the tip of the nose, the height is known to be two digits. The distance between the eyes is four digits. |10|

The eye-socket is two digits wide. The two eyes are each two digits, and the **pupil** <note>original: *tārā*</note> is one-third of that. The **sight** <note>the iris</note> is one-fifth of the pupil. The opening of the eye is one digit. |11|

From end to end, the eyebrows are ten digits long. The line of the eyebrow is half a digit wide. The space between the eyebrows is two digits, and each eyebrow is four digits in length. |12|

The hairline should be made equal to the curve of the eyebrows and half a digit wide. At the corner of the eye, one should place the **Karavīraka** <note>a technical term for a specific anatomical marking or fold near the eye</note> measuring one digit. |13|

The head is thirty-two digits in circumference and fourteen digits in length. In **painting** <note>original: *citrakarma*</note>, only twelve digits are visible, though twenty are seen in total <note>referring to the perspective of the curve</note>. |14|

**Nagnajit** has stated that the face, including the hair-covered part, is sixteen digits in length. The neck is ten digits wide and twenty-one digits in circumference. |15|

From the throat to the heart is twelve digits; from the heart to the navel is the same measure. From the center of the navel to the penis, the distance is said to be the same. |16|

The thighs are twenty-four digits long, and the shanks are the same. The kneecaps are four digits, and the feet are equal to that in height. |17|

The feet are twelve digits long and six digits wide. The big toe is three digits long and five digits in circumference. The second toe is three digits long. |18|

The remaining toes should be made smaller by one-eighth part in succession. The height of the big toe is said to be one and a quarter digits. |19|

Experts say the nail of the big toe is three-quarters of a digit. The remaining nails are half a digit, or slightly less, in order. |20|

The circumference at the top of the shank is said to be fourteen digits, and the width is five. In the middle, it is seven digits wide and twenty-one digits in circumference. |21|

The width at the middle of the knee is eight digits, and the circumference is twenty-four. The thigh is fourteen digits wide at the middle, and its circumference is double that. |22|

The hips are eighteen digits wide and forty-four digits in circumference. The navel is one digit in depth and the same in width. |23|

The middle of the waist, through the navel, is forty-two digits in circumference. The distance between the two breasts is sixteen digits, and the height to the armpits is six digits...

# The Varāhī Saṃhitā

### Chapter on the Characteristics of Images

[24-25] The shoulders should be made with a width of one *vasti* <note>approximately 9 inches</note>. The upper arms and forearms are twelve digits in length. The upper arms are six digits wide, while the forearms are four digits wide.

[26] The circumference of the arm is sixteen digits at the base and twelve digits at the wrist. The palm of the hand is six digits in width and seven digits in length.

[27] The middle finger is five digits long. The index finger is shorter than the middle finger by half a phalange <note>the segment of a finger</note>. The ring finger is equal to the index finger, and the little finger is shorter than those by one phalange.

[28] The thumb consists of two phalanges, while the remaining fingers should be made with three phalanges each. The measurement of the nails for all fingers should be half the length of a phalange.

[29] An image should be fashioned with ornaments, dress, and decorations appropriate to the region. An image endowed with the correct characteristics <note>lakṣaṇas</note> brings prosperity by its very presence.

[30] Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and Bali, the son of Virocana, should be one hundred and twenty digits in height. Other superior, medium, and inferior figures are reduced in height by increments of twelve digits.

[31] The Lord Viṣṇu should be made with eight, four, or two arms. His chest should be marked with the *Śrīvatsa* <note>a sacred curl of hair</note> and his breast adorned with the *Kaustubha* gem.

[32] He should be dark like the linseed flower <note>original: "atasī-kusuma-śyāma"</note>, wearing yellow garments, with a placid countenance. He wears earrings and a crown, and possesses a sturdy neck, chest, shoulders, and arms.

[33] In his right hands, he holds a sword, a mace, and an arrow, while the fourth hand is held in the gesture of peace <note>śāntida-mudrā</note>. In his left hands, he holds a bow, a buckler, a discus, and a conch.

[34] If one desires a four-armed Viṣṇu, one right hand is in the peace gesture and the other holds a mace; on the left side, he holds the conch and the discus.

[35] In a two-armed image, the right hand is in the peace gesture and the other holds the conch. Thus should the image of Viṣṇu be made by those seeking prosperity.

[36] Baladeva <note>Balarāma</note> should be made holding a plow, with eyes rolling from intoxication. He wears a single earring and his body is as white as a conch, the moon, or a lotus stalk.

[37] The goddess Ekānaṃśā should be placed between Baladeva and Kṛṣṇa. Her left hand rests on her hip and the other holds a lotus.

[38] If she is made with four arms, her left hands hold a book and a lotus; her two right hands offer a boon to seekers and hold a rosary.

[39] If she has eight arms, the left hands hold a lotus, a water-pot, a bow, and a book. The right arms are equipped with the boon-granting gesture, an arrow, a mirror, and a rosary.

[40] Sāmba should be made holding a mace, and Pradyumna should be handsome and holding a bow. Their wives should be fashioned holding a buckler and a sword.

[41] Brahmā is four-faced, holds a water-pot, and is seated on a lotus. Skanda has the appearance of a youth, carries a spear <note>śakti</note>, and has a peacock for his banner.

[42] Indra’s elephant <note>Airāvata</note> is white and has four tusks. Indra himself holds a thunderbolt. A third eye placed horizontally on his forehead is his distinguishing mark.

[43] On Śambhu’s <note>Śiva's</note> head is the crescent moon; he has the bull for his banner and a third eye placed vertically. He holds a trident and the *Pināka* bow. Alternatively, his left half may consist of the Daughter of the Mountain <note>Pārvatī, in the Ardhanārīśvara form</note>.

[44] The Buddha should have the palms of his hands and soles of his feet marked with lotuses. He has a serene expression and very short hair. He is seated on a lotus seat and appears like the father of the world.

[45] The God of the Arhats <note>a Jina/Tīrthaṅkara</note> should be made with arms reaching to his knees <note>ājānulamba-bāhu</note>, marked with the *Śrīvatsa*, and possessing a tranquil form. He is sky-clad <note>naked</note>, youthful, and handsome.

[46] The nose, forehead, shanks, thighs, cheeks, and chest of the Sun <note>Sūrya</note> should be prominent. He should wear the "Northern dress" <note>udīcya-veṣa, often interpreted as boots and a quilted tunic</note>, covering him from the feet to the chest.

[47] He holds two lotuses by their stalks in his hands and wears a crown. His face is adorned with earrings, he wears a long dangling necklace, and is surrounded by birds <note>or attendants</note>.

[48] His face has the luster of the interior of a lotus; he is protected by a bodice, has a smiling, pleasant face, and a halo shining with gems. Such a Sun brings good fortune to the maker.

[49] An image one cubit high is peaceful; one two cubits high grants wealth. Images of three or four cubits lead to safety and abundance.

... [If the artisan makes an image] of a low-caste woman, there is fear of the king; if she has deformed limbs, the maker becomes incapable; if she has a very thin belly, there is fear of hunger; and if the body is emaciated, there is loss of wealth. || 49-50 || If the image has a wound or scar, one should predict the death of the maker by a weapon. An image leaning to the left destroys the wife; one leaning to the right destroys the maker's lifespan. || 51 || An upward gaze causes blindness; a downward gaze causes constant anxiety. In all idols, the good and bad effects are similar to those described for the Sun god. || 52 || One should determine the circumference of the <term>Lingam</term> <note>The symbolic representation of Shiva</note> by its length and divide it into three parts. The bottom part should be square, the middle part octagonal, and the top part circular. || 53 || The square part is buried in the earth; the middle part is placed within the cavity of the pedestal. The visible height of the pedestal should be equal on all sides from the cavity. || 54 || A <term>Lingam</term> that is thin and long destroys the country; one lacking sides destroys the city. A <term>Lingam</term> with a crack or wound on its head leads to total destruction. || 55 || The group of Mothers <note>The Matrikas</note> should be made with the specific symbols and features corresponding to the gods of their names. Revanta <note>Son of the Sun god</note> should be depicted on horseback with a retinue engaged in hunting and sport. || 56 || Yama <note>God of Death</note> holds a staff and rides a buffalo; Varuna <note>God of the Waters</note> rides a swan and holds a noose. Kubera <note>God of Wealth</note> has a human vehicle, wears a crown tilted to the left, and has a large belly. || 57 || The lord of the spirits <note>Ganesha</note> should have an elephant's face, a protruding belly, and carry an axe. He has a single tusk and holds a radish root with dark blue leaves. || 58 ||

# Thus ends the 58th Chapter, titled "Characteristics of Idols," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. || 58 ||

---

The extremely fine dust seen in a ray of sunlight entering through a lattice window is known as a <term>Paramanu</term> <note>Atom/Particle</note>; it is the first of all measurements. || 1 || Eight <term>Paramanus</term> make one particle of dust (<term>Raja</term>); eight <term>Rajas</term> make one hair-tip (<term>Balagra</term>); eight <term>Balagras</term> make one nit (<term>Liksha</term>); eight <term>Likshas</term> make one louse (<term>Yuka</term>); eight <term>Yukas</term> make one barley-corn (<term>Yava</term>); and eight <term>Yavas</term> make one <term>Angula</term> <note>Digit/Finger-width</note>. In this way, the measurement increases eightfold at each step. This defines the <term>Angula</term> count. || 2 || From the height of the temple door, subtract one-eighth; one-third of the remainder is the measurement for the <term>Pindika</term> (the pedestal of the idol). The <term>Pratima</term> (the idol itself) should be double the measurement of the <term>Pindika</term>. || 3 || Whatever height is determined for the idol, divide it into twelve parts, and then divide each of those parts into nine. That single unit is one <term>Angula</term>. This is because all idols are one hundred and eight <term>Angulas</term> tall by their own proportions. The teacher named Nagnajit has said that the face of the idol should be twelve <term>Angulas</term> wide and fourteen <term>Angulas</term> long. This measurement belongs to the Dravidian tradition. || 4 || The nose, forehead, chin, neck, and ears of the idol should each be made four <term>Angulas</term> long. The jaws should be two <term>Angulas</term> long, and the width of the chin is two <term>Angulas</term>. || 5 || The forehead is eight <term>Angulas</term> wide; on both sides of the forehead, make the temples two <term>Angulas</term> each. The length of the temples should be four <term>Angulas</term>, and the ears should be two <term>Angulas</term> wide. || 6 || The edge of the ear, starting from the corner of the eye along the line of the eyebrow, should be four and a half <term>Angulas</term>. The ear-hole and the <term>Sukumaraka</term> (the fleshy part near the ear canal) should be aligned with the eye-line. || 7 || The sage Vashistha says that the distance between the eye and the end of the ear should be four <term>Angulas</term>. The lower lip should be one <term>Angula</term> and the upper lip half an <term>Angula</term>. || 8 || The <term>Goccha</term> <note>The philtrum or area above the lip</note> should be half an <term>Angula</term> wide. The mouth should be four <term>Angulas</term> long and one and a half <term>Angulas</term> wide. An open mouth, such as for deities like Narasimha, should be three <term>Angulas</term> wide.
