9. The two nostrils should be made two <term>angulas</term><note>An 'angula' is a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger.</note> each, and from the tip of the nostrils, the nose should also extend two angulas. The height of the nose should be two angulas, and a distance of four angulas should be kept between the two eyes.

10. The eye socket should be two angulas, each of the two eyes two angulas, the pupil equal to one-third of the eye, and the iris <insert>the visual point</insert> equal to one-fifth of the pupil; the width of the eye should be one angula.

11. From the end of one eyebrow to the end of the other, a distance of ten angulas should be maintained. The width of the eyebrow should be half an angula, the space between the two eyebrows two angulas, and the length of each eyebrow should be four angulas.

12. Above the forehead, the hairline should be made equal to the span of the eyebrows, and the hairline itself should be half an angula wide. At the outer corner of the eye, there should be a <term>karviraka</term><note>A specific anatomical point or marking near the temple.</note> of one angula, which is also called the <term>mushika</term>.

13. The head should be made thirty-two angulas long and fourteen angulas wide. If a painting is being made, then twelve angulas of the head are visible, while the twenty angulas that remain at the back are not seen.

14. The master <term>Nagnajit</term><note>An ancient authority on Indian art and architecture (Vastu Shastra).</note> has stated the width of the face, including the hairline, to be sixteen angulas. The width of the neck is ten angulas and its length is said to be twenty-one angulas.

15. From the middle of the throat to the heart, a distance of twelve angulas should be kept. From the heart to the navel, and from the center of the navel to the center of the penis, the distance is also said to be exactly twelve angulas.

16. The thighs and the shanks should each be made twenty-four angulas long. The kneecap above the joints should be four angulas, and the feet should also be four angulas <insert>in height</insert>.

17. The feet should be made twelve angulas long and six angulas wide. The big toes of both feet should be made three angulas long, and the <term>pradeshini</term> (the toe next to the big toe) should also be kept three angulas long.

18. The remaining three toes should be made in sequence, each reducing by one-eighth part from the length of the <term>pradeshini</term>. The height of the big toe is said to be one and a quarter angulas; the height of the other toes should be understood according to this proportion.

19. Those who know the characteristics of icons have stated the length of the big toe's nail to be three-quarters of an angula, and the length of the nails of the remaining toes should be half an angula each, or they may be slightly reduced in sequence so that the toes and nails appear beautiful.

20. The thickness of the front part of the shank is fourteen angulas and its width is said to be five angulas. The width of the middle part of the shank is seven angulas and its thickness is said to be twenty-one angulas.

21. The width of the middle of the knee is eight angulas and its thickness is twenty-four angulas. The thighs are fourteen angulas wide at the middle, and their circumference is twenty-eight angulas.

22. The width of the waist is eighteen angulas and the circumference of the waist is forty-four angulas. The width and the depth of the navel are each one angula.

23. Taking the navel as the center, the circumference of the middle region is forty-two angulas. The distance between the two breasts is sixteen angulas, and above the breasts, the armpits are six angulas each diagonally.

24. The length of the shoulders starting from the neck should be kept at eight angulas. It is proper to make the upper arms and the forearms twelve angulas long each. The width of the upper arm should be six angulas and that of the forearm four angulas.

25. At the base of the upper arm, the circumference should be sixteen angulas, and near the <term>prakoshtha</term> (wrist), it should be twelve angulas. The width of the palm should be six angulas and the length seven angulas.

26. The finger next to the thumb is the <term>pradeshini</term> (index), the one after that is the <term>madhyama</term> (middle), the one after that is the <term>anamika</term> (ring), and the finger after the ring finger is called the <term>kanishtha</term> (little). Each finger has three <term>pauruve</term> (phalanges/joints). The middle finger should be made five angulas long. If half of the middle phalanx of the middle finger is subtracted, that is the length of the index finger...

# Chapter 58 (213)
## With Hindi Commentary

The <term>ring finger</term> <note>original: "Anamika"</note> should be equal in length to the index finger. By reducing the length of the ring finger by one <term>phalange</term> <note>original: "Pauruva"; the segments of a finger</note>, the length of the little finger is determined. ||27|| The <term>thumb</term> should be made with two <term>phalanges</term>, and the remaining four fingers should each have three <term>phalanges</term>. The length of the nails on all fingers should be equal to half of their respective <term>joints</term> <note>original: "Parva"</note>. ||28||

The ornaments, dress, decorations, and physical form of the idol should be crafted according to the customs of one's own region. A deity resides in an idol endowed with the correct scriptural characteristics; therefore, such an idol brings all kinds of prosperity to its maker. ||29||

The idol of Lord Rama, the son of Dasharatha, and Bali, the son of Virochana, should be made one hundred and twenty <term>digits</term> <note>original: "Angul"; a traditional unit of measurement based on finger-width</note> long. Generally, an idol of one hundred and eight <term>digits</term> is considered excellent, ninety-six <term>digits</term> is medium, and eighty-four <term>digits</term> is considered inferior.

The idol of Lord Vishnu should be made with <term>eight arms</term>, <term>four arms</term>, or <term>two arms</term>. The chest of the idol should be adorned with the mark known as <term>Srivatsa</term> <note>a symbolic mark on the chest of Vishnu</note> and the <term>Kaustubha gem</term>. ||30||31||

The color of the idol should be like the flower of the flax plant <note>original: "Atasi"; a deep blue or violet hue</note>, and it should be dressed in yellow garments. The idol should have a cheerful face and wear earrings and a crown. In the three right hands of the eight-armed form, place a sword, a mace, and an arrow; the fourth hand should be made in the gesture of granting peace, known as the <term>Abhaya Mudra</term> <note>the "fear-not" hand gesture</note>. In the four left hands, place a bow, a shield, a discus, and a conch. ||32||33||

If one wishes to make a <term>four-armed</term> idol, one right hand should be in the gesture of granting peace (boon-giving) and the other should hold a mace. In the lower left hand, place a conch, and in the other, a discus. ||34||

For a <term>two-armed</term> idol, the right hand should be in the peace-giving gesture and the left hand should hold a conch. Men desiring prosperity should fashion the idol of Vishnu in this manner. ||35||

The idol of Baladeva <note>Balarama</note> should hold a plow in his hand, and his eyes should be made rolling as if from intoxication. He should wear earrings in his ears. The color of the idol should be white like a conch, the moon, or a <term>lotus stalk</term> <note>original: "Mrinal"</note>. ||36||

Between the idols of Baladeva and Krishna, one should place an idol of the goddess Nanda <note>Ekanansha</note>, with her left hand placed on her hip and her right hand holding a lotus. ||37||

If a <term>four-armed</term> idol of <term>Ekanansha</term> is made, she should hold a book and a lotus in her two <term>left hands</term>, and in her two right hands, she should hold a rosary and grant boons to seekers. ||38||

In the <term>eight-armed</term> form of <term>Ekanansha</term>, the four left hands should hold a water-pot, a bow, a lotus, and a book; the four right hands should hold the <term>gesture of boons</term>, an arrow, a mirror, and a <term>rosary</term> <note>original: "Akshasutra"</note>. ||39||

The idol of Samba should hold a mace, and the idol of Pradyumna should hold a bow and arrow. Both these idols should be <term>two-armed</term> and made with beautiful forms. The idols of the wives of Samba and Pradyumna should be made holding shields. ||40||

The idol of Brahma should hold a water-pot in one hand, have four faces, and be seated on a lotus-shaped throne. The idol of Kartikeya should be in the form of a youth, holding a <term>spear</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> in his hand and a banner featuring a peacock. ||41||

The idol of Indra's elephant, Airavata, should be white and have four tusks. The idol of Indra should hold a <term>thunderbolt</term> <note>original: "Vajra"</note> in his hand and have a third eye placed horizontally in the middle of his forehead; this is the identifying mark of that idol. ||42||

The idol of Lord Shiva should bear a <term>crescent moon</term> on his head, have the symbol of a <term>bull</term> <note>original: "Vrish"</note> on his banner, and a vertical third eye on his forehead. He should hold a trident in one hand and the bow named <term>Pinaka</term> in the other. Alternatively, the left half of Shiva's idol may be made as the left half of Parvati <note>referring to the Ardhanarishvara form</note>. ||43||

The hands and feet of the idol of Lord Buddha should be marked with lotus lines; the idol should be serene, with hair hanging down, and such a Buddha—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of iconography and the proportions of divine images from the Varāhamihira Saṃhitā (Bṛhat Saṃhitā). It follows previous descriptions of celestial beings and focuses here on specific deities and the consequences of improper craftsmanship.</meta>

# The Varāhamihira Saṃhitā
## Chapter 58: Characteristics of Divine Images

The image <note>original: "pratima" - a consecrated icon or statue</note> should appear as if it were the manifest Father of the World <note>referring to Brahma</note>, seated upon a lotus throne. **(44)** One should fashion the image of the Lord Arhat <note>original: "Arhantadeva" - a Jain Tirthankara</note> with arms reaching down to the knees, adorned with the Shrivatsa mark <note>a sacred symbol on the chest</note>, possessing a peaceful countenance, sky-clad <note>original: "digambara" - naked, specifically referring to the Digambara Jain tradition</note>, youthful, and endowed with excellent form. **(45)**

For the image of the Sun <note>Surya</note>, the nose, forehead, shins, thighs, cheeks, and chest should be made prominent. The attire of the Sun’s image should be made according to the fashion of the people of the Northern lands; from the feet up to the chest, the image should be covered by a garment <note>original: "cholaka" - a tunic or vestment typical of Central Asian influence on Surya iconography</note>. **(46)** He should be made to hold two lotuses with their stems in both arms, wear a crown, have his face adorned with earrings, wear a long necklace around his neck, and have a girdle <note>original: "vihanga" or "sarasan"</note> wrapped around his waist. **(47)**

The luster of the face should be like the inner glow of a lotus. The image should be covered by a bodice <note>original: "kanchuka"</note>, and the face should appear joyful with a gentle smile. A Sun image whose collection of rays is as radiant as jewels brings auspiciousness to its makers. **(48)** A Sun image one cubit high is auspicious; two cubits high bestows wealth; three cubits high brings safety, and four cubits high ensures a plentiful harvest. **(49)**

An image with extra limbs causes fear of the king; one with missing limbs keeps the maker diseased; one with a thin belly causes fear of hunger; and the destruction of wealth follows the making of an image with emaciated limbs. **(50)** Death by a weapon should be predicted for the maker of a scarred or damaged image. An image leaning to the left destroys the maker's wife, and one leaning to the right destroys his lifespan. **(51)** If the gaze of the image is directed upward, the maker may go blind; if the Sun's gaze is directed downward, the maker will suffer anxiety. These are the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of the Sun's image; similar results should be understood for the images of other deities as well. **(52)**

Measuring the circumference of the circular Linga <note>the symbolic form of Shiva</note> in length with a thread, one should divide that thread into three parts. Divide the Linga itself into three equal parts accordingly: the middle third of the Linga should be octagonal <note>original: "astasra"</note> and the top third should be made round. **(53)** The square bottom portion of the Linga should be buried in the earth; the middle octagonal portion should be placed within the cavity of the pedestal <note>original: "pindika" or "jalahari"</note>; the remaining third circular portion should remain above. A pedestal should be fashioned on all four sides of the cavity, equal in height to the visible circular portion of the Linga. **(54)**

A thin and long Shiva-linga destroys the country; one that is deficient on both sides destroys the city. A Linga that has a wound or crack on its head destroys its master. **(55)**

The Divine Mothers <note>original: "Matrigana"</note> should be fashioned with the same characteristic marks as the gods of their respective names: for example, the form of Brahmi should be like Brahma, Indrani like Indra, and so on. However, their breasts and other features should be fashioned so that the female form is beautifully rendered. The image of Revanta <note>a son of Surya</note> should be shown mounted on a horse, with a retinue depicted as if engaged in a hunt. **(56)**

The image of Yama <note>God of Death</note> should hold a staff in his hand and be mounted on a buffalo. The image of Varuna <note>God of the Waters</note> should be mounted on a swan and hold a noose. The image of Kubera <note>God of Wealth</note> should be mounted on a man, wear a crown tilted to the left, and have a large belly. **(57)**

The image of Ganapati <note>Ganesha</note> should have the face of an elephant and a long belly; he should hold an axe in his hand, be shown with a single tusk, and hold a radish root <note>original: "mulakakanda"</note> and a blue lotus root. **(58)**

-> Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the venerable teacher Varahamihira. **(58)** <-

# Now begins the Fifty-Ninth Chapter

## Entering the Forest

On a day favorable to the craftsman, at an auspicious moment purified by the astrologer, and observing the lucky omens and signs prescribed for a journey, the entry into the forest should take place. ||1||

Trees growing in the following places must be avoided: along the path to a cemetery, near temples, by anthills, in pleasure gardens, within the hermitages of ascetics, at <term>Chaityas</term> <note>sacred spots or shrines marked by a tree or monument</note>, at the confluence of rivers, or those nourished by water from jars. ||2||

Also to be avoided are trees that are stunted, those grown into or suppressed by creepers, those struck by lightning or broken by the wind, those fallen of their own accord or crushed by elephants, and those that are withered, scorched by fire, or serve as a <term>Madhunnilaya</term> <note>original: "मधुन्निलय" - a dwelling for honeybees/beehives</note>. ||3||

Such trees should be rejected. Those with glossy leaves, flowers, and fruits are auspicious. Having approached the desired tree, one should perform a worship service with offerings and flowers. ||4||

Trees such as Deodar <note>Himalayan Cedar</note>, Sandalwood, Shami, and Madhuka are auspicious for the <term>Brahmin</term> <note>priestly</note> class. For the <term>Kshatriya</term> <note>warrior/ruling</note> class, Arishta, Ashvattha, Khadira, and Bilva bring prosperity. ||5||

For the <term>Vaishya</term> <note>merchant/farmer</note> class, Jivaka, Khadira, Sindhuka, and Syandana yield auspicious results. For the <term>Shudra</term> <note>laborer</note> class, Tinduka, Kesara, Sarja, Arjuna, Mango, and Shala are recommended. ||6||

Because a <term>Linga</term> or an image must be installed in the same orientation as the tree stood, one must mark the directions on the tree—the top and the bottom—before it is felled. ||7||

Having worshipped the tree with offerings of <term>Paramanna</term> <note>rice boiled in milk/kheer</note>, sweetmeats, boiled rice, curd, sesame-meat preparations, cakes, wine, flowers, incense, and perfumes; ||8||

And having performed worship at night to the Gods, Ancestors, Pishachas, Rakshasas, Nagas, Asuras, Ganas, Vinayaka, and others, one should touch the tree and say: ||9||

"O Tree! You have been chosen for the making of an image of such-and-such a Deity. Salutations to you! Please accept this worship performed according to the sacred rites." ||10||

"May those spirits who dwell here, having accepted this duly offered sacrifice, take up residence elsewhere. May they forgive us today; salutations to them!" ||11||

In the morning, after sprinkling the tree with water and smearing the axe with honey and clarified butter, one should begin cutting from the northeast, moving in a clockwise direction. ||12||

If the tree falls toward the East, Northeast, or North, it brings prosperity. If it falls toward the Southeast and subsequent directions, it results in fire, famine, disease, and the loss of horses. ||13||

Whatever has not been mentioned here regarding the entry into the forest—such as the omens of the fall, the cuts, or the hollows in the tree—I have previously explained in the chapters on Indra's Banner and Architecture; those rules should be applied here as well. ||14||

**Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Entering the Forest," in the Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira.**

[Hindi Commentary Summary]: The sculptor should enter the forest on an auspicious day and hour determined by an astrologer. Trees from cemeteries, temples, or those damaged by nature (lightning, wind, fire) or inhabited by bees must be avoided. Specific trees are assigned to the four social classes (Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras). Ritual offerings must be made to the spirits inhabiting the tree to ask them to relocate before the tree is cut with a consecrated axe.

These are auspicious; that is, a Brahmin should fashion divine images from their wood. The Neem, Peepal, Khair <note>Acacia catechu</note>, and Bel trees are those that bring growth and prosperity to the Kshatriyas (the warrior/ruling class) ||5||. The Jīvaka, Khair, Sindhuka, and Syandana trees give auspicious results to the Vaishyas (the merchant class). The Tendu, Nagkeshar, Sarja, Arjun, and Sal trees are auspicious for the Shudras (the laboring class) ||6||. One should install the *lingam* <note>a symbolic representation of Shiva</note> or the statue according to the original directions of the tree; in the same way, the feet of the statue should be fashioned from the upper part of the tree. For this reason, before cutting, it is proper to mark the four directions and the upper and lower sections of the tree ||7||. One should worship the tree with offerings of rice-pudding, sweets, cooked rice, *ullopika* <note>a specific type of traditional food preparation</note>, and other edibles, along with wine, flowers, incense, and perfumes ||8||. After worshipping the Gods, Ancestors, Pishachas, Rakshasas, Nagas, Asuras, and Vinayakas <note>various classes of divine and supernatural beings</note> at night, one should touch the tree and recite this mantra ||9||: "O Tree! You have been chosen for the worship of [Name of Deity], I bow to you. Please accept this worship according to the sacred rites. May the beings who dwell upon this tree accept this ritual worship and find residence elsewhere. May they forgive me today; I bow to them." In place of "[Name of Deity]," one should use the name of the specific god in the genitive case ||10||11||. At dawn, one should water the tree, smear the axe with honey and ghee <note>clarified butter</note>, and then first strike the tree with that axe in the Northeast corner, thereafter cutting the remainder of the tree in a clockwise direction ||12||. If the felled tree falls toward the East, Northeast, or North, it brings prosperity; if it falls in the five directions starting with the Southeast, the results are, respectively: destruction by fire, disease, and the loss of horses ||13||. In this "Chapter on Entering the Forest," whatever we have not mentioned—namely the auspicious and inauspicious results of the tree's fall, its cutting, or the "womb" of the tree—all of that we have previously described in the "Chapter on Indra's Banner" and the "Chapter on the Science of Architecture" <term>Vastu Vidya: the ancient Indian system of architecture and design</term>; they should be understood here in the same manner ||14||.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the Northwestern region, on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the Great Master Varāhamihira ||59||.

### Now Begins the Sixtieth Chapter
### The Consecration of the Image

->A wise man should construct the *mandapa* <note>a temporary ritual pavilion or hall</note> for the preliminary consecration rites in either the Northern or Eastern direction. It should be equipped with four ceremonial arches and covered with the leaves of auspicious trees ||1||. In the Eastern part of the pavilion, variegated garlands and banners are prescribed. In the Southeast, they should be "empty" <note>perhaps meaning plain or thin</note>; in the South and Southwest, they should be black ||2||. In the Western direction, they should be white; in the Northwest, they should be pale gray. On the Northern side, they should be variegated, and in the Northeast, they should be yellow ||3||. An image made of wood or clay bestows long life, prosperity, strength, and victory. For the welfare of the people, an image made of jewels is auspicious, while one made of gold brings nourishment and growth ||4||. An image made of silver brings fame; one made of copper brings the increase of progeny. An image or *lingam* made of stone brings great gain of land ||5||. An image damaged by a "pin" or "stake" <note>referring to flaws in the material or construction</note> destroys the chief man and his lineage. One damaged by a hollow or pit causes diseases and unending calamities ||6||. In the middle of the pavilion, [one should] sta-<-

# Chapter 60: The Installation of Deities

### (Page 217)

Having smeared the sacrificial altar <note>original: "sthandila"</note> with cow dung and strewn it with sand and sacred Kusha grass, the priest should place the image upon it, with its head resting on a "propitious seat" <note>a specific ritual posture or throne</note> acting as a pillow and its feet pointing toward the south. **(7)**

The image should be bathed with decoctions made from the bark of the Plaksha, Udumbara, Shirisha, and Vata trees <note>four types of sacred fig and acacia trees</note>, and with water mixed with the "auspicious" group of all-medicinal herbs. **(8)**

One must also use earth <note>mud</note> taken from the tusks of an elephant, the horns of a bull, a mountain peak, a termite mound, the confluence of rivers, and lotus ponds, along with the five products of the cow <note>milk, curd, ghee, urine, and dung</note> and water from sacred pilgrimage sites. **(9)**

The image, facing east, should be bathed with water containing gold and gems, accompanied by fragrances, the sounding of various musical instruments, the chanting of "Auspicious Day!" <note>original: "punyaha"</note>, and the resonance of the Vedas. **(10)**

In the eastern direction, the chief Brahmins should mutter hymns addressed to Indra; in the south-east, hymns addressed to Agni. These priests must be honored with sacrificial fees. **(11)**

The Brahmin should offer oblations into the fire using the specific hymns belonging to the deity being installed. I have already described the omens related to the fire in the chapter on the "Raising of Indra's Banner." **(12)**

If the fire is choked with smoke, swirls to the left <note>counter-clockwise</note>, or repeatedly throws out sparks, it is not auspicious. A lapse in the memory of the priest or his stumbling is also declared to be inauspicious. **(13)**

After the bath, the installer should clothe the image in new garments, adorn it, worship it with flowers and perfumes, and place it upon a well-spread bed. **(14)**

After the deity has "slept" <note>a ritual rest</note> and been kept awake with beautiful dances, songs, and vigils, the installation should take place at the exact time prescribed by the astrologer. **(15)**

Having worshipped the image with flowers, clothes, and ointments to the sound of conchs and trumpets, one should carefully lead it around the temple in a clockwise direction. **(16)**

After making a grand offering <note>original: "bali"</note> and honoring the Brahmins and the assembled guests, a piece of gold should be placed in the cavity of the pedestal before the image is set. **(17)**

By specifically honoring the installer, the astrologer, the Brahmins, the assembly, and the architect, the patrons become sharers of blessings in this world and attain heaven in the next. **(18)**

The devotees of Vishnu <note>Bhagavatas</note> should install Vishnu; the Magas <note>sun-priests</note> should install the Sun; those who wear sacred ashes should install Shiva; those who know the "Circle of the Mothers" <note>original: "mandalakrama"</note> should install the Mother Goddesses; and Brahmins should install Brahma. The followers of the Buddha <note>original: "Shakyas"</note>, who are peaceful in mind, should install the Buddha, the friend of all; and the "Naked Ones" <note>Jains</note> should install the Jinas. Each deity should be installed by those who follow their specific traditional rites. **(19)**

The installation of deities is best performed during the northern transit of the sun, in the bright fortnight, when the moon is auspicious and Jupiter is in a favorable sign. **(20)**

It should be done during a fixed ascendant <note>Lagna</note> or a fixed division, with benefic planets in the 5th, 9th, or center houses, and malefic planets in the 3rd, 6th, or 11th houses, under stable, soft, or short constellations, on a day other than Tuesday. **(21)**

I have composed this general summary for the benefit of the people. The details regarding the preliminary consecration and the placement of the image have been described extensively by Savitra. **(22)**

---

### Thus ends the Sixtieth Chapter, titled "The Installation of Deities," in the Brihat Samhita by Shri Varahamihira.

...destroys both the man and his lineage. If an idol has a hollow or a pit, it causes incurable diseases and various types of calamities. ||6||

In the center of the <term>Adhivasa</term> <note>preliminary consecration</note> pavilion, one should prepare a <term>Sthandila</term> <note>a leveled square piece of ground for a sacrificial fire</note>, plaster it with cow dung and other materials, spread sand over it, and place Kusha grass upon the sand. The idol should then be laid down upon it. The head of the idol should be placed upon a <term>Bhadrasana</term> <note>a royal throne or auspicious seat</note> and the feet of the idol should be placed upon a pillow or bolster. ||7||

One should prepare <term>Kashayajala</term> <note>astringent water made from decoctions</note> using the leaves of the Pakar, Peepal, Gular, Siris, and Banyan trees. Along with Kusha grass, one should use auspiciously named herbs such as Jaya, Punarnava, and Vishnu-kanta. ||8||

Earth dug up by an elephant and a bull, earth from lotus-filled ponds, and water from holy pilgrimage sites mixed with <term>Panchagavya</term> <note>the five products of the cow: milk, curd, ghee, urine, and dung</note> ||9||

And water containing gold and jewels—with all of these, one should bathe the idol. It should be installed with its head facing the East while various musical instruments like trumpets are played, and Brahmins perform the <term>Punyahavachana</term> <note>recitation of prayers for an auspicious day</note> and chant the Vedas. ||10||

Excellent Brahmins should chant the mantras of Indra in the East and the mantras of Agni in the South-East corner; the patron should worship those Brahmins with sacrificial fees (<term>dakshina</term>). ||11||

The Brahmin should perform the fire sacrifice (<term>havan</term>) with the mantras of whichever deity is being installed. We have already described the auspicious and inauspicious signs of the fire in the <term>Indradhwajadhyaya</term> <note>The Chapter on Indra's Banner</note>. ||12||

If, at the time of the sacrifice, the fire is choked with smoke, its flame turns to the left, it makes frequent noises, or sparks fly from it, then it is not auspicious. It is also inauspicious if the one performing the sacrifice loses his memory (forgets the mantras) or if he slips or moves from the place where he sat to perform the sacrifice. ||13||

After bathing the idol, it should be dressed in new clothes, adorned with ornaments and such, and worshipped with flowers and perfumes. The person performing the installation should then place the idol upon a well-prepared bed. ||14||

Having thus performed the <term>Adhivasa</term> of the reclining idol with vigils including dance and song, one should install it at the auspicious moment (<term>muhurta</term>) indicated by the astrologer. ||15||

Having worshipped the idol with flowers, clothes, and sandalwood paste, it should be lifted from the consecration pavilion, carried clockwise around the temple, and carefully taken into the <term>Garbhagriha</term> <note>the "womb-chamber" or innermost sanctum</note>. At that time, conches, trumpets, and other instruments should be played. ||16||

Going there, after offering many sacrifices, one should worship the Brahmins and the "Sabhyas" (the respectable men present in the assembly) with clothes and gifts. A piece of gold should be placed in the pit of the <term>Pindika</term> <note>the pedestal or base</note>, and the idol should be installed upon it. ||17||

One should especially worship the installer, the astrologer, the Brahmins, and the craftsmen. In this way, the man who performs the <term>Devapratishtha</term> <note>consecration of a deity</note> partakes in blessings in this world and attains a place in heaven in the afterlife. ||18||

The installation of Vishnu should be done by <term>Bhagavatas</term> (Vaishnavas); the installation of the Sun by <term>Magas</term> <note>Brahmins originally from Shakadvipa</note>; the installation of Shiva by ash-wearing Brahmins (Pashupatas); the installation of the Matrikas (Mother Goddesses) like Brahmi by those who know the sequence of the Mandala (circle of worship); the installation of Brahma by Vedic Brahmins; the installation of the "All-Benevolent" Buddha by the calm-minded <term>Shakyas</term> <note>Buddhist monks, often identified by red robes</note>; and the installation of the Jinas by <term>Namans</term> <note>Digambara Jain monks</note>. Whichever deity a man is a devoted follower of, he should perform all the rites of installation for that deity according to the specific rules of his own sect. ||19||

It should be during the <term>Uttarayana</term> <note>the northern transit of the sun</note>, in the bright half of the month, when the Moon is in the <term>Shadvarga</term> <note>six divisions of a sign</note> of Jupiter, in a fixed Ascendant and a fixed Navamsha, and when gentle planets are in the 5th, 9th, 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses. ||20||

Malefic planets should be in the 3rd, 6th, 10th, and 11th houses. The constellations should be either of the two Uttaras, Rohini, Mrigashira, Revati, Chitra, Anuradha, Shravana...

# Now Begins the Sixty-First Chapter
## Characteristics of Cows

The sage Parashara spoke to Brihadratha regarding the characteristics of cows; that which was said is presented here. I shall describe in summary those auspicious signs, following the traditional scriptures. || 1 || Cows that have tearful, dull, or dry eyes, or eyes like a mouse, are not givers of auspiciousness. So too are those with shaking or flat horns, those of a variegated color, or those whose color resembles that of a donkey. || 2 || Those with ten, seven, or four teeth; those with long, drooping heads or sunken backs; those with short, thick necks; those whose bodies are shaped like a barley-corn (thick in the middle); and those with cracked hooves [are inauspicious]. || 3 || Those with dark-gray or excessively long tongues; those with very small or very large and heavy ankles; those with an oversized hump or a wasted body; and those with missing or extra limbs are not desired. || 4 ||

A bull is likewise inauspicious if it has thick and excessively long testicles, or a chest covered in prominent veins. One with a thick head, swollen cheeks, or one who urinates in three streams [is also rejected]. || 5 || A bull with eyes like a cat, or one that is tawny or variegated, is not auspicious for a Brahmin <note>the priestly class</note>. One with a black lip, palate, and tongue, who breathes like a dog, is a destroyer of the herd. || 6 || One with a thick, bird-like penis, a white belly, and the color of a black antelope—even if born in one's own home—such a bull should be abandoned as it brings destruction to the herd. || 7 || A bull whose body is covered in dark-gray spots, or one that looks like reddish-ash and has cat-like eyes, does not bring good fortune even to Brahmins if accepted. || 8 || Those that lift their feet as if they are lame when yoked, have weak necks, glassy eyes, or are stunted in their hindquarters, are not capable of bearing loads. || 9 ||

[Conversely], those with soft, well-formed, copper-colored lips; thin, firm buttocks; and copper-colored palates and tongues [are auspicious]. Those with thin, short, and high-set ears; well-shaped bellies; and clearly defined shanks; || 10 || those with reddish, well-knit hooves; broad chests; large humps; glossy, smooth skin and hair; and copper-colored horns; || 11 || those with thin eyebrows and tails; eyes with reddish corners; great breath capacity; shoulders like a lion; and thin, small dewlaps—these are honored and move gracefully. || 12 || Bulls that have hair-whorls turning to the left on their left side and to the right on their right side are givers of prosperity, especially those with shanks resembling those of a deer. || 13 || Those with eyes like beryl, jasmine, or bubbles, with thick eyelids and uncracked heels, are all praised as excellent load-bearers. || 14 || One with wrinkles on the nose, a face like a forest-dweller (monkey), white on the right side, the color of a red or blue lotus or lac, and a tail like a fine cloth, possesses speed like a horse. || 15 || One with hanging testicles, a belly like a sheep, and a compact chest and groin, should be known as capable of enduring long journeys with loads; in speed, he is equal to a horse and yields auspicious results. || 16 || A bull of white color, with yellowish eyes, copper-colored horns and eyes, and a large face, is named "Hansa" (Swan); he is said to bring auspicious results and increase the herd. || 17 ||

We now summarize the characteristics of cows as told by the sage Parashara to his disciple Brihadratha, drawing from that text. Although all cows are generally considered auspicious, the scriptures describe their specific favorable and unfavorable marks. || 1 ||
Cows whose eyes are filled with tears, are cloudy, or appear dry are not auspicious. Those with eyes like a mouse are also not favorable, nor are those whose horns are loose or flat. A cow whose color is a mix of black and red, or resembles the color of a donkey, is likewise inauspicious. || 2 ||
A cow is not auspicious if she has ten, seven, or four teeth in her mouth; if her face is overly long or "munda" <term>Munda: hornless or blunt-headed</term>; if her back is hunched; if her neck is short and thick; if her middle section is shaped like a barley corn <note>meaning excessively thick in the center</note>; if her hooves are badly cracked; if her navel is dark and very long; if her dewlaps are either too small or too large; if her hump is excessively high; if her body remains perpetually thin; or if any limb is missing or extra. || 3 || 4 ||
A bull possessing the aforementioned traits is also inauspicious. Furthermore, one with thick and very long testicles, a chest covered in prominent veins, or cheeks covered in thick veins is unfavorable. Also avoided is a bull that "excretes from three places" <note>original: "tri-sthana-mehana"</note>, meaning tears drip from both eyes while urine falls from the penis simultaneously. || 5 ||
A bull with eyes like a cat, or one that is a tawny or brownish-red color, is not auspicious even for a Brahmin <note>the priestly class</note>, let alone for other castes. One whose lips, palate, and tongue are black, and a bull that is "shvasana" <note>fearful or panting heavily</note>, brings destruction to his herd. || 6 ||
Even if born in one's own home, a bull should be discarded if its dung, the tip of its penis, and its horns are thick, if it has a white belly, and if its body color is a mixture of black and white; such a beast also destroys the herd. || 7 ||
A bull whose body is covered in black flower-like spots and has eyes like a cat will not be auspicious, even if accepted by Brahmins. || 8 ||
Bulls that lift their feet under a load as if they are struggling to pull them out of deep mud are undesirable. Those with weak necks, glassy eyes, or short or sunken backs are not capable of carrying loads. || 9 ||
Those with soft, well-joined lips of a copper hue, small haunches <term>Sphik: the fleshy part of the hips</term>, a copper-colored palate and tongue, and ears that are small, thin, and high-set are excellent. They should have a handsome belly and straight thighs. || 10 ||
Bulls are good if they have copper-colored, well-joined hooves, a firm chest, a large hump, and skin and hair that are glossy, soft, and thin. Their body and horns should also be copper-colored. || 11 ||
Those with thin tails that touch the ground, whose inner corners of the eyes are red, who take deep breaths, have shoulders like a lion, a thin and small dewlap, and a graceful gait are considered superior bulls. || 12 ||
Bulls are auspicious if they have hair-whorls <term>Avarta: a natural cowlick or circular pattern of hair</term> that turn to the left on their left side and to the right on their right side, and whose thighs resemble those of a ram. || 13 ||
Those whose eyes are like the Vaidurya gem <note>Chrysoberyl or Cat's eye stone</note> <unclear>...</unclear>

Those bulls whose eyes resemble the *Nivari* flower <note>original: "नवारीपुष्प" - likely a reference to a white jasmine-like flower</note>, meaning they have white lines surrounding the outer edges of the eyes; those whose eyes resemble water bubbles; those with thick eyes and bodies; and those whose rear hooves are not cracked—all such bulls are auspicious and capable of carrying heavy loads. || 14 || A bull that has folds on its nose, a face like a cat, a white right side, a complexion like a blue lotus or red lac, a fine tail, and the speed of a horse in its gait || 15 || with long testicles, a belly like a ram, and whose <term>Vankshana</term> (the middle part between the hind thighs and the testicles) and <term>Kroda</term> (the middle part between the front thighs) are compact—such a bull is capable of carrying loads and traveling long distances. A bull with the speed of a horse is always auspicious. || 16 || A bull that is white in color, with copper-colored horns and eyes and a large mouth, is called a 'Hamsa' (Swan); it is auspicious and increases the size of its herd. || 17 || A bull whose tail touches the ground, who has copper-colored horns, red eyes, and is endowed with a <term>Kakuda</term> (hump) soon makes its owner wealthy. || 18 || Regardless of its body color, a bull with four white feet is auspicious. If a bull with exclusively auspicious marks cannot be found, one may choose a bull of mixed results—that is, one with both auspicious and inauspicious marks—provided the auspicious marks are more numerous. || 19 ||

### Now Begins the Sixty-Second Chapter
#### Characteristics of Dogs

> A dog that has five claws on three of its feet, but six claws on the front right foot; whose lips and the tip of the nose are copper-red; who moves with the gait of a lion and walks sniffing the ground; whose tail is bushy with hair; whose eyes resemble those of a bear; and whose ears are long and soft—such a dog quickly brings abundant prosperity to the home of its master. || 1 || A female dog that has five claws on each foot except the front left foot, which has six claws; who has white rings around the eyes like the *Mallika* flower; who has a curved tail, a reddish-brown (tawny) color, and long ears—such a female dog protects the kingdom of its master. || 2 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "Characteristics of Dogs," in the Brihat Samhita by Shri Varahamihira. || 62 ||

A dog that has five claws on three of its feet and six claws on the front right foot; whose lips and the tip of the nose are red like copper; whose gait is like a lion's and who walks while sniffing the earth; whose tail is very bushy with hair; who has eyes like a bear and ears that are long and soft—such a dog increases the wealth in the house of the master who feeds it. || 1 || A female dog that has five claws on three of its feet and six claws on the front left foot; who has white lines outside the eyes like the *Mallika* flower; whose tail is crooked; who is tawny in color and has long ears—such a female dog protects the kingdom of the one who nourishes her. || 2 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Hindi commentary on the Brihat Samhita composed by Acharya Varahamihira, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. || 62 ||

# Chapter 63
## Characteristics of Roosters

A <term>rooster</term><note>Sanskrit: kukkuta</note> that has straight feathers and toes, with a face, nails, and crest as red as copper, and is white in color, is auspicious. One who crows with a pleasant voice at the end of the night <note>dawn</note> brings about the growth of the king, the kingdom, and the horses. || 1 || A bird whose neck is shaped like a grain of barley, or whose red color is like a ripe jujube fruit, who has a large head, and is beautiful with many colors <note>such as white, yellow, red, and black</note>, is considered excellent for battle. One whose color is like honey or like a black bee also brings victory in war. Any rooster other than these is not auspicious; specifically, one with a thin body, a weak voice, or a lame foot is not favorable. || 2 || And a hen who makes soft and beautiful sounds, has a glossy body, and beautiful face and eyes—such a hen grants kings long-lasting wealth, fame, victory, strength, and prosperity. || 3 ||

**Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "Characteristics of Roosters," in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā composed by Śrī Varāhamihira. || 63 ||**

->Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the Hindi commentary composed by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, inhabitant of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Bṛhat Saṃhitā composed by the great teacher Śrī Varāhamihira. || 63 ||<-

# Chapter 64
## Characteristics of Turtles

A <term>turtle</term><note>Sanskrit: kūrma</note> that is the color of crystal or silver, variegated with blue streaks, shaped like a water-pot, and possesses a beautiful back-bone <note>the ridge of the shell</note> is auspicious. Or one whose body is like the dawn <note>reddish</note> and speckled with marks the size of mustard seeds, brings greatness to all kings when kept in the palace. || 1 || One whose body is dark like kohl or a black bee, variegated with spots, and has a body free of defects, a head like a serpent, and a thick neck—he also leads to the expansion of the kingdom for kings. || 2 || One with the luster of a cat's eye gem, a thick neck, a triangular shape, hidden orifices, and a beautiful back-bone is praised. For the sake of auspiciousness, kings should keep such a turtle in a pleasure-pond or a vessel filled with water. || 3 ||

**Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Turtles," in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā composed by Śrī Varāhamihira. || 64 ||**

# Chapter 65 with Hindi Commentary

A tortoise that is white like crystal or silver, marked with blue lines, shaped like a water-pot, possessing a beautiful spine, or one that is red and speckled with spots like mustard seeds—if such a <term>Kurma</term><note>Sanskrit: tortoise</note> resides in a house, it brings greatness among all kings. || 1 || A tortoise whose body is dark like kohl or a black bee, variegated with spots, with all limbs fully formed, a head like a snake, and a thick neck—such a tortoise serves to increase the kingdom of kings. || 2 || A tortoise with the luster of a <term>Vaidurya</term><note>Cat's eye gem or chrysoberyl</note> gem, a thick neck, a triangular shape, whose orifices are hidden, and who has a beautiful spine—a king should keep such a tortoise in his pleasure-pool or in a large pot filled with water for the sake of auspiciousness. || 3 ||

### Now, the Sixty-Fifth Chapter
->Signs of Goats<-

I shall now describe the auspicious and inauspicious signs of goats. Those with nine, ten, or eight teeth in their mouths are blessed and should be kept in the home; those with seven teeth should be discarded as they are inauspicious. || 1 || A black circular mark on the right side of a white goat brings auspicious results. For those goats that are the color of a deer, or are black or red, a white mark is also a giver of good fortune. || 2 || The fleshy protuberance that hangs from the throat of goats like a nipple is known as a <term>Mani</term><note>Literally "jewel," referring here to the throat wattles of a goat</note>. One such wattle brings auspicious results; those with two or three wattles are considered most blessed. || 3 || All hornless goats are givers of good, as are those that are entirely white or entirely black. Those that are half-black and half-white, or half-brown and half-black, are also blessed. || 4 || The goat that walks at the head of the herd and is the first to enter the water is auspicious; so too is one with a white head, or one who has a <term>Kruttika</term><note>A mark resembling the Pleiades star cluster</note> mark on its head. || 5 || One with flower-like marks on the throat or head, or one colored like sesame paste with copper-colored eyes, is praised. So is a white goat with black legs, or a black goat with white legs. || 6 || A white goat with black testicles and a black band around its middle, or one that walks with a sound and moves slowly, is a beautiful and good goat. || 7 || One with hair and legs like a deer, or one who is pale in the front and blue/dark in the rear, is a goat that brings good fortune. On this subject, there is also a verse spoken by <term>Garga</term><note>An ancient sage and authority on omens</note>: || 8 || The "Striker" (<term>Kuttaka</term>), the "Crooked" (<term>Kutila</term>), the "Matted" (<term>Jatila</term>), and the "Dwarf" (<term>Vamana</term>)—these four are the sons of Prosperity; they truly do not dwell where Misfortune resides. || 9 || Now, the unpraiseworthy: those with a voice like a donkey, those with glowing/red tails, those with bad nails, those of dull color, those with clipped ears, those with heads like elephants, and those with black palates and tongues. || 10 || Those goats endowed with praised colors and wattles, the hornless ones, and those with copper-colored eyes—when honored in the homes of men, they create happiness, fame, and prosperity. || 11 ||

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "Signs of Goats," in the Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira. || 65 ||

Do not keep those with seven teeth because they are inauspicious. || 1 || If there is a black circle on the right side of a white-colored goat, it is auspicious. For a goat...

If the color of a goat is blue-black like a deer, black, or red, then a white circle on its right side is also auspicious. || 2 || The fleshy growth hanging from the necks of goats, similar to a teat, is called a *mani* <note>literally "jewel" or "pendant"</note>. # Now begins the Sixty-Sixth Chapter
## Characteristics of Horses

> A horse with a long neck, eyes, and chest; broad loins, heart, and forehead; thin skin, hair, and tail; beautiful hooves, gait, and mouth; short ears, lips, and tail-bone; rounded shanks, knees, and thighs; and even, white teeth—such a horse, perfect in all limbs, always leads to the destruction of a king's enemies. || 1 || Whorls of hair <note>natural hair patterns/cowlicks used for divination</note> located on the tear-ducts, jaw, cheeks, heart, eyes, throat, temples, waist, bladder, or knees are inauspicious. Similarly, they are inauspicious on the scrotum, navel, hump, anus, or the left flank. || 2 || Those whorls located on the upper lip, throat, or ears, or situated in the middle of the back or above the eyes, are very auspicious, as are those on the lips, thighs, arms, belly, and sides, including the forehead. || 3 || Among these, there is one certain whorl on the upper lip and in the hair of the forehead. There are two each on the nostrils, the temples, the head, and the chest. || 4 || With six teeth...

Hindi Commentary Included — Chapter 66

> A foal has teeth as white as jasmine; at two years, they turn the color of astringent juice <note>original: "kashaya" - a reddish-brown or dark hue</note>. When the central and then the outer incisors fall out and regrow, the horse is three to five years old. Following the sequence of these incisors, and counting in three-year increments, the colors change to black, yellow, and white; then they become glassy, honey-colored, or shell-like, followed by the appearance of hollows, loosening, and finally the falling out of the teeth. Know this to be the progression of age. || 5 ||

# Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Horses," in the Brihat Samhita by Shri Varahamihira. || 66 ||

A horse whose neck and <term>akshikuta</term> <note>the bony socket or orbit of the eye</note> are long; whose <term>trika</term> <note>the lower back or sacral region</note> and chest are broad; whose palate, lips, and tongue are red like copper; whose skin, mane, and tail-hair are fine; whose hooves, gait, and mouth are beautiful; and whose ears, lips, and tail-bone are small—here the word "tail" refers specifically to the central bone of the tail—is highly auspicious. A horse with rounded, even thighs, knees, and shanks, white teeth, and a beautiful form, free from any inauspicious hair-whorls, brings daily destruction to the enemies of the king who owns him. || 1 ||

It is inauspicious to have hair-whorls <note>circular patterns of hair growth, often used in divination</note> in the following places: where tears fall, the jaw, the cheeks, the heart, the throat, the <term>protha</term> <note>the lower part of the nose/snout</note>, the temples, the waist, the bladder area, the knees, the scrotum, the navel, the <term>kakuda</term> <note>the nape of the neck near the shoulders</note>, the anus, the right flank, and the feet. || 2 ||

A hair-whorl is considered auspicious if it is located on the <term>prapana</term> <note>the upper lip</note>, the throat, the ears, the middle of the back, near the eyebrows above the eyes, the lips, the hindquarters, the forelegs, the left flank, the sides, and the forehead. || 3 ||

There are ten essential hair-whorls on a horse's body known as <term>dhruvavarta</term> <note>fixed or constant whorls</note>. Among them, one whorl is on the upper lip and one on the forehead below the hair. There are two whorls each in the following four places: the <term>randhra</term> <note>the area between the flank and navel</note>, the <term>uparandhra</term> <note>just above the randhra</note>, the head, and the chest. Thus, these are the ten fixed whorls. || 4 ||

In a horse's row of teeth, if the six teeth between the two canines are white, it is a one-year-old foal. If those same six teeth are "kashaya" <note>dark reddish-brown</note> in color, it is a two-year-old horse. In both rows of teeth, the two central teeth are called <term>sandansha</term> <note>central incisors</note>; the tooth on either side of the central ones is the "middle" tooth, and the ones on the outer edges are the "end" teeth. If the central incisors fall out and regrow, the horse is four years old; if the end teeth fall out and regrow, it is five. Following the sequence of the central incisors, the age increases by three years based on color changes. This means: if <term>kalika</term> <note>black spots</note> appear on the central incisors, the horse is six; if on the middle teeth, seven; and if on the end teeth, eight. Similarly, yellow spots on the central, middle, and end teeth indicate ages nine, ten, and eleven respectively. White spots on these teeth indicate ages twelve, thirteen, and fourteen. Glassy-colored spots indicate ages fifteen, sixteen, and seventeen. Honey-colored <note>original: "maakshika"</note> spots indicate ages eighteen, nineteen, and twenty. Shell-white spots indicate twenty-one, twenty-two, and twenty-three. If hollows/pits appear in the teeth, the age is twenty-four, twenty-five, and twenty-six. If the teeth begin to loosen, the age is twenty-seven, twenty-eight, and twenty-nine. When the teeth begin to fall out—specifically, if the central incisors fall, the horse is thirty; if the middle ones fall, it is thirty-one; and...

If the last teeth fall out, the horse's life is thirty-two years; this is the maximum lifespan of horses. For this reason, the signs for knowing the stages of life up to thirty-two years have been written. || 5 ||

### Now begins the Sixty-Seventh Chapter
### The Characteristics of Elephants <note>Sanskrit: Gaja-lakshanam</note>

Those with tusks colored like honey, well-proportioned bodies, neither overweight nor weak, capable of endurance, with symmetrical limbs, a spine curved like a bow, and hindquarters like those of a boar are of the **Bhadra** <note>literally "auspicious" or "noble"</note> type. || 1 || The **Manda** <note>literally "slow" or "heavy"</note> type of elephant has a loose chest and folds around the middle, a long belly, thick skin and neck, thick flanks and root of the tail, and a gaze like that of a lion. || 2 || The **Mriga** <note>literally "deer-like" or "forest-dwelling"</note> type has a short lower lip, tail-hair, and penis; their legs, neck, teeth, trunk, and ears are also small, but their eyes are large. Those elephants possessing mixed characteristics of these three types are called **Sankirna** <note>literally "mixed" or "hybrid"</note>. || 3 || The height of a Mriga elephant is five cubits, its length is seven, and its circumference is eight cubits. For the Manda and Bhadra types, these measurements increase by one and two cubits respectively. The Sankirna elephant has no fixed measurements. || 4 || The color of the musth <note>rutting secretion</note> of a Bhadra elephant is green; that of a Manda is like the color of turmeric (yellow); the musth of a Mriga is said to be black, and that of a Sankirna elephant is of mixed colors. || 5 ||

Those with copper-colored lips, palates, and mouths; eyes like a sparrow; smooth, elevated, and sharp tusks; broad and long faces; a spine that is curved like a bow, long, hidden, and well-set; and temples shaped like a tortoise covered with thin, single hairs— || 6 || with broad ears, jaws, navels, foreheads, and private parts; with eighteen or twenty nails that are elevated like a tortoise shell; with trunks that are well-fleshed, round, and marked with three lines; with beautiful tails and musth and breath from the trunk that smells fragrant— || 7 || with long fingers <note>the "fingers" or lobes at the tip of the trunk</note> and blood-red trunk-tips; who trumpet with a sound like a water-laden cloud; and who have large, long, and round necks—such elephants are auspicious for a king. || 8 || Those that are devoid of musth, or have too many or too few nails or limbs; those that are humpbacked, dwarfed, or have tusks like a ram's horns; those whose sheath, testicles, or trunk-tip are missing; those with dark-blue, blue, spotted, or black palates— || 9 || those with very small or crooked tusks, those born without tusks <note>Matkuna</note>, impotent elephants, female elephants possessing male characteristics, and pregnant elephants—a king should send these to a foreign land, for they bring extremely unfavorable results. || 10 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, named "The Characteristics of Elephants," in the *Brihat Samhita* composed by the illustrious Varahamihira. || 67 ||

There are four types of elephants: **Bhadra**, **Manda**, **Mriga**, and **Sankirna**. Now their characteristics are described in order. Those elephants whose teeth <insert>tusks</insert> are the color of honey, whose limbs are all well-divided <note>distinct and well-proportioned</note>, whose bodies are neither too fat nor weak, who are capable (fit for work), possessed of symmetrical limbs, whose spine <term>Prishthavamsha|the backbone</term> is shaped like a bow, and whose hindquarters <term>Jaghana|the hip or pelvic region</term> are like those of a boar—those elephants belong to the **Bhadra** caste. || 1 || The **Manda** caste elephant has loose folds on the chest and middle part, a long stomach, a thick neck and skin, thick flanks <term>Kukshi|the belly or cavity of the abdomen</term> and tail-root <term>Pechaka|the root of an elephant's tail</term>, and a lion-like gaze. This is the sign of a Manda. || 2 || For **Mriga** caste elephants, the lower lip, the hair of the tail, and the penis <term>Medhra|male organ</term> are small; the legs, neck, teeth, trunk, and ears are also small, and the eyes are large. These are the signs of the Mriga. [Elephants with] mixed signs of these three castes...

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the lifespan of horses and begins a detailed classification of elephants into four types (Bhadra, Manda, Mriga, and Sankirna) based on physical dimensions, temperament, and secretions.</summary>
<keywords>elephant classification, Varahamihira, Brihat Samhita, Bhadra, Manda, Mriga, Sankirna, elephant anatomy, musth, royal omens</keywords>

--- Page 229 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse on elephant classification and begins a new chapter on human physiognomy from Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita.</meta>

<page-num>227</page-num>
<header>With Hindi Commentary, Chapter 68</header>

Those elephants that possess all the characteristics previously mentioned should be known as the **Mixed** <note>Sankirna</note> class. ||3|| The height of a **Deer-class** <note>Mriga</note> elephant is five cubits <note>hatha: a traditional unit of length, approx. 18 inches</note>, its length from the base of the tail to the frontal globes of the head is seven cubits, and its girth at the middle is eight cubits. By increasing these measurements by one cubit, one finds the proportions of the **Sluggish-class** <note>Manda</note>, and by increasing them by two cubits, one finds the proportions of the **Noble-class** <note>Bhadra</note>. Thus, the girth of a Sluggish-class elephant is nine cubits. The Noble-class elephant is seven cubits in height, nine cubits in length, and ten cubits in girth. There is no fixed rule for the height and other dimensions of the Mixed-class elephants; they are of indefinite proportions. ||4|| The ichor <note>mada: the musth fluid secreted by elephants</note> of a Noble-class elephant is green; that of a Sluggish-class elephant is yellow like turmeric; and that of a Deer-class elephant is black. The ichor of a Mixed-class elephant is of mixed colors, meaning it displays several hues. ||5||

Those elephants whose lower lips, palates, and mouths are red like copper; whose eyes resemble those of common house sparrows; who possess tusks with glossy and elevated tips; who have a wide and long face; a back-bone that is high like a bow, long, well-concealed, and firm; frontal globes shaped like a tortoise; and whose hair follicles on the frontal globes contain a single fine hair each— ||6|| whose ears, jaws, navel, forehead, private parts, and penis are large; who possess eighteen or twenty nails that are elevated in the middle like a tortoise; whose trunk is round and marked with three vertical lines; and whose ichor flowing from the trunk is fragrant—such elephants are excellent. ||7|| The tip of the trunk is called the *pushkara*, and at the end of the *pushkara* is the "finger." Elephants whose "finger" is long, whose *pushkara* is red, whose roar <note>brimhita</note> sounds like the thundering of a water-laden cloud, and whose neck is very long and round, are auspicious for a King. ||8||

An elephant that never enters musth; one whose nails or limbs are deficient or excessive (meaning fewer than eighteen or more than twenty nails); whose limbs are disproportionately small or large compared to the body; elephants that are hunchbacked <note>kunja</note>; those with tusks resembling the horns of a ram; those whose testicles are visible; those lacking a *pushkara*; and those whose palates are dark, blue, variegated, or black— ||9|| those with small tusks; those that are tuskless <note>matkuna or makuna</note>; or those that are impotent <note>shandha</note>—all these, as well as any cow-elephant that possesses male characteristics (such as large tusks or entering musth), and any pregnant cow-elephant, should be sent out of the kingdom by the King. If they remain in the kingdom, they produce very evil results. An elephant whose chest and hips are narrow, whose back is high, who is below standard proportions, and whose navel is high, is called **Hunchbacked** <note>Kunja</note>. One that is correct in length and girth but very deficient in height is called a **Dwarf** <note>Vamana</note>. One that has all the perfect characteristics but lacks tusks is called **Tuskless** <note>Matkuna</note>. An elephant whose legs strike each other while walking is called **Impotent** <note>Shandha</note>. ||10||

### Now begins the Sixty-Eighth Chapter
### The Characteristics of Men <note>Purusha Lakshanam</note>

> An expert in the science of bodily marks <note>Samudrika-shastra</note>, after duly observing the height, weight, gait, joints, essence, color, gloss, voice, nature, and temperament in order, as well as the "field" <note>the body</note> and its cleanliness, can predict the past and the future. ||1|| Feet that do not sweat, have soft soles, are the color of the interior of a lotus, have closely set toes, beautiful copper-colored nails, and good heels; which are warm and free from visible veins— <note>The text breaks off here mid-description of auspicious feet</note>

The feet of a lord of men <note>original: *manujeshvara*; a king or great leader</note> have hidden ankles and are raised like the back of a tortoise. ## 2 ##

Feet that are shaped like winnowing fans, rough, with pale nails, crooked, covered in prominent veins, shriveled, or with widely spaced toes, bring the misery of poverty. Those with feet that are raised while walking <note>high arches or a specific gait</note> or are the color of astringent wood-apple are destined for the destruction of their lineage. Those with feet that resemble overripe clay in luster or are yellow-hued are said to be "slayers of Brahmins" <note>a term for a grave sinner</note> and will engage in forbidden relations. ## 3 ##

Kings possess calves that are round with very sparse hair, and thighs that resemble the trunk of an elephant. Their knees are well-fleshed and symmetrical. Those devoid of wealth have calves resembling those of dogs or jackals. ## 4 ##

One hair per pore is the mark of kings; two hairs per pore belong to scholars and Vedic priests <note>original: *shrotriyas*</note>. Those with three or more hairs per pore are poor and suffer from diseases. Such hair, as well as that on the head, is considered censurable. ## 5 ##

Fleshless knees lead to death in a foreign land; small knees bring little fortune; and those with huge, distorted knees are poor. Men are conquered by women if their knees are sunken, while those with symmetrical knees attain a kingdom, and those with large knees enjoy long life. ## 6 ##

A man with a small penis is wealthy but childless; a thick one indicates lack of wealth. If it is short, he lacks sons and money; if crooked, the opposite is true (he has sons). Poverty follows a downward-curving organ, while few sons result from one covered in veins. One with thick knots <note>possibly referring to the texture or glands</note> is happy, but a soft one leads to death by urinary diseases <note>original: *prameha*; often associated with diabetes or similar ailments</note>. ## 7 ##

Kings have organs hidden within a sheath <note>like a horse or bull</note>. Those with long or broken-looking organs are devoid of wealth. Those with straight, round, small, and lightly veined organs are wealthy. ## 8 ##

A man with a single testicle dies by water; one with unequal testicles is a womanizer; one with symmetrical testicles is a ruler of the earth. Short life is predicted for those with uplifted testicles, while one with long, hanging testicles lives a hundred years. ## 9 ##

Those with reddish glans are wealthy; those with pale or dirty-colored ones are destitute. Those whose urine makes a sound are happy, while those with a silent stream are poor. ## 10 ##

Those whose urine flows in two, three, or four streams, or turns to the right, should be known as lords of the earth. Those with scattered, spray-like urine are devoid of wealth. ## 11 ##

A single, forceful stream of urine that twists indicates a man who will have beautiful wives and sons. Those with glossy, raised, and symmetrical glans enjoy wealth, women, and gems. ## 12 ##

If the center of the glans is depressed, men become fathers of only daughters and remain poor. Those with a raised center are owners of many cattle, and if it is not overly prominent, they are wealthy. ## 13 ##

Those with a shriveled bladder-head are poor and unfortunate. Those whose semen smells like flowers are to be recognized as kings. ## 14 ##

If it smells like honey, one gains much wealth; if like fish, many children. Thin semen produces daughters, while semen smelling like meat belongs to a great enjoyer of life. ## 15 ##

If it smells like wine, he is a performer of sacrifices; if like salt, he is poor. One who is quick to climax in union lives long; otherwise, he has a short life. ## 16 ##

One with very fleshy buttocks is poor; one with moderately fleshy buttocks is endowed with happiness. One with buttocks like a tiger's is a warrior; one with frog-like buttocks is a ruler of men. ## 17 ##

A man with a waist like a lion is a lord of men; one with a waist like a monkey or a young camel is abandoned by wealth. A flat belly brings enjoyment; one shaped like a pot or a jar belongs to the poor. ## 18 ##

Those with flawless flanks are wealthy; those with sunken or crooked flanks are deprived of enjoyments. Symmetrical sides bring abundance; sunken sides bring lack. ## 19 ##

Those with raised bellies are lords of the earth; those with hard or uneven bellies are poor. Those with "snake-bellies" <note>long and thin</note> are poor and gluttonous. ## 20 ##

Men with round, raised, and wide navels are happy. A small, invisible, or shallow navel brings distress. ## 21 ##

A navel situated in the middle of a fold that is uneven causes pain and poverty. A leftward-turning navel indicates deceit; a rightward-turning one indicates intelligence. ## 22 ##

A navel extended to the side grants long life; one extended upwards makes one a lord rich in cattle; one extended downwards makes one a ruler of men. A navel resembling the heart of a lotus makes one a king. ## 23 ##

One, two, three, or four folds on the belly indicate, respectively: death by a weapon, a woman-chaser, a teacher, or a man with many sons. A man with [many folds] is a scholar or a king...

# Chapter 68: The Signs of Men (Continued)

...uneven folds of skin. ||24|| Men with uneven folds on their belly are known to approach women they should not <note>original: "agamyabhigaminah" - referring to prohibited social or moral unions</note> and are prone to sin. Those with straight, even folds enjoy happiness and possess a natural aversion to the wives of others. ||25||

Those with fleshy, soft flanks and hair that curls in a clockwise direction <note>original: "pradakshinavarta" - a traditional sign of auspiciousness</note> become kings. Those with the opposite characteristics are destitute, devoid of happiness, and remain servants to others. ||26||

Men with nipples that are not raised or prominent are fortunate; those with uneven or long nipples are poor. Kings and happy men possess nipples that are thick, well-developed, and slightly recessed. ||27||

The heart <note>referring here to the chest area</note> of a king is elevated, broad, steady (not trembling), and fleshy. In base men, it is the opposite: covered in coarse hair and showing prominent veins. ||28||

Those with an even chest possess wealth; those with thick, fleshy chests are brave; those with thin chests are penniless. Men whose chests are uneven are destitute and likely to meet their end by a weapon. ||29||

A man with uneven collarbones is devoid of wealth; if the joints of the bones are visible and knotted, he is poor. One with elevated collarbones enjoys life's pleasures; one with sunken collarbones is poor, while one with thick, fleshy collarbones is wealthy. ||30||

A man with a flat neck is poor; so is one whose neck shows dry, prominent veins. A man with a neck like a buffalo's is a brave warrior who may die by the sword. One with a neck like a bull's is equally courageous. ||31||

A man with a neck shaped like a conch shell <note>original: "kambu-griva" - considered a mark of great beauty and status</note> becomes a king. One with a long, dangling neck is a glutton. A back that is not hunched and is free of hair belongs to the wealthy; any other kind brings bad luck. ||32||

Armpits that do not sweat, are fleshy, elevated, fragrant, and covered in soft, even hair belong to the wealthy. Any other characteristics indicate those lacking in means. ||33||

The shoulders of a poor man are thin, covered in hair, slumped, or small. The shoulders of the happy and powerful are broad, continuous (not bony), and well-knit. ||34||

Arms that resemble an elephant's trunk, are rounded, and reach down to the knees <note>original: "ajanubahu" - a classic sign of a great hero or divine being</note> belong to the lords of the earth. The arms of base men are hairy and short. ||35||

Long fingers indicate a long life; those that are curved or well-turned belong to the fortunate. Fine, slender fingers belong to the intelligent, while flat fingers belong to those who serve others. ||36||

Those with thick fingers lack wealth; those with fingers that bend outward die by weapons. Men with hands resembling a monkey's are wealthy; those with hands like a tiger's are sinful. ||37||

Kings have hidden wrist joints and well-knit knuckles. If the wrists are small, the hands may be lost (severed); if they are loose and make a cracking sound, the person is penniless. ||38||

Men with sunken palms are devoid of paternal wealth. Those with palms that are slightly hollowed in the center are wealthy, and those with raised (convex) palms are generous givers. ||39||

Those with uneven palms are poor; those with palms as red as lacquer <note>original: "lakshabha" - a deep, healthy red</note> are lords. Those with yellow palms approach forbidden women, and those with rough palms are destitute. ||40||

Nails that look like husks belong to the impotent; flat or cracked nails belong to those abandoned by fortune. Discolored or ugly nails belong to the deceptive, while copper-colored nails belong to kings. ||41||

Those with barley-corn shaped marks <note>term: "yava" - a grain-shaped island in the lines of the thumb indicating prosperity</note> on the thumb are wealthy; if the mark is at the base of the thumb, they will have sons. Those with long joints in their fingers are fortunate and long-lived. ||42||

Smooth, deep lines on the palm belong to the wealthy; the opposite is true for the poor. Fingers with wide gaps between them indicate poverty, while fingers that fit tightly together belong to those who accumulate wealth. ||43||

Three lines rising from the wrist and going toward the palm belong to a king. A man with the sign of a pair of fish on his hand is always performing charity. ||44||

Wealthy men have marks shaped like a diamond (Vajra); the learned have marks like a fish's tail. Marks resembling a conch, a parasol, a palanquin, an elephant, a horse, or a lotus belong to a king. ||45||

Those with marks like a water-pot, a lotus stalk, a flag, or a goad become guardians of treasure. Those with marks like a garland are wealthy, and a swastika shape brings power and sovereignty. ||46||

Lines resembling a wheel, a sword, an axe, a javelin, a spear, or a bow make one a commander of an army. A mark shaped like a mortar makes one a performer of sacrifices. ||47||

Those with marks resembling a sea-monster (Makara), a flag, or a granary possess great wealth. One with a mark like a sacrificial altar is a performer of fire-rituals. ||48||

Lines shaped like a pond or a temple bring prosperity; triangular marks are also significant. Lines at the base of the thumb indicate the number of sons...
