# The Varahi Samhita
## Chapter on Human Physiognomy (Continued)

<page-num>(230)</page-num>

Fine lines on the palm indicate the birth of daughters. <note>Verse 49</note> Lines reaching the forefinger belong to those who live a hundred years, provided the base of the thumb is well-formed. If these lines are broken, it indicates a fall from one's position or land. Those with too many or too few lines are destitute. <note>Verse 50</note>

With very thin and long chins, men are without wealth; with fleshy chins, they possess riches. Those with lower lips resembling the Bimba fruit <note>a bright red tropical fruit, *Coccinia grandis*</note> and which are not crooked become kings; those with thin lips are poor. <note>Verse 51</note> Those with lips that are cracked, divided, discolored, or rough are abandoned by wealth. Smooth, thick, even, and very sharp teeth are auspicious. <note>Verse 52</note>

A tongue that is red, long, smooth, and very even is known to belong to those who enjoy life's pleasures. A white, black, or rough tongue—and likewise the palate—belongs to those without wealth. <note>Verse 53</note> A mouth that is handsome, gentle, well-closed, clean, smooth, and even belongs to kings. The opposite belongs to those who suffer hardships, and a very large mouth belongs to the unfortunate. <note>Verse 54</note>

A mouth shaped like a woman's belongs to the childless; a circular mouth indicates a deceptive nature. A long mouth belongs to the destitute, and those with mouths like a coward's are performers of sinful deeds. <note>Verse 55</note> A square mouth belongs to the cunning, and a sunken mouth to those without sons. A very small mouth belongs to the miserly, while a full and lovely mouth belongs to those who enjoy life. <note>Verse 56</note>

Beards and mustaches that are not split at the ends, are glossy, soft, and well-trimmed are auspicious. Those with red, rough, or very sparse facial hair should be known as thieves. <note>Verse 57</note> With fleshless ears, one meets a sinful death; with flat ears, one enjoys many pleasures. Short ears belong to misers, and those with ears shaped like a cone <term>Shanku-shravana</term> <note>ears that taper or stand up like a spike</note> are kings. <note>Verse 58</note>

Those with hairy ears live long; those with large ears possess wealth. Those with ears covered in prominent veins are cruel, while those with hanging, fleshy ears are happy. <note>Verse 59</note> One who enjoys life has cheeks that are not sunken; a minister has cheeks full of flesh. One with a nose like a parrot's beak <note>aquiline or hooked</note> experiences happiness, and one with a dry (thin) nose lives long. <note>Verse 60</note>

One with a nose that appears "cut" or broken pursues forbidden partners; a long nose brings good fortune. A crooked nose indicates a thief, and a flat nose indicates the death of one's wife. <note>Verse 61</note> Those with noses that are not crooked at the tip are wealthy; those whose noses turn to the right are cruel gluttons. A straight nose with small nostrils and beautiful wings belongs to the fortunate. <note>Verse 62</note>

For the wealthy, a sneeze occurs once, or in two or three bursts, and is resonant and pleasant. For those who live long, a sneeze is loud and continuous. <note>Verse 63</note> Those with eyes like lotus petals are wealthy; those with eyes red at the corners possess great fortune. Those with eyes yellow like honey possess great means, but those with eyes like a cat's are sinful. <note>Verse 64</note>

Those with eyes like a deer's or circular eyes, or those with squinted eyes, are thieves. Those with squinting <term>kekara</term> eyes are cruel, while those whose gaze resembles an elephant's are kings. <note>Verse 65</note> Deep-set eyes bring power; those with eyes the color of the blue water-lily are learned. Those with extremely black pupils face the risk of their eyes being plucked out. <note>Verse 66</note>

Large eyes lead to the position of a minister, and brownish-gray eyes bring good luck. A dejected look belongs to the destitute, while a glossy and wide gaze belongs to those who enjoy great wealth. <note>Verse 67</note> Those with very raised eyebrows have short lives; those with broad and raised eyebrows are very happy. Those with uneven eyebrows are poor, while those with eyebrows raised like the crescent moon are wealthy. <note>Verse 68</note>

Those with long, joined eyebrows are wealthy; those with broken eyebrows are deprived of money. Those whose eyebrows are depressed in the middle are attached to forbidden women. <note>Verse 69</note> Those with high and broad temples are blessed; those with sunken temples are abandoned by children and wealth. Those with uneven foreheads are poor, while those with foreheads like a half-moon are wealthy. <note>Verse 70</note>

A forehead broad like a mother-of-pearl shell indicates a teacher; one covered in veins indicates a devotion to unrighteousness. Those with prominent veins are rich, as are those whose veins are shaped like a swastika. <note>Verse 71</note> Those with sunken foreheads suffer imprisonment and execution and are intent on cruel deeds. Kings have high foreheads, while misers have narrow, constricted ones. <note>Verse 72</note>

Laughter that is not dejected, without tears, and glossy brings good fortune to men. Rough, dejected laughter with many tears is not auspicious for men. <note>Verse 73</note> Auspicious laughter is without body-shaking; laughter with closed eyes belongs to the sinful. Frequent laughter belongs to the wicked, and constant laughter to the insane.

# Chapter 68 (with Hindi Commentary)

...at the end. ||74|| Three long lines on the forehead indicate those who live a hundred years. If there are four lines, it indicates kingship <note>literally: "lordship of the earth"</note> and a lifespan of ninety-five years. ||75|| With broken lines, one goes to forbidden women <note>indicates a lack of moral restraint</note>; even without lines, the lifespan is ninety. With lines reaching the hairline, the lifespan is eighty years. ||76|| With five lines, the life is seventy years; with one line, it is sixty. With many lines, it is fifty <note>literally: "half of a hundred"</note>, and with curved lines, it is forty. ||77|| With lines touching the eyebrows, the life is thirty; with lines curved to the left, it is twenty. With very small or faint lines, the life is short; for intermediate numbers of lines, the result should be inferred accordingly. ||78||

Those with rounded heads are wealthy in cattle; those with umbrella-shaped heads are kings. Those with flat heads are killers of their fathers and mothers <note>likely a metaphor for bringing ruin to the lineage</note>; those with skull-shaped heads <note>sunken or bony</note> meet an early death. ||79|| A pot-shaped head indicates a love for meditation; a double-headed <note>misshapen or bifid appearance</note> person is a sinner abandoned by wealth. A slightly depressed head belongs to the great, but a very deep depression brings disaster. ||80||

One who has hair where each strand grows from a single pore, and is glossy, black, curled, with intact tips, soft, and not too thick, is a happy man or a king. ||81|| Hair that has many roots in one pore, is uneven, reddish-brown, thick, split at the ends, rough, short, very curly, or extremely dense, belongs to those without wealth. ||82|| Whichever limb is dry, lacking flesh, and covered in prominent veins is said to be inauspicious; the opposite of this is entirely auspicious. ||83||

A king is broad in three parts, deep in three, raised in six, short in four, red in seven, and long and subtle in five. ||84|| The chest, forehead, and face—these three being broad is praised in men. The navel, the voice, and the inner character <term>Sattva: the quality of purity and strength</term>—these three are directed to be deep in men. ||85|| The chest, armpits, nails, nose, mouth, and the nape of the neck—these six should be raised. Four parts—the penis, the back, the neck, and the shanks—being short is beneficial. ||86|| The corners of the eyes, feet, palms, palate, lower lip, tongue, and nails—these seven being red brings happiness. Five things—teeth, finger joints, hair, skin, and nails—being subtle <note>fine or delicate</note> are not found in the miserable. ||87|| The jaw, eyes, arms, nose, and the space between the breasts—these five are long in kings, but not in others. ||88||

Thus ends the section on the Body <term>Kshetra: the physical field</term>.

Now, the Shadow <term>Chhaya: the aura or luster of the skin</term>, which reveals good and bad results, should be observed in humans, animals, and birds by those skilled in signs. It radiates the qualities of one's inner energy <term>Tejas</term> outward, like the light of a lamp inside a vessel of crystal or gems. ||89|| A shadow that is glossy on the teeth, skin, nails, and hair, and is fragrant, arises from the Earth element. It brings contentment, wealth, and daily progress in righteousness <term>Dharma</term>. ||90|| A shadow that is glossy, white, clear, and green-tinted is pleasing to the eye; it brings good fortune, gentleness, happiness, and prosperity. Like a mother, it is the producer of all success and bestows good results on embodied beings. ||91|| A shadow that is fierce, unassailable, the color of a lotus, gold, or fire, and joined with valor and majesty, is of the Fire element; it brings quick victory and the attainment of desired goals. ||92|| A shadow that is dirty, rough, black, and smells foul arises from the Air element; it causes death, imprisonment, disease, and loss of wealth. A shadow that is clear like crystal, extremely noble, and of pure color is like a treasury of blessings from the Sky element. ||93||

Some say there are ten shadows arising in sequence from Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether, corresponding to the Sun, Moon, Vishnu, Indra, and Yama; this is the summary of their signs and fruits. ||94||

Thus ends the section on Gloss <term>Mrja: cleanliness or luster</term>.

Those whose voices sound like an elephant, a bull, a chariot, a drum, or a lion are kings. Those with voices like a donkey, or which are cracked and rough...

# Varahi Samhita
<page-num>232</page-num>

...deprived of food and happiness. (95) **Thus ends the section on Voice.** <note>original: "iti svarah"</note>

There are seven "essences" <term>sara: the fundamental constitutional strengths of a person</term> in living beings: fat, marrow, skin, bone, semen, blood, and flesh. The results of these are summarized as follows: (96)

Those with the essence of **blood** are identified by red palates, lips, teeth, gums, tongues, eyes, nails, hands, and feet; they possess great happiness, many wives, wealth, and sons. (97) Those with the essence of **skin** have glossy skin; they are wealthy, and if the skin is soft and thin, they are fortunate and wise. Those with the essence of **marrow and fat** have handsome bodies and are endowed with sons and wealth. (98) One with the essence of **bone** has thick bones and joints; he is strong, learned, and handsome. **Thus ends the section on Essence.** Those with an abundance of heavy **semen** are fortunate, wise, and beautiful. (99)

He who has the essence of **flesh** has a well-developed body, is learned, wealthy, and handsome. Regarding **compactness** <term>samhati: the firmness or structural integrity of the body</term>, those with well-knit joints are known to enjoy happiness. (100) **Thus ends the section on Compactness.**

**Glossiness** <term>sneha: a quality of luster or oiliness</term> can be observed in five places: speech, tongue, teeth, eyes, and nails. Those who possess glossiness in these areas are endowed with children, wealth, and good fortune; those who are "dry" or rough in these areas are impoverished. (101) **Thus ends the section on Glossiness.**

The **complexion** <term>varna</term> that is radiant and glossy belongs to kings; a medium complexion belongs to those with children and wealth; a dull or dry complexion belongs to the poor. A pure complexion brings good fortune, while a mottled one does not. (102) **Thus ends the section on Complexion.**

The **facial resemblance** <term>anukam: the likeness of a human face to an animal</term> should be judged from the face. Those with faces like a bull, an ox, a tiger, a lion, or a Garuda <note>a divine eagle-like bird</note> possess irresistible prowess, conquer their enemies, and become lords of men. (103) Those with faces resembling a monkey, a buffalo, a boar, or a goat enjoy sons, wealth, and happiness. Those with faces and bodies resembling a donkey or a young camel are devoid of wealth and happiness. (104) **Thus ends the section on Facial Resemblance.**

The **height** <term>unmanam: vertical measurement</term> of men is 108, 96, or 84 digits <note>angulas: a traditional unit of measure roughly equal to a finger's width</note>, categorized as excellent, average, and inferior respectively, measured by their own fingers. (105) **Thus ends the section on Height.**

Regarding **weight** <term>manam</term>, one who weighs half a *bhara* <note>a traditional unit of weight</note> enjoys happiness; one who weighs less than that suffers misery. Those who are very wealthy weigh one *bhara*, and a universal ruler weighs one and a half *bharas*. (106) A woman at twenty years and a man at twenty-five years, or in the fourth part of their lifespan, are eligible for these measurements of height and weight. (107) **Thus ends the section on Weight.**

The **temperament** <term>sattva: the inner psychological and elemental nature</term> of men is influenced by the five elements—Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether—and corresponds to the natures of gods, humans, demons, spirits, elephants, and animals. This is the characteristic of both. (108)

One with the **Earth nature** has the scent of beautiful flowers, enjoys pleasures, has good breath, and is steady. One with the **Water nature** drinks much water, speaks kindly, and enjoys juicy foods. (109) One with the **Fire nature** is restless, very sharp, fierce, hungry, and eats much. One with the **Air nature** is wandering, active, and quickly falls under the power of anger. (110)

One with the **Ether nature** is clever, has an open mouth, is skilled in the science of sound, and has porous limbs. A man with a **Divine nature** is charitable, mildly angry, and fond of affection. (111) One endowed with a **Human nature** is fond of music and ornaments and is always inclined toward sharing. (112)

One with the nature of **Demons** <note>Rakshasas</note> is fiercely angry, acts wickedly, and is sinful. One with a **Spirit nature** <note>Pishacha</note> is restless, smeared with dirt, talks excessively, and has a bloated body. (113) One who is timid, hungry, and eats much is known to have the nature of **Animals**. Thus is the nature of men described, which those skilled in characteristics call "Sattva." (114) **Thus ends the section on Temperament.**

Kings have a **gait** <term>gati</term> similar to that of a tiger, a swan, a great elephant, a bull, or a peacock. Those whose walk is silent and steady are also lords; those who walk with a quick, hopping gait are poor. (115) **Thus ends the section on Gait.**

When a man receives a vehicle when tired, food when hungry, drink when thirsty, and protection in times of fear—those skilled in the characteristics of men say that such a man is truly fortunate. (116)

<header>With Hindi Commentary, Chapter 68</header>

# **I have briefly stated these characteristics after observing the opinions of the sages. By studying this, a man becomes esteemed by kings**
# **and beloved by all people. || 197 ||**

## Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Characteristics of Men," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira. || 68 ||

<note>Varahamihira was a 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath. The Brihat Samhita is his "Great Compilation" of various sciences.</note>

A clever man who knows the <term>Samudrika Shastra</term> <note>The ancient Indian science of body features and palmistry</note> can predict the past and future good or bad fortunes of men by first observing their height (measured in fingers), weight, gait, <term>samhati</term> <note>the well-knit quality of the joints</note>, essence, color, voice, nature, <term>sattva</term> <note>a quality of the mind that prevents despair and fear</note>, <term>anuka</term> <note>traits carried from a previous birth</note>, the ten types of "fields" such as the feet (which will be described later), and <term>mrija</term> <note>the physical luster or aura composed of the five elements</note>. || 1 ||

Feet that are free from sweat, possessed of soft soles, glowing like the center of a lotus, with toes closely joined together, having shiny and red-colored nails, beautiful heels, free from prominent veins, with <term>nigudha gulph</term> <note>hidden or well-fleshed ankles that do not protrude</note>, and arched like the back of a tortoise—these are the feet of a king. A man whose feet possess these marks becomes a ruler. || 2 ||

If the feet are shaped like a <term>shurpa</term> <note>a winnowing basket; wide at the front</note>, have white nails, are crooked, covered in veins, dry, and have widely spaced toes, they bring poverty and sorrow. Feet arched in the middle like a frog cause one to be constantly traveling on the road. Feet of a <term>kashaya</term> <note>astringent or brownish-red</note> color indicate the end of a lineage; that is, the family of a man with such feet does not continue. He whose soles have the luster of baked clay commits <term>brahmahatya</term> <note>the grave sin of killing a learned priest</note>, and a man with yellow-colored feet is attracted to forbidden women. || 3 ||

A man with sparse and fine hair on the legs, beautiful thighs shaped like an elephant's trunk, and fleshy, symmetrical knees—one with all these marks becomes a king. Those whose shanks resemble those of a dog or a jackal are devoid of wealth. || 4 ||

Those who have only one hair in each <term>romakupa</term> <note>hair follicle</note> on their shanks become kings; those with two hairs per follicle become scholars and <term>shrotriyas</term> <note>those well-versed in Vedic oral tradition</note>; those with three or four hairs per follicle are poor and miserable. From this, one should also understand the good and bad effects of the hair on the head. || 5 ||

He who has no flesh on his knees dies while traveling abroad; one with small knees is fortunate. Those with jagged or ugly knees are poor. Those whose knees are sunken are dominated by women; one with fleshy knees attains a kingdom, and those with large knees are long-lived. || 6 ||

A man with a small <term>linga</term> <note>penis</note> is wealthy but childless. One with a thick <term>linga</term> is poor. He whose <term>linga</term> tilts to the left is devoid of wealth and sons. If it tilts to the right, he will have sons. He whose <term>linga</term> hangs very low is poor. If it is covered in veins, the man will have few sons. One whose <term>linga</term> has a thick knot or gland is happy. A man with a soft <term>linga</term> dies of diseases like <term>prameha</term> <note>urinary disorders or diabetes</note>. || 7 ||

Those whose <term>linga</term> is retracted or hidden in a sheath (like a horse's) become kings. Those with long and "broken" <term>lingas</term> are poor. Those with straight, round, small, or vein-covered <term>lingas</term> are wealthy. || 8 ||

A man with only one <term>vrishana</term> <note>testicle</note> dies by drowning in water. If the testicles are uneven (one small, one large), he is a womanizer...

Those whose *glans* is depressed in the middle become fathers of daughters—meaning only daughters are born to them—and such men are also poor. By having symmetrical flanks, one becomes wealthy; if the flanks are low and crooked, one is poor. If the *kakshya* is elevated, they become kings. Those whose *kakshya* is uneven are harsh men. He whose navel spirals counter-clockwise is a rogue. If the navel spirals clockwise, he possesses excellent intelligence. A navel that is long on both sides grants a long life. If the navel is long upwards, it endows the man with prosperity; if it is long downwards, it endows him with many enjoyments. # Varahi Samhita

Those who consort with forbidden women <note>original: "agamya stri"</note> have a lifespan of ninety years. Even if there are no lines on the forehead, the lifespan is ninety years. The place where the hair begins is called the hairline <note>original: "keshanta"</note>. If a line on the forehead reaches the hairline, the lifespan is eighty years. || 76 ||

If there are five lines on the forehead, the lifespan is seventy years. If the ends of all lines meet, the lifespan is sixty years. If there are many lines, such as six or seven, the lifespan is fifty years. If there is a crooked line on the forehead, the lifespan is forty years. || 77 ||

If a line touches the eyebrow, the lifespan is thirty years. If there is a crooked line on the left side, the lifespan is twenty years. If the line is short, the lifespan is less than twenty years. If there are few lines—meaning only one or two—the lifespan is also less than twenty years. One should estimate the age between these lines. For example, if there are three lines, one should predict a lifespan of one hundred years; for four lines, ninety-five years; and for three and a half lines, ninety-seven and a half years should be estimated. Know the others similarly. || 78 ||

Those with round heads possess many cows. If the head is broad at the top like the shape of a ceremonial umbrella <note>original: "chhatra"</note>, they become kings. Men with flat heads kill their parents. Those whose heads are shaped like a skull <note>original: "karoti"</note> live for many days. || 79 ||

Those whose heads are shaped like a pot <note>original: "ghata"</note> are sinful and poor. Those with a low or indented head are prestigious men, but if it is extremely low, they cause calamities. || 80 ||

Men are happy or become kings if their hair grows one strand per pore, and is black, glossy, slightly curled at the ends, not split, soft, and not very thick. || 81 ||

Hair that grows in clusters from a single pore, is uneven in length, tawny <note>original: "kapila"</note> in color, thick, split at the ends, dry, short, very curly, and very dense belongs to the poor. || 82 ||

Any limb that is dry, lacking flesh, and covered in visible veins is inauspicious. A limb that is glossy, well-nourished, and free of visible veins is auspicious. || 83 ||

A man becomes a king if he has broad limbs, three deep parts, six raised parts, four short parts, seven reddish parts, five long parts, and five subtle or thin parts. || 84 ||

The chest, forehead, and face—if these three parts are broad, they are excellent. The navel, the voice, and the inner character <note>original: "sattva," referring to the quality of the mind</note>—if these three are deep, the man is superior among men. || 85 ||

The chest, the armpits <note>original: "kakshya"</note>, the nails, the nose, the mouth, and the nape of the neck <note>original: "krikatika" or Adam's apple area</note>—these six parts should be raised. The penis, the back, the neck, and the shanks—if these four are short, it is auspicious. || 86 ||

The corners of the eyes, the soles of the feet, the hands, the palate, the lower lip, the tongue, and the nails—if these seven parts are reddish, they bring happiness. The teeth, the joints of the fingers, the hair, the skin, and the nails—these five are not thin in miserable men; that is, those in whom these five are thin <note>original: "sukshma"</note> remain happy. || 87 ||

The jaw, the eyes, the arms, the nose, and the space between the two breasts—these five long parts are not found in men other than kings. Thus, the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of the body's limbs have been told. || 88 ||

Those who know the signs <note>physiognomists</note> should observe the "shadow" <note>original: "chhaya," referring to the aura or luster of the body</note>, which indicates auspicious and inauspicious results in humans, animals, and birds. Like the light of a lamp inside a crystal jar, it resides within the body yet illuminates the qualities of its brilliance outwardly. || 89 ||

When the "Earth shadow" is upon a man, his teeth, skin, nails, and hair remain glossy, and there is a fragrance in the body. That Earth shadow brings contentment <note>original: "tushti"</note>, gain of wealth, and prosperity; it increases righteous conduct day by day. || 90 ||

The "Water shadow" is glossy, white, clear, and green, and is pleasing to the eyes. That shadow brings good fortune to all men...

# Chapter 68: With Hindi Commentary
<page-num>239</page-num>

Affection and tenderness bring happiness and prosperity; they are the fulfillers of all tasks and, like a mother, grant auspicious fruits to men and other living beings. || 91 || The shadow of Fire (wrathful) is <term>unassailable</term> <note>original: "adhṛṣyā" - meaning one who cannot be insulted or overpowered</note>; it possesses a complexion like a lotus, gold, or fire, and is endowed with brilliance, valor, and majesty. Such a fire-shadow grants victory to beings and quickly achieves desired goals. || 92 || The shadow of Wind is filthy, harsh, black, and foul-smelling; that shadow causes death, imprisonment, disease, misfortune, and the destruction of wealth. The shadow of Ether (Sky) is exceedingly pure like crystal; that shadow is fortunate, very generous, a virtual treasury of blessings, and transparently clean. || 93 ||

The five shadows of Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Ether have been described in order. Some sages, such as Garga and others, speak of ten shadows; in their opinion, there are five shadows of Earth etc., and five shadows of the Sun, Vishnu, Indra, Yama, and the Moon. However, because the characteristics and fruits of these shadows are equal to those of the Earthly shadows, we have condensed the ten shadows into five. This is the description of <term>Mṛjā</term> <note>The luster or cleansing quality associated with the five great elements</note>. || 94 ||

Those whose voice is like that of an elephant, a bull, a fleet of chariots, a kettle-drum, a mridangam drum, a lion, or a cloud, become kings. Those whose voice is cracked and harsh are devoid of wealth and happiness. This is the description of the Voice. || 95 ||

<term>Fat</term> <note>meda - the oily substance within the bones</note>, <term>Marrow</term> <note>majjā - the oily substance within the skull/large bones</note>, <term>Skin</term> <note>tvacā</note>, <term>Bone</term> <note>asthi</note>, <term>Semen/Vitality</term> <note>vīrya</note>, <term>Blood</term> <note>rudhira</note>, and <term>Flesh</term> <note>māṃsa</note>—these seven are the <term>Sāras</term> <note>essences or constitutional strengths</note> in the bodies of living beings. Now, their fruits are told in brief. || 96 ||

Men whose palate, lips, teeth, flesh, tongue, corners of the eyes, anus, hands, and feet are reddish in color possess the essence of Blood; they are endowed with great happiness, wives, wealth, and sons. || 97 || If the skin is glossy, one becomes wealthy. If the skin is soft, one is fortunate/charming, and if the skin is thin, one becomes a scholar. Those in whose bodies Marrow and Fat are the primary essences possess beautiful bodies. || 98 || In those with the essence of Bone, the bones are thick; such a man is strong, reaches the end of knowledge (highly educated), and is handsome. Those whose semen is abundant and thick possess the essence of Vitality; such men are charming, learned, and handsome. || 99 || A creature with a well-nourished body possesses the essence of Flesh; such a man is learned, wealthy, and handsome. This is the description of the Essences. The well-knit quality of the joints of the limbs is called <term>Saṃghāta</term> <note>compactness</note>; men with such compactness are enjoyers of happiness. || 100 ||

One should observe the glossiness residing in these five: speech, tongue, teeth, eyes, and nails. Those in whom these five are glossy are endowed with sons, wealth, and good fortune; if they are dry/harsh, they are poor. || 11 || <note>Printed as 11, likely intended to be 101</note> Whether the body color be fair or dark, a glossy and radiant complexion belongs to kings. A medium complexion (neither dry nor glossy) belongs to those with sons and wealth. A dry complexion belongs to men devoid of wealth. A glossy complexion is auspicious; a mixed complexion (dry in some places, glossy in others) is not auspicious. This is the description of Complexion. || 102 ||

By looking at the face, know the <term>previous birth</term>. Those whose faces are like a cow, bull, tiger, lion, or eagle had an auspicious previous birth; these men possess irresistible majesty, conquer their enemies, and become kings. || 103 || Those whose faces are like a monkey, buffalo, boar, or goat are endowed with scriptures, wealth, and happiness; their previous birth is of a medium grade. Those whose faces and bodies are like a donkey or camel are poor and devoid of happiness; their previous birth is inauspicious. This is the description of <term>Anūka</term> <note>the "after-image" or reflection of a previous incarnation</note>. || 104 ||

A man who is one hundred and eight fingers high (measured by his own fingers) is excellent. One who is ninety-six fingers high is medium, and one eighty-four fingers high is inferior. This is the description of Height. One should measure from the tip of the foot to the middle part of the head. || 105 ||

<page-num>240</page-num>
<header>The Varahi Samhita (Brihat Samhita)</header>

Two thousand *palas* <note>A traditional unit of weight; one *pala* is approximately 48 grams</note> constitute one *bhara*. A man whose body weight is half a *bhara* enjoys happiness; if it is less than this, he remains miserable. Those whose weight is one full *bhara* (two thousand *palas*) become extremely wealthy. Those whose body weight is one and a half *bhara* (three thousand *palas*) become sovereign emperors (*Chakravarti* kings). **|| 106 ||** Women should be measured and weighed at the age of twenty, and men at the age of twenty-five. Alternatively, they should be measured and weighed when one-fourth of their lifespan—as determined by astrology and calculations—has passed. **|| 107 ||** The essences (*sattva* or inner natures) of earth, water, fire, air, ether, gods, humans, demons, spirits, and animals/birds are found within men. Their characteristics are described as follows: **|| 108 ||** A man with the nature of **Earth** has a fragrance like beautiful lotus flowers; he is a seeker of pleasure, has fragrant breath, and a steady temperament. A man of **Water** nature drinks much water, speaks sweetly, and takes delight in eating sweet flavors. **|| 109 ||** A man of **Fire** nature is restless, extremely sharp, and cruel; he cannot endure hunger and eats excessively. A man of **Air** nature is fickle, physically weak, and quickly overcome by anger. **|| 110 ||** A man of **Ether** (Space) nature is skillful in all tasks, keeps an open mouth, is expert in the science of sound and song, and has porous limbs. A man of **Divine** nature is charitable, rarely angry, and full of affection. **|| 111 ||** A man of **Human** nature loves music and ornaments; he is virtuous and constantly performs favors for his kinsmen. **|| 112 ||** A man of **Demonic** nature is very wrathful, wicked, and sinful. A man of **Spirit** (*Pishacha*) nature is restless, has an unclean body, talks excessively, and possesses stout limbs. **|| 113 ||** A man of **Animal** (*Tiryak*) nature should be known as fearful, unable to endure hunger, and a glutton. Thus are the natures of men described, which scholars of human characteristics declare to be true. This concludes the description of natures (*sattva*). **|| 114 ||** Those whose gait resembles that of a tiger, a swan, an elephant in rut, a bull, or a peacock become kings. Those whose walk is silent and slow also become wealthy. Men who walk hurriedly or jump like frogs are poor. This concludes the description of gait. **|| 115 ||** A man who receives a vehicle when tired, food when hungry, water when thirsty, and protection in times of fear—all at the exact moment of need—is called "Blessed" (*Dhanya*) by those who know human signs. **|| 116 ||** Having observed the opinions of many sages, I have stated these human characteristics in brief. By reading this, a man becomes respected by kings and beloved by all people. **|| 117 ||**

### Now begins the Sixty-Ninth Chapter
## Characteristics of the Five Great Men
<note>The *Pancha Mahapurusha* Yoga: a fundamental concept in Vedic astrology where five specific planetary combinations create extraordinary individuals.</note>

> When the non-luminary planets <note>Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note> are powerful, situated in their own zodiac signs or signs of exaltation, and occupy the cardinal houses (*Kendras*), five types of excellent men are born. I shall now describe them. **|| 1 ||** By Jupiter, the *Hansa* type is formed; by Saturn, the *Shasha* type; by Mars, the *Ruchaka* type; and by Mercury, the *Bhadra* type... <note>The text cuts off before mentioning Venus, which forms the *Malavya* type.</note>

# Chapter 69: Characteristics of the Five Great Men

(241)
-> **With Hindi Commentary** <-

The **Malavya** <note>One of the five types of "Great Men" in Vedic astrology</note> is born when Venus is strong and exalted. ||2|| 

Strength of character and physical vigor are derived from the Sun, while mental strength comes from the power of the Moon. A man’s characteristics are determined by the specific zodiac signs and planetary divisions occupied by these two luminaries. ||3|| 

The nature, radiance, color, and temperament of a person are shaped by the elements <note>The Mahabhutas: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether</note> associated with the ruling planets. If the Sun and Moon are weak, the person will possess a mixture of these various traits rather than a distinct "Great Man" profile. ||4|| 

From Mars comes spirit and energy; from Mercury comes weight or gravity; from Jupiter comes the voice; from Venus comes grace and luster; and from Saturn comes the complexion. The virtues or defects of these planets determine whether a person is good or bad. ||5|| 

Those with mixed characteristics do not become kings, though they may enjoy happiness during the planetary periods <note>Dasha: cycles of time ruled by specific planets</note> of favorable planets. Differences in status arise from whether planets are in enemy houses, debilitated, exalted, or aspected by benefics or malefics. ||6|| 

The height and arm-span of a **Hansa** type is 96 digits <note>Angula: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly the width of a finger</note>. The **Shasha**, **Ruchaka**, **Bhadra**, and **Malavya** types each increase in height by three digits respectively <note>i.e., Shasha is 99, Ruchaka 102, Bhadra 105, and Malavya 108 digits</note>. ||7|| 

One who is dominated by **Sattva** <note>The quality of purity and goodness</note> possesses compassion, stability, honesty, and devotion to Brahmins and the Divine. One dominated by **Rajas** <note>The quality of passion and activity</note> is skilled in poetry and arts, fond of women, and extremely brave. ||8|| 

One dominated by **Tamas** <note>The quality of darkness and ignorance</note> is a deceiver of others, foolish, lazy, prone to anger, and sleeps excessively. Through various combinations of these three qualities—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—seven distinct types of temperaments are formed. ||9|| 

### The Malavya Man
The **Malavya** has arms as long and graceful as an elephant's trunk, with hands reaching to the knees. His limbs and joints are well-fleshed and symmetrical; he has a beautiful body with a slender waist. His face is thirteen digits long, and his ear-openings are three digits apart. He has bright eyes, handsome cheeks, even white teeth, and lips that are not too fleshy. ||10|| 

He rules over the regions of Malwa, Bharuch, Gujarat, Lata, and Sindh. He is a king who acquires wealth through valor, resides near the Pariyatra mountains, and is highly intelligent. ||11|| 

This Malavya man lives for seventy years and eventually gives up his life peacefully at a holy pilgrimage site <note>Tirtha: a sacred place, often by a river</note>. These characteristics have been fully described; now I shall speak of the remaining men. ||12|| 

### The Bhadra Man
The **Bhadra** type has well-developed, symmetrical, and long arms. His height is equal to his arm-span. His cheeks are covered with soft, fine, and dense hair. ||13|| 

His strength lies in his skin and reproductive essence <note>Shukra: vital fluid or essence</note>. He has a broad and thick chest, great courage, and a face resembling a tiger's. He is stable, forgiving, proud, grateful, walks with the gait of a lordly elephant, and is well-versed in many sciences. ||14|| 

He is wise, handsome, with beautiful temples and forehead. He is an expert in the arts, patient, and has a well-formed belly. His hands and feet have the luster of the interior of a lotus. He is a practitioner of yoga, has a fine nose, and even, joined eyebrows. ||15|| 

His body scent resembles freshly watered earth, saffron, an elephant in rut, or agarwood. His hair is dark, curly, and beautiful. His private parts are well-concealed, like those of a horse or an elephant. ||16|| 

The palms of his hands and soles of his feet are marked with signs of a plow, a pestle, a mace, a sword, a conch, a wheel, an elephant, a crocodile, or a lotus. He shares his wealth with others, but being of independent mind, he does not tolerate his own kinsmen if they interfere. ||17|| 

His height is 106 digits, and his weight is proportionate. He becomes the ruler of the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha: the central heartland of ancient India</note>, and if other auspicious signs are present, he may rule the entire earth. ||18|| 

Having enjoyed the earth won by his bravery, at the age of eighty, the Bhadra gives up his life at a holy pilgrimage site and goes to the abode of the gods. ||19|| 

### The Shasha Man
The **Shasha** type has slightly protruding but small teeth, narrow eyes, and a quick gait. He is devoted to science, metallurgy, and trade. He has full cheeks but is deceitful. He is a commander of armies, fond of physical intimacy, attracted to the wives of others, and restless. He is brave, devoted to his mother, and fond of forests, mountains, and rivers. ||20|| 

He is 92 digits tall. His movements are cautious, and he is skilled in finding the weaknesses of others. His strength lies in his marrow. He moves quietly and is not very heavy. ||21|| 

He is slender in the waist. On his hands or feet, there are lines shaped like a shield, a sword, a lute, a bed, a garland, or a drum. There are also upward-pointing lines resembling a trident. ||22||

# The Great Compendium of Varahamihira
## Chapter 69: Characteristics of the Five Great Men

...or he may suffer from discharges from the hips or piercing pains in the body. Thus, the **Rabbit** type <note>original: *Shasha*</note> lives for seventy years before departing for the abode of the Son of the Sun <note>The god of death, Yama</note>. ||23||

With a reddish complexion, full cheeks, a high nose, and a face like gold; with a rounded head and eyes the color of honey, and all nails appearing red; his hands and feet are marked with the signs of a garland, a goad, a conch, a pair of fish, a skull-topped staff <note>original: *khatvanga*</note>, a water-pot, and lotuses. He possesses a voice as sweet as a swan, beautiful feet, and clear, calm senses—this is the **Swan** type <note>original: *Hamsa*</note>. ||24||

He delights in being near water, his strength lies in his virility, and his weight is measured at sixteen hundred *palas* <note>A traditional unit of weight; approximately 160 lbs / 72 kg</note>. His height is declared by the wise to be ninety-six digits <note>original: *angulas*</note>. ||25||

The **Swan** rules over the lands of the Khasas, Shurasenas, Gandharas, and the region between the Ganges and Yamuna rivers. Having exercised kingship for ninety years, he meets his end in a forest. ||26||

With beautiful brows and hair, a dark-reddish complexion, a neck like a conch shell, and a long face; he is brave, cruel, an excellent counselor, a leader of thieves, and fond of physical exercise. ||27||

The length of the **Radiant** type's <note>original: *Ruchaka*</note> face is equal to his width, showing a squareness in the middle parts. He has thin skin, and his strength lies in his blood and flesh. He is a slayer of enemies whose goals are achieved through bold daring. ||28||

His hands and feet are marked with the signs of a cot, a lute, a bull, a bow, a thunderbolt, a spear, the moon, and a trident. He is a devotee of elders, Brahmins, and the gods. His height is one hundred digits, and his weight is one thousand *palas*. ||29||

Skilled in mantras and magic, with thin knees and shanks, the **Radiant** king rules over the Vindhya and Sahya mountains and the city of Ujjain. Having reached seventy years, he meets his death by a weapon or by fire. ||30||

There are five other types: the **Dwarf**, the **Deformed**, the **Hunchback**, the **Circular**, and the **Partial**. These are the attendants of the previously mentioned kings and are known as the "Mixed" types. Hear now their characteristics. ||31||

The **Dwarf** <note>original: *Vamanaka*</note> has well-formed limbs but a broken back; he is somewhat sunken in the middle of his thighs and armpits. He is a famous follower of the **Noble** <note>Bhadra</note> type of king, wealthy, charitable, and a devotee of Vishnu. ||32||

The one called **Deformed** <note>original: *Jaghanya*</note> serves the **Garland** <note>Malavya</note> type. His ears resemble the crescent moon; he is fragrant, but his strength is derived from others. He is a backbiter, a poet, with rough skin and thick fingers. ||33||

He is cruel, wealthy, dull-witted, and famous; he has a similar complexion to his master and is fond of joking. On his chest, feet, and hands are the marks of a sword, a spear, a noose, a battle-axe, and a goad. This is the **Deformed** type. ||34||

The one named the **Hunchback** <note>original: *Kubja*</note> is well-formed in the lower body but wasted and bent in the upper half. He serves the **Swan** type. He is an atheist, yet learned, brave, an informant, and grateful. ||35||

He is an expert in the arts, fond of quarrels, has many servants, and is conquered by women. After being honored by the world, he suddenly renounces it. This is the **Hunchback**, who is always energetic. ||36||

The one named **Circular** <note>original: *Mandalaka*</note> is a follower of the **Radiant** type. He is an expert in magic and is devoted to the rituals of spirits and vampires <note>original: *kritya-vetala*</note> and various sciences. ||37||

He has the appearance of an old man, with hair that is stiff and rough. He is skilled in destroying enemies. His mind is fixed on Brahmins, gods, sacrifices, and yoga, yet he is dominated by women and is highly intelligent. ||38||

The one called **Partial** <note>original: *Sami*</note> has a very deformed body and follows the **Rabbit** type. He is indeed unfortunate, yet charitable; he completes great undertakings and possesses qualities similar to the **Rabbit** type. ||39||

# Chapter 69: With Hindi Commentary
<page-num>243</page-num>

If the five planets—Mars and the others—are endowed with strength of position, direction, motion, and time <note>These refer to the four types of planetary strength: Sthana, Dik, Cheshta, and Kala Bala</note>, and are situated in their own zodiac sign or their sign of exaltation while occupying the first, fourth, seventh, or tenth house <note>The cardinal houses or 'Kendras'</note>, then five types of "Noble Men" are born, whom we shall now describe. ||1||

When Jupiter is powerful and situated in its own sign or exaltation in a cardinal house, that man is a **Hamsa** type; if Saturn is so placed, he is a **Shasha** type; if Mars, he is a **Ruchaka** type; if Mercury is powerful, he is a **Bhadra** type; and if Venus is so placed, he is a **Malavya** type. ||2||

From the strength of the Sun comes a man's complete inner essence <term>Sattva: the quality of purity and spirit</term>, and from the strength of the Moon come the qualities of the body and mind. A man possesses the elements, primordial nature, luster, complexion, temperament, and physical characteristics of whichever planet's sign, decan <term>Drekkana: a 10-degree division</term>, ninth-part <term>Navamsha</term>, twelfth-part <term>Dvadasamsha</term>, or thirtieth-part <term>Trishamsha</term> the Sun and Moon are occupying. If the Sun and Moon are strong in these divisions, the man possesses the full characteristics of that planet; however, if the Sun and Moon are weak, the man will possess mixed or "blended" characteristics. ||3||4||

From Mars comes valor; from Mercury, gravity; from Jupiter, the voice; from Venus, affection; and from Saturn, luster. If Mars and the other planets are strong, these qualities like Sattva are excellent; if they are weak, there is a lack of such qualities. ||5|| Men with mixed characteristics do not become kings; they merely enjoy happiness during the periods <term>Dasha: planetary cycles</term> of the aforementioned planets like Mars. Variations or "blending" in men occur due to a planet's placement in an enemy's sign, moving from exaltation to debilitation or vice versa, and the aspects of benefic or malefic planets. ||6||

The height of a **Hamsa** man is ninety-six digits <term>Angul: a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's width</term>, and his arm span <note>The width when both arms are extended</note> is also ninety-six digits. By increasing this measure by three digits for each subsequent type, one finds the height and span for the **Shasha**, **Ruchaka**, **Bhadra**, and **Malavya** types respectively. ||7||

A man of **Sattvic** (pure) nature possesses compassion, stability, honesty toward all living beings, and devotion to priests and deities. A **Rajasic** (passionate) man is attached to poetry, arts like dance and music, rituals, and women, and is extremely heroic. ||8|| A **Tamasic** (dark/ignorant) man is a deceiver of others, foolish, lazy, irritable, and sleeps excessively. By the combination of these three qualities—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—men of mixed temperaments are formed. There are four such combinations (Sattva-Rajas, Sattva-Tamas, Rajas-Tamas, and Sattva-Rajas-Tamas) and the three pure qualities previously mentioned, making seven types of men in total. ||9||

The arms of a **Malavya** man are like an elephant's trunk, reaching down to his knees. All the joints of his limbs are well-fleshed and firm. His body is symmetrically beautiful with a slender waist. Measured vertically, his face from chin to forehead is thirteen digits, and the diagonal width from the chin to the ear-hole is ten digits. This man's face is characterized by bright eyes, beautiful cheeks, even and white teeth, and a thin lower lip. ||10|| That **Malavya** man rules over the regions of Malwa, Maha, Kutch (Bharuch), Saurashtra (Surat), Laat, and Sindh. He acquires wealth through his prowess and becomes a king. He protects those living in the Pariyatra mountains and is endowed with noble intelligence. ||11|| After enjoying a lifespan of seventy years, this **Malavya** man gives up his life at a holy pilgrimage site. The characteristics of the Malavya type have been well described; now the characteristics of the remaining men, starting with Bhadra, are told. ||12||

A **Bhadra** man has firm, even, round, and long arms. His height is equal to his arm span. His cheeks are covered with soft, fine, and thick hair. Through the influence of Mercury, a man with these characteristics is known as a **Bhadra**. ||13||

The **Bhadra** <note>The "Auspicious" type, governed by Mercury</note> man possesses the essence of skin and strength; he has a broad and well-developed chest and is endowed with great courage. His face resembles that of a tiger; he is of a steady nature, patient, righteous, grateful, walks with the gait of a lordly elephant, and is well-versed in many scriptures. ||14|| He is intelligent, has a beautiful body, a handsome forehead and temples, is skilled in arts such as dance and song, possesses fortitude, a well-formed abdomen, and a luster like the interior of a lotus. He has well-proportioned hands and feet, is a yogi, has a beautiful nose, and even, joined eyebrows. ||15||

His body carries a fragrance like that of earth sprinkled with fresh rain, or like the scent of cassia leaves, saffron, elephant ichor <note>The aromatic secretion of an elephant in rut</note>, or aloe-wood. His head hair grows singly from each pore, and is black and curly. His private parts are concealed like those of a horse or an elephant. ||16|| Lines resembling a plow, a pestle, a mace, a sword, a conch, a discus, an elephant, a sea-monster <term>Makara: a legendary sea-creature in Hindu mythology</term>, a lotus, and a chariot are found on his hands and feet. Other men enjoy his wealth; he does not tolerate his kinsmen and is independent in his actions. ||17||

He is eighty-four <term>Angul: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly the width of a finger</term> tall. The weight of this man’s body is one <term>Tula: a unit of weight equal to two thousand Palas</term>. He becomes a king of the Middle Country <note>Madhyadesha, the central region of ancient India</note>. Previously, the height of men starting from the **Shasha** type was said to increase by three fingers each up to one hundred and eight fingers; if this **Bhadra** man reaches a height of one hundred and eight fingers, he becomes a universal emperor <term>Chakravarti: a supreme ruler whose chariot wheels roll everywhere without obstruction</term>. ||18|| After enjoying the earth acquired through his valor, the **Bhadra** man gives up his life at a holy pilgrimage site at the age of eighty and goes to heaven. ||19||

The man named **Shasha** <note>The "Hare" type, governed by Saturn</note>, born of the influence of Saturn, has slightly protruding teeth, and somewhat small nails and teeth. If his eye sockets are well-developed, he is swift-footed. He is devoted to science, metallurgy, and trade; he has full cheeks, achieves his own goals, is a commander of armies, fond of sexual union, attached to others' wives, restless, brave, devoted to his mother, and fond of forests, mountains, rivers, and active pursuits. ||20|| The **Shasha** man is ninety-two fingers tall. He is suspicious in all matters and knows the weaknesses of others. He possesses the essence of marrow, has a steady gait, and is not very stout. ||21||

The **Shasha** man’s middle part is slender. On his feet or hands, there are lines or upward-pointing marks in the shape of a shield, sword, lute, bed, garland, drum, and trident. ||22|| The **Shasha** man becomes a king of the lands of the barbarians <note>original: "Mlechchha-desha," referring to non-Vedic or foreign regions</note> or a local chieftain elsewhere. His body suffers from pain in the hips, secretions, and colic. In this manner, the **Shasha** man falls under the power of death at the age of seventy. ||23||

The **Hamsa** <note>The "Swan" type, governed by Jupiter</note> man, born of the influence of Jupiter <note>Original text says Shasha-purusha, likely a typo for Hamsa-purusha given the context of Jupiter and the subsequent verse</note>, has a reddish face, full cheeks, a high nose, a golden luster, and a round head. His eyes are the color of honey and all his nails are reddish. He has a sweet voice like a swan, beautiful feet, and all his senses are clear. ||24|| This **Hamsa** man has a fondness for water and possesses the essence of semen. Sages say his height is ninety-six fingers. ||25|| The **Hamsa** man rules over the lands of Khasa, Shurasena, Gandhara, Kandahar, and Antarvedi. After enjoying his kingdom for ninety years, he meets death in the forest. ||26||

The man named **Ruchaka** <note>The "Radiant" type, governed by Mars</note>, born of the influence of Mars, has beautiful eyebrows and hair. He is of a reddish-dark complexion, has a neck like a conch shell, and a long face. He is brave, cruel, an excellent minister, a leader of thieves, and industrious. ||27|| The length of the **Ruchaka's** face...

The measurement of the squareness of the middle part [of the body] is determined by this. Four times the height of the face constitutes the thickness of the middle part. Such a person possesses moderate luster, has blood and flesh as their primary constitutional strength <note>Sanskrit: *Sāra* - the essential quality of the body</note>, is a slayer of enemies, and achieves his goals through courage. || 28 ||

The hands and feet of a **Ruchaka** man are marked with lines in the shapes of a staff with a skull (*Khatvanga*), a lute (*Veena*), a bull, a bow, a thunderbolt, a spear, the moon, and a trident. He is a devotee of Gurus, Brahmins, and the Gods; he stands one hundred digits (*Angul*) tall, and his body weight is one thousand *Palas* <note>An ancient unit of weight</note>. || 29 ||

That **Ruchaka** man is skilled in mantras and occult rites such as *marana* (lethal magic) and *uchatana* (causing distraction or ruin). His knees and shins are slender. After enjoying sovereignty over the lands of the Vindhya mountains, the Sahyadri range, and Ujjain, the **Ruchaka** king meets his end at the age of seventy through weapons or fire. || 30 ||

Apart from these five Great Men (*Mahapurushas*), there are five types of men known as "Mixed" (*Sankirna*). These are the **Vamanaka**, **Jaghanya**, **Kubja**, **Mandalaka**, and **Saami**. These are the servants of the five aforementioned kings. Now hear the characteristics of these five: || 31 ||

The **Vamanaka** (Dwarf) has all limbs complete, but his back is hunched. He is somewhat deficient in the thighs, middle section, and the space between the armpits. This man known as **Vamanaka** is famous; among the five kings, he is a follower of the **Bhadra** king. He is prosperous, charitable, and a devotee of Lord Narayana (Vishnu). || 32 ||

The man named **Jaghanya** is a servant of the **Malavya** king. His ears resemble the half-moon; he is endowed with a pleasant scent, has semen as his primary constitutional strength, is a backbiter (informant), and a scholar. His bodily luster is dry, and the fingers of his hands are thick. || 33 ||

That man is cruel, wealthy, of coarse intellect, and famous. His complexion is like the color of copper, and he has a fondness for laughing. On the chest, feet, and hands of that **Jaghanya** man, there are lines in the shape of a sword, a spear, a noose, and an axe. || 34 ||

The **Kubja** (Hunchback) man is well-formed below the navel but somewhat wasted and bent above the navel. He serves the **Hansa** king. He is an atheist, wealthy, learned, cruel, an informant, and grateful. || 35 ||

**Kubja** men are experts in the arts, fond of quarrels, possessed of many servants, and are conquered by women (henpecked). He honors people and then suddenly abandons them. This described **Kubja** man remains full of enthusiasm at all times. || 36 ||

The man named **Mandalaka** is a servant of the **Ruchaka** king. He is knowledgeable in occult rites (*Abhichara*), skilled in the invocation of spirits (*Kritya*) and the raising of vampires (*Vetala*), and is a lover of the sciences. || 37 ||

He has an appearance like an old man, with hard and dry hair. He is skilled in destroying enemies, a Brahmin, and applies his intellect to the gods, sacrifices, and Yoga. He is conquered by women and is highly intelligent. || 38 ||

The man named **Saami** has an extremely deformed body. He is a servant to the **Shasha** king, is charitable, and completes great tasks after starting them. In terms of qualities, that **Saami** man is equal to the **Shasha** king himself. || 39 ||

---

# Varahi Samhita
## Chapter 70
### The Characteristics of Women

If a young woman’s feet are glossy, elevated, thin, and have copper-colored nails; if they are even, well-fleshed, beautiful, and have hidden ankles; and if the toes are closely set and the soles have the luster of a lotus—a man should marry her if he desires to become a lord of the earth. (1)

Feet marked with the signs of a fish, a goad <note>a tool used to guide elephants</note>, a lotus, a grain of barley, a thunderbolt, a plow, or a sword, which do not sweat and have soft soles, are highly praised. The shanks should be hairless, without visible veins, and well-rounded. The two knees should be symmetrical with joints that are not prominent. (2)

The thighs should be firm, like the trunk of an elephant, and hairless. The private parts should be wide, shaped like a leaf of the sacred fig tree. The hips and forehead should be broad and elevated like the shell of a tortoise, and the clitoris <note>original: "mani"</note> should be hidden; such features bring great fortune. (3)

A waist that is broad and well-fleshed, and heavy hips, support a girdle of bells. The navel of a woman is praised when it is deep, wide, and circles toward the right. (4)

A woman’s middle should have three folds <note>a traditional mark of beauty in ancient India</note> and be hairless. The breasts should be rounded, firm, equal in size, and hard. A chest that is hairless and soft, and a neck shaped like a conch shell, bring wealth and happiness. (5)

The lower lip should resemble the *Bandhujiva* flower <note>a bright red flower</note>, be fleshy, and have the beautiful shape of a *Bimba* fruit. The teeth of women should be even and resemble jasmine buds; such teeth grant the husband happiness and immense wealth. (6)

Speech that is kind, honest, and as sweet as the call of a cuckoo or a swan, and which is not dejected, brings great joy. The nose should be symmetrical with even nostrils and beautiful. The eyes should possess the captivating luster of blue lotus petals. (7)

The eyebrows are praised when they do not meet, are not too thick, and do not hang down, but are shaped like the crescent of the new moon. A forehead shaped like a half-moon, hairless, neither sunken nor too protruding, is auspicious. (8)

The pair of ears is praised when they are well-fleshed, soft, even, and well-attached. The hair should be glossy, black, soft, curled, and grow from single roots to bring happiness. The head should be symmetrical. (9)

If on the feet or the palms there are marks of a golden pitcher, a throne, a horse, an elephant, a chariot, a wish-fulfilling tree, a sacrificial post, an arrow, a garland, an earring, a fly-whisk, a goad, a barley grain, a mountain, a flag, a gateway, a fish, a *swastika* <note>an ancient symbol of well-being</note>, an altar, a fan, a conch, an umbrella, or a lotus—such women attain the status of a queen. (10)

Hands with hidden wrist joints, resembling the interior of a young lotus, with thin and long fingers, belong to the wives of kings. A palm that is neither sunken nor raised and is endowed with good lines ensures a woman will not be widowed for a long time and will enjoy the happiness of children and wealth. (11)

A line rising from the wrist and going to the middle finger on the palm of a woman—or a line rising upward on the sole of the foot—brings the joy of sovereignty to either a woman or a man. (12)

A line originating from the base of the little finger and reaching the space between the forefinger and middle finger indicates a long life. If the line is shorter, the lifespan is reduced accordingly. (13)

At the base of the thumb, the lines indicate offspring: thick lines represent sons and thin lines represent daughters. If these lines are unbroken in the middle, the children will have long lives; if they are broken or short, their lives will be brief. (14)

Thus, the auspicious signs of women have been described. Those that are the opposite are considered inauspicious. I shall now briefly recount those specific features that yield unfavorable results. (15)

If a woman’s little toe or the toe next to it does not touch the ground, or if the second toe <note>the "index" toe</note> is longer than the big toe, she will be of loose character and very sinful. (16)

Shanks that are bulging, veiny, or dry; shanks that are hairy or excessively fleshy; private parts that circle to the left, are sunken, or small; and a belly shaped like a pot—these belong to women who suffer. (17)

A short neck leads to poverty; a very long neck leads to the destruction of the family.

# Chapter 70 with Hindi Commentary

A woman with a very thick neck displays a fierce and violent nature. || 18 || She whose eyes are squinted <note>original: "kekara"</note> or reddish-brown <note>original: "pingala"</note> is of bad character; the same applies to one with dark, wandering eyes. Those who have deep dimples in their cheeks when they smile are undoubtedly said to be unchaste <note>original: "bandhaki," a term for a woman of loose morals</note>. || 19 || A pendulous forehead brings harm to the brother-in-law; a pendulous belly brings harm to the father-in-law; and pendulous buttocks bring harm to the husband. A woman with an excessively hairy upper lip or one who is exceptionally tall is not auspicious for her husband. || 20 || Breasts that are hairy, discolored, or uneven bring misery, as do uneven ears. Teeth that are thick, projecting <note>original: "karala"</note>, uneven, or have dark gums lead to suffering and a tendency toward theft. || 21 || Women whose hands resemble those of carnivorous animals—such as wolves, crows, herons, snakes, or owls—or whose hands are dry, veiny, and uneven, will be devoid of happiness and wealth. || 22 || She who has a protruding upper lip and hair with rough ends is fond of quarreling. Generally, defects reside in those who are ill-formed, for where there is beauty <note>original: "akriti," referring to a balanced form</note>, there virtues dwell. || 23 || The feet including the ankles are designated as the first part; the shanks along with the knees are the second. The private organs and the scrotum <note>Note: Though the text mentions male parts here, in this context of general physiognomy, it refers to the pelvic region</note> are the third; the navel and the waist are called the fourth. || 24 || The abdomen is called the fifth; the heart and the breasts are the sixth. The collarbones are the seventh; the lips and the neck are the eighth. || 25 || The eyes and eyebrows are the ninth; the forehead and the head are the tenth. Inauspicious signs in these ten parts yield inauspicious results, while auspicious signs yield happiness. || 36 || <note>The numbering jumps from 25 to 36 in the source, likely a scribal or printing error.</note>

The soles of her feet should possess the luster of a lotus. || 1 || Those feet are best which bear the marks of a fish, a goad, a lotus, a barley grain, a thunderbolt, a plow, or a sword; they should not sweat and should have soft soles. The shanks should be hairless, without visible veins, beautiful, and rounded. Both knees should be even and their joints should not be thick. Both thighs should be firm, resembling the trunk of an elephant and hairless. The private parts should be shaped like a peepal leaf and broad. The hips and waist should be broad and elevated like the shell of a tortoise; such hidden features bring great fortune <note>original: "Lakshmi"</note>. || 2-3 || Women with broad, well-fleshed, and heavy buttocks, adorned with a waist-belt <note>original: "kanchi-kalap"</note>, and who possess a deep, wide navel that turns to the right, are auspicious. || 4 || A woman whose middle section has three folds <note>term: "trivali" — three folds of skin on the abdomen, considered a mark of beauty in ancient India</note>, is hairless, and has breasts that are round, firm, even, and hard, is auspicious. A hairless and soft chest, and a neck resembling a conch shell with three lines, brings wealth and happiness. || 5 || If the lower lip is as red as the Bandhujiva flower, fleshy, and beautiful like a Bimba fruit, and the teeth are even and like jasmine buds, she brings her husband happiness and great wealth. || 6 || She who is straightforward, free from deceit, and whose voice is as pleasant as a cuckoo or a swan and lacks any tone of misery, brings great joy. One with a beautiful nose with even nostrils is excellent. A gaze that rivals the beauty of blue lotus petals is auspicious. || 7 || Eyebrows are auspicious if they do not meet, are not too wide or long, and are curved like the crescent moon. ...nor is a high forehead considered auspicious. <note>Verse 8</note> Both ears are auspicious if they are lightly fleshed, soft, symmetrical, and close to the head. Hair that is glossy, very dark, soft, curly, and grows with a single strand from each pore brings happiness. The head is also auspicious if it is even—neither sunken nor protruding. <note>Verse 9</note>

Those women who have marks on their soles or palms in the shape of a *bhringara* <term>ritual water vessel</term>, a seat, a horse, an elephant, a chariot, a wood-apple tree, a sacrificial pillar, an arrow, a garland, earrings, a fly-whisk, a goad, a barley grain, a mountain, a flag, a ceremonial arch, a fish, a swastika, a sacrificial altar, a fan, an umbrella, or a lotus—such women become queens of kings. <note>Verse 10</note>

Hands belonging to queens have concealed wrists (meaning the joints are not protruding) and fingers with long, slender joints resembling the interior of a young lotus. A woman whose palm is neither too deep nor too high and is marked with excellent lines does not become a widow; she enjoys the happiness of children and wealth for a long time. <note>Verse 11</note>

In either a woman or a man, a line that rises from the wrist and reaches the middle finger, or a vertical line on the sole of the foot, brings the happiness of sovereignty. <note>Verse 12</note>

The span of life is determined by the line that starts from the base of the little finger and goes to the middle of the middle finger. If that line is complete, the lifespan is full; if the line is short, the lifespan should be known as correspondingly shorter. <note>Verse 13</note>

At the base of the thumb are the lines of progeny; among them, the large lines represent sons and the small lines represent daughters. Those lines in the middle that are unbroken belong to those with long lives; broken or short lines indicate short-lived offspring. <note>Verse 14</note>

The auspicious signs of women have been stated; signs contrary to these are inauspicious. We shall now briefly describe those signs that are particularly inauspicious. <note>Verse 15</note>

A woman whose little toe or the toe next to it (the ring toe) does not touch the ground, or whose second toe is longer than the big toe, is considered unchaste and sinful. <note>Verse 16</note>

Women suffer grief if their calves are pulled upward and covered in veins, or if their thighs are dry, hairy, or excessively stout. Similarly, those with pubic hair that swirls to the left, or who have a sunken or small vulva, or a stomach shaped like a pot, endure misery. <note>Verse 17</note>

A woman with a short neck is poor; a very long neck causes the ruin of the family; one with a thick neck is of a cruel nature. <note>Verse 18</note>

A woman whose eyes are squinted or tawny, or whose eyes are dark and restless, is unchaste. A woman whose cheeks develop dimples when she laughs is undoubtedly unchaste. <note>Verse 19</note>

One with a long forehead brings harm to her husband's younger brother; a long belly brings harm to the father-in-law; and a woman with long buttocks brings harm to her husband. A woman with much hair on her upper lip or one who is excessively tall is not auspicious for her husband. <note>Verse 20</note>

A woman whose breasts and ears are hairy, dirty, protruding, or of unequal size (one small, one large) suffers distress. One whose teeth are covered with dark flesh is a thief. <note>Verse 21</note>

Those women who have lines on their hands shaped like flesh-eating birds (such as vultures), wolves, crows, herons, snakes, or owls, or whose hands are dry, veiny, and irregular, are devoid of happiness and wealth. <note>Verse 22</note>

A woman whose upper lip is protruding and whose hair ends are coarse is fond of quarreling. Generally, defects are found in unattractive women, whereas in those of excellent beauty...

...possess these qualities. ||23|| For the purpose of determining the "Dasha" <note>A period of time in Vedic astrology where specific influences prevail</note> of body parts, the body is divided into ten sections: The feet and ankles are the first part; the shanks including the kneecaps are the second part; the genitals, thighs, and scrotum are the third part; the navel and waist are the fourth part. ||24|| The abdomen is the fifth part; the heart and breasts are the sixth part; the shoulders and the clavicle (the junction of the shoulders) are the seventh part; the lips and neck are the eighth part. ||25|| The eyes and eyebrows are the ninth part; and the forehead and head are the tenth part. If the limbs starting from the feet are endowed with inauspicious marks, the fruit of their specific Dasha period will be auspicious <note>This suggests a compensatory astrological principle where certain physical defects might result in positive timing later in life</note>. ||26||

# Now begins the Seventy-First Chapter
## Signs of Tears in Garments

The gods reside in the corners of a garment; humans reside in the middle area between the edges and the fringe. The remaining three parts are the portions of the *Nishacharas* <note>Night-walkers or demons</note>; the same applies to beds, seats, and sandals. ||1|| If a garment is stained with ink, cow dung, mud, and the like, or if it is torn, burnt, or burst, one should understand the omen. The effect is full in a new garment, moderate in one slightly worn, and minimal in one long-used. The sin or merit (inauspicious or auspicious result) is most significant regarding the upper garment. ||2|| If a tear occurs in the portions assigned to the *Rudrakshas* <note>The demonic/fierce portions</note>, it signifies death; in the human portion, it signifies the birth of a son and glory; in the portion of the gods, it signifies enjoyment; and at the edges, it signifies an increase in enjoyment—though they say all results at the edges are temporary. ||3|| Even if a tear occurs in the divine portion, if its shape resembles a vulture, a water-bird, an owl, a pigeon, a crow, a beast of prey, a jackal, a donkey, a camel, or a snake, it brings fear equal to death to men. ||4|| If the shape of the tear resembles an umbrella, a flag, a *Swastika* <note>An ancient symbol of well-being</note>, a *Vardhamana* <note>A specific auspicious diagram</note>, a *Shrivatsa* <note>The mark of Vishnu</note>, a water-pot, a lotus, or a ceremonial arch, it bestows wealth upon men before long, even if the tear is in the demonic portion. ||5||

<column-break/>

Wearing a new garment under the *Ashwini* nakshatra <note>Star constellation</note> brings many clothes; under *Bharani*, it takes away one's livelihood; under *Krittika*, it is consumed by fire; under *Rohini*, it brings success in undertakings. ||6|| Under *Mrigashira*, there is danger from mice; under *Ardra*, there is loss of life; under *Punarvasu*, there is the arrival of good fortune; and under *Pushya*, there is a union with wealth. ||7|| Under *Ashlesha*, the garment is lost; under *Magha*, one should predict death; under *Purva Phalguni*, there is danger from the king; and under *Uttara Phalguni*, there is the arrival of wealth. ||8|| Under *Hasta*, success in work is achieved; under *Chitra*, there is the arrival of good things; under *Svati*, there is good food; and under *Vishakha*, one becomes popular among people. ||9|| Under *Anuradha*, there is a meeting with friends; under *Jyeshtha*, the garment is destroyed; under *Mula*, there is a danger of drowning; and under *Purva Ashadha*, there is illness. ||10|| Under *Uttara Ashadha*, one receives sweet food; under *Shravana*, there is eye disease; under *Dhanishta*, the acquisition of grain is known; and under *Shatabhisha*, there is great fear caused by poison. ||11|| Under *Purva Bhadrapada*, there is fear arising from water; under *Uttara Bhadrapada*, there is the birth of a son; and under *Revati*, they say one acquires gems—provided one desires to wear a new garment. ||12|| According to the opinion of the Brahmins, a garment given by a king or obtained during a marriage ceremony may be worn even if the astrological qualities are lacking; wearing such a new garment will yield desired results. ||13|| It is praised to wear a new garment even during inauspicious constellations if it is for a marriage, for honoring a king, or if approved by Brahmins. ||14||

->Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, named "Signs of Tears in Garments," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. ||71||<-

# The Brihat Samhita
<note>original: "Varahi Samhita" - another name for the Brihat Samhita by Varahamihira</note>

Divide a new garment into nine parts to contemplate its effects: the four parts at the corners of the garment are inhabited by the **Gods**, the two parts at the ends of the borders <note>the edges or hems</note> are inhabited by **Humans**, and the three parts in the center are inhabited by **Demons**. The beginning of the cloth is called the *pashanta* and the end is called the *dashanta*; similarly, one should divide a bed, a seat, and sandals into nine parts to contemplate their fruits. || 1 ||

If a new garment is stained with ink, cow dung, mud, etc., or if it is cut, burnt, or torn, it results in entirely inauspicious fruits. If the garment is somewhat old, the ill effect is slight; if it is very old, the ill effect is negligible. This result is more pronounced in the case of an *uparna* <note>an upper garment or shawl worn over the shoulders</note>. || 2 ||

If there are holes or tears in the **Demonic** portions of the garment, the owner may face disease or death. If there are holes in the **Human** portions, it leads to the birth of a son and an increase in splendor. If there are holes in the **Divine** portions, there is an increase in enjoyments. However, if there are holes at the very edges of all parts, the sage Garga and others declare it to have an evil result. || 3 ||

If a hole takes the shape of a heron, a frog, an owl, a pigeon, a crow, meat-eating vultures, a jackal, a donkey, a camel, or a snake—even if it occurs in the **Divine** portion—it causes fear equal to death for men; what then to say if it occurs in the other portions? || 4 ||

If a hole takes the shape of an umbrella, a flag, a swastika, a *vardhamana* <note>a clay bowl or platter</note>, a wood-apple tree, a water-pot, a lotus, or a festoon, it quickly grants wealth to men even if it is in the **Demonic** portion; what then to say if it is in the other portions? || 5 ||

Wearing a new garment during the <term>Nakshatra</term> <note>Lunar mansion/constellation</note> of **Ashwini** brings many more clothes; in **Bharani**, it leads to the loss of clothes; in **Krittika**, the cloth may be burnt; in **Rohini**, there is the acquisition of wealth. || 6 ||

In **Mrigashira**, there is fear of mice damaging the cloth; in **Ardra**, death; in **Punarvasu**, the attainment of auspiciousness; in **Pushya**, gain of wealth. || 7 ||

Wearing it in **Ashlesha** leads to the destruction of the garment; in **Magha**, death; in **Purva Phalguni**, fear from the king; in **Uttara Phalguni**, the acquisition of wealth. || 8 ||

In **Hasta**, success in work is achieved; in **Chitra**, the attainment of auspiciousness; in **Swati**, obtaining excellent food; in **Vishakha**, becoming dear to people. || 9 ||

In **Anuradha**, meeting with friends; in **Jyeshtha**, the depletion of the garment; in **Mula**, drowning in water; in **Purva Ashadha**, the onset of disease. || 10 ||

In **Uttara Ashadha**, obtaining sweet food; in **Shravana**, eye disease; in **Dhanishta**, gain of grain; in **Shatabhisha**, great fear of poison. || 11 ||

In **Purva Bhadrapada**, fear of water; in **Uttara Bhadrapada**, the birth of a son; and if a man wears a new garment in the **Revati** Nakshatra, he obtains jewels. || 12 ||

Wearing a new garment even during an inauspicious Nakshatra is auspicious if done by the command of a <term>Brahmin</term> <note>a member of the priestly/scholarly class</note>. A garment given by a King or received during a marriage should be accepted even during a bad Nakshatra, as it yields auspicious results. || 13 ||

In marriage, in the honor of a King, and by the command of Brahmins, wearing a garment even in a bad Nakshatra yields auspicious results. || 14 ||

->Thus ends the seventy-first chapter in the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the venerable Acharya Varahamihira. || 71 ||<-
