### Now Begins the Seventy-Second Chapter
#### Characteristics of the Fly-Whisk

> It is said that the gods created the *Chamari* <note>The Yak (Bos grunniens)</note> in the caves of the Himalayan mountains for the sake of their hair. The hair produced from their tails are yellowish, black, and white. ||1|| Glossiness, softness, abundance of hair, purity <note>meaning the hairs are not tangled</note>, a small central bone attachment, and whiteness are described as the wealth of qualities for these whisks. Those that are pierced, short, or sparse are not auspicious. ||2|| The handle of this whisk should be one and a half cubits, one cubit, or equal to a <term>Ratni</term> <note>A specific measurement: the length of a closed fist with the arm extended, roughly 15-18 inches</note> in length. It should be made of auspicious wood, covered in gold or silver, and studded with various gems for the benefit of kings. ||3|| For staffs, umbrellas, elephant-goads, canes, bows, canopies, spears, banners, and <term>Chowries</term> <note>Fly-whisks used as symbols of royalty and divinity</note>, the handles should be colored according to the social orders: pale-red for the first, tawny like honey for the second, and black for the others, to ensure prosperity. ||4|| If the joints of these handles are even-numbered, starting from two and increasing by two up to twelve, they bring destruction of the mother, loss of land, loss of wealth, ruin of the lineage, disease, and death respectively. ||5|| Success in journeys, destruction of enemies, great profit, acquisition of land, increase in livestock, and the attainment of desired objects are the results for the owners when the joints are odd-numbered, starting from three and increasing by two. ||6||

->Thus ends the seventy-second chapter titled "Characteristics of the Fly-Whisk" in the Brihat Samhita of Sri Varahamihira.<-

---

The gods created the Yak cows in the caves of the Himalayan mountains for the purpose of making fly-whisks. The hair of their tails is yellow, black, and white ||1||. If the whisk hair is oily, soft, and plentiful, clear (meaning pure and not tangled together), has a small bone at the base where the hair is attached, and is white in color, these are called the "wealth of qualities." Such hair is auspicious. Whisk hair that is broken, torn, short, or falling out is not auspicious ||2||. One should make the handle of that whisk one and a half cubits, one cubit, or equal to a <term>Ratni</term> in length. Making the handle from excellent wood, plating it with gold or silver, and embedding it with jewels is beneficial for kings (a closed fist is called a <term>Ratni</term>) ||3||. Staffs, umbrellas, goads, canes, bows, canopies, spears, banners, and <term>Chowries</term>—the handles for all these should be made for Brahmins; for Kshatriyas, they should be the color of sinew (mixed yellow and red); for Vaishyas, the color of honey; and for Shudras, black handles are appropriate ||4||. If these handles have even-numbered joints, increasing by two from two up to twelve, the results are as follows: a two-jointed handle causes the loss of the mother, four joints cause loss of land, six joints cause loss of wealth, eight joints cause death and ruin of the family, ten joints cause the onset of disease, and a twelve-jointed handle causes death ||5||. From three joints onwards, increasing by two (odd numbers), the results for the owners are: a three-jointed handle brings victory in travel, five joints bring destruction of enemies, seven joints bring great profit, nine joints bring acquisition of land, eleven joints bring an increase in cattle, and a thirteen-jointed handle brings the attainment of desired objects ||6||.

->Thus ends the seventy-second chapter in the Hindi commentary on the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihira, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region.<-

## Chapter Seventy-Three

### Characteristics of the Umbrella
<note>The umbrella (Chatra) was a primary symbol of sovereignty and status in ancient India.</note>

An umbrella should be constructed from the feathers of swans, roosters, peacocks, or cranes. It should be covered all around with a fresh, white silk cloth <note>original: "dukūla"</note> || 1 ||

It should be adorned with pearls, draped with hanging garlands, and fitted with a handle made of crystal. The staff should be six cubits <note>term: "hasta" (cubit) — a measurement from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches</note> long, plated in pure gold, and consist of either seven or nine joints || 2 ||

The width of the umbrella should be half the length of the staff (three cubits). It should be well-joined, decorated with gems, and lofty. Such an umbrella brings welfare and victory to the King || 3 ||

For the Crown Prince, the Queen, the General, and the Commander of Justice <note>term: "Dandanayaka" — a high-ranking official or magistrate</note>, the staff should be four and a half cubits long, and the width of the umbrella should be two and a half cubits || 4 ||

For others of high rank, the sun-shielding umbrella should be decorated at the top with "grace-bands" <note>original: "prasadapatta" — ornamental fillets or headbands described in previous chapters</note>, adorned with hanging gem-garlands, and made of peacock feathers || 5 ||

For ordinary men, a four-sided (square) umbrella should be made to ward off cold and sun. For Brahmins <note>the priestly class</note>, the umbrella should be perfectly circular and equipped with a handle || 6 ||

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter of the Bṛhat Saṃhitā by Shri Varāhamihira, titled "Characteristics of the Umbrella." || 73 ||

## Chapter Seventy-Four

### Praise of Women

In the conquest of the earth, the city is the essence; in the city, the house; in the house, a specific chamber. Even there, the bed is the best part, and upon the bed, a woman radiant with jewels is the very essence of royal pleasure || 1 ||

Jewels adorn a woman, but a woman is not merely adorned by the luster of gems <note>i.e., her natural beauty surpasses the gems</note>. Women captivate the heart even without jewels, but jewels offer no delight without the company of a woman || 2 ||

For those who must suppress their outward appearance <note>maintain a "poker face"</note>, those rising to conquer enemy forces, those contemplating the complexities of statecraft, and those weighing what has been done and what is yet to be done—

# Chapter 74: In Praise of Women

Entangled in a hundred branches of business and affairs, kings who follow the counsel of ministers and are constantly suspicious of everyone around them live in a vast ocean of sorrow. For them, the only small drop of happiness is the embrace of a beloved woman. (3)

Whether heard, seen, touched, or even just remembered, women bring joy to men. The Lord of the World <note>The Creator, Brahma</note> has created no gem superior to woman. For her sake, both religious merit and wealth are pursued, as well as the joys of having children. Therefore, women should be honored as the Goddesses of Fortune in the home, treated with constant respect and provided with riches. (4)

Those who speak of the faults of women, ignoring their virtues in the name of the path of renunciation <note>The ascetic path of Vairagya</note>, are—in my opinion—wicked people. Their words are not born of truth or goodness. (5)

Tell me truly: what fault is there in women that has not been practiced by men? It is only through sheer audacity that men disparage women, even though women possess superior virtues. Indeed, Manu <note>The ancient lawgiver</note> has stated this as well: (6)

The Moon gave them purity; the Gandharvas <note>Celestial musicians</note> gave them refined speech; and Agni <note>The Fire God</note> gave them total purification. Therefore, women are eternally pure. (7)

Brahmins are pure at their feet; cows are pure on their backs; goats and horses are pure in their mouths; but women are pure in every limb. (8)

Women are an incomparable source of purity; they are never defiled. Month after month, their menstrual flow washes away their impurities. (9)

Those households where women are not honored and thus pronounce a curse, perish utterly as if struck by a dark power. (10)

Whether as a wife or a mother, the very existence of men is due to women. O ungrateful men! How can you find happiness while slandering them? (11)

The scriptures declare that the fault of infidelity is equal for both husband and wife. Men pay no heed to this law, yet in this regard, women are superior <note>because they generally maintain their vows while men do not</note>. (12)

A man who violates his marriage vow must wear the skin of a donkey with the hair turned outward and beg for alms for six months, saying "Give to one who has strayed," before he is purified. (13)

The desire for love does not leave a man even in a hundred years. Men only cease their pursuits through physical inability, whereas women cease through their own fortitude and restraint. (14)

Oh, the audacity of the wicked who slander innocent women! They are like thieves who, while they themselves are stealing, shout at others, "Stop, thief!" (15)

The sweet, flattering words a man speaks to a woman in private are forgotten by him later. But women, out of gratitude for past kindness, will even embrace the lifeless bodies of their husbands and enter the Seven-Tongued Fire <note>The funeral pyre</note>. (16)

A man who enjoys the "gem of a woman" is a king unto himself, even if he possesses nothing else. The essence of a kingdom is food and women; all else is merely fuel for the fire of greed. (17)

To hold a young woman in the prime of youth, who speaks with a soft, sweet, and gentle voice—I believe such pleasure is not to be found even in the abode of the Creator. (18)

Tell me, what happiness is there in the abode of the Creator, where one must serve those served by gods, sages, perfected beings, and celestial singers, compared to the joy of a man who holds a woman? (19)

From the Creator down to the smallest insect, this entire world is bound together by the union of male and female. Why feel shame here, when even the Four-Faced Lord <note>Brahma</note> was driven by the beauty of a young woman to grow four faces just to look at her? (20)

->Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "In Praise of Women,"<-
->in the Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira, within the section on the Inner Court.<-

---

Even if a King conquers the entire earth, his capital city is the essence of it. In that city, his home is the essence; in the home, his private quarters; in those quarters, his bed; and on that bed, the essence is a woman adorned with jewels. This is the true essence of the joy of sovereignty.

# The Varahamihira Samhita
## (Page 254)

...and all other objects are essence-less. ||1|| A woman adorns jewels; women are not merely adorned by the luster of jewels. The reason is that a woman, even without jewels, captivates the heart, whereas jewels cannot captivate the heart without being in contact with a woman’s body. ||2||

For kings—who must hide their expressions of joy or sorrow, who rise to conquer the strength of enemies, who are agitated by the branches of hundreds of tasks (done or undone), who contemplate the systems of governance, who follow the policies dictated by ministers, and who remain suspicious even of their own sons and wives—for such kings, who are submerged in an ocean of sorrow, the embrace of a woman is the only small measure of happiness. ||3||

The Creator <note>Vidhatā/Brahma</note> has not fashioned any jewel other than woman, the mere hearing of whom, the touching of whom, the seeing of whom, or the remembering of whom brings immediate joy to the heart. It is for the sake of woman that men pursue Virtue <term>Dharma: religious and moral duty</term> and Wealth <term>Artha: material prosperity</term>. The gain of sons and the pleasures of the senses are obtained through woman alone. A woman is the Fortune <note>Lakshmi: the goddess of prosperity and the home</note> of the household; therefore, it is proper to honor women at all times with respect and luxury. ||4||

It is the firm conviction of our school of thought that those men who, abandoning the virtues of women, speak of their faults through the path of renunciation <note>Vairagya: the ascetic path of detachment</note>, are wicked men. For this reason, the words of those wicked people are not authoritative. ||5||

If you are detached, then speak the truth yourself: what fault is there in women that was not first committed by men? (All faults were first committed by men, and later women learned them from men). Men have overcome women through audacity; in reality, women possess more virtues than men. Even Manu, the chief teacher of the Law Books <term>Dharmashastra: ancient legal and ethical texts</term>, has said this regarding this subject: ||6||

The Moon gave them purity, the Gandharvas <note>celestial musicians</note> gave them refined speech, and Agni <note>the Fire God</note> gave women the ability to consume all things (purification); therefore, women are equal to gold. ||7||

The feet of Brahmins, the backs of cows, and the mouths of goats and horses are sacred, but all the limbs of women are sacred. ||8||

There is no other substance as pure as women; they can never be defiled, because month after month they have their menses, which takes away all their sins. ||9||

Those houses which a noble woman <term>Kulastri: a woman of good family/lineage</term>, when disrespected, curses—those houses, as if struck by a malevolent spirit <note>Kritya: a destructive deity or spell</note>, meet with destruction on all sides. ||10||

Whether she be a wife or a mother, the birth of men happens from women alone; that is, one is born in the form of a son from a wife, and one is born directly from a mother. O ungrateful men! How can any good come to you by slandering your wife and mother? ||11||

In the Law Books, the fault is said to be equal for men and women in the case of adultery; however, men see no fault in their own adultery with other women, yet they see fault when a woman is with another man. Therefore, women are superior to men. ||12||

That man who, abandoning his own wife, associates with another woman, must wear the skin of a hairy donkey with the fur facing outward and wander for six months saying "Give me alms" <note>original: "Bhikshandehi"</note>—that is, he must beg for food—only then does he become pure. ||13||

Even after a hundred years pass, the lust of men does not leave them; however, men desist only because the strength of the body declines, whereas women desist through their own patience and fortitude. ||14||

Look! The wickedness of those villains who slander innocent women is just like a thief who, while stealing, shouts at the master of the house, "Hey thief! Stand still!" All these are the words of the Law Books. ||15||

The sweet words a man speaks to a woman in private when overcome by passion, he does not speak those same words from his heart (later); yet a woman, out of her gratitude, embraces her dead husband and enters the fire <note>A reference to the historical practice of Sati, framed here as an act of ultimate devotion</note>. ||16||

Even a poor man who enjoys an excellent woman...

...is the king, because the essence of a kingdom consists of only two things: food and an excellent woman. All other materials—elephants, horses, gems, and gold—are merely wood to ignite the fire of greed <note>original: "trishna," meaning insatiable desire or thirst</note>. ||17|| It is our belief that the happiness derived from embracing a young, gentle, beautiful, and delicate woman who speaks softly and has high breasts is a happiness not found even in the world of Brahma <note>Brahmaloka, the highest heaven</note>. ||18|| In the world of Brahma, gods, sages, perfected beings, and celestial singers merely offer respect to the respectable and serve those worthy of service; what other happiness is there in that realm that cannot be obtained by embracing a woman in solitude? ||19|| From the creator Brahma down to the smallest insect, the entire world is bound by the union of male and female. ### Now begins the Seventy-Fifth Chapter
## On the Acquisition of Fortune and Beauty
<term>Saubhagyakaranam: The art of becoming beloved or fortunate in love.</term>

The pleasure of love is natural and complete for a fortunate man, but for others, it is a mere shadow because their minds are not united. A woman bears a child resembling the man whom she contemplates in her heart, even if he is far away. || 1 || Just as a branch of a tree broken off and planted in the earth, or a seed sown in it, does not become something else, so too the soul is born again through women; any variation therein is due to the quality of the "field" <note>the womb or the mother</note>. || 2 || The soul joins with the mind, the mind with the senses, and the senses with their objects—this sequence is instantaneous. This very union is the power of the mind; is there anything unreachable? Wherever the mind goes, there the soul has gone. || 3 || This soul, residing in the heart, is extremely subtle and can be grasped only by a steady mind through constant practice. Since one becomes that which he meditates upon, young women have attained the state of being fortunate <note>beloved</note> through such focus. || 4 ||

Courtesy <note>Dakshinya: sincerity and kindness</note> is the sole cause of being beloved; behavior contrary to that causes hatred. Through the use of spells, medicines, and deceptive tricks, many evils arise, but never true peace or happiness. || 5 || By abandoning pride, one attains the state of being a favorite; egoism brings about misfortune. An arrogant man accomplishes his tasks with great difficulty, whereas one who speaks kindly achieves them with ease. || 6 || True brilliance <note>Tejas</note> is not the love of reckless violence, nor is it speaking unpleasant or untruthful words. Those who complete their work without arrogance and do not boast are the truly brilliant ones. || 7 || He who desires universal popularity and fortune should speak of the virtues of everyone in their absence. He who speaks of the faults of others acquires many faults himself, even those he does not actually possess. || 8 || The world follows a man who is inclined to help everyone. The fame gained by helping even one's enemies in their times of distress cannot be matched by any small act of merit. || 9 ||

---

<note>1. This is an illustrative story: Once, while Mahadeva was seated in Kailash with Parvati on his lap, a celestial nymph named Tilottama began to circumambulate him. Out of respect/fear of Parvati, Mahadeva could not turn his head to look at her, but as she moved around him, a new face manifested in whichever direction she went. In this way, Mahadeva became four-faced.</note>

**Varahi Samhita**

**Even when one attempts to conceal them, virtues naturally increase and flourish. Only those who desire to destroy the virtues of others descend into the state of being a wicked person. || 10 ||**

## Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Creation of Good Fortune," in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira. || 75 ||

For a fortunate <note>Sanskrit: *subhaga*; one who is well-liked or possesses auspicious qualities</note> man, all the pleasures of the God of Love are supreme. However, for an unfortunate man, because a woman’s heart is not devoted to him, he experiences only a mere shadow of pleasure during intimacy, not true happiness. At the time of union, a woman conceives a child resembling the man she contemplates in her mind, even if he is far away. || 1 || Just as the specific graft or seed sown in the earth produces that exact tree and no other, so it is with women. The soul itself is reborn as the offspring; the variation occurs only due to the quality of the "field" <note>The mother's womb is traditionally compared to a field (*kshetra*)</note>. Just as trees are excellent in some soils and ordinary in others, the same should be understood regarding women. || 2 ||

The soul moves with the mind, the mind with the senses, and the senses with their objects, such as sound. This is the rapid sequence of the soul’s movement, and this is *Yoga* <note>Here referring to the union or connection of faculties</note>. No place is inaccessible to the mind, and wherever the mind goes, the soul follows. || 3 || This individual soul <term>Jivatma (the individual living soul as distinct from the universal spirit)</term>, in its extremely subtle form, resides within the heart amidst the Supreme Soul. One should perceive it with a steady mind through constant practice. Whatever a person meditates upon, they become one with that; therefore, a woman meditates only upon a fortunate man. || 4 ||

Acting in accordance with a woman's heart is the primary cause of "good fortune" <note>meaning being loved or attractive</note>; that is, a man becomes fortunate through courtesy and kindness <term>Dakshinya (sincerity, gallantry, or consideration)</term>. Conversely, acting against a woman's heart leads to <term>Vidveshana (causing hatred or aversion)</term>, making the man unfortunate. Using mantras, medicines, or deceptive magical practices <term>Indrajala (sorcery or illusion)</term> for subjugation <note>Vashikarana</note> only results in numerous faults and does no good. The primary means of winning a woman is courtesy, not spells or drugs. || 5 ||

By abandoning ego, a man becomes dear to everyone; through ego, he becomes disliked by all. An arrogant man accomplishes his tasks with great difficulty, while a sweet-spoken man achieves his goals with ease. || 6 || There is no true brilliance in acting without reflection, nor are the harsh words of the wicked considered superior. Those who do not boast even after completing a task are truly radiant. Talkative men possess no true luster. || 7 || A man who desires to be loved by all should praise everyone in their absence. People naturally attribute many faults to those who criticize others behind their backs. || 8 ||

All people will help a man who is intent on helping everyone. The fame gained by helping an enemy in their time of distress is not the result of minor merit; such an opportunity arises only through great past virtues. || 9 || No matter how much a wicked person tries to hide the virtues of the righteous, those virtues will only grow, like a fire covered by grass. He who seeks to erase the virtues of others only gains the reputation of a villain; the virtues themselves cannot be destroyed by anyone. || 10 ||

## Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter in the Hindi commentary on the Brihat Samhita, composed by Shri Varahamihira and translated by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. || 75 ||

# Now begins the Seventy-Sixth Chapter
## Aphrodisiacs <note>Sanskrit: *Kāndarpikam*, relating to Kandarpa/Kamadeva, the god of love.</note>

If the female's seed <note>original: *rakta*, referring to menstrual blood/ovum</note> is in excess at the time of conception, a female is born; if the male's seed <note>original: *shukra*, semen</note> is in excess, a male is born; if both are equal, a hermaphrodite is produced. Therefore, one should utilize elixirs <term>Rasayanas: Ayurvedic rejuvenation therapies</term> that increase the male seed. || 1 ||

The roof of a palace, the rays of the moon, wine with blue water-lilies, a beloved wife languid with passion, the lute <note>original: *vallaki*, a type of veena</note>, talk of love in private, and flower garlands—this collection is the snare of the God of Love. || 2 ||

He who consumes the powder of iron, honey-colored pyrite <note>original: *mākshika-dhātu*</note>, honey, mercury, chebulic myrobalan, bitumen <note>original: *shilajatu*</note>, and false black pepper <note>original: *vidanga*</note> mixed with clarified butter for twenty-one days—even if he is burdened by old age, even if he is eighty years old—he pleases a woman like a young man. || 3 ||

He who drinks milk boiled with the roots of cowhage <note>original: *kapikacchu*</note> does not suffer exhaustion with women. Or, one may eat black gram cooked in milk and clarified butter in portions of six mouthfuls, followed by a drink of milk. || 4 ||

One should take the powder of the *Vidarika* tuber <note>Pueraria tuberosa</note>, repeatedly soaked in its own juice and dried, and drink it with boiled milk and sugar; such a man can satisfy many women. || 5 ||

One who licks the powder of Indian gooseberry <note>original: *dhātri-phala*</note> well-mixed with its own juice, honey, sugar, and clarified butter, and then drinks milk according to his digestive capacity, may enjoy love as much as he desires. || 6 ||

A lover who repeatedly soaks sesame seeds in milk boiled with goat testicles, dries them well, and then eats them and drinks milk—what can even a sparrow <note>symbol of high virility in Sanskrit poetry</note> do to compete with him? || 7 ||

Men who eat *Shashtika* rice <note>rice that ripens in sixty days</note> with clarified butter and black gram soup, and drink milk afterward, spend their nights awake with the God of Love. || 8 ||

A mixture of sesame, *Ashwagandha*, cowhage roots, *Vidarika*, and *Shashtika* rice flour, ground with goat's milk and cooked in clarified butter, makes a fried cake <note>original: *shashkulika*</note> that is highly aphrodisiac. || 9 ||

By using the small caltrop <note>original: *gokshura*</note> with milk, or eating the tubers of *Vidarika*, one does not grow weary, provided he can digest it. If his digestion is weak, here is a powder for that: || 10 ||

A powder of Bishop’s weed <note>original: *ajmoda*</note>, salt, chebulic myrobalan, ginger, and long pepper, taken with wine, buttermilk, or warm water, kindles the digestive fire of the stomach. || 11 ||

A man who eats excessively sour, bitter, salty, or pungent foods, or too many alkaline dishes and leafy vegetables, becomes devoid of vision and virility; even if young, he makes many excuses when meeting a woman, just like an old man. || 12 ||

### Now begins the Seventy-Seventh Chapter

## The Preparation of Perfumes <note>Ghandhayukti</note>

> Garlands, scents, incense, fine clothes, and ornaments do not look beautiful on one with white hair. Therefore, one should attend to hair dye just as one attends to eye-salve and ornaments. || 1 || Cook *Kodrava* <note>Kodo millet</note> grains in an iron vessel until they are white, along with iron powder. Grind this finely and apply it to the head of a person with white, acidic hair <note>referring to hair chemistry or premature greying</note>. Cover it again with leaves for another two watches. When washed, the head will attain a deep black color. || 3 || Afterward, for the fragrant bath of the head—

After removing the smell of iron and acidity from the head with oils, one should enjoy the pleasures of the kingdom in the inner quarters <note>the harem or private royal chambers</note> using heart-pleasing scents and various types of incense. || 4 ||

A head-bath fit for kings is made of equal parts of cinnamon, *kushtha* <note>Saussurea lappa</note>, *renuka* <note>scented seeds</note>, *nalika* <note>a fragrant bark</note>, *sprikka* <note>Trigonella corniculata</note>, *rasa* <note>myrrh or resin</note>, *tagara* <note>Valeriana wallichii</note>, and *balaka* <note>Valeriana hardwickii</note>, mixed with saffron and *patra* <note>Cinnamomum tamala</note>. || 5 ||

A powder made of madder, "tiger-nail" <note>a dried shellfish operculum used as a fixative</note>, pearl-oyster shell, cinnamon, *kushtha*, and *rasa*, when mixed with oil and heated by the rays of the sun, creates an oil that smells like the *Champaka* flower. || 6 ||

Equal parts of *patra*, *turushka* <note>liquid storax</note>, *balaka*, and *tagara* create a scent that kindles desire. This same mixture, when combined with *bakula* <note>Mimusops elengi</note> and fumigated with *katuka* <note>bitter herbs</note> and asafoetida, changes its character. With *kushtha*, it smells like a blue lotus; with sandalwood, it becomes the aforementioned *Champaka*; and with jasmine, cinnamon, and coriander, it is known as the *Atimuktaka* <note>mountain jasmine</note> scent. || 7 ||

One part of *kunduruka* <note>frankincense</note>, a quarter part of "tiger-nail," and half a part of *turushka*, combined with sandalwood and *priyangu* <note>Aglaia elaeagnoidea</note>, creates a scent to be used as incense when mixed with molasses and "tiger-nail." || 8 ||

*Guggulu* <note>Indian bdellium</note>, *balaka*, lac, *musta* <note>nut-grass</note>, "tiger-nail," and sugar, in increasing order of proportions, form an incense. Another pill-shaped incense is made from *mamsi* <note>spikenard</note>, *balaka*, *turushka*, "tiger-nail," and sandalwood. || 9 ||

By using myrobalan, conch shell, *musta*, resin, and liquid storax, along with molasses and blue lotus, and increasing the proportions starting from a quarter-part, many enchanting incenses are produced. || 10 ||

With four parts each of white sandalwood, *shaila* <note>bitumen or lichen</note>, and *musta*, and one part each of *shrivasa* <note>turpentine resin</note>, *sarja* <note>sal resin</note>, "tiger-nail," and *guggulu*, then awakened <note>scent-enhanced</note> with camphor and mixed with honey, this incense is called "Anger-Coverer" <note>Kopacchada</note>, a favorite of kings. || 11 ||

A powder made of cinnamon, *ushira* <note>vetiver</note>, and *patra*, with half a part of fine cardamom, and awakened with musk and camphor, makes an excellent scented powder for clothes. || 12 ||

*Musta*, *balaka*, *shaileyaka*, *kachura*, *ushira*, *nagapushpa*, "tiger-nail," *sprikka*, *agaru* <note>agarwood</note>, *damanaka*, "tiger-nail," *tagara*, and coriander... || 13 ||

...along with camphor, *choraka*, and sandalwood—these sixteen ingredients may be varied at will. By choosing four ingredients at a time in proportions of one, two, three, or four parts, an "Ocean of Perfumes" <note>Gandharnava</note> is created. || 14 ||

Because of its very intense smell, one part of coriander should always be used. Camphor should be used in a smaller amount, while others may be given in two or three parts. || 15 ||

These should be fumigated with *shrivasa*, *sarja*, molasses, and "tiger-nail" in sequence, not while in a mass. The "awakening" scent should be given with musk combined with camphor. || 16 ||

In this system, there are four thousand, seventy thousand, one hundred thousand, and seven hundred and twenty varieties of perfumes <note>174,720 total combinations</note>. || 17 ||

If each ingredient is used in one part, or combined in two, three, or four parts, it creates a six-fold fragrance; similarly, it produces variations in two, three, and four parts. || 18 ||

From the combination of four substances, twenty-four scents arise; thus for the remaining groups, there are ninety-six in total here. || 19 ||

In a group of sixteen substances, when varied by choosing four at a time, eighteen hundred and twenty combinations are born. || 20 ||

Since the group of four-fold choices is divided into ninety-six varieties, that number should be multiplied by ninety-six to find the total number of perfumes. || 21 ||

Garlands, scents (perfumes, etc.), incense, clothes, and ornaments do not grace a man with white hair. Therefore, just as one makes an effort to apply collyrium to the eyes and wear ornaments, one should also make an effort to dye the hair. ॥ 1 ॥ Cook *Kodo* rice in vinegar in an iron vessel. Then, mix iron powder into that rice, grind it very finely, and set it aside. Afterward, moisten the hair with vinegar, apply the previously prepared paste, and sit with green leaves (such as castor leaves) wrapped over it. ॥ 2 ॥ After midday has passed, wash off this paste and apply a paste of *Amala* <note>Indian gooseberry</note>, wrap it with leaves again, and sit for another midday period. When the head is washed afterward, the hair becomes black. Once the hair is black, one should bathe the head, use fragrant oils, delightful scents, and various types of incense to remove the foul smell of iron and vinegar. Then, the King may enter the inner apartments and enjoy royal pleasures with his queens. ॥ 4 ॥ Take equal parts of cinnamon, *Kustha*, *Renuka*, *Nalika*, *Sprikka*, *Bolam*, *Tagara*, *Netrawala*, *Nagakeshara*, and *Gandhapatra*. Grind them, apply to the head, and wash. This is described as a head-bath worthy of Kings. ॥ 5 ॥ Take equal parts of madder, *Vyaghranakha*, *Shakti*, cinnamon, *Kustha*, and *Bolam*. Reduce them to powder and put them in sweet oil. If heated in the sun, that oil acquires the fragrance of Champaka flowers. ॥ 6 ॥ If one mixes *Patra*, *Sihlak*, *Netrawala*, and *Tagara* in equal parts, it becomes a scent that stimulates the God of Love <note>Kamadeva</note>. # Chapter 77: With Hindi Commentary
## (Page 261)

If one gives a fumigation of **Bitter Guggulu** <note>Indian Bdellium-tree resin</note>, a perfume is created with a scent similar to the **Bakula** flower <note>Spanish Cherry or Mimusops elengi</note>. By adding **Kuth** <note>Costus root</note> to this, the scent becomes like the **Blue Lotus**. By adding **White Sandalwood**, the scent becomes like the **Champaka** flower. If **Nutmeg**, **Cinnamon**, and **Coriander** are added to this, the scent becomes like the **Atimuktaka** flower <note>a type of jasmine or mountain creeper</note>. ||7||

Take **Fennel** and **Kunduraka** <note>resin of the Deodar tree</note> at one-quarter part each; **Nakha** <note>literally "nail," referring to the operculum of a shell used in incense</note> and **Silhaka** <note>Liquidambar orientalis or Altingia excelsa resin</note> at half a part (i.e., two-quarters) each; and **White Sandalwood** and **Gandhapriyangu** <note>a fragrant medicinal plant</note> at one-quarter part each. Prepare the perfume and fumigate it with **Jaggery** and **Nakha**. ||8||

Take **Guggulu**, **Netrawala** <note>Pavonia odorata</note>, **Lac**, **Musta** <note>Nut grass</note>, **Nakha**, and **Sugar** in equal parts to make an incense. Another incense ball <note>Pinda-dhupa</note> is made by taking equal parts of **Jatamansi** <note>Spikenard</note>, **Netrawala**, **Silhaka**, **Nakha**, and **Sandalwood**. ||9||

Take these nine substances: **Haritaki** <note>Chebulic Myrobalan</note>, **Shankha** <note>Conch shell powder</note>, **Nakha**, **Drava** <note>Myrrh or liquid resin</note>, **Netrawala**, **Jaggery**, **Kuth**, **Shailaka** <note>Lichen</note>, and **Musta**. Start with one part and increase up to nine. For example, one part Haritaki, two parts Shankha, three parts Nakha, and so on. By increasing the parts of Jaggery and Kuth, a second variety is made; by increasing Shailaka and Musta, a third. Or, one part Haritaki and two parts Shankha make one incense; adding three parts Nakha makes a second; adding four parts Myrrh makes a third. In this way, many delightful incenses are created. ||10||

Take **Sugar**, **Shaileya** <note>Lichen</note>, and **Musta**; four times their amount of **Shrivasa** <note>Turpentine resin</note> and two parts **Sarja** <note>Sal tree resin</note>; and two parts **Nakha** and **Guggulu**. Grind these and give them a "scent-awakening" <note>Bodha</note> with **Camphor** (meaning scent it with camphor powder), then mix with **Honey** to form a ball. This incense, named **Kopacchada**, is worthy of Kings. ||11||

Take three parts each of **Cinnamon**, **Khus** <note>Vetiver</note>, and **Patra** <note>Malabathrum leaf</note>, and half a part of **Small Cardamom**. Powder them all and give a "scent-awakening" with **Musk** and **Camphor**. This creates an excellent **Patvasa**—a powder used for scenting clothes. ||12||

**Musta**, **Netrawala**, **Shaileyaka**, **Kachur** <note>White Turmeric</note>, **Khus**, **Nagakesar** flowers, **Vyaghranakha** <note>Tiger-nail shell</note>, **Sprikka** <note>Delphinium brunonianum</note>, **Agarwood**, **Damanaka** <note>Artemisia</note>, **Nakha**, **Tagar** <note>Valerian</note>, **Coriander**, ||13|| **Camphor**, **Chora** <note>Angelica glauca</note>, and **White Sandalwood**. These are the sixteen fragrant substances. By selecting any four substances from these and varying their proportions as one, two, three, or four parts, the **Gandharnava** <note>literally "Ocean of Perfumes"</note> is created. ||14||

Among these, **Coriander** has an extremely strong scent; for this reason, one should always take only one part of Coriander. **Camphor** also has a very intense scent, so it is appropriate to take even less than one part. One should never take two or three parts of these two, otherwise they will suppress the scents of all other substances. ||15||

Fumigate all perfume ingredients with **Shrivasa**, **Resin**, **Jaggery**, and **Nakha**, but give each of these four fumigations separately, not mixed together. Afterward, give the "scent-awakening" with **Camphor** and **Musk**. ||16||

From these fragrant substances, **174,720** types of perfumes can be created. ||17||

If one takes one part of one substance and two, three, and four parts of the other substances, six types of perfumes are formed. In the same way, if one takes two, three, and four parts of that substance in sequence and mixes them with two parts of the others, six more perfumes are formed. ||18||

By mixing four substances, there will be twenty-four variations for a single substance; these together make ninety-six variations. ||19||

If one takes the sixteen types of fragrant substances mentioned and makes combinations of four substances each, there are 1,824 <note>likely a calculation of combinations</note> perfumes. ||20||

Ninety-six variations have been mentioned for the scent of four substances, and 1,820 variations occur by mixing different sets of four substances. Therefore, by multiplying 1,820 by 96, the previously mentioned perfume total of 174,720 is proven. ||21||

To understand the variations of perfumes, both the mathematical method <term>Ganita</term> and the permutation table <term>Prastara</term> are explained.

# Varahi Samhita

Write a vertical column of numbers starting from one up to the total number of substances. Add the bottom one to the two above it to make three; then add those three to the three above them to make six; add those to the four above them to make ten. Continue this summation in this manner, omitting the final number. Then, perform the summation of this new column, again omitting the final number. Continue creating as many columns as the number of substances you wish to select to find the variations. The number remaining at the top of the final column, after omitting the last, will be the total number of variations. <note>This describes a method of calculating combinations, similar to Pascal's Triangle, used here to determine how many different perfumes can be made from a set of ingredients.</note> ||22||

Take Aloe wood, Patra <gloss>scented leaf</gloss>, Turushka <gloss>liquid storax/Sihlak</gloss>, and Shaileya in parts of two, three, five, and eight. Take Priyangu, Musta, Rasa, <gloss>Bale</gloss>, and Kesh-Hiber in parts of five, two, eight, and three. ||23||

Take Sprikka, Cinnamon, Tagara, and Jatamansi in parts of four, one, seven, and six. Take White Sandalwood, Nakha, Shrivasa, and Kunduru in parts of seven, six, four, and one. ||24||

In the <term>Kachchaputa</term> <note>A grid-like arrangement or "box" used for mixing</note> of these sixteen substances, as written below, whenever the sum of the parts of any four substances equals eighteen, many types of <term>Gandhayoga</term> <note>perfume combinations</note> are formed. ||25||

Afterward, combine those perfumes with Nakha, Tagara, and Sihlak. Awaken <note>intensify the scent</note> them with Nutmeg, Camphor, and Musk, and fumigate them with incense made of Jaggery and Nakha. Because the sum equals eighteen when added from any direction in the <term>Kachchaputa</term>, these perfumes are called <term>Sarvatobhadra</term> <note>meaning "auspicious from all sides" or a perfect square</note>. ||26||

In this same <term>Kachchaputa</term>, take any four substances and scent them with Nutmeg, Musk, and Camphor. Soak them in Sahakara <gloss>the juice of highly fragrant mangoes and honey; they then produce many scents equal to the Parijata flower</gloss>. These are all <term>Mukhavasa</term> <note>mouth fresheners</note>, meaning the mouth becomes fragrant through these Parijata-scents. ||27||

By adding Sarja-rasa (resin) and Shrivasa to the perfumes mentioned in the first <term>Kachchaputa</term>, various types of incense are made. If one does not add Shrivasa and Sarja-rasa but instead adds Netrawala and Cinnamon, powders suitable for bathing are created; that is, one should apply them to the head and body before bathing. ||28||

From the <term>Kachchaputa</term> of these nine substances—Lodhra, Khus, Tagara, Aloe wood, Musta, Patra, Priyangu, Vana <gloss>a fragrant substance named Paripelva</gloss>, and Haritaki—take any three substances to make a perfume. ||29||

Mix them with one part Sandalwood, one part Sihlak, half a part Nakha, and a quarter part of Fennel. If you fumigate them with Guggulu and Jaggery, eighty-four perfumes are formed, smelling like the Bakula flower. By taking three substances at a time from nine, there are eighty-four variations; this should be verified by the previously mentioned method of <term>Prastara</term> <note>mathematical permutation/combination table</note>. ||30||

Take <term>Dantakasthas</term> <note>tooth-sticks or herbal toothbrushes</note>, soak them in cow urine mixed with Haritaki powder for seven days, and then place them in scented water. ||31||

Take equal parts of Cardamom, Cinnamon, Patra, Anjana, Honey, Black Pepper, Nagakesar, and Kushtha to make scented water. Soak those tooth-sticks in that scented water for some time. ||32||

Then take four parts Nutmeg, two parts Patra, one part Cardamom, and three parts Camphor. Make a fine powder of these and rub it over the tooth-sticks. Afterward, dry them in the sun and store them. ||33||

For the man who uses these prepared tooth-sticks, his body color becomes excellent, the luster of his face improves, his mouth becomes clean and fragrant from within, and his speech becomes so sweet that it brings pleasure to those who hear it. ||34||

# Now Begins the Seventy-Eighth Chapter

### The Union of Men and Women

> Her own queen killed King Viduratha with a weapon hidden in her braided hair. It is said that a disaffected queen killed the King of Kashi with an anklet smeared with poison. || 1 ||

> When disaffected women can cause such life-threatening harm, what is the need to mention other faults? Therefore, men must carefully examine whether women are truly affectionate or disaffected. || 2 ||

> Gestures reveal the affection born in the heart: exposing the navel, thighs, or breasts; adjusting the garments; loosening the hair; and casting side-long glances with trembling eyebrows. || 3 ||

> Spitting loudly, laughing boisterously, shifting on the bed or seat, stretching and yawning, asking for small or easily available things, hugging and kissing children, looking at a female friend while facing the man, casting glances when he is turned away, praising his virtues, and scratching the ear—these are signs of an affectionate woman. || 4 ||

> Know these to be the actions of an affectionate woman: she speaks sweet words, gives her own wealth, feels delighted upon seeing him, loses her anger, and wipes away faults by praising his virtues. || 5 ||

> She honors his friends and hates his enemies; she remembers his deeds and feels dejected when he is away. She offers her breasts and lips, embraces him, perspires, and is the first to initiate a kiss. || 6 ||

> The signs of a disaffected woman are: a face with a constant frown, turning her back, forgetting what has been done, lack of excitement, being difficult to please, befriending his enemies, and speaking harsh words. || 7 ||

> Upon being touched or looked at, she shakes her limbs in annoyance; she acts with pride and does not stop him when he leaves. After a kiss, she wipes her mouth, and she wakes up after him but gets out of bed before him. || 8 ||

> A female mendicant, a wandering nun, a nurse, a young girl, a washerwoman, a flower-seller, a woman of ill-repute, a female friend, and a barber-woman—all these may act as <term>messengers</term><note>dūtya: intermediaries or go-betweens in romantic affairs</note>. || 9 ||

> (Because such messengers are the cause of the destruction of noble families, women should be protected from them with great effort for the sake of the family's lineage, fame, and honor. || 10 ||)

> Night-time strolls, staying awake late, feigning illness, visiting others' houses, festivals, and gatherings are all occasions for secret meetings; women should be <gloss>1</gloss> protected during these times. || 11 ||

# Varahamihira’s Brihat Samhita

...she acts with languid grace, yet is devoid of shame; she bows her face in modesty. She performs various gestures with many-fold emotions and acts with great respect. Having understood the nature of the man, she follows his lead with tireless movements. **(12)**

The virtues of women include youth, beauty, dress, courtesy, specialized knowledge <note>original: "vijnana," referring to the arts or sciences</note>, and playful grace. Those endowed with these qualities are known as "Gem-like Women" <note>original: "Stri-ratna"</note>; other types of women may bring affliction to a clever man. **(13)**

One should not use vulgar language, nor should the body be smeared with dirt. One should not speak ill of her limbs or relatives. While in private, one should not dwell on other tasks, for the mind is the very root of the God of Love <note>original: "Hara-dagdha-murti," literally "the one whose body was burnt by Shiva," referring to Kamadeva</note>. **(14)**

She who exhales in unison with the man, who is skilled in providing her arm as a pillow and offering her breast, whose hair is fragrant, who shares the same passions, who falls asleep only after he sleeps and wakes before him—she is the ideal. **(15)**

Those of wicked nature should be avoided, as well as those who lack patience during the time of embrace. Those whose menstrual blood is scented or appears blue, yellow, or dark copper in color are not praised. **(16)**

She who sleeps excessively, has an excess of bile or blood, or suffers from discharges of wind and phlegm; she who eats voraciously, has a foul-smelling body due to sweat, or has short or prematurely gray hair— **(17)**

She whose flesh is flabby, who has a large belly, or who makes a "khikkhi" sound <note>likely referring to a wheezing or harsh respiratory sound</note>; those women who possess the sinful characteristics described in the science of feminine marks <note>term: "Stri-lakshana" — the traditional study of physical traits that indicate character or destiny</note>—with such women, one should not practice the duties of love. **(18)**

That blood which resembles the blood of a rabbit or the juice of lac <note>a red resin</note>, and which leaves no stain on a garment after being washed, should be considered pure. **(19)**

That which ceases after three days without pain or sound <note>referring to the menstrual cycle</note> leads to conception without doubt through union with a man. **(20)**

For three days, the woman should not indulge in bathing, wearing garlands, or applying ointments. She should bathe on the fourth day according to the instructions mentioned in the scriptures. **(21)**

She should bathe with water mixed with the medicinal herbs mentioned for the "Pushya-bath" <note>a ritual bath taken when the moon is in the Pushya constellation</note>; the mantra to be used there is the same as the one specified for that ritual. **(22)**

It is said that conception on even-numbered nights results in male children, and on odd-numbered nights, in female children. Long-lived, handsome, and happy children are born from unions on the later even nights. **(23)**

If the seed stays on the right side of the womb, a male is born; on the left, a female; if on both sides, twins. If it enters the middle of the womb, it should be understood that a sterile or third-gender child <note>original: "napumsaka"</note> is born. **(24)**

When the auspicious planets are in the centers or trines <note>astrological houses 1, 4, 7, 10 and 1, 5, 9</note>, and the Ascendant and Moon are joined by benefics, while malefic planets are in the 3rd, 11th, or 6th houses, one should engage in union during the yogas <note>astrological alignments</note> for the birth of a son. **(25)**

A man should never inflict wounds with nails or teeth upon a woman during her fertile period <note>term: "Ritu-samaya" — the 16 days following the start of menstruation</note>. This period lasts sixteen days, but the first three nights are forbidden for union. **(26)**

For this reason, men must examine with great effort whether a woman is affectionate or disaffected. **(2)** All the expressions of an affectionate woman reveal the love born of the God of Love. Such women display their navel, arms, breasts, and ornaments; they reveal signs such as adjusting their clothes, binding their hair, loosening their hair, raising their eyebrows, and looking with trembling side-glances. **(3)** Clearing the throat loudly, laughing boisterously, approaching the bed or seat, stretching the limbs...

Yawning, asking for small and easily obtainable things, hugging and kissing a child sitting in front of her, looking at her beloved in the presence of a female friend, looking at the beloved out of the corner of her eye when the friend turns her face away, praising the beloved's virtues, and scratching her ear—all these are signs of an **attached** <note>original: "anurakta" - a woman who is in love or devoted</note> woman. ||4|| An attached woman speaks sweet words, offers her wealth, feels joy upon seeing him, and, being free from anger, hides all his faults by calling them virtues. ||5||

Honoring the husband's friends, hating the husband's enemies, remembering the husband, feeling sorrow in the heart when the husband goes abroad, offering her breasts for embracing and her lips for drinking, perspiring during the first meeting with her lord, and kissing the husband's face first of her own accord—these are the actions of **affectionate** <note>original: "anurāgiṇī"</note> women. ||6||

Raising the eyebrows, turning the face away, forgetting the beloved, showing disrespect, remaining dissatisfied, befriending those who are the husband's enemies, and speaking harsh words; ||7|| trembling the body upon touching or seeing the husband, acting with pride (such as saying, "What are you? No one is as beautiful as I am"), not asking the husband to sit when he is walking, wiping the mouth after the husband has kissed it, sleeping before the husband sleeps and waking up after him—all these are the actions of a **disaffected** <gloss>1</gloss> woman. ||8||

A beggar woman, a female ascetic, a maidservant, a wet-nurse, a washerwoman, a gardener woman, a wicked-bodied woman (one with physical defects like being one-eyed or hunchbacked), a female friend, and a barber woman—these serve as **messengers** <term>dūtī: a female go-between or confidante who carries messages between lovers</term>. ||9|| These messengers are the cause of the destruction of family members. For this reason, to increase the lineage, fame, and honor, women should be protected from the clutches of these messengers with great effort. ||10||

Going out of the house at night, making the excuse of illness to stay awake (pretending not to feel well), visiting others' houses, and attending festivals like weddings or times of calamity—all these are times for women's **secret rendezvous** <note>original: "saṃketa" - a pre-arranged meeting place or time for lovers</note>; therefore, women should be protected during these times as well. ||11||

Furthermore, one who is filled with a shyness mixed with lethargy, who does not speak of sexual union but cannot leave it either, who abandons shame during the act of love, and who bows her head in modesty once the act is finished; the woman who playfully performs various types of love-acts with respect and behaves according to the man's nature—meaning she is sad when her lord is sad and happy when he is happy—it is only with such a woman that it is proper to engage in **love-play** <note>original: "rati" - pleasure or sexual union</note>. ||12||

Due to the possession of all virtues such as youth, beauty, dress, cleverness, specialized knowledge, and grace, women are given the title of **"Gem"** <note>meaning they are considered the finest of their kind</note>; for a clever man, women with opposite qualities become like a disease. ||13||

It is not proper to discuss vulgar body parts (such as the anus) with a woman who speaks crudely or keeps her limbs dirty; nor is it proper to speak **tales of desire** <note>original: "smarakathā" - erotic conversation or talk of the god of love</note> with a woman sitting in a solitary place who is thinking of some other task, because the mind itself is the root of **the God of Love** <note>original: "Kāmadeva"</note>. ||14|| One who breathes in unison with the man...

She who places her husband's head upon the pillow of her arm, who presses his chest with her breasts, who keeps her hair fragrant and remains ever near with beautiful affection; she who sleeps only after her master <note>original: "swami," referring here to the husband</note> has slept and wakes before her master wakes—she alone is truly affectionate. ||15|| It is right to abandon a woman of wicked nature who cannot endure the pressure of love-making. The fertile period lasts for sixteen days; among these, one should not approach a woman during the first three nights. ||26||

# Chapter 79: Characteristics of Beds and Seats

<page-num>267</page-num>
<header>With Hindi Commentary, Chapter 79</header>

Trees that are home to honeybees or birds; those situated in sacred groves, cremation grounds, or on pathways; those entangled with upward-growing dry creepers; ॥ 3 ॥
Those that are thorny, or grow at the confluence of great rivers; those born in temple precincts; those that are not auspicious; and those that have fallen toward the West—these should be avoided. ॥ 4 ॥
From the use of beds and seats made of forbidden trees, the destruction of the family follows. Disease, fear, expense, quarrels, and various other misfortunes arise. ॥ 5 ॥
If the wood was cut previously, it should be examined at the start of the work. If a young boy climbs upon it <note>This is considered a spontaneous omen or 'nimitta'</note>, it bestows sons and cattle. ॥ 6 ॥
Seeing white flowers, an intoxicated elephant, curds, unbroken grain, a full pot, or jewels at the start of the work should be known as auspicious. ॥ 7 ॥
A "Work-Digit" <term>Karmangula: a unit of measurement</term> is equal to eight barley-corns placed side-by-side, stripped of their husks. A bed made one hundred digits long for kings brings victory. ॥ 8 ॥
The same length reduced by six, then by twelve, and then by eighteen <note>i.e., 94, 88, and 82 digits</note> are for the king's son, the minister, the commander of the army, and the royal priest respectively. ॥ 9 ॥
The width is stated by Vishvakarma <note>The divine architect</note> to be the length minus one-eighth. The height of the legs, including the joints and the head-piece, should be one-third of the length. ॥ 10 ॥
A couch made entirely of *Shriparni* <term>Gmelina arborea</term> wood bestows wealth; one made of *Asana* <term>Terminalia tomentosa</term> removes disease; and one made of the heartwood of *Tinduka* <term>Diospyros melanoxylon</term> brings prosperity. ॥ 11 ॥
That which is constructed solely of *Shishapa* <term>Dalbergia sissoo</term> brings various types of growth. One made of Sandalwood destroys enemies and bestows virtue, fame, and long life. ॥ 12 ॥
A couch made of *Padmaka* <term>Prunus cerasoides</term> grants long life, prosperity, learning, and wealth. One made of *Shala* <term>Shorea robusta</term> or *Shaka* <term>Teak</term> brings well-being. ॥ 13 ॥
A king who occupies a couch made of pure Sandalwood, inlaid with gold and adorned with various gems, is honored even by the gods. ॥ 14 ॥
*Tinduka* and *Shishapa* are not auspicious when joined with other woods; nor are *Shriparni*, *Devadaru* <term>Himalayan Cedar</term>, or *Asana*. ॥ 15 ॥
However, *Shaka* and *Shala* are auspicious both when joined together and when used separately. Similarly, *Haridraka* and *Kadamba* are praised both separately and together. ॥ 16 ॥
A couch made entirely of *Syandana* <term>Dalbergia oudheinensis</term> is not auspicious; one made of *Amba* <term>Mango</term> destroys life. *Asana* joined with other wood quickly produces many defects. ॥ 17 ॥
For trees like *Amba*, *Syandana*, and Sandalwood, the legs are auspicious if made from *Syandana*. A bed or seat made entirely from a fruit-bearing tree yields desired results. ॥ 18 ॥
Ivory is highly praised for use in combination with all the aforementioned trees. Decorative work should be performed with excellent ivory. ॥ 19 ॥
Leaving aside a portion of the ivory at the root equal to twice its circumference, the remainder may be used. A little more should be left for marsh-dwelling elephants, and a little less for mountain-dwelling ones. ॥ 20 ॥
If, when the ivory is cut, shapes like the *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious mark</note>, the *Vardhamana* <note>a mystical diagram</note>, an umbrella, a banner, or a fly-whisk are seen, it brings health, victory, increase in wealth, and happiness. ॥ 21 ॥
Shapes resembling weapons bring victory; the *Nandyavarta* <note>a labyrinthine symbol</note> brings the recovery of lost lands; a shape like a clod of earth brings the acquisition of lands previously possessed. ॥ 22 ॥
A female form brings one's own destruction; a water-pot brings the birth of a son; a full jar brings the discovery of treasure; and a staff brings obstacles to a journey. ॥ 23 ॥
Shapes of a lizard, monkey, or snake bring poverty, famine, and disease, or subjection to enemies. Shapes of a vulture, owl, crow, or hawk bring pestilence among the people. ॥ 24 ॥
If a noose or a headless trunk appears, there is danger for the king's servants; if the ivory is bloody, dark, grey, rough, or foul-smelling, it is inauspicious. ॥ 25 ॥
A cut that is white, even, fragrant, and glossy is a bringer of good fortune. The effects of auspicious or inauspicious cuts in ivory apply to the beds as well. ॥ 26 ॥
In joining the side-rails, the teacher says wood with the grain running clockwise is best. If the grain runs counter-clockwise or in only one direction, there is fear from spirits...

# Varahi Samhita
## Chapter 79: Characteristics of Beds and Seats

...[The wood] is ruined. || 27 || If there is a knot <note>original: "granthi" - a knot or burl in the timber</note> at the foot of the bed facing downwards, it causes lameness in one leg. If there are two such knots, the body does not digest food properly; if there are three or four, it leads to misery, slaughter, or imprisonment. || 28 || A hollow or discolored knot at the head of the bed causes disease. If there are two "pot-shaped" knots at the foot, it causes abdominal diseases. || 29 || Below the "pot" is the shank; a knot there causes fear for one's own shanks. A knot at the base of that support causes the loss of wealth. || 30 || A knot in the region of the "hoof" <note>the base of the leg</note> is said to cause pain to hoofed animals (livestock). Knots located in the three parts of the pole or the head are not auspicious. || 31 ||

The types of holes or defects are described as: *Nishkuta*, *Kolaksha* (boar-eye), *Shukaranayana* (pig-eye), *Vatsanabha* (calf-navel), *Kalaka*, and *Dundubhaka*. || 32 || A *Nishkuta* hole is hollow like a pot in the middle and narrow at the mouth. A blue-colored hole the size of a kidney bean or a mung bean is called *Kolaksha*. || 33 || *Shukaranayana* is uneven, discolored, and one and a half finger-joints long. A hole that turns to the left, is cracked, and measures one finger-joint is called *Vatsanabha*. || 34 || The one called *Kalaka* is black, and the one that splits the wood in two is *Dhundhuka*. A hole that is the same color as the wood is not considered so sinful. || 35 ||

Loss of wealth occurs from the *Nishkuta* defect; destruction of the family from *Kolaksha*. Fear of weapons comes from *Shukara*, and fear of disease from *Vatsanabha*. || 36 || The *Kalaka* and *Dhundhuka* defects, or wood bored by insects, are not auspicious. Wood that is full of knots is generally not good for any purpose. || 37 || A bed made from one type of tree is blessed; made from two types, it is even more blessed. Three types of wood bring an increase in progeny, and four types bring the highest fame. || 38 || If a bed is crafted from five types of wood, the one who sleeps there faces death <note>original: "panchatvam" - literally 'becoming the five elements'</note>. If constructed from the wood of six, seven, or eight trees, it leads to the destruction of the family. || 39 ||

**Thus ends the 79th Chapter of the Brihat Samhita by Shri Varahamihira, titled "Characteristics of Beds and Seats."**

A bed one hundred such fingers long brings victory to kings. || 8 || The beds of princes, ministers, commanders, and priests should be made according to the following order...

| One should construct [beds] ninety, eighty-four, seventy-eight, and seventy-two fingers <note>The "finger" or *angula* is a traditional unit of measurement</note> in length. ||9|| By subtracting one-eighth of the bed's half-length from that half-length, the remainder is the width of the bed. The height of the legs, including the side-rails and the headboard, should be equal to one-third of the length. This has been stated by Vishvakarma <note>The divine architect of the gods</note>. ||10|| Beds made of *Shriparni* <note>Gmelina arborea</note> or the heartwood of *Tinduka* <note>Diospyros embryopteris</note> grant the gift of wealth, and a bed made from the wood of the *Asana* tree <note>Terminalia tomentosa</note> removes diseases. ||11|| A bed made solely of *Shisham* <note>Dalbergia sissoo</note> wood brings various types of prosperity. A sandalwood bed, besides being a destroyer of enemies, grants righteousness, fame, and long life. ||12|| A bed made of *Padma* <note>likely Prunus cerasoides</note> gives long life, beauty, knowledge, and wealth; a bed made of *Shala* <note>Shorea robusta</note> or Teak is auspicious. ||13|| Even the gods worship a king who sleeps on a bed made solely of sandalwood, plated with gold, and studded with wonderful gems. ||14|| If a bed or stool is made of *Tinduka*, *Shisham*, *Shriparni*, *Devadaru* <note>Himalayan Cedar</note>, or *Asana* wood without mixing in any other wood, it is a bringer of good fortune. ||15|| The mixing of Teak and *Shala* wood, or using them separately, is auspicious; similarly, the mixing or separate use of *Haridraka* <note>Adina cordifolia</note> and *Kadamba* wood is also good and auspicious. ||16|| All types of beds made from the wood of the *Syandana* tree are not auspicious; a bed of *Amba* <note>Mango</note> wood takes away life; if another wood is mixed with *Asana*, it quickly produces many defects. ||17|| If the legs of beds made from the wood of *Amba*, *Syandana*, and Sandalwood are made specifically of *Syandana* wood, they are auspicious; and if beds and seats are made from the wood of any other fruit-bearing trees, the desired results are obtained. ||18|| The combination of ivory with all the types of trees mentioned above is excellent; it is proper to decorate it using the finest ivory. ||19|| One should leave a portion from the base of the tusk equal to twice the measurement of the circumference at the base, and construct the work from the remaining part; however, for elephants from marshy lands, leave a little more, and for mountain-dwelling elephants, leave a little less. ||20|| If, while cutting the ivory, marks resembling the *Shrivatsa* <note>an auspicious symbol/curl</note>, *Vardhamana* <note>a clay bowl</note>, umbrella, banner, or fly-whisk appear, they bring health, victory, increase in wealth, and happiness. ||21|| A weapon-shaped mark brings victory; a mark shaped like a *Nadyavarta* <note>a whirlpool-like pattern</note> brings the recovery of a lost kingdom; and a clod-shaped mark brings the attainment of a kingdom previously held. ||22|| A mark in the form of a woman brings one's own destruction; if a mark like a *Bhringara* <note>a ceremonial water vessel</note> appears, a son is born. A pot-shaped mark brings the attainment of gems, and a staff-shaped mark causes obstacles in a journey. ||23|| Marks resembling a chameleon, monkey, or snake bring famine, disease, and deception by enemies. Marks resembling a vulture, owl, crow, or hawk cause a plague among men. ||24|| If a mark of a noose or a headless torso appears when cutting the ivory, it signifies the death of the king; if blood comes out, it brings calamity to the people; and if it is blackish-yellow, dry, and foul-smelling, it is inauspicious. ||25|| If the hollow of the tusk is even, white, fragrant, or glossy, it is auspicious; know this for the seat. The auspicious and inauspicious holes described for the seat are also fruitful regarding the bed. ||26|| In the joining of the *Isha* <note>See footnote 1</note>, a clockwise direction is best.

This is the arrangement established by the ancient teachers. Contrary to this, if the wood is joined improperly, or if the tops of the head and foot boards face the same direction, the person sleeping on such a bed will suffer from fear caused by spirits <note>original: "bhuta"; refers to ghosts or supernatural entities</note>. || 27 || If one leg of the bed or seat is placed upside down (meaning the tip of the leg is made from the root-end of the wood and the base of the leg from the tip-end), it leads to the failure of the feet. If two legs are upside down, the sleeper cannot digest food. If three or four legs are upside down, it results in distress, slaughter, and imprisonment. || 28 || If the head of the leg has a hole or a knot of an ugly color, it causes disease. A knot in the "pot" <note>the rounded, decorative bulbous part of a furniture leg</note> of the leg causes stomach ailments. || 29 || The wooden part below the "pot" is called the shank <term>jangha: the lower leg portion of the furniture</term>. If a bed is made with defects here, it creates fear in the sleeper's own shanks. The middle part of the shank is called the base; a knot in this base leads to the depletion of wealth. || 30 || A knot in the "hoof" <note>the very bottom of the leg</note> is said to cause suffering to one's hooved animals. If there is a knot on the third part of the side-rails or the headboard, it is not auspicious. || 31 || *Nishkuta, Kolaksha, Shukaranayana, Vatsanabha, Kalaka,* and *Dhundhuka*—these are the names given to the various types of holes or defects in brief. || 32 || If a hole is wide in the middle like a jar but has a narrow mouth, it is the *Nishkuta* defect. A hole the size of a pea or black gram and blue in color is called *Kolaksha*. || 33 || An uneven, discolored hole one and a half finger-joints long is *Shukaranayana* <note>literally "boar's eye"</note>. A hole one finger-joint long that spirals to the left is famous as *Vatsanabha*. || 34 || A black-colored hole is known as *Kalaka*, and one that is particularly shattered or split is called *Dhundhuka*. However, a hole that is the same color as the wood does not produce such intense inauspicious results. || 35 || The *Nishkuta* hole leads to loss of wealth; *Kolaksha* (shaped like a boar's eye) leads to the destruction of the family; the *Shukara* hole leads to fear of weapons; and the *Vatsanabha* hole leads to fear of disease. Furthermore, the worm-eaten *Kalaka* and *Dhundhuka* holes are also not givers of good fortune. Wood that is filled with many knots is never auspicious in any circumstance. || 36 || 37 || A bed made from the wood of a single tree is blessed. A bed made from two trees is even more blessed. A bed made from three trees increases the number of sons. A bed made from four trees brings excellent wealth and fame. || 38 || A man who sleeps on a bed made from the wood of five trees meets his end <note>meaning death or ruin</note>. Sleeping on a bed made from six, seven, or eight types of wood leads to the destruction of the entire lineage. || 39 ||

### Chapter Eighty

### Examination of Diamonds <note>Vajra-Pariksha</note>

Good fortune comes to men through auspicious gems, and misfortune through inauspicious ones. Therefore, those who understand the matter should examine the destiny that resides within gems. || 1 || The word "gem" <term>ratna: literally 'jewel' or 'best of its kind'</term> is applied to elephants, horses, and women when they possess special qualities. However, in this context, we deal with the authority on lithic gems, beginning with the diamond. || 2 || Some say gems were born from the demon Bala <note>referring to the myth where the body of the demon Vala/Bala turned into gemstones</note> or from the sage Dadhichi. Others say the variety of stones is produced by the inherent nature of the earth. || 3 || Diamonds, sapphires...

# Chapter 80: The Examination of Diamonds

The wearing of auspicious gemstones brings prosperity to kings, while wearing inauspicious ones leads to misfortune; for this reason, the destiny associated with gems should be examined by learned scholars of gemology. <note>Verse 1</note> Although the word "gem" <note>Sanskrit: *ratna*</note> is used to denote excellence in all things—such as "gem of an elephant," "gem of a horse," or "gem of a woman"—in this context, the term refers specifically to precious stones like diamonds. <note>Verse 2</note> Some hold the opinion that gems originated from the demon named Bala; others say they were produced from the bones of the sage Dadhichi; while others claim the variety in all gems arises from the natural properties of the earth itself. <note>Verse 3</note>

The gems are named as follows: Diamond, Sapphire, Emerald, <insert>Red Agate</insert>, Ruby, Bloodstone, Chrysoberyl, Pulaka, Vimalaka, Rajamani <note>Royal Gem</note>, Quartz Crystal, and Moonstone. <note>Verse 4</note> Also Saugandhika, Gomedaka <note>Hessonite</note>, Conch-shell, Mahaneela, Topaz, Brahmamani, Jyotirasa, Sasyaka, Pearl, and Coral. <note>Verse 5</note>

Pure diamonds are found on the banks of the Vena River; those resembling the Shirisha flower <note>Albizia lebbeck, a pale greenish-yellow</note> come from the Kosala region; slightly reddish diamonds come from Saurashtra; and black diamonds from Surparaka. <note>Verse 6</note> Diamonds from the Himalayas are slightly copper-colored; those from Matanga are the color of the Valla flower; those from Kalinga are yellowish, and those produced in the Paundra region are dark/grey. <note>Verse 7</note>

The diamond belonging to Indra is six-sided and white; that of Yama is the shape of a grain and black; that of Vishnu is the color of a banana stalk and of various shapes. <note>Verse 8</note> The diamond of Varuna is shaped like a woman’s private parts or a Karnikara flower; that of Agni is shaped like a water-chestnut <note>Sringataka</note> or like a tiger's eye. <note>Verse 9</note> The diamond of Vayu is said to be shaped like a barley grain and has the luster of an Ashoka flower. There are three types of origins: rivers, mines, and scattered deposits. <note>Verse 10</note>

Red and yellow diamonds are auspicious for the Kshatriyas <note>the warrior/ruling class</note>; white for the Brahmins <note>the priestly class</note>; Shirisha-colored for the Vaishyas <note>the merchant class</note>; and those resembling a sword-blade <note>dark/blue-black</note> are recommended for Shudras. <note>Verse 11</note>

A diamond weighing twenty grains of rice <note>where 8 white mustard seeds equal 1 rice grain</note> is valued at two hundred thousand <note>pieces of gold/currency</note>; as the weight decreases by two grains, the value decreases. <note>Verse 12</note> The value follows a scale of three-quarters, a half, one-third, one-fifth, one-sixteenth, one-twenty-fifth, one-hundredth, and one-thousandth. <note>Verse 13</note>

A diamond that cannot be pierced by any material, is light enough to float on water, is oily/glossy like a ray of light, and resembles lightning, fire, or a rainbow, is said to be beneficial. <note>Verse 14</note> Those containing "crow's feet" <note>cracks</note>, inclusions like flies or hair, or mixed with grit/sand, or those that are double-faceted, stained, dull, or cracked are not auspicious. <note>Verse 15</note> Those with bubbles, broken tips, flattened shapes, or elongated like a chisel—for all such defects, the value is reduced by one-eighth. <note>Verse 16</note>

Experts say that women desiring sons should not wear certain diamonds; however, those shaped like a water-chestnut, a triangle, or a coriander seed, or those resembling the hips, are auspicious for those seeking offspring. <note>Verse 17</note> A diamond with inauspicious marks causes the loss of kinsmen, wealth, and life. A beneficial diamond destroys the fear of lightning, poison, and enemies, and brings great enjoyment to kings. <note>Verse 18</note>

---

->Thus ends the Eightieth Chapter of the Brihat Samhita by Varahamihira, titled "The Examination of Diamonds."<-

The wearing of auspicious gems brings welfare to kings, while inauspicious ones bring bad luck; therefore, scholars of gems must examine the destiny residing in them. (1) In all things like elephants, horses, and women, the word "gem" is used to denote excellence (such as elephant-gem, horse-gem, woman-gem, etc.), but here the word "gem" refers specifically to stones like diamonds. (2) Some believe gems come from the demon Bala, some say from the bones of Sage Dadhichi, and some say the variety in gems is due to the nature of the soil. (3) Diamond, Sapphire, Emerald, Karkentana, Ruby, Bloodstone, Chrysoberyl, Pulaka, Vimalaka, Rajamani, Crystal, Moonstone. (4) Saugandhika, Gomedaka, Conch, Mahaneela, Topaz, Brahmamani, Jyotirasa, Sasyaka, Pearl, Coral—all these are called gems. (5) Pure diamonds are produced on the banks of the Vena River; diamonds like the Shirisha flower are produced in the Kosala country; slightly reddish diamonds are from Saurashtra (Surat)...

...is produced in that country. Black-colored diamonds are produced in the Surparaka <note>Sopara, an ancient port near modern Mumbai</note> region. || 6 || Diamonds produced on the Himavan <note>Himalaya</note> mountains are somewhat reddish in color. The diamond known as 'Matanga' is like the flower of the Valla plant. Somewhat yellow diamonds are produced in the Kalinga <note>Ancient region in modern Odisha/Andhra Pradesh</note> country. Gems produced in the Paundra <note>Ancient Bengal/Bihar region</note> country are dark-colored <note>original: "shyam-rang"</note>. || 7 ||

The deity of a six-angled diamond is Indra. The deity of a white-colored diamond is Yama. A diamond with a mouth shaped like a serpent, or colored black or like the stalk of a banana tree (blue and yellow), has Vishnu as its presiding deity; that is, Lord Vishnu is its god. Thus, the deities and shapes of all have been described. || 8 ||

A diamond shaped like the female vulva is associated with Varuna; it can also be like the Karnikara flower. Diamonds shaped like a water chestnut <note>Sringataka</note> or like the eye of a tiger have Agni <note>the Fire God</note> as their deity. || 9 ||

All diamonds colored like the Ashoka flower or like a grain of barley are named Vayavya <note>associated with Vayu, the Wind God</note>. The three sources of diamond production are the flow of rivers and such, mines, and scattered <note>original: "prakirnaka"</note> (found spread over certain lands). || 10 ||

Red and yellow diamonds bring prosperity to the Kshatriyas <note>the warrior/ruling class</note>. White diamonds bring prosperity to the Brahmins <note>the priestly/scholarly class</note>. Green diamonds, like the Shirisha flower, bring good fortune to the Vaishyas <note>the merchant/landowner class</note>, and blue diamonds, like the color of a sword, give auspicious results to the Shudras <note>the laborer/artisan class</note>. || 11 ||

Eight grains of white mustard are equal to one grain of rice. A diamond weighing twenty such rice-grains is valued at one hundred thousand rupees. For every two rice-grains less in weight—that is, 18, 16, 14, and so on—the price will be, in order: a quarter less, a third less, a half, three-quarters less, a fifth part, a sixteenth part, a twenty-fifth part, a hundredth part, and a thousandth part of the previously mentioned price. || 12 || 13 ||

A diamond that cannot be broken by any object, which floats in ordinary water like a ray of light, is oily/smooth <note>original: "snigdha"</note>, and possesses colors like lightning, fire, or a rainbow, is beneficial. || 14 ||

Diamonds that contain "crow's feet" <note>cracks</note>, marks like flies, hair, or metallic streaks, or those pierced by gravel, or those with two threads in every corner, or those that are elongated, dull, lusterless, and crumbling, are not auspicious. || 15 ||

Or diamonds that are split at the front like a water bubble, or are flat, or long like the Vasi-fruit—these diamonds are also not auspicious. The price of diamonds with all these [negative] marks should be determined by reducing the fixed price by one-eighth in sequence; that is, the price of a diamond with a "crow's foot" mark will be less, and a diamond with a fly-mark will not even be worth an eighth part of that value. || 16 ||

Some scholars who know the essence of diamonds say that women desiring sons should not wear even an ordinary diamond. However, wearing diamonds shaped like a water chestnut, a triple-nut <note>triputa</note>, a grain, or a crescent <note>shreni</note> is auspicious for women desiring sons. || 17 ||

By wearing a diamond with bad characteristics, the brothers, kinsmen, wealth, and life of kings are destroyed. By wearing a diamond with auspicious characteristics, the fear of thunderbolts, poisons, and enemies is destroyed, and one's enjoyments increase greatly. || 18 ||
