# Now begins the Eighty-First Chapter
## The Examination of Pearls

Pearls are produced from elephants, serpents, oysters, conch-shells, clouds, bamboos, whales, and hogs. Among these, those produced from oysters are the most excellent. <note>The text lists eight traditional sources of pearls in ancient Indian gemology, though modern science recognizes only the oyster/mollusk variety.</note> ||1||

There are eight sources (mines) of pearls: Sri Lanka, Paraloka, Saurashtra, Tamraparni, Parasava, Kaubera, Pandya-vataka, and Haima. ||2||

Pearls from **Sri Lanka** are of many shapes, glossy, like the color of a swan, and large. Those from **Tamraparni** are slightly copper-red, white, and free from dark spots. ||3||

Pearls from **Paraloka** are black, white, or yellow, mixed with gravelly textures, and irregular in shape. Those from **Saurashtra** <note>Modern Gujarat</note> are neither too large nor too small, and resemble the color of butter. ||4||

Pearls from **Parasava** <note>Likely referring to Persia/the Gulf</note> are brilliant, white, heavy, and possess great qualities. Those from **Haima** <note>The Himalayas</note> are light, fragile, curd-like in color, and large but irregular in shape. ||5||

Pearls from **Kaubera** are irregular, black or white, light, and of standard brilliance. Those from **Pandya-vataka** are like the fruit of the Neem tree, or like the seeds of the Triputa or coriander. ||6||

Pearls belonging to the deity **Vishnu** are dark like the Atasi flower; those of **Indra** are like the moon; those of **Varuna** are like yellow orpiment; and those of **Yama** are black. ||7||

Pearls belonging to the deity **Vayu** (the Wind) are copper-red like a ripe pomegranate or the Gunja berry. Those belonging to **Agni** (Fire) should be known by their brilliance like smokeless fire or a lotus. ||8||

### The Valuation of Pearls
<note>The following verses describe a complex pricing system based on weight (Mashakas and Dharanas) and quality.</note>

For a single pearl weighing four *Mashakas* and possessing brilliance and good qualities, the price is said to be 5,300 *Karshapanas* <note>An ancient silver or copper coin</note>. ||9||

As the weight decreases by half a *Mashaka*, the prices are 3,200, 2,000, 1,300, 800, 300, and 53 *Karshapanas* respectively. ||10||

For a pearl weighing four *Krishnalas*, the price is 90. For one weighing three and a half *Gunjas*, the price is 70. ||11||

The price for a pearl of three *Gunjas* with good qualities is 50 *Rupakas*. For one weighing two and a half *Gunjas*, the price is 25 *Rupakas*. ||12||

A *Dharana* is the tenth part of a *Pala*. If thirteen beautiful pearls weigh one *Dharana*, their price is 325 *Rupakas*. ||13||

If sixteen pearls weigh a *Dharana*, the price is 200. If twenty pearls, the price is 170. If twenty-five pearls weigh that much, the price is 130. ||14||

If thirty pearls weigh a *Dharana*, the price is 70. If forty, the price is 50. If sixty (or five less than sixty), the price is 40. ||15||

If eighty pearls weigh a *Dharana*, the price is 30. For groups of 200, 300, 400, or 500 pearls weighing a *Dharana*, the prices are 12, 6, 5, and 3 respectively. ||16||

Pearls with the luster of a cuckoo's tail are called *Ravaka*. From the thirteenth group onwards, they are called *Siktha*. Beyond that, they are called *Nigara* and *Churnas* (powder/seed pearls). ||17||

This price is stated for pearls of good quality weighing a *Dharana*. For those of intermediate or inferior quality, the price should be reduced accordingly. ||18||

For pearls that are black, white, yellow, or copper-colored, or slightly irregular, the price is reduced by one-third. For those that are very irregular or yellow, the price is reduced by one-sixth or one-half. ||19||

### Rare Non-Oyster Pearls

Elephants born of the lineage of Airavata, on days of the Pushya or Shravana constellations, or during the Sun's northern course, or during solar or lunar eclipses—these are "Noble Elephants." ||20||

It is said that pearls are produced in their temples (foreheads) and at the base of their tusks. These are numerous, large, of various shapes, and highly brilliant. ||21||

No price can be set for these, nor should they be perforated, as they are exceedingly brilliant. When worn by kings, they bring sons, victory, and health, and are highly sacred. ||22||

A pearl from a **boar** is found at the root of the tusk, resembling the moon's luster and possessing many virtues. A pearl from a **whale** (Timijam) resembles a fish's eye, is large, sacred, and highly virtuous. ||23||

Pearls produced like hailstones from the seventh layer of the wind... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the description of celestial or atmospheric pearls.</note>

# 274
## Varāhamihira’s Compendium (Brihat Samhita)

It is seen; it is said to be snatched from the sky, possessing the brilliance of lightning and born from the clouds. <note>Verse 24 refers to the rare 'cloud pearl' or celestial pearl.</note> ||24|| Among the serpents born of the lineages of Takshaka and Vasuki <note>Famous mythical serpent kings</note> who move at will, smooth and blue-tinted pearls are produced within their hoods. ||25|| If the god [Indra] suddenly sends rain upon a commendable, silver-like piece of ground, that [pearl] should be known as being born of the Nagas <note>Serpents</note>. ||26|| It dispels uneven fortune, destroys enemies, and spreads one's fame; a serpent-born pearl worn by kings brings victory and fulfills all desires. ||27||

The pearl born from bamboo is known to be like camphor or crystal, flat and uneven. That born from a conch shell is like the moon, round, brilliant, and beautiful. ||28|| Pearls born from the conch, fish, bamboo, elephant, boar, serpent, and clouds are not to be perforated <note>Because of their extreme rarity and sacred nature</note>; because of their infinite virtues, no price has been fixed for them in the scriptures. ||29|| All these are of great merit, bestowing sons, wealth, beauty, and fame; they destroy the diseases and grief of kings and are the givers of desired objects. ||30||

A decoration of one thousand and eight strings, four cubits long, is named *Indracchanda*. Half of that is *Vijayacchanda*. ||31|| A necklace of one hundred and eight strings is a *Hara*; eighty-one strings is *Devacchanda*; sixty-four strings is an *Ardhahara*; and fifty-four strings is a *Rashmikalapa*. ||32|| Thirty-two strings is called a *Guccha*; twenty is known as an *Ardhaguccha*; sixteen is a *Manavaka*; and twelve is an *Ardhamanavaka*. ||33|| Eight strings is named *Mandara*; a five-stringed necklace is called a *Haraphalaka*; and twenty-seven pearls [in a single string] is a *Nakshatramala* <note>Literally 'Garland of Stars'</note>. ||34||

When combined with intervening gems or gold beads, it is called a *Manisopana* <note>Gem-staircase</note>; if it has a central gem <term>Taralaka</term> <note>A large central pendant or 'shaking' gem</note>, it is known as *Catukara*. ||35|| An *Ekavali* is a single string of pearls of any desired number, one cubit long; if it is joined with a gem in the middle, experts in ornamentation call it a *Yashti*. ||36||

### Thus ends the eighty-first chapter of the Illustrious Varāhamihira’s Brihat Samhita, titled "The Examination of Pearls."

---

Pearls are produced from elephants, serpents, oysters, conch shells, clouds, bamboo, fish, and boars. Among all these, the pearl produced from the oyster is the most excellent. ||1|| Sri Lanka, Paraloka, Saurashtra, Tamraparni, Parasava, Kaubera, Pandyavataka, and Haima—these eight places are the sources of pearls. ||2|| Pearls of various shapes, smooth, white like a swan, and large are produced in the land of Sri Lanka. Those named *Tamra* are somewhat red or black, lacking luster, yet white. ||3|| Pearls known as *Paraloka* are black, white, or yellow, containing grit and uneven; those known as *Saurashtra* are neither too large nor too small and possess a luster like butter. ||4|| *Parasava* pearls are brilliant, white, heavy, and of great quality; *Haima* pearls are small, fragile, with a luster like curd, yet large and of excellent shape. ||5|| *Kaubera* pearls are black or white, uneven, small in size but brilliant; pearls from the Pandyavataka region are like the *Triputa* fruit or coriander powder. ||6||

A *Vaishnava* pearl (whose presiding deity is Vishnu) is dark like a flax flower; an *Indra* pearl is like the moon; a *Varuna* pearl has the brilliance of yellow orpiment; and a *Yama* pearl is black. ||7|| A *Vayu* pearl is like the seed of a ripe pomegranate, or the color of copper; and an *Agni* pearl is brilliant like a smokeless fire or a lotus. ||8|| A single pearl weighing four <term>Mashas</term> <note>An ancient unit of weight, roughly 1 gram</note> that possesses brilliance and quality is valued at 5,300 rupees.

### Now Begins the Eighty-Third Chapter
#### The Examination of Rubies <note>original: *Padmaraga* - literally "Lotus-colored"</note>

> **Rubies originate from Saugandhika, Kuruvinda, and Crystal sources. Those born from Saugandhika possess the luster of bees, collyrium <note>eye-black</note>, lotuses, or the juice of the Jambu fruit. || 1 || Those born from Kuruvinda are mottled, of duller luster, and pierced by mineral impurities. Those born from Crystal are brilliant, of various colors, and highly pure. || 2 || Glossiness, a spreading radiance, transparency, luminosity, heaviness, good shape, internal glow, and deep color—these are the qualities of all excellent gemstones. || 3 || Being turbid, dull in luster, full of scratches, containing air bubbles, broken, poorly cut, unpleasing, or containing sandy grit—these are the defects of gems. || 4 || A gem with the color of a bee or a peacock's neck, brilliant like the flame of a lamp, is said to exist on the heads of serpents; it is known to be of immeasurable value. || 5 || The sovereign who wears such a gem will never suffer from the ill effects of poison or disease. In his kingdom, the gods will always send rain, and by the power of that gem, he shall destroy his enemies. || 6 || The value of a single gem weighing one *pala* <note>an ancient unit of weight</note> is twenty-six thousand [gold pieces]. For a ruby weighing three *karshas*, twenty thousand is prescribed. || 7 || For half a *pala*, twelve *karshas*—**

# Chapter 82: The Examination of Rubies (Padmaraga)

One <term>Karsha</term><note>A traditional unit of weight, approximately 12 grams</note> is worth six thousand. That which weighs eight <term>Mashakas</term><note>A smaller unit of weight; 1/12th of a Tola</note> is valued at three thousand. ||8|| Four Mashakas are worth one thousand, while two are valued at five hundred. For those with intermediate qualities—whether superior or inferior—the price should be calculated proportionately. ||9|| A stone lacking in color is worth half; one lacking luster is worth an eighth part. A stone with few virtues and many flaws receives only a twentieth part of the base value. ||10|| A ruby that is smoky, heavily scarred, and possesses few virtues also fetches only a twentieth part. Thus has the valuation of rubies been described by the ancient teachers. ||11||

-> Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Examination of Rubies," in the *Brihat Samhita* by Shri Varahamihira. <-

Rubies are born from three types of stones: Saugandhika, Kuruvinda, and Crystal. Rubies produced from Saugandhika stone are as lustrous as a bumblebee, collyrium <note>dark eye-salve</note>, a rain cloud, or the Jambu fruit. ||1|| Rubies produced from Kuruvinda stone come in various colors, possess a duller luster, and are often stained by mineral impurities. Rubies produced from Crystal are multi-colored, brilliant, and pure. ||2|| A ruby that is oily <note>smooth/glossy</note>, shining with its own radiance, clear, bright, heavy, well-shaped, glowing from within, and richly colored is considered to possess the finest qualities. ||3|| A ruby that is turbid, dim, covered in streaks, mixed with earth or minerals, fractured, unfit for piercing, or gritty is not pleasing; these are the defects of the gems. ||4|| A gem colored like a bumblebee or a peacock’s throat, brilliant like the flame of a lamp, is born in the heads of serpents; such a gem is priceless. ||5|| The King who wears that priceless gem can never be harmed by poison or disease. By the power of that gem, the gods will grant regular rain in his kingdom, and his enemies will be destroyed. ||6|| It is said that a ruby weighing one <term>Pala</term><note>Approximately 48 grams</note> is worth 26,000 rupees. A ruby weighing three Karshas is worth 20,000 rupees. ||7|| A ruby weighing half a Pala is worth 12,000; one weighing a full Karsha is worth 6,000 rupees; and a ruby weighing eight Mashas is worth 3,000 rupees. ||8|| A ruby weighing four Mashas is worth 1,000 rupees, and one weighing two Mashas is worth 500 rupees. One must judge the value of the gem according to the increase or decrease of its qualities. ||9|| The price of a ruby with poor color is half; for one without brilliance, the price is one-eighth; and for a ruby with few virtues and many defects, the price is one-twentieth. ||10|| A ruby that is somewhat smoky in color, heavily scarred, and possesses few virtues receives only a twentieth part of the value. Thus have the ancient teachers well-instructed. ||11||

-> Thus ends the eighty-second chapter of the Hindi commentary on the *Brihat Samhita* composed by Shri Varahamihiracharya, written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, a resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region. <-

### Chapter Eighty-Four
### The Characteristics of Lamps

> A lamp whose flame turns toward the left, possesses dull rays, emits sparks, is small in size, and—even when supplied with clean oil and a proper wick—extinguishes quickly, foretells sinful or calamitous results. So too does a lamp that makes noise, trembles, has scattered rays, or fails without the interference of insects or wind. ||1||
> A lamp with a concentrated flame, a long body, no flickering, and great brilliance; one that is silent, beautiful, turns toward the right <note>The clockwise or rightward motion (Pradakshina) is traditionally considered auspicious in Indic sciences.</note>, and possesses the luster of beryl or gold; such a lamp quickly manifests the arrival of Prosperity <term>Lakshmi; the goddess of wealth and fortune</term> and shines with beautiful fame. The remaining characteristics should be interpreted by applying the same logic used for the characteristics of fire. ||2||

**Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter of the Brihat Samhita by Shri Varahamihira, titled "The Characteristics of Lamps." ||84||**

A lamp whose flame turns to the left, is joined with dim rays, from which sparks emerge, which is small, and which—despite being joined with pure oil and a wick—extinguishes quickly; one that is shaky and noisy, whose rays are scattered, and which meets its end quickly without a moth falling into it or a breeze blowing; that lamp reveals sinful fruits. || 1 ||
A lamp with a unified flame, a long form, free of trembling, brilliant, silent, and beautiful, whose flame moves toward the right and has a light like beryl <term>Vaidurya; often identified as chrysoberyl cat's eye</term> and gold, and which shines with beauty and readiness—that lamp quickly reveals the coming of Lakshmi. All other characteristics should be revealed by combining them with the characteristics of fire according to logic. || 2 ||

**Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the teacher Shri Varahamihira. ||84||**

# Now Begins the Eighty-Fifth Chapter
## Characteristics of the Tooth-stick

There are thousands of varieties of tooth-sticks <note>Sanskrit: *dantakastha*; twigs used for oral hygiene</note> derived from creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, and trees. To avoid an overly lengthy discussion on all their possible effects, I shall describe only those that grant desired results. ||1||

One should not use a tooth-stick from a tree that is unknown, nor one that still has leaves attached. One should avoid those with an even number of joints <note>nodes or knots in the wood</note>, those that are split, those that have dried up while still on the tree, or those stripped of their bark. ||2||

Using tooth-sticks from the *Vaikankata* <note>Flacourtia sapida</note>, *Shriphala* <note>Coconut or Wood Apple</note>, or *Kashmari* <note>Gmelina arborea</note> trees brings divine luster. The *Kshema* tree brings a good wife. The Banyan tree (*Vata*) brings growth, the *Arka* <note>Calotropis gigantea</note> brings great brilliance, the *Madhuka* <note>Mahua</note> brings sons, and the *Kakubha* <note>Arjuna tree</note> makes one beloved by others. ||3||

Prosperity comes from the *Shirisha* and *Karanja* trees. Success in one's desires is achieved through the *Plaksha* <note>Wavy-leaf fig</note>. Using the Jasmine (*Jati*) tooth-stick brings honor among people, and the Sacred Fig (*Ashvattha*) is said to grant preeminence. ||4||

Health and long life come from the Jujube (*Badari*) and the Brihati <note>Indian Nightshade</note>. Increase in wealth and power comes from the *Khadira* <note>Catechu</note> and *Bilva* <note>Bael</note> trees. Desired objects are obtained through the *Atimuktaka* <note>Mountain Creeper</note>, and the same results are gained from the *Kadamba* tree. ||5||

Wealth is gained from the Neem tree, and food is obtained from the *Karavira* <note>Oleander</note>. The *Bhandira* tree also provides an abundance of food. Using the *Shami* tree destroys enemies, as does the *Arjuna* and the *Shyama* <note>Black creeper</note>—these lead to the destruction of those who hate you. ||6||

Dignity is said to come from the *Shala*, *Ashvakarna*, *Bhadradaru* <note>Himalayan Cedar</note>, and *Atarushaka* trees. One becomes a favorite of all people by using the *Priyangu*, *Apamarga*, *Jambu* <note>Java Plum</note>, and Pomegranate (*Dadima*) trees. ||7||

Facing either the North or the East, and holding a specific wish in one's heart, one should use a blameless tooth-stick while sitting comfortably. After use, it should be washed and discarded in a clean place. ||8||

If the discarded stick falls toward the user, or stays in a peaceful direction, it is auspicious. If it stands upright, it is extremely fortunate. Any other way is declared inauspicious, though a stick that stands and then falls is said to bring delicious food. ||9||

->**Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Tooth-stick," in the Brihat Samhita of Shri Varahamihira.**<-

### Now begins the Eighty-Sixth Chapter

### Chapter on the Mixed Results of Omens

The views held by Venus, Indra, Jupiter, Kapisthala, and Guru; the opinions expressed by Rishabha, Bhaguri, and Devala; || 1 || having seen the views of Bharadwaja and what was spoken by King Dravyavardhana, the King of Kings of Avanti; || 2 || the views of the Seven Sages <note>The Saptarishi</note>, both in Sanskrit and Prakrit <note>the vernacular languages</note>, and those things said by Garga and other authors of travel-manuals; || 3 || having seen all these, Varahamihira has composed this entire collection of omens with affection, for the supreme knowledge of his disciples. || 4 || The good or bad karma created by men in other previous births—omens reveal the ripening <term>paka: the fruition of past actions</term> of that karma for those who are traveling. || 5 || Whether they belong to the village, the forest, the water, the earth, or the sky; whether they move by day, by night, or both; their sounds, movements, and looks are to be understood through their gender: male, female, or hermaphrodite. || 6 || Because of the distinct nature of their species and their lack of fixed positions, their individual identity is sometimes not perceived. Regarding the general characteristics, there are these two verses by the Sages: || 7 || Those with thick, raised, and broad shoulders, thick necks, broad chests, and voices that are slight, deep, and resonant are males, possessing steady valor. || 8 || Those with thin chests, heads, and necks, and fine mouths, feet, and gaits, who speak continuously and softly, are females; anything other than these is a hermaphrodite. || 9 || One should observe whether they frequent villages or forests from common worldly knowledge. Desiring to be brief, I speak only of what is necessary for a journey. || 10 || Regarding the King traveling with his armies, or the deity in a city, or the leader of a caravan, the omens apply equally, but are more significant based on caste, knowledge, and age. || 11 || The results in different directions are based on whether the omen is past, present, or future. The directions are classified as "Blazing" <note>Angara: burning</note>, "Illuminated" <note>Dipta</note>, and "Smoky" <note>Dhumini</note>; the others are "Peaceful" <note>Shanta</note>. || 12 || One should predict the good or bad results for the three periods of time <note>past, present, future</note> based on the fifth direction. For the remaining directions, one should speak of the good or bad results based on proximity. || 13 || Results occur quickly if the omen is near or in a low place, and after a long time if it is high or far away. One should also state the results based on the omen's location, growth, or injury. || 14 || The "blazing" <note>intensity</note> of an omen is determined, in increasing order of importance, by the moment, the lunar day, the asterism, the wind, the sun, and the deity. An omen is also "blazing" through its action, gait, position, state, voice, and movement. || 15 || Even a peaceful omen is of five kinds: "Mild" if it eats grass or fruit; "Fierce" if it eats meat or impure things; and "Mixed" if it is known to eat grain. || 16 ||

# Chapter 86: On Omens (with Hindi Commentary)

Animals and birds are most powerful when situated in auspicious and pleasing places such as palaces, mansions, or near trees bearing excellent nectar, milk, fruits, or flowers. **(17)** They are also potent when in their natural habitats, such as mountains or water, during their appropriate seasons. Among these, the strength of omens increases progressively from a eunuch <note>original: "kliba"</note> to a woman, and then to a man. **(18)**

Omens are effective when the creatures possess their natural speed, breed characteristics, strength, posture, joy, temperament, and voice. They are favorable when moving in their natural terrain; otherwise, they should be disregarded. **(19)**

### Strength by Direction

| Direction | Powerful Omens / Sounds |
| :--- | :--- |
| **East** | Cocks, elephants, *pirili* birds, peacocks, *vanjula* birds, *chikkara* deer, the roar of a lion, and the *kutapuri* bird. **(20)** |
| **South** | Jackals, boars, *harita* pigeons, crows, *koka* ducks, and the tawny owl; also the sounds of pigeons, wailing, or harsh cries. **(21)** |
| **West** | Cows, hares, curlews <note>original: "krauncha"</note>, foxes, swans, ospreys, and *kapinjala* partridges; also the sounds of cats, festive music, singing, and laughter. **(22)** |
| **North** | Woodpeckers, deer, *khunu* deer, unclooven-hoofed animals (horses), cuckoos, blue jays <note>original: "chasha"</note>, porcupines, and the sounds of auspicious blessings, bells, or conchs. **(23)** |

### Invalid Omens
A domestic animal found in the forest or a wild animal found in a village is not to be considered. Diurnal creatures (active by day) are not omens at night, nor are nocturnal creatures omens by day. **(24)** Creatures that are in pairs (mating), diseased, terrified, fighting, hungry for meat, separated by a river, or intoxicated are never to be accepted as omens. **(25)**

### Seasonal Exceptions
The following are "fruitless" (invalid) during specific seasons:
*   **Winter:** *Rohita* deer, goats, donkeys, *kuranga* deer, and hares.
*   **Spring:** Crows and cuckoos. **(26)**
*   **Rainy Season (Bhadrapada):** Boars, dogs, and wolves.
*   **Autumn:** Lotus-dwelling birds, cows, and curlews.
*   **Monsoon (Shravana):** Elephants and *chataka* birds. **(27)**
*   **Early Winter (Hemanta):** Tigers, bears, monkeys, leopards, lions, and burrowing animals. All young animals (infants) are also considered fruitless. **(28)**

### The Thirty-Two Divisions of Directions
Between the East and South-East, one finds the treasurer, the fire-user, and the ascetic. **(29)** Between the South and South-West are the artisan, the monk, the naked mendicant, and the woman; further along are the elephant-driver, the cowherd, and the virtuous. **(30)** Between the South-West and West are the wanton woman, the woman recently delivered of a child, and the thief. Between the West and North-West are the vintner, the bird-catcher, and the cruel man. **(31)** Beyond that are the poison-healer, the cattle-owner, and the magician; then the wealthy man, the fortune-teller, and the florist. **(32)** Finally, the devotee of Vishnu, the wanderer, and the horse-groom. Thus, thirty-two variations are described starting from the East. **(33)**

The King, the Prince, the Commander, the Messenger, the Merchant, the Spy, the Brahmin, and the Elephant-Superintendent are assigned to the East and other directions respectively. **(34)** Whether a person is moving or standing, an expert in omens should predict an encounter based on the direction in which the bird or animal cries. **(35)**

### Sounds and Gender
Broken, terrifying, piteous, burnt, harsh, or rattling sounds are undesirable. Auspicious sounds are peaceful, joyful, and full of natural vigor. **(36)** The female jackal, the *shyama* bird, the *ratna*, the musk-shrew, the tawny owl, the house lizard, the sow, and the cuckoo—along with those having masculine names—are favorable on the **left**. **(37)** Those with feminine names, such as the vulture, the dog, the monkey, and the *chikkara*, along with the peacock, the *shrikantha*, and the hawk, are favorable on the **right**. **(38)**

Sounds of whistling, clapping, auspicious chants, singing, conchs, and water are favorable if they sound masculine; other sounds are favorable if they sound feminine. **(39)** In terms of musical notes <note>The text refers to the Indian solfège system</note>, the *Madhyama* (Ma), *Shadja* (Sa), and *Gandhara* (Ga) are auspicious. The *Rishabha* (Re) note is also beneficial. **(40)**

### Specific Creatures
The *Bharadvaja* lark, the goat, and the peacock are auspicious whether heard, mentioned, or seen. The mongoose and blue jay are lucky, but the chameleon brings sin if seen ahead. **(41)** Mentioning the hedgehog, snake, hare, boar, or iguana is auspicious, but seeing them or hearing them is not. The monkey and bear are unfavorable if they appear in front. **(42)**

Odd numbers of deer, mongooses, and birds are favorable on the right. The blue jay and mongoose are favorable on the left. The *Bhrigu* (sage/planet Venus) is favorable in the afternoon. **(43)** The *chikkara*, the *kutapuri*, and the *pirili* are favorable on the right during the day...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on omens (Shakuna) from the Varahi Samhita (also known as the Brihat Samhita) by the polymath Varahamihira. It focuses on the specific movements and positions of animals and birds as signs for travelers and kings.</meta>

# The Varahi Samhita

-> Page 282 <-

Animals with keen sight and those that live in burrows are always auspicious. **(44)** In the East, a white horse is best; in the South, the flesh of a dog <note>original: "shvamamsam"; likely referring to the sight of it or a specific omen involving it</note>. In the West, a young maiden is auspicious, and in the North, cows, Brahmins, and holy men. **(45)** A net or a dog's foot are not desired in the East or South, as they signify death by weapons. In the West, a eunuch or a servant are ill-omened; in the North, a threshing floor, a seat, or a plow are unfavorable. **(46)**

In matters of work, social gatherings, battles, entering a place, or finding a lost path, the following specific movements should be observed: **(47)** During the day, the deer, the *Ruru* <note>a species of antelope</note>, and monkeys should be regarded as they are during a departure. In the first part of the day, the blue jay, the *Vanjula* bird, and the cock are significant. **(48)** In the latter part of the night, the son's son <note>possibly a specific bird name or a corruption in the OCR</note>, the owl, and the *Pingala* <note>spotted owlet</note> are observed. All these are considered reversed <note>inauspicious</note> when occurring in the company of women. **(49)**

When visiting a king, the omens should be taken as if one were departing on a journey. This also applies to entering mountains, forests, or bathing in rivers. **(50)** An omen moving from left to right is auspicious, but those moving directly in front or behind are not. If they are "blazing" <term>dipta: a technical term in omenology meaning an animal is agitated, facing the sun, or making harsh sounds</term> with activity, they signify destruction for the traveler and are called *Parigha* <note>the "iron bar" omen</note>. **(51)** If those same omens are "calm" <term>shanta: the opposite of dipta; peaceful in sound and movement</term> in their cries and actions, they are called "Gateways of the Omen" and lead to the success of one's goals. **(52)**

Some authorities desire the "Gateway of the Omen" to be formed by birds of the same species standing on both sides, characterized by calm actions and sounds. **(53)** If one omen permits departure while another forbids it, this is a conflict; it is inauspicious for the traveler, or one must follow the stronger omen. **(54)** If an omen first appears as one for "entering" and then becomes one for "departing," it predicts success with ease. The reverse indicates failure upon entry. **(55)** If an omen first allows passage but then blocks it, it foretells the death of the traveler at the hands of an enemy, or perhaps a riot or disease. **(56)**

Omens on the left that are "blazing" <gloss>agitated/harsh</gloss> announce fear. A blazing omen at the start of an undertaking is like a grass fire at the end of the year. **(57)** Depending on the lunar day, the day of the week, the asterism, the location, and the movement, blazing omens respectively bring fear to wealth, the army, strength, the body, and desired actions. **(58)** When omens are blazing during the sound of thunderclouds, there is fear from the wind. Blazing omens at the two twilights <note>dawn and dusk</note> create fear arising from weapons. **(59)**

If omens are seen on funeral pyres, hair, or skulls, they grant death, imprisonment, or slaughter. If situated on thorns, wood, or ashes, they give quarrels, exhaustion, and sorrow. **(60)** Blazing omens situated in hollows or unstable places cause unknown fears. Calm omens in such places are simply fruitless. **(61)** Those making loud noises or carrying food are known to give failure or success respectively. One who leaves their place to travel is praised; otherwise, it signifies a return. **(62)**

Quarrels occur when the voice is blazing; conflict occurs when the location is blazing. A voice that is high at first and low afterward indicates a thief. **(63)** A blazing omen crying out from a single spot for seven days causes the destruction of a village. For cities and kings, this destruction follows a season, a half-year, or a year. **(64)** All animals that eat the flesh of their own kind cause famine—except for snakes, mice, cats, and fish <note>original: "prithuroma", literally "broad-scaled"</note>. **(65)** Animals mating with other species portend the destruction of the country, except for the birth of mules or unnatural mating among humans. **(66)**

Fears of bondage and slaughter arise from omens touching the feet, thighs, or head. From omens involving flowers, meat, or grain, there come rains, theft, or the capture of the wounded. **(67)** Through cruel or evening-spoiled omens, or those involving the behavior of chief kings, and through those of long duration, the arrival of men from various directions is known. **(68)** If the omen is strong and associated with good objects, good things will arrive. One who is radiant but looks down submissively is gentle, yet may perform cruel deeds. **(69)** A blazing omen in an intermediate direction, echoed by one on the left, tells of the abduction of a woman. **(70)** A calm omen followed by a "fifth-position" blazing one brings victory or the arrival of a man; the reverse causes harm. **(71)** A cry from both the left and right indicates fear for both oneself and the enemy.

It categorizes omens into "blazing" (agitated) and "calm" states to interpret their prophetic meaning.</summary>

If all these [birds/animals] cry out with a balanced or uniform tone, they foretell death. ||72|| If they are at the top, middle, or root of a tree, they signify the arrival of elephants, horses, or charioteers respectively. If they are on long lotuses or those with stolen <note>damaged or plucked</note> tips, they signify the arrival of men, boats, or palanquins. ||73|| If the omen occurs on a cart, on high ground, or in the shade, it is associated with a parasol <note>a symbol of royalty or high status</note>. Having observed what Rishabha <note>a legendary seer</note> said to Bhaguri and Devala according to the views of Venus, Indra, Jupiter, Kapisthala, and Garuda; ||1|| and having looked at the views of Bharadwaja, and what the Great King of Ujjain, Shri Dravyavardhana, said, as well as the views of the Seven Sages <note>the Saptarshis</note> composed in Prakrit and Sanskrit, and what Garga and other travelers have said—having seen all that, I, Varahamihira, have composed this "Collection of All Omens" endowed with excellent knowledge for the pleasure of my disciples. ||2||3||4|| The good and evil deeds that humans have performed in previous births are revealed by birds and other creatures at the time of one's journey through the ripening of that karma; this is what is known as *Shakuna* <term>Shakuna: the science of omens based on the behavior of animals and birds</term>. ||5|| The movements, gazes, sounds, and utterances of creatures—whether village-dwellers, forest-dwellers, water-dwellers, land-dwellers, sky-dwellers, day-active, night-active, or active in both—reveal whether they are male, female, or hermaphrodite. ||6|| Because of differences in species and lack of fixed states, it is not always clear which among these creatures is male, female, or hermaphrodite; for this reason, the Sages have composed two verses stating their general characteristics. ||7|| Those creatures that are thick-set, tall, with broad shoulders, large necks, beautiful chests, somewhat deep voices, and steady prowess—those creatures are male. ||8|| Those with weak chests, weak heads, and weak necks, small mouths, small feet, little prowess, and who always make sweet sounds should be understood as female; and those in whom the characteristics of both male and female are found should be understood as hermaphrodite. ||9|| Which omen belongs to the village and which to the forest will be known through common worldly practice. Since I am a summarizer, I shall only speak on the subject for the purpose of travel. ||10|| The fruit of the omen falls upon oneself on a path, upon the King in an army, upon the deity (city lord) in a city, upon the chief in commerce, and among equals, upon the one who is greatest in caste, knowledge, or age. ||11|| From sunrise until one watch <note>approx. 3 hours</note> of the day has passed, the North-East is "released by the sun," the East is "possessed by the sun," and the South-East is "approached by the sun." In this way, through the eight watches, the sun moves through the directions starting from the East...

The sun moves through the quarters; the direction from which the sun has already passed is called **Angarini** <note>literally "glowing like charcoal"</note> (the direction abandoned by the sun). The direction in which the sun is currently situated is called **Dipta** <note>blazing or illuminated</note> (the sun-attained direction). The direction toward which the sun is about to move is named **Dhumita** <note>smoky</note> (the sun-approaching direction). The remaining five directions are considered **Shanta** <note>calm or peaceful</note>. If an ill omen occurs in the direction the sun has left, its effects are considered to have already passed; in the direction where the sun is present, the omen’s fruit occurs that very day; in the direction the sun is approaching, the fruit of the omen should be known to occur in the future. || 12 ||

The auspicious or inauspicious results from the fifth direction relative to the *Angarita* and others are always equal at all times, and the results of the remaining two directions should be interpreted according to the nearest direction. || 13 ||

The result of an omen occurring nearby or below happens quickly, while the result of an omen occurring high up or far away happens with delay. An omen reveals its fruit based on the growth or decay of its location; that is, if the omen sits in a place that grows daily, such as a tree, the result is auspicious. Sitting in a place that diminishes daily is a giver of inauspicious results. || 14 ||

The moment, the lunar day <term>Tithi: a Vedic lunar day</term>, the constellation <term>Nakshatra: lunar mansion</term>, the wind, and the sun—these five are successively called **Devadipta** <note>divinely illuminated</note>. Movement, position, state, voice, and gesture—when these are intensified, they are called **Kriyadipta** <note>action-illuminated</note> in sequence. These are the ten types of "illuminated" states. || 15 ||

The ten types of omens mentioned above that eat grass and fruit are **Saumya** <note>gentle/benign</note> and peaceful. Those that eat meat, excrement, and other impure substances are **Raudra** <note>fierce/terrible</note>. Those that eat grain are called **Mishra** <note>mixed—neither gentle nor fierce</note>. || 16 ||

It is excellent if omens are seated on palaces, temples of deities, flags, auspicious objects, or beautiful places, or if they sit on trees laden with honey, sap, milk, fruits, or flowers. || 17 ||

Diurnal <note>daytime</note> omens are powerful when seated atop mountains (at a height) during their time. Nocturnal <note>nighttime</note> omens are powerful when seated near water. Among these creatures, males and females are more powerful than those of neutral gender. || 18 ||

When endowed with (movement) caste, strength, position, joy, essence, and voice, they are powerful; when moving in a natural direction from their own ground, they are strong. When lacking speed and such, they are devoid of strength. || 19 ||

The rooster, elephant, *pirili* <note>a type of bird</note>, peacock, *vanjula* <note>willow-bird</note>, *chikkara* <note>a species of deer or bird</note>, the lion-roar bird, and the *karayika*—all these omens are powerful in the **East**. || 20 ||

The jackal, owl, green pigeon, crow, ruddy sheldrake, *rikshu*, *pingala* (a type of owl/bird), and the pigeon—all these creatures are powerful in the **South** when crying or making harsh sounds. || 21 ||

In the **West**, the cow, rabbit, crane, fox, swan, osprey, *kapinjala* (white partridge), and cat are powerful, as are festivals, musical instruments, songs, and laughter. || 22 ||

The woodpecker, deer, mouse, buck, horse, cuckoo, blue jay, porcupine, auspicious sounds, and the sounding of conchs and bells are powerful in the **North**. || 23 ||

One should not accept a forest omen occurring in a village, nor a village omen occurring in the forest. It is also improper to consider a daytime omen at night or a nighttime omen during the day. || 24 ||

One should never consider omens that are in pairs (mating), afflicted by disease, terrified, fighting, seeking meat, on the opposite bank of a river, or intoxicated. || 25 ||

The red deer, goat, donkey, horse, antelope, camel, buck, and rabbit should not be considered during the *Shishira* <note>late winter</note> season. In the *Vasanta* <note>spring</note> season, the crow and cuckoo are considered fruitless. || 26 ||

In the month of *Bhadrapada* <note>August-September</note>, the boar, dog, and wolf; in the *Sharad* <note>autumn</note> season, the heron, cow, and crane; and in the month of *Shravana* <note>July-August</note>, the elephant and the *chataka* <note>Jacobin cuckoo</note> should not be taken as omens. || 27 ||

In *Hemanta* <note>early winter</note>, the tiger, bear, monkey, leopard, buffalo, snake, child, and all deformed humans are fruitless. || 28 ||

In the division between the East and the South-East <note>Agni corner</note>, following the clockwise order <term>Pradakshina: circumambulation from left to right</term>, the treasurer, those who live by fire (blacksmiths, etc.), and the ascetic are situated. || 29 ||

In the middle section are the artisan, the beggar, and the naked woman—these three. Sounds that are broken, terrifying, miserable, pained, harsh, weak, or shrill are not auspicious; however, sounds made by creatures that are calm and joyful in nature are auspicious. || 36 || From the left side, the female jackal, the sinful woman, the quarrelsome woman, the shrew, the lizard, the sow, and the cuckoo are auspicious, as are birds with masculine names. || 37 || The Bhasa bird, the dog, the monkey, the Shrikarna bird, the Chikka-deer, the peacock, the Shrikanta, the Pippika, the Ruru-deer, and the hawk—these are considered feminine in gender; they are auspicious when appearing on the right. || 38 ||

The sound of the Bharadwaja bird, the goat, and the peacock is blessed when heard or seen in front; however, the appearance of a mongoose, a blue jay <note>Nilkanth</note>, or a chameleon in front at the time of a journey brings misfortune. || 41 || It is auspicious to speak the names of the hedgehog, the snake, the rabbit, the boar, and the iguana at the time of a journey, but their crying or their sight is not desirable; for the monkey and the bear, the result is the opposite <note>their sight is good, but their names are not</note>. || 42 ||

Sage Bhrigu says that in the afternoon, it is beneficial for deer, mongooses, and egg-born creatures (birds) to be positioned in a clockwise manner even if they are in an odd number; the appearance of a blue jay along with a mongoose on the left side gives auspicious results. || 43 || During the day, the Chikka-deer, the Kutapuri, and the Pirili appearing on the right, and at all times, snakes and tusked animals appearing on the right path, is auspicious. || 44 ||

In the East, horses and the Chinese; in the South, a corpse and meat; in the West, a maiden and curd; and in the North, cows, Brahmins, and holy men give the best results. || 45 || In the East and South, a net, dog tracks, weapons, and a killer; in the West, liquor and a eunuch; and in the North, a villain, a seat, and a plow are not auspicious. || 46 ||

At the time of performing a task, meeting someone, entering a battle, or searching for lost property, if the rules mentioned for a journey are reversed, it is auspicious. That is, what was fixed as auspicious or inauspicious for a journey will be auspicious or inauspicious here in that order. In the remaining parts, the <term>Naptuka</term> <note>a specific type of bird, possibly a nightjar</note>, the owl, and the <term>Pingala</term> <note>the spotted owlet</note> should be considered auspicious; however, for women, all omens should be interpreted in the opposite manner. ||49|| When going to have an audience with a King or entering a house, all omens should be observed just as they are for a journey. Similarly, when climbing a mountain, entering a forest, or crossing a river, one should observe omens as one does during travel. ||50|| If <term>Kriyadipta</term> <note>omens "blazing" or excited by their specific actions or movements</note> omens move toward both the left and right directions, they are beneficial. If those same two move both ahead and behind, they are called <term>Parigha</term> <note>literally "an iron bar" or "obstruction"</note>, which causes the destruction of the traveler. ||51|| However, if those same two omens remain in their respective sections—that is, the one on the left stays left and the one on the right stays right—and they make sounds or movements in a calm manner, it is called a "Gate" (Dvara) omen, and they fulfill the purpose of the traveler. ||52|| Some say that if "Gate" omens of the same species, calm in movement and silent, are situated on both sides of the traveler, they are auspicious. ||53|| If one omen gives permission for the journey and another omen forbids the journey, that omen is designated as <term>Virodha</term> <note>contradiction or opposition</note>; it is highly inauspicious for the one departing. ||54|| If an omen first enters and then departs, success is achieved with ease; however, in the case of entry (such as entering a home), the opposite of this leads to the fulfillment of the task. ||55|| If an omen first grants permission for the journey and then later forbids it, the traveler faces death at the hands of an enemy, or suffers from weapons and disease. ||56|| Omens situated on the left side in a <term>Dipta</term> <note>literally "blazing"; refers to an inauspicious or agitated direction/state</note> direction reveal fear; if an omen is "blazing" right at the start, it causes fear regarding that task for one year. ||57|| Based on the date, wind, sun, lunar mansion, location, and movement, "blazing" omens are respectively terrifying for wealth, the army, strength, limbs, loved ones, and actions. ||58|| If an omen is "blazing" due to the sound of clouds, there is fear from the wind; an omen "blazing" during both twilights causes fear arising from weapons. ||59|| If an omen sits upon a funeral pyre, hair, or a skull, it brings death, imprisonment, and slaughter. Sitting on a thorny tree, wood, or ashes, it gives distress, toil, and sorrow. ||60|| If all the aforementioned "blazing" omens sit upon worthless stones, it indicates an undistinguished soldier; however, a "calm" (Shanta) omen reduces all the stated [negative] effects. ||61|| Omens that are making noise and those that are eating should be known as providers of failure and success respectively. If an omen moves from its place while making a sound, it indicates a journey; if it returns to the same place, it confirms someone's arrival. ||62|| A <term>Svaradipta</term> <note>blazing by voice/sound</note> omen indicates distress; a <term>Sthanadipta</term> <note>blazing by location</note> omen is <term>Vigrahasuchaka</term> <note>an indicator of war or conflict</note>. If an omen first makes a high-pitched sound and then a low-pitched sound, the traveler will be a victim of theft. ||63|| If an omen remains "blazing" and sounding from one location for a week, it destroys the village; if it sounds "blazing" in one place for two years, six months, or one year, it respectively destroys the city, the country, and the kings. ||64|| Except for snakes, rats, cats, and fish, if any omens begin to eat the flesh of their own kind, they are <term>Durbhikshakari</term> <note>bringers of famine</note>. ||65|| Except for the mating of humans with different species (such as with a mare) or the production of a mule (where a mare mates to produce a mule), if omens and species mate outside their kind, the country is destroyed. ||66|| If an omen passes over the feet, thighs, or head...

<header>With Hindi Commentary Chapter 86 (287)</header>

If the omen <note>original: "shakuna" - refers here to a bird or animal acting as a sign</note> is seen binding, striking, or causing fear, it indicates imprisonment or danger. If seen drinking water, it foretells rain. If seen eating grass, it indicates a theft will occur. If seen eating meat, it predicts a wound on the body. If seen eating grain, the omen indicates a meeting with a relative. ॥67॥

If this omen is situated in the "Blazing" <note>term: Dipta - a direction or state associated with the sun's position, usually considered ill-omened</note> directions, it is respectively cruel, fierce, and faulty or wicked. If situated in the "Smoky" directions, it indicates a prominent king or a servant. If in the "Calm" <note>term: Shanta - directions not facing the sun, usually auspicious</note> directions, it signifies the arrival of a man after a long time. If the omen is situated in the "Glow" <note>term: Angarini - 'charcoal-like' or burning direction</note> direction, it proves the arrival of the local people along with everyone else. ॥68॥

If the omen is wealthy <note>meaning robust or appearing prosperous</note> and powerful, then a man with wealth arrives that day. If it is radiant, looking downward (appearing humble), or gentle, then there is fear in fierce business dealings. ॥69॥

If a "Blazing" omen situated in an intermediate direction <note>term: Vidisha - the corners like NE, SE, SW, NW</note> moves to the left and cries out, it indicates the acquisition of a woman from a man of famous birth in that direction. ॥70॥

If there is a "Calm" omen in any direction, and if it is answered by a "Blazing" omen in the fifth direction from it, it grants victory. If the opposite occurs, it indicates the arrival of a man from that direction or is harmful. ॥71॥

If there are cries in the left and right sections, and then the omen on the left side speaks afterward, they reveal fear from oneself and from enemies. If all these make an equal sound, they reveal death. ॥72॥

If the omen is perched on the top, middle, or root of a tree, then respectively a man riding an elephant, a horse, or a chariot arrives. If the omen is on a long object, on a lotus or similar flower, or on the edge of a doorframe, then a man riding a boat or a palanquin arrives. ॥73॥

If the omen is perched in the high part or the shadow of a cart in the East or an intermediate direction, then a man accompanied by a ceremonial umbrella arrives in one, three, five days, or one week. ॥74॥

Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirriti, Varuna, Pavana, Chandra, and Shankar are the eight lords of the eight directions starting from the East. Among them, all cardinal directions are male and intermediate directions are female. ॥75॥

By dividing the eight directions into thirty-two variations—such as a wooden plank, a split bamboo, the sky, water-born, an arrow, leather, and a strip of cloth; or exercise, a peacock, chirping, distress, a lotus, a chain, a mantra, and the sound of a cow; or red, yellow, black, white colors, and mixed colors in the corners; and a flag, burnt, a cremation ground, a cave, water, a mountain, a sacrifice, and anger—all these signs are placed in order. Then, through these, one reveals the fear of union or the imagined fear of another place. ॥76॥77॥78॥

And in order: in the Northeast, a great woman and a young girl; in the Southeast, a deformed and foul-smelling woman; in the Southwest, a woman in blue clothes and a wicked woman; in the Northwest, a tall woman and a widow. The union occurs with a woman of the direction in which the omen resides, or that woman causes anxiety. ॥79॥

Furthermore, in this directional circle, in order: handsome forms, gold, the sick, or women; or sheep, rams, vehicles, sacrifices, herds of cows; or the Banyan, the red Lodhra, yellow bamboo, the Mango tree, Khadir, Bel, and Arjun—these are the eight trees of the directions. (Depending on the direction of the omen, the gain or loss of silver, gold, etc., occurs under the tree of that direction according to the omen). ॥80॥

->resident of Moradabad in the North-Western region, on the Brihat Samhita composed by Sri Varahamihiracharya. ॥86॥<-

Varahi Samhita

# Chapter 87

### Omens: The Inner Wheel <note>Sanskrit: *Antarachakram*. This refers to a conceptual map used to interpret the cries or sightings of birds based on their specific compass direction.</note>

In the **East**, if a bird cries in a peaceful direction, it foretells the arrival of a king’s associate, the gaining of honor, and the acquisition of gems and wealth. (1) In the section immediately following that, there will be the arrival of gold and the fulfillment of desired goals. In the third section, there will be the arrival of weapons, wealth, and betel nuts. (2) In the fourth section, one sees a sleek-looking <term>Brahmin</term> <note>A member of the priestly class</note> or a consecrated fire-priest. In the corner <note>Southeast</note>, one sees a dependent or a monk, and acquires gold and iron. (3)

In the first section of the **South**, one sees a king or a son, and achieves success in desired aims. Beyond that, one acquires wealth through women and obtains mustard and barley. (4) In the fourth section from the corner, one recovers wealth previously lost; or, a traveler receives some fruit or another. (5) Due **South**, there is success in travel and the acquisition of peacocks, buffaloes, and roosters. In the second part from the South, there is a meeting with wandering performers, bringing auspiciousness and joy. (6)

Further on, there is success, a meeting with fishermen, and the acquisition of partridges. In the next, one sees a wandering ascetic and obtains ripe mangoes. (7) In the **Southwest**, one gains a woman, horses, ornaments, and a messenger’s letter. Beyond this, one sees a leather-worker and obtains leather goods. (8) In the third part from the Southwest, one sees monkeys and monks. In the fourth part from the corner, one acquires fruits, flowers, and ivory carvings. (9)

In the **West**, one obtains gems born of the ocean and lapis lazuli. Beyond this, there is a meeting with forest-dwellers, hunters, or thieves, and the acquisition of meat. (10) Further on, one sees those afflicted by "wind-diseases" <note>Sanskrit: *Vata*; likely referring to respiratory or neurological conditions in this context</note> and obtains sandalwood and agarwood. Above that, one acquires weapons and books, and meets with a friend. (11)

In the **Northwest**, one obtains sea-foam, fly-whisks, and woolen goods, and meets a scribe. In the next, one gains earthenware, and the instruments of bards and drummers. (12) In the third from the Northwest, there is a meeting with a friend and the acquisition of wealth. Beyond that, one gains clothes and horses, and meets with a dear friend. (13)

One obtains curd, rice, and parched grain, and sees a sick person or a Brahmin. Immediately after, wealth is gained and a merchant arrives. (14) In the next, there is a meeting with a courtesan, a young lad, or a servant, and the acquisition of dried flowers and fruits. Beyond that, one sees a painter and obtains fine cloth. (15)

In the **Northeast**, one meets a temple priest and gains grain, gems, and cattle. In the first part toward the East, one gains cloth and meets a harlot. (16) Beyond that, there is a meeting with a washerman and the arrival of water-based goods. After this, a meeting with those who work with elephants and the acquisition of a cow. (17)

This directional wheel, divided into thirty-two parts, is also mentioned in the context of <term>Vastu-bandhana</term> <note>The ritual binding or architectural planning of a site</note>. The results for those situated in the spokes and the hub are categorized in nine ways. (18) In the **Hub**, there is a meeting with kinsmen and friends, bringing great satisfaction. If a bird cries there, it signifies the arrival of silk cloth and a meeting with a king. (19)

In the **Southeast spoke**, there is a meeting with an owl-catcher, a carpenter, a laborer, a horse, or a charioteer; one also acquires goods made by them or a horse. (20) Having fixed the rim and the hub, in the spoke to the **South**, there is a meeting with righteous people and a gain of merit. (21) In the **Southwest**, a meeting with camels, performers, or <term>Kapalika</term> ascetics <note>A specific sect of Shiva-worshippers known for carrying skulls</note> is indicated; one also gains a bull and food such as beans and pulses. (22) In the spoke of the **West**, there is an association with farmers; one gains products of the sea, essence, glass, fruits, and wine. (23) One also sees porters, carpenters, and beggars...

# Chapter 87: With Hindi Commentary
**10**

->**The Results of Omens in the Inner Circle**<-

If the bird is situated in the North-West <note>Vayu-dik</note>, one obtains the Tilaka flower and the flowers of the Naga and Punnaga trees. **[24]** In the North <note>Kauberi</note>, a bird in a "quiet" <note>Shanta: a favorable or peaceful direction</note> quarter indicates the gain of wealth. It also foretells a meeting with a devotee of Vishnu <note>Bhagavata</note> and those wearing yellow garments. **[25]** In the North-East <note>Aishane</note>, one encounters a woman engaged in religious vows <note>Vrata</note>. One should also expect the acquisition of black iron, clothing, and bells. **[26]**

In the Southern eighth-part, if the bird is in the second, sixth, third, seventh, or eighth positions, the result of a journey is middling. In the North, if in the second position, and in all remaining positions, the journey is highly auspicious. **[27]** Within the center <note>the "navel" or Nabha</note>, it gives auspicious results in six specific movements. However, in both the North-West and South-West, the journey brings distress. **[28]**

These results have been stated for the "quiet" <note>Shanta</note> directions; now I shall describe the results for the "blazing" <note>Dipta: unfavorable or agitated</note> directions. In the East, there is fear from the king <note>Narendra</note> and an encounter with enemies. **[29]** In the direction immediately following that, there is loss of gold and fear for goldsmiths. In the third part, there is loss of wealth, quarrels, and the fury of weapons. **[30]**

In the fourth part, there is fear of fire, and in the South-East <note>Agneya</note>, there is fear of thieves. In the second part from that corner, there is loss of wealth and the death of a prince. **[31]** In the third and fourth parts, there is the destruction of a woman's fetus. There is also the ruin of goldsmiths and artisans, and the fury of weapons. **[32]** In the fifth part, one should predict fear of the king, plague <note>Mari</note>, and the sight of a corpse. In the sixth, fear is known for celestial musicians <note>Gandharvas</note> and actors. **[33]**

In the seventh part of the "blazing" direction, there is fear for fishermen and bird-catchers. Following that, the disruption of meals and fear of Jain monks <note>Nirgrantha</note> is mentioned. **[34]** In the South-West <note>Nairrita</note>, there is a quarrel, bloodshed, and the fury of weapons. In the subsequent part, leather goods are destroyed and there is fear for leather-workers. **[35]**

In the next part, there is fear for wandering ascetics <note>Parivrajaka</note> and Buddhist monks <note>Shravana</note>; in the one after that, fear of starvation. In the West <note>Varunya</note>, there is fear of rain, and in the next, fear of thieves. **[36]** In the next parts, there is the destruction of those affected by wind, then of weapons, books, and those suffering from wind-related diseases. In the corner, books are destroyed, followed by fear of poison, thieves, and storms. **[37]**

Beyond that, loss of wealth and conflict with friends is to be known. Near that, the killing of horses and fear for the royal priest <note>Purohita</note> is proclaimed. **[38]** In the North, there is the stealing of cows and injury by weapons; in the next, the destruction of a caravan and loss of wealth. Nearby, there is fear of dogs, and for wind-god worshippers, Brahmins, slaves, and courtesans. **[39]**

Near the North-East, omens regarding variegated clothes and painted walls are mentioned. In the North-East itself, there is fear of fire and the defilement of noble women. **[40]** Near that same spot, the birth of sorrow and the death of a woman occurs. Above that, fear is known for washermen and those who live in marshy areas. **[41]**

There is fear for elephant-drivers and the death of elephants at the completion of the circle. In the interior, if "blazing," the death of the wife is certain in the East. **[42]** In the South-East, there is the fury of weapons and fire, the death of horses, and fear for artisans. In the South, the destruction of righteousness <note>Dharma</note>; in the next, the slaughter of attackers and pure people. **[43]**

In the West, there is fear for laborers, and in the North-West corner, the death of donkeys and camels. In this very place, there is fear of cholera <note>Visuchika</note> and poison for men. **[44]** In the Northern half, there is harassment of Brahmins; in the North-East, mental anguish. There is distress for village cowherds there, and in the center <note>Nabha</note>, suicide <note>Atmavadha</note>. **[45]**

(Thus ends the second chapter titled "The Inner Circle" in the section on All Omens.)

...there is an outbreak of violence with weapons. ||30|| If an omen occurs in the fourth part of the East, there is fear of fire; in the South-East corner <note>Agneya-kona</note>, there is fear of thieves. If the omen occurs in the second part of this same corner, it leads to the loss of wealth and the destruction of the King's son. ||31|| If an omen occurs in the third part of the South-East corner, it causes the destruction of the wombs of women <note>miscarriage or infertility</note>; in the fourth part, it leads to the destruction of goldsmiths and artisans, and an outbreak of weapons. ||32|| If an omen occurs in the fifth part of this same direction, there is fear of the King and the sight of one dead from a plague <note>Mari</note>. In the sixth part, fear of the *Dom* <note>a specific social group often associated with cremation rites</note> and *Gandharvas* <note>celestial musicians/performers</note> is known. ||33|| If a "blazing" <note>dipta: a harsh or ill-omened cry</note> omen occurs in the seventh part of the East, there is fear from fishermen and bird-catchers. In the eighth part, it leads to the destruction of food and fear from a fool. ||34|| If an omen occurs in the South-West corner <note>Nairitya-kona</note>, it brings distress, bleeding, and violence with weapons. In the West, it signifies the destruction of leather goods and fear of the tanner. ||35|| In the second part of the West, there is fear of ascetics and Buddhist monks; in the third part, fear of fasting <note>starvation</note>. If a blazing omen occurs in the West, there is fear of excessive rain, and in the next part, fear of dogs and thieves. ||36|| In the following direction, there is destruction of people afflicted by wind-related diseases <note>Vayu-grasa</note>, and in the part after that, destruction of weapons, books, and messengers. If a blazing omen occurs in the North-West corner <note>Vayu-kona</note>, books are destroyed; in the next part, fear arises from poison, thieves, and wind. ||37|| In the next part, wealth is lost and one should expect quarrels with friends. In the following part, it reveals the killing of horses and fear for the royal priest. ||38|| If a blazing omen occurs in the North, there is cattle-lifting and injury by weapons. In the next part, trade is struck and wealth is lost. In the adjacent part, there is fear from *Vratya* <term>Vratya: Brahmins who have lost their caste status due to missing initiatory rites</term>, servants, and the dogs of widows. ||39|| Near the North-East corner <note>Ishan-kona</note>, there is fear regarding paintings, clothing, and artists. If a blazing omen occurs in the North-East corner itself, fire-fear and the defilement of noble women is foretold. ||40|| In the part adjacent to this direction, sorrow arises and women perish. In the next part, fear from washermen and gardeners <note>Kachhi</note> is known. ||41|| At the conclusion of the directional wheel <note>Dik-chakra</note>, an omen brings fear of falling from an elephant or the death of an elephant. If a blazing omen occurs on the eastern spoke of the center, the death of a woman is certain. ||42|| In the middle of the South-East, there is the wrath of weapons and fire, the death of horses, and fear for artisans. In the South, there is the destruction of righteousness <note>Dharma</note>, and in the next part, death by fire, sudden attack <note>avaskanda</note>, or rogues. ||43|| On the western spoke, there is fear for artisans; in the North-West, the killing of donkeys and camels, and for humans, fear of cholera <note>Visuchika</note> and poison. ||44|| In the North, a blazing omen brings loss of wealth and suffering to Brahmins; in the North-East, it brings mental anguish. If a blazing omen occurs at the "navel" <note>the very center of the diagram</note>, there is suffering for villagers and cowherds, and death for the traveler. ||45||

->Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter in the Hindi commentary by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-West, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the venerable Acharya Varahamihira. ||87||<-

# Chapter Eighty-Eight

## On the Sounds of Omens

The Shyama <note>Indian Robin</note>, the Dhwanvan <note>a type of crane</note>, the Vanjula <note>Water-cane bird</note>, the Peacock, the Shrikarna <note>Green Woodpecker</note>, the Chakravaka <note>Ruddy Sheldrake</note>, the Blue Jay, the Andiraka, the Wagtail, the Parrot, the Crow, and the three types of Pigeons; the Bharadvaja <note>Skylark</note>, the Potter-bird <note>Hoopoe</note>, the Wild Cock, the Donkey, the Harita <note>Green Pigeon</note>, the Vulture, the Monkey, the Phenta, and the Kukkuta-purnakuta—these are declared to be **diurnal** <note>active during the day</note> creatures. ||1||

The Vixen, the Pingala <note>Spotted Owlet</note>, the Chappika, the Bat, the Owl, and the Hare are **nocturnal** <note>active at night</note>. If any of these move about outside of their natural time, it portends the destruction of the country or its ruler. ||2||

Horses, men, snakes, camels, leopards, lions, bears, iguanas, wolves, mongooses, deer, dogs, cows, tigers, swans, spotted deer, jackals, and the "other-reared" <note>Cuckoo</note>—these, along with cats, cranes, and boars, may be seen both by **day and night**. ||3||

The birds known as Bhasha, Kutapuri, Karabaka, and Karayika are collectively called *Purnakuta*. The Owl is also known by names such as Chetaka, Pingalika, Pechika, and Hukka. ||4||

The female pigeon is called *Kapotaki*. The Shyama is also known as *Vanjulaka* and *Khadirachanchu* <note>Catechu-beaked</note>. The Musk-shrew is called *Nrupasuta* <note>King's daughter</note>, and the Donkey is termed *Baleya*. ||5||

The bird that frequents broken riverbanks and ponds is called *Ekaputraka*. The *Rala* is known as the "quarrel-maker"; it is two inches long, stays on the ground, and chirps like a cricket at night. ||6||

The *Durbalika* is the same as the *Bhandika*; for those in the East, seeing it on the south is auspicious. The *Chikkara* is a species of deer, and the *Kukuvaku* is another name for the Cock. ||7||

The "Pit-cock" is famously known as the *Kulala-kukkuta* <note>Hoopoe</note>. The "Wall-fish" should be understood as the common House Lizard. ||8||

The *Dhwanvan* is called "Divine." The *Kroda* is the Boar, and the *Gaurastra* is the Wild Ox. The *Sarameya* is the Dog, and the *Sukarika* is the common Sparrow. ||9||

In this manner, one should learn the local names used in various regions from experts. To understand the meaning of the sounds of omens, these names must be carefully considered and applied according to the scientific treatises. ||10||

The sound of the Vanjula is *Tittidi* when "blazing" <note>dipta: usually inauspicious or intense</note>, and *Kilikili* when "full" <note>purna: auspicious</note>. The sounds of the Hawk, Parrot, Vulture, and Crow are considered "blazing" if they differ from their natural notes. ||11||

If a pigeon enters a vehicle, a seat, a bed, or a house, or if it settles on a lotus, it portends evil for men. The timing of the result varies by species: ||12||

For a pale white pigeon, the result occurs within a year; for a variegated one, within six months; for a saffron-grey one, the result of the pigeon's omen is felt immediately. ||13||

The sound *Chich-chid* of the Shyama is "full" <note>auspicious</note>; the sound *Shula-shula* brings wealth. The sound *Chach-cha* is "blazing," while *Chikkigiti* indicates a meeting with a loved one. ||14||

The sound *Guggu* of the Green Pigeon is "full"; all its other sounds are "blazing." For the Bharadvaja <note>Skylark</note>, any variety in its notes is declared to be auspicious. ||15||

The *Kish-kishi* sound of the Karayika is "full"; the sound *Kaha-kaha* is auspicious. The sound *Kara-kara* brings only safety but does not ensure the success of the intended business. ||16||

The sound *Kotukli* brings safety; *Katukli* indicates rain. The sound *Kotikili* is fruitless, and the *Gum* sound is "blazing" <note>inauspicious</note>. ||17||

Seeing the "Divine bird" <note>Dhwanvan</note> on the left is praised. If it is seen perched a cubit high, success is certain. If it is perched even higher, the Earth, bounded by the oceans, will surely come under the observer's control. ||18||

A snake coming toward a traveler indicates an encounter with enemies, imprisonment, or death. If it moves to the left, it is not favorable for success in coming or going. ||19||

The Wagtail <note>Khanjanaka</note> brings kingship if seen on lotuses, the heads of horses, elephants, or snakes, or on heaps of grain or green grass. However, if seen on ashes, bones, wood, chaff, hair, or dry grass, it brings sorrow. ||20||

# The Varahi Samhita

...for one year. ||20||

The sound of the <term>partridge</term><note>Sanskrit: *tittiri*</note> described as "kili-kili-kili" is considered peaceful and brings auspicious results; any other sound is the opposite. The <term>rabbit</term><note>Sanskrit: *shashaka*</note> is said to bring auspicious results if it moves to the left side at night while making its sound. ||21||

The "kili-kili" cry of a <term>monkey</term><note>Sanskrit: *kapi*</note> is considered "blazing" <note>A technical term in omenology meaning harsh or ill-omened</note> and is not said to grant good results for a traveler. However, the "chugla" sound of a monkey is called auspicious, as is the similar sound made by a potter-cock <note>likely a species of wild fowl or coucal</note>. ||22||

If a <term>blue jay</term><note>Sanskrit: *chasha*; the Indian Roller</note> approaches a man from the right with its mouth full of worms, grasshoppers, or ants, or if it makes a "svastika" <note>a cross-like flight pattern</note> for one about to depart, it brings great wealth and gain without delay. ||23||

If the <term>blue jay</term> is seen fighting with a crow on the right side, it indicates the defeat or even the death of the person setting out. If the positions are reversed, victory is predicted for him. ||24||

If the blue jay makes a "ke-ke" sound like a full pot on the left side, it brings victory. If its cry is "kra-kra," it is "blazing" and not for one's welfare; however, the mere sight of this bird is always auspicious for a traveler. ||25||

The <term>male lapwing</term><note>Sanskrit: *andiraka*</note> is considered "full" <note>auspicious</note> when it cries "stauti," but is "blazing" <note>inauspicious</note> with the sound "ttit-ttit-tibha." The "phesta" sound is auspicious when the bird is on the right side; otherwise, its cry holds no special significance. ||26||

The cry of the <term>shrikarna</term> bird on the right side sounding like "kva-kva-kva" is declared auspicious. The sound "chikki-chiko" is middling, while all other sounds are considered fruitless. ||27||

Even for the weak, the sound "chirilu-chirvil" is said to give desired results if heard from the left. If the bird moves from the left to the right, it grants success in one's work shortly. ||28||

If a bird makes the "chikki-chika" sound and moves from the left to the right side, it brings safety and prosperity. If it moves in the opposite direction, it leads to the fear of death or imprisonment. ||29||

The <term>myna bird</term><note>Sanskrit: *sarika*</note> that cries "kra-kra" or "tre-tre" rapidly and without fear predicts that the traveler will soon see blood flowing from his limbs. ||30||

The "chirvil" sound of the <term>phentaka</term> bird from the left is called beautiful/auspicious; any other sound is called "blazing." ||31||

For one staying in place, a superior sound from the left is desired; the "Om-kara" sound <note>resembling the sacred syllable Om</note> is beneficial for a traveler. Beyond this, the braying of a <term>donkey</term> is said to be "blazing" in all circumstances. ||32||

The <term>antelope</term><note>Sanskrit: *kuranga*</note> crying "aa" and the spotted deer crying "oo" are considered "full" <note>auspicious</note>. Other sounds are called "blazing." Full sounds are auspicious; blazing sounds bring sinful or negative results. ||33||

When <term>roosters</term><note>Sanskrit: *tamrachuda*, literally "copper-crested"</note> cry "ku-ku-kuv" out of fear at night, it brings danger. However, when healthy birds make their natural sounds at the end of the night (dawn), it brings prosperity to the nation, the city, and the king. ||34||

The <term>chippika</term><note>likely a species of owlet or nightjar</note> makes various sounds; of these, "kulu-kulu" is auspicious, while the rest are not. The cry of a cat is never auspicious for a traveler, and the sneeze of a cow brings certain death to one setting out. ||35||

The <term>owl</term><note>Sanskrit: *uluka*</note> cries "hum-hum-glug-lug" with joy when desiring its mate; the sound "guru-lu" is "full," while "kis-kisi" is always "blazing." A sound like "bala-bala" indicates a quarrel, and a single cry is for evil; "tata-tata" and other blazing sounds are not auspicious. ||36||

The warbling of the <term>crane</term><note>Sanskrit: *sarasa*</note> brings desired results if the pair cries together. A single cry is not auspicious, unless another bird responds to that single cry after a long interval. ||37||

The <term>spotted owlet</term><note>Sanskrit: *pingala*</note> brings auspiciousness with the sounds "chirvil-virvil." All other sounds are designated as "blazing"...

# Chapter 88: With Hindi Commentary

### Verse 38-39
If a female jackal <note>original: *shikhi-virutam*</note> howls, it forbids travel. If she makes the sound "Kushu-Kushu," it foretells a quarrel. I shall now describe the method by which she reveals the success of a desired task.

### Verse 40-41
At the time of evening twilight, one should approach the tree where she resides. After purifying oneself, one should worship the gods—starting with Brahma <note>the Creator</note>—and the tree itself with new clothes and fragrant offerings. At midnight, standing in the South-East <note>the direction of Agni, the fire god</note>, one should assign the directions of the sky and ask about the intended matter using this mantra so she may hear:

### Verse 42-44
"O Auspicious One, know that I have urged you for this purpose. O Blessed One, you are celebrated as the knower of all beings. I take my leave now and shall return in the morning. Standing in the South-East, I will ask you again. You ought to explain what I ask of you, O Auspicious One, through your own movements so that I may understand clearly."

### Verse 45-46
If, after saying this, the creature atop the tree makes the sound "Chiril-Virilvi," it signifies the fulfillment of the goal. If she makes a "Dishikar" sound or "Kucha-Kucha," it indicates great distress or confusion. If she remains silent or gives a low sound, the goal is achieved as intended. Other results should be interpreted based on the previously mentioned directions of the compass. Furthermore, the result is excellent, middling, or poor depending on whether she sits on an upper, middle, or lower branch.

### Verse 47
One should understand the results of the house-lizard <note>original: *griha-godhika*</note> based on its position within the circle of directions, whether inside or outside. The musk-shrew <note>original: *chuchundari*</note> is considered "blazing" <note>inauspicious/intense</note> when it makes a "Chichid" sound, but "full" <note>auspicious</note> when it makes a "Tittid" sound.

**(Thus ends the third chapter on the sounds of omens in the Universal Augury)**

->**Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the Brihat Samhita composed by Shri Varahamihira.**<-

***

The Shyama bird, hawk, falcon, Vanjula, peacock, Shrikarna, Ruddy goose, Indian roller, Andiraka, wagtail, parrot, crow, three types of pigeons, Bharadvaja, potter-bird, rooster, donkey, green pigeon, vulture, monkey, Phenta bird, Kukkuta, Karayika, and sparrow—all these creatures are called "day-walkers" <note>diurnal</note> because they graze or move during the day. **(1)**

The fox, Pingala <note>spotted owlet</note>, Chippika bird, bat, owl, and hare—all these creatures move at night <note>nocturnal</note>. If an omen-creature moves outside its natural time, it causes the destruction of the country or the downfall of kings. **(2)**

The horse, man, snake, camel, leopard, lion, bear, monitor lizard, wolf, mongoose, deer, dog, goat, cow, tiger, swan, spotted deer, jackal, porcupine, cuckoo, cat, crane, and boar—these creatures move both day and night; they are "dual-walkers" <note>amphibious/cathemeral</note>. **(3)**

The Bhasha, Kubapuri, Karabaka, and Karayika are known as "Purnakuta" <note>full-peak omens</note>. The owl is known by names such as Kochari, Pingalika, Pechika, and Hakka. **(4)**

The female pigeon is called Shyama, and the Vanjula bird is called Khadirachunchu. The musk-shrew is called "King's Daughter" <note>original: *nripasuta*</note> and the donkey is called Baleya. **(5)**

The bird that breaks pond-banks <note>the snipe</note> is called "Only Son," and the Kalahakarika <note>quarrel-maker</note> is called Rala. The Rala's body is two fingers long; at night, it makes a sound like a golden vase on the ground. **(6)**

According to the people of the Eastern countries, the Durbalika is named Bhandika; its appearance on the right is auspicious. The sound of the Chikkara refers to the deer species, and the Kukuvaku refers to the rooster species. **(7)**

The ditch-cock is named the potter-cock. By the name of the house-lizard...
