<meta>This page continues the instructions for the Nakshatra-Purusha vow (the ritual of the Constellation-Man) and concludes the main body of the Brihat Samhita, transitioning into the author's concluding remarks.</meta>

(342)
->Barahi Samhita<-

A Brahmin who possesses knowledge of the sciences should be given a vessel filled with clarified butter <note>ghee</note> and gold, along with clothes and gems. ||7||

A man desiring to attain beauty and grace should worship Brahmins by donating food mixed with milk and clarified butter, along with jaggery, and likewise donate silver and garments to them. Starting from the constellation <term>Nakshatra: the 27 lunar mansions of Hindu astrology</term> corresponding to the feet of the "Constellation-Man," he should fast month by month in sequence. According to the prescribed rites, he should worship Lord Vishnu and the specific constellation associated with each limb of the deity. ||8|| By performing this worship, a man becomes long-armed, with a broad and firm chest, a face like the moon, beautiful white teeth, a gait like a majestic elephant, large eyes like lotus petals, and a form like Kamadeva <note>the Hindu god of love</note>, capable of captivating the hearts of women. ||9|| If women perform this vow, they attain a face as radiant as the clear full moon of autumn, large eyes like lotus petals, beautiful teeth, lovely ears, and hair on the head as black as the belly of a bumblebee. ||10|| They will speak with a voice as sweet as the Indian cuckoo <note>Kokila</note>, possess lips with the redness of copper, hands as soft as lotus leaves, and similar feet; they will be slightly bent in the middle from the weight of their breasts, with a deep and circular navel. ||11|| With thighs like the trunk of a banana tree, beautiful hips, and feet with lovely and well-joined fingers. ||12|| For as long as the garland of stars wanders in the sky, beautifying this world with its radiance, the performer of this vow wanders in the sky as a star until the end of the <term>Kalpa: an eon or a 'day of Brahma'</term>. That wise soul, at the beginning of the next eon, becomes a sovereign Universal Emperor <note>Chakravarti Raja</note>. ||13|| In all the months starting from Margashirsha <note>roughly November-December</note>, one should worship Lord Vishnu using these names in order: Keshav, Narayan, Madhav, Govind, Vishnu, Madhusudan, Trivikram, Vaman, ||14|| Shridhar, Hrishikesh, Padmanabha, and Damodar. ||15|| The person who fasts according to the rules on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight <note>Dwadashi</note> and worships Keshava while chanting the specific name of Vishnu assigned to that month, attains His abode. Having attained that state, there is no longer any fear of rebirth. ||16||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter in the Hindi commentary written by Pandit Baldev Prasad Mishra, resident of Moradabad in the North-Western province, on the Brihat Samhita composed by the venerable teacher Varahamihira. ||105||

### Chapter One Hundred and Six

### Conclusion

By churning the ocean of the Science of Light <note>Jyotish or Astrology/Astronomy</note> with the Mandara Mountain of my intellect, I have brought forth this Moon of Scripture to provide light to the world. ||1||

While composing this scripture, I have not discarded the works of the ancient teachers. O virtuous people, look upon their works and this one, and then strive as you desire. ||2|| Or rather, a virtuous person spreads [the merit of others] greatly—

# Chapter 106: Conclusion

->With the Hindi Commentary<-

Seeing even a small virtue within an ocean of faults, the virtuous man magnifies it; the base man does the opposite. This is the inherent nature of the good and the wicked. || 3 ||

Gold in the form of poetry attains its true purity only after being heated in the fire of the wicked man’s criticism. Therefore, one should diligently recite their work to the malicious. || 4 ||

Whatever parts of this book might perish over time from the written manuscript, let them be preserved through the oral tradition of learned scholars. Whatever I have done poorly here, or left undone, let the wise correct it, setting aside any resentment. || 5 ||

This knowledge has been compiled by a mind graced through prostrating at the feet of the Sun, the Sages, and the Guru. Salutations to the ancient authors! || 6 ||

->Thus ends the Epilogue.<-

### Table of Contents of the Treatise

First, the introduction to the science, then the laws of the calendar and the course of the Sun. Then the movements of the Moon, Rahu <note>the ascending node</note>, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Ketu <note>the descending node or comets</note>. || 1 ||

The course of the Sage Agastya <note>the star Canopus</note> and the Seven Sages <note>the Big Dipper</note>; the "Tortoise" division of the earth <note>a method of mapping regions of India to the stars</note>; the grouping of constellations, the planetary orbits, and the conflict of the planets. || 2 ||

The conjunction of the planets with the Moon; the yearly results for the houses; the planets appearing in the shape of a "Shringataka" <note>a triangular or horned formation</note>; and the formation of rain-clouds. || 3 ||

The quantity of rainfall; the conjunctions of the Moon with the stars Rohini, Svati, and Ashadha; the signs of famine and plenty; the flowering of plants; the omens of twilight and the burning of the horizons. || 4 ||

Earthquakes; the characteristics of meteors and halos; the rainbow and the "City of the Gandharvas" <note>mirages</note>; mock suns; thunderbolts; and the prices of crops and commodities. || 5 ||

The festival of Indra’s Banner; the lustration ceremony; the omens of the wagtail; portents; and the variegated colors of the peacock. The dimensions of the royal umbrella and the throne; the characteristics of swords; and architecture <term>Vastu</term>. || 6 ||

The dowsing of underground water; gardening; the features of temples; the preparation of "Adamantine Glue" <note>a durable ancient cement</note>; the making of idols; the entry into the forest; and the consecration of divine temples. || 7 ||

The signs of cows, dogs, roosters, tortoises, goats, and men. The five types of great men; the signs of women; and the tearing of garments. || 8 ||

The examination of fly-whisks and staffs; the praise of women; the art of winning affection; aphrodisiacs and perfumes; the union of men and women; and the rules for couches and seats. || 9 ||

The examination of diamonds, pearls, rubies, and emeralds. The signs of lamps; the cleaning of teeth; and miscellaneous omens. || 10 ||

The circle of the quarters; the cries of birds and the behavior of dogs; the cries of the jackal; the movements of wild deer, horses, and elephants; and the lore of the crow. || 11 ||

The ripening of results; the qualities of the constellations, lunar days, and half-days; the results of birth under certain stars; the transit of planets; and the "Constellation Man" <note>mapping the stars to the human body</note>. || 12 ||

One hundred and six chapters have been set forth here in due order. The number of verses composed is just under four thousand. || 13 ||

->Thus ends the Table of Contents.<-

For this reason, this book should be shared with wicked people only with great effort <note>The author suggests caution in sharing sacred or powerful knowledge with those who might misuse it</note> ||4||

## Appendix to Chapter 104

### The Science of Prosody

The proper arrangement of <term>short and long syllables</term> <note>original: "laghu-guru-vinyas"; the foundational rhythmic units of Sanskrit and Hindi poetry</note> is called meter. <term>Meter</term> <note>original: "chhanda"</note> is of two types: prose and verse. That which has four quarters <note>lines</note> is verse, and anything different from that is prose. The categories known as *Vritta* and *Jati*...

<summary>The author, Baldev Prasad of Moradabad, concludes his commentary in 1895 CE under the patronage of Gangavishnu and introduces an appendix on the technical rules of poetic meter.</summary>
<keywords>Baldev Prasad, Moradabad, 1895 CE, Vikram Samvat 1952, Gangavishnu, Prosody, Meter, Syllabic weight, Hindi literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Sanskrit prosody (the study of poetic meters) within the Varahi Samhita. It establishes the foundational definitions required to understand the mathematical structure of the verses that follow.</meta>

# Varahi Samhita
<page-num>346</page-num>

There are two types of verse. That in which the number of syllables is fixed is called <term>Vritta</term> <note>syllabic meter</note>, and that which is formed by the count of beats is called <term>Jati</term> <note>quantitative meter based on matras or time-units</note>. <term>Vritta</term> is of three types: even, uneven, and semi-even. That which has an equal number of syllables in all four quarters <note>padas</note> is "even" <note>Samavritta</note>; that in which the first and third quarters, and the second and fourth quarters are equal, is "semi-even" <note>Ardhasamavritta</note>; and that in which all four quarters are different is called "uneven" <note>Vishamavritta</note>.

**Heavy (Guru):** The vowels A, I, U, Ri, E, Ai, O, Au, Am, Ah <note>long vowels and those with nasalization or aspiration</note> are these characters; characters joined with these vowels, the character preceding a conjunct consonant, and the character at the end of a verse quarter (optionally) are considered "heavy" <note>long/stressed</note>.

**Light (Laghu):** Characters other than the "heavy" ones are "light" or short.

**Pause (Yati):** The resting place of the tongue—that is, the stopping point—is the <term>Yati</term> <note>caesura</note>.

**Measure (Matra):** A short character is one measure, a heavy character is two measures, and a prolonged <note>Pluta</note> character is three measures.

**Feet (Gana):** The "feet" used in <term>Vritta</term> consist of groups of three characters; the "feet" used in <term>Jati</term> consist of four measures each. For example: three heavy syllables make a *Ma-gana*, and three light syllables make a *Na-gana*. 
*   **Bha:** initial-heavy
*   **Ya:** initial-light
*   **Ja:** middle-heavy
*   **Ra:** middle-light
*   **Sa:** end-heavy
*   **Ta:** end-light
*   **Ga:** one heavy
*   **La:** one light. 

We shall indicate these using the heavy sign (2) and the light sign (1).

For example: **Ma**-222; **Na**-111; **Bha**-211; **Ya**-122; **Ja**-121; **Ra**-212; **Sa**-112; **Ta**-221; **Ga**-2; and **La**-1.

Among these feet—**Ma, Sa, Ja, Bha**—these four (namely: all-heavy, end-heavy, middle-heavy, and initial-heavy) and the all-light foot make five types of feet that appear in <term>Jati-vritta</term>. However, whereas previously each foot was made of 3 characters, here it will be 4 measures; that is the only difference. Their signs in order are as follows:

->(Being quantitative meter) (22) (112) (121) (211) (1111)<-

The characteristics of the meters written by the author are now stated according to their verse numbers.

**2-3.** In this chapter, while first naming the meter, the author has written the name of the **'Mukhachapala'** meter by saying "May the noble ones <note>Aryas</note> forgive the flickering of my mouth <note>original: "mukha-chapalatvam kshaman-tvaryah"</note>." Therefore, the characteristics of the **Arya** meter are stated first.

**Arya:** The meter which contains a total of 57 measures—that is, 14.25 feet—is the **Arya**. In its first half, there are 30 measures (7.5 feet), and in the second half, there are 27 measures, but specifically 7.5 feet. (By this foot-count, the sixth foot of the second half will be a single light syllable; thus, one light syllable alone constitutes the sixth foot).

# Appendix

In the *Arya* <note>a specific style of Sanskrit meter based on syllabic weight or "matras"</note> meter, the odd-numbered feet (1st, 3rd, 5th, and 7th) must not be a *madhyaguru* (the *ja-gana* pattern: short-long-short). Even-numbered feet may be used as desired; however, in the first half, the sixth foot may be either a *madhyaguru* (*ja*) or entirely short syllables (*na-la*).

There are nine variations of the *Arya* meter: 1. *Pathya*, 2. *Vipula*, 3. *Chapala*, 4. *Mukha-chapala*, 5. *Jaghana-chapala*, 6. *Giti*, 7. *Upagiti*, 8. *Udgiti*, and 9. *Aryagiti*.

**Pathya**—When the pause <term>yati: a rhythmic caesura or breath-break</term> occurs after the first three feet in both the first and second halves of the verse, it is called *Pathya*.

**Vipula**—When there are three feet in the middle but no pause (*yati*) occurs, it is called *Vipula*.

**Chapala**—When the second and fourth feet in both halves of the verse are *madhyaguru* (the *ja* pattern), it is called *Chapala*.

**Mukha-chapala**—When only the first half of the verse follows the characteristics of the *Chapala* meter, it is a *Mukha-chapala Arya*.

**Jaghana-chapala**—When only the second half follows the characteristics of the *Chapala* meter, it is a *Jaghana-chapala Arya*.

**Giti**—When the second half of the verse is equal in structure to the first half, it is a *Giti Arya*.

**Upagiti**—When the first half is equal in structure to the second half of a standard *Arya*, it is an *Upagiti*.

**Udgiti**—An *Arya* where the first half is structured like a standard second half and the second half is structured like a standard first half—meaning the first half has 27 beats and the second half has 30 beats—is called *Udgiti*.

**Aryagiti**—When the eighth foot in both the first and second halves consists of four beats—totaling 32 beats per half and 64 beats in the full verse—it is called *Aryagiti*.

4 **Shardulavikridita**—<note>The "Tiger's Sport" meter</note> Patterns: *ma, sa, ja, sa, ta, ta, ga*—Pause (*yati*) at 12 and 7 syllables. [Syllabic weights: 2 2 2, 1 1 2, 1 2 1, 1 1 2, 2 2 1, 2 2 1, 2].

5 **Sragdhara**—Patterns: *ma, ra, bha, na, ya, ya, ya*—Pause at 7, 7, 7.

6 **Suvadana**—Patterns: *bha, ra, bha, na, ya, bha, la, ga*—Pause at 7, 7, 6.

7 **Suvritta** or **Meghavisphurjita**—Patterns: *ya, ma, na, sa, ra, ra, ga*—Pause at 6, 6, 7.

8 **Shikharini**—Patterns: *ya, ma, na, sa, bha, la, ga*—Pause at 6, 11.

9 **Mandakranta**—Patterns: *ma, bha, na, ta, ta, ga, ga*—Pause at 4, 6, 7. <note>Famous as the meter of Kalidasa's Meghaduta</note>

10 **Vrishabhacharita** or **Harini**—Patterns: *na, sa, ma, ra, sa, la, ga*—Pause at 6, 4, 7.

11, 12 **Upendravajra**—Patterns: *ja, ta, ja, ga, ga*.

13 **Prasabha**—Patterns: *na, na, ra, la, ga*—Its other name is **Bhadrika**.

14 **Malati**—Patterns: *na, ja, ja, ra*.

42 **<term>Shriputa</term>**; — na, na, ma, ya — caesura <note>a rhythmic pause</note> at 8, 4.

43 **<term>Vaishvadevi</term>**, — ma, ma, ya, ya — caesura at 5, 7.

44 **<term>Urmimala</term>** <note>"Garland of waves"</note>, — bha, bha, ta, ga, ga. Its other name is **<term>Vatormi</term>** <note>"Wind-tossed wave"</note>.

(This is a **<term>Vishama-vritta</term>** <note>an uneven or irregular meter where the four lines of a stanza differ in structure</note>).

52 **<term>Narkutaka</term>**, — na, ja, bha, ja, ja, la, ga — caesura at 7, 10. The other name is **<term>Nardataka</term>**.

53 **<term>Vilasa</term>** — **<term>Upajati</term>**, — an extraordinary usage. That in which the four quarters <note>lines</note> do not have equal meters is called an Upajati.

56 **<term>Vaktra</term>**, — that which has eight syllables in each quarter; from the initial syllable onwards there should be no *na-gana* or *sa-gana*, and after the [specified] syllable there should be a *ya-gana*, and (there is no fixed rule for the [other] syllables); that is Vaktra.

59 **<term>Vaitaliya</term>**, — this is a **<term>Matra-vritta</term>** <note>a meter based on the count of beats/duration rather than the number of syllables</note>. That which has 14 beats in the first and third feet and 16 beats in the second and fourth feet is Vaitaliya. However, its specialty is that its beats will be a mixture of only short <note>laghu</note> or only long <note>guru</note> sounds, and all even-numbered beats must not be dependent on the following beat; that is, characters with 3, 5, 7 etc. beats should not become long by being joined to the preceding beat. At the end of its foot, ra, la, and ga-gana must certainly be placed.

60 **<term>Aupachhandasika</term>**; — by adding one extra long syllable <note>guru</note> at the end of the Vaitaliya meter, the meter named Aupachhandasika is formed.

61 **<term>Chandavrishtiprayata</term>**, (**<term>Dandaka-bheda</term>** <note>a variety of the 'Dandaka' or long-form meter</note>). The general rule for Dandaka is to have 27 syllables; 1—therein are two *na-ganas* followed by seven *ra-ganas*. After placing the *ganas* in this manner, if one adds *ra-ganas* according to their wish, it will still be the Chandavrishtiprayata Dandaka. There is no rule for how many syllables it may contain (each quarter of this particular verse contains 102 syllables). Dandaka is a type of meter that follows the poet's will.

62 **<term>Varnadandaka</term>**, — na, na, bha, bha, bha, bha, bha, bha, ga.

63 **<term>Samudradandaka</term>** <note>"Ocean-Dandaka"</note>, — na, na, ra, ja, ra, ja, ra, ja, ra, ja, ra, ja, ra, la, ga.

<header>The Varahi Samhita</header>

Now, the subject of *Chhandovichiti* <note>The science of prosody or the analysis of poetic meters</note>, specifically regarding *Prastara* <note>The mathematical process of mapping out all possible combinations of long and short syllables in a meter</note>, is being described in brief.

The six fundamental elements of meter are: *Prastara* (permutation table), *Nashta* (finding a form from a number), *Uddishta* (finding a number from a form), *Ekadvayadi-lagakriya* (calculating combinations of specific numbers of short/long syllables), *Sankhya* (total count), and *Adhvayoga* (the space occupied by the table).

### 1. Prastara (Permutation)
The systematic arrangement of short and long syllables to expand a meter is called *Prastara*. This means determining how many variations a verse-quarter (*charana*) of a specific syllable count can have based on the placement of long and short syllables. The method to gain this knowledge is called *Prastara*.

The rule for it is as follows: First, place as many "long" symbols <note>original: "guru" (heavy/long syllable), represented by '2' or 'S'</note> as there are syllables in the verse-quarter. Subsequently, place a "short" symbol <note>original: "laghu" (light/short syllable), represented by '1' or 'I'</note> below the first long symbol encountered. For the symbols following it (to the right), keep them exactly as they were in the row above. For any positions preceding the newly placed short symbol (to the left), replace whatever was there with long symbols. Continue this process of placing a short symbol under the first available long symbol and filling the preceding spots with long symbols until all positions are filled with short symbols. The total number of rows generated represents the total possible variations.

For example:—

A three-syllable verse-quarter begins with three long symbols: 2 2 2. Place a short symbol under the first long one and complete the row: 1 2 2. Next, place a short symbol under the first available long symbol (the second one) and keep the following symbol as it was. Since the first position is now empty, place a long symbol there: 2 1 2. Continue this process until all symbols are short. As shown:—

| Row Number | Syllable Pattern | Gana (Metrical Foot) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | 2 2 2 | *Ma-gana* |
| 2 | 1 2 2 | *Ya-gana* |
| 3 | 2 1 2 | *Ra-gana* |
| 4 | 1 1 2 | *Sa-gana* |
| 5 | 2 2 1 | *Ta-gana* |
| 6 | 1 2 1 | *Ja-gana* |
| 7 | 2 1 1 | *Bha-gana* |
| 8 | 1 1 1 | *Na-gana* |

<note>The table illustrates the eight standard "Ganas" or triplets of syllables used in Sanskrit poetry to define meters.</note>

<summary>This page explains the mathematical method of Prastara, used to calculate all possible variations of long and short syllables within a poetic meter. It specifically demonstrates how to derive the eight standard three-syllable metrical feet (Ganas).</summary>
<keywords>Prastara, Sanskrit prosody, Varahi Samhita, Gana, metrical feet, Guru and Laghu, poetic meter, combinatorics</keywords>

# Appendix

If one wishes to know the <term>Chhandabheda</term> <note>variations of poetic meter</note> by cutting the <term>Prastara</term> <note>the systematic expansion or table of all possible combinations of long and short syllables</note> in this manner, there is a high probability of error. A simple remedy for this is as follows: place numbers above the syllables of a foot, starting from the first syllable and doubling the value for each subsequent one (1, 2, 4, 8...). By doubling the final number reached, the total number of possible variations is determined. For example, in a <term>Tryakshara</term> <note>three-syllable meter</note>, the numbers would be 1, 2, 4. Doubling the last number (4) results in 8; therefore, there are eight types of variations in a <term>Tryakshara-vritti</term> <note>a three-syllable rhythmic structure</note>. However, if one wishes to know exactly how many variations contain a specific number of <term>Guru</term> <note>heavy/long syllables, marked —</note> or <term>Laghu</term> <note>light/short syllables, marked ऽ</note>, one should calculate according to the rules of <term>Bhaskaracharya</term>’s <note>a famous 12th-century Indian mathematician</note> work, the <term>Lilavati</term>, specifically the rule: "The figures starting from one and increasing by one, placed in reverse order and divided by the figures in direct order..." and so on. Due to the fear of excessive length, the entirety of that method is not described here. Knowledge of this can also be gained through the <term>Meru</term> <note>the "Mountain" or Pascal's Triangle</note>, <term>Khandameru</term>, or <term>Pataka</term> <note>diagrammatic methods for calculating permutations</note>, but those too are extremely detailed and thus have not been written down.

**2. Nashta** <note>literally "lost"; the process of finding the form of a meter given its index number</note>—If someone asks what the specific arrangement of long and short syllables is for a particular number in a sequence of meters, the method by which the answer is found is called <term>Nashta</term>.

The rule is as follows: if the given number is even (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, etc.), first place a <term>Laghu</term> (short) mark. Then halve that number; if the result is also even, place another <term>Laghu</term>. If the result is odd (1, 3, 5, 7, etc.), place a <term>Guru</term> (long) mark. Then, add 1 to that odd number and halve it; if that result is odd, place a <term>Guru</term>, and if even, place a <term>Laghu</term>. Continue this until the total number of syllables for that meter is reached.

For example, what is the form of the 4th variation in a <term>Tryakshara-vritti</term>? Here, 4 is an even number, therefore: <term>Laghu</term>. Half of four is 2, which is also even, so another <term>Laghu</term>. Half of two is 1, which is odd; thus, a <term>Guru</term>. In this way, we get [Short, Short, Long]. This is the fourth variation of the three-syllable meter. And if someone asks what the seventh is? Since 7 is <term>Ayugma</term> <note>odd</note>, the first is a <term>Guru</term>. Adding 1 to it makes 8, half of which is 4 (even), so the next is a <term>Laghu</term>. Half of that is 2 (even), so another <term>Laghu</term>. This seventh variation is [Long, Short, Short].

**<term>Uddishta</term>** <note>literally "pointed out"; the process of finding the index number given a specific arrangement of syllables</note>—If someone asks, "What is the sequence number of a meter with this specific arrangement of long and short syllables?" the method by which that number is known is <term>Uddishta</term>. The rule is to place doubling numbers (1, 2, 4...) above the syllables of the foot. Then, add together all the numbers that sit above the <term>Laghu</term> (short) marks. Finally, add 1 to that <term>Samashti</term> <note>total/sum</note>. The resulting number is the position of that specific arrangement in the expansion.

For example, what is the index of the <term>Tryakshara-vritti</term> [Short, Short, Long]? Place the doubling numbers 1, 2, 4 above them. By adding the numbers above the first two short syllables...

<summary>This page explains the mathematical principles of Sanskrit prosody, specifically how to calculate the total number of possible meters and how to convert between a meter's index number and its specific pattern of long and short syllables.</summary>
<keywords>prosody, Sanskrit meter, mathematics, Bhaskaracharya, Lilavati, Prastara, Nashta, Uddishta, permutations, syllables</keywords>

<header>Varahi Samhita</header>

3, and by adding one to it, it becomes 4; therefore, it is understood that this is the 4th variation of the <note>original: "tryaksharavrittika"</note> three-syllable meter, and so on.

If one wishes to understand the wonderful details of <term>Prosody</term> <note>Chanda-shastra: the ancient science of poetic meters</note>, such as the sequences of long and short syllables, the calculation of variations, the spatial representation of meters, and the various mathematical diagrams like the <term>Matrix of Syllabic Lengths</term> <note>Matra-meru</note>, the <term>Pyramidal Grid</term> <note>Meru</note>, the <term>Broken Pyramid</term> <note>Khanda-meru</note>, and the <term>Flag Diagram</term> <note>Pataka</note>, then it would be necessary to translate the entire science of prosody. Such a translation is extremely necessary for those who recite the Vedas, but it is not of great necessity for the general public. Keeping this in mind, and for fear of making this work too long, I have not deemed it appropriate to write more on the subject here.

->-**Baldev Prasad Mishra.**<-
